Alle origini della pittura senese (Siena, Santa Maria della Scala, 2003–04) with Bagnoli, Bellosi and Michel Laclotte, to mount Omaggio a Giovanni Pisano at Pistoia in 2017, and, with Bagnoli and Max Seidel, the monographic Ambrogio Lorenzetti at Santa Maria della Scala (22 October 2017 – 8 April 2018).

His principal books are Le occasioni del Sodoma. Dalla Milano di Leonardo alla Roma di Raffaello (Donzelli, 1996); Scultura gotica in Toscana. Maestri, monumenti, cantieri del Due e Trecento (Silvana, 2005), the product of a decade's work, which runs from the Pisani to Andrea Pisano at Orvieto in 1347–48 and places a long series of chapters on Sienese sculpture at its centre; Scultura gotica senese, 1260–1350 (Allemandi, 2011), written with the collaboration of Francesco Aceto, Claudia Bardelloni and Silvia Colucci; and Il duomo nuovo di Siena. La fabbrica, le sculture, i maestri, le dinamiche di cantiere (Silvana, 2019), a reconstruction of the abandoned enlargement voted by the Sienese commune in 1339 and of the workshop practices it reveals. He has also edited the modern reissues of two of Bellosi's classics, La pecora di Giotto and Buffalmacco e il Trionfo della Morte, for Abscondita, adding an extended postface to the first.

For the sculpture of Trecento Siena his most consequential single study is the long article "Per la scultura senese del Trecento: Agostino di Giovanni," published in Prospettiva 108 (2002). Together with the chapters of the 2005 and 2011 books it reopened a question that Enzo Carli had appeared to settle in 1960 by reducing Agostino di Giovanni to the single signed Tarlati monument of 1330 and a handful of grudging possibilities. Bartalini's method there is characteristic: he sets the father's manner — an alignment of plastic volumes upon a flat ground, clear in plane and solid in body — against the atmospheric, "pictorial" relief of his son Giovanni d'Agostino, and uses that contrast as a positive criterion for dividing hands within a family workshop where documents cannot. The result has been a substantial return of works to Agostino, and a catalogue that now oscillates between father and sons rather than resting where Carli left it; Bartalini has been correspondingly firm in rejecting accretions he judges unfounded, among them the 1982 proposal to give the Gandoni and de' Bonandrei tombs in Bologna to the shop of Agostino and Agnolo di Ventura. On the effort to give Agnolo di Ventura an independent profile of his own he is equally measured: what has been recovered of that shadowy partner amounts, in his phrase, to no more than "una traccia."

Alongside the research he has carried a considerable institutional load. He sat on the scientific committee, established by the Opera della Metropolitana of Siena with the Soprintendenza, that supervised the investigation and restoration of Nicola Pisano's pulpit in Siena Cathedral in 2016–18; he collaborated for nearly thirty years (1989–2018) with the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz on Die Kirchen von Siena; and he has been a member of the scientific committee of Prospettiva since 1998, and of Matèria. Revista internacional d'Art and La Diana since 2013 and 2020. He teaches in the inter-university doctoral programme in art history "Pegaso" (Florence, Pisa and Siena) and has supervised a long series of theses on Trecento sculpture and painting in central Italy.

Becherucci, Luisa

Florence, 29 May 1904 – Florence, 19 March 1988

Luisa Becherucci was an Italian art historian and museologist whose career was built almost entirely around the museums and monuments of her native Florence. She trained under Pietro Toesca, writing a degree thesis on the sculptures of Florence Cathedral, and completed a diploma in advanced studies in Rome under Adolfo Venturi — placing her, by formation, within the two dominant schools of early twentieth-century Italian art history. Her early research followed from this training and concentrated on fifteenth-century Florentine architecture and sculpture, before extending to the architecture and sculpture of the sixteenth century and, in particular, Mannerism, the subject of her 1944 book Manieristi toscani.

She entered the Soprintendenza in 1933, serving first as an inspector in Naples and then in Emilia-Romagna, where she collaborated on the landmark 1938 exhibition on Melozzo da Forlì organised under Roberto Longhi's direction. She returned to Florence's Soprintendenza ai Monumenti in 1939. In 1955 she directed the reorganisation of the Museo Nazionale di San Marco, and in 1957 she succeeded Roberto Salvini as director of the Galleria degli Uffizi, a post she held until 1969. Her scholarship on Trecento Florentine painting engaged directly with the workshop of Andrea di Cione: with Anna Padoa Rizzo, she was among the modern scholars who firmly reaffirmed Orcagna's authorship of the Santa Croce murals — the Triumph of Death, the Last Judgement and the Hell — first recorded by Ghiberti, while additionally identifying the hand of Nardo di Cione in their execution.

Becherucci's directorship at the Uffizi coincided with the catastrophic flood of the Arno on the night of 3–4 November 1966. She went to the gallery as the waters rose, helping to coordinate the rescue of paintings and archival material from the flooded lower rooms, and in the aftermath she organised the exhibition Dipinti salvati dalla piena dell'Arno, which presented recovered works to the public and documented the first campaigns of emergency restoration — an episode now widely regarded as a turning point in the modern history of art conservation.

After museology was established as a university discipline in Italy in 1967, Becherucci was among its first teachers, lecturing at the International University of Art and at the universities of Pisa, Florence and Urbino. In 1972 she founded, and co-directed with Luciano Berti, the journal Museologia. She had earlier co-founded the Soroptimist International Club of Florence in 1949, serving as its vice-president and then, from 1952 to 1955, its president. She died in Florence in 1988; her university lectures were published posthumously as Lezioni di museologia, 1969–1980.

Beckwith, John

Whitby, 2 December 1918 - London, 20 February 1991

John Gordon Beckwith was an English museum curator and art historian who spent his entire career at the Victoria and Albert Museum, where he became one of the twentieth century's leading authorities on Byzantine and early medieval ivory carving and on early Byzantine art more generally, publishing accessible synthetic surveys alongside close curatorial studies of individual objects.

Born in Whitby, North Yorkshire, on 2 December 1918, Beckwith was abandoned by his father at the age of two and raised in Whitby by his paternal grandmother; his Roman Catholic faith won him a scholarship to Ampleforth College, the Benedictine boarding school in Yorkshire. He went up to Exeter College, Oxford, to read History, but his studies were interrupted by the Second World War, in which he served in the infantry with the Duke of Wellington's Regiment and was severely wounded during the Normandy invasion, sustaining a permanent injury to his right hand; his brother was killed in the war. Returning to Oxford after his recovery, he completed his degree in modern history and, through his friendships there with the historian Gervase Mathew and the art historian Otto Pächt, developed the interest in Byzantine and medieval art that would define his career, though he never went on to take a doctorate.

In 1948 Beckwith was appointed an assistant keeper in the Department of Textiles at the Victoria and Albert Museum, where he specialised in medieval and Byzantine textiles, before transferring in 1955 to the Department of Architecture and Sculpture under John Pope-Hennessy to take up the study of medieval ivory carving that became his principal scholarly identity. He was promoted Deputy Keeper of the department in 1958 and Keeper in 1974, a post he held until his retirement in 1979; he also served as Slade Professor of Fine Art at the University of Oxford in 1978-79.

His publications combined broad, vividly written synthesis with detailed attributional work on individual carvings and their patronage. They include The Andrews Diptych (London: H.M. Stationery Office, 1958); Caskets from Cordoba (London: Victoria and Albert Museum, 1960); The Art of Constantinople: An Introduction to Byzantine Art, 330-1453 (London: Phaidon, 1961); Early Medieval Art: Carolingian, Ottonian, Romanesque (London: Thames and Hudson, 1964); Early Christian and Byzantine Art (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1970, in the Pelican History of Art series); and his most substantial original contribution, Ivory Carvings in Early Medieval England (London: Harvey Miller and Medcalf, 1972). His attributions of individual ivories to specific workshops and periods, including his proposals on the Codex Aureus of Echternach's treasure binding, were confident and often influential, but also, in the judgement of later specialists, controversial and not always borne out by subsequent scholarship.

Beckwith was elected a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London in 1968 and a Fellow of the British Academy in 1974. He died in London on 20 February 1991, and an obituary appeared in The Times on 27 February 1991.

Bellosi, Luciano

Scandicci, 7 July 1936 – Florence, 26 April 2011

Luciano Bellosi was one of the most distinguished Italian art historians of the twentieth century, renowned for his scholarship on medieval and early Renaissance painting, especially the Tuscan tradition from the Duecento to the Quattrocento. His work combined connoisseurial sharpness with rigorous historical method, placing him in the lineage of the major Italian historians of style and attribution.

Born in Scandicci near Florence, Bellosi studied at the University of Florence and graduated in 1963 under Roberto Longhi with a thesis on Lorenzo Monaco. Longhi's teaching shaped Bellosi's method: primacy of direct visual analysis, close formal comparison, and reconstruction of artistic personalities through works themselves before documentary confirmation. After military service (1963-1964), he began the institutional and academic path that would define his career.

From 1969 to 1979 Bellosi worked at the Soprintendenza alle Gallerie di Firenze, gaining sustained firsthand contact with major public collections. In 1979 he moved to the University of Siena, where he taught medieval art history, directed the Department of Archaeology and Art History (1983-1986), and trained generations of scholars until his early retirement in 2002. He often described his method as detective-like: reading paintings with the eye first, then testing hypotheses against texts and archives.

His first major book, Buffalmacco e il Trionfo della Morte (Einaudi, 1974), was a landmark reconstruction and won the Premio Viareggio Opera Prima di Saggistica the same year. He later published La pecora di Giotto (Einaudi, 1985), with influential arguments on Giotto's workshop and attribution, and Cimabue (Federico Motta, 1998), still a standard reference for the painter's oeuvre and historical position. His collected essays, "I vivi parean vivi": scritti di storia dell'arte italiana del Duecento e del Trecento (2006), brought together decades of core research on thirteenth- and fourteenth-century painting.

Bellosi's scholarship also extended beyond Tuscany. He published an influential 1975 Prospettiva study on the Limbourg Brothers and the Tres Riches Heures, and in later years wrote important work on the young Giovanni Bellini in relation to Andrea Mantegna. He contributed regularly to journals including Paragone, Prospettiva, Bollettino d'Arte, The Burlington Magazine, and Revue de l'Art.

He was also a major exhibition curator, responsible for projects such as Lorenzo Ghiberti: Materia e ragionamenti (Florence, 1978), Pittura di luce (Florence, 1990), Una scuola per Piero (Florence, 1992), Francesco di Giorgio e il Rinascimento a Siena (Siena, 1993), and in 2003 both Masaccio e le origini del Rinascimento (San Giovanni Valdarno) and Duccio. Alle origini della pittura senese (Siena), the latter a major international event. Active in scholarly institutions and conferences, including the 1985 international conference on Simone Martini, Bellosi was a member of the Accademia degli Intronati. After his death in 2011, his library of about 8,000 volumes and his archive were donated to the University of Siena, where they remain an enduring resource for research.

Belting, Hans

Andernach, 7 July 1935 - Berlin, 10 January 2023

Hans Belting was one of the greatest art historians of the twentieth century: a German scholar trained in medieval studies, he became, over the course of his career, one of the most original and influential theorists of Bildwissenschaft - the "science of the image" - capable of reformulating the methodological foundations of art history from an anthropological, cultural, and global perspective.

Belting was born on July 7, 1935, in Andernach, Rhineland, at a time when the region was still in the shadow of World War II. He studied art history at the universities of Mainz and Rome - a choice that would prove decisive for his deep connection to Italian medieval art - and earned his doctorate at the University of Mainz in 1959, with a dissertation on the early medieval frescoes of the Basilica of the Holy Martyrs in Cimitile, near Naples. His Habilitation, the postdoctoral qualification required in the German university system, was dedicated to medieval Beneventan painting. Shortly thereafter, he received a fellowship at the Center for Byzantine Studies at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington, an institute affiliated with Harvard and still today one of the world's leading centers for medieval and Byzantine studies.

Returning to Germany in 1965, Belting founded the Department of Byzantine Art at the University of Hamburg before being appointed professor at Heidelberg. From 1980 to 1992, he held the chair of Art History at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat in Munich - the same chair once held by Heinrich Wolfflin and Hans Sedlmayr, two of the greatest art theorists of the German tradition. It was a clear signal: Belting was not merely a specialist in the Middle Ages, but a continuator of that tradition of theory and method that had made German Kunstwissenschaft a global model.

In 1992, he left Munich to take on an even more ambitious intellectual challenge: he was among the founders of the Hochschule fur Gestaltung (University of Art and Design) in Karlsruhe, where he established a new doctoral program in Kunstwissenschaft und Medientheorie (Art History and Media Theory) from scratch, in close collaboration with the renowned ZKM - Zentrum fur Kunst und Medientechnologie. In this cutting-edge context, Belting was able to engage with photography, video, and digital art, expanding his research from medieval miniatures to contemporary media. He remained in Karlsruhe until his retirement in 2002.

After his formal academic retirement, his activity did not slow down. From 2002 to 2003, he held the European Chair at the College de France in Paris. From 2004 to 2007, he directed the Internationales Forschungszentrum Kulturwissenschaften (IFK) in Vienna, an international center for cultural studies. A member of the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and the Academia Europaea, he was elected an Honorary Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1992 and was a recipient of the Ordre Pour le Merite fur Wissenschaften und Kunste, Germany's highest honorary distinction for scientists and artists.

The cornerstone of Belting's thought is the monumental Bild und Kult. Eine Geschichte des Bildes vor dem Zeitalter der Kunst, published in German in 1990 and translated into English in 1994 as Likeness and Presence: A History of the Image before the Era of Art. The central thesis of the work is as simple as it is revolutionary: before the Renaissance, sacred images - icons, altarpieces, figurative reliquaries - were not works of art in the modern sense of the term, but rather living presences, objects of worship endowed with miraculous power, perceived by the faithful as direct interfaces with the divine. The history of Western art, according to Belting, begins precisely when this cultic dimension separates from the aesthetic one: with the Renaissance, the sacred image becomes a work of art - that is, an object of aesthetic and authorial contemplation - and loses its function as a transcendent presence. The transition is not progress, but a profound transformation of the relationship between image, body, and religious community. The book also redefined the origins of easel painting and profoundly influenced studies of Italian and Byzantine medieval iconography.

In 1987, Belting published Das Ende der Kunstgeschichte? (The End of the History of Art?), in which he challenged the Hegelian teleology that dominated the discipline: the idea that art history advanced along a linear path toward modern art as its culmination. For Belting, the contemporary no longer lent itself to being narrated with the old historical-artistic tools, and art criticism was slowly replacing art history in discourse on the present. The question posed by the title remained programmatic: not a declaration of the discipline's death, but an invitation to re-establish its foundations.

This invitation took systematic form in Bild-Anthropologie (2001), translated as An Anthropology of Images: Picture, Medium, Body. Here Belting proposed a general theory of the image that transcended Western art history: images do not exist in a vacuum, but always in relation to a medium (the surface that bears them) and a body (the human body that perceives and produces them). This triad - image, medium, body - became the backbone of his Bildwissenschaft and also profoundly influenced cognitive studies and international visual studies.

In 2008 (German edition) and 2011 (English edition with Belknap/Harvard), Florenz und Bagdad: Eine westostliche Geschichte des Blicks (Florence and Baghdad: Renaissance Art and Arab Science) was published, one of the most original and debated works of his mature period. In it, Belting demonstrated how the linear perspective of the Italian Renaissance - from Brunelleschi to Alberti - was not an autonomous European invention, but derived crucially from the mathematical theory of vision developed by the Arab optician and mathematician Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, 10th-11th centuries). Perspective was thus the product of an encounter between cultures, not the triumph of a Western genius. The book openly engaged in the debate on the need for a truly global art history, capable of overcoming Eurocentrism.

In 2013, Belting received the I Tatti Mongan Prize from the Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies (Villa I Tatti) in Florence, an award that once again celebrated his Italian medievalist roots. In 2015, he was awarded the prestigious Balzan Prize for European art history (1300-1700), with a citation highlighting his unique contributions to the study of the visible, the function of images in the Western world, and his innovative interpretations across cultures and eras. The Courtauld Institute of Art had already awarded him an honorary doctorate in Literature from the University of London in 2003.

Hans Belting died in Berlin on January 10, 2023, at the age of 87, after a long illness. He left behind a bibliography of over thirty books translated into numerous languages, an international school of thought, and a series of methodological questions - on the nature of images, the significance of the Middle Ages for modernity, and the relationship between European art and Islamic culture - that continue to shape the debate in contemporary art history.

Benazzi, Giordana

Ferrara - Perugia, 4 February 2026

Giordana Benazzi was one of Italy's most dedicated art historians in the fields of medieval and Renaissance art, and a central figure in the protection and interpretation of Umbria's cultural heritage. After her death in Perugia on 4 February 2026, she was widely remembered for combining rigorous scholarship with a long and concrete commitment to conservation practice in the region.

Born in Ferrara, she completed her university formation in Florence, earning a Laurea in Filosofia at the Università degli Studi di Firenze between 1967 and 1971 under Eugenio Garin. She later specialized in art history with Mina Gregori. This dual formation, philosophical and art-historical, shaped the interdisciplinary method that marked her scholarship on medieval and Renaissance works.

Benazzi later settled in Perugia, where she served for approximately thirty years as a funzionario at the Soprintendenza per i Beni Architettonici, il Paesaggio, il Patrimonio Storico, Artistico e Etnoantropologico dell'Umbria. In that role she supervised major restoration campaigns involving the Duomo and Rocca of Spoleto, pictorial cycles and artworks in Gubbio, and the Palazzo Trinci complex in Foligno. Her work after the 1976, 1979, and 1997 earthquakes was repeatedly described as an exemplary case of technical competence and dedication under difficult conditions.

Her publications and curatorial activity made her a major reference point for Umbrian medieval and Renaissance studies. She curated the exhibition on Nicolo Alunno in Foligno (2004) and "Gubbio al tempo di Giotto" in Gubbio, and co-edited with Francesco Federico Mancini the major volume Il Palazzo Trinci di Foligno (Perugia, Quattroeme, 2001, 729 pp.). Her collaboration with Vittorio Sgarbi on Marchigian artistic culture, including "Da Giotto a Gentile / Pittura e scultura a Fabriano tra Due e Trecento" (Fabriano, 2014), further confirmed her specialization in medieval sculpture, especially scultura lignea. She also contributed to projects linked to the Museo Diocesano in Foligno and to the exhibition Segni di Croce.

Among her most noted contributions was the study of a gonfalon in Gubbio that she identified as a probable early work by Raphael; after its presentation in Gubbio, the work entered major national and international exhibitions. Even after retirement, she remained active in cultural life: in 2018 she was among the founders of the Associazione Umbra Federico II di Svevia Hohenstaufen in Perugia, and she supported projects such as "Castelli eugubini sulla Via di Francesco" (Gubbio, 2024; reprised in Valfabbrica, 2025), alongside documentary initiatives on Umbrian history and art from Antiquity to the Renaissance. Her funeral was held on 6 February 2026 in the Cattedrale di San Lorenzo (Duomo di Perugia), a monument emblematic of the heritage she had spent her life preserving.

Berenson, Bernard

Butrimonys (Lithuania), 26 June 1865 - Fiesole, 6 October 1959

Bernard Berenson was one of the most influential art historians and connoisseurs of the twentieth century and, during his lifetime, the most authoritative international voice on Italian Renaissance painting. Born Bernhard Valvrojenski into a Jewish family in Lithuania, he later became a central figure in the way European and American scholars, collectors, and museums identified, valued, and interpreted early Italian art.

His family emigrated to Boston in 1875 after severe financial losses, and the surname was changed to Berenson. From early youth he demonstrated extraordinary linguistic ability and broad humanistic interests. He studied at Harvard, graduating in 1887 with training in literature and history, and initially moved toward literary criticism. Financial support from Boston patrons, especially Isabella Stewart Gardner and Thomas Sergeant Perry, enabled extended travel in Europe, where his intellectual focus shifted decisively from literature to painting.

Berenson developed a method of attribution that combined Giovanni Morelli's comparative analysis of recurring anatomical details with a psychological reading of artistic personality associated with John Addington Symonds. This synthesis made his connoisseurship unusually systematic while preserving interpretive nuance, and helped define modern attribution practice in Italian art history.

His major early books established his authority rapidly: The Venetian Painters of the Renaissance (1894), The Florentine Painters of the Renaissance (1896), and Lorenzo Lotto: An Essay in Constructive Art Criticism (1895). He became especially known for rigorous reattribution lists that reduced inflated traditional catalogues and imposed stricter standards of authorship. His monumental The Drawings of the Florentine Painters (1903), later expanded in 1938, remains one of the landmark works of twentieth-century art-historical scholarship.

Berenson's influence extended beyond academia into the international art market. As adviser to Lord Duveen and to major American collectors, including Isabella Stewart Gardner and Henry Walters, he shaped acquisitions that would become foundational holdings in American museums. At the same time, his financial arrangements with the trade, particularly undisclosed commissions linked to authentication, generated lasting controversy over the relationship between scholarship and the art market. His authority was also publicly tested in the famous La belle ferronniere litigation associated with Duveen and Andree Hahn.

In 1900 he married Mary Whitall Smith; in the following years they established themselves at Villa I Tatti near Fiesole, transforming it into a major center of study, collecting, and intellectual sociability. During the Second World War, Berenson remained at I Tatti under increasingly dangerous conditions due to anti-Jewish persecution. His wartime observations were later published in Rumour and Reflection, 1941-1944 (1952).

At his death in 1959, Berenson bequeathed Villa I Tatti, together with its collections, gardens, and extraordinary library, to Harvard University. It became the Harvard Center for Italian Renaissance Studies, one of the most important institutions in the world for Renaissance scholarship. Through his writings, attributions, and institutional legacy, Berenson decisively shaped modern understanding of Italian Renaissance art.

Berger, Samuel

Beaucourt, 1843 - Paris, 1900

Samuel Berger was a French Protestant theologian and one of the founding figures of the modern historical study of the Latin Bible. He taught church history at the Faculté de théologie protestante de Paris, and his scholarship combined the philological rigor of French érudition with a Protestant scholar's close attention to the history of the biblical text as such.

His major work, Histoire de la Vulgate pendant les premiers siècles du moyen âge (Paris, 1893), remains a foundational study of how Jerome's Latin Bible was transmitted, corrupted, and revised across the early medieval West, and it is still cited as a point of departure for the textual history of the Vulgate more than a century after its publication.

Berger's contribution to the study of the Codex Amiatinus was precise and consequential. In examining the recovered original dedication verses transcribed in the anonymous Vita Ceolfridi — the text that Fenton John Anthony Hort had brought to bear on the manuscript's erased dedication — Berger corrected an early reading of the abbot's people as Britonum ("of the Britons") to the correct Anglorum ("of the English"), a small but important emendation for the manuscript's Northumbrian identification. He also noted the comparative textual weakness of the Amiatinus's rendering of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, an observation that remains part of the standard account of the manuscript's uneven textual quality across its different books. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for further detail.

Bertelli, Carlo

Rome, 1930

Italian art historian and former public official, widely recognised as a leading specialist in late antique and medieval art, with significant contributions to conservation, photography as historical evidence, and institutional reform in Italy's cultural heritage management. Bertelli studied literature at the University of Rome (La Sapienza), graduating in 1954, and pursued advanced specialisation at the Warburg Institute in London, where he trained under Pietro Toesca, Otto Pächt, Richard Krautheimer, and Mario Salmi. This interdisciplinary formation equipped him to bridge iconographic analysis with material history, particularly in early Christian and medieval painting. He married Ilaria Toesca, herself an art historian, and was the brother of the historian Sergio Bertelli.

From 1956 to 1977 Bertelli edited entries for Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'arte antica, while serving as inspector at the Istituto Centrale per il Restauro from 1958, focusing on unpublished medieval icons and Roman early medieval painting, including the Madonna di Santa Maria in Trastevere (1961). As director of the Gabinetto Fotografico Nazionale (1963–1973), he elevated photography to a rigorous historical tool, a project crystallised in L'immagine fotografica: 1845–1945 (1979). He subsequently directed the Calcografia Nazionale (1973–1975), merging it into the Istituto Nazionale per la Grafica.

Appointed Superintendent for Artistic and Historical Heritage in Milan and Western Lombardy (1978–1984), Bertelli spearheaded the modernisation of the Pinacoteca di Brera and the critical restoration framework for Leonardo's Last Supper. His tenure emphasised systematic recovery of Lombard medieval sites, aligning administrative duties with the scholarly rigour inherited from Cesare Brandi. These efforts earned him honours including the Sanseverino Prize for his Piero della Francesca monograph and gold medals from Italian cultural ministries.

Transitioning to academia after 1984, Bertelli taught at the University of Lausanne until 1995 and subsequently at the Accademia di Architettura in Mendrisio, Switzerland, as professor emeritus of art history at the Università della Svizzera italiana. His principal monographs include Il ciborio della Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio (1981), Piero della Francesca (1991), Lombardia medievale (2003), and Wolvinio e gli angeli (2006). He also curated the major exhibition Il futuro dei Longobardi (2000). His work integrates paleochristian iconography, Renaissance attribution, and archival photography, and constitutes an essential methodological framework for understanding artists such as the Maestro di Galliano and the broader tradition of Lombard monumental painting.

Best, Richard Irvine

Derry, 17 February 1872 – Dublin, 25 September 1959

Richard Irvine Best was an Irish Celtic scholar, bibliographer and civil servant, one of the central figures of early twentieth-century Irish manuscript studies. Largely self-trained, he began his career cataloguing manuscripts at the National Library of Ireland, rising to become its Director from 1924 to 1940. In 1903 he helped found, with Kuno Meyer, the School of Irish Learning in Dublin, and he worked closely for decades with Osborn Bergin on the editing and facsimile publication of early Irish literary manuscripts, including the Book of Leinster and Lebor na hUidre.

Best's decisive contribution to the study of the Book of Dimma was his article "On the Subscriptiones in the 'Book of Dimma,'" published in Hermathena (volume 44) in 1926. By close examination of the manuscript's four gospel colophons, Best demonstrated that in three of them the name Dimma had been written over an erasure, substituted for an earlier scribe's name in a deliberate later alteration, while the intact colophon at the end of Luke preserved the original name Dianchride. The discovery overturned centuries of belief that the book was a seventh-century relic of Saint Crónán's own scribe, and it remains the founding study of the manuscript's modern, critical historiography.

Best was also a formidable bibliographer, compiling successive volumes of the standard Bibliography of Irish Philology and of Printed Irish Literature, works that remained essential research tools for Celtic studies for much of the twentieth century.

Betham, William

Suffolk, England, 22 May 1779 – Dublin, 26 October 1853

William Betham was an English-born genealogist, antiquary and heraldic official who spent most of his career in Ireland, serving as Ulster King of Arms from 1820. An indefatigable collector, he amassed one of the largest private accumulations of genealogical and manuscript material in nineteenth-century Ireland, much of it later dispersed through sale.

Betham acquired the Book of Dimma sometime before 1826, in the chain of ownership recorded by Trinity College Dublin that runs from the Roscrea priest William Meagher through Henry Monck Mason to Betham himself. He attempted to sell the manuscript at auction as lot 444 on 4 July 1830; it failed to find a buyer at that sale and was purchased directly from him by Trinity College Dublin on 29 March 1836. Betham's own publications, notably Irish Antiquarian Researches (1826–27), are characteristic of the antiquarian scholarship of the period, combining genuine documentary transcription with speculative and often unreliable etymological and historical argument. His chief importance to the study of the Book of Dimma lies not in interpretation but in provenance: he is the last private owner through whose hands the manuscript passed before entering institutional custody.

Bieler, Ludwig

Vienna, 20 October 1906 – Dublin, 2 May 1981

Ludwig Josef Georg Bieler was born in Vienna on 20 October 1906 and educated at the Landstrasser Gymnasium before reading classical philology at the Universities of Vienna, Tubingen, and Munich under Ludwig Radermacher, Otto Weinreich, and Paul Kretschmer. He took his doctorate at Vienna in 1929 with a dissertation on the sixth-century St Samson of Dol — an early sign of the interest in the Latin hagiography of the Celtic-speaking world that would define his career. He remained at Vienna as a lecturer in classical philology through the 1930s.

The day after the Anschluss, on 12 March 1938, Bieler left for Switzerland. He was Catholic and, under the racial categories of the Nuremberg Laws, classified as "Aryan," so his departure was a matter of principle rather than persecution in the narrowest legal sense: he judged, correctly, that a scholar committed to intellectual freedom could not continue to work under National Socialism. His opposition to Nazi ideology led to his suspension and formal expulsion from the university the following month. In 1939 he married Eva Uffenheimer, a Froebel-trained teacher and Jewish refugee from Vienna, and in 1940 the couple settled in Ireland.

Bieler joined the National University of Ireland, teaching palaeography and medieval Latin, fields for which his Viennese training and his early thesis on an Insular saint had prepared him unusually well. Except for a single year, 1947–48, spent at the University of Notre Dame, he remained in Ireland for the rest of his working life, retiring in 1977. In 1954 he declined an offer of a professorship at Graz: Ireland, adopted in flight from Vienna, had become the permanent centre of his scholarly world, and neither the University of Vienna nor any other Austrian institution ever recovered him, notwithstanding his election as a corresponding member of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in 1964.

It was above all Bieler who, in the second half of the twentieth century, established Hiberno-Latin literature as a rigorous field of classical philology rather than an antiquarian sideline of Irish studies. He applied to early medieval Irish Latin texts the same exacting methods of textual criticism that Central European scholarship applied to classical authors, and in doing so brought the subject to international scholarly attention. His output included Theios Aner, a study of the late-antique concept of the divine man, editions such as the Four Latin Lives of St Patrick and, for the Scriptores Latini Hiberniae series of the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, The Irish Penitentials (1963).

His culminating achievement was The Patrician Texts in the Book of Armagh (Scriptores Latini Hiberniae X, Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1979), with a contribution by Fergus Kelly — the standard critical edition of Muirchu's Vita, Tirechan's Collectanea, the Liber Angeli, the Additamenta, and the Notulae. Where John Gwynn's 1913 diplomatic edition had transcribed the whole codex, Bieler's edition subjected the hagiographical core of the Patrician dossier to full critical apparatus, translation, and commentary, and it remains the point of departure for all serious work on the texts. On the vexed question of how many hands wrote the manuscript, his judgement — formed primarily from the texts rather than from the letterforms — was that Ferdomnach worked with one or two assistants, an intermediate position between John Gwynn's view of a single scribe and E. A. Lowe's attribution of three.

Bieler died in Dublin on 2 May 1981, having done more than any other twentieth-century scholar to place the critical study of Hiberno- Latin literature on a secure philological footing. The dual itinerary of the Book of Armagh's two great modern editors — an Irish clergyman-scholar born within sight of Trinity College, and a Viennese classicist who found in Ireland the refuge that let his scholarship flourish — is itself a fitting emblem of how thoroughly the field he founded has always depended on exchange across national and confessional lines.

Bietti, Monica (Bietti Favi, Monica)

Florence, 1953

Monica Bietti, known in the academic publications of the early phase of her career as Monica Bietti Favi, was born in Florence in 1953. She graduated in 1978 from the University of Florence with a degree in art history, summa cum laude, under the supervision of Mina Gregori, one of the most authoritative art historians of 20th-century Italy, specializing in 17th-century Lombard and Tuscan painting. Her training with Gregori instilled in Bietti a rigorous method based on documentary analysis and attributionism, a tradition characteristic of the school of Roberto Longhi. It is no coincidence that, after graduation, she received a fellowship at the Roberto Longhi Foundation for Art History Studies in Florence, one of Italy's most exclusive centers for advanced training, which has educated generations of world-class art historians.

In the early phase of her career, Bietti signed her contributions with the compound name Monica Bietti Favi. The article "Gaddo Gaddi: a hypothesis," published in Arte Cristiana, LXXI, no. 694 (1983), pp. 49-52, dates from this period; it presented new documentary evidence supporting the identification of the Florentine painter and mosaicist Gaddo Gaddi, active between the late 13th and early 14th centuries. The article, still cited today in the international critical bibliography, including the entry Taddeo Gaddi in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani) and studies published by Cambridge University Press, marked her entry into the debate on 14th-century Florentine painting. During this same period, she contributed to the collective publication La Misericordia di Firenze: Archivio e raccolta d'arte (1981), also signed under the name Bietti Favi.

Between 1982 and 1983, Bietti served as director of the Civic Museum of Modena, a position that conferred upon her, at an early stage, management and curatorial responsibilities of national significance. This was a transitional phase between her academic and institutional careers, which would be definitively consolidated in 1983, the year she joined the Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Activities.

From 1983 onward, Bietti spent her entire career as an art historian with the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts, and Landscape for the metropolitan city of Florence and the provinces of Pistoia and Prato. Starting in 1986, she oversaw the preservation of the Val di Sieve region, the city of Florence, and the Municipal Museums, a role that involves not only the supervision of works of art but also the oversight of construction projects in areas of historical and artistic interest. From 2000 to 2015, she directed the Museum of the Last Supper at Ognissanti, which houses one of Domenico Ghirlandaio's absolute masterpieces, the Last Supper from 1480, as well as frescoes by Botticelli.

One of Bietti's most significant institutional achievements was the reopening and revitalization of the Casa Martelli Museum, a Florentine noble residence that had been closed for decades. Bietti coordinated the complete restoration, cataloging, and inventory of the collections, leading to the museum's public opening in 2009. Casa Martelli houses paintings by Piero di Cosimo, Pontormo, Luca Giordano, and Salvator Rosa, and its restoration was considered one of the most successful projects to transform a historic home into a museum in Florence during the 2000s.

Since 2004, Bietti has served as director of the Medici Chapels Museum, the monumental complex attached to the Basilica of San Lorenzo that houses the Medici tombs designed and partially sculpted by Michelangelo, the New Sacristy with its famous allegories of Day, Night, Dawn, and Twilight, and the magnificent Chapel of the Princes. In this capacity, she has curated internationally acclaimed exhibitions, including the one dedicated to Ferdinando I de' Medici (2009), marking the 400th anniversary of the Grand Duke's death, and the one on Leo X (2012), on the 500th anniversary of his election to the papal throne, organized in collaboration with Nicoletta Baldini.

Since 2010, she has also been entrusted with the stewardship of the Laurenzian Complex, the Basilica of San Lorenzo, the Laurentian Library, and the adjoining museums, one of the world's most concentrated collections of artistic and literary heritage.

The catalog of exhibitions curated by Bietti is extraordinarily rich and diverse. Among the most important exhibitions are: Saved from the Waters. Works of Art Restored and to Be Restored Thirty Years After the Flood (Florence, 1996), dedicated to the recovery of the artistic heritage flooded in 1966; From Pontormo & for Pontormo (Florence, 1996); Death and Glory. Medici Funeral Apparatus for Philip II of Spain and Margaret of Austria (Florence and Valladolid, 1999); and the traveling exhibition Pinocchio from Birth to the Present, which toured six Japanese national museums in 2004-2005 before being presented at Palazzo Pitti in 2006-2007. She also organized the international conference Around Filippo Lippi's Martelli Annunciation. Reflections Following the Restoration, whose proceedings were published by Mandragora.

Bietti has overseen major restorations of works and spaces under her care. These include the restoration of Sagrestia Nuova by Michelangelo, which restored the legibility of the complex's marbles and frescoes, and numerous interventions on the paintings in the Ognissanti Last Supper and the Medici Chapels.

Her bibliography includes contributions to exhibition catalogs, specialized journals, and monographs. Among her major works are: Ferdinando I de' Medici (1549-1609) (exhibition catalog, 2009); The Casa Martelli Museum in Florence; On Filippo Lippi's Martelli Annunciation; the anthology Grand Duke Cosimo I de' Medici and the Dynastic Political Program in the San Lorenzo Complex in Florence (Florence University Press), which she edited; and the very recent San Lorenzo in Florence: the Basilica, the Museums, the Library (Mandragora, 2026), previewed at the Opera Medicea Laurenziana.

In 2018, she was elected Honorary Academician of the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno di Firenze, the oldest art academy in the Western world, founded in 1563 by Cosimo I de' Medici and Giorgio Vasari. She has also received the Award from the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington, D.C., the title of Grand Dame of the Supreme Order of the Knights Hospitaller of Saint Martin de Tours (March 10, 2010), and the "Pinocchio di Carlo Lorenzini" Award in 2011. She has been a supporter of Advancing Women Artists (AWA) since the association's founding in 2006, contributing to the recovery of works by women artists from the storage facilities of Florentine museums.

Bigaroni, Marino

Izzalini di Todi, 27 March 1919 - Santa Maria degli Angeli, 4 April 2016

Born Luigi Bigaroni in the hamlet of Izzalini near Todi, he entered the Order of Friars Minor in 1934, taking the religious name Marino, and took a degree in classical letters at the Sapienza University of Rome. Ordained priest, he celebrated his first Mass on 4 July 1943 in the parish church of his native Izzalini. For decades he taught classical literature in Franciscan secondary schools, notably at the liceo of Assisi, before retiring from teaching on grounds of age.

Freed from the classroom, Bigaroni devoted his final decades to the Biblioteca Francescana at the Chiesa Nuova in Assisi, which he directed as librarian and expanded from some 4,000 to 24,000 volumes, all catalogued and eventually computerised — turning a modest conventual collection into a working research library for Franciscan studies. From this base he produced more than forty essays and editions on the topography, architecture and cult sites of Franciscan Umbria, among them Montesanto di Todi da monastero a rocca dell'Albornoz (1981), San Damiano - Assisi, la chiesa prima di San Francesco (1983), Contributi per la biografia ed il culto di Iacopone da Todi (1985), La Chiesa di San Giorgio in Assisi ed il primo ampliamento della cinta medievale (1990), and La "Domus comunis Assisii" (2001).

His most consequential editorial work was Compilatio assisiensis, the collection of testimony by Brother Leo and his companions on the life of Francis, transmitted in a Perugia manuscript and previously circulated under titles such as Legenda Antiqua and Legenda Perugina; Bigaroni's first edition appeared in 1975, followed in 1992 by a complete critical edition with facing Italian translation that remains a standard reference among the early Franciscan sources. He is also credited with recovering the melody transmitted for the Cantico di frate Sole. Alongside Hans-Rudolf Meier and Elvio Lunghi, he co-authored the standard modern monograph La basilica di Santa Chiara in Assisi (Quattroemme, Perugia, 1994), contributing the reconstruction of the church's documented origins and building history on which the current scholarly chronology of the basilica rests. In the aftermath of the 1997 earthquake he took part in explorations beneath Santa Chiara that brought to light a wooden coffin associated by tradition with the bodies of Francis and Clare; study of the discovery remained unfinished at his death in 2016.

Bikiaris, Dimitrios Nikolaos

Milea, Larisa, 20 July 1965

Dimitrios Nikolaos Bikiaris was born on 20 July 1965 in Milea, Larisa, Thessaly, Greece. He obtained his degree in chemistry and then his Doctor of Philosophy from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in 1988, with a thesis on the synthesis of diepoxy derivatives and their application in tuning the properties of polyesters — doctoral work that established the core vocabulary of his scientific career: a vocabulary rooted in the synthesis and characterisation of polymeric materials across a remarkably wide range of applications, from industrial plastics to pharmaceutical drug carriers, from biodegradable packaging to the binding media of Byzantine frescoes.

Bikiaris became Assistant Professor in the Chemistry Department of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in 2000 and has since risen to the rank of full Professor, currently holding the chair of Professor of Polymer Chemistry and Technology and directing the Laboratory of Chemistry and Technology of Polymers and Colors. The laboratory name — combining polymers and colours — reflects a research identity that from the outset brought together the synthesis and characterisation of macromolecular materials with the scientific analysis of colouring substances, a combination that made Bikiaris a natural partner for the Byzantine heritage science programme at Ormylia. In the second half of the 1990s, working simultaneously at the Aristotle University and at the newly established Diagnostic Research Centre for Icons at the Sacred Convent of the Annunciation in Ormylia — his institutional affiliation in these publications given as the Diagnostic Centre for the Research and Study of Byzantine Hagiography — he joined the founding team of the Ormylia Art Diagnosis Centre alongside Sister Daniilia and Sophia Sotiropoulou.

The first and most methodologically influential of his contributions to Byzantine heritage science appeared in 2000: "Ochre-differentiation through micro-Raman and micro-FTIR spectroscopies: application on wall paintings at Meteora and Mount Athos, Greece," published in Spectrochimica Acta Part A: Molecular and Biomolecular Spectroscopy, with Bikiaris as first author and co-authored by Sister Daniilia, Sotiropoulou, Katsimbiri, Pavlidou, Moutsatsou, and Chryssoulakis. The most widely used inorganic pigments of Byzantine and post-Byzantine painting are earth pigments called ochres — red and yellow ochres, limonite, goethite, raw and burnt sienna, caput mortuum, and hematite. The paper proposed a technique of differentiation allowing one to distinguish among all the different kinds of iron oxides used as pigments, calculating ratios between the main spectroscopic peaks from micro-Raman spectra and confirming elementary composition through SEM-EDS. This paper is today one of the most widely cited references in the entire literature of Byzantine wall painting analysis, appearing in the bibliography of virtually every subsequent study that employs vibrational spectroscopy to characterise iron oxide pigments in Orthodox sacred art: its methodological contribution was to transform the identification of ochre-family pigments from a qualitative art-historical judgement into a quantitative, reproducible chemical procedure. In the same year Bikiaris was listed among the authors of the landmark Protaton study — the systematic technical examination of the frescoes attributed to Manuel Panselinos — published in the Journal of Cultural Heritage, which established the mixed binding media technique as the foundation of Palaiologan monumental workshop practice.

Bikiaris extended the analytical chemistry of his Byzantine work into the study of post-Byzantine and modern Greek painting, including an investigation of old varnishes from six paintings in the collection of the Teloglion Foundation of Arts at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, and a diagnostic study of the artistic technique and materials of Nikolaos Gyzis — the nineteenth-century Academic painter — published in 2008 in collaboration with Sotiropoulou and others.

While his contributions to Byzantine heritage science represent a significant and internationally influential strand of his work, they form only a fraction of a scientific output of extraordinary scale and range. His research interests include the synthesis and characterisation of polyesters, copolymers, biobased polymers, composites, and nanocomposites, as well as 3D printing, polymer recycling, the modification of natural polymers, the use of polymers for contaminant removal, microplastics, and the application of new biocompatible polymers in tissue engineering and pharmaceutical technology. A particular focus is the synthesis and characterisation of novel polymers from monomers derived from biomass — especially polyesters from FDCA (furan-2,5-dicarboxylic acid), bio-derived polymers that offer a potential substitute for petroleum-based PET with improved barrier properties and full biodegradability — and the preparation and optimisation of biodegradable polymeric drug carriers for sustained release.

The scale of Bikiaris's scientific output places him among the most internationally productive chemists in Greece: more than 550 papers in international scientific journals, over 25,000 citations, an h-index of 85 (Scopus), four chapters in international scientific books, 15 international patents, and participation in more than 60 research projects. He is included in the top 2% of cited scientists worldwide and ranks first at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in the Stanford University global ranking of scientists. In 2017 he was awarded the Prize of Excellence in Research on Natural Sciences by the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. He serves as Section Editor-in-Chief for the Biobased and Biodegradable Polymers section of the MDPI journal Polymers and sits on the editorial boards of several international publications in polymer chemistry and materials science.

Bikiaris's position in the intellectual landscape of Byzantine heritage science is that of the materials chemist whose early engagement with the Ormylia team provided the quantitative, reproducible analytical backbone for a field that was, in the late 1990s, still finding its methodological footing. His ochre-differentiation paper in particular has achieved the status of a reference standard, cited reflexively in Byzantine painting analyses across Europe, Russia, the Balkans, and the Middle East wherever iron oxide pigments are identified by vibrational spectroscopy. The connection between his primary polymer chemistry programme and his heritage science work is not incidental: the chemistry of binding media in Byzantine frescoes — egg proteins, animal glues, oil glazes — involves exactly the kind of macromolecular characterisation that his laboratory specialises in, and his ability to bring the full technical arsenal of a modern polymer chemistry department to bear on medieval sacred art gave the Ormylia team a scientific depth that few comparable heritage institutions could match.

Binaghi Olivari, Maria Teresa

d. 20 August 2021

Maria Teresa Binaghi Olivari was an Italian art historian and heritage official whose career was bound up with the study and conservation of Lombard art, and in particular with the Pinacoteca di Brera and the wider Milanese Soprintendenza. A word of caution at the outset: biographical documentation on her is thin. The fullest single source is the obituary Franco Moro published in Il Giornale dell'Arte in September 2021, supplemented by her own professional self-description and her bibliographic footprint. Her date and place of birth are not recorded in the sources available, and this gap is best flagged rather than filled with conjecture.

By her own account, Binaghi Olivari served as a funzionario storico dell'arte (art-historical officer) at the Soprintendenza per i Beni Artistici e Storici in Milan from 1969 to 1998, rising eventually to the rank of soprintendente aggiunto (deputy superintendent) over what her obituarist counted as more than forty years of service. Moro records that she trained under, and was shaped by, the examples of Gian Alberto Dell'Acqua, Franco Russoli, and Carlo Bertelli - three dominant figures in mid-twentieth-century Milanese museum culture and Brera scholarship. That lineage situates her firmly within the Brera-Poldi Pezzoli axis of Lombard connoisseurship rather than the academic university system.

Her published interests were unusually wide, spanning roughly six centuries, though the center of gravity lay in the Lombard Renaissance. According to Moro, her earliest work, from 1965, addressed the thirteenth-century sculptor Guido Bigarelli da Como; she then turned to Bernardino Luini - a projected monograph that, tellingly, she never brought to completion - and to the Lombard woodcarvers (intagliatori). In her later years her attention shifted toward subjects often neglected as marginal: the history of Milanese embroiderers and of the first museum restorers. One fruit of this late direction was her 2018 identification, in the parish church of Caglio above Lake Como, of four canvases painted in 1776 by the young Andrea Appiani - the pursuit of a restorer's biography leading to an attributional discovery.

Her most cited contributions belong to the study of painting in Milan around 1500. She was among the authors of the landmark catalogue Zenale e Leonardo. Tradizione e rinnovamento della pittura lombarda (Museo Poldi Pezzoli, 4 December 1982 - 28 February 1983), where her attributional arguments - for instance connecting works to Bernardo Zenale's circle and tracing Bramantino's and Luini's inflections in provincial cycles such as those at Gravedona - are still engaged with by specialists today. She also wrote on the artistic and cultural situation of Milan under French occupation, in her essay I francesi a Milano (1499-1525): arti figurative e moda (1979), and, reflecting her interest in textiles, co-edited studies of lace and its symbolism with Alessandra Mottola Molfino (I pizzi: moda e simbolo). She authored a well-known guide to the Brera picture gallery (The Pinacoteca of Brera, with a preface by Carlo Bertelli). In 1992 she supervised the celebrated restoration of Luini's Pelucca frescoes, carried out by Pinin Brambilla. Decades on, she was still active as a member of the working group for the 2010-11 exhibition Il Rinascimento nelle terre ticinesi. Da Bramantino a Bernardino Luini at Rancate.

Moro's obituary is candid about a professional disappointment - that the top superintendency she was equipped for never came - and warm about her personality, remembering her sharp wit and the cropped, jaunty haircut by which colleagues had known her since the 1980s. The portrait that emerges is of a rigorous heritage professional who did much of her most valuable work on precisely the unglamorous, archival edges of the discipline: restorers, embroiderers, and provincial attributions.

Bioletti, Susie

active early 21st century

Susie Bioletti is a conservator and conservation scientist who has led preservation and conservation work at the Library of Trinity College Dublin, with particular responsibility for the library's collection of early Irish manuscripts. Her work sits at the intersection of conservation practice and technical art history, applying non-destructive scientific analysis to questions that have traditionally been addressed only through connoisseurship or documentary inference.

With Allyson Smith, Bioletti carried out pigment analysis of the Book of Dimma and related pocket gospel books as part of Trinity's early Irish manuscripts project of the 2010s, published as "Shining a Light on the Pigments of Early Irish Manuscripts" in An Insular Odyssey: Manuscript Culture in Early Christian Ireland and Beyond (2017). Their analysis overturned the long-held assumption that the intense blue found in these manuscripts derived from imported lapis lazuli, showing instead that the illuminators achieved a comparable effect with an indigo blue mixed with gypsum — a finding that substantially revised scholarly understanding of the materials, trade networks and technical resourcefulness of early Irish scriptoria.

Bischoff, Bernhard

Altendorf (Altenburg), 20 December 1906 - Munich, 17 September 1991

Bernhard Bischoff was born on 20 December 1906 in Altendorf, an administrative division of Altenburg in Thuringia, and died in Munich on 17 September 1991. He was the son of Emil Bischoff and Charlotte von Gersdorff, who died giving birth to him. He received a Pietistic education during his youth, a background that shaped both his ethical seriousness and his familiarity with the Christian textual tradition from which medieval Latin culture drew its deepest sustenance. He married Hanne Oehler in 1935 and lived the majority of his life in Bavaria.

Bischoff studied under Paul Lehmann at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat Munchen, the third successive holder of the chair in Medieval Latin Philology inaugurated by Ludwig Traube. The Munich tradition of palaeography thus formed an unbroken three- generation lineage from Traube to Lehmann to Bischoff. Each generation deepened the science established by its predecessor: Traube created the philological foundations, Lehmann built the bibliographical infrastructure of medieval library catalogues, and Bischoff developed comprehensive control of the manuscript record itself.

Before completing his doctorate in 1933 under Lehmann, Bischoff was recruited by E. A. Lowe as an assistant for Codices Latini Antiquiores (CLA). He worked on the project until 1972 and conceived his later ninth-century cataloguing work as its continuation beyond CLA's chronological boundary. Lowe's project covered pre-ninth-century manuscripts; Bischoff's contribution focused on the Carolingian period, the most productive era of Latin manuscript production before the twelfth century. In 1982 he received the gold medal of the Bibliographical Society and reflected publicly on this formative collaboration.

From 1947 until retirement in 1974, Bischoff held the chair for Medieval Latin Philology at Munich, succeeding his teacher Lehmann. Between 1953 and 1975 he trained generations of medievalists from across Europe and North America in manuscript methods. He was especially renowned for mastery of Carolingian manuscripts, and students who studied with him in Munich understood they were entering an unusually exacting and influential palaeographical school.

Among those shaped by his teaching were Rosamond McKitterick, who studied with him in 1974-75 before finishing her Cambridge doctorate, David Ganz, and a wide international network that transmitted Munich methods into universities and research institutes across Britain, Ireland, Germany, France, Italy, and North America. In 1953 Bischoff was elected to the central board of the Monumenta Germaniae Historica (MGH), contributing especially to the Antiquitates series.

His first major independent achievement was Die sudostdeutschen Schreibschulen und Bibliotheken in der Karolingerzeit: Part I on Bavarian dioceses (1940; revised 1960 and 1974) and Part II on predominantly Austrian dioceses (1980). This work established a systematic map of Carolingian scriptoria and libraries in the southeast German sphere, including Regensburg, Freising, Salzburg, Augsburg, and Passau. The method combined close analysis of hands, localisation of undated manuscripts, and reconstruction of scriptorial networks as historical geography.

The three volumes of Mittelalterliche Studien (1966, 1967, 1981) represent the broadest expression of his scholarship. These essays range across Latin exegesis, Carolingian transmission of the Fathers, diffusion of Isidore, Greek learning in the early Middle Ages, Insular scholarship on the Continent, Merovingian minuscule, Alcuin and liturgical reform, and localisation of major classical and patristic manuscripts. Two studies were especially influential: his work on Greek knowledge in the Carolingian world and "Wendepunkte in der Geschichte der lateinischen Exegese im Fruhmittelalter" (Sacris Erudiri 6, 1954).

Bischoff's handbook Latin Palaeography: Antiquity and the Middle Ages, translated into English by Daibhi O Croinin and David Ganz and into French by Jean Vezin and Hartmut Atsma, became the standard introduction to the history of Latin script. It integrates technical script analysis with the cultural history of books, schools, churches, and courts, moving from writing materials and codicological form to Roman, national, Carolingian, Gothic, and humanist script traditions. The English edition appeared in 1990, one year before his death.

His largest late project was the Katalog der festlandischen Handschriften des neunten Jahrhunderts (mit Ausnahme der wisigotischen), the continental ninth-century continuation of CLA. Bischoff worked over decades to examine nearly every relevant manuscript witness, ultimately documenting close to 7,000 codices. The four published volumes appeared in 1998, 2004, 2014, and 2017, with posthumous editorial completion by Birgit Ebersperger.

This catalog transformed the field. References to the relevant Katalog entry became standard practice in Carolingian manuscript scholarship because Bischoff's descriptions provide the baseline for dating, localisation, and scriptorial comparison. His photographic memory and long direct experience in libraries enabled him to identify scribal hands, reunite membra disiecta, and test hypotheses at a level of precision rarely equaled.

His books and papers are now divided principally between the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek in Munich, the MGH, and the Universitatsbibliothek Leipzig. The Leipzig library preserves his personal research collection of approximately 5,700 volumes.

The English volume edited and translated by Michael Gorman (Cambridge, 1994) assembled seven of Bischoff's major Carolingian essays, including studies of cultural transmission from the sixth to ninth centuries, the court libraries of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, and centres of learning beyond court. These essays remain fundamental for reconstructing Carolingian intellectual infrastructure from manuscript evidence.

Bischoff received extensive international recognition: membership in the Bavarian Academy of Sciences (1956), Royal Irish Academy (1957), Medieval Academy of America (1960), German Archaeological Institute (1962), American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1968), and American Philosophical Society (1989), as well as honorary doctorates from Dublin, Oxford, Cambridge, and Milan. The Dublin honor had particular symbolic significance given his sustained work on Insular script and Irish learning on the Continent.

Bischoff's historical position is exceptional: he was not only the leading Latin palaeographer of the twentieth century, but the scholar who gave Carolingian studies its most reliable manuscript foundation. Because Carolingian civilisation is known primarily through surviving codices, his command of script, transmission, and localisation profoundly influenced neighbouring disciplines including medieval theology, liturgy, philology, and the history of learning.

For historians of medieval art and illuminated manuscripts, his work remains indispensable at every level. The Schreibschulen established key scriptorial geographies; Latin Palaeography supplied analytical tools; Mittelalterliche Studien clarified intellectual contexts; and the ninth-century Katalog became the practical entry point for identifying and dating Carolingian codices. No sustained work on Carolingian manuscripts, illuminated or otherwise, can proceed without his framework.

Bocchi, Francesco

Florence, 1548 – Florence, 1618

Francesco Bocchi was a Florentine writer and critic whose Le bellezze della città di Fiorenza (1591) is among the earliest works in the modern genre of the art guidebook, describing the paintings, sculptures and buildings of Florence church by church and quarter by quarter for the benefit of the cultivated visitor. Trained in Florence and active in its literary academies, Bocchi brought to the description of art a rhetorical and theoretical seriousness unusual for a topographical guide, treating individual works as objects worthy of sustained critical argument rather than mere itemised notice.

That seriousness is most fully realised in his earlier Eccellenza della statua del San Giorgio di Donatello (1584), a monographic treatise devoted entirely to a single sculpture at Orsanmichele — one of the first instances in European literature of a whole critical essay built around one work of art. Bocchi's Bellezze was substantially expanded, corrected and brought up to date by Giovanni Cinelli Calvoli in a much enlarged 1677 edition, commonly cited as "Bocchi–Cinelli," which nearly doubled the original text with new documentary and topographical material and became the standard reference edition for the following century. Because it records the location, condition and attribution of works before the redecorations, demolitions and losses of later centuries, the Bocchi–Cinelli guide remains a primary source for reconstructing the original disposition of Florentine church decoration, including campaigns that no longer survive in situ.

Bogaert, Pierre-Maurice

active late 20th-21st century

Pierre-Maurice Bogaert is a Belgian Benedictine monk of the abbey of Maredsous and one of the leading contemporary historians of the Latin Bible in the Middle Ages. Long associated with the Revue Bénédictine, the scholarly journal published by his own monastic community and a central venue for research on patristic and early medieval biblical scholarship, he has built a career on the close study of the biblical text's transmission, translation, and canonical status across the Latin West.

His work ranges widely across the history of the Vulgate and the Vetus Latina, with particular attention to the Book of Baruch and to the formation of the biblical canon in Latin Christianity. His synthetic chapter, "The Latin Bible, c. 600 to c. 900," in The New Cambridge History of the Bible (Cambridge, 2013), is among the most authoritative recent overviews of the subject and situates individual manuscripts, including the Codex Amiatinus, within the broader currents of early medieval biblical scholarship.

Bogaert's chapter is particularly valuable for its account of the three principal Latin psalter traditions — the Roman, the Gallican, and Jerome's iuxta Hebraeos — and of the Amiatinus's position among them as a rare and imperfect witness to the Hebraicum version, a distinction frequently blurred in general literature on the manuscript. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion.

Bologna, Ferdinando

L'Aquila, 27 September 1925 – Ocre, 3 April 2019

Ferdinando Bologna was one of the greatest Italian art historians of the twentieth century, a student of Pietro Toesca and a collaborator of Roberto Longhi, whose career spanned over sixty years across the fields of medieval and modern art and the theory of art historiography, always characterized by philological rigor and a broad historical perspective.

Born in L'Aquila on September 27, 1925, Bologna earned his degree in Rome under the guidance of Pietro Toesca, the great systematizer of medieval Italian painting, from whom he absorbed the attribution method based on rigorous stylistic analysis and archival documentation. At just twenty-five years old, in 1950—the very year of its founding—he joined the editorial staff of the journal Paragone, established by Roberto Longhi as an instrument of cultural struggle and the renewal of Italian art historiography. His association with Longhi was decisive: Bologna absorbed his ability to combine philology and critical sensibility, but over time developed an independent vocation for the historical-social analysis of art, distancing himself from his mentor's pure aesthetics in favor of an interpretation more materialistically rooted in the conditions of production and patronage.

After a brief stint as a young official at the Superintendency of Naples—a city that would remain at the center of his interests throughout his life—Bologna rapidly advanced through the university ranks, becoming a full professor of Medieval and Modern Art History at the University of Naples in 1965. He later taught at the universities of Salerno, Messina, and Siena, where he was among the founders of the School of Specialization in Art History established by Giovanni Previtali. In 1984, he assumed the chair of Medieval and Modern Art History at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, of which he was one of the founders, holding that position until his retirement and remaining professor emeritus until his death. The city of Naples conferred upon him honorary citizenship in 1997, an extremely rare honor that attests to the deep bond between the scholar and the southern region he had loved most.

Bologna's most enduring contribution to medieval studies is undoubtedly La pittura italiana delle origini (1962, reprinted in 1978), a seminal work in which he reconstructs, with a broad perspective, the roots of the Italian pictorial tradition, from early medieval cycles to the emergence of the Romanesque and Proto-Gothic styles, situating Italian painting within the broader context of the late medieval Mediterranean. This is complemented by crucial studies on the Angevin court of Naples—the volume I pittori alla corte angioina di Napoli (1969) remains an indispensable reference for anyone studying 14th-century art in southern Italy—and on the relationship between Naples and the major Mediterranean routes of painting, analyzed in the volume Napoli e le rotte mediterranee della pittura (1977). Also significant were his contributions on Giotto (Novità su Giotto, 1969) and on Simone Martini, of whom he presented a historiographically more accurate portrait than the prevailing interpretations.

A common thread runs through Bologna's entire scholarly output: the historiographical vindication of the art of southern Italy, traditionally neglected by criticism centered on Florence and Rome. His study of the ceiling of the Sala Magna at the Steri in Palermo (The Ceiling of the Sala Magna at the Steri in Palermo and Sicilian Feudal Culture in the Late Middle Ages, 1975, now in its fourth edition) is a paradigmatic example of this approach: Bologna decodes the complex figurative program of the 14th-century ceiling as a mirror of Sicilian feudal culture at the moment of its decline, interweaving art history, political history, and the history of mentalities with a methodology that was pioneering at the time. Similarly, his studies on Francesco Solimena (1958), on Roviale Spagnolo and 16th-Century Neapolitan Painting (1959), and on Gaspare Traversi in the European Enlightenment (1980) demonstrate a constant focus on modern Neapolitan art, in the conviction that it deserved the same critical standing reserved for the northern schools.

Bologna was also a theorist of historiographical method, author of some of the most stimulating contributions on the problem of art history as a discipline. In the volume From the Minor Arts to Industrial Design: History of an Ideology (1972), he investigated the genesis of the concept of "decorative arts" and its ideological function within the capitalist system, anticipating issues that would become central to the international debate of the 1980s. With Methods of Studying Italian Art and the Methodological Problem Today (1979, for Einaudi's Storia dell'arte) and La coscienza storica dell'arte d'Italia (1982), he took a clear stand against what he called Warburgian-derived iconological "mentalism"—the, in his view, casual use of iconology as an interpretive key independent of the material history of the works. He edited the ambitious UTET series Storia dell'arte in Italia (eight volumes, 1980–1988), which remains a standard reference work in Italian university libraries.

In the 1990s, Bologna explored the theme of naturalism in painting with the volume L'incredulità del Caravaggio e l'esperienza delle "cose naturali" (1992), in which he interpreted Caravaggio's realism not as an individual aesthetic choice but as a response to a collective cultural need of post-Tridentine Catholicism, rooted in the tangible concreteness of Franciscan preaching and in the Lombard tradition of observing nature. He also curated the exhibition Battistello Caracciolo and Early Naturalism in Naples (1991), a further contribution to the appreciation of the Neapolitan Caravaggio period. Ferdinando Bologna passed away on April 3, 2019 in Ocre, Abruzzo, at the age of ninety-four, leaving behind a scientific library of extraordinary scope and a school of students who have continued his southern-focused approach to the history of Italian art.

Boskovits, Miklós

Budapest, 1935 – 2011

Hungarian-born Italian art historian renowned for his rigorous scholarship on Tuscan painting from the Duecento through the early Trecento, establishing himself as a pivotal figure in the attribution of anonymous masters and the refinement of chronologies of Sienese and Florentine primitives. Born in Budapest on October 11, 1935, Boskovits fled Hungary amid the 1956 revolution and settled in Italy, where he pursued classical studies and art history at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan. Working within the intellectual legacy of Pietro Toesca and under the influence of Cesare Brandi, he developed a method that blended connoisseurship, archival rigour, and close stylistic analysis. He later held a professorship at the same university, where he taught courses on Giotto and the Florentine primitives.

Boskovits revolutionised attributions in medieval Tuscan painting and worked in close collaboration with Luciano Bellosi as one of the foremost experts on the period. Their analyses underpinned the reattribution of Cimabue's Castelfiorentino Madonna (c. 1283–1284), distinguishing it from Duccio's Crevola Madonna through nuanced comparisons of drapery, halo treatment, and iconographic detail. His seminal article Su Niccolò di Buonaccorso, Benedetto di Bindo and Sienese Painting in the Early Fifteenth Century (Paragone, 1980) dissected Trecento Sienese developments, while broader studies on Bartolomeo Bulgarini and Niccolò di Buonaccorso clarified workshop practices and stylistic evolutions in the aftermath of the Black Death. His oeuvre emphasised the interplay of Florentine innovation — Giotto's naturalism — with Sienese Gothic elegance, reshaping understandings of figures such as the Master of the Bambino Vispo.

As professor emeritus at the Università Cattolica, Boskovits contributed to catalogues for major exhibitions and institutions, influencing the restoration and museum display of Duecento–Trecento panels. His methodology bridged Brandi's restoration theory with the iconographic precision associated with Carlo Bertelli, as seen in collaborative contexts on Lombard and Sienese heritage. His multi-volume Italian Paintings before 1400 for the National Gallery of Art in Washington remains a fundamental reference tool. He died in 2011, leaving a corpus that continues to guide scholars navigating the anonymous masters of medieval Tuscany.

Bottari, Stefano

Fiumedinisi, 6 March 1907 - Bologna, February 1967

Stefano Bottari was an Italian art historian and critic, the leading twentieth-century interpreter of Norman and Swabian art in Sicily and the Italian South, and — at the end of his life — of Nicola Pisano.

He was born at Fiumedinisi, in the province of Messina, on 6 March 1907, and remained attached throughout his life to the nearby village of Itala, where he carried out some of his earliest fieldwork: his first publication, in 1931, concerned figured plaster fragments of Arab-Norman work found there. He began his studies with a course in architecture at the University of Messina before transferring to letters at Catania, where he graduated on 5 November 1931 with a thesis on Michelangelo.

The architectural training is not incidental. It shows in everything he later wrote about buildings — the Norman churches of Sicily and Calabria, the cathedral of Messina, the Swabian castles — where the analysis is structural before it is decorative, and where plan and section carry as much argument as ornament.

His first books were not monographs but methodological essays: La critica figurativa e l'estetica moderna (Bari, 1935) and I miti della critica figurativa (Messina, 1936). The lineage here runs from Benedetto Croce and from Matteo Marangoni, and it commits him early to a position — that the critical act and the historical act are the same act — which he never abandoned.

The corollary was a lifelong concern with teaching.
