His Storia dell'arte (Milan: Principato, 2 vols., 1937-40) became one of the most widely used Italian secondary-school manuals of its generation and was still being reissued and expanded twenty years later, as Storia dell'arte italiana (3 vols., 1954-57). He wrote repeatedly on the method and the efficacy of teaching art history in schools, sharing much of his methodological ground with Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti; in the mid-1960s he argued publicly for the renewal of the istituti d'arte along lines rooted in the material traditions of Italian artistic culture. Among Italian art historians of the interwar generation he was one of the most seriously engaged with the school as an institution — a strand of his work recovered in recent scholarship by Simonetta Nicolini.

He also worked on cataloguing and restoration, notably as consultant to the Pinacoteca Zelantea at Acireale, and between 1945 and 1946 published a considerable body of political and civic journalism in La Sicilia, La Nuova Europa, L'Opinione, La Città libera and Risorgimento liberale — the liberal and Actionist press of the immediate post-war.

He held teaching appointments at Messina from 1935 and at Catania from 1937, entering the university roll as professor of art history in 1939, with the chair at Catania. The Sicilian phase lasted two decades.

On 1 November 1956 he took over the direction of the Institute of Medieval and Modern Art History at Bologna — the institute named for Igino Benvenuto Supino — and from 1 February 1957 held the chair of medieval and modern art history in the Faculty of Letters, a post he retained until his death. From the academic year 1957-58 he also taught in the Faculty of Magistero, and from 1 November 1959 directed the Scuola di perfezionamento in medieval and modern art history.

He arrived at Bologna into a particular vacuum. Roberto Longhi had left the Bologna chair in 1949 for Florence, having transformed it; the Longhian lesson needed to develop on its own terms. In 1958 Bottari founded, with the archaeologist Luciano Laurenzi, the journal Arte antica e moderna, which became the central organ of art-historical study at Bologna in those years.

The scholarship

The Norman and Swabian South. This is the body of work for which he is indispensable:

  • Chiese basiliane della Sicilia e della Calabria (1939)
  • Il Duomo di Messina (1939)
  • I mosaici della Sicilia (1943)
  • L'architettura della Contea. Studi sulla prima architettura normanna nell'Italia meridionale e in Sicilia (Catania: Muglia, 1948)
  • Monumenti svevi di Sicilia (1950; reprinted Catania: Pellicanolibri, 1984)

L'architettura della Contea is the fundamental study of the first Norman building campaigns in the South and in Sicily — the architecture of the county before the kingdom — and remains the point of departure for the subject.

Sicilian painting and Antonello. Antonello da Messina (Messina, 1939), revised as Antonello (1953); La pittura del Quattrocento in Sicilia (1954); La cultura figurativa in Sicilia (1954). Together these effectively constituted Sicilian Quattrocento painting as a field.

Nicola Pisano and Bologna. The last phase of his work turned to thirteenth-century sculpture. He published "L'arca di San Domenico in Bologna" in the Salmi Festschrift of 1961 and then the monograph L'arca di S. Domenico in Bologna (Bologna, 1964). Alongside this he was accumulating a series of studies on Nicola Pisano which he intended to draw together into a single monograph. He died before doing so. The Faculty of Letters at Bologna gathered the scattered essays and published them posthumously as Saggi su Nicola Pisano (Bologna, 1969), stating in its preface that death had interrupted a project which would have given a complete image of the artist and of what it called a fundamental knot in Italian art.

That trajectory — three decades on the Norman and Swabian monuments of the Mezzogiorno, then the Arca di San Domenico, then Nicola — is worth registering in itself. Bottari came to Nicola from the South, which is to say from the sculptural and architectural culture in which the sculptor's own formation is most plausibly to be sought.

He died at Bologna in February 1967, at fifty-nine. He was commemorated by Francesco Arcangeli before the Accademia delle Scienze dell'Istituto di Bologna for the academic year 1966-67, and by Cesare Gnudi in the Atti e Memorie of the Deputazione di Storia Patria per le Province di Romagna in 1968. A collection of his shorter and more personal writings appeared as Schegge di varia umanità, which carries a bibliography of his work.

Bourke, Cormac

Dublin, active late 20th-21st century

Cormac Bourke is an Irish archaeologist born in Dublin, specialising in medieval studies, early church history, and insular Christianity. His career has been defined by an unusually sharp methodological focus: rather than broad historical surveys, he works at the precise intersection of material culture and religious practice, reading saints' relics, liturgical objects, and metalwork as primary historical documents. He is currently based in Belfast and is recognised as one of the foremost authorities on early medieval Irish sacred objects.

Bourke served for twenty-six years as Curator of Medieval Antiquities at the Ulster Museum, Belfast, a tenure that gave him unparalleled hands-on access to the collections of early insular metalwork and relics held in Northern Ireland. Following his retirement from the Ulster Museum, he moved to the antiquities department of the National Museum of Ireland, where he has continued his active research and curatorial work. In both institutions he has combined object-based scholarship with public engagement, participating in lectures and interpretive projects that bring early medieval material culture to wider audiences.

The intellectual core of Bourke's work is the archaeology of saints' relics and the devotional objects associated with them. His publications range across early Irish hand-bells, insular croziers, Celtic brooches, crucifixion plaques, and cumdachs (elaborate book-shrines). His magnum opus in this field is The Early Medieval Hand-bells of Ireland and Britain (Wordwell Books, 2020; revised 2022), a 708-page study that the National Museum of Ireland described as "the most authoritative study ever undertaken on medieval hand-bells" and "an immense achievement both nationally and internationally". Hand-bells were emblematic objects of early Irish monastic life, and Bourke's exhaustive catalogue and analysis of surviving examples transformed a relatively under-studied category of object into a richly documented chapter in the history of insular Christianity.

In the field of Columban scholarship specifically, Bourke edited the landmark volume Studies in the Cult of Saint Columba (Four Courts Press, 1997), which brought together twelve original essays by leading specialists covering the saint's life, the history of Iona, and the wider Columban monastic federation. He has also published directly on Adomnan's Vita Columbae, including the article "A play on a letter in Adomnan's Life of Saint Columba" (Innes Review, 2019), which examines a subtle textual detail within the primary hagiographic source. His essay "Peregrinatio Columbae" (2004) explored the theology and practice of holy pilgrimage in the Columban tradition, contributing to the broader debate about Irish peregrinatio pro Christo as a form of spiritual exile.

One of the more distinctive threads in Bourke's scholarship is his attention to the transmission of Irish sacred objects beyond Ireland and Britain. His article "The early Irish reliquary in Bobbio" (Archivum Bobiense, 1994-95) examined an Irish relic container preserved at the monastery of Bobbio in northern Italy, founded by St. Columbanus - a find of direct relevance to the study of Irish monastic influence on the Continent. His work on "Clonmore and Bobbio: two seventh-century shrines" (2001-02) extended this line of inquiry, comparing Irish shrine-making traditions with surviving Lombard-era parallels. More recently, in 2025, he published a major article in the Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy reinterpreting the Shrine of St. Brigid's Shoe, a metalwork object from County Galway that had been misunderstood since the eighteenth century, providing its first complete description and historical interpretation.

Though Bourke's primary expertise is material rather than textual, his scholarship intersects meaningfully with the world of illuminated manuscripts. His 2024 article "Stolen by night in 1007: a crux in the history of the Book of Kells" (Riocht na Midhe, 2024) addressed a key episode in the transmission history of the Columban codex, re-examining the documentary evidence for the famous theft of the manuscript. This work situates him as a valuable voice in the broader scholarly debate about the Book of Kells' origins and custody within the Columban monastic network.

His article output has appeared consistently in the Ulster Journal of Archaeology, the Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, the Journal of the Royal Society of Antiquaries of Ireland, and in major edited volumes published by Brill, Four Courts Press, and Yale University Press. He contributed the entry on St. Patrick to the Dictionary of Irish Biography (Royal Irish Academy / Cambridge University Press, 2009), and the entry on liturgical staves to The Eerdmans Encyclopedia of Early Christian Art and Archaeology (2017). His Academia.edu profile lists over seventy-seven research papers and has accumulated more than 15,000 public views, placing him in the top 3% of researchers on the platform.

Brandi, Cesare

Siena, 1906 – Vignano, 1988

Born on April 8, 1906, in Siena, Brandi graduated in literature from the University of Florence in 1928, following studies that also included law at the University of Siena. He began his career in the Administration of Antiquities and Fine Arts, starting in Siena in 1930 where he catalogued paintings for the Academy of Fine Arts, and later moving to Bologna in 1933 as an inspector, during which he organised early restoration workshops and exhibitions such as the Exhibition of Riminese Painting of the Fourteenth Century in 1935. These formative roles immersed him in practical conservation challenges, shaping his later theoretical innovations amid Italy's rich medieval and Renaissance heritage.

In 1939, Brandi became the inaugural director of the Istituto Centrale per il Restauro (Central Institute for Restoration) in Rome — a position he held until 1959 — transforming it into a global benchmark for conservation science. Proposed for the role by fellow critic Giulio Carlo Argan, he designed the institute to integrate phenomenological philosophy with hands-on techniques, addressing postwar damages to frescoes in places like Mantua and Viterbo. His tenure extended to UNESCO collaborations from 1948, international consultancies, and the role of Superintendent of Antiquities and Fine Arts from 1953, earning honours such as the Feltrinelli Prize for art criticism in 1958, shared with Argan.

Brandi's enduring legacy stems from his theory of restoration, first outlined in the 1963 book Teoria del Restauro, which posits that restoration must respect an artwork's historical authenticity, aesthetic unity, and material integrity — often summarised as the "duality of matter and form." Drawing from philosophers including Heidegger, Husserl, Hegel, and Croce, he argued for interventions that reveal rather than replace the object's temporal patina, influencing Italy's 1972 restoration charter and worldwide conservation practice. Major publications such as Le due vie (1966) and Teoria generale della critica (1974) further explored aesthetics and criticism, sparking debates with thinkers including Roland Barthes.

As a professor of medieval and modern art history — first as a free lecturer at the University of Rome from 1934, then holding chairs at Palermo (1961) and Rome's La Sapienza — Brandi mentored generations of scholars while producing essays on artists such as Filippo de Pisis and catalogues of Tuscan collections. He founded journals including L'Immagine (1947–1950) and the institute's Bollettino, blending criticism with travelogues and poetry that reflected his phenomenological approach to art's encounter with time. He died on January 19, 1988, in Vignano, leaving an adopted son, Vittorio Brandi Rubiu, who also pursued art history.

Bretholz, Berthold

Freiberg, 9 July 1862 – Brno, 27 November 1936

Berthold Bretholz was born on 9 July 1862 in Freiberg, Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, into a Jewish family with deep roots in the region's mercantile community. His father Sigmund was a wool merchant and his mother Henriette the daughter of a merchant from Tysmenitz. He died on 27 November 1936 in Brno, Czechoslovakia; his son Wolfgang Bretholz (1904–1969) became a journalist.

After studying history and law at the University of Vienna, Bretholz worked for two years at the Institut für Österreichische Geschichtsforschung and then for five years as a collaborator on the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in Berlin, where he worked on the Concilia volumes. The Institut für Österreichische Geschichtsforschung — founded by Theodor von Sickel and modelled on the French École des Chartes — was the principal training ground for diplomatic and palaeographic method in the Habsburg Empire, and Bretholz's passage through it gave his subsequent archival and editorial work a rigorous technical foundation. On the recommendation of Sickel, he was appointed Landeshistoriker — state historian — of Moravia in 1892.

From 1895 Bretholz directed the Brno city archive and from 1897 the Moravian provincial archive, of which he was director from 1909 until his retirement in 1926. Under his stewardship he rebuilt the provincial archive into the central archival centre of Moravia. From 1909 he taught as honorary and later extraordinary professor at the German Technical University in Brno, and was a corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences in Vienna. From 1905 he belonged to the Commission for the Recent History of Austria, and from 1907 to the Austrian Archive Council as a full member.

His most forensically significant archival achievement was the exposure of his predecessor's fraudulent documentary corpus. Antonín Boček, who had served as Moravian archivist in the early nineteenth century, had fabricated a substantial number of medieval documents pertaining to Moravian history, presenting them as authentic charters. Bretholz applied the diplomatic and palaeographic methods acquired in Vienna and Berlin to demolish the evidentiary basis on which earlier Moravian historiography had partly rested. This exposure was not merely a scholarly correction; it required the methodical dismantling of a legacy deeply embedded in Moravian historical self-understanding, and it demonstrated a critical independence that Bretholz maintained throughout his career.

The contribution for which Bretholz occupies a permanent place in the historiography of medieval Central Europe is his critical edition of the Chronica Boemorum — the Chronicle of the Czechs — by Cosmas of Prague, published in the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1923 as volume 2 of the new series Scriptores rerum Germanicarum (MGH SS rer. Germ. n.s. 2), produced in collaboration with W. Weinberg. Cosmas was born around 1045, educated in Liège, and upon his return to Bohemia became a priest and, from 1086, a prebendary at Prague. He completed the first book of the Chronicle in 1119, starting with the creation of the world and the earliest deeds of the Czechs up to Saint Adalbert; the second and third books carry the history of Bohemia forward to 1125, the year of his death.

The Chronicle of the Czechs is a masterwork of medieval historical writing — deeply erudite, consciously researched, and narrated in high rhetorical style, at times slipping into rhymed prose or verse. Regarded as the foundational narrative of Czech history, it is the source of the oldest stories about the land, people, and rulers of Bohemia and Moravia, and its Latin demands not only textual but also literary and philological competence in an editor. Bretholz's edition, with its apparatus of manuscript variants, its forty-page prolegomena examining the chronicle's manuscript tradition and identifying Cosmas's classical and biblical sources, and its discussion of the provost Severus of Mělník, the master Gervase, and the abbot Clement of Břevnov — the dedicatees of the individual books — supplied the text on which all modern scholarship on Bohemian medieval history has subsequently rested. The edition remains the standard critical text, reprinted without substantial revision and cited as the reference edition in all subsequent translations, including the recent bilingual Latin-English edition published by Central European University Press.

Parallel to his archival directorship, Bretholz produced an extensive body of historical writing on the Bohemian and Moravian lands. From 1893 he published a detailed history of Moravia and edited an enormous quantity of archival sources, including the Codex Diplomaticus et epistolaris Moraviae (volumes XIV–XV, 1903) and the Libri citationum et sententiarum (volume VII, 1911). In 1912 he published Geschichte Böhmens und Mährens bis zum Aussterben der Přemysliden 1306, followed by the ambitious four-volume Geschichte Böhmens und Mährens (1921–1925), covering the period up to the modern era.

It was in these works that Bretholz advanced the argument that would mark his historiographic legacy with deep ambiguity. The "Bretholz theory," expounded mainly in the four-volume history, ascribed the descent of the Bohemian and Moravian Germans not to medieval colonists but to Teutonic tribes who had settled the area before the advent of the Czechs — a continuous inheritance from a pre-Slavic Germanic population that had never departed. The theory was empirically insupportable and its rejection by specialists on both sides of the ethnic divide was swift, including by German historians at the Prague German University such as Wilhelm Wostry. Yet its political consequences outlived its scholarly rebuttal: the theory became an important argument of extremist German nationalists in Czechoslovakia, and the Nazi regime incorporated it into its own ideology while simultaneously erasing Bretholz's name from the historiography on account of his Jewish origin. Few ironies in the history of Central European scholarship are more pointed.

On 1 December 1892, the year of his appointment as state historian, Bretholz converted to Lutheranism of the Augsburg Confession — a step common among Central European Jewish professionals seeking entry into public academic life under the late Habsburgs. This conversion did not dissolve his attachment to Jewish culture and history, which reasserted itself with force in the final years of his career. He wrote Geschichte der Juden in Mähren im Mittelalter (1934) and edited Quellen zur Geschichte der Juden in Mähren (1935), and contributed to the yearbooks of the Jewish historical society. These works, produced as the political situation in Central Europe darkened catastrophically, constituted an act of scholarly restitution — a recovery of the documentary and narrative record of Moravian Jewish life in the medieval period, carried out with the same archival precision that had characterised his entire career.

Bretholz's scholarly output spans three distinct but interconnected areas. As an archivist he transformed the Moravian provincial archive into a modern research institution and produced critical editions of documentary sources that underpinned the entire subsequent study of Moravian medieval history. As a textual critic his edition of Cosmas of Prague for the MGH remains, a century after its publication, the authoritative text of the most important medieval Bohemian chronicle. And as a historian — however contested his settlement thesis — he produced a comprehensive narrative history of Bohemia and Moravia whose documentary apparatus set the standard for the field. For medievalists working on Central European history, hagiography, or the transmission of Latin historiographic culture eastward from the Carolingian heartlands, Bretholz's work remains a constant point of reference: as editor, as archivist, and as a figure whose career was shaped — and ultimately deformed — by the intersection of scholarship and political identity in the last decades of the Habsburg world.

Brogi, Francesco

active Siena, 1862–1897

Italian scholar active in Siena in the second half of the nineteenth century, compiler of the Inventario generale degli oggetti d'arte della provincia di Siena, the first systematic survey of the paintings, sculptures, and liturgical furnishings preserved in the churches, confraternities, and public collections of the Sienese contado. Brogi carried out the fieldwork underlying the inventory between 1862 and 1865, travelling through the towns and parishes of the province to record, describe, and attribute works then still largely undocumented; the survey was not published until 1897, when it appeared in Siena as a single volume that remains a standard reference for provenance research.

Little is recorded of Brogi's own biography, but the inventory itself testifies to a conscientious and encyclopedic method: entries proceed town by town and building by building, noting condition, attribution as then understood, and location, so that many works later moved, dispersed, or destroyed can be traced back to a specific altar or chapel. It was Brogi, for instance, who first recorded the Montepulciano panel now known as the Coronation of the Virgin with Eleven Angels — later reattributed across four painters' names before settling, provisionally, on Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio — noting it in the Cappella della Concezione of the Arciconfraternita della Misericordia as a work "in the manner of Simone Martini," the earliest attributional judgment on record for that panel. For this reason the Inventario has retained a documentary value out of proportion to its modest, list-like format, and it continues to be cited wherever a nineteenth-century witness to the state and early attribution of Sienese paintings is needed.

Brown, Michelle P.

b. 1959

Distinguished British scholar specialising in medieval manuscripts, Professor Emerita of Medieval Manuscript Studies at the School of Advanced Study, University of London, and formerly Curator of Illuminated Manuscripts at the British Library (1986–2004), where she managed, preserved, and promoted access to the Library's holdings of illuminated manuscripts, including contributions to digitisation projects. At the University of London she taught on the History of the Book MA programme and supervised doctoral research on palaeography, book history, and medieval art; she has also held visiting professorships at University College London and Durham University, and was awarded the Sandars Readership in Bibliography at Cambridge (2008–2009). Additional roles include Lay Canon at St Paul's Cathedral and director of the Hereford Mappa Mundi Trust; she remains active as an independent scholar.

Her research spans the transition from Late Antiquity to the Early Middle Ages — the Conversion period, biblical and liturgical manuscripts, Anglo-Saxon and Celtic cultures, and early East–West relations, including ongoing work on manuscripts at St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai. Her principal publications include Understanding Illuminated Manuscripts (1994), The Lindisfarne Gospels: Society, Spirituality and the Scribe (2003) — the standard monographic treatment of Eadfrith's manuscript, which established the eremitic devotional interpretation of its creation — The Luttrell Psalter facsimile (2006), Manuscripts from the Anglo-Saxon Age (2008), and Bede and the Theory of Everything (2021). A Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries (FSA), she also works as a historical consultant and on-screen expert for radio and television, making manuscript studies accessible to broader audiences.

Brown, Thomas Julian

24 February 1923 – 19 January 1987

Thomas Julian Brown, FBA, FSA, FKC, known as Julian Brown, was an English palaeographer, celebrated above all for his work on Insular and Anglo-Saxon script. He held the chair of Palaeography at King's College London from 1961 until his retirement in 1984.

He was born on 24 February 1923, the son of a land agent and of Helen Brown, who received the MBE for wartime service in the WRVS. His half-sister by his father's first marriage, Mabel Raven "Betty" Brown (later Gilson, 1909–1965), became a botanist and fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge. He was educated at Westminster School and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he read Classics, graduating in 1948 after wartime service with the Border Regiment from 1942 to 1945.

In 1950 he became an Assistant Keeper in the Department of Manuscripts at the British Museum, where he remained until 1960, developing his expertise through direct work with the manuscripts themselves. In 1953 the Museum launched the project to publish a facsimile of the Lindisfarne Gospels with a volume of commentary; because the other departmental staff were overcommitted, the palaeographical commentary fell to Brown, who had had no formal training in the subject and had been in post only three years. It appeared in 1960 in the second volume of Evangeliorum Quattuor Codex Lindisfarnensis, and made his reputation.

He was elected a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries in 1956 and a Fellow of King's College London in 1975. In 1977 he delivered the James P. R. Lyell Lectures in Bibliography at Oxford, on "The Insular System of Scripts, c.600–c.850"; he served as President of the Bibliographical Society in 1986–87, and was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1982.

Brown's importance lies in having given Insular palaeography a coherent developmental framework. Working outward from the Lindisfarne commentary, he proposed a phased account of how the Insular grades of script — half-uncial, the various minuscules — arose and interrelated across Ireland, Northumbria, and Pictland, and he insisted that codicological evidence (parchment preparation, ruling, pricking, quire structure) be read alongside letter-forms as historical testimony. Two of his most cited papers are "The Irish Element in the Insular System of Scripts to c. AD 850" (1976), given at the International Conference on Ireland in Early Medieval Europe and published in Die Iren und Europa im früheren Mittelalter, and "Tradition, Imitation and Invention in Insular Handwriting of the Seventh and Eighth Centuries" (1983). He understood and articulated the continuity from Late Antiquity into the early Middle Ages, and sought to show that the study of manuscripts could yield a broader picture of learning in Northumbria, Ireland, and the land of the Picts in the early Christian centuries.

A Palaeographer's View: The Selected Writings of Julian Brown, edited by Janet Bately, Michelle P. Brown, and Jane Roberts with a preface by Albinia C. de la Mare, was published posthumously by Harvey Miller in 1993 (371 pp., ISBN 0-905203-20-8). Its contents include his inaugural lecture in the London chair, Latin Palaeography since Traube; "Names of Scripts: A Plea to All Medievalists"; the four-part "Aspects of Palaeography" (on the definition of the discipline, an overview, Latin and Western European vernacular, and punctuation); "Northumbria and the Book of Kells"; "The Distribution and Significance of Membrane Prepared in the Insular Manner"; and an historical introduction to the use of Classical Latin authors in the British Isles from the fifth to the eleventh century. The volume also brought previously unpublished material into print, including the 1977 Lyell Lectures and the 1978 R. W. Chambers Memorial Lecture.

The standard memoir is J. J. G. Alexander, "Thomas Julian Brown, 1923–1987", Proceedings of the British Academy 75 (1989), pp. 341ff.

Bruce-Mitford, Rupert

1914 - 1994

Rupert Bruce-Mitford was a leading British archaeologist of the twentieth century, best known for directing the excavation, study, and eventual full publication of the Sutton Hoo ship burial, the seventh-century East Anglian royal grave whose treasures transformed understanding of early Anglo-Saxon England. He served as Keeper of Medieval and Later Antiquities at the British Museum, where the Sutton Hoo finds are held, and his three-volume publication of the site (1975–1983) remains the definitive scholarly account.

Bruce-Mitford's expertise extended beyond archaeology proper into the study of early medieval manuscripts and metalwork as related bodies of evidence for Anglo-Saxon material culture and artistic practice. In his Jarrow Lecture of 1967, The Art of the Codex Amiatinus, he offered the first sustained modern art-historical treatment of the manuscript's decoration, and it remains a foundational text in the field even where its central thesis has since been contested.

That thesis concerned the celebrated Ezra miniature. Bruce-Mitford argued that the image essentially reproduced an author-portrait of Cassiodorus taken over from the lost Codex Grandior of Vivarium, with the nine volumes visible in the bookcase behind the seated figure representing Cassiodorus's own novem codices, and the scholar himself merely relabelled as Ezra when the image was copied at Wearmouth-Jarrow. The position was influential for decades and was sharply contested by Paul Meyvaert in 2005, who argued instead for a miniature newly conceived in Northumbria; the debate between the two positions remains, in current scholarship, formally unresolved. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the Ezra portrait and its contested identity.

Burresi, Mariagiulia

active late 20th-21st century

Mariagiulia Burresi is one of the leading historians of medieval art in central Italy, recognized nationally for her studies on painting, sculpture, and the artistic heritage of Pisa between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries.

Burresi earned a degree in Humanities with a specialization in Art History from the University of Pisa in 1970, graduating with highest honors. She furthered her academic training with a postgraduate course in Art History at the University of Florence between 1974 and 1975. Between 1968 and 1976, she taught at the Ministry of Education.

In 1977, she began her long career as Coordinating Director of Art History at the Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Activities, a role she held for over thirty years, until 2010. In this capacity, she served as an official at the Superintendence for Artistic and Historical Heritage of Pisa and Livorno and held the position of Director of the National Museum of San Matteo in Pisa, one of the most important museums for medieval Tuscan painting. In 2011-2012, she was again called upon as an expert consultant by the same Superintendence.

Her scholarly work has focused primarily on medieval Pisan art, with particular attention to mural painting, Gothic sculpture, religious architecture, and art collections. One of her most celebrated contributions is the monograph Santa Maria della Spina in Pisa (Silvana Editoriale, Milan, 1990), in which she addressed, with philological rigor, the issues related to the construction phases of this extraordinary Gothic chapel, combining historical-critical analysis with previously unpublished photographic documentation.

In collaboration with Antonino Caleca, an internationally renowned scholar, Burresi edited the volume Medieval Frescoes in Pisa (2003), a fundamental resource on the city's mural painting featuring the publication of numerous previously unpublished works. Together with Caleca, she also edited the catalog for the exhibition Cimabue in Pisa: 13th-Century Pisan Painting from Giunta to Giotto (2005), which brought together over a hundred works of painting, sculpture, and goldsmithing from thirteenth-century Pisa at the Museum of San Matteo.

Burresi served as editor of numerous exhibition catalogs of high scholarly merit. In 1983, she edited Andrea, Nino, and Tommaso: Pisan Sculptors (Pontedera), dedicated to the great masters of Pisan Gothic sculpture. In 1992, she edited Nel secolo di Lorenzo: restauri di opere d'arte del Quattrocento. She then worked on Il modello e la copia: dai quadroni del Duomo di Pisa tra Settecento e Ottocento (1993-1994, Museo dell'Opera del Duomo) and the essay Alla ricerca di un'identità: le pubbliche collezioni d'arte a Pisa fra Settecento e Novecento (1999), a contribution of great historiographical interest on the reception of the Pisan "primitives" in public collections.

Also noteworthy is her editing of the Inventario dei beni artistici nel Compartimento di Pisa (1860-1863) by the painter Marianini, published in 2007, a nineteenth-century inventory of extraordinary documentary value for reconstructing the original locations of many works that were later dispersed. In 2017, she edited the volume Di antichissima fondazione: il Palazzo del Governo di Pisa (Pacini Editore), confirming her commitment to promoting the city's architectural heritage.

Her contribution to the historiography of medieval Pisa is recognized as indispensable by the academic community. Laura Fenelli, in the critical review Fifteen Years of Art-Historical Studies on the Medieval Period in Pisa published in Predella, ranks Burresi among the leading figures in research on medieval art in Pisa, emphasizing how her works have "for decades shed light on key moments in the history of medieval art in the city." The CNR journal RiMe cites her in connection with studies on the Sacre Passioni and the Deposition of Christ in Pisa Cathedral, attesting to the iconographic breadth of her research.

Burresi thus embodied with rare consistency the dual vocation of the art historian in the service of both scientific research and the public preservation of heritage, leaving a lasting mark on the knowledge and safeguarding of medieval art in Pisa.

Bury, John Bagnell

Clontibret, County Monaghan, 16 October 1861 – Rome, 1 June 1927

John Bagnell Bury was born on 16 October 1861 at Clontibret, County Monaghan, the son of the Reverend Edward John Bury, an Anglican rector, and Anna Rogers. Educated at Foyle College, Londonderry, he proceeded to Trinity College Dublin, where he was elected a scholar in 1879 and graduated with honours in classics in 1882. He was elected a Fellow of Trinity in 1885, the same year he married his second cousin Jane Bury, with whom he had one son. His younger brother, Robert Gregg Bury, became a classicist and translator of Plato in his own right.

Bury's early scholarship was classical rather than medieval: as an undergraduate he edited Euripides' Hippolytus (1881), and he went on to edit Pindar's Nemean Odes (1890) and Isthmian Odes (1892), works that established him as a classical philologist of the first rank before he had turned thirty. But his ambitions widened quickly. At Trinity he held, in remarkable simultaneity, the Erasmus Smith's Professorship of Modern History from 1893 and the Regius Professorship of Greek from 1898, both until 1902, when he was appointed Regius Professor of Modern History at the University of Cambridge and a Professorial Fellow of King's College, a chair he held until his death.

Bury did more than any English-language historian of his generation to establish Byzantine history as a serious field of academic study in Britain, above all through his monumental History of the Later Roman Empire (1889, substantially revised in a two-volume edition covering 395–800) and his multi-volume History of the Eastern Roman Empire and History of the Later Roman Empire from the Death of Theodosius I to the Death of Justinian. He produced a landmark scholarly edition of Gibbon's History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1896–1900, revised 1909–1914), annotating Gibbon's text with the century of subsequent scholarship the eighteenth-century original could not have known, and he co-founded and helped launch the Cambridge Ancient History in 1919. His History of Greece to the Death of Alexander the Great (1900) remained a standard student text for decades. Later works, including A History of Freedom of Thought (1913) and The Idea of Progress (1920), display the same preoccupation with tracing the long-term movement of ideas that runs through all his historical writing.

Bury's guiding conviction, stated with characteristic bluntness in his 1902 Cambridge inaugural lecture, was that "history is not a branch of literature" but "simply a science, no less and no more" — a programmatic rejection of the belletristic tradition of historical writing in favour of rigorous, source-critical method. That method he turned directly on the Patrician dossier in The Life of St Patrick and His Place in History (1905), a critical study that subjected Muirchu's Vita, Tirechan's Collectanea, and the associated hagiographical material preserved in the Book of Armagh to the same sceptical historical analysis he applied to imperial Rome and Byzantium. On the abbreviated text of Patrick's own Confessio as it survives in the Book of Armagh, Bury held, together with John Gwynn, that the Armagh scribe himself was responsible for the omissions — a view later contested by Ludwig Bieler, who argued instead that the abbreviation was already present in Ferdomnach's exemplar.

Bury was elected a Fellow of the British Academy and received honorary doctorates from Glasgow (1901), Oxford (1902), and Aberdeen (1905). Privately an agnostic of firm conviction, he maintained throughout his career a historian's insistence on evidence over inherited authority, whether the subject was the fifth-century Roman frontier or the fifth-century Irish church. Among those who came under his influence at Cambridge was the future Byzantinist Steven Runciman. Bury died in Rome on 1 June 1927 and is buried in the city's Protestant Cemetery; his widow, Jane, saw several of his works through posthumous publication.

Bussagli, Marco

Rome, 9 December 1957 -

Marco Bussagli was born in Rome on December 9, 1957. He holds a degree in Art History and is a full professor at the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome. A fellow at the Warburg and Courtauld Institute in London in 1989, he collaborated with the Italian Encyclopedia Institute from 1985 to 2009.

His teaching profile is broad and multidisciplinary: he has taught Art History and Iconology at the Universities of Macerata, La Sapienza in Rome, and L.U.M.S.A. in Palermo. He has held the chair of Artistic Anatomy at the Academy of Fine Arts in Rome since 1997.

He has more than 200 publications to his credit, including scientific texts, encyclopedia entries, popular articles, and books, translated into English, French, German, Polish, Russian, Japanese, and Korean.

Among his most significant works is The History of Angels: A Tale of Images and Ideas, a seminal work on medieval religious iconography. In this essay, Bussagli explores archaeology, the Scriptures, and art in search of the ancestral imagery from which the first depictions of angels emerged, creatures mediating between the particular and the Absolute, who have populated religious spaces since the eras preceding the Babylonian captivity.

In the realm of large-scale publishing, he served as Scientific Director and author of I Grandi Temi della Pittura for De Agostini, a 60-volume work. He has also collaborated with RAI and contributes regularly to Il Giornale dell'Arte.

Bussagli has curated some of the most significant exhibitions of recent decades.

In 2000, with Mario D'Onofrio, he curated the exhibition Le ali di Dio (Bari and Mont-Saint-Michel).

In 2008, with Claudio Strinati, he curated Il '400 a Roma (Museo del Corso).

In 2011, with Maria Grazia Bernardini, he curated Il Rinascimento a Roma nel segno di Michelangelo e Raffaello (Fondazione Roma).

He then curated the three most recent exhibitions on Maurits Cornelis Escher in Italy, including the one in Rome at the Chiostro del Bramante and the one in Reggio Emilia with Piergiorgio Odifreddi. He published the volume Bosch. Tavole di diverse bizzarrie with Giunti Gruppo Editoriale.

In addition to his scholarly work, Bussagli is also a visual artist: as a painter, he exhibited at the 1986 Venice Biennale. He finds time to draw, paint, write essays and articles, and curate exhibitions throughout Italy.

C

Calabresi, Ilio

Montepulciano, 8 July 1931 – Sarteano, 27 February 2014

Italian medievalist, palaeographer, and philologist, and the foremost twentieth-century historian of Montepulciano and the Valdichiana. Calabresi devoted his scholarly life to the institutional and legal history of the late medieval commune, working from the documentary record of Montepulciano's own archives; his principal and most ambitious undertaking, the Glossario giuridico dei testi in volgare di Montepulciano, occupied him for decades and was left incomplete at its fourth volume. His book Montepulciano nel Trecento: contributi per la storia giuridica e istituzionale (1987) remains a standard reference for the town's fourteenth-century institutions, and he published widely on regional history, guild organization, and Tuscan folk tradition. Alongside this historical work, Calabresi was a linguist of note: he collaborated with Piero Fiorelli on the phonetic transcriptions introduced in the tenth edition (1970) of the Zingarelli dictionary, the first large-scale application of that transcription system to the Italian language.

Calabresi's command of the Montepulciano archives also made him the natural discoverer of documents bearing on the town's artistic history. In 1981 he brought to scholarly attention, in a notice in the newspaper La Nazione, a payment recorded in the Apodisse dei Priori of 1374–1375 to "magistro Jacobo de Senis pictore" for a now-lost fresco of a Maestà with saints in the Palazzo Nuovo dei Priori — the documentary anchor for Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio's activity in Montepulciano, and one of the pieces of evidence connecting the painter to the town that also preserves his celebrated Coronation of the Virgin. He died in Sarteano in 2014; his personal library and archive, recognized as an irreplaceable resource for the history of the Valdichiana, passed to the Comune di Montepulciano, and the Fondazione Ilio Calabresi was established in his honor in Acquaviva in 2010.

Caleca, Antonino

Italian scholar of art history and visual culture, particularly active in the study of medieval and Renaissance Tuscan art, image theory, and the history of Pisa. Describing himself as a researcher in art history and in the philosophy of visual language, he combines close empirical work on monuments, paintings, and objects with sustained reflection on how images shape perception and meaning.

Caleca began his professional life in heritage and museum practice, serving as conservator of artistic heritage in western Tuscany, especially in the province of Pisa. This institutional experience gave him direct and prolonged contact with collections, archives, and local cultural bodies, and it informed the curatorial and archival sensitivity visible throughout his later publications. In the early 2000s he also taught in the Department of Communication Science at the University of Pisa and later at the University of Siena, where he offered courses in art history and urban history that linked visual form to broader social and political processes.

His scholarship spans several connected fields: Pisan Romanesque and Gothic architecture; civic and religious monuments as instruments of power, identity, and urban memory; and the visual construction of the city through maps, views, and narrative imagery from the Middle Ages to the early modern period. He has also studied objects and ornament, and has addressed the philosophical and hermeneutic implications of visual representation, particularly in relation to memory, mediation, and the image of the city. In the 1990s he served as co-director of Critica d'Arte and later its new series, collaborating with Giuseppe Cuscito and Giovanni C. F. Villa; as co-director of the Storia dell'arte series (Viella, Rome), he helped shape volumes that connect Italian and international scholarship on the long duration of image-making in Italy and the Mediterranean. Alongside journal essays and conference papers, he has contributed to exhibition catalogues and collective volumes on Tuscan art, establishing a profile that moves fluently between museum practice, urban visual history, and theory of the image.

Cameron, Alan

13 March 1938 - 31 July 2017

Alan Cameron was one of the most formidable classical scholars of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, a historian and philologist whose work ranged from Hellenistic poetry to Byzantine circus factions, with the whole cultural and political world of late antiquity in between. His scholarship is especially notable for its recurring impact on the study of late antique intellectual, religious, and artistic culture, where he repeatedly used exacting philology to dismantle entrenched interpretive narratives.

He was born on 13 March 1938 and educated at St Paul's School in London between 1951 and 1956. There he and Martin West, later one of the other great classical philologists of the generation, founded an astronomical society, an early sign of the minute observational habits that would mark both men's careers. Cameron later paid explicit tribute to the formidable schoolmaster W. W. Cruickshank, a teacher he regarded as central to his formation. He went on to New College, Oxford, where he took firsts in Honour Moderations in 1959 and in Literae Humaniores in 1961. At Oxford he attended Eduard Fraenkel's celebrated and intimidating seminars, while Arnaldo Momigliano took a direct interest in his earliest papers. He later named Fraenkel, Momigliano, and Cruickshank together in the preface to his book on Callimachus. He never completed a doctorate, a fact he later recalled with some pride and amusement.

Cameron's academic career moved quickly and internationally. He began as Lecturer at Glasgow in 1961, then became Lecturer and later Reader in Latin at Bedford College, London, from 1964 to 1972. From 1972 to 1977 he held the Chair of Latin at King's College London. In 1977 he crossed to Columbia University as Charles Anthon Professor of Latin Language and Literature, remaining there until his retirement in 2008. His honors reflect the exceptional range of his authority: Fellow of the British Academy in 1975, Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1978, Fellow of the American Philosophical Society in 1992, and recipient of the British Academy's Kenyon Medal for Classical Studies and Archaeology in 2013. In 1998 he married Carla Asher, who survived him. He died in New York on 31 July 2017 at the age of seventy-nine, while being treated for complications of ALS.

The range of his scholarship was extraordinary. His essential books include Claudian: Poetry and Propaganda at the Court of Honorius (1970), which made the late antique poet a historical source rather than a literary ornament; Porphyrius the Charioteer (1973); Bread and Circuses (1974); Circus Factions: Blues and Greens at Rome and Byzantium (1976), where he demolished the long-popular idea that the circus factions were simply fronts for organised religious or political parties; Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993, with Jacqueline Long); The Greek Anthology from Meleager to Planudes (1993); Callimachus and His Critics (1995); Greek Mythography in the Roman World (2004); The Last Pagans of Rome (2011); and Wandering Poets and Other Essays on Late Greek Literature and Philosophy (2015). Across these works the method is strikingly consistent: exact philology used to overturn a widely accepted but, in his view, weakly supported orthodoxy.

His most consequential intervention for late antique cultural history was The Last Pagans of Rome, an immense and combative book in which he attacked the still-popular narrative of a heroic, self-conscious pagan senatorial resistance in the fourth-century West, culminating in the battle of the Frigidus. Cameron argued instead that no such organised final stand existed, that the paganism of the Roman aristocracy was often social, cultivated, and antiquarian rather than ideologically militant, and that the Christianisation of the elite was both earlier and less dramatically contested than standard narratives had allowed. The book is exemplary of his historical style: patient, overwhelming in documentation, and openly revisionist.

For scholars of late antique art, Cameron's importance lies partly in this broader dismantling of inherited narratives, but also in his repeated engagement with visual and material culture as evidence. His work on late antique ceremonial, elite self-representation, public spectacle, and literary-historical context bears directly on the world in which ivories, manuscripts, inscriptions, consular diptychs, and monumental imagery were produced and read. Even when writing as a philologist rather than as an art historian, he persistently altered the historical framework within which late antique art must be interpreted.

Camón Aznar, José

Zaragoza, 1898 - Madrid, 1979

Spanish art historian, critic, and writer, and one of the most prolific and wide-ranging figures in twentieth-century Spanish art history. Born in Zaragoza in 1898, he took a degree in law at the University of Zaragoza but never practised, turning instead to Philosophy and Letters, in which he took his doctorate; in 1924 he won the chair of Theory of Literature and the Arts at the University of Salamanca. He taught at Zaragoza from 1939 and in 1942 obtained the chair of Art History at the Universidad Complutense in Madrid, where he became dean of the Faculty of Philosophy and Letters. He was elected to the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando, to the Royal Academy of History (1963), and to the Royal Academy of Moral and Political Sciences.

From 1951 until his death Camón Aznar directed the Fundación Lázaro Galdiano in Madrid, and in the summer of 1954 he founded its art journal Goya, which remains one of the principal Spanish periodicals in the field. His published work ranges across the whole of Spanish art, with monographs on El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya — the last including the posthumous Goya, cinco estudios (1978) — alongside broad surveys such as Pintura medieval española. His own collection formed the nucleus of the museum opened in Zaragoza in 1979, known since 2015 as the Museo Goya – Colección Ibercaja – Museo Camón Aznar.

Within the study of the Beatus manuscripts, Camón Aznar is remembered chiefly for his reading of the cryptic date in the colophon of the Morgan Beatus (New York, Pierpont Morgan Library, MS M.644), which he argued yielded a date of 958. This is the latest of the several datings that the ambiguous arithmetical formula has generated, standing against both the literal reading of Spanish Era 964 (AD 926) and the stylistic dating of about 940–945 advanced by John Williams and now generally preferred. His proposal is chiefly valuable as a demonstration of how unstable the cryptogram is as evidence for the manuscript's date.

Campbell, Caroline

active 21st century

Caroline Campbell is a British art historian, curator, and museum director whose career has moved across three of the United Kingdom's leading collections of European art. Trained in art history at the Courtauld Institute of Art, she built her early career as a curator of Italian and Spanish paintings before 1500 at the National Gallery, London, where she organised exhibitions on subjects including Andrea Mantegna and the visual culture of Renaissance marriage and the domestic interior, before being appointed the Gallery's Director of Collections and Research.

In 2017 Campbell became Director of the Courtauld Gallery, overseeing its reopening after a major renovation, and in 2023 she moved to Oxford as Director of the Ashmolean Museum. Alongside her curatorial and administrative career she has continued to publish on early Italian Renaissance painting; she co-edited, with Joanna Cannon and Stephan Wolohojian, the catalogue accompanying Siena: The Rise of Painting, 1300–1350, the exhibition shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the National Gallery, London, in 2024–25, that reasserted the centrality of Sienese painting to the origins of the Italian Renaissance tradition.

Cannon, Joanna

active late 20th-21st century

Joanna Cannon is a British art historian and professor whose work has profoundly shaped the study of late medieval Italian art, especially the painting and architecture of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italy. She has been a central figure at the Courtauld Institute of Art in London for decades, influencing several generations of scholars working on communal Italy, mendicant orders, and the intersection of art, spirituality and technical analysis.

Joanna Cannon studied both as an undergraduate and a postgraduate at the Courtauld Institute of Art, completing her PhD there in 1980. She began teaching at the Courtauld in 1977, an unusually early appointment that underlines how quickly she established herself as a specialist, and she has remained there throughout her career. In 2014 she was appointed Professor in the History of Art, consolidating her long-standing role in the institution's teaching and research culture. Within the Courtauld she served as Head of the Classical, Byzantine and Medieval Section from 2004 to 2008 and later as Head of Examinations between 2012 and 2014, roles that reflect her leadership in curriculum and institutional governance.

Her influence extends beyond formal titles. She has been a convenor of the seminar group "Giotto's Circle," an important forum for medieval art historians, and has been heavily involved in organizing research events, including acting as local organizer of the annual "ICMA at The Courtauld" lecture and co-organizing workshops such as "Art, Architecture and the Indulgence." A festschrift, "Late Medieval Italian Art and Its Contexts: Essays in Honour of Professor Joanna Cannon," attests to the depth of her impact on her students and colleagues, many of whom contributed essays reflecting the breadth of topics she has helped open up in early Italian art history.

Cannon's research focuses on the art and architecture of Italy in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, with a strong emphasis on the ways visual evidence can be used as a historical source. She is particularly interested in how historical circumstances - political, social, religious - shape the formal development of art, and conversely how artistic forms can illuminate civic religion and lay spirituality in the Italy of the communes. Another hallmark of her work is the integration of technical art history into interpretive narratives: she has been concerned with how detailed knowledge of materials, techniques and physical condition can inform questions of dating, authorship and function.

This methodological orientation has led her to collaborate closely with conservators and scientists. Together with Aviva Burnstock and Caroline Campbell she directed an Andrew W. Mellon Foundation-funded project to create a research website on the Master of the Fogg Pieta/Maestro di Figline, focusing on technical aspects of works attributed to this problematic figure across international collections. She is also a trustee of the Caroline Villers Research Fellowship, which specifically promotes research in technical art history, reinforcing her commitment to bridging connoisseurship, historical inquiry and scientific investigation.

Among Cannon's most important publications is the monograph Religious Poverty, Visual Riches, published in 2013, which examines how richly endowed visual programmes coexisted with and articulated ideals of religious poverty in late medieval Italy. This work has been described as seminal in showing how images and architectural settings mediated civic religion and religious experience, especially among the laity, emphasizing the role of visual culture in communal devotion. Her overall output spans more than fifty publications over roughly six decades, consistently returning to the intersection of art and spirituality.

More recently, she has been closely associated with the research and exhibition project Siena: The Rise of Painting, 1300-1350, undertaken with Caroline Campbell and Stephan Wolohojian for the National Gallery, London. This project, culminating in a 2024-2025 catalog and exhibition, explores a crucial turning point in Italian art through masterpieces by Duccio, Simone Martini, the Lorenzetti brothers and their contemporaries, situating Sienese painting within broader artistic and devotional contexts. Reviews highlight its "important new scholarship," suggesting that Cannon's long engagement with Sienese art has fed directly into a synthetic reappraisal accessible to both specialists and a wider public.

Cannon's teaching has been central to her reputation. The essays gathered in Late Medieval Italian Art and Its Contexts: Essays in Honour of Professor Joanna Cannon are all written by scholars who completed their doctorates under her supervision, indicating the scale of her influence as a doctoral supervisor. The volume's contributions span panel and wall painting, architecture, sculpture, metalwork, manuscripts and gilded glass across the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, reflecting the range of media and topics she encourages her students to explore. Commentators note that her scholarship and teaching together have "shaped the historical study of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italian art," and the festschrift explicitly positions itself as a response to her "extraordinary contribution" to early Italian art studies.

Beyond her immediate students, Cannon has been active in broader scholarly networks. She has been closely associated with initiatives in medieval and Byzantine studies, and recent notices, such as a 2026 announcement by the Society for the Promotion of Byzantine Studies on the death of her husband, the art historian John Lowden, underline her position within an international community of medievalists. Through seminars, public lectures, exhibition collaborations and research networks, she has helped keep Trecento studies at the forefront of methodological innovation and interdisciplinary dialogue.

Cardwell, Emily

active 21st century

Emily Cardwell is a scholar of early medieval Northumbrian intellectual and manuscript culture whose recent work has extended the roster of identifiable scribes and exegetes associated with the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow, the community that produced the Codex Amiatinus. Her research is characteristic of a current strand of scholarship that reopens apparently settled questions about the scale and organization of the Wearmouth-Jarrow scriptorium through fresh palaeographic and codicological analysis.

In her 2025 article "Biblical Exegesis at Wearmouth-Jarrow before Bede? The Hereford Commentary on Matthew," published in Early Medieval Europe, Cardwell examines a fragmentary commentary and its palaeographic relationship to the Amiatinus and its sister pandects. She argues that, beyond the seven scribal hands conventionally identified in the Amiatinus itself, an eighth and a ninth hand can be distinguished among the surviving leaves of the companion Bibles, with a possible tenth in the related Hereford fragment. The finding reinforces the picture of Wearmouth-Jarrow as a house that trained a substantial cohort of scribes to a common, exacting standard, rather than relying on one or two exceptional calligraphers. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller context.

Carli, Enzo

Pisa, August 20, 1910 - Siena, September 26, 1999

Enzo Carli was one of the leading Italian art historians of the twentieth century, an authority on the study of medieval Sienese and Pisan art, as well as a museum director, curator, and extraordinarily prolific writer.

He graduated from the University of Pisa, where he was first a student of Mario Salmi, one of the founders of modern Italian medieval art history, and later of Matteo Marangoni. His thesis was dedicated to the Sienese sculptor Tino di Camaino (1285-1337), a choice that perfectly foreshadowed the two geographical and stylistic poles around which his entire research would revolve: Pisa and Siena, and the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Alongside his university studies, he cultivated music, studying piano and composition, and poetry with equal passion, two dimensions that accompanied his intellectual life until the end.

From 1933, he taught art history in Florentine high schools, gaining experience through direct contact with Tuscany's artistic heritage. In 1937, he was appointed Superintendent in L'Aquila, and in 1939 he was transferred to Siena, the city that became his permanent home and the center of his work for over sixty years. In Siena, he directed the Pinacoteca Nazionale until 1952 and the Museo dell'Opera Metropolitana del Duomo until 1973, two institutions that housed the masterpieces of medieval Sienese painting, from Duccio to Simone Martini, and from Pietro to Ambrogio Lorenzetti. That long tenure at the helm of Siena's museums allowed him to develop a direct, daily, and inexhaustible knowledge of the original works, which translated into a level of meticulousness in attribution and description that was rare indeed.

In 1942, he obtained a teaching qualification in Medieval and Modern Art History, which he exercised at the Faculty of Letters of the University of Pisa. In 1962, he won a university competition and was appointed to the Faculty of Letters of the University of Genoa; subsequently, he taught Art History at the University of Siena, thus combining his museum work with his academic career.

His approach to the study of artistic phenomena was always rooted in a historicism of Crocean descent: rigorous formal analysis, historical contextualization, and attention to the expressive quality of the work, without veering into formalism or sociological interpretations.

His bibliographic output was vast, over 500 titles, including monographs, specialized essays, catalogs, and popular texts. His fundamental contributions primarily concern Sienese art: I capolavori dell'arte senese (Milan, 1946), La pittura senese (Milan, 1955), and numerous monographs on individual masters, including Duccio, Simone Martini, the Lorenzetti, Giovanni di Paolo, and Sassetta. On the Pisan front, he dealt with equal depth with Romanesque sculpture, the Camposanto Monumentale, and Duecento painting. In collaboration with Gian Alberto Dell'Acqua, he edited Storia dell'arte ad uso dei licei, a textbook published in multiple volumes and editions between 1952 and 1986, which educated generations of Italian students.

In 1980, he received the President of the Republic Award as an emeritus member of the Accademia dei Lincei. In 1995, the Accademia dei Lincei awarded him the Feltrinelli Prize for Art and Poetry Criticism, one of the most prestigious honors in Italian culture, crowning a career of exceptional consistency and breadth. He died in Siena on September 26, 1999, and is buried in the Monumental Cemetery of Pisa. In his memory, his children established the Enzo Carli Fund at the University of Siena Library, which houses his books, papers, and scholarly correspondence.

Carr, Annemarie Weyl

active late 20th–21st century

Annemarie Weyl Carr, University Distinguished Professor of Art History Emerita at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Texas, has worked on the history of Middle Byzantine art, especially manuscripts; on art and issues of cultural interchange in the eastern Mediterranean Levant in the era of the Crusades, above all on the island of Cyprus; and on women artists in the Middle Ages. Her career, spanning more than five decades, constitutes perhaps the single most sustained and wide-ranging body of English-language scholarship on Byzantine Cypriot art produced in the modern era.

Carr received her BA from Swarthmore College and her MA and PhD from the University of Michigan. Her doctoral thesis, "The Rockefeller McCormick New Testament: Studies Toward the Reattribution of Chicago, University Library, MS. 965" (1973), systematically revisited the attribution of a richly decorated 12th-century Byzantine Gospel manuscript through detailed art-historical analysis of its miniatures, engaging codicology, iconographic analysis, stylistic comparison across the corpus of Middle Byzantine illumination, and provenance history. It was a doctoral thesis that announced, from the first page, a scholar committed to working at the intersection of object analysis and cultural history. She served on the SMU faculty from 1972 to 2008, becoming University Distinguished Professor Emerita, and also taught as visiting professor at the universities of Chicago, Michigan, Pittsburgh, and Delaware, and as Visiting Professor at Dumbarton Oaks (autumn 2009) and Yale (autumn 2008). She is a member of the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton. In 2006 she received the Lifetime Achievement Award for Teaching from the College Art Association of America.

What distinguishes Carr's approach throughout her career is a consistent preoccupation with the reception of images — not merely what Byzantine objects looked like or how they were made, but what they did: how they were used devotionally, how they moved across cultural boundaries, what happened to them when they passed from a Greek Orthodox community into a Crusader one, and what their afterlives — their continued veneration, their theft, their rescue, their return — reveal about the communities that made and treasured them. Her work focuses on the object but considers the audience, looks at the copy for retention or rejection of the original form and meaning, and always seeks to understand the relationship between intent and perception, examining the elusive nature of "centre" and "periphery" across manuscript production, icons, and the dissemination of style and meaning.

Her first book, developed from doctoral research and subsequent work on the corpus of Middle Byzantine manuscripts, remains indispensable for the study of provincial illumination during the Komnenian period. Byzantine Illumination, 1150–1250: The Study of a Provincial Tradition (University of Chicago Press, 1987) established Carr as the leading Anglophone authority on manuscript production in the Middle Byzantine provinces — the same cultural world and historical moment as the Enkleistra frescoes of 1183 and the Lagoudera cycle of 1192. The book's central argument — that provincial manuscript illumination develops distinctive local characteristics that cannot be reduced to dependence on Constantinopolitan models — challenged a long-standing tendency to treat metropolitan production as normative and provincial work as merely derivative.

The most dramatically narrative of Carr's scholarly engagements concerned the 13th-century frescoes of the church at Lysi, Cyprus, looted after the 1974 Turkish invasion and subsequently acquired by the Menil Foundation in Houston to prevent their further dispersal on the international art market. In 1991 she published A Masterpiece of Byzantine Art Recovered: The Thirteenth-Century Murals of Lysi, Cyprus (with Laurence J. Morrocco; University of Texas Press) in association with the Menil Foundation, which had built a special Byzantine Fresco Chapel in Houston to house the rescued frescoes under a twenty-year loan agreement with the Church of Cyprus. When the loan period expired, the frescoes were returned to Cyprus — an act of restitution Carr had consistently advocated. She wrote the essay "The Byzantine Fresco Chapel: Lysi in the Art of Cyprus" for Art and Activism: Projects of John and Dominique de Menil (Menil Collection / Yale University Press, 2010), pp. 158–67, and edited and contributed "How Icons Look" to Imprinting the Divine: Byzantine and Russian Icons from the Menil Collection (Menil Foundation / Yale University Press, 2011), pp. 18–33.

Cyprus and the Devotional Arts of Byzantium in the Era of the Crusades (Ashgate, 2005) collects Carr's major articles on Cypriot Byzantine art across several decades, including "Byzantines and Italians on Cyprus: Images from Art," Dumbarton Oaks Papers 49 (1995): 339–57. This Variorum volume represents the most comprehensive assembly of her arguments about Cyprus as a site of cross-cultural artistic exchange — a place where Greek Orthodox, Latin Catholic, and Armenian Christian traditions intersected under Crusader and Lusignan rule, producing hybrid objects and practices that neither tradition alone could have generated. Her most recent edited book, Famagusta: Art and Architecture (Brepols, 2014), extended this engagement into the architectural and artistic culture of the greatest Lusignan-era city.

The work that most directly places Carr at the intersection of every biographical thread in this series is her co-editorship, with Andréas Nicolaïdès, of Asinou Across Time: Studies in the Architecture and Murals of the Panagia Phorbiotissa, Cyprus (Dumbarton Oaks / Harvard University Press, 2012), to which she contributed three chapters and an appendix. The volume also contains Ioanna Kakoulli, Christian Fischer, and Jeffrey Mazurek's technical examination of the Asinou murals. Nicolaïdès is the author of the foundational 1996 Dumbarton Oaks Papers study of Lagoudera. The Asinou volume thus assembles, within a single publication, virtually the entire scholarly network traced through this biographical series — art historians, conservation scientists, iconographers, and materials analysts, united by a common devotion to a single mountain church in the Troodos range.

Carr has been editor of the journal Gesta, President of the International Center of Medieval Art, and a long-standing trustee of the Cyprus American Archaeological Research Institute in Nicosia — the same institution of which Ioanna Kakoulli was a Board member from 2011. Carr is the natural closing figure for this biographical constellation. Her work encompasses every dimension of the world it has traced: the illuminated Byzantine manuscript that was her doctoral object; the Komnenian wall paintings of Cyprus whose context she has spent a career elucidating; the Crusader political framework within which those paintings were commissioned; the post-1974 cultural heritage crisis whose victims she has documented and mourned; and the scholarly community — Hawkins, Mango, Nicolaïdès, Kakoulli, Fischer, Winfield — whose work on the Troodos churches she has sustained, supported, and co-edited across five decades. No single scholar has done more to make the painted world of medieval Cyprus legible to the international scholarly community.

Carver, Martin

b. 8 July 1941

Martin Oswald Hugh Carver, FSA, Hon FSA Scot, FBA — who publishes as M.O.H. Carver — was born on 8 July 1941 to Colonel John Hobart Carver and Jocelyn Louisa Grace Carver (nee Tweedie), and is the grandson of the Olympic rower Oswald Carver. He was educated at Ladycross School, Seaford, and Wellington College, Berkshire.

Carver's early career was in the Army rather than academia. After Sandhurst he was commissioned into the Royal Tank Regiment in July 1961, was made lieutenant in 1963 and captain in 1967, and by 1969 was Adjutant of the 4th Royal Tank Regiment. He left the Army in the rank of captain on 1 July 1972, counting fifteen years as an army officer. He characteristically notes that he holds no degree in archaeology — his formal training in the discipline was at Shrivenham and Durham.

He practised as a freelance archaeologist from 1973 to 1986, founding the Birmingham University Field Archaeology Unit (BUFAU, later Birmingham Archaeology) to undertake contract work, and was the first secretary of the Institute of Field Archaeologists. In 1992 he created Field Archaeology Specialists Ltd (FAS, now FAS Heritage), which he chairs. This period produced his urban-archaeology work, summarised in Underneath English Towns (1987) and Arguments in Stone (1993). Throughout, he championed evaluation and project design as the key elements of a "value-led" archaeology — a methodological position later developed in Archaeological Investigation (2009) and Making Archaeology Happen: Design versus Dogma (2011).

Carver is best known for directing a new campaign of research at Sutton Hoo from 1983, excavating over a hectare between 1983 and 1993 using a then-innovative approach to evaluation, project design, and integrated fieldwork. The project produced the edited volume The Age of Sutton Hoo (1992), the popular Sutton Hoo: Burial Ground of Kings? (1998), the full report Sutton Hoo: A Seventh-Century Princely Burial Ground and Its Context (British Museum Press, 2005), and later The Sutton Hoo Story: Encounters with Early England (Boydell, 2017). From 1986 he presented four episodes of BBC2's Chronicle, and he is now a director of The Sutton Hoo Ship's Company, which is building a full-size seaworthy replica of the Mound 1 ship.

Carver was Professor of Archaeology at the University of York from 1986, serving as Head of Department from 1986 to 1996, and has been Emeritus since 2008. He introduced courses in World Archaeology and Field Archaeology and has served on UK, Irish, Danish, and European research councils, including the AHRC, the Irish Research Council, Denmark, Sweden, and ERC Panel H6 (2009-2015). He edited Antiquity from 2002 to 2012, personally handling some 800 articles.

From 1994 to 2007 he led excavations at Portmahomack on Tarbat Ness, Easter Ross, centred on a sixth- to tenth-century Pictish settlement and monastery, co-directed with Justin Garner-Lahire and Cecily Spall. As at Sutton Hoo, the project was framed as a study of shifting ideology and allegiance, feeding into the edited volume The Cross Goes North: Processes of Conversion in Northern Europe, AD 300-1300 (Boydell, 2003). It resulted in Portmahomack: Monastery of the Picts (Edinburgh University Press, 2008; 2nd ed. 2016) and the full monograph, co-authored with Garner-Lahire and Spall, Portmahomack on Tarbat Ness: Changing Ideologies in North-east Scotland, Sixth to Sixteenth Century AD (Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, 2016), which is available open-access.

Since 2008 Carver has worked as a full-time writer, speaker, and broadcaster. In 2014 he launched Sicily in Transition (SICTRANSIT, ERC 693600) with Alessandra Molinari (Roma Tor Vergata) and Girolamo Fiorentino (Lecce), examining the experience of farmers and merchants under successive Byzantine, Islamic, and Norman regimes. His career synthesis, Formative Britain: An Archaeology of Britain, Fifth to Eleventh Century AD (Routledge, 2019, xxix + 735 pp.), is organised around three "Formative" phases (fifth-seventh, seventh-ninth, and ninth-eleventh centuries) and four themes: personhood; settlement and economy; cemeteries as ritual places; and monumentality, sculpture, churches, and illuminated books.

Carver was elected FSA on 8 January 1981, was made Hon FSA Scot on St Andrew's Day 2011, and became FBA on 23 July 2020. He lives at Ellerton, East Yorkshire, with the archaeologist, translator, and editor Madeleine Hummler.

Carver's excavated monastery at Portmahomack is the archaeological foundation of Victoria Whitworth's 2025 hypothesis, set out in The Book of Kells: Unlocking the Enigma (Head of Zeus, October 2025). Whitworth argues that Portmahomack is the most likely place of manufacture of the Book of Kells, citing the site's vellum production, elaborate inscribed carving matching the manuscript, and a fine sculptor's chisel found in the vellum workshop, against the "plainness and legibility" of Iona's lettering.

Casazza, Ornella

Rezzoaglio (Genoa), 1943 – Florence, March 2020

Ornella Casazza was one of the most celebrated and respected Italian restorers of the twentieth century, widely recognized as a leading authority in the conservation of pictorial heritage. Although born in Rezzoaglio in Liguria in 1943, she spent almost her entire professional life in Florence, where she developed the career that would place her at the center of postwar restoration culture in Italy and abroad.

Her formation unfolded in a decisive historical context. Living in Florence at the time of the catastrophic flood of 4 November 1966, she experienced directly the emergency that transformed the discipline of conservation and brought her into contact with Umberto Baldini and the restoration environment that later shaped the Opificio delle Pietre Dure's post-flood methodologies. After a long workshop apprenticeship, she entered the Opificio officially in 1974, following a national competitive examination.

The range and quality of her interventions are exceptional. Her work on Cimabue's Crucifix in Santa Croce became a key site for the refinement of lacuna reintegration methods, while the restoration of Botticelli's Primavera was presented as a methodological landmark in the 1982 exhibition Method and Science. The most internationally celebrated project of her career, however, was the direction of the restoration of the Brancacci Chapel frescoes by Masaccio, Masolino, and Filippino Lippi in Santa Maria del Carmine, a campaign considered exemplary for both technical innovation and historical results. She also directed the restoration of Masaccio's San Giovenale Triptych, a fundamental work for early fifteenth-century Florentine painting.

Casazza's contribution was as theoretical as it was practical. Through sustained work on flood-damaged paintings and on major medieval and Renaissance panels, she helped define and stabilize the methods of chromatic selection and chromatic abstraction, approaches that made visual reintegration possible without falsifying the original. In this sense, her work belongs to the broader methodological transformation associated with the Florentine school of restoration in the second half of the twentieth century. Antonio Paolucci would later remember her as a restorer of exceptional standing with international recognition.

After advancing through further competitive appointments, Casazza also held major institutional roles, including leadership of advanced-technology research for conservation in Florence and direction of the Museum of Silver and Porcelain at Palazzo Pitti. She curated projects that connected restoration, decorative arts, and modern production, and remained active as a teacher and author in Italy and abroad, with publications on conservation, iconography, and painting techniques that remain widely cited. She died in Florence in March 2020. The 2021 volume L'eredità culturale di Ornella Casazza, edited by Lura Felici, stands as the principal collective tribute to her life and legacy.

Cassidy, Brendan

active late 20th–21st century

Brendan Cassidy is an Irish-born art historian whose career moved from Trecento Florentine sculpture to Anglo-Saxon stone crosses to the Grand Tour, three fields that share little beyond the fact that he wrote a standard reference work in each of them. Before any of that he taught chemistry in Ghana, West Africa — an interlude seldom omitted from accounts of his career, since it sits so oddly beside the medievalism and eighteenth-century connoisseurship that followed.
