He returned to university study to take an M.A. in art history at Edinburgh and a Ph.D. at Cambridge, where his dissertation was devoted to Andrea Orcagna's tabernacle at Orsanmichele. That research, expanded and reworked, became "Orcagna's Tabernacle in Florence: Design and Function," Zeitschrift für Kunstgeschichte 55 (1992), 180–211 — still, alongside the Fabbri–Rutenburg article of a decade earlier, one of the two studies named as essential in the modern literature on the monument.

Cassidy was a Research Associate at the Warburg Institute, University of London, from 1985 to 1988, and then Director of the Index of Christian Art at Princeton University from 1988 to 1995 — a post that put him at the centre of Anglo-American iconographic scholarship rather than at its Italian Trecento margin. In that capacity he edited The Ruthwell Cross: Papers from the Colloquium Sponsored by the Index of Christian Art, Princeton University, 8 December 1989 (Princeton: Index of Christian Art, Department of Art and Archaeology, Princeton University, 1992), the volume that remains a standard point of reference on the Northumbrian high cross and its inscriptions, and a second colloquium volume on iconographic method, Iconography at the Crossroads (1993).

In 1996 he joined the University of St Andrews, where he was Professor of Art History until his retirement in 2018, teaching late-medieval and early Renaissance Italian art alongside a second, later-acquired specialism in the cultural relations between Italy and Britain in the eighteenth century. The Trecento work culminated in Politics, Civic Ideals and Sculpture in Italy, c. 1240–1400 (Turnhout: Harvey Miller/Brepols, 2007), a wide-ranging study of Italian public sculpture — from the Holy Roman Empire and the Angevin kingdom of Sicily to the central and north Italian communes — read as an instrument of civic and political self-presentation, the same interpretative question, applied more broadly, that had organised his reading of the Orsanmichele tabernacle two decades before.

The Grand Tour side of his output is anchored by The Life & Letters of Gavin Hamilton (1723–1798): Artist & Art Dealer in Eighteenth-Century Rome (London: Harvey Miller, 2012), a two-volume edition, in 855 pages, of an introductory biographical essay and a corpus of more than three hundred annotated letters by and to the Scottish painter, antiquarian and dealer who supplied British collectors from Rome for half a century. A shorter synthesis of the same territory, "The Lure of 'Magick Land': British Artists and Italy in the Eighteenth Century," appeared as a chapter in A Companion to Nineteenth-Century Art (Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell, 2016).

Castaldi, Lucia

active late 20th-21st century

Lucia Castaldi is an Italian philologist specializing in medieval Latin literature and the transmission of early medieval texts, associated with the University of Cagliari and with the broader Italian tradition of filologia mediolatina — the rigorous, manuscript-based study of Latin textual transmission across the Middle Ages. Her work addresses the hagiographic and exegetical traditions of the early medieval West, with particular attention to questions of authorship, attribution, and the material history of the manuscripts that preserve these texts.

Castaldi was a co-editor, with Luigi G. G. Ricci and Rosanna Minello, of La Bibbia Amiatina: Riproduzione integrale su CD-ROM del manoscritto Firenze, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Amiatino 1 (Florence, 2000), the complete digital facsimile of the Codex Amiatinus that made the manuscript's every page available for close study without recourse to the fragile original. The facsimile has been an important research tool, not least for the study of the disordered opening quire and the offsets — the ghostly impressions left by painted surfaces on facing leaves — that bear on the reconstruction of the quire's original order. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion.

Castelfranchi Vegas, Liana

Milan, 1924 - 2013

Liana Castelfranchi, who published chiefly as Liana Castelfranchi Vegas, was an Italian art historian and for over a decade holder of the chair of medieval art history at the Università degli Studi di Milano, where her wide-ranging synthetic studies of medieval and early Renaissance art - from Ottonian goldsmiths' work and manuscript illumination to Trecento and Quattrocento panel painting - reached a broad Italian readership through the Milanese publisher Jaca Book over more than three decades.

Born in Milan in 1924, she studied at the Università degli Studi di Milano and took her degree under Maria Luisa Gengaro, the medievalist and Byzantinist who helped shape the Milanese school of medieval art history in the mid-twentieth century. She began her teaching career at the Università di Verona, where she taught medieval art history, before returning to Milan, where from 1986 she held the chair of medieval art history at the Università statale for twelve years.

Her research interests were unusually broad within the medieval field. Much of her early work concerned Trecento and Quattrocento painting and, in particular, the artistic exchange between Italy and the lands north of the Alps, as well as the grafting of Tuscan pictorial culture onto Trecento Lombardy; in 1966 Roberto Longhi invited her to contribute the volume Il gotico internazionale in Italia to his series La pittura italiana, an early mark of scholarly recognition. She wrote extensively on manuscript illumination of the Visconti period and on Michelino da Besozzo, and produced the study of Italo-Flemish exchange Italia e Fiandra nella pittura del Quattrocento (1983).

In her later career she turned increasingly to the early Middle Ages and to the so-called minor arts - goldsmiths' work, ivory carving, enamelling and manuscript painting - publishing the synthesis L'arte ottoniana intorno al Mille (Milan: Jaca Book, 2002), a survey of Ottonian art around the year 1000 that treats the extraordinary vitality of these luxury media as the era's supreme artistic achievement and situates the Echternach scriptorium's golden Gospels, including the Codex Aureus of Echternach, within the wider panorama of Reichenau, Trier, Cologne and the Lombard centres; and Lo splendore nascosto del Medioevo: arti minori (2005), which extended the same argument across the medieval centuries. Her other books include L'arte del Medioevo (1994) and L'arte medievale in Europa, both widely used as general surveys in Italian university teaching.

Liana Castelfranchi Vegas died in 2013, leaving a body of synthetic scholarship, largely published through Jaca Book, that remains a standard Italian-language point of reference for medieval and early Renaissance art across a wider chronological and geographical range than most of her specialist contemporaries attempted.

Castelnuovo, Enrico

Rome, 26 May 1929 - Turin, 15 June 2014

Enrico Castelnuovo (1929-2014)

Enrico Castelnuovo was one of the most influential Italian art historians of the twentieth century and, arguably, the scholar who did most to renew the study of medieval art in Italy after the Longhian generation. Trained as a connoisseur under Roberto Longhi, he moved decisively beyond connoisseurship toward a storia sociale dell'arte - a social history of art nourished by the Annales school, by economic and institutional history, and by Pierre Bourdieu's sociology of the artistic field. His enduring contribution is a way of asking questions: about artistic geography, about the status and working conditions of the medieval artist, and about the frontier zones where distinct figurative cultures collide.

Note on homonyms. He is not to be confused with Enrico Castelnuovo (1839-1915), the Venetian novelist (I Moncalvo), nor with Guido Castelnuovo (1865-1952), the mathematician. His own son, Guido Castelnuovo, is a historian of the late medieval period at the Universite d'Avignon.

Early life and formation

Castelnuovo was born in Rome on 26 May 1929. His formative academic years were spent in Turin, where he graduated in Lettere in 1951 with a thesis on Andrea Pisano, supervised by Anna Maria Brizio (then holder of the chair of medieval and modern art history) with Aldo Bertini as co-supervisor. That first subject is worth noting: he entered the discipline through Trecento sculpture.

In 1954 he took his perfezionamento at Florence under Roberto Longhi, with a thesis on the Sienese painter Matteo Giovannetti and his activity at the papal court of Avignon. In the same year Brizio appointed him assistente volontario at Turin. The Longhian training in the discipline of the eye never left him, but he came to treat it as a starting point rather than a destination.

The Avignon thesis became the book that made his name - Un pittore italiano alla corte di Avignone: Matteo Giovannetti e la cultura in Provenza nel sec. XIV - published in the early 1960s and reissued in a substantially expanded edition in 1991. It already contains the seed of his whole method: an Italian painter at a transalpine court, working at the meeting point of two cultures, studied as much through the mechanisms of patronage and mobility as through style.

Academic career

  • Lausanne, 1964-1983 (academic years 1964-65 to 1982-83): his longest tenure, and the base from which he built a European rather than merely Italian network. His Lausanne pupils became a school in their own right.
  • Geneva, 1970-1971.
  • Turin, from 1979 to 1982-83: he returned to hold the chair of medieval and modern art history for roughly four years.
  • Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa, from 1983 (academic year 1983-84) until his retirement at the statutory age limit in 2004, as professor of medieval art history. He was subsequently made professor emeritus.
  • Ecole Normale Superieure, Paris, 1994: invited to teach on the chaire Condorcet.

He sat on the editorial board of Paragone - the Longhi journal - and contributed to a wide range of Italian and international periodicals.

Method: artistic geography and the social history of art

Centro e periferia (1979)

Castelnuovo's single most consequential text is the long essay written jointly with the historian Carlo Ginzburg, Centro e periferia, published in Giovanni Previtali's volume of the Einaudi Storia dell'arte italiana (Materiali e problemi. Questioni e metodi, Parte I, vol. 1, Turin 1979, pp. 285-352).

The essay dismantles the assumption - inherited from Vasari onward - that Italian art history is the story of a few dominant centres from which quality radiates outward, with everything else understood as delay, provincialism, or decline. Castelnuovo and Ginzburg reframe the centre/periphery relation as a structure of symbolic domination: peripheries are not merely belated, they resist, select, reinterpret, and sometimes generate. Artistic geography becomes a historical problem rather than a map of rankings.

Its diffusion marks its importance: French translation in Actes de la recherche en sciences sociales 40 (1981) as Domination symbolique et geographie artistique dans l'histoire de l'art italien; German as Zentrum und Peripherie (Berlin 1987); English as Symbolic Domination and Artistic Geography in Italian Art History, Art in Translation 2 (2009). Officina Libraria reissued it as a standalone volume in 2019, forty years on.

Related methodological work

  • Arte delle citta, arte delle corti tra XII e XIV secolo, in Federico Zeri (ed.), Storia dell'arte italiana (Einaudi, 1983), pp. 167-227 - the civic workshop and the courtly commission as two distinct systems of production.
  • Arte, industria, rivoluzioni: temi di storia sociale dell'arte (Einaudi) - extending the social history of art into the modern era and industrial design.
  • Sustained work on the status of the medieval artist, the portrait and its social function, and on frontier cultures and artistic geography.

Medieval subjects

  • Stained glass: Vetrate medievali. Officine, tecniche, maestri (1994) - a study of workshops, techniques, and masters that treats glass as a craft system rather than a minor art.
  • Alpine figurative culture: Il Gotico nelle Alpi 1350-1450, the major Trento exhibition of 2002 (with Francesca de Gramatica), the fullest application of his centre/periphery thinking to a real territory. Earlier, Giacomo Jaquerio e il Gotico internazionale (Turin, Palazzo Madama, 1979, with Giovanni Romano).
  • The medieval artist: Artifex bonus. Il mondo dell'artista medievale (2004), a collective portrait of the artist as craftsman, contractor, and social actor.
  • Syntheses: with Giuseppe Sergi he directed the four volumes of Arti e storia nel Medioevo (Einaudi, 2002-2004), an attempt to integrate art history with general medieval history rather than run them in parallel.
  • Historiography: with Alessio Monciatti, Medioevo/Medioevi. Un secolo di esposizioni d'arte medievale (2008) - how the Middle Ages have been constructed through exhibitions.

He also directed major reference works: the Il Duecento e il Trecento (1986) and Ottocento (1990) volumes of Electa's La Pittura in Italia; the Storia del disegno industriale (1989-1991); and the Larousse-Einaudi Dizionario della pittura e dei pittori (1989-1994).

The Camposanto of Pisa

With Paola Barocchi he promoted the programme of study and restoration of the Camposanto Monumentale of Pisa, whose frescoes had been catastrophically damaged in 1944. The resulting volume, Il Camposanto di Pisa, was edited in collaboration with Clara Baracchini (1996). It is a model of the kind of project he favoured: technical, collaborative, and institutionally grounded.

Why he matters for Trecento sculpture

For work on Giovanni di Balduccio, Castelnuovo is not a source of attributions but of framing. A Pisan sculptor formed in the orbit of Giovanni Pisano and Tino di Camaino, who transplants a Tuscan sepulchral language to Visconti Milan, is precisely the phenomenon Centro e periferia was written to explain - not "Tuscan quality exported to a lesser northern centre," but a negotiated encounter in which Lombardy selects, adapts, and redirects what it receives. Likewise, Arte delle citta, arte delle corti supplies the distinction between communal and signorial patronage that the Arca di San Pietro Martire at Sant'Eustorgio sits astride. And his beginnings with a thesis on Andrea Pisano place him, at the outset, in exactly the sculptural milieu at issue.

Honours and legacy

  • Premio Feltrinelli for art criticism, Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei, 1991, jointly with Paola Barocchi.
  • Corresponding member of the Accademia dei Lincei; member of the Accademia delle Scienze di Torino, the Accademia di San Luca, and the Accademia del Disegno of Florence.

He died in Turin on 15 June 2014. In 2016 his son Guido donated his archive, photographic collection (fototeca), and personal library to the University of Turin, where they are held in the Archivio Storico. A commemorative conference held at Lausanne on 13 May 2015 produced the volume Per Enrico Castelnuovo. Da Losanna, le vie della storia dell'arte (Viella), with contributions from his Lausanne, Turin, and Pisa pupils.

Cavalcaselle, Giovanni Battista

Legnago, 22 January 1819 - Rome, 31 October 1897

Giovanni Battista Cavalcaselle was an Italian writer, critic, and art historian, born at Legnago on 22 January 1819 and dead in Rome on 31 October 1897, who is widely regarded as one of the founders of modern Italian art history and art criticism. He is especially famous for his long collaboration with Joseph Archer Crowe, with whom he produced major histories of Italian and Flemish painting that remained influential well into the twentieth century.

Cavalcaselle studied at the Accademia di Belle Arti in Venice, but from an early stage his real formation came from direct travel and close observation of artworks across Italy rather than from academic routine alone. Treccani describes him as moving from town to town on foot, visiting churches, convents, palaces, and collections, and recording newly seen works in sketches and notes that became the foundation of his later method.

In 1846-47 he traveled through Germany, especially Munich, Dresden, Leipzig, and Berlin, expanding his knowledge of northern collections and meeting the English art enthusiast Joseph Archer Crowe. When the revolutions of 1848 broke out, he returned to Italy, took part in the anti-Austrian uprising, later fought for the Roman Republic, and was eventually condemned to death in absentia by the Austrians, forcing him into exile. By 1850 he was living in London in difficult circumstances, supported only modestly by relatives and by the network of friends he had formed abroad.

In London, Cavalcaselle renewed his connection with Crowe, and together they published Early Flemish Painters in 1856, followed by the major History of Painting in Italy beginning in 1864. Their partnership later produced A History of Painting in North Italy, as well as substantial studies on Titian and Raphael, and these works helped establish a more empirical and comparative way of writing art history in English. Even though many of their individual attributions have since been revised, modern scholars still cite them because of the extraordinary breadth of firsthand looking on which their books were based.

Cavalcaselle's reputation rested above all on his powers of attribution and connoisseurship, and Italian scholarship has often treated him as a founder of modern art criticism for that reason. His sketchbooks and notes, preserved in Venice, are considered vital evidence of both his visual method and his vast range of knowledge. He also contributed to the development of restoration thinking, proposing more updated criteria at a time when the conceptual basis of restoration was still unsettled in Italy.

After Italian unification, Cavalcaselle entered public service and from 1875 to 1893 worked in Rome as a central inspector in the state administration responsible for excavations, museums, antiquities, and fine arts. In that role he traveled widely through the newly unified kingdom, advising on museum organization, acquisitions, and urgent restorations, and in some cases personally supervising interventions. For a scholar of medieval and early Renaissance art, his importance lies not only in the books he wrote, but in the union he forged between travel, archival diligence, visual analysis, attribution, and cultural administration.

Cecchetti, Bartolomeo

Venice, 2 September 1838 - Rome, 16 March 1889

Bartolomeo Cecchetti was born in Venice on September 2, 1838, to Rosa Pancrazio and Pietro Cecchetti, a cultivated man active in local periodicals. He grew up in an intellectual environment open to the influence of writers and scholars.

From 1848 to 1855 he attended the S. Caterina high school, then left at seventeen to begin as an apprentice at the General Archive of the Frari. He soon attended the paleography school established in 1854 and directed by C. Foucard, whose technical training and liberal-patriotic outlook deeply shaped his method and historical interests. He earned a diploma as a judicial paleographer and a teaching qualification.

After a brief period in the Registry Office of the Lieutenancy and the State Accounting Office (January 1857 to October 1861), he returned to the Archives in 1860 to replace Foucard, dismissed for excessively liberal views, as professor of paleography. He held the post until 1872, adding lectures on Venetian history. From 1863 he worked permanently in the Archives, directed the historical-diplomatic section, and quickly advanced. In 1876 he became director of the Venice State Archives, remaining in office until his death.

One of the most dramatic episodes of his life came in 1866, when he opposed the transfer to Vienna of major archival holdings ordered by Austrian authorities. Arrested during the night of August 7-8, he was imprisoned on San Giorgio and deported to Trieste, where he remained until September 23, when he was released through diplomatic intervention. Back in Venice, he immediately resumed duty, and the Italian government later recognized his role by appointing him to a commission charged with identifying documents and artworks removed from the Veneto up to 1866.

As official and then director, Cecchetti pursued two main goals: reordering the Republican-era fonds and expanding holdings through new acquisitions, while also pressing the ministry for better staffing and improved conditions at the Frari. Among his enduring institutional achievements were the creation, with R. Tredelli, of the Paleographic Museum of the Veneto Region and the Regina Margherita Diplomatic Hall, the reorganization of the Legislative Library, and the acquisition of the Venetian Republic's collection of weights and measures.

From 1871 he contributed to Archivio Veneto, becoming its director in 1884. The journal became the principal vehicle of his scholarly production and a crucial medium for publishing Venetian documentary sources. Active in Venice's liberal cultural circles and a contributor to Il Pensiero di Venezia, he met his wife Anna Mander there, poet and journalist, with whom he shared a life devoted to archival work, historical research, and civic ideals.

Cecchetti published more than 150 titles spanning archival theory, paleography, political-institutional history, and medieval Venetian social life. Key works include Program of the I.R. School of Paleography in Venice (1861-62), The Royal General Archive of Venice (1873, with T. Toderini), The State Archive of Venice in the Decade 1866-1875 (1876), and Statistics of the Archives of the Venetian Region 1820-1880 (1881). For political and institutional history, The Doge of Venice (1864) and The Republic of Venice and the Court of Rome in Religious Relations (1874) are central references.

His studies on everyday medieval life, especially The Life of the Venetians in 1300, published in installments in Archivio Veneto between 1884 and 1887, are still valuable source repositories for later scholarship. He also contributed to The Basilica of St. Mark in Venice (1880), edited by Camillo Boito and published by Ferdinando Ongania. Bartolomeo Cecchetti died in Rome on March 16, 1889; he was succeeded at the Frari by Federico Stefani, and his archival legacy continued through students such as Giuseppe Giomo and Riccardo Predelli.

Chatzidakis, Manolis

Heraklion, 1909 – Athens, 1 March 1998

Manolis Chatzidakis (Greek: Μανόλης Χατζηδάκης) was born in 1909 in Heraklion, Crete, and died on 1 March 1998 in Athens. He was a Greek Byzantinist who made significant contributions to the history of art in Greece, specialising in Byzantine and post-Byzantine painting. He is buried at the First Cemetery of Athens.

He studied at the University of Athens, graduating in 1933, and was associated with Antonis Benakis, the Greek industrialist and founder of the Benaki Museum, who offered him a scholarship to study at the École du Louvre in Paris. There he studied under Gabriel Millet and André Grabar — two of the most influential figures in twentieth-century Byzantine art history. Millet had established the systematic photographic survey of Byzantine monuments across Greece and the Balkans, while Grabar was redefining the very interpretive frameworks of early Christian and medieval art. At the École du Louvre, Chatzidakis also obtained a degree in Islamic art, and additionally received a degree in classical Arabic at the School of Oriental Languages — a breadth of linguistic and cultural formation that set him apart from most of his contemporaries and gave his work an unusually wide comparative range.

Chatzidakis served as director of the Benaki Museum from 1941 to 1973 — a tenure of more than three decades that transformed the institution into one of the foremost centres for Byzantine and post-Byzantine studies in the world. Simultaneously, he served as director of the Byzantine Museum of Athens and held the positions of head of Byzantine Antiquities and General Superintendent of Antiquities, a remarkable concentration of curatorial authority reflecting the degree to which Greek cultural institutions had come to depend on his expertise. He helped organise and structure the framework of museums in Greece during the twentieth century and was instrumental in founding the Hellenic Institute of Byzantine and Post-Byzantine Studies in Venice and the National Hellenic Research Foundation.

Chatzidakis's most enduring scholarly achievement lies in his systematic reconstruction of Greek painting in the centuries following the fall of Constantinople. His most notable contribution to Greek art history was the magisterial Greek Painters after the Fall of Constantinople (1450–1830), in which he documented hundreds of hitherto almost unknown Greek painters. The volumes were published in 1987 and 1997, with a third volume completed by Eugenia Drakopoulou in 2010; the encyclopaedia features biographical details and an index of artistic works cataloguing portable icons, church frescoes, and other artistic productions. This work earned him the comparison, in the critical literature, to Giorgio Vasari — the Renaissance biographer of artists — for the sheer ambition of its documentary scope. His pivotal publications on post-Byzantine Cretan icon painting in the 1970s laid the foundation of a now well-established research field that has consolidated the contribution of Venetian Crete's artistic production to European culture.

He was a major contributor to uncovering and researching the early Cretan work of El Greco relative to the Cretan School. His studies helped situate Domenikos Theotokopoulos firmly within the tradition of Venetian Crete before his departure for Italy and Spain, providing the art-historical context that transformed the understanding of El Greco's formation as a painter.

Among his most celebrated monographic studies is his investigation of Theophanes the Cretan, the major fresco painter of sixteenth-century Mount Athos. Chatzidakis published The Cretan Painter Theophanes: The Final Period of his Art in the Frescoes in Stavronikita Monastery (Mount Athos, 1986), as well as an earlier essay on the painter in Nea Estia (1963) and multiple contributions to the comprehensive volumes of Greek national history. In this detailed study, Chatzidakis assessed Theophanes's work with particular attention to what he called the anthropocentric quality of the painter's art, stressing his ceaseless concern for the human figure within the devotional space of the monastery.

Chatzidakis also edited and contributed to the landmark series Byzantine Art in Greece, producing comprehensive monographs on individual monuments including Hosios Loukas, Naxos, Kastoria, Patmos, and Mystras. His Mystras: The Medieval City and the Castle (Athens, 1992) and The Great Meteoron: History and Art (Athens, 1990, with D. Sofianos) exemplify his ability to combine archaeological precision with accessible historical narrative, making his books indispensable reference tools for both scholars and museum visitors.

Throughout his lifetime Chatzidakis was awarded the Order of the Phoenix, the Herder Prize (1965), and the Order of George I. He received honorary doctorates from the Universities of Brussels and Athens. He was an associate member of the Academy of Sciences of Vienna, secretary of the Society of Byzantine Studies, secretary and later president of the Christian Archaeological Society, and a member of the German Archaeological Institute. He is considered the twentieth-century Giorgio Vasari and Bernardo de' Dominici of Greek art history — scholars who, in their respective eras, gave systematic and lasting form to biographical and critical knowledge of their national artistic traditions. His work remains the essential point of departure for any serious study of Byzantine and post-Byzantine painting in Greece.

Chazelle, Celia

active late 20th-21st century

Celia Chazelle is an American historian of the early medieval West, Professor Emerita of History at The College of New Jersey, and one of the leading specialists in the intersection of theology, liturgy, and visual art in the Carolingian and Anglo-Saxon periods. Her work is distinguished by a consistent methodological commitment: reading images and diagrams not as illustrations of a text fixed in advance but as arguments in their own right, produced within specific theological controversies and institutional settings and meant to be read against them.

Chazelle built her early reputation with a sustained study of Carolingian responses to the Crucifixion, culminating in her monograph The Crucified God in the Carolingian Era: Theology and Art of Christ's Passion (Cambridge University Press, 2001). The book traces how ninth-century debates over the nature of Christ's suffering and the theology of the Eucharist — including the dispute between Paschasius Radbertus and Ratramnus of Corbie — shaped, and were shaped by, contemporary depictions of the crucified Christ, and it established Chazelle as a scholar capable of moving fluently between doctrinal history and the close reading of images. She co-edited, with Simon Doubleday, Felice Lifshitz, and Amy G. Remensnyder, the collective volume Why the Middle Ages Matter: Medieval Light on Modern Injustice (Routledge, 2012), which argued for the relevance of medieval studies to contemporary questions of poverty, race, gender, and violence.

Chazelle's most sustained later project has been the Codex Amiatinus, the great single-volume Bible produced at the Northumbrian monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow around the year 700 and sent, unsuccessfully in its original intention, as a gift for the tomb of St Peter in Rome. Her article "Ceolfrid's Gift to St Peter: The First Quire of the Codex Amiatinus and the Evidence of Its Roman Destination," published in Early Medieval Europe 12 (2003), argued that the manuscript's celebrated Ezra portrait and the surrounding prefatory apparatus were designed with the papacy specifically in view, presenting the image of the restorer and custodian of Scripture to the pope who was to receive the book. A further essay, "Christ and the Vision of God: The Biblical Diagrams of the Codex Amiatinus" (2006), extended this reading to the manuscript's schematic diagrams of the biblical canon, treating them as vehicles of theological argument about the structure of revelation and the vision of God rather than as neutral scholarly apparatus.

This body of work reached its culmination in The Codex Amiatinus and its "Sister" Bibles: Scripture, Liturgy, and Art in the Milieu of the Venerable Bede (Leiden: Brill, Commentaria 10, 2019), a monograph of more than 650 pages that is now the standard comprehensive treatment of the manuscript and of the two lost companion pandects commissioned alongside it by the abbot Ceolfrith. The book draws together the codicological, textual, art-historical, and liturgical evidence bearing on the three Bibles, situates them within the intellectual world of Bede and the library of Wearmouth-Jarrow, and has become the indispensable point of reference for subsequent scholarship on the manuscript, including its complicated modern historiography — the erased dedication, the nineteenth-century recognition of the codex's true Northumbrian origin by Giovanni Battista de Rossi and Fenton John Anthony Hort, and the long misattribution to sixth-century Italy that preceded it. For the fuller narrative, see the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database, which draws extensively on Chazelle's findings for its account of the manuscript's scale, its prefatory quire, and the current state of the field.

Chelazzi Dini, Giulietta

active 20th–21st century

Giulietta Chelazzi Dini is an Italian art historian and museum official whose long career was centred on the study, conservation, and public presentation of Sienese art. For many years she held senior responsibility within the Italian state superintendency for the artistic and historical heritage of Siena and its province, a position that gave her direct custodial and scholarly access to the city's museums, churches, and archives across a career spanning several decades.

Her most influential contribution to the study of Sienese Gothic painting was as editor of Il Gotico a Siena, the catalogue of the landmark 1982 Siena exhibition that reassessed the Sienese Trecento school and, in the specific case of Luca di Tommè, reversed the long-standing view of him as a subordinate hand, granting him autonomy of language and a distinctive chromatic sensibility. She also contributed the entry on Luca di Tommè to the Enciclopedia dell'Arte Medievale (1997), a standard reference synthesis of the documentary and critical literature on the artist.

Chiappelli, Alessandro

Pistoia, 20 November 1857 - Florence, 4 November 1931

Alessandro Chiappelli was an Italian philosopher, historian of ideas, and senator of the Kingdom of Italy whose principal scholarly life was devoted to the history of ancient and modern philosophy, but who also contributed, through a family enterprise of local erudition centred on his native Pistoia, occasional but consequential pieces of documentary art history. It is in this latter, more incidental capacity that he enters the present database: his 1900 article on early paintings in the Pistoiese church of San Giovanni Fuorcivitas published the mid-fourteenth-century document recording a debate over the finest painter "from Giotto onward," a text that names several Sienese masters among the best and remains a key piece of evidence for the extra-Sienese reputation of painters such as Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio.

Born into a Pistoiese family of some intellectual distinction—his father, Francesco Chiappelli, was a noted physician and physiologist—Alessandro was educated at the Liceo Forteguerri in his native city before proceeding to the Istituto di Studi Superiori in Florence, where he read philosophy and letters under the neo-Kantians Felice Tocco and Francesco Fiorentino and studied ancient thought with the classicist Domenico Comparetti. This formation set the course of his career: a philosopher trained in the German idealist tradition but equally attentive to classical philology and to the history of early Christian literature.

Chiappelli's academic career took him first to Padua (1883) and then to Florence (1885), before he was called, in 1887, to the chair of the history of philosophy at the University of Naples, where he also taught pedagogy and directed an attached museum. He held the Naples chair until 1908, when he resigned it to devote himself entirely to research and writing, though he continued to lecture on the history of the Christian church at Pisa, Bologna, and Florence. In recognition of his scholarly standing he was made a national member of the Accademia dei Lincei in 1899 and was elected to the Società Reale di Napoli, the Accademia delle Scienze di Torino, the Accademia Pontaniana of Naples, and the Accademia della Crusca of Florence. On 30 December 1914 he was named a senator of the Kingdom of Italy, taking his seat in the twenty-fourth legislature the following March.

His published output ranged across ancient Greek philosophy—Plato, the Stoics, the pre-Socratics—early Christian literature and thought, the modern idealist and "theistic" reaction to positivism and Marxism, and studies of Dante and of Renaissance and nineteenth-century literary figures including Leopardi. Among his books are Studi d'antica letteratura cristiana (1887), Guerra, amore ed immortalità (1916), and La crisi del pensiero moderno (1920).

The Pistoiese art-historical strand of his work is best understood through his family. His brother Luigi Chiappelli, a historian of medieval law, founded the Società Pistoiese di Storia Patria in 1898 together with a third brother, Alberto, and from 1901 directed its journal, the Bullettino Storico Pistoiese; Alessandro collaborated closely in this civic scholarly project and served for many years as the society's president, and it was in the Bullettino's inaugural volumes that he placed his 1900 notice on Taddeo Gaddi and the early paintings of San Giovanni Fuorcivitas. His personal papers, including correspondence with Benedetto Croce, Antonio Fogazzaro, and Antonio Salandra, are held at the Biblioteca Comunale Forteguerriana in Pistoia.

Chiodo, Sonia

active late 20th-21st century

Sonia Chiodo (full name: Stella Sonia Chiodo) is one of Italy's leading historians of medieval art, specializing in Tuscan painting and miniature art from the 12th to the 15th centuries. She currently serves as Associate Professor of Medieval Art History (SSD L-ART/01) in the SAGAS Department (History, Archaeology, Geography, Art, and Performing Arts) at the University of Florence.

Chiodo graduated in 1992 from the University of Florence with a thesis on late-Gothic Florentine painting, titled The Master of the Madonna Straus. Continuities and Innovations in Florentine Painting at the Turn of the Fifteenth Century, under the guidance of the renowned art historian Mina Gregori, earning the highest honors with distinction.

In 1996, she earned a diploma from the School of Archival Science, Paleography, and Diplomatics at the State Archives of Florence, thereby refining the documentary and paleographic skills essential for research on medieval art. The following year, in 1997, she also earned a diploma with highest honors from the School of Specialization in Art History at the University of Florence.

In 2004, she earned her Ph.D. with a dissertation titled The Master of the Accademia's Misericordia. Trends in Florentine Painting of the Third Quarter of the Fourteenth Century, a work that would lay the groundwork for some of her most important monographic studies on post-plague Florentine painting. Between 1994 and 1996, she was a fellow at the prestigious Roberto Longhi Foundation for Art History Studies in Florence, a leading institution for the training of Italian art historians.

From 1999 to 2001, and then from 2004 to 2006, Chiodo was a research fellow at the University of Florence; on September 1, 2006, she became a Researcher in Medieval Art History at the same university.

On October 1, 2018, she was promoted to the position of Associate Professor of Medieval Art History, a role she still holds today. Since 2021, she has directed the Graduate School of Art Heritage at the University of Florence, further solidifying her role in training new generations of art historians.

She is head of the Corpus of Florentine Painting Laboratory within the LIEC (Interdisciplinary Laboratory on Cultural Heritage) of the SAGAS Department, and is a member of the editorial board of the journal Paragone. Arte. She served on the Executive Board of the University Council of Art Historians (CUNSTA) from 2018 to 2023.

One of the most significant scholarly achievements associated with Chiodo's name is her direction of the Corpus of Florentine Painting, the monumental cataloging project initiated by Richard Offner between 1930 and 1965, and subsequently continued by Miklos Boskovits from 1984 to 2011.

From 1997 to 2011, Chiodo actively collaborated with Boskovits on numerous volumes of the project, publishing in 2011 the volume Painters in Florence after the "Black Death": The Master of the Misericordia and Matteo di Pacino (Section IV, vol. IX), which sheds new light on little-studied aspects of Florentine painting of the late 14th century. In 2012, she took over the direction of the entire project, succeeding Boskovits, within the association chaired by Andrea De Marchi.

Starting in 2013, Chiodo designed and coordinated the creation of the Corpus's digital photo library (www.corpuspitturafiorentina.it), a pioneering initiative in the field of Digital Humanities applied to medieval art history, which made the historical archive's photographic collection accessible online.

Medieval miniatures represent one of the most fruitful areas of Chiodo's research. In 2009, she received PRIN (Project of National Interest) funding for the study of the illuminated manuscripts of Santa Croce in Florence.

In 2016, she curated the exhibition Ad usum fratris. Miniatures in the Laurentian Manuscripts of the Santa Croce Library (10th-13th Centuries), accompanied by a scholarly reference catalog. In her studies of miniatures, Chiodo pays particular attention to the relationship between text and images, the cultural context of production, and patronage, applying a rigorous method that combines philological analysis and archival research.

In 2020, she curated the exhibition Storie di pagine dipinte. Miniature recuperate dai Carabinieri at the Galleria Palatina in Florence, dedicated to ancient illuminated manuscripts stolen and recovered by the Carabinieri's Cultural Heritage Protection Unit. The exhibition, organized in collaboration with the University of Florence's School of Specialization, drew attention to the fragility of the historical and artistic heritage and the need for its protection.

As part of the 2021 Dante celebrations, Chiodo curated, together with Luca Azzetta and Teresa De Robertis, the exhibition "Honorable and Ancient Citizen of Florence": The Bargello for Dante at the Bargello National Museum, dedicated to iconographic representations of the poet.

Among her most cited contributions is the essay A Tribute to Dante: The Giottesque Portrait in the Palazzo del Podesta in Florence, published in the anthology New Horizons in Trecento Italian Art. From 2013 to 2019, she served as a member of the scientific committee of the Ente Nazionale Giovanni Boccaccio, overseeing the project Boccaccio visualizzato, and from 2019 to 2022, she served on the board of directors of the same organization.

The international dimension of her work is also evident through her affiliation with the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz (KHI), the prestigious German institute for art research based in Florence, where the Corpus of Florentine Painting is headquartered.

She is regularly invited to leading international conferences, including the symposium Siena: The Rise of Painting, 1300-1350 (2025), and actively contributes to the international debate on medieval Italian painting. Her academic profile on Academia.edu has over 300 followers and 46 published works, reflecting a broad international research network.

Ciatti, Marco

Prato, 1955 – Prato, 2024

Italian art historian and one of the most influential figures in twentieth- and early twenty-first-century Italian restoration and conservation, whose career combined institutional leadership, scholarly publishing, and hands-on direction of major campaigns at the Opificio delle Pietre Dure in Florence. He graduated with honours in Literature, specialising in art history, from the University of Florence, and from 1980 served as an art historian within the Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Activities. From 1981 he worked within the Superintendence for Artistic and Historical Heritage in Siena, in the restoration team, an experience that grounded his later theoretical positions in the practical demands of monumental and panel painting conservation. In 1984 he joined the Opificio delle Pietre Dure, where he eventually became head of the restoration workshops for paintings on canvas and panel and for textile artefacts, supervising campaigns on major works by Beato Angelico, Botticelli, Caravaggio, Giotto, Raphael, Mantegna, and others — many of them damaged by the catastrophic 1966 Florence flood. From 2012 to 2022 he served as Superintendent of the Opificio, consolidating its international standing as one of Europe's foremost centres for the scientific study and technical restoration of portable paintings and textiles.

Ciatti's contribution to the scholarly literature on restoration methodology was substantial and sustained. From 1997 he edited the annual journal OPD Restauro and coordinated the Opificio's two principal publication series, Storia e teoria del restauro and Problemi di conservazione e restauro, through which he promoted a rigorous integration of conservation science, art-historical analysis, and restoration theory that distinguished the Florentine school from more purely technical or aesthetic approaches. He taught History and Theory of Restoration and History of Artistic Techniques at the universities of Florence, Siena, Bologna, and Milan, as well as at the Polytechnic, training successive generations of restorers and art historians in the interdisciplinary framework that characterised his own practice. He was elected a member of the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno and a corresponding member of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei, recognitions that affirmed his standing within Italian academic culture alongside his institutional achievements. He died in Prato on 20 April 2024.

Coakley, John W. (John Wayland Coakley)

active late 20th-21st century

John W. Coakley is an American historian of Christianity whose scholarship has done much to shape the modern study of medieval religious women, hagiography, and the vexed question of female spiritual authority within a clerical, male-dominated Church. He held the L. Russell Feakes Memorial Professor of Church History chair at New Brunswick Theological Seminary in New Jersey, where he taught for some three decades before his retirement, and where he remains Professor Emeritus.

Coakley earned his bachelor's degree from Wesleyan University before pursuing graduate theological training at Harvard Divinity School, where he took both the M.Div. and the Th.D.; he also holds an M.L.I.S. from Rutgers University. Before turning to academic life he served for several years as a parish minister in Massachusetts, an experience of pastoral practice that informed his later scholarly attentiveness to the practical, day-to-day dynamics between religious women and the male clergy who guided, confessed, and wrote about them.

His scholarly path toward the study of medieval holy women began with the essay "Friars as Confidants of Holy Women in Medieval Dominican Hagiography," contributed to the influential collective volume Images of Sainthood in Medieval Europe, edited by Renate Blumenfeld-Kosinski and Timea Szell (Cornell University Press, 1991), which examined the collaborative and often uneasy textual partnerships between female mystics and their male confessor-scribes. He then co-edited, with E. Ann Matter, Creative Women in Medieval and Early Modern Italy: A Religious and Artistic Renaissance (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1994), a volume that brought together historians of religion and of art to reassess the creative agency of Italian women, both religious and lay, across several centuries.

Coakley's central and most widely acclaimed contribution is Women, Men, and Spiritual Power: Female Saints and Their Male Collaborators (Columbia University Press, 2006), a study of nine female mystics active between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries, read through the writings composed about them, and sometimes with them, by the male clerics who served as their confessors and hagiographers. Among the case studies at the heart of the book is Angela of Foligno, whose Memoriale was set down by an anonymous Franciscan "frater scriptor," a textual relationship of collaboration and mediation that Coakley treats as paradigmatic of the larger problem the book addresses: how spiritual authority could be claimed by women whose voices reached posterity chiefly through male-authored texts. Coakley works from the text established in Giovanni Pozzi's critical edition of the Memoriale, Il libro dell'esperienza (1992), the standard modern edition of Angela's book. The book was met with strong critical praise; Barbara Newman, writing in the Catholic Historical Review, called it "the capstone of a well-established scholarly edifice and a spur to further research," concluding that "Coakley's elegant study belongs in every medievalist's library," while Donna Trembinski, in the Canadian Journal of History, praised it as "a well-researched and insightful exploration" that "fills a void in the research on female mystics."

Alongside his work on medieval sainthood, Coakley pursued a parallel scholarly interest in the history of American Reformed Protestantism. He co-edited, with Renee S. House, Patterns and Portraits: Women in the History of the Reformed Church in America (Eerdmans, 1999), and edited on his own Concord Makes Strength: Essays in Reformed Ecumenism (Eerdmans, 2002). With Andrea Sterk he co-edited Readings in World Christian History, Volume I: Earliest Christianity to 1453 (Orbis Books, 2004), a sourcebook designed to accompany global histories of the early and medieval Church and notable for its deliberate inclusion of women's voices, still rare in general church histories of the period. He later wrote New Brunswick Theological Seminary: An Illustrated History, 1784-2014, a history of the institution where he spent his teaching career, tracing its evolving relationship with the Reformed Church in America.

Taken as a whole, Coakley's scholarship occupies a distinctive place in the historiography of medieval religious women: rather than treating hagiographical texts as transparent windows onto female mystical experience, or dismissing them as mere instruments of clerical control, he reads them as sites of genuine, if unequal, collaboration between women seeking spiritual expression and the men charged with authenticating and transmitting it. This approach has proved especially productive for the study of figures such as Angela of Foligno, whose textual legacy, like that of many of her contemporaries, cannot be separated from the confessors and scribes who set it in writing.

Cole, Bruce

Cleveland, Ohio, 1938 – Indianapolis, Indiana, 2018

American art historian whose career traced an arc from the intimacy of Trecento Florentine and Sienese panel painting to the highest levels of American cultural policy — a trajectory that made him, in the words of the National Endowment for the Humanities, both a prolific scholar of the Italian Renaissance and a consequential public servant. He died on 8 January 2018 in Indianapolis, aged seventy-nine.

Born in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1938, Cole did not in his early years have much interest in art. His conversion came suddenly and memorably during his undergraduate years at Case Western Reserve University, where a chance encounter with a reproduction in a classroom book changed the direction of his life. Cole could remember the day in class that he opened a book and saw The Meeting of Saint Anthony and Saint Paul — a fifteenth-century narrative painting depicting the monastic Saint Anthony on a long journey as he seeks out Saint Paul the Hermit. While looking at this picture, Cole was bitten by the art-history bug.

Cole earned a bachelor's degree from Case Western Reserve University, a master's from Oberlin College, and a doctorate from Bryn Mawr College. His dissertation examined the work of the fourteenth-century Florentine painter Agnolo Gaddi (c.1350–1396). The choice of subject was characteristic: not one of the canonical giants of the period, but a major workshop master whose relationship to Giotto's inheritance and to his own father Taddeo Gaddi raised precise questions about continuity, workshop practice, and the transmission of style — questions that placed Cole squarely within the tradition of Florentine Trecento connoisseurship.

The biographical intersection with Florence was formative, and it came at a historic moment. He was in Florence in 1966 as a fellow at the Kunsthistorisches Institut, a research library for Renaissance art, when the Arno River flooded the city. Fifty years later, reflecting on that catastrophe, Cole recalled "conservators and scholars from all over the world who flocked to the city, bringing their technical know-how to rescue the city's art. It was an international rescue mission that affirmed the universal importance of art for all humanity, something worth recalling in these days of its wanton destruction by the enemies of civilization."

The event placed Cole — like Erling Skaug, who was also present in Florence that November — at the epicentre of one of the twentieth century's defining encounters between the scholarly community and the fragility of the cultural heritage it studied. For two years, Cole was the William E. Suida Fellow at the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz.

Cole was appointed Assistant Professor of art history at the University of Rochester, NY in 1969 before joining the faculty at Indiana University in 1973. There he was appointed Professor in 1977 and Distinguished Professor in 1988. In 1971, Cole received a research fellowship from NEH, followed by grants and fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the American Council of Learned Societies, the Kress Foundation, the American Philosophical Society, and the Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies at UCLA. At Indiana, one of the largest art history graduate programmes in the country, he became one of the most productive scholarly presences in the field of Italian medieval and Renaissance art.

Cole's bibliography of fifteen books constitutes one of the most comprehensive bodies of accessible scholarship on Italian art of the period from Nicola Pisano to Titian produced by an American scholar of his generation. It ranges from focused monographs on individual artists to broad synthetic surveys intended for students and general readers.

His published dissertation, Agnolo Gaddi (Clarendon Press, 1977), remains the standard monograph on its subject. Giotto and Florentine Painting, 1280–1375 (Harper and Row, 1976) established the scholarly framework within which he would operate throughout his career — a focus on the critical decades from Cimabue's generation to the consolidation of Giotto's legacy in the hands of the major Trecento workshops. Two volumes on Siena followed: Sienese Painting from Its Origins to the Fifteenth Century (1980) and Sienese Painting in the Age of the Renaissance (1985), together constituting a comprehensive survey of the Sienese school from Duccio to Sodoma.

Masaccio and the Art of Early Renaissance Florence (1980) addressed the pivotal generation of the early Quattrocento, while The Renaissance Artist at Work: From Pisano to Titian (1983) — telling how the artists learned their craft, the organization of their workshops, and the guilds they belonged to; how their customers or patrons treated them and where their work was displayed; how art was made — tempera, oil, panel, canvas, fresco; and surveying the characteristic types of Renaissance art: altarpieces, portraits, tombs, busts, doors, fountains, medals — became one of the most widely used introductions to the material culture of Renaissance artistic production. Italian Art, 1250–1550: The Relation of Renaissance Art to Life and Society (1987) provided chapters on Italian Renaissance art in relation to domestic life, worship, civic life, death and afterlife, and Renaissance images and ideals, firmly situating objects within the social fabric that had generated them.

Piero della Francesca: Tradition and Innovation in Renaissance Art (1991), Giotto: The Scrovegni Chapel (1993), and Studies in the History of Italian Art, 1250–1550 (1996) continued the series, while The Informed Eye: Understanding Masterpieces of Western Art (1999) extended his range beyond Italian art to the broader canon of Western painting. His work was used by PBS as the basis for a television series — a measure of his capacity to communicate scholarly knowledge to wide audiences long before he assumed public office.

Cole was a founder and co-president of the Association for Art History and a member of the Accademia Senese degli Intronati, the oldest learned society in Europe.

The trajectory of Cole's career changed decisively in the autumn of 2001. Shortly after the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, Cole left the University to become Chairman of the National Endowment for the Humanities. He would go on to occupy the role for over seven years between December 2001 and early 2009, becoming the institution's longest-serving chair.

His NEH chairmanship was defined by two signature initiatives. The first, We the People, sought to place the treasures of American heritage before all Americans, establishing an annual Heroes of History lecture, an essay contest for high school students, and a programme to distribute classic children's books to libraries and schools across the country.

The second, Picturing America, was its visual complement: Cole's love of the masterpieces of Western art inspired him to create the enormously successful Picturing America initiative, which brought reproductions of forty important works of American art to K-12 classrooms and libraries, accompanied by humanities-rich educational and curricular resources for teachers. The programme reached some 80,000 classrooms and public libraries across the country.

Cole also left an institutional legacy of considerable forward vision: he was an early champion of the digital humanities, establishing the NEH Office of Digital Humanities during his tenure. Under his leadership, the NEH also developed the Chronicling America online database of historic American newspapers and established a partnership with the National Science Foundation to document endangered languages.

In 2008, President Bush awarded Cole the Presidential Citizens Medal "for his work to strengthen our national memory and ensure that our country's heritage is passed on to future generations." The Presidential Citizens Medal is the second-highest civilian honour the President can confer. In the same year, he was decorated as a Knight of the Grand Cross, the highest honour of the Republic of Italy — a distinction that acknowledged a life's work in the service of Italian cultural heritage and its transmission to American students and readers.

Following his departure from NEH in 2009, Cole served as President and CEO of the American Revolution Center, and in 2012 joined the Ethics and Public Policy Center as a Senior Fellow. In 2013, President Barack Obama appointed Cole to the Eisenhower Memorial Commission.

In 2017, in one of his final acts of public generosity, Cole donated his personal library of 2,000 volumes of special and rare books to Christopher Newport University. A scholar of Italian Renaissance and American art, Cole had spent over sixty years amassing a collection that began when he was a young man in Cleveland, Ohio.

Bruce Cole belongs to a generation of American art historians — alongside Millard Meiss, John Pope-Hennessy, Frederick Hartt, and later John T. Paoletti — who built the university-level study of Italian medieval and Renaissance art in the United States into a mature and methodologically sophisticated discipline. His particular contribution was the consistent accessibility of his scholarship: rigorous in its archival and connoisseurial foundations, but always oriented toward the reader who needed a reliable guide through the complex terrain of Trecento and Quattrocento Italy. The breadth of his bibliography — covering Giotto, the Gaddi workshop, the Lorenzetti, Masaccio, Piero della Francesca, and Titian — reflects not intellectual dilettantism but an unusually systematic ambition to map the entire span of Italian panel painting from its medieval origins to its Cinquecento culmination. In the specific field of Sienese Trecento painting, his two surveys remain indispensable introductions for English-language readers. The coincidence of his scholarly formation in Florence during the 1966 flood, at the very institution where Erling Skaug was also at work, places him within the same remarkable generation of scholars whose encounter with the city's art — in conditions of emergency — forged a lifelong personal and professional bond with the Italian cultural heritage.

Coletti, Luigi

Treviso, 1886 – Treviso, 1961

Luigi Coletti was one of the most important Italian art historians of the twentieth century, specializing in medieval and Venetian art, with a particular focus on fourteenth-century painters and the so-called Italian primitives. His work became a central reference for scholarship on Italian painting between the Romanesque and Gothic periods.

Born in Treviso to a family from Cadore with a long-standing local tradition, Coletti entered the city's intellectual world early, coming into contact during his school years with figures such as Luigi Bailo and Augusto Serena. His academic formation followed an unusual path: he completed a law degree at the University of Padua in 1909, while already publishing studies on local art. Friendships formed after the First World War, especially with Giuseppe Fiocco and later Carlo Gamba Ghiselli, decisively shaped his methodological and critical orientation.

In 1919, Coletti was appointed chair of the commission for the reorganization of the Treviso Civic Museum, and in 1932 he obtained a lectureship in art history, succeeding Abbot Bailo as curator of the Museum and Civic Art Gallery. His curatorial activity was both scholarly and operational: he led the reordering of civic collections, promoted conservation campaigns for the walls of Fra Giocondo and the Loggia dei Cavalieri, and initiated restoration work at San Francesco. He also acquired the Bampo manuscript on local art for the Municipal Library and founded the Museo della Casa Trevigiana in Ca' de Noal.

The high point of his scholarship was the trilogy on the Italian Primitives: Dal romanico a Giotto (1941), I senesi e i giotteschi (1946), and I padani (1947). Together these volumes offered a systematic account of medieval Italian painting from Romanesque beginnings to the Gothic developments of the mid-fourteenth century, combining stylistic analysis, regional comparison, and historical framing of the Sienese, Florentine, and Padanian schools.

In 1946, Coletti accepted a university chair in Trieste, deliberately choosing the city during a politically sensitive phase to contribute to its cultural and institutional consolidation within the Italian sphere. Elected dean, he is remembered for balancing academic leadership with a commitment to ideological pluralism in teaching. During the Second World War he had already played a key role in the protection of Treviso's artistic patrimony, coordinating the evacuation and safeguarding of artworks between 1940 and 1943.

Author of more than 150 publications, including articles, essays, and monographs, Coletti worked across medieval and Venetian Renaissance art, with important studies on Lorenzo Lotto, Tommaso da Modena, Veronese, and Canova. He served on the editorial board of Arte Veneta, on the board of the Institute of Art History of the Cini Foundation, and as chairman of the board of trustees of the Trieste Museum. Retiring from university teaching in 1957, he remained active in Treviso, continuing to supervise the final reorganization of the Civic Museums until his death.

Colgan, John

c. 1592, County Donegal – 15 January 1658, Louvain

John Colgan was an Irish Franciscan friar and hagiographer, a member of the community of Irish Franciscans at St Anthony's College, Louvain, in the Spanish Netherlands — the principal continental centre of Irish Counter-Reformation scholarship in the seventeenth century. He continued the great manuscript-collecting and historical project begun at Louvain by Brother Michael O'Clery, compiler of the Annals of the Four Masters, and Hugh Ward, drawing on materials gathered from religious houses and private collections throughout Ireland and the Irish diaspora.

Colgan's major publications were Acta Sanctorum Hiberniae (Louvain, 1645), covering the lives of Irish saints commemorated between January and March, and Triadis Thaumaturgae Acta (the Trias Thaumaturga, 1647), collecting the lives of Patrick, Brigid and Columba. It was through Colgan's compilation, and its later popularisation in English by writers such as William Betham, that the legend of Saint Crónán, the scribe Dimma, and the forty-day miracle of the gospel book's copying reached the wide antiquarian and popular readership from which it entered general circulation as fact.

Colgrave, Bertram

Derry, 1889 - Cambridge, 13 January 1968

Bertram Colgrave was one of the twentieth century's foremost authorities on the Latin hagiographic literature of early Anglo-Saxon England, best known for his critical editions of the lives of saints Cuthbert, Wilfrid, Guthlac, and Gregory the Great, and above all for his landmark edition of Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People.

Colgrave was born in 1889 in Derry, Ireland, and pursued a distinguished academic formation at two of England's leading universities. After completing his first degree, he went on to study Anglo-Saxon and Middle English at Clare College, Cambridge, where he developed the deep philological training in Old and Middle English that would underpin his entire scholarly career. He taught briefly at Merchiston Castle School near Edinburgh from 1916 to 1918, before moving into the full-time academic life that defined him.

Colgrave spent the central decades of his career at Durham University, and his close association with Durham was not merely institutional but deeply personal. Durham Cathedral is the resting place of Saint Cuthbert, and Colgrave wrote in the preface to his edition of the Two Lives of Saint Cuthbert that editing those texts was "almost a pious duty for one who lives under the shadow of Durham Cathedral". He became one of the university's leading scholars of early medieval hagiography, wrote the official guide to the city and diocese of Durham, and on his retirement in 1954 was celebrated as one of the institution's most distinguished figures.

His most enduring contribution to medieval studies was the preparation of scrupulously edited, bilingual Latin-English critical editions of foundational texts of early Northumbrian Christianity. His edition of the Two Lives of Saint Cuthbert, presenting both the anonymous Life composed by a monk of Lindisfarne between 698 and 705 and Bede's polished prose Life of 721, remains a standard scholarly reference. Taken together, the two texts illuminate the golden age of Northumbrian monasticism and the ecclesiastical tensions between Celtic and Roman practice, resolved in the generation after Whitby.

He also prepared editions of the Latin Life of Wilfrid by Eddius Stephanus, the Life of Guthlac by Felix, and the earliest Life of Gregory the Great by the anonymous monk of Whitby, works that form the core corpus of early Anglo-Saxon hagiography. His greatest posthumous achievement was the monumental critical edition of Bede's Ecclesiastical History, co-edited with R. A. B. Mynors and published by Oxford University Press in 1969, the year after his death. In the Oxford Medieval Texts series, with facing Latin text and Colgrave's English translation, it has remained continuously in print and is cited in virtually all anglophone scholarship on early medieval England.

Beyond editorial work, Colgrave served from 1950 to 1963 as the founding editor-in-chief of Early English Manuscripts in Facsimile, a landmark series that made major Anglo-Saxon manuscripts accessible to scholars internationally. This role placed him at the intersection of palaeography, codicology, and literary history, the same intersection in which illuminated manuscript studies are grounded. After retiring from Durham in 1954, he held visiting professorships at the University of North Carolina, the University of Texas, the University of Kansas, the University of Colorado, and Mount Holyoke College, carrying the study of Bede and early English hagiography to American audiences.

Colgrave died on 13 January 1968 in Cambridge. His editions remain indispensable tools for scholars working on early medieval England, Northumbrian Christianity, and the Latin literary culture of the seventh and eighth centuries, a body of work whose care, erudition, and longevity place him among the major medievalists of the twentieth century.

Constable, Giles

London, 1 June 1929 – Princeton, 17 January 2021

Giles Constable FBA, born on 1 June 1929 in London, was one of the most distinguished and influential medieval historians of the twentieth century, whose prolific scholarship fundamentally reshaped the study of religious and intellectual life in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. He died on 17 January 2021 in Princeton, New Jersey, at the age of 91.

Constable came from a family already distinguished in the world of art and scholarship: his father, William George Constable, was a noted art historian, and his mother was Olivia Roberts. This cultivated background nurtured in him a lifelong sensitivity to the interconnections between religious culture, material art, and intellectual history — a sensibility that would prove enormously productive throughout his career. He received his undergraduate degree (A.B.) from Harvard University in 1950, spent 1952–53 at Cambridge, and returned to Harvard to complete his Ph.D. in 1957.

Constable's teaching career began at the University of Iowa (1955–58), before he joined the faculty of Harvard University in 1958, where he remained for over two decades. At Harvard he rose to hold the prestigious Henry Charles Lea Professorship of Medieval History from 1966 to 1977 — the oldest and most distinguished chair in medieval studies at an American university. His Harvard years were enormously productive, establishing him as the preeminent American authority on the religious history of the central Middle Ages.

From 1977 to 1984 he served as Director of Dumbarton Oaks Research Library and Collection in Washington D.C., the Harvard-affiliated research institute devoted to Byzantine, pre-Columbian, and garden studies. This role gave him both administrative authority and the resources to pursue wide-ranging collaborative scholarship, and it deepened his already considerable familiarity with Byzantine history and culture. In 1985 he joined the permanent faculty of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton — one of the world's most celebrated centers of pure research — as Professor in the School of Historical Studies, a post he held until becoming Professor Emeritus in 2003.

The animating center of Constable's scholarship was the religious and cultural history of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, a period he regarded as one of the most creative and transformative in the entire history of Western Christianity. He was particularly fascinated by the Abbey of Cluny and its great abbot Peter the Venerable (c. 1092–1156), whose intellectual and spiritual world he explored with a depth and precision that no previous scholar had matched. Cluny, as the head of the largest monastic network in medieval Europe, represented for Constable the fullest expression of the Benedictine ideal — and also its most productive tensions with the newer religious movements of the age.

His most celebrated single work is The Reformation of the Twelfth Century (1996), a sweeping and erudite synthesis that interpreted the explosion of new religious orders, hermit movements, and spiritual experiments in the 1100s as a coherent reforming impulse comparable in scope to the Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century. The book became a standard reference for all students of medieval religious history. His two-volume critical edition of Peter the Venerable's letters, published by Harvard University Press in 1967, remains the authoritative text. Together with Robert Benson he edited the landmark collaborative volume Renaissance and Renewal in the Twelfth Century (1982), a collection that brought together the finest medievalists of the era and consolidated the scholarly argument for a genuine "twelfth-century renaissance".

His scholarly range extended well beyond monasticism. Together with Alexander Kazhdan he co-authored People and Power in Byzantium (1982), an introduction to Byzantine studies that opened a productive dialogue between Western medieval history and the Byzantine tradition. He also wrote authoritatively on the Crusades, on the history of monastic tithes, on medieval attitudes to wealth, poverty, and social order, and on the methodological and historiographical challenges of medieval studies itself.

Constable devoted enormous energy to the infrastructure of the discipline. For twenty years, from 1958 to 1978, he served as Assistant Editor of Speculum, the flagship journal of the Medieval Academy of America — work that shaped the intellectual standards of the field for a generation. He sat on the editorial boards of the Journal of Ecclesiastical History, Medievalia et Humanistica, and the Revue Mabillon, among others. He also served on the scientific council of the Revue d'Histoire Ecclésiastique.

As a visiting professor he lectured at Saint John's University in Collegeville, the Catholic University of America, Georgetown University, Princeton University, and Arizona State University — bringing his scholarship to a wide range of academic communities.

The breadth and depth of Constable's contributions were recognized by learned societies across the world. He was elected a Fellow of the Medieval Academy of America, the American Historical Association, the American Philosophical Society, the British Academy (FBA), the Royal Historical Society, the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in Paris, the Bavarian Academy of Sciences, and two of Italy's most prestigious scholarly institutions: the Instituto Lombardo and the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei. Honorary doctorates were conferred upon him by the University of Paris I, Georgetown University, Longwood University, and the Pontifical Institute of Medieval Studies in Toronto.

Giles Constable's legacy rests on his extraordinary capacity to combine meticulous archival and textual scholarship with broad synthetic vision. He did not merely edit documents or compile facts: he asked large questions about the nature of medieval religious experience, the meaning of monastic reform, and the relationship between institutional structures and individual spirituality, and he answered those questions with lucidity and authority. For scholars engaged in the study of medieval manuscript culture, religious iconography, and the ecclesiastical world of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, Constable's work remains an indispensable intellectual companion — a guide to the spiritual and cultural landscape within which the great artists and illuminators of the medieval centuries worked and believed.

Conti, Alessandro

Florence, 1946 - Siena, 5 May 1994

Alessandro Conti was an Italian art historian and the founding figure of the modern history of restoration as a scholarly discipline. He trained in one of the most demanding lineages of Italian connoisseurship, studying under Francesco Arcangeli, Paola Barocchi, Roberto Longhi, and Giovanni Previtali.

His academic career moved across three chairs that reflected the full range of his method: scienza e tecnica del restauro at Bologna, Storia dell'arte moderna at Milan, and finally Storia della critica d'arte at Siena, where he was teaching at the time of his death at only forty-eight.

His signal contribution was Storia del restauro e della conservazione delle opere d'arte (Electa, 1973; revised and expanded in 1988), the book that made the history of restoration a fully legitimate field of study. The project was undertaken at Roberto Longhi's urging, and Longhi provided the introductory essay for the first edition. Conti traced both the evolution of restoration theory and its concrete application, following debates through nineteenth-century Italy into the criteria that shaped twentieth-century conservation. The volume remains a standard reference. He complemented it by editing the Einaudi anthology Sul restauro (1988), which brought together key theoretical texts.

What set Conti apart was his refusal to separate connoisseurship and material science. He insisted on the physical reality of the artwork, combining archival and literary-source research with the study of workshop recipes, pigment and varnish alteration, and the damage left by poorly executed restorations. A physicist who knew him described his method as genuinely scientific in a systems-theory sense: each object treated as a unicum, to be understood in its own context.

His range was wide. Major works include La miniatura bolognese. Scuole e botteghe, 1270-1340 (1981), a rigorous account of Bolognese illumination in its most creative half-century; Michelangelo e la pittura a fresco. Tecnica e conservazione della Volta Sistina (1986), published while the Sistine cleaning was under way; Guida agli artisti del Quattrocento a Firenze (1989); I dintorni di Firenze (1983); and a monograph on Pontormo, published posthumously in 1995. His 1969 Paragone note on a Trecento drawing also remained important in later Pacino di Bonaguida scholarship.

The measure of his standing is visible in the memorial literature: Paola Barocchi wrote ricordi of him in both Prospettiva and Anagke; the Scuola Normale of Pisa dedicated a volume of the Quaderni del Seminario di Storia della Critica d'Arte to him, Ad Alessandro Conti (1946-1994) (1996); and Massimo Ferretti later framed the history of restoration itself as a line running "from Alessandro Conti to Roberto Longhi."

Cormack, Robin Sinclair

b. 27 September 1938

Robin Sinclair Cormack, FSA (born 27 September 1938) is one of Britain's foremost classicists and art historians, internationally recognized for his groundbreaking scholarship in Byzantine art, icon studies, and the cultural history of the Eastern Christian world. His career, spanning more than five decades, placed him at the heart of the Courtauld Institute of Art and cemented his reputation as a leading authority on the visual culture of Byzantium.

Cormack received his secondary education at Bristol Grammar School before reading classics at Exeter College, Oxford. He then pursued graduate study at the Courtauld Institute of Art, University of London, where he completed his doctoral dissertation on the art of Thessaloniki in the aftermath of iconoclasm. The dissertation was supervised by two giants of Byzantine studies, Hugo Buchthal and Cyril Mango, and it was Mango who first encouraged Cormack to extend his research at Dumbarton Oaks, the pre-eminent research center for Byzantine studies in Washington, D.C.

Cormack joined the Courtauld Institute as a lecturer in 1966, a position he held until 1982. During this period he took a formative leave of absence in the academic year 1972-73, when he became a visiting fellow in Byzantine studies at Dumbarton Oaks, an experience that profoundly shaped his research trajectory. He subsequently spent three years as a reader at the Warburg Institute, another prestigious center for cultural and classical studies, and also held a fellowship at Robinson College, Cambridge between 1984 and 1985.

He returned to the Courtauld as reader and then professor, eventually being appointed to a full Chair in the History of Art in 1991, a position he held until his retirement in 2004. During his tenure, he also served as the Institute's deputy director from 1999 to 2002. His photographs documenting architectural monuments are preserved in the Courtauld's Conway Library, currently being digitized as part of the broader Courtauld Connects project.

Rather than retreating from academic life, Cormack's retirement in 2004 opened a new phase of active scholarship.
