He was awarded a Leverhulme Emeritus Fellowship (2004-2006) and a scholarship at the Getty Research Institute in Los Angeles (2005-06), followed by an appointment as Special Professor in Classics at the University of Nottingham (2005-2008). He returned to Dumbarton Oaks once more as a visiting scholar in 2011. Since then, he has been an invited lecturer in the Faculty of Classics at the University of Cambridge, where his wife, the classicist Mary Beard, is Professor of Classics, and holds the title of Professor Emeritus in the History of Art at the University of London, as well as Senior Academic Visitor at Wolfson College, Cambridge.

His ongoing research centers on the cultural history of Saint Catherine's Monastery on the Sinai Peninsula, one of the oldest and most important repositories of Byzantine icons and manuscripts in the world, tracing its significance from Late Antiquity to the present.

Beyond his scholarly writing, Cormack made a significant contribution to the public understanding of Byzantine art through his curatorial work. His interest in exhibitions began in his student years, when he worked at the Institute of Contemporary Arts (ICA) under Roland Penrose and Herbert Read. His first independent exhibition featured Bulgarian icons in Edinburgh in the 1970s. He later served as a consultant to the Royal Academy of Arts, London for the landmark exhibitions From Byzantine to El Greco (1987) and The Art of Holy Russia: Icons from Moscow 1400-1660 (1998). His most celebrated curatorial achievement was co-curating, with Professor Maria Vassilaki of the University of Thessaly and the Benaki Museum, the Royal Academy's monumental exhibition Byzantium 330-1453 (2008-2009), which brought together iconic works from across the former Byzantine world.

Cormack's bibliography reflects a career dedicated to making Byzantine art accessible to both scholars and general readers. His debut monograph, Writing in Gold: Byzantine Society and its Icons (Oxford University Press, 1985), set a new standard for contextualizing icons within Byzantine social and religious life and was translated into French. Painting the Soul: Icons, Death Masks, and Shrouds (Reaktion Books, 1997) won the Runciman Award in 1998. His volume Byzantine Art (Oxford University Press, 2000), part of the Oxford History of Art series, became an essential introductory text for students of the field.

He also authored Icons (British Museum Press, 2007) and co-edited the Oxford Handbook of Byzantine Studies (2008) with Elizabeth Jeffreys and John Haldon. Together, these works constitute a body of scholarship that has shaped how Byzantine art is studied, taught, and appreciated internationally.

Cormack married Annabel Shackleton in 1961; they had a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Justin. After the dissolution of that marriage, he married the classicist and public intellectual Mary Beard in 1985; together they have a daughter, Zoe, and a son, Raphael Cormack (born 1987), who has himself become a scholar and translator. Cormack is a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London (FSA).

Corsano, Karen

active late 20th century

Karen Corsano is the author of one of the most influential single articles in the modern study of the Codex Amiatinus's prefatory quire: "The First Quire of the Codex Amiatinus and the Institutiones of Cassiodorus," published in Scriptorium 41 (1987). The article argued for a close and direct dependence of the Amiatinus's opening images and diagrams on material drawn from Cassiodorus's sixth-century monastery of Vivarium in Calabria, reconstructing in detail how the lost Codex Grandior and its accompanying apparatus might have shaped the Northumbrian book's design.

Corsano's argument set the terms for much of the subsequent debate on the question of the Amiatinus's models. Paul Meyvaert's major studies of 1996 and 2005 both engaged directly and critically with her conclusions, qualifying the degree of direct Cassiodoran dependence she proposed while accepting the broader Vivarium connection her work had helped to establish. The disagreement between the two positions — a closer transcription of Cassiodoran material against a more thoroughly Northumbrian redesign — remains one of the genuinely open questions in current scholarship on the manuscript's opening quire. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller account of this debate.

Crowe, Joseph Archer

London, 25 October 1825 – Gamburg an der Tauber, 6 September 1896

Joseph Archer Crowe was an English journalist, diplomat, and art historian whose work with Giovanni Battista Cavalcaselle helped give art history in English a more rigorous, evidence-based method. Born in London on 25 October 1825 and dead at Gamburg an der Tauber, in present-day Germany, on 6 September 1896, he belonged to that rare nineteenth-century generation whose careers moved easily between politics, letters, and scholarship.

Crowe was born into a cultivated and cosmopolitan family as the son of the journalist Eyre Evans Crowe, and he spent much of his boyhood in France, especially in Paris, where his father worked as a correspondent and where the family home became a meeting place for liberal and artistic circles. His education was directed largely by his father, and this early exposure to languages, journalism, and continental culture gave him an unusually international outlook for an English writer of his time. He was also the brother of the painter Eyre Crowe, so the visual arts were part of his family world from the beginning.

After returning to England in the 1840s, Crowe entered journalism, working for the Morning Chronicle and the Daily News before serving as a correspondent for the Illustrated London News during the Crimean War. He later reported for The Times during the Indian Mutiny and the Austro-Italian War, and he was present at the Battle of Solferino, an experience that placed him close to one of the defining military events of nineteenth-century Europe. This journalistic training sharpened the habits of close observation and factual scrutiny that later marked his writing on painting and attribution.

In 1860 Crowe entered the British diplomatic service as consul-general for Saxony at Leipzig, beginning a second career that ran alongside his scholarly work for decades. He later served at Dusseldorf, then as commercial attache in Berlin and Vienna, and eventually held responsibility for commercial affairs across Europe; he also represented Britain at the Danube Conference in 1883, the Samoa Conference in 1889, and the Telegraph Congress in Paris in 1890. His public service was recognized with appointment as Companion of the Bath in 1885 and Knight Commander of the Order of St. Michael and St. George in 1890, and his private life included a marriage in 1861 to Asta von Barby, with whom he had a large family.

Crowe's lasting fame rests above all on his partnership with Giovanni Battista Cavalcaselle, the Italian critic and connoisseur with whom he collaborated on a series of major works that transformed the study of European painting. Their first major book, The Early Flemish Painters of 1856, was followed by A New History of Painting in Italy from the Second to the Sixteenth Century and then by A History of Painting in North Italy, as well as substantial monographs on Titian and Raphael. In these works, Crowe supplied much of the prose structure and literary form, while the collaboration as a whole depended on sustained travel, firsthand viewing, stylistic comparison, and the attempt to reconstruct the historical development of individual artists.

What made Crowe important was not simply the number of books he wrote, but the method those books embodied: a disciplined reliance on direct visual examination, chronology, and connoisseurship rather than on inherited tradition alone. Even though many individual attributions made by Crowe and Cavalcaselle have been revised by later scholars, their work still stands near the beginning of modern art-historical writing in English because it treated painting as something to be studied critically, comparatively, and historically. Crowe published his memoirs, Reminiscences of Thirty-Five Years of My Life, in 1895, one year before his death, leaving behind the image of a Victorian scholar whose authority was built as much on travel and observation as on reading and theory.

Cuppini, Luciano

active second half of the 20th century

Luciano Cuppini was an Italian art historian active in Verona during the second half of the twentieth century, serving as a key link between the great tradition of Longhian criticism and local research on Venetian medieval and Renaissance art. Although he never held a university chair, his influence was exerted with extraordinary effectiveness through his teaching and scholarly contributions, leaving a lasting mark on Veronese art historiography.

Cuppini trained as a direct student of Roberto Longhi, the greatest Italian art historian of the twentieth century, known for his method based on close examination of works and a stylistic analysis of extraordinary acuity. This apprenticeship left an indelible mark on Cuppini's method: his ability to interpret pictorial and sculptural forms, to identify individual artists and workshops, and to link archival documents to anonymous artistic figures directly reflects the Longhi school. The correspondence preserved at the Longhi Foundation in Florence documents a letter-writing relationship between the two dating back at least to 1950, attesting to an intellectual association that continued even after their formative years.

Upon returning to Verona, Cuppini began a career as a teacher of art history at the Liceo Classico Scipione Maffei, one of the city's most prestigious schools, historically linked to Verona's antiquarian and literary culture. His teaching was instrumental in shaping a generation of art historians: among his students was Paola Marini, who would later direct the Civic Art Museums of Verona from 1997 to 2015 and subsequently the Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice until 2018. Cuppini was thus not only a researcher but also an educator capable of transmitting the rigor of the attribution method to future professionals in Italian cultural heritage.

On the scholarly level, Cuppini focused on two major thematic areas. The first concerns medieval painting and sculpture in Verona: together with Maria Teresa Cuppini, presumably a close collaborator or family member, he developed in the 1950s and 1960s the critical identification of the sculptural corpus of Giovanni di Rigino, the leading fourteenth-century Veronese sculptor and creator of signed works, thereby contributing to defining the artistic character of Verona under the Scaliger dynasty. His studies on the Arca di Cangrande I della Scala proposed specific attributions for the equestrian statues and funerary reliefs that subsequent critics would debate and, in part, revise.

The second area concerns thirteenth-century Italian painting in the broadest sense. In 1952, he published the essay Ranieri di Ugolino (Commentari, vol. 3, pp. 7-13), in which he identified the Pisan painter Ranieri di Ugolino with the so-called Master of San Martino, the creator of the large panel preserved at the National Museum of San Matteo in Pisa. This proposal, shared by Garrison and supported by Battisti in 1963, did not gain definitive acceptance from subsequent critics, but it attests to the breadth of Cuppini's interests, which ranged from local Veronese painting to thirteenth-century Pisan panel paintings.

A little-known but significant aspect of Cuppini's life is his collecting. In 1993, he donated to the Castelvecchio Museum in Verona a substantial private collection of ancient drawings, which remains a valuable documentary resource for the study of Venetian graphic art. This donation, likely made shortly before his death, was an act of returning to the Veronese community the heritage he had accumulated over decades of study and research.

Luciano Cuppini's legacy can be measured on two distinct yet complementary levels. As a researcher, his contributions to our understanding of Scaliger sculpture and thirteenth-century Pisan painting remain key references in the scholarly literature, cited in major studies on medieval art in Verona and Tuscany. As a teacher and mentor, his influence lives on in the careers of his students and in the direction of art studies in Verona during the second half of the twentieth century, at a time when the city was establishing its own museums and cultural institutions. He epitomizes the figure of the high-profile local scholar who, despite not holding a university chair, worked with a methodological rigor fully comparable to that of his academic colleagues.

Curzi, Gaetano

b. Rome, 29 April 1967

Gaetano Curzi is an Italian medievalist who teaches at the Università "G. d'Annunzio" of Chieti-Pescara. He took his doctorate in art history in 1999 through a consortium of the Universities of Rome "La Sapienza", Florence and Parma, with a thesis on the painting of the military orders in Europe and the Holy Land, focused on the Templar case.

His career began outside the university. From 1990 to 1999 he was an editor of the Enciclopedia dell'Arte Medievale at the Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana — for which he wrote entries including those on Crusader religious architecture and sculpture and on Templar painting and sculpture. From June 1999 to November 2001 he served at the Soprintendenza ai Beni Artistici e Storici di Napoli as a funzionario storico dell'arte, with responsibility as curator of the early paintings at the Museo di Capodimonte.

He became a researcher in medieval art history in October 2002, based at Chieti-Pescara until 2008 and at the University of Siena from 2008 to 2011, then associate professor from March 2011 to May 2018. He now teaches Byzantine art history and comparative medieval art history in Europe at Chieti-Pescara.

His work runs along two main lines. The first is the visual culture of the crusades and the military orders: his monograph La pittura dei Templari (Silvana, 2002) was the first systematic treatment of the pictorial decoration of Templar buildings, covering cycles at Cressac, Montsaunès and San Bevignate in Perugia and fragments and documented lost works across France, Spain and Italy. He has published later essays on crusades, military orders and warrior saints, and on figurative graffiti in Tarquinia.

The second is the art of Abruzzo and the Regno — a field directly relevant to this site. Key titles include Arredi lignei medievali. L'Abruzzo e l'Italia centromeridionale. Secoli XII–XIII (Silvana, 2007), and a series of studies and edited volumes on Abruzzese medieval art, codices, and regional architecture and patronage.

He has sat on scientific committees for exhibitions such as Tavole miracolose. Le icone medievali di Roma e Lazio (Palazzo Venezia, 2012–13) and Calabria angioina (1266–1382) (Altomonte, 2023–24), and co-edited the Festschrift for Alessandro Tomei, Storia dell'arte on the road.

D

Dalarun, Jacques

Boulogne-Billancourt, 1 November 1952

Jacques Dalarun is a French medievalist, one of the leading living historians of medieval religious life, hagiography, and the Franciscan movement. A member of the Institut de France (elected to the Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres in 2013) and a Corresponding Fellow of the Medieval Academy of America since 2018, he built his career largely within the French research system rather than a conventional university chair.

Trained at the Université Paris-I Panthéon-Sorbonne, Dalarun passed the agrégation in history in 1975 and earned his doctorate in medieval history in 1984 under the direction of Pierre Toubert, with a thesis on the reforming hermit-preacher Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the abbey of Fontevraud. He was a member of the École française de Rome from 1986 to 1989 and returned there as director of medieval studies from 1990 to 1997. In 1997 he joined the Centre national de la recherche scientifique (CNRS) as a director of research, a position he held until 2018, serving also as director of the Institut de recherche et d'histoire des textes (IRHT) and, from 1998 to 2004, vice-president of the governing council of the École nationale des chartes. He has held visiting professorships in Italy, the United States (notably St. Bonaventure University, New York), Japan, Australia, Lebanon, New Zealand, and Togo, and was awarded the Franciscan Institute Medal in 2016 and made a Chevalier de la Légion d'honneur in 2017.

Dalarun's scholarship moved from the Gregorian reform movement in western France — beginning with his prize-winning study of Robert of Arbrissel, L'impossible sainteté (1985) — to the study of female religious experience in thirteenth- to fifteenth-century Italy (Clare of Rimini, Micheline of Pesaro), and finally to a sustained, decades-long reexamination of Francis and Clare of Assisi. His method combines social and cultural history, philology, codicology, and a sharply critical historiographical eye toward the layered, often self-serving textual traditions surrounding medieval saints. He has identified numerous previously unknown medieval sources, most famously announcing in 2014 the rediscovery of Thomas of Celano's Vita brevior of Francis of Assisi — hailed by André Vauchez as "a major event for Franciscan history" and, on Dalarun's advice, subsequently acquired by the Bibliothèque nationale de France.

For the study of Angela of Foligno, Dalarun is a central and provocative voice. His 1995 essay "Angèle de Foligno a-t-elle existé?" — a title he later described as a deliberate boutade — reframed the central historiographical problem not as doubt over a historical tertiary's existence but as the uncertain relationship between the woman and the Liber attributed to her, subjecting the traditional Ferré chronology of her life to sharp critique. With Romana Guarnieri he convened the December 1995 Roman round table that produced the essential collective volume Angèle de Foligno: Le dossier (co-edited with Giulia Barone, École française de Rome, 1999), which remains the standard critical reassessment of her manuscript tradition, authorship, and cult.

Daniilia, Sister

active late 20th–21st century

Sister Daniilia is a Greek Orthodox nun and conservation scientist affiliated with the 'Ormylia' Art Diagnosis Centre at the Sacred Convent of the Annunciation in Ormylia, Chalkidiki, northern Greece. The Convent of the Annunciation — one of the most significant women's monasteries in Greece, founded in 1974 as a dependency of the Holy Monastery of Simonopetra on Mount Athos under the spiritual guidance of Elder Aimilianos Simonopetritis — combines Orthodox faith with scientific work and social outreach. The Art Diagnosis Centre was founded in 1996 under the auspices of the Sacred Convent and operates as a branch of the non-profit ORMYLIA Foundation, conducting interdisciplinary research in the analytical investigation, documentation, and preservation of artworks and monuments of cultural heritage, with particular expertise in Byzantine iconography. Sister Daniilia has been, from the earliest years of the Centre's existence, its leading scientific figure and the principal author of its foundational publications. She has collaborated with researchers from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the National Technical University of Athens, the University of Ioannina, and European institutions including the CNR in Perugia.

Sister Daniilia's scholarly contribution belongs to a discipline that did not exist before the late twentieth century and that she has helped to define: the systematic application of analytical chemistry and materials science to the study of Byzantine and post-Byzantine sacred art. Her research applies an arsenal of techniques — micro-Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (μFTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray analysis (SEM-EDS), gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC/MS), ultraviolet fluorescence microscopy, and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) — to answer questions that neither art historians nor conservators alone could resolve: what pigments did Byzantine painters use, what binding media held those pigments to wood and plaster, how have these materials degraded over time, and can we determine whether a given work is authentic and, if so, by whom?

The most celebrated of her early publications — and the one that established her international reputation — is the technical examination of the frescoes of the Protaton Church at Karyes on Mount Athos: "Panselinos' Byzantine wall-paintings of the Protaton Church, Mount Athos, Greece: a technical examination" (Journal of Cultural Heritage 1(2), 91–110, 2000), co-authored with Sotiropoulou, Bikiaris, Chryssoulakis, Salpistis, Karagiannis, Price, and Carlson. The paper presents an examination and technical analysis of fifteen representative thematic scenes covering approximately 65 square metres of these monumental works, documenting both original and subsequently restored areas through visible and ultraviolet photography, infrared reflectography, and colour measurements, while identifying pigments, binders, and layer stratigraphy through micro-Raman spectroscopy, μFTIR, X-ray diffraction, and SEM-EDS. The most consequential finding — established through gas chromatography-mass spectrometry — was that egg together with a modest amount of animal glue served as the organic binding media, and that the scenes were initially begun on wet plaster but completed after drying using these protein binding media. In other words, the workshop responsible for the Protaton frescoes used a mixed al fresco/al secco technique that defied the binary categories into which Byzantine painting had previously been placed, a finding of the first importance for both conservation strategy and the understanding of medieval Greek workshop practice. This study established the methodological template for all subsequent work at the Ormylia Centre. A complementary study followed in 2007 — "The Byzantine wall paintings from the Protaton Church on Mount Athos, Greece: tradition and science," Journal of Archaeological Science 34 (2007) — extending the investigation to the Chapel of St. Euthymios in Thessaloniki, stylistically attributed to the School of Panselinos, through a MOLAB project combining XRF, mid-FTIR, and UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy with laboratory study of selected cross-sections. The connection between the Protaton frescoes and the Chapel of St. Euthymios — both associated with the Macedonian School workshop of Michael Astrapas — means that Sister Daniilia's scientific work intersects directly with the attribution debates explored by art historians including Vapheiades and Marković: where they approach the question through signatures and stylistic analysis, she approaches it through material fingerprints.

One of the most significant applications of Sister Daniilia's methodology came through her collaboration with Robin Cormack and Maria Vassilaki on the technical analysis of El Greco's Baptism of Christ. By observing cross-sections under the optical microscope and analysing the materials through μRaman and μFTIR spectroscopies and HPLC, it was possible to reveal the "fingerprints" of the artist's brushwork, demonstrating that El Greco succeeded in combining traditional techniques of Byzantine icon-painting with the innovative practices of Venetian Renaissance art. The study, published in the Benaki Museum Journal in 2005, provided the first scientific corroboration of the attribution that art historians had long argued on stylistic grounds.

Sister Daniilia's research extends beyond monumental painting to the equally fragile medium of the illuminated manuscript. Her 2007 paper in the Journal of Raman Spectroscopy presents the results of research on two full-page medieval miniatures painted on isolated sheets of paper, establishing methodology for in-situ examination that avoids the need for micro-sampling — a critical consideration given the exceptional fragility and sanctity of the objects. A major methodological consolidation came in 2004 with a chapter in the authoritative Elsevier volume on non-destructive microanalysis: "Diagnostic methodology for the examination of Byzantine frescoes and icons: non-destructive investigation and pigment identification," in Non-Destructive Microanalysis of Cultural Heritage Materials, vol. XLII, Janssens and Van Grieken, eds. (Elsevier, Amsterdam, 2004), pp. 565–604 — a chapter that drew together the methodology developed at the Ormylia Centre across its first decade and has served as a primary reference for heritage science laboratories working on Byzantine material across Europe and beyond. Her 2010 review in Accounts of Chemical Research, co-authored with Sophia Sotiropoulou, brought the scientific study of Byzantine art to the attention of the international chemical research community through one of the flagship journals of the American Chemical Society. Her research further encompasses the analytical investigation of Cretan School icons and a study of the old katholikon of St. Stephen's Monastery at Meteora, tracing the technical transition from Byzantine to post-Byzantine painting methods in the Ottoman-period monasteries of Thessaly.

Sister Daniilia occupies a position in Byzantine studies that is, in the most literal sense, unique: she is the only scientist working at the intersection of Orthodox monastic life and peer-reviewed analytical chemistry who has built a sustained research programme specifically focused on Byzantine and post-Byzantine sacred art. The Ormylia Art Diagnosis Centre she represents has become one of the most cited laboratories in the heritage science literature dealing with Greek Orthodox material culture, and her publications appear in journals ranging from the Journal of Cultural Heritage and the Journal of Archaeological Science to the Journal of Raman Spectroscopy and Accounts of Chemical Research. Her work demonstrates that the Orthodox tradition of monastic service — of placing knowledge and skill at the disposal of the community and the sacred — can, in the right institutional context, produce scientific contributions of genuine international significance.

Darby, Peter

active 21st century

Peter Darby is a British historian of early medieval England associated with the University of Nottingham, specializing in the intellectual and theological world of the Venerable Bede, particularly Bede's engagement with biblical chronology and eschatology. His monograph Bede and the End of Time (Farnham: Ashgate, 2012) reassessed Bede's apocalyptic thought against the background of Insular computistical and exegetical traditions, and he co-edited, with Faith Wallis, the collective volume Bede and the Future (2014).

Darby's article "The Codex Amiatinus Maiestas Domini and the Gospel Prefaces of Jerome," published in Speculum 92 (2017), analyses the great image of the enthroned Christ that stands at the head of the New Testament in the manuscript, arguing that its composition — fusing Old Testament prophetic vision with New Testament fulfilment through the surrounding evangelist symbols — answers closely to the prefatory statements Jerome himself supplied for the Gospels. The reading exemplifies the broader shift in Amiatinus scholarship toward treating its images as exegetically motivated arguments rather than as decorative or merely reproductive elements. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion.

De Angelis, Luigi

Citta della Pieve, 1759 - Siena, 13 August 1832

Luigi De Angelis was one of the most significant figures in Sienese culture at the turn of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: theologian, librarian, scholar, and art historian, he played a decisive role in preserving Siena's artistic and literary heritage during the Napoleonic period.

Born in 1759 in Citta della Pieve (Perugia), where his father held a papal office, he moved with his family in 1764 to Piancastagnaio, in the Sienese area. Orphaned young, he found support with the Preti Ricci family of Abbadia San Salvatore. On 17 February 1775, still a teenager, he entered the convent of San Francesco in Siena as a novice, beginning a solid Franciscan ecclesiastical career.

After advanced theological studies, he earned a degree in Dogmatic Theology at the College of Saint Bonaventure in Rome in 1786. From 1791 he taught Philosophy and Moral Theology in the seminaries of Foligno and Florence, and in 1792 returned to Siena as custodian of the Franciscan custody.

His ascent in the Franciscan hierarchy was rapid: guardian of the monastery in 1798, examiner of clergy for the Diocese of Siena in 1801, and definitor for the Province of Tuscia in 1802. His scholarly prestige and ties with ruling elites led to his appointment, on 14 April 1803, to the chair of Dogmatic Theology at the University of Siena by Maria Luisa of Bourbon, regent queen of the Kingdom of Etruria. In 1805 he was also charged with reviewing librettos for operas and theatrical performances in Siena.

When the French administration abolished the University of Siena in 1808, De Angelis lost his chair but reoriented his career with remarkable diplomatic skill. On 11 March 1810 he was appointed librarian of the Public Library of Siena, reopened on 4 April 1810 as an institution of the Civic Community. In that office he transformed the library into a major center for collecting manuscripts, incunabula, and artworks from Napoleonic suppressions, expanding holdings from roughly ten thousand to more than forty-five thousand volumes.

His impact on art preservation was equally decisive. Paintings gathered from suppressed religious institutions, together with earlier collections assembled by Giuseppe Ciaccheri, formed the founding nucleus of what became the National Art Gallery of Siena. De Angelis can therefore be regarded as the effective founder of Siena's first public art museum.

With the reopening of the University in 1814, he resumed teaching theology while also serving as curator of the Cabinet of Fine Arts. In Sienese art historiography, he continued the municipal scholarly tradition associated with figures such as Giulio Mancini and Guglielmo Della Valle, promoting the reevaluation of Sienese painting against the dominant Florentine model. He devoted special attention to Fra Giacomo da Torrita (Jacopo Torriti), authoring Notizie istorico-critiche and praising him as a master of the renewal of Italian mosaic art and a precursor to Simone Martini.

He was also the first scholar to recognize the historical and artistic value of the Biccherna Panels, at a time when they were still largely neglected by critics.

Among his principal publications are Discorso storico su l'Università di Siena (Siena, 1810), Ragguaglio del nuovo Istituto delle Belle Arti stabilito in Siena con la descrizione della sala nella quale sono distribuiti cronologicamente i quadri dell'antica Scuola Senese (Siena, 1816), and Capitoli dei Disciplinati della venerabile Compagnia della Madonna sotto le volte dell'Imperiale e Reale Spedale di Santa Maria della Scala di Siena (Siena, 1818), which includes on pages 153-282 an important catalogue of Italian-language manuscripts in the Siena Municipal Library that remains a key reference for researchers. He also left an unpublished manuscript, Di Giulio Mancini elogio, later published and studied as evidence of his commitment to revaluing Sienese art history.

In 1825 he was appointed provost of the collegiate church of Santa Maria in Provenzano in Siena. The following year he purchased, with his own funds, the ruined chapel of San Francesco all'Alberino, restored it, and dedicated to it the monograph Dell'albero di San Francesco vicino alle mura di Siena (Siena, 1827). He died in Siena on 13 August 1832 and was buried in that same chapel. His biography has been comprehensively reconstructed by Alessandro Leoncini in Luigi De Angelis. A Life Between University, Library, and Art Gallery (University of Siena, 2014), presented at the Biblioteca degli Intronati in March 2015.

De Benedictis, Cristina

active from the 1970s; Professor of Museology, University of Florence

Cristina De Benedictis is an Italian art historian whose career divides, with unusual clarity, into two phases: an early formation as a specialist in Sienese Trecento painting, and a subsequent career-defining shift into museology and the history of collecting, the field in which she taught for over thirty years as professor of Museologia e critica artistica e del restauro at the University of Florence.

Her early work belongs to the connoisseurial tradition of Sienese studies. La pittura senese 1330-1370 (Florence, 1979) surveyed the generation of painters active between the death of the Lorenzetti and the last quarter of the century, Luca di Tommè among them, and remains a point of reference in the bibliography on the period notwithstanding the more specialised monographs that followed it, such as Sherwood A. Fehm's 1986 catalogue of Luca's own work.

From the 1990s De Benedictis's principal published work moved toward museology and the history of collecting. Her manual Per la storia del collezionismo italiano: fonti e documenti (first published 1994; 2nd ed., Milan, 1998; reissued Florence, 2015) traces the phenomenon of collecting from the Trecento to the eighteenth century, from Medicean taste and artists' workshops to the formation of the modern museum gallery. She edited a modern edition of Marco Antonio Michiel's Notizia d'opere del disegno (Florence, 2000) and, with Maria Grazia Marzi, the digitised Epistolario of the antiquarian Anton Francesco Gori (Florence, 2004), and she directed the Florentine monograph series Le voci del Museo. A festschrift, Scritti di museologia e di storia del collezionismo in onore di Cristina De Benedictis (Edifir, 2013), gathered essays by colleagues and former students in recognition of her thirty years of teaching in the discipline.

De Francovich, Géza

Gorizia, 1902 – Rome, 1996

Géza de Francovich was one of the most wide-ranging and methodologically rigorous Italian art historians of the twentieth century, whose scholarly interests spanned from Romanesque sculpture to the art of the ancient Near East.

De Francovich was born on August 28, 1902, in Gorizia — then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire — into an aristocratic family of Hungarian origin. He attended the German-language section of the Staatsgymnasium in Gorizia before the First World War disrupted his youth. After the conflict, he moved to Florence, where he completed his university degree in 1925. His formation thus combined Central European cultural sensibility with a deep immersion in the Italian art historical tradition, an unusual and productive duality that would shape his entire career.

Following his graduation, de Francovich took up a post as inspector at the Soprintendenza of Perugia from 1926 to 1928. He was subsequently recruited by the philosopher Giovanni Gentile to serve as a contributor to the Enciclopedia Italiana, where he worked alongside some of the leading art historians of the time — Pietro Toesca, Lionello Venturi, and Mario Salmi — whose assistant he also became at the University of Rome. He obtained his libera docenza (the Italian qualification for independent university teaching) from 1937, and from 1956 to 1972 he held the chair of medieval art history at the Università degli Studi di Roma "La Sapienza".

De Francovich's research was characterized by a rigorous historical method that placed artistic objects firmly within their broader ideological and cultural contexts. His thematic range was exceptional: he moved from Lombard Carolingian and Ottonian art to Romanesque wood sculpture, from Byzantine ivory carving to Achaemenid and Sasanian art, always grounding his analysis in direct examination of the monuments themselves. His 1937 article "A Romanesque School of Wood Carvers in Central Italy," published in the Art Bulletin, established an early international reputation. His most celebrated work remains the monumental two-volume Benedetto Antelami, architetto e scultore e l'arte del suo tempo (1952), a landmark study of the great Romanesque sculptor, sponsored by Bernard Berenson.

De Francovich traveled extensively throughout his career, conducting fieldwork not only across Europe but throughout the former Byzantine Empire and the Middle East. In 1966, he coordinated a team of Italian scholars from La Sapienza in a series of study trips to the historic regions of Armenia, resulting in extensive photographic documentation of medieval churches and monasteries. For the Italian National Research Council (CNR), he directed the multi-volume projects Studi di architettura medievale armena (4 vols., 1971–73) and Studi sulla pittura medievale campana (3 vols., 1974–81). His intellectual journey concluded with Santuari e tombe rupestri dell'antica Frigia (1990), a study of rock-cut sanctuaries in ancient Phrygia (modern Turkey), published when he was nearly ninety years old. He died in Rome on November 24, 1996.

De Lagarde, Paul

Berlin, 2 November 1827 - Göttingen, 22 December 1891

Paul de Lagarde (born Paul Anton Bötticher, and known for most of his career under the name he adopted from a great-aunt) was a German orientalist and biblical philologist who held the chair of Oriental Languages at the University of Göttingen from 1869 until his death. He was a pioneer of the critical study of the Septuagint and of the Syriac and Latin biblical versions, and his editorial and text-critical work on these traditions was, by the technical standards of his own field, genuinely important and influential on later scholarship.

It is necessary to record, without euphemism, that Lagarde was also a virulent German nationalist and antisemitic polemicist whose political writings — calling, among other things, for the exclusion and destruction of Jews from German national life — were influential on later völkisch and National Socialist ideology and are rightly remembered as a discreditable and dangerous body of work, wholly separate from and not excused by his technical contributions to biblical philology.

In the context of the Codex Amiatinus, Lagarde is remembered for a much narrower matter: an isolated early dissent from the confident nineteenth-century consensus that the manuscript was a sixth-century Italian production. This dissent did not, by itself, dislodge the prevailing attribution or supply the positive evidence needed to establish the manuscript's true Northumbrian origin; that demonstration required the convergence of physical examination and textual recovery achieved by Giovanni Battista de Rossi and Fenton John Anthony Hort in the 1880s. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database, which notes Lagarde's dissent as one isolated voice within the longer historiography of the manuscript's misattribution and its correction.

De Marchi, Andrea

Biella, 1962

Andrea De Marchi is one of Italy's leading scholars of medieval art history and currently serves as Full Professor of Medieval Art History at the University of Florence. Trained in Siena under Luciano Bellosi, he developed within one of the most rigorous traditions of Italian medieval art criticism, combining close stylistic reading with documentary and liturgical contextualization.

After serving as an inspector at the Soprintendenza of Pisa (1994-1995), he was researcher at the University of Lecce (1995-2000) and then professor at the University of Udine (2000-2006), before moving to Florence. He is affiliated with the SAGAS Department (History, Archaeology, Geography, Art, and Performing Arts), based at Via Gino Capponi 9, Florence.

De Marchi's research focuses primarily on painting, drawing, and miniature art from the Gothic to the Renaissance, with particular attention to the decoration of mendicant churches, especially Franciscan contexts, in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. A further central axis of his work is the evolution of the altarpiece from Gothic to Renaissance forms, examined through workshop practice, patronage, and the liturgical functions of images.

He has also made significant contributions to philological and attributional questions, especially in the reconstruction of fragmented contexts and dismembered works. His method repeatedly links objects to their original spatial and devotional settings, clarifying how artistic programs were read and used inside ecclesiastical spaces.

His first major monograph, Gentile da Fabriano. Viaggio nella pittura italiana alla fine del gotico (1992; reissued 2006), remains a fundamental reference for late Gothic painting. He later published major studies on fifteenth-century painting in the Marche, including Pittori a Camerino nel Quattrocento (2002) and, with Matteo Mazzalupi, Pittori ad Ancona nel Quattrocento (2008). He was also co-author, with Francesco Caglioti, of the exhibition project on Verrocchio at Palazzo Strozzi (Florence, 2019).

Since 2015, De Marchi has chaired the Association "Corpus of Florentine Painting," the long-term project dedicated to digitizing and critically updating the historic corpus of medieval and Renaissance Florentine painting begun in the early twentieth century. He also supervises doctoral research on late Gothic and early Renaissance Sienese painting, reflecting an active and ongoing role in advanced scholarly training.

Particularly relevant for manuscript and materials-based studies is his 2016 essay Aureola e grandine. La materia che cattura la luce e la trasfigura: esperienze nella pittura tardogotica, in which he investigates the relationship between matter, light, and spiritual transfiguration in late Gothic painting.

De Rossi, Giovanni Battista

Rome, 23 February 1822 - Castel Gandolfo, 20 September 1894

Giovanni Battista de Rossi was the foremost Italian archaeologist and epigrapher of the nineteenth century and the founder, in any disciplined modern sense, of Christian archaeology. His rediscovery and systematic exploration of the catacombs of Rome, and his decipherment and publication of the city's Christian inscriptions, placed the study of the early Church on an evidentiary footing it had not previously possessed, and his methods — patient topographical reconnaissance, exhaustive collation of texts, and a refusal to publish beyond what the material itself could support — became the working standard of the field.

Born in Rome on 23 February 1822 into a family of the professional middle class, de Rossi showed an early and abiding fascination with the physical remains of the ancient and early Christian city. As a young man he came under the influence of Giuseppe Marchi, a Jesuit scholar of Christian antiquities, and it was in the company of Marchi that de Rossi made, in 1849, the discovery that determined the direction of his life's work: a fragment of an inscribed marble slab, found in a vineyard on the Via Appia, that he correctly identified as part of the tombstone of Pope Cornelius and as evidence for the long-lost location of the catacomb of Callixtus. Systematic excavation of the site began in 1854 and continued, under de Rossi's direction, for decades.

De Rossi's principal scholarly monument is the Inscriptiones Christianae urbis Romae septimo saeculo antiquiores, a corpus of the dated and datable Christian inscriptions of Rome down to the seventh century, published in two volumes (1857 and 1861, with later supplements) and still a foundational reference for the epigraphy of early Christian Rome. In parallel he produced the three-volume La Roma sotterranea cristiana (1864–1877), a comprehensive topographical and historical account of the catacombs that combined excavation reports, inscriptions, and early Christian art into a single synthetic argument about the organization and beliefs of the Roman Church in its first centuries. He founded and for many years edited the Bullettino di archeologia cristiana, the journal that gave the new discipline its regular forum. Pope Pius IX created for him the post of custodian of the sacred cemeteries, and Leo XIII, under whom de Rossi's authority in matters of Christian antiquity was unrivalled, drew on his expertise repeatedly for the Vatican's own scholarly enterprises.

It was in service of one such enterprise that de Rossi made his contribution to the study of a manuscript far removed, on its face, from the Roman catacombs: the great Bible then known as the Codex Amiatinus and universally assigned, on the strength of its script and its dedication page, to sixth-century Italy. Working from the eighteenth-century observation of the Laurentian librarian Angelo Maria Bandini that the manuscript's dedicatory verses had been altered, and connecting this with Bede's statement that the Northumbrian abbot Ceolfrith had carried a pandect of Jerome's version to Rome as a gift for the tomb of St Peter, de Rossi proposed in 1886, and set out formally two years later in a contribution to the jubilee volume presented to Leo XIII by the Vatican Library (Al sommo pontefice Leone XIII omaggio giubilare della Biblioteca vaticana, Rome, 1888), that the codex was in fact Ceolfrith's gift, its dedication tampered with to disguise an Anglo-Saxon origin behind the name of a Lombard abbot. The proposal, though not yet proof, redirected attention to the erased verses and to the neglected Vita Ceolfridi, and it was on this foundation that Fenton John Anthony Hort shortly afterward demonstrated the case conclusively by recovering the manuscript's original wording. See Fenton John Anthony Hort for the completion of the argument, and, for the fuller account of the episode, the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database.

De Rossi held no university chair for most of his career, working instead within the ambit of the Vatican Library and the papal antiquities administration, but his influence on the academic study of early Christianity was pervasive, and he corresponded and collaborated with the leading historians, theologians, and archaeologists of his generation across Europe. He died at Castel Gandolfo on 20 September 1894, honored as the scholar who had given Christian Rome back its own documented history, and his identification of the true origin of the Amiatine Bible stands as one of the more unexpected extensions of that lifelong project into the manuscript culture of Anglo-Saxon Northumbria.

Del Migliore, Ferdinando Leopoldo

Florence, 1628 – Florence, 1696

Ferdinando Leopoldo Del Migliore was a Florentine antiquarian and genealogist whose Firenze città nobilissima illustrata (1684) is a systematic topographical description of Florence's churches, palaces, streets and monuments, organised quarter by quarter in the erudite antiquarian manner of the later seventeenth century. Drawing on archival research, inscriptions, and direct inspection of the buildings themselves, Del Migliore recorded the location, patronage and, where known, authorship of paintings, sculptures and tombs across the city with a documentary thoroughness that places his work alongside Bocchi–Cinelli and, a generation later, Richa among the indispensable topographical sources for Florentine art history.

The value of Del Migliore's testimony lies precisely in its descriptive comprehensiveness at a fixed moment before the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century remodellings, demolitions and dispersals that altered or destroyed so much of what he saw: church interiors subsequently reordered, altarpieces moved or lost, decorative campaigns overpainted or removed. For the reconstruction of the original setting and condition of Trecento and later Florentine church decoration, his Firenze illustrata remains, alongside the other great topographical guides of the period, a primary point of reference for modern scholarship.

Delisle, Léopold

Valognes, 24 October 1826 - Paris, 22 July 1910

Léopold Victor Delisle was born on 24 October 1826 in Valognes, a small Norman town in the Manche department of northwestern France, into a family of modest provincial bourgeoisie with deep roots in the Norman countryside. This origin proved formative in ways that went beyond mere geography: Normandy, with its extraordinary density of medieval abbeys, its rich documentary heritage stretching back to the Carolingian era, and its particular place in the history of French feudalism, provided the young Delisle with his first intellectual landscape and would remain a central preoccupation of his scholarship throughout his life.

His early education at the collège of Valognes and subsequently at Caen distinguished him as a student of exceptional memory and philological aptitude. On the advice of local scholars who recognized his unusual gifts, he was directed toward Paris and the institution that would definitively shape his career: the École nationale des Chartes, the specialized school founded in 1821 for the training of archivists, palaeographers, and historians capable of working directly with primary medieval sources.

Delisle entered the École des Chartes in 1844 and graduated in 1847, submitting as his thesis a study that already announced the scope and seriousness of his historical ambitions: Études sur la condition de la classe agricole et l'état de l'agriculture en Normandie au Moyen Âge (published in expanded form in 1851). This work — a systematic analysis of medieval agrarian structures in Normandy based on direct examination of charters, cartularies, and administrative records — was immediately recognized as a contribution of lasting value to the economic and social history of medieval France. Its methodology, grounded in exhaustive archival research and a refusal to speculate beyond what the documents could support, established the characteristic virtues of all Delisle's subsequent scholarship.

At the École des Chartes, Delisle benefited from the teaching of Jules Quicherat, one of the founding figures of French medieval archaeology, and from the broader intellectual atmosphere of an institution devoted to what the French called érudition in its most rigorous sense: the patient, meticulous, deeply learned study of primary sources without concession to eloquence at the expense of accuracy. This formation instilled habits of mind — archival thoroughness, critical scepticism toward received attributions, the systematic comparison of witnesses — that Delisle would deploy at an almost incomprehensible scale of productivity over the following six decades.

In 1852, Delisle was appointed to the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris — then housed in the Palais Mazarin on the rue de Richelieu — as an assistant in the manuscript department. He would remain in that institution for the rest of his professional life, ascending through successive positions until his appointment as Administrateur général (Director General) in 1874, a post he held with distinction until his retirement in 1905. For more than half a century, Delisle and the Bibliothèque nationale were virtually synonymous in the minds of European scholars.

His most enduring institutional achievement was the three-volume (plus atlas) Le Cabinet des manuscrits de la Bibliothèque nationale (1868–1881), a work of extraordinary scope that constituted the first systematic history of the formation of the manuscript collections held by France's national library. Drawing on decades of archival investigation, Delisle traced the provenance of thousands of manuscripts — their monastic, royal, and private origins; their paths of acquisition through the upheavals of the Renaissance, the Wars of Religion, the Revolution, and the Napoleonic confiscations; and the history of the cataloguing efforts that had preceded his own. The Cabinet des manuscrits remains to this day the indispensable starting point for any inquiry into the history of French manuscript collections, and a model of what institutional bibliographical history can achieve.

Among the most dramatic episodes of Delisle's career was his central role in addressing the consequences of one of the most audacious manuscript thefts in modern history. Guglielmo Libri, an Italian mathematician and bibliophile who had served as Inspector General of French Libraries under the July Monarchy, had systematically stolen hundreds of manuscripts and rare books from French provincial libraries and archives during his official inspection tours in the 1830s and 1840s. Libri, having been exposed and forced to flee to England, had sold a large portion of his fraudulently acquired collection to Lord Ashburnham, the English bibliophile, who thus became the unsuspecting possessor of stolen French national heritage.

Delisle undertook the painstaking work of identifying the stolen items by systematically comparing Libri's sale catalogues against the records of French libraries and archives, matching individual manuscripts to their original institutional homes through codicological analysis, ex-libris, and the evidence of older catalogues. His report, produced with meticulous documentary precision, constituted an irrefutable indictment and provided the legal and scholarly basis for the French government's eventual negotiation for the repatriation of the Ashburnham-Libri collection in 1888. A parallel inquiry into the Barrois collection, another assemblage of manuscripts of partly dubious provenance held at Ashburnham Place, resulted in the return of further materials. Delisle published his findings in the Catalogue des manuscrits des fonds Libri et Barrois (1888), transforming a legal and diplomatic affair into a permanent scholarly resource.

This episode illustrated a characteristic of Delisle's intelligence rarely found in combination: the ability to bring the full resources of palaeographical and codicological scholarship to bear on questions with immediate practical and juridical consequences.

For historians of medieval art and book illumination, Delisle's most consequential contributions lie in his systematic study of the great manuscript libraries of medieval French royalty and nobility, and in his foundational work on the identification and dating of illuminated manuscripts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

His Recherches sur la librairie de Charles V (2 volumes, 1907) reconstructed, from inventory records, accounts, and surviving manuscripts, the extraordinary royal library assembled by Charles V of France (1338–1380) — a collection of some 1,200 volumes, mostly housed in the Louvre, that constituted the most important secular library in fourteenth-century Europe and the direct ancestor of the Bibliothèque nationale itself. Delisle's reconstruction identified the surviving manuscripts from this dispersed collection, analysed the illuminators and scribes who had worked for the royal workshop, and situated Charles V's patronage within the broader context of late fourteenth-century Parisian book culture. The work provided the essential framework within which subsequent art historians — from Henri Martin to François Avril — would develop the detailed study of Parisian Gothic illumination.

His Notice de douze livres royaux du XIIIe et du XIVe siècle (1902) presented in meticulous detail twelve manuscripts of exceptional quality from the royal French collections, including liturgical books, Books of Hours, and Psalters, analysing their decoration, their scribal hands, and their relationship to royal patronage. This work exemplifies Delisle's approach to illuminated manuscripts: grounded always in documentary evidence (inventory entries, colophons, heraldic identification), proceeding from the particular to the general, and attentive to the relationship between the material object and its historical context.

Of particular importance for the history of Flemish and Franco-Flemish illumination was Delisle's early recognition of the exceptional significance of the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, the magnificent Book of Hours produced for Jean, Duke of Berry by the Limbourg Brothers around 1410–1416. Delisle's analysis of the duke's inventories and his identification of the manuscript's place within the broader context of Berry's extraordinary patronage laid the groundwork for all subsequent scholarship on this supreme monument of late medieval illumination.

Alongside his work at the Bibliothèque nationale, Delisle maintained throughout his life an intense commitment to the documentary history of medieval Normandy, producing a series of studies that transformed the understanding of Norman institutional, ecclesiastical, and cultural history.

His Cartulaire normand de Philippe-Auguste, Louis VIII, saint Louis et Philippe le Hardi (1852) edited a fundamental collection of royal acts relating to Normandy under the Capetian monarchy. His work on the Catalogue des actes de Philippe-Auguste contributed to the monumental enterprise of editing the royal French charters. His studies of Norman abbeys — including Saint-Wandrille, Jumièges, and Mont-Saint-Michel — illuminated the role of Norman Benedictine monasticism in the preservation and production of manuscripts from the Carolingian era onward.

The Rouleaux des morts du IXe au XVe siècle (1866), an edition of the extraordinary medieval mortuary rolls circulated among monasteries to announce the deaths of abbots and request prayers, was both a significant contribution to liturgical history and a palaeographical achievement of the first order, requiring the analysis of documents from dozens of different scriptoria across a period of six centuries.

Among Delisle's most technically demanding contributions to palaeography was his systematic study of Carolingian manuscripts, and in particular his investigation of the great pandect Bibles produced under the influence of Alcuin of York at Tours in the early ninth century. His essay on Les Bibles de Alcuin and his broader work on Tours manuscripts established essential criteria for distinguishing the output of the Touraine scriptoria from related Carolingian centres, and contributed to the understanding of the role of Alcuin's reform in the standardization of the Carolingian minuscule — the script that would become the foundation of all Western book hands through the medieval period and, via humanist revival, of modern Roman typography.

This work situated Delisle within the broader tradition of Carolingian palaeographical scholarship that extended from Mabillon through Traube and into the twentieth century, and demonstrated his command of the earliest stratum of the medieval Latin manuscript tradition as well as its later developments.

In 1856, at the age of thirty, Delisle was elected a member of the Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres — France's premier learned society for historical, philological, and archaeological scholarship — a recognition of the extraordinary maturity and authority of his early work. He would eventually serve as the Academy's Secrétaire perpétuel (Permanent Secretary), the most senior administrative position in the institution, from 1876 to 1907, transforming it into a major centre for the coordination of collaborative scholarly enterprises.

In this role, Delisle oversaw and contributed to a series of monumental collective projects that defined the infrastructure of French medieval studies for generations: the continuation of the Recueil des historiens des Gaules et de la France, the Notices et extraits des manuscrits de la Bibliothèque nationale, and the broader programme of cataloguing French manuscript collections in provincial libraries — an enterprise that would eventually produce the multivolume Catalogue général des manuscrits des bibliothèques publiques de France, still an essential reference tool.

Delisle's published output — exceeding 800 items by the end of his life, ranging from brief notices to multi-volume monographs — is distinguished by qualities that reflect both his formation and his temperament. He combined an almost supernatural memory for manuscript details with a principled refusal to claim more than the evidence could support. His prose, though never elegant in the French literary sense, is a model of scholarly exactitude: every assertion documented, every attribution argued from physical evidence, every identification supported by multiple converging criteria.

His approach to illuminated manuscripts was pioneering in its insistence on the codicological totality of the object: script, parchment quality, quire structure, rubrics, calendar saints, heraldry, ownership inscriptions, and binding evidence were all brought to bear in establishing date, origin, and provenance — a method that anticipates the systematic codicological analysis that would be theorized by scholars such as Léon Gilissen and Albert Derolez in the twentieth century.

He was also exceptional among nineteenth-century scholars in the breadth of his international scholarly relationships. He corresponded regularly with English, German, Italian, Belgian, and Dutch medievalists, contributed to foreign learned journals, and participated in the international congresses of orientalists, bibliographers, and historians that were a feature of late nineteenth-century intellectual life. His international standing was recognized by election to numerous foreign academies and by honorary degrees from universities across Europe.

Delisle retired from the Bibliothèque nationale in 1905, after more than fifty years of service, but continued to work with undiminished energy. His last major publication, the Recherches sur la librairie de Charles V, appeared in 1907, when he was eighty years old, and demonstrated no diminution of the analytical power that had characterized his work half a century earlier.

He died in Paris on 22 July 1910, aged eighty-three, mourned by the entire community of European medieval scholarship as the greatest librarian and manuscript scholar of his era. His funeral at the Institut de France brought together historians, philologists, archivists, and diplomats from across the continent in tribute to a career of extraordinary length, breadth, and sustained excellence.

The legacy of Léopold Delisle operates on several distinct levels, each of lasting significance.

As an institutional figure, he transformed the Bibliothèque nationale from a relatively passive repository into an active research institution, establishing cataloguing standards, accessioning procedures, and curatorial practices that continue to shape the library to this day. His conception of the national library as a centre of scholarship rather than merely a storehouse of books influenced the development of major research libraries across Europe.

As a palaeographer and codicologist, his systematic analysis of Latin script traditions and his development of provenance methodology established criteria and approaches that remain foundational. His work on Carolingian manuscripts, royal French libraries, and the Norman documentary tradition defined entire subfields of medieval studies.

As a historian of illuminated manuscripts, his reconstructions of the libraries of Charles V and the Duke of Berry, and his identification of key illuminated manuscripts through documentary analysis, provided the essential framework within which the art history of French and Flemish Gothic illumination was subsequently developed by Henri Martin, Paul Durrieu, François Avril, and Miranda Snijders, among many others.

For anyone working today in medieval manuscript studies — whether as palaeographer, codicologist, art historian, or archivist — Delisle's work remains a constant point of reference: a standard of scholarly rigour, archival thoroughness, and interpretive restraint that the intervening century of methodological development has refined but not superseded.

Della Valle, Guglielmo

Moncalvo, 1746 - Turin, 1805

Guglielmo della Valle was an Italian art writer and Conventual Franciscan friar, now regarded as a key figure in eighteenth-century Italian art historiography. His importance for medieval art studies lies in his pioneering archival research on early Sienese and Tuscan painting, carried out well before the discipline assumed its modern academic form.

Likely born in 1745-1746 in Moncalvo, in the Monferrato region, to Guglielmo Antonio Della Valle and Anna Maria De Ferrari, he entered the Franciscan convent in Pinerolo in 1762 at a young age. As a Conventual friar he traveled extensively across Italy, studying firsthand the works of the major schools of Florence, Siena, and Pisa. In Rome, he became assistant to the Order and general secretary in 1783, and in 1784 he was appointed prior of the convent of the Twelve Apostles.

His principal achievement is the three-volume Lettere sanesi sopra le belle arti (Rome, 1782-1786), a monumental publication of enduring value for its documentary and archival content. The first volume addresses general methodological and historical issues; the second, composed of twenty-three monographs, concentrates largely on Sienese painting; and the third, with thirty-three letters, examines specific painters and sculptors, mostly Sienese, including a foundational letter to Abbot Lanzi on the Tuscan schools.

Della Valle advanced an original and controversial historiographical thesis, arguing that the Sienese school was older and more autonomous than the Florentine one, and that Florentine painting had effectively declined after Cimabue while Sienese traditions endured longer. Although later scholarship rejected this larger framework for lack of sufficient documentary support, several of his insights proved remarkably prescient: he identified the influence of Giunta Pisano on Cimabue, that of Nicola and Giovanni Pisano on Giotto, and emphasized the Roman component in Giotto's formation through figures such as Pietro Cavallini and Jacopo Torriti.

In 1791 he edited an important version of Vasari's lives, revising and updating descriptions through his own research. This edition remained a significant bibliographic reference for art criticism well into the late nineteenth century and confirms his role as a transitional figure between antiquarian erudition and modern historical method.

Delpriori, Alessandro

Fabriano (Marche), active 21st century

Alessandro Delpriori is one of Italy's most active art historians in the field of medieval and late Gothic painting in central Italy, with particular attention to the schools of Umbria and the Marche between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries. Originally from Fabriano, a city central to the history of Italian late Gothic painting, he has developed a scholarly profile in which local artistic traditions are read within broader interregional networks of production, patronage, and stylistic exchange.

He completed his secondary studies at the "V. Volterra" scientific high school in Fabriano (diploma, 1996), then earned a degree in History and Conservation of Cultural Heritage at the University of Macerata (2004). He subsequently obtained a PhD in Art History at the University of Florence between 2008 and 2010. This training consolidated his specialization in medieval and late Gothic visual culture, with a focus on attributional issues, workshop dynamics, and the reconstruction of regional artistic identities in central Italy.

Delpriori is currently Professor and Researcher in Art History at the University of Camerino, where since 2015 he has taught in the Bachelor's program in Technology and Diagnostics for Conservation and Restoration. He has also taught at the University of Macerata and at the University of Florence. Alongside academic teaching, he has held significant institutional roles: from 2008 to 2011 he served as director and curator of the collections of the Cariverona Foundation and the Domus Foundation for Modern and Contemporary Art in Verona; from 2011 to 2014 he was curator of the Frascione Collection in Florence, overseeing research, cataloging, and restoration projects.

He collaborates with the Cini Foundation in Venice on the updating of catalogues of works and is a member of the Board of Directors of the Museum System of the Province of Macerata. His principal research interests include medieval painting and sculpture in central Italy, with specific studies on Gentile da Fabriano, fourteenth-century wooden sculpture in Umbria and the Marche, the Master of the Fabriano Crucifix, Luca di Paolo, Lorenzo d'Alessandro, and the early activity of Raphael in the Marche context. His scholarly output includes monographs, essays, and papers, including approximately thirty-three contributions published on his Academia.edu profile.

Among his best-known publications are volumes such as The School of Spoleto, Masterpieces of the 14th Century, Luca di Paolo and the Renaissance in the Marche, Lorenzo d'Alessandro, and Capriccio and Nature. He has curated major exhibitions, including Masterpieces of the 14th Century. Giotto's Workshop, Spoleto, and the Apennines, and has participated in public scholarly forums such as the Passaggi Festival (2023). Between 2014 and 2019 he also served as Mayor of Matelica, combining academic research with civic and administrative responsibility. His profile is therefore notable for the integration of specialist art-historical scholarship and sustained commitment to local cultural governance.

Demus, Otto

1902 – 1990

Otto Demus was an Austrian art historian and Byzantinist widely regarded as one of the towering figures of twentieth-century medieval art scholarship. Hans Belting famously described him as "the eye" of art history in his areas of study, in recognition of Demus's exceptional visual acuity and connoisseurship.

Demus studied art history at the University of Vienna between 1921 and 1928 under Josef Strzygowski and received his doctorate summa cum laude. He is generally considered part of the second Vienna School of Art History, rooted in the theoretical legacy of Alois Riegl and committed to understanding the artwork as a functional perceptual whole rather than as a merely documentary object. In keeping with this approach, Demus consistently analyzed how figures, architecture, and light operated together in decorative programs to produce a unified visual and spiritual experience.

After the annexation of Austria in 1938, Demus refused to cooperate with the Nazi regime and emigrated to England in 1939. During the war years in London, he worked on what became his most theoretically foundational book, Byzantine Mosaic Decoration (1947), a project first conceived during his earlier fieldwork in Greece, Sicily, and Venice in the 1920s and 1930s.

Among Demus's most original and lasting contributions is the concept of the space icon (Raum-Ikone). In his analysis of middle Byzantine mosaic programs, he argued that Byzantine artists did not rely on Western linear perspective, which draws the eye into illusionistic depth, but instead employed a "negative perspective" in which figures seem to project outward toward the beholder. In this reading, curved apses, vaults, and domes become active collaborators with mosaic imagery, producing a strong sense of presence in the real space of the worshipper and fundamentally reframing the image-viewer relationship in Byzantine art.

Two monument groups occupied decades of his research: the Basilica of San Marco in Venice and the Norman churches of Sicily. His four-volume The Mosaics of San Marco in Venice remains the authoritative study of the basilica's decoration, and he was the first scholar to assess fully the central role of mosaic as San Marco's most indigenous and aesthetically accomplished medium. In The Mosaics of Norman Sicily (1949), he examined the transfer of Byzantine craftsmen and models into the Norman kingdom and the resulting hybrid artistic language.

In 1966 Demus delivered the Metropolitan Museum of Art lectures in New York that became Byzantine Art and the West (1970), widely regarded as a major work of twentieth-century Byzantine scholarship. The book traces, from the seventh to the thirteenth century, the sustained dialogue between Byzantine and Western artistic models.

After returning to Vienna, Demus was appointed Professor of Art History at the University of Vienna in 1963. Together with manuscript specialist Otto Pacht, the pair known as die zwei Ottos transformed the Vienna Institute into what contemporaries described as a Mekka der Mittelalterkunstgeschichte, an international center for medieval art historical study spanning both monumental and manuscript traditions.

Diebold, William J.

b. 1958

William J. Diebold is an American historian of medieval art, Jane Neuberger Goodsell Professor of Art History and Humanities Emeritus at Reed College, whose work divides between the art of the early Middle Ages and the uses to which the Middle Ages have been put by the modern world. He was educated at Yale College and took his M.A. and Ph.D. at Johns Hopkins.

Word and Image: An Introduction to Early Medieval Art, 600–1050 (2000) is the book by which he is most widely known. Organised around the relation between text and image rather than around dynasties or regions, it is capacious enough to hold both the oral culture behind the Sutton Hoo treasure and the emphatically literate art of the Carolingian and Ottonian courts, and it traces the fortunes of Gregory the Great's dictum on images from the seventh century through to the Romanesque. Alongside it stands a long series of studies of Carolingian and Ottonian manuscripts and ivories and of medieval writing about art.

His second field is the modern reception of the medieval, and in particular the appropriation of medieval art in twentieth-century Germany — work published under titles such as "The Nazi Middle Ages" and in the volume Medieval Art, Modern Politics, co-edited with Brigitte Buettner. It is scholarship about scholarship and about the political conditions under which objects acquire their meanings, a preoccupation that connects him to the historiographical turn in medieval studies more broadly.

That preoccupation explains his role in the Autun debate. Reviewing Linda Seidel's Legends in Limestone in The Medieval Review (2000), he gave the most substantial specialist assessment the book received: he granted that, on ordinary medieval conventions, the Gislebertus of the inscription might perfectly well have been a patron rather than an artist, and observed that the displacement of the artist by the patron was in any case familiar to medievalists rather than the scandal some general readers took it to be — a judicious separation of the book's genuine historiographical contribution from the specific identification it proposed.

Diehl, Charles (Michel-Charles)

Strasbourg, 4 July 1859 - Paris, 1 November 1944

Charles Diehl, whose full name was Michel-Charles Diehl, was the most important French Byzantinist of his generation and one of the key figures in the history of Byzantine art and civilization studies. Born in Strasbourg on July 4, 1859, his academic and scholarly career spanned more than half a century of tireless research.

Diehl completed his secondary education in Strasbourg, Nancy, and Paris with brilliant results, and in 1878 he was admitted to the prestigious École Normale Supérieure in Paris. His doctoral thesis, published in 1888 under the title Études sur l'administration byzantine dans l'exarchat de Ravenne, marked his official entry into Byzantine studies and remains to this day a benchmark for the history of the Exarchate of Ravenna, a subject of great importance for those interested in the medieval art of northern Italy.

In 1899, when the first chair of Byzantine History in France was established at the Sorbonne, Diehl was appointed to fill it, holding the position until 1934. From this position of exceptional influence, he trained generations of French, Italian, Greek, and Romanian scholars, thereby founding a true school of European Byzantine studies. In 1910, he was elected a member of the Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres, of which he served as president in 1920-1921.

Diehl's scholarly output was extraordinarily vast and touched on every aspect of Byzantine civilization. His Manuel d'art byzantin (1910, second edition 1915) was the first systematic handbook on Byzantine art and remained an indispensable reference work for decades. The essay Byzance. Grandeur et décadence (1919), translated into Italian as La civiltà bizantina in 1962 and into English by Naomi Walford in 1957, cemented his international fame.

Among the popular works that made him well known even outside the academic world, Figures byzantines (1906-1908, in two series) and Theodora, impératrice de Byzance (1904) stand out; these works of elegant historical prose evoked the personalities of the Eastern Empire with a literary vividness rare among professional historians. Diehl also wrote an important volume on the history of Venice, Une république patricienne (1915), which demonstrates his ability to look beyond strictly Eastern boundaries.

Diehl was not an armchair scholar: he conducted field research campaigns in Greece, North Africa, and Ravenna. Between 1907 and 1909, he directed the restoration of the Byzantine church of Hagia Sophia in Thessaloniki, and the Greek city honored his work by naming a street after him near that very church. His study L'Afrique byzantine (1896) opened new perspectives on the legacy of Byzantium throughout the Mediterranean.

Charles Diehl died in Paris on November 1, 1944. In his will, he bequeathed 240,000 francs to the Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres for the establishment of a prize for the best works on Byzantine history and culture, a gesture that encapsulates his lifelong dedication to the discipline he had helped to found. His work, combining the rigor of archival research with accessible prose and a comprehensive vision of Byzantine civilization, remains a model of how medieval art history can be both science and literature.

Dionysios of Fourna

Fourna (Agrafa), c. 1670 - c. 1745

Dionysios was born around 1670 in Fourna, in the mountainous Agrafa region of central Greece, then under Ottoman control. Little is known about his family background, but Agrafa was culturally significant: relatively isolated from direct Ottoman administration, it served as a refuge for Greek Orthodox monastic and intellectual life during the centuries of Turkokratia.

He entered monastic life at a young age and formed within the living tradition of Byzantine ecclesiastical art preserved in monasteries of mainland Greece and Mount Athos. The name Dionysios was common among Orthodox monks; "of Fourna" distinguishes him from other bearers of the same monastic name.

The decisive phase of his artistic development unfolded on Mount Athos, the monastic peninsula that for centuries functioned as a spiritual and artistic center of Orthodox Christianity. There he encountered the post-Byzantine painting tradition associated with figures such as Manuel Panselinos of Thessaloniki and the masters of the Cretan School, whose idiom had shaped Athonite fresco production since the sixteenth century.

Dionysios is believed to have worked under, or at minimum studied closely, the legacy of Georgios and Frangos Katelanos and related Athonite-Cretan workshop practice. He painted extensively, though attribution remains difficult because of the collaborative and often anonymous structure of Byzantine and post-Byzantine workshops.
