The catalogue also extends to miniature painting, making it directly relevant to the study of Italian illuminated manuscripts in which gilded surfaces were decorated by related punch methods and occasionally with the same tools found in panel painting.

Fuchs, Robert

b. 1949

Robert Fuchs is a German analytical chemist and, alongside the art historian Doris Oltrogge, one half of the most productive chemist/art-historian partnership in the technical study of medieval book illumination. For nearly three decades he held the chair for the restoration and conservation of written material, graphics, photographs and book painting at the Fachhochschule Köln - later the Technische Hochschule Köln - where he built the non-destructive analytical laboratory that underlies most modern technical scholarship on the materials of medieval manuscripts.

Fuchs studied chemistry and Egyptology at the Eberhard Karls Universität Tübingen, deliberately pairing his science coursework with seminars in art history and archaeology; he felt most at home in Egyptology, then chaired by the noted Egyptologist Helmut Brunner. He completed his Diplom in 1980 with a thesis on the structure and properties of the green pigments antlerite and Casselmann's green, and took his doctorate in 1983 in chemistry with Egyptology as a subsidiary subject - an unusual combination that reportedly gave the science faculty's board some difficulty in approving. His dissertation, supervised by Joachim Strähle, was on the structure and properties of lanthanide acetates, solving the single-crystal structures of highly coordinated organometallic rare-earth-metal acetates; the electrical conductivity of the chain structure of scandium acetate proved of particular interest for further research.

As a fellow of the Fritz Thyssen Foundation at the University of Würzburg, Fuchs took on the scientific and technical entries for the Lexikon der Ägyptologie, contributing more than twelve articles on materials used in ancient Egypt, from ochre to tin; his entry on "Technik" (technique), summarising the technical and technological achievements of five thousand years of ancient Egyptian civilisation, ran to forty-five columns and was the longest single article in the entire reference work.

In 1984 Fuchs realised a project he had originally planned in Würzburg with the art historian Heinz Roosen-Runge, the leading authority on the technique of medieval book painting as recorded in historical sources: an interdisciplinary research centre devoted to that subject. Roosen-Runge's sudden death forced a change of venue, and under the auspices of the Nobel laureate Manfred Eigen of the Max Planck Institute, the DFG-funded project found a new home at the University of Göttingen as the Forschungsstelle für Technik mittelalterlicher Buchmalerei (Research Unit for the Technique of Medieval Book Painting), with Oskar Glemser supervising the chemistry, Karl Arndt the art history, and Helmut Vogt the library side of the work. Fuchs was its lead researcher from 1984 to 1989, paired throughout with an art-historical partner - first Solange Michon, then, from 1986, Doris Oltrogge - in what was for a long time the only DFG-funded interdisciplinary research team combining the humanities and the natural sciences. The unit's method, which became the template for Fuchs's later career, was to collect and interpret medieval recipes and technical instructions, reconstruct the pigments and paint samples they described, compare the samples non-destructively against original manuscripts, artificially age the samples through climate testing to study damage mechanisms, and only then test candidate conservation treatments on the samples before ever applying them to an original.

That final step - the move from laboratory reconstruction to practical conservation - found an institutional home in 1989, when the Fachhochschule Köln established a chair for the restoration and conservation of written material, graphics, photographs and book painting within its department of restoration and conservation of art and cultural property. Fuchs held this chair from 1989 to 2017 and succeeded in integrating the Göttingen research unit into it, bringing with it the specially built, DFG-funded instrumentation for wholly non-destructive analysis that became the foundation of the Laboratory for the Non-Destructive Analysis of Works of Art, expanded continuously since. He directed the Cologne Institute of Conservation Sciences (CICS) itself from 2009 to 2015, and sat on the Senate of the Technische Hochschule Köln from 2011 to 2016. Over his active career he trained more than 172 students to the diploma, BA and MA levels and guided a number to the doctorate, and he published the results of his research in more than 200 scholarly contributions.

Since 1984 Fuchs's research has centred on book painting and coloured graphic art, and on writing and ink materials and their conservation; since 1986 this work has been carried out with Oltrogge and other collaborators as a continuous interdisciplinary programme on medieval book painting, art-technological written sources, and historical materials. Their joint publications include technical studies of the Master of the Registrum Gregorii, of manuscripts from Ottonian Hildesheim associated with Bishop Bernward, of the World Chronicle of Rudolf of Ems, and - the study for which Fuchs is most cited in the literature on the Codex Aureus of Echternach - Die Maltechnik des Codex Aureus aus Echternach: ein Meisterwerk im Wandel (Nuremberg: Verlag des Germanischen Nationalmuseums, 2009), the systematic technical examination of every painted and ornamental page of the Nuremberg manuscript.

Fuchs was a Getty Foundation fellow in 1991, chaired the Arbeitskreis Archäometrie (Working Group on Archaeometry) within the Analytical Chemistry division of the German Chemical Society (GDCh) from 2002 to 2014, and served on advisory boards including those overseeing fire-damage management at the Herzogin Anna Amalia Bibliothek in Weimar and, after the catastrophic 2009 collapse of the Historical Archive of the City of Cologne, the archive's own advisory board and the board of trustees of the city's Stiftung Stadtgedächtnis. He is also active in the working group Antike Pigmente (Ancient Pigments), devoted to translating ancient pigment-recipe texts from Theophrastus to Heraclius. Fuchs was emeritated on 1 September 2017. In retirement he continues to research nineteenth- and twentieth-century colour materials under the BMBF-funded programme WELTBUNT, and works as an expert witness in the investigation of art forgeries and in damage assessments for archives and libraries destroyed by disaster; in 2018/2019 the GDCh named him its Fresenius Lecturer.

G

Galatariotou, Catia

active 1984–1993 and beyond

Catia Galatariotou is a British Byzantine scholar whose work, concentrated in roughly a decade of exceptional productivity between 1984 and 1993, made a lasting and methodologically innovative contribution to the study of Byzantine hagiography, monastic culture, gender, and social history. She is best known as the author of The Making of a Saint: The Life, Times and Sanctification of Neophytos the Recluse (Cambridge University Press, 1991), which remains the standard monograph on the saint. Her work connects directly to the wider scholarly constellation assembled here — she cites Mango and Hawkins's 1966 Dumbarton Oaks Papers study of the Enkleistra frescoes as a cornerstone reference throughout her research.

Galatariotou completed her doctoral thesis, "Neophytos the Recluse: A Cultural Study of a Byzantine Holy Man," at the University of Birmingham, Centre for Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies, in 1985–1986. Her first articles appeared in print even before her thesis was complete, indicating a scholar whose ideas were already fully formed at a precocious stage. Alongside work by Alexander Kazhdan, her articles on Byzantine sexuality were recognised as among the pioneering contributions to the use of hagiographic material for the social history of Byzantium.

What distinguished her scholarship from the first was a commitment to reading Byzantine hagiographic texts not merely as pious narratives or historical chronicles, but as windows into Byzantine mentality, social structure, and cultural construction. She brought to bear on medieval Greek sources the theoretical tools of Western social history and gender studies — above all the work of Peter Brown on holy men and Evelyne Patlagean on family and social structures — and applied them with rigour and sensitivity to the peculiarities of the Byzantine Orthodox world.

Her first major article, "Holy Women and Witches: Aspects of Byzantine Conceptions of Gender" (Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies 9, 1984–85, pp. 55–94), opened a domain — Byzantine women's history — that she recognised as almost entirely unexplored, examining the binary structure of female representation in Byzantine religious literature and arguing that these oppositions mapped onto fundamental anxieties in Byzantine patriarchal culture.

In 1987 she published two landmark studies simultaneously. "Byzantine Ktetorika Typika: A Comparative Study" (Revue des Études Byzantines 45, 1987, pp. 77–138) presented a comprehensive list of monastic foundation charters and established a typology distinguishing "aristocratic" from "non-aristocratic" typika, each containing clauses that reveal distinct attitudes towards spirituality, the lay world, the ephoros, administration, and the individual monk. This typology, rigorously argued from the full corpus of surviving documents, has proved durable and continues to structure scholarly discussion of Byzantine monastic foundation charters. In the same year she published "Structural Oppositions in the Grottaferrata Digenes Akrites" (Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies 11), a structuralist analysis of the Byzantine epic demonstrating the range of her methodological interests beyond hagiography.

Her most daring article, "Eros and Thanatos: A Byzantine Hermit's Conception of Sexuality" (Byzantine and Modern Greek Studies 13, 1989, pp. 95–138), examined the conception of sexuality of one Byzantine individual as reconstructed from his voluminous writings: Neophytos the Recluse of Cyprus. Galatariotou argued that focusing on Neophytos offered the rare opportunity of examining the thought-patterns of a Byzantine man from close quarters concerning a subject as important, as intimate, and as elusive as sexuality — for very few Byzantines discussed it in writing, and even fewer in a manner as personal, direct, and extensive as Neophytos. "Travel and Perception in Byzantium" (Dumbarton Oaks Papers 47, 1993, pp. 221–241) extended her inquiry into a new domain, using Byzantine literary and hagiographic sources to reconstruct how Byzantines conceptualised movement through physical and cultural space — a subject closely related to the biography of a hermit whose enforced rootedness became the ground of his spiritual life.

The Making of a Saint (Cambridge University Press, 1991; xvi + 310 pp., thirteen plates) poses the central question: how does an individual become a saint? The book operates on multiple levels simultaneously: it is a biography of Neophytos drawing on his own extensive corpus of writings; a social history of twelfth- and thirteenth-century Cyprus at the intersection of Byzantine administration, Latin Crusader rule, and an assertively Orthodox monastic culture; an analysis of the mechanisms by which sanctity was constructed and validated in the Byzantine world; and a study of the psychological and cultural formation of a remarkable individual self. Galatariotou reads Neophytos's texts — his Typikon, his homilies, his scriptural commentaries, his historical chronicle — with the sensitivity of a literary critic and the analytical rigour of a social historian, extracting from them a portrait of Byzantine mentality of singular intimacy and depth. The book was reviewed in Church History, the Journal of Ecclesiastical History, and the American Historical Review — an unusually wide reception for a Byzantine monograph.

Galatariotou's work belongs to the intellectual moment when Byzantine studies opened decisively to the methods of French Annales social history, British women's and gender history, and the anthropologically-inflected study of holy men pioneered by Peter Brown. Her typology of ktetorika typika remains a standard reference in the study of Byzantine monastic institutions. Her work on Neophytos established the saint as a central figure for the study of Byzantine subjectivity, sexuality, and cultural identity. Her current research interests — Pope Leo the Great, Gregory the Great, and Evagrius Ponticus — suggest a trajectory that has moved from Byzantine studies into the broader field of late antique Christian thought, leaving her Byzantine publications standing as a self-contained and formidable body of work, complete in itself.

Gameson, Richard

active late 20th-21st century

Richard Gameson is a British historian of the medieval book, Professor at Durham University, and one of the most prolific contemporary scholars of Anglo-Saxon manuscript culture. He has served as general editor of the multi-volume Cambridge History of the Book in Britain and has published extensively on the manuscripts associated with Canterbury, on the St Augustine Gospels, and on the broader material and economic conditions of early medieval book production.

His article "The Cost of the Codex Amiatinus," published in Notes and Queries in 1992, remains the standard study of the resources required to produce the Codex Amiatinus and its two lost sister pandects. Building on figures proposed by Rupert Bruce-Mitford, Gameson calculated that the three books together required some 1,545 animal skins, and — against the popular impression of a ruinously expensive undertaking — argued that the enterprise was well within the sustainable capacity of a monastery holding at least 150 hides of land, given that a slaughtered animal yielded far more than parchment alone. His careful, unsensational arithmetic remains the foundation for how the manuscript's material cost is now understood, correcting a good deal of loose popular claim in the process. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion, including the corrected account of the Aldfrith land grant that Gameson's work helps to contextualize.

Ganz, David Michael

Welwyn, 1952 -

David Michael Ganz FSA was born in Welwyn in 1952 and educated at Merton College, Oxford, where he received a BA in History in 1973 and a DPhil in 1980. His doctoral dissertation examined the monastery of Corbie and its intellectual and scribal culture in the Carolingian period, a subject that remained central throughout his career and placed him directly in the methodological line opened by Bernhard Bischoff's work on scriptoria and manuscript localization.

He served as a research assistant at the University of St Andrews (1979-1980), then moved to North America. From 1980 to 1997 he taught in the Department of Classics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he became associate professor in 1989. Those years provided the institutional context in which he brought his major study of Corbie to completion and established a durable presence in the international Carolingianist community.

One of Ganz's most consequential contributions came in 1990 with the English translation of Bischoff's Paläographie des römischen Altertums und des abendländischen Mittelalters, produced with Daibhi O Croinin and published by Cambridge University Press as Latin Palaeography: Antiquity and the Middle Ages.

The impact of this translation was immediate and long-lasting. Bischoff's handbook had already become the standard introduction to Latin palaeography in German and French, but Anglophone students were still largely dependent on older manuals. By making the most advanced synthesis of Latin script history available in English, Ganz and his co-translator transformed palaeographical training across Britain, Ireland, North America, and beyond.

Ganz's role in the translation was not merely linguistic. As a specialist trained in manuscript method and deeply engaged with Carolingian material, he ensured technical precision across difficult passages involving script typology, dating criteria, and codicological terminology. For generations of readers, his name on the volume served both as assurance of reliability and as an introduction to his own scholarship.

In the same year he published his principal monograph, Corbie in the Carolingian Renaissance (Beihefte der Francia 20, Sigmaringen: Jan Thorbecke Verlag, 1990), expanding his Oxford doctoral research into the most complete English-language study of a single Carolingian scriptorium.

The Abbey of Corbie, founded in the seventh century on the Somme near Amiens, was crucial for the history of medieval writing because it produced an exceptionally large surviving manuscript corpus and because it preserves the earliest datable experiments in Caroline minuscule, the script that became dominant in the medieval Latin West and foundational for later Roman typeforms.

Under Abbot Maurdramnus (771-781), Corbie developed the so-called Maurdramnus script, among the earliest securely datable Caroline minuscule forms. Ganz's study integrates institutional history, palaeography, textual transmission, and library reconstruction to show how the scriptorium functioned as both a production center and an intellectual laboratory.

A distinctive strength of the monograph is its attention to reading practices: marginal annotations, glosses, quotation habits, and manuscript use. Through evidence tied to figures such as Ratramnus of Corbie and Hadoard, Ganz demonstrated that the physical and textual dimensions of manuscripts are inseparable and that marginalia are themselves primary witnesses to Carolingian thought.

In 1997 Ganz moved to King's College London as the fourth holder of the Professorship of Palaeography, established in 1949 after Francis Wormald and subsequently held by Julian Brown and Albinia de la Mare. The post was the only dedicated professorship of palaeography in the English-speaking world. Appointed jointly in English and Classics, he developed and taught major courses in the History of the Book with sustained manuscript teaching in London collections.

He held the chair until its abolition in 2010, a decision that prompted substantial international protest from manuscript scholars and Carolingian historians. The episode became a widely cited case in debates over the institutional marginalization of technical auxiliary disciplines, especially those requiring prolonged direct work with original manuscripts.

Ganz's scholarly relationship to Bischoff remained explicit throughout his career. His work on Corbie extended the framework of scriptorial analysis developed in Bischoff's Schreibschulen and later catalog projects, while his reviews of the Katalog der festlandischen Handschriften des neunten Jahrhunderts modelled rigorous engagement that combined high praise for its foundational achievement with careful critical observation.

He also taught at the Ecole des Chartes in Paris and as Visiting Professor at the Medieval Institute of the University of Notre Dame, and held research fellowships from the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the Manuscripts Department of the Staatsbibliothek Preussischer Kulturbesitz in Berlin. He was elected to the Comite internationale de paleographie latine (1997) and became a Corresponding Member of the Monumenta Germaniae Historica (2016).

Among his influential essays, "Mass production of early medieval manuscripts: The Carolingian Bibles from Tours" in The Early Medieval Bible: Its Production, Decoration, and Use (Cambridge, 1994) examined how the Tours scriptorium organized large- scale production of pandect Bibles in the first half of the ninth century, addressing logistical questions of parchment supply, scribal labor, and distribution central to Carolingian book culture.

His broader publication record includes chapters in the New Cambridge Medieval History, Cambridge History of the Book in Britain, Cambridge History of Libraries in Britain and Ireland, the New Cambridge History of the Bible, and the Oxford Handbook of Latin Palaeography. His translation Two Lives of Charlemagne: Einhard and Notker the Stammerer (Penguin Classics, 2008), with a substantial introduction, made the two principal narrative sources for Charlemagne accessible to a wide readership. In the same year he co-edited with Paul Fouracre Frankland: The Franks and the World of the Early Middle Ages (Manchester University Press, 2008).

David Ganz's place in manuscript studies rests on three intersecting achievements: opening Bischoff's palaeographical synthesis to the English-speaking world through translation; producing the definitive English study of Corbie as a Carolingian intellectual and scriptorial center; and representing, as the final holder of the King's chair, the institutional high point of palaeography as a distinct discipline in Anglophone higher education. For art historians of illuminated manuscripts, his work remains foundational because it provides the technical dating and contextual tools required for secure visual and codicological analysis.

Garibaldi, Vittoria

Rome, 5 February 1950

Vittoria Garibaldi is one of Italy's most distinguished art historians, renowned for her expertise in medieval and Renaissance painting, her long stewardship of Umbria's cultural heritage, and her role in bringing Central Italian art to international audiences. Born on 5 February 1950 in Rome, she pursued her academic formation at the Sapienza University of Rome, where she also taught.

Garibaldi obtained a degree in Modern Letters in 1974 and subsequently a degree in Art History from the University of Rome "La Sapienza" in 1977, where she also taught between 1974 and 1977 before entering the Italian Ministry of Cultural Heritage. She later won the competitive "Art Historians" examination of the MiBAC (Ministero per i Beni e le Attività Culturali) in 1991, consolidating her position within Italy's state heritage administration.

Garibaldi's career at the intersection of scholarship and institutional responsibility defined several decades of cultural life in Central Italy. From 1988 to 2011, she served as Director of the Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria in Perugia, simultaneously holding the position of Superintendent for the Historical, Artistic, and Ethno-Anthropological Heritage of Umbria. Between 2008 and 2011 she also served as Director of the Galleria Nazionale delle Marche in Urbino.

The Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria, housed in the Palazzo dei Priori, houses one of the most important collections of art in Italy, comprising nearly three thousand works: paintings, sculptures, ceramics, ivories, bronzes, textiles, drawings, and prints, both displayed and held in reserve.

Following her formal superintendency, she continued her engagement with Umbrian cultural heritage as technical-scientific director of the diagnostics laboratory for cultural heritage in Spoleto, and as coordinator of ICOM Umbria.

Garibaldi's scholarship is characterized by rigorous archival research combined with deep connoisseurship, with a particular focus on the Umbrian School from the 13th through 16th centuries. She co-curated a series of landmark exhibitions, often in collaboration with Francesco Federico Mancini, professor of Modern Art History at the University of Perugia.

Among these were Benedetto Bonfigli e Perugia (Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria, 1996-97), a monographic exhibition on the fifteenth-century Perugian master; Perugino il divin pittore (2004), a major retrospective at Perugia, co-edited with Francesco Federico Mancini and published by Silvana Editoriale; Arnolfo di Cambio: una rinascita nell'Umbria medievale (Perugia and Orvieto, 2005-06), co-curated with Bruno Toscano; Pintoricchio (Perugia and Spello, 2008), a comprehensive retrospective co-edited with Mancini; Piermatteo d'Amelia e il Rinascimento nell'Umbria meridionale (2009-10), co-curated with Francesco Federico Mancini; Luca Signorelli "de ingegno et spirto pelegrino" (Perugia, Orvieto, Città di Castello, 2012), co-edited with F. De Chirico, T. Henry, and F.F. Mancini; and Le Pérugin, maître de Raphaël (Musée Jacquemart-André, Paris, 12 September 2014 - 19 January 2015), for which she served as general commissioner, co-curating with Nicolas Sainte-Fare Garnot.

Her monumental scholarly project, the Catalogo generale della Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria, resulted in a foundational reference work. The catalogue, conceived and realized by Garibaldi, follows the path traced by two earlier volumes by Francesco Santi (1969 and 1985), but substantially revises, deepens, and expands the historical, technical-scientific, and documentary understanding of the museum's holdings in light of current research. The first volume, Dipinti e sculture dal XIII al XV secolo, was presented in December 2015 at the Sala dei Notari of the Palazzo dei Priori in Perugia, published by Quattroemme Editore.

Garibaldi's interests span the full arc of Umbrian artistic production, from its Romanesque roots through the Renaissance, with particular sensitivity to the Giottesque tradition and its Umbrian diffusion. In a 2021 lecture for the network of Umbrian ecclesiastical museums, she discussed the works of the Maestro di Cesi, a follower of Giotto, preserved in the Museo Diocesano di Spoleto, observing that Giotto's arrival in Umbria in the 1290s was revolutionary, decisively departing from the Byzantine tradition and reshaping the region's visual culture permanently.

Garibaldi is a descendant of the legendary Giuseppe Garibaldi, the nineteenth-century military hero and architect of Italian unification, a lineage that lends a particular symbolic resonance to her lifelong dedication to Italy's national cultural patrimony.

Selected publications include: Perugino (with Simonetta Innamorati), Silvana, Milan, 2004; Perugino, Giunti (Dossier d'arte series); Perugino, Scala Group (Pittori del Rinascimento series), 2004; Arnolfo di Cambio: una rinascita nell'Umbria medievale (with Bruno Toscano), Silvana, 2005; Pintoricchio (with F.F. Mancini), Silvana, 2008; Piermatteo d'Amelia e il Rinascimento nell'Umbria meridionale (with F.F. Mancini), Silvana, 2009; Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria: Dipinti e sculture dal XIII al XV secolo. Catalogo generale, Vol. 1, Quattroemme, 2015.

Vittoria Garibaldi stands as a pivotal figure in the historiography of Umbrian art, bridging meticulous connoisseurship, institutional responsibility, and public engagement over a career spanning more than four decades. For anyone researching anonymous medieval masters of Central Italy, as in work on the Maestro di San Felice di Giano, her catalogue and exhibition work remain indispensable primary references.

Garrison, Edward B.

Chicago, 1900 – London, 1981

American art historian who made foundational contributions to the study of medieval Italian painting, particularly through his meticulous documentation of Romanesque panel paintings and twelfth-century manuscripts from central Italy. Born in Chicago in 1900, Garrison initially pursued a business career before pivoting in 1945 to art history, earning an MA from New York University's Institute of Fine Arts. He then immersed himself in Italy, collaborating with Richard Offner on the Corpus of Florentine Painting (Volume V, 1943–1945), which honed his expertise in Duecento and Trecento primitives. This transition reflected a broader postwar scholarly migration to Italy's artistic heartland, where Garrison's independent research thrived without institutional ties.

His breakthrough came with Italian Romanesque Panel Painting: An Illustrated Index (1949), a pioneering catalogue that systematically inventoried surviving panels from the eleventh and twelfth centuries, providing scholars with their first comprehensive visual reference for styles bridging Byzantine and proto-Renaissance forms. Between 1953 and 1962 he issued four volumes of Studies in the History of Medieval Italian Painting, featuring photographs of Tuscan and Papal States miniatures, wall paintings, and initials — unprecedented in scope and enabling precise stylistic comparisons across regions including Umbria and Latium. Later compilations, such as Early Italian Painting: Selected Studies (1984, posthumous, 2 vols.), consolidated his essays on panels, frescoes, and manuscripts, emphasising iconographic and formal evolutions. His 1953 identification of connections between the Sarzana Cross and the Passionary P+ manuscript initiated the scholarly programme of reconstructing the broader artistic activity of Maestro Guglielmo.

Travelling extensively in Italy, Garrison amassed a vast photographic archive of medieval artworks, donated in 1962 to the Courtauld Institute of Art in London, where he served as honorary curator of the Garrison Collection. This resource — now undergoing digitisation as part of the Conway Library project — captured details often overlooked in earlier studies, supporting attributions of anonymous masters and illuminating workshop practices in Romanesque illumination. His method integrated visual analysis with historical context, influencing successors such as Miklós Boskovits in their pursuit of chronological clarity for Tuscany's early painting schools. An honorary member of the Courtauld from 1979, Garrison died in London on October 16, 1981; his indices remain an indispensable reference for any researcher working on Italian Romanesque and early Duecento painting.

Gelli, Giovan Battista

Florence, 12 August 1498 – Florence, 24 July 1563

Giovan Battista Gelli was born in Florence on 12 August 1498 and died there on 24 July 1563. He came from an artisan family and was trained as a shoemaker — a biographical fact his contemporaries never let him forget, and which he turned to advantage in the plain-spoken, vernacular manner of his writing. Essentially self-taught, he made his way in the 1520s into the Orti Oricellari, the Florentine literary circle that preceded the Accademia Fiorentina and counted Machiavelli among its members, and there began delivering lezzioni of his own on literary, historical and philosophical questions. He joined the Accademia Fiorentina on 25 December 1540 and became, with Pierfrancesco Giambullari and Carlo Lenzoni, one of its dominant figures under the patronage of Cosimo I.

His literary reputation rests on the dialogues of the 1540s: I capricci di Giusto bottaio (1548) and La Circe (1549), both ethical and philosophical in cast, together with the comedies La sporta (1543) and L'errore. He also translated Euripides' Hecuba from Latin, and lectured publicly on Dante's Commedia before the Academy — a body of commentary later gathered as the Letture edite e inedite... sopra la Commedia di Dante (ed. C. Negroni, 1887). His writing on Florentine antiquity is more compromised: his account of the city's origins depends on the forgeries of Annio da Viterbo, which claimed to demonstrate that Tuscany had been settled by Noah and his descendants after the Flood.

For art history his significance lies in a small manuscript work, the Vite d'artisti fiorentini. Published by Girolamo Mancini in 1896 as Venti vite d'artisti (Florence, M. Cellini), it runs from Cimabue and Giotto through Maso, Stefano, Taddeo and Agnolo Gaddi, Orcagna, Buonamico, Starnina, Lippo and Dello Delli to Ghiberti and Brunelleschi. Mancini identified his exemplar with the codex Salvino Salvini had recorded in the Strozzi library as no. 952, containing a dedicatory letter to Francesco di Sandro and the same twenty lives. Composed before Vasari's Vite, the text belongs with Antonio Billi's Libro and the Anonimo Magliabechiano among the Florentine sources that transmitted — and shaped — the memory of Trecento painting; Peter Murray argued that Gelli may have used a lost second copy of Ghiberti's Commentarii for his life of that artist.

Standard citation: G. B. Gelli, Vite d'artisti, ed. G. Mancini, «Archivio Storico Italiano», XVII (1896), pp. 32–62.

Gill, Meredith J.

active late 20th-21st century

Meredith J. Gill is an American art historian specializing in Italian art and architecture of the late Middle Ages and the Renaissance, with a particular focus on the relationship between image, theology, and philosophy. She is Professor Emerita in the Department of Art and Archaeology at the University of Maryland, College Park.

Gill earned her Ph.D. in art history from Princeton University, one of the most rigorous centers for the study of Italian Renaissance art in the United States. She built her academic career at the University of Maryland, where she taught fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian art and supervised numerous doctoral dissertations, including that of Caroline Dubinsky, which focused on medieval art history. In addition to teaching, her interdisciplinary approach - which encompasses social history, religion, the history of science, and gender in the history of images - has made her a mentor to generations of students. She is a member of the board of directors of the Digital Art History Association, affiliated with the College Art Association.

Gill's interests focus on the connections between art and spirituality in late medieval and Renaissance Italy, with a special focus on Augustinian theology, Neoplatonic philosophy, and religious iconography. A central question running through her research is how images - frescoes, altarpieces, pictorial cycles - functioned as vehicles for philosophical and theological thought, rather than merely as illustrations of sacred texts. This perspective places her in close methodological affinity with art historians such as Hans Belting, whose study of the cultic and anthropological function of medieval images constitutes a fundamental theoretical reference point.

Gill's first major book, Augustine in the Italian Renaissance: Art and Philosophy from Petrarch to Michelangelo (Cambridge University Press, 2005), traces the visual and intellectual legacy of Saint Augustine in Renaissance Italy from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. The work demonstrates how Augustine's legacy - his philosophy of time, memory, and grace - permeated not only Petrarch's literature and the theology of the mendicant orders, but also the visual language of artists such as Michelangelo and Botticelli. The volume helped redefine Augustinianism as a key interpretive framework for the Italian Renaissance.

The second major work, Angels and the Order of Heaven in Medieval and Renaissance Italy (Cambridge University Press, 2014), examines angelic iconography from Dante to Raphael, analyzing how the figure of the angel functioned as an intellectual marker to define Renaissance conceptions of the cosmos, grace, and divine order. Gill carefully distinguishes the medieval angelological tradition - rooted in Dionysius the Areopagite, Thomas Aquinas, and scholastic theology - from the Renaissance tradition, in which the angel takes on Neoplatonic and humanistic connotations stemming from the rediscovery of the thought of Pico della Mirandola and Ficino. From Fra Angelico's cycle of angel musicians to Raphael's angels, the book has been hailed by critics as a contribution of great methodological elegance, capable of weaving together visual and textual sources with rare precision.

She also co-edited, together with the classicist Karla Pollmann, the interdisciplinary volume Augustine Beyond the Book (Brill), which brings together studies on the reception of Augustine in medieval, Renaissance, and modern contexts. She contributed important essays to the collective volume Rome: Artistic Centers of the Italian Renaissance, edited by Marcia Hall for Cambridge University Press, where she focused on the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and to The Renaissance World, edited by John Jeffries Martin for Routledge.

Gill has published articles in international scholarly journals, including Renaissance Studies, where she serves on the advisory board. A notable essay, co-authored with William E. Wallace, appeared on JSTOR and explores the relationship between the late Michelangelo and religious piety, a topic in which the two scholars examined the artist's final paintings and sculptures in light of Reformation spirituality. Her articles cover topics ranging from Augustinian theology in Tuscan art to monastic patronage, from Marian iconography in fifteenth-century Rome to the relationship between Humanism and patristic thought in Italian visual culture.

Given her specialization in Italian medieval art, religious iconography, and manuscripts as vehicles for philosophical and theological texts, her research serves as a particularly significant point of reference for the study of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century authors active in central Italy.

Gillis, John

active early 21st century

John Gillis is a book conservator whose work at the Library of Trinity College Dublin has focused on the physical care and technical study of the library's early Irish manuscripts. As part of Trinity's early Irish manuscripts project of the 2010s, he disbound, conserved and rebound the Book of Dimma in 2016, work that involved close first-hand examination of the manuscript's quire structure, parchment and multiple scribal hands.

With Bernard Meehan, Gillis co-authored "Examining the Book of Dimma, the Scribe Dianchride and the Gospel of John," a chapter in An Insular Odyssey: Manuscript Culture in Early Christian Ireland and Beyond (2017). Their study identified five distinct scribal hands responsible for the manuscript, established that the gospels of Matthew and Mark were largely the work of one scribe and Luke of another, and gave the fullest modern codicological account of the manuscript, including the case for treating John as a once physically separate unit. Their conclusions, and the debate they subsequently attracted from scholars such as Bart Jaski, represent the most substantial advance in Book of Dimma scholarship since Richard Irvine Best's exposure of the colophon forgery in 1926.

Girelli, Francesca

active 21st century

Francesca Girelli is an Italian medieval art historian trained at the University of Genoa, where she took her degree and completed her doctorate in art history in 2019. She belongs to the Genoese school of medieval sculpture studies formed around Clario Di Fabio, with whom, together with Gianluca Ameri, she co-authored the 2020 Art & Dossier monograph on Giovanni Pisano. She is currently a research fellow (assegnista di ricerca) at Genoa, working on the PRIN project MemId: Memoria e Identità - a study of the reuse, reworking, and re-display of medieval sculpture in the early modern period, run in partnership with the universities of Trento and Naples Federico II. She has also begun teaching at Genoa, holding the graduate course Arti Monumentali del Medioevo europeo and lecturing on Italian Gothic sculpture within the university's Scuola di Specializzazione in Beni Storico-Artistici.

Her principal field is Italian Gothic sculpture between the Duecento and Trecento, with a particular focus on the Pisan and Genoese milieux and on artists who moved between Tuscany, Liguria, and Lombardy; alongside this she works on Romanesque wooden sculpture in France (twelfth-thirteenth centuries). Her scholarship has appeared in leading journals including the Bollettino d'Arte, Paragone, Convivium, Sculpture Journal, and Arte Lombarda.

Her signature contribution to date is the 2023 monograph Giovanni di Balduccio prima di Milano. La scalata al successo, 1326-1335 (Perugia, Aguaplano), the first book-length study of the Pisan sculptor's Tuscan years before the Milanese commissions — most famously the Arca di San Pietro Martire in Sant'Eustorgio — that made his reputation. It reconstructs the patronage networks that propelled his early career, and she has pursued the same figure in related essays, including a study of the Arca di Sant'Agostino in Pavia and its authorship. Other attributional work includes essays on Goro di Gregorio and, in Arte Lombarda (2021), a Madonna assigned to the workshop of the anonymous Master of the Loggia degli Osii.

On the museum side, between 2021 and 2024 she served as a scientific consultant for the reinstallation of the monumental tomb of Cardinal Luca Fieschi at the Museo Diocesano di Genova and for the partial reopening of Genoa's Museo di Sant'Agostino. Her interest in the afterlife of medieval objects - how sculpture was reused, recut, and recontextualised in later centuries to serve civic and family memory - is now the connective thread of much of her output. She is also a co-editor of the recent Festschrift for her mentor, Sulla scultura. Studi in onore di Clario Di Fabio (Milan, Dario Cimorelli, 2025).

Giorgi, Silvia

active 21st century

Silvia Giorgi is an Italian art historian specializing in medieval panel painting, with particular scholarly focus on the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Her research concentrates on the study of Italian panel painting across multiple geographical centers — Bologna, Siena, Spoleto — and on the broader artistic transitions of the Romanesque-Gothic period. She is recognized as a specialist in attributional analysis and stylistic chronology during this formative era of Italian art.

Giorgi's scholarly work has been cited in major publications on thirteenth-century Sienese painting, particularly in studies devoted to the work of Guido da Siena. She contributed to the exhibition catalog Duccio: Alle origini della pittura senese, a comprehensive volume that examines the development of Sienese painting from its earliest manifestations. Through this and related publications, she has established herself as a reference point in the literature on Duecento Italian art and the emergence of regional stylistic identities in central Italy.

Giorgi's most significant contribution to medieval art history is her entry on Rainaldetto di Ranuccio, written for the General Catalog of the National Art Gallery of Bologna. In this work, she advances a major chronological hypothesis through rigorous comparative analysis. Giorgi argues that the Fabriano Cross predates the documented Bolognese cross — which is dated to April 1265 — by approximately five years, placing it around 1260. This dating represents a revival and refinement of a hypothesis originally formulated by the American scholar Edward B. Garrison in 1949.

Her methodology exemplifies high-level Italian medieval art-historical scholarship, grounded in precise formal analysis and close visual comparison. The dating of the Fabriano Cross rests on detailed stylistic examination of Christ's abdomen and a cross-reading of the inscriptions appearing on both crosses, demonstrating the kind of disciplined connoisseurial work that has long characterized Italian studies in panel painting. Through arguments of this type — combining technical observation with documentary evidence and comparative methodology — Giorgi contributes to the ongoing refinement of chronologies for early Italian panel painting and helps illuminate the networks of artistic exchange between regional centers during the critical period of the Duecento.

Gnoni Mavarelli, Cristina

Perugia, 1957 – Florence, 10 November 2023

Cristina Gnoni Mavarelli was an Italian art historian and state museum official who, across four decades of service within the Italian Ministry of Culture, pursued a career of remarkable range and intellectual consistency — moving between scholarly research, monumental restoration, museum direction, and exhibition curatorship with the same characteristic combination of precision, generosity, and passion. Born in Perugia in 1957, she adopted Florence as her home, and it was to Florentine and Tuscan art — above all the Quattrocento, the circle of Filippo Lippi, and the devotional heritage of medieval Siena — that she returned throughout her professional life. She died in Florence on 10 November 2023, aged sixty-five, while still in active service. The announcement of her death was made by Eike Schmidt, director of the Gallerie degli Uffizi.

Gnoni graduated from the University of Florence under the supervision of Maria Grazia Ciardi Dupré, with an initial scholarly interest focused on French and Flemish Books of Hours — the devotional object par excellence of late medieval lay piety, where Flemish naturalism and French elegance converge in a miniature space. This training in illuminated manuscripts gave her scholarly formation a richly material and cross-cultural dimension that would inform her later curatorial sensibility throughout her career.

Gnoni entered the roles of the Soprintendenza Beni Storico Artistici as a funzionario storico dell'arte, with a first posting at Mantua, then at Siena, where she was responsible for the protection and valorization of monumental complexes including Sant'Agostino and the Contrada oratories with their related museums, as well as nine municipalities of the Province of Grosseto. The Sienese years were foundational: working within the dense web of medieval and Renaissance monuments concentrated in that city and its territory, she developed the close familiarity with Sienese painting that would later inform her direction of the Pinacoteca Nazionale.

From 2000, Gnoni Mavarelli transferred to the Soprintendenza for the provinces of Florence, Prato, and Pistoia, where she also held the post of Director of the exhibitions office and of the stolen art archive. The defining undertaking of this period was monumental: together with Isabella Lapi Ballerini, she directed the restoration of the fresco cycle by Filippo Lippi in the Duomo of Prato, completed in 2007. The Lippi frescoes in the choir of Prato Cathedral — depicting the lives of St. John the Baptist and St. Stephen, painted between 1452 and 1465 — are among the supreme achievements of Florentine narrative painting in the Quattrocento. Her leadership of this project established her as one of the foremost living authorities on Filippo Lippi, a distinction the Uffizi's director acknowledged at the time of her death.

The decades of her oversight of Prato produced a sustained engagement with the city's artistic patrimony that went well beyond the cathedral. She served as a member of the museum commission for the new Museo Civico, co-editing with Maria Pia Mannini the scientific catalogue Il museo di Palazzo Pretorio a Prato (Giunti, 2015). During the years of the museum's closure she brought its collections before international audiences through touring exhibitions — at the Musée du Luxembourg in Paris (2009), CaixaForum in Barcelona (2008), and museums in Tokyo and Hiroshima (2005–06). In collaboration with Andrea De Marchi she conceived and curated the exhibition Da Donatello a Lippi: Officina pratese (2013–14), which marked the Palazzo Pretorio's reopening. She also curated Legati da una cintola (Mandragora, Florence, 2017), dedicated to the sacred cult of the Prato relic, the Holy Belt of the Virgin, and its extraordinary artistic consequences.

In parallel, she took on wider institutional responsibilities: serving by ministerial appointment on the commission for the patrimonial evaluation of the Richard-Ginori museum at Sesto Fiorentino (2012), contributing to the volume La fabbrica della bellezza (Mandragora, 2017). From 2015 she entered the Polo Museale Regionale della Toscana, directing the Cenacolo d'Ognissanti, the Cenacolo di Andrea del Sarto, the Galleria Mozzi-Bardini, the Villa Medicea di Cerreto Guidi, and the Museo della Caccia e del Territorio.

From 2018 she assumed the direction of the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Siena — a significant homecoming after her earlier years in the territory. Under her aegis was presented the restoration she had promoted of the Croce del Carmine by Ambrogio Lorenzetti, one of the most significant rediscoveries of Sienese panel painting to emerge in recent years. In the final chapter of her career, at the Gallerie degli Uffizi–Palazzo Pitti, she became Curator of seventeenth-century painting. At the time of her death she was preparing, jointly with Anna Maria Guiducci, a major exhibition on seventeenth-century Sienese art for the Uffizi diffusi programme.

Her bibliography reflects the full range of her institutional commitments. Her monographic works include Restauri e recuperi in terra di Maremma (Il Leccio, 2003), Il museo Bandini di Fiesole (Polistampa, 2011), and the elegant Falchi, girifalchi e astori al tempo di Pisanello e Leonardo (Edifir, 2019), at the intersection of natural history, court culture, and the visual arts. From 2013 she was a member of CIHA — the Comité International de l'Histoire de l'Art — and in the year of her death was appointed an Honorary Academician of the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. She remained professionally active until the very end: in the spring of 2023 she accompanied paintings to an exhibition in Madrid, and in September delivered a final text.

Gnudi, Cesare

Ozzano dell'Emilia, 9 July 1910 - Bologna, 19 January 1981

Cesare Gnudi (1910-1981) was an Italian art historian and heritage official whose career combined rigorous connoisseurship with a major institutional role in the protection and presentation of Italian art. He served as Superintendent of the Galleries of Bologna and as director of the Pinacoteca Nazionale, and he is remembered for a body of scholarship that ranged from Romanesque and Gothic sculpture to Bolognese Trecento painting and the Emilian Baroque.

Born on 9 July 1910 at Ozzano dell'Emilia, near Bologna, he was the son of Rinaldo Gnudi, a pharmacist, and Rosa Rimondini. He graduated in art history at the University of Bologna in 1932 under Igino Benvenuto Supino, whose historical-philological method left a lasting mark on him. He then continued his formation in Rome at the Scuola di perfezionamento in storia dell'arte, the school founded by Adolfo Venturi for the training of scholars in heritage care and university teaching, where Pietro Toesca was director during Gnudi's attendance.

His early outlook combined historicism and Crocean idealism with a firm democratic and anti-fascist conviction. That dual formation - Supino's connoisseurship on one side, Croce's sensitivity to style and quality on the other - remained visible throughout his career and informed both his scholarship and his public role.

Gnudi built his career inside the Italian heritage administration. In the early 1950s he became Superintendent of Fine Arts in Bologna and devoted exceptional energy to the reorganization of the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna, which he rethought on modern historical-critical lines. His superintendency also drove a broad campaign of restoration across Emilia and Romagna, bringing renewed attention to the Riminese painters, Vitale da Bologna, the frescoes of Palazzo Schifanoia, and later Emilian masters from Niccolo dell'Abate and Pellegrino Tibaldi to the Carracci.

His most influential institutional invention was the cycle of Biennali d'Arte Antica, exhibitions mounted at two-year intervals, chiefly in the Archiginnasio, that paired scientific rigor with real public appeal. Beginning with Guido Reni in 1954 and continuing with the Carracci, the ideal of classicism in seventeenth-century Italy, and Il Guercino in 1968, these exhibitions did as much as his books to reshape the twentieth-century reception of Bolognese and Emilian art. The cycle followed the model of public scholarship demonstrated by Roberto Longhi and helped consolidate Bologna as a major centre for art-historical exhibition making.

For medievalists, Gnudi's central contribution lies in sculpture. His monograph Nicola Arnolfo Lapo. L'arca di San Domenico in Bologna (1948) is a foundational study of the Arca di San Domenico, in which he attempted to distinguish the hand and design of Nicola Pisano from those of collaborators such as Arnolfo di Cambio, Lapo, and Fra Guglielmo. The work entered directly into the long debate over the shrine and over the early careers of Arnolfo and Fra Guglielmo, and much of his reconstruction has remained durable, even though the division of hands on the Arca continues to be contested.

Earlier, his first book, Niccolo dell'Arca (1942), had treated the late Gothic and early Renaissance Bolognese sculptor, while his later essays extended to painting. He contributed the volume on Gothic art with Jacques Dupont to Skira's The Great Centuries of Painting (1954), wrote the admired essay Grandezza di Simone on Simone Martini, and explored Giotto's beginnings in relation to the Gothic world of the North. After withdrawing from administrative work, he returned to the medieval sculpture of France and Italy, publishing on the choir sculpture of Notre-Dame and on the rediscovered sculptures of Notre-Dame shortly before his death; these essays were gathered posthumously in L'arte gotica in Francia e in Italia (1982).

Gnudi's authority extended well beyond Bologna. He sat on the Consiglio Superiore delle Belle Arti, was active in UNESCO, ICOMOS, and the Comite International d'Histoire de l'Art, served on the Consiglio Nazionale per i Beni Culturali e Ambientali, and was elected a national member of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei in 1973. A discerning collector, he donated his personal holdings - including works by Giorgio Morandi and Seicento Bolognese painting - to Bologna's Galleria d'Arte Moderna, while part of his library and photographic archive passed to the research library at Palazzo Ghisilardi-Fava. His influence ran through a generation of Emilian scholars, and his method remains a reference point for the study of medieval sculpture and Emilian art.

Godman, Peter

Auckland, 1955 -

Peter Godman was born in Auckland in 1955. He pursued his academic formation in Britain, lecturing at Cambridge and Oxford universities before moving onto a chair. He was Fellow and Tutor at Pembroke College, University of Oxford. He took up a professorship at the University of Tubingen from 1989 to 2002, where he held the chair as Professor of Medieval and Renaissance Latin, before subsequently moving to Rome. He now lectures at the University of La Sapienza in Rome. He specialises in medieval and modern religious history.

The intellectual thread running through Godman's entire career, from the Carolingian court of Charlemagne through Florentine humanism and Counter-Reformation censorship to the Vatican's posture towards National Socialism, is his preoccupation with the relationship between Latin intellectual culture and political power: the conditions under which scholars, poets, and theologians wrote, what was permitted and prohibited, how the language of learning was deployed in the service of ambition, patronage, and authority, and how the tensions between freedom of thought and institutional control generated the most distinctive achievements of each period he has studied.

Godman's first major publication was an edition and English translation of Alcuin's De pontificibus et sanctis Ecclesiae Eboracensis carmina (The Bishops, Kings, and Saints of York, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1982). This poem, a verse history of the church of York from its Roman foundations to the time of Alcuin's own formation, cast in a Latin hexameter that attempts to reproduce the diction and manner of Virgil and Ovid, is the longest surviving poem of the Carolingian period and one of the most important documents of Anglo-Latin culture at the moment of its decisive engagement with the Continent. Alcuin (c. 735-804) went from York to the court of Charlemagne in 782, becoming the principal intellectual of the Carolingian reform movement; the poem he had composed before his departure served as his scholarly credential and his cultural manifesto.

Godman's edition, with its full critical apparatus, substantial introduction, and facing-page English translation, established him as a Latin Carolingianist of the first rank. Its treatment of Alcuin's relationship to the classical tradition, and of the way in which eighth-century Northumbrian Latin culture both absorbed and adapted the models of Virgil, Ovid, and Venantius Fortunatus, set the analytical agenda for his subsequent work on Carolingian poetry.

Poetry of the Carolingian Renaissance (1985), the most widely used English-language collection of Carolingian Latin verse, remains Godman's most-cited work and the text through which generations of students have first encountered the poetic culture of the eighth and ninth centuries. Published simultaneously in London (Duckworth) and Norman, Oklahoma (University of Oklahoma Press), it presented for the first time in a single volume, with facing-page English translations and full critical apparatus, a representative selection of the major poets of the Carolingian renaissance: Paul the Deacon, Theodulf of Orleans, Alcuin, Angilbert, Moduin, Ermoldus Nigellus, Walafrid Strabo, Sedulius Scottus, John the Scot (Eriugena), and others.

The introduction was itself a substantial scholarly contribution, offering a reinterpretation of the Carolingian renaissance that emphasised its creative engagement with the classical tradition rather than its mere imitative reproduction of it, and that stressed the specifically political and courtly functions of the poetry: its role as an instrument of legitimation, of royal encomium, and of the negotiation of relationships between court intellectuals and their Frankish patrons. The anthology was reviewed by Rosamond McKitterick in the Journal of Ecclesiastical History in 1986, and by the time Godman published his analytical monograph two years later, it had become the standard teaching text for the field.

Poets and Emperors: Frankish Politics and Carolingian Poetry (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987) extended this programme into a sustained argument. Godman's analysis focuses on the character of the classical tradition in the early Middle Ages, creatively adapted to "barbarian" literary tastes, and the refashioning and invention of poetic form in response to contemporary political affairs.

The book moved through the Carolingian period from the court of Charlemagne to that of Charles the Bald, tracing the changing nature of court poetry, panegyric, elegy, epistle, satire, as the political circumstances of the dynasty changed. From the confident imperialism of Charlemagne's Aachen poets to the bitter exilic poetry of Ermoldus Nigellus, from the delicate negotiations of Louis the Pious's court to the politically charged art-patronage of Charles the Bald, Godman showed how Carolingian Latin poetry was not a serene academic exercise in classical imitation but a politically engaged art form produced in the heat of dynastic competition and ideological contest.

Godman co-edited with Roger Collins the large collected volume Charlemagne's Heir: New Perspectives on the Reign of Louis the Pious, 814-840 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1990), assembling leading scholars of Carolingian history and culture to reassess the reign of Louis the Pious. The volume's essay by Elizabeth Sears on the dedicatory image of Hrabanus Maurus's De laudibus sanctae crucis, which Godman disputed in footnotes, illustrated the interlocking networks of Carolingian scholarship in which his work was embedded.

After 1990, Godman's interests expanded to twelfth-century and early modern Latin intellectual culture. From Poliziano to Machiavelli: Florentine Humanism in the High Renaissance (Princeton University Press, 1998) offered the first intellectual history of Florentine humanism from the later fifteenth century to 1527 and drew overdue attention to Marcello Virgilio Adriani, Poliziano's successor and Machiavelli's colleague at the Florentine Chancery. The book received the Roland H. Bainton Prize for History in 1998.

The Silent Masters: Latin Literature and Its Censors in the High Middle Ages (Princeton University Press, 2000) marked his first sustained engagement with the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The book examines the tension between literary experiment and competing regimes of authority, arguing that the relationship between writer and censor, initially metaphorical, became progressively institutional. Latin texts from Peter Abelard and Bernard of Clairvaux to the Archpoet, John of Salisbury, and Alan of Lille are translated into English and interpreted both as literary works and as evidence for the cultural history of the High Middle Ages.

In the same year, Godman published The Saint as Censor, a major study of Robert Bellarmine and Roman censorship grounded in newly opened archives of the Roman Inquisition and the Index of Prohibited Books. By editing and interpreting unpublished archival sources, the book re-evaluated Counter-Reformation censorship, including Bellarmine's position as censor for the Index, consultor to the Holy Office, and later cardinal-inquisitor.

This archival engagement continued in Hitler and the Vatican: Inside the Secret Archives that Reveal the New Story of the Nazis and the Church (New York: Free Press, 2004), which examined the Vatican's policy of non-confrontation with National Socialism and the role of Eugenio Pacelli, later Pius XII, in shaping that policy. The book reached a broad readership beyond specialist circles and was translated into several languages.

Godman later returned to the twelfth century with Paradoxes of Conscience in the High Middle Ages: Abelard, Heloise, and the Archpoet (Cambridge University Press, 2009), an account of the relationship between ethics and literature focused on authenticity, sincerity, dissimulation, and fictio. He portrayed Abelard as a critic of hypocrisy and Heloise as a major moral thinker, setting both against the Archpoet's ironical literary posture.

The Archpoet then became the center of Godman's monograph The Archpoet and Medieval Culture (Oxford University Press), the first full-length study devoted to this pseudonymous twelfth- century poet associated with Rainald of Dassel. Godman argued that the Archpoet's writings articulate a brilliant intellectual counter-culture in medieval Germany, one that refashioned available political, social, and religious roles to create an alternative to clerical conformity.

Peter Godman's career represents one of the most sustained and wide-ranging engagements with the Latin intellectual tradition in modern scholarship. From Alcuin at the court of Charlemagne to the Archpoet at the court of Rainald of Dassel; from Poliziano and Machiavelli in Florentine circles to Bellarmine as cardinal-inquisitor; from Vatican archival records on Nazi Germany to the ethics of conscience in Abelard and Heloise, the unifying thread is his analysis of how minds of exceptional Latin learning operated within, against, and around institutions of power.

His work on the Carolingian period, especially Poetry of the Carolingian Renaissance and Poets and Emperors, has been directly productive for the study of early medieval culture in its full breadth, connecting the literary record of the Carolingian court to the art-historical record with which Kessler, McKitterick, Bischoff, and Perrin were simultaneously engaged. His edition of Alcuin's York poem demonstrated with particular clarity how Latin literary culture functioned simultaneously as aesthetic achievement and political instrument, a lesson that reverberates through the illustrated manuscripts, figured poems, dedicatory images, and inscribed tituli of the Carolingian visual world.

Gordon, Dillian Rosalind

active late 20th-21st century

Dillian Rosalind Gordon OBE is a British art historian and curator whose work has been central to the modern understanding and cataloguing of early Italian painting, especially the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries. She is best known for her long career at the National Gallery, London, where she became the leading specialist on Italian paintings before 1460 and produced some of the institution's most important scholarly catalogues.

Dillian Gordon studied Modern and Medieval Languages at Girton College, Cambridge, an unusually philological starting point for a future curator of early Italian art and one that equipped her with strong linguistic and textual skills. She subsequently moved to the Courtauld Institute of Art, University of London, where she completed an MA in 1972 with a dissertation on the gilded glass Madonna in the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, signalling an early interest in Marian imagery and precious devotional objects. Gordon then pursued doctoral research, again at the Courtauld, and in 1979 was awarded a PhD with a thesis entitled "Art in Umbria c.1250-c.1350," an ambitious regional study that laid the foundations for her later work on central Italian painting. This combination of language training and specialised art-historical formation positioned her perfectly for a museum career focused on close visual analysis, documentary research and careful attribution studies.

In 1978 Gordon joined the National Gallery in London as a curator of early Italian paintings, entering a department whose holdings stretch from the Duecento to the early Renaissance. Over the next three decades she gradually became the central figure in the Gallery's work on Italian pictures before 1460, eventually holding the post of Curator of Italian Paintings before 1460 and overseeing research, display and cataloguing in this area. Nicholas Penny, later Director of the National Gallery, has noted that Gordon was the first woman to serve as a curator at the institution, underlining both the historical weight of her appointment and the example she set for subsequent generations of female museum professionals. Within the Gallery she was deeply involved in important acquisitions of early Italian works, in the organisation of exhibitions, and in the re-thinking of attributions and datings within the permanent collection. Colleagues have repeatedly stressed her meticulous approach to cataloguing, which combined connoisseurship, technical evidence and documentary research, and helped to stabilise the scholarly record on many complex or fragmentary works.

Gordon retired from her curatorial position in 2010 but maintained close ties with the National Gallery and continued to research and write on thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italian painting. Her post-retirement publications, often linked to exhibitions or catalogue projects, demonstrate an ongoing engagement with issues of workshop practice, iconography and the reconstruction of dispersed altarpieces. Living in Oxford, she has remained active within the broader scholarly community, contributing essays and co-authored volumes that build on the technical and historical work undertaken at the National Gallery in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

Gordon's most substantial scholarly legacy lies in the multi-volume catalogues of Italian paintings at the National Gallery, which have become standard references for specialists in Trecento and Quattrocento art. She is the author of The Italian Paintings before 1400 (London, 2011), a comprehensive catalogue that systematically re-examines the Gallery's holdings of early Italian works, often revisiting attributions and integrating technical imaging and conservation findings into the art-historical discussion. Earlier, she co-authored The Fifteenth Century Italian Paintings, Volume I with Susanna Avery-Quash, further consolidating the documentation and interpretation of the National Gallery's Quattrocento collection. These catalogues are not merely inventory tools but substantial monographs on individual panels and groups of works; they have been praised within the National Gallery itself as among the most important scholarly catalogues produced by any curator there.

Beyond collection catalogues, Gordon has written and co-written a series of more focused books and essays on individual masterpieces and themes. She is the author of The Wilton Diptych: Making & Meaning, a detailed study of the celebrated late fourteenth- century portable altarpiece now in the National Gallery, in which she examines not only the painting's technique and materials but also its iconography and likely function as a devotional object for King Richard II. In this work Gordon argues that the diptych was almost certainly commissioned for Richard's private devotions and explores the interplay of English and French artistic influences in its style, emphasizing the "sophisticated combination of northern and Italian methods" that scholars have identified. Her publication 100 Great Paintings: Duccio to Picasso reflects a broader curatorial remit, presenting key works from different periods in a form accessible to a wider public while maintaining a high level of scholarly accuracy.

Gordon's research has consistently focused on early Italian painting, with a particular emphasis on the Duecento and Trecento and on questions of attribution, provenance and the original configuration of complex altarpieces. Her doctoral work on Umbrian art between about 1250 and 1350 already indicated a concern with regional schools, stylistic networks and the relationships between major and minor masters. Later, at the National Gallery, she became known for reconstructions of dispersed polyptychs and horizontal narrative cycles, including work on ensembles that once included Giotto's Pentecost and panels by Ugolino di Nerio, thereby illuminating the original liturgical and visual contexts of now- isolated paintings. Such reconstructions, grounded in meticulous comparison of panel sizes, carpentry, style and iconography, have contributed to a more coherent understanding of Trecento workshop practice and patronage.

Her study of the Wilton Diptych and related publications on English and Italian connections around 1400 also show a sustained interest in artistic exchange across regions and in the devotional uses of small-scale objects. In combination with catalogue essays on individual works, such as paintings attributed to Andrea di Bonaiuto and others, these studies reflect her ability to move from large structural questions about collections to finely grained analyses of a single panel. Within the National Gallery and more broadly, Gordon has been recognised as a model of scholarly rigor and cautious, evidence-based connoisseurship, qualities that have influenced cataloguing standards well beyond the field of early Italian painting.

In recognition of her services to early Italian painting, Dillian Gordon was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2011, shortly after her retirement from the National Gallery. This honour reflects not only her curatorial achievements but also the impact of her publications, which have become indispensable to scholars, students and curators working on medieval and early Renaissance Italian art. The National Gallery itself has highlighted the exceptional quantity and quality of her catalogues, noting that she has authored more scholarly catalogues than any curator there apart from Martin Davies, a key figure in the institution's earlier history. Her work continues to shape the way early Italian paintings are presented and interpreted, both in London and in the many museums and collections that rely on National Gallery scholarship as a benchmark. Living in Oxford and still active as a researcher and author, Gordon remains an important reference point for ongoing debates about attribution, dating and the interpretation of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italian painting.

Gorman, Michael

active late 20th-21st century

Michael Gorman is an American-born medievalist specializing in the textual and manuscript history of early medieval biblical exegesis, with particular attention to the Carolingian and Anglo-Saxon commentary traditions and to the works attributed, correctly or incorrectly, to Bede and his contemporaries. Working largely outside conventional university tenure, he has built a reputation as one of the field's most exacting and often polemical correctors of received attributions, frequently overturning long-standing consensus through direct manuscript examination.

His long article "The Codex Amiatinus: A Guide to the Legends and Bibliography," published in Studi Medievali in 2003, is an indispensable resource for the modern study of the manuscript. It combines a careful account of the nineteenth-century discovery of the manuscript's true origin with a patient, often pointed dismantling of the garbled and inaccurate versions of that story that continue to circulate in encyclopedic and popular literature. Gorman's article exemplifies the historiographical vigilance the Codex Amiatinus in particular seems to demand, given how persistently its history has been simplified or misreported. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database, which draws on Gorman's bibliographic guide at several points in correcting claims common in general literature.

Gounaris, Georgios

active late 20th – early 21st century

Greek archaeologist and professor of Byzantine Archaeology at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki whose scholarly life was dominated by a sustained, decades-long excavation at Philippi — the Macedonian city on the Via Egnatia where the Apostle Paul preached in approximately 49–50 AD and established what is traditionally regarded as the first Christian community in Europe. His excavation campaigns at the site, his publications on its early Christian and Byzantine monuments, and the archaeological guide he co-authored with his daughter Emmanouela Gounari constitute a contribution to early Byzantine Macedonian archaeology whose importance both for the discipline and for Christian history is difficult to overstate.

The most important monument Gounaris excavated and published at Philippi was the Octagon — a large octagonal martyrium-church of the later fourth or early fifth century built directly over the site of an earlier sacred precinct believed to mark where Paul first preached. One of the grandest early Christian buildings in the eastern Mediterranean, the Octagon's plan — inscribed within a larger structure and carrying the regular symbolism of eight as the number of resurrection and new creation — placed it within the prestigious tradition of imperial octagonal martyria, from the Anastasis Rotunda in Jerusalem to the great baptisteries of Milan and Rome. His 1990 monograph Το βαλανείο και τα βόρεια προσκτίσματα του Οκταγώνου των Φιλίππων (The Bath and the Northern Annexes of the Octagon at Philippi; Archaeological Society at Athens) addressed the practical and liturgical infrastructure attached to the main structure, and his 1984 article on bronze brooches from the Octagon and central Macedonia (Βυζαντιακά 4) applied the material evidence to the typological study of late antique metalwork in the region.

From 1988 until the final years of his career, Gounaris directed the University Excavations of Philippi under the auspices of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. He published successive campaign results systematically in Egnatia, the annual of the university's Department of History and Archaeology: reports covering 1997–99 (including a remarkable mosaic floor with a chariot-race representation), 2000–02, 2003–05, and 2006–07. The later phases of excavation documented a glasswork building with an important ceramic assemblage — including a significant quantity of Macedonian Grey Ware — and traced the urban development of Philippi across the full arc from the Roman colonial period through the early Byzantine centuries: the transformation of a Roman colony into a Christian episcopal city, the construction and modification of its great basilicas and martyria, and the contraction of settlement in the later Byzantine period.

The most accessible synthesis of his understanding of Philippi as an archaeological landscape was the Philippi: Archaeological Guide, co-authored with Emmanouela Gounari and published in English translation (by Sophia Tromara; University Studio Press, Thessaloniki, 2004). He also wrote two university textbooks in Byzantine archaeology used across several Greek universities, extending his scholarly influence beyond the circles of specialists following the Philippi excavation publications. The memorial volume in his honour, Lepetymnos: Studies in Archaeology and Art in Memory of Georgios Gounaris: Late Roman, Byzantine, Post-Byzantine Period, edited by Athanasios Semoglou, Ioanna P. Arvanitidou, and Emmanouela G. Gounari, brings together Greek and international contributors — including the New Testament scholar Peter Pilhoffer, whose contribution "Georgios Gounaris in Philippi: A Retrospective on Half a Century of Research" situates his excavations within the broader history of Pauline scholarship at the site.

Grabar, André

Kiev, 1896 – Paris, 1990

Pioneering French art historian of Russian origin, renowned for his foundational studies on Byzantine and early Christian art. Born on July 26, 1896, in Kiev — then part of the Russian Empire — he fled the Bolshevik Revolution in 1917 and eventually settled in Paris, where he immersed himself in the city's scholarly circles. He studied at the University of Paris (Sorbonne), earning his doctorate in 1931 with a dissertation on early Christian iconography that established him as a leading authority in the field. He taught at the École des Hautes Études and later at the Collège de France from 1946 until his retirement, shaping generations of scholars through a rigorous methodology that blended formal analysis, liturgical context, and cultural history. His tenure at the Bibliothèque Byzantine in Paris further amplified his influence, as he curated resources that became essential for Byzantine studies worldwide.

His seminal works — including L'empereur dans l'art byzantin (1936) and The Beginnings of Christian Art, 200–395 (1967) — redefined the field by arguing that early Christian imagery drew from imperial Roman symbolism to assert theological authority, famously interpreting the haloed emperor as a precursor to the Christ Pantocrator icon. He also explored monastic art and relic cults, linking them to broader socio-political shifts in the Christian East. Later studies on L'art paléochrétien and Byzantium emphasised art's role in imperial ideology and popular devotion, challenging purely aesthetic readings. His interdisciplinary approach — integrating archaeology, texts, and theology — influenced subsequent scholars and remains vital for understanding the transitions from late antiquity to the Romanesque era. He died on October 2, 1990, in Paris.

Gregori, Mina

Cremona, 7 January 1924 - Florence, 8 January 2022

Mina Gregori was one of the most influential Italian art historians of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, internationally recognized above all for her scholarship on Caravaggio and the seventeenth-century Lombard and Tuscan schools. Her work combined rigorous connoisseurship, archival precision, and a sustained commitment to museum and exhibition practice.

Trained in the Longhian tradition, Gregori was among the closest pupils of Roberto Longhi. She absorbed and refined the method centered on direct visual analysis of the work of art, historical context, and strict philological control of attributions.
