This formation placed her at the center of postwar Italian art-historical scholarship and made her a key transmitter of Longhi's methodological legacy to later generations.

Gregori taught for decades in the Italian university system and became a central scholarly reference for early modern painting studies. Her publications and lectures shaped the international discussion on Caravaggio, his workshop circle, and the broader diffusion of naturalism in seventeenth-century Italy. She worked constantly at the intersection of attribution, chronology, and patronage context, producing studies that remain standard points of departure in the field.

A major part of her scholarly profile was curatorial. Gregori directed and co-curated significant exhibitions in Italy and abroad, where she translated specialist research into coherent public narratives without sacrificing critical rigor. Her exhibition work was especially important in reassessing lesser-known Caravaggesque painters and in re-evaluating the relationship between regional schools and major artistic centers.

She also played a crucial institutional role in the preservation and development of Longhi's intellectual heritage. Through her long activity at the Fondazione di Studi di Storia dell'Arte Roberto Longhi in Florence, she helped sustain one of the principal research environments for the study of Italian painting, supporting advanced scholarship, young researchers, and high-level publication projects.

Gregori's legacy lies not only in specific attributions or catalogues, but in a broader model of scholarly practice: disciplined looking, historical responsibility, and continuity between research, teaching, conservation, and public dissemination. For historians of Italian painting, she remains a foundational figure in the modern history of the discipline.

Grivot, Denis

Rully, 3 November 1921 – Autun, 9 July 2008

Denis Grivot was a French Catholic priest, canon and maître de chapelle of the cathedral of Saint-Lazare at Autun, honorary conservator of antiquities and objets d'art for the department of Saône-et-Loire, and the author of some thirty books on the Romanesque art of Burgundy. With the Courtauld scholar George Zarnecki he wrote the monograph that gave the sculptor of Autun his modern identity, and for six decades he was the cathedral's resident interpreter — the man who knew its stones, its archives, and its capitals more intimately than anyone of his generation.

He was born on 3 November 1921 at Rully, in the Côte chalonnaise, into a family of wine merchants. His primary education was at the maîtrise, the choir school of Autun cathedral, an institution to which he would remain attached for the rest of his life; his secondary studies were at the petits séminaires of Rimont and of Semur-en-Brionnais, and his higher studies at Saint-Sulpice in Paris, a formation he would later turn to unexpected account in a book on Talleyrand. Ordained priest in 1947, he was immediately appointed vicar of Saint-Lazare and director of its maîtrise, a post whose survival he is generally credited with having secured through the income and prestige of his own publications.

The work with which his name is permanently associated is Gislebertus, sculpteur d'Autun, published in French by the Trianon Press in 1960 and in English the following year as Gislebertus, Sculptor of Autun. The project was conceived by Arnold Fawcus, the Trianon Press's founder, who brought together Grivot — the canon with unrestricted access to the building and its documentation — and Zarnecki, then the leading specialist in Romanesque sculpture in Britain; the photographic campaign was carried out by Gérard Franceschi, and Paul Deschamps supplied the preface. The volume catalogued the whole surviving corpus of capitals, tympana and lintel fragments, argued from close stylistic comparison that the great majority were the work of a single hand, and read the inscription Gislebertus hoc fecit beneath the feet of Christ as that sculptor's own proud signature.

The effect of the book on the wider literature was out of all proportion to its modest physical format. It established Gislebertus as the earliest Romanesque sculptor whose personality could be reconstructed in detail, and in doing so it made Autun the standard case study for the emergence of individual artistic identity in the twelfth century — a status the monument has never lost. Later scholarship has been considerably less confident: Linda Seidel's Legends in Limestone (1999) reread the inscription as a commemoration of a lay benefactor rather than a craftsman's signature, and revisionists including Xavier Barral i Altet have treated the whole construction as a product of modern rather than medieval assumptions about authorship. What has survived intact from Grivot and Zarnecki's volume is its descriptive catalogue, still the point of departure for any account of the sculptural programme.

Grivot's remaining output was largely regional, devotional and popular in the best sense. His survey of the churches and chapels of Saône-et- Loire was the work that earned him appointment as conservator of antiquities and objets d'art for the department, and he produced a long series of guides, iconographic studies — among them a book on the devil in the cathedral — and local histories, written with a lightness of touch that concealed a great deal of first-hand observation. He was elected to the Académie du Morvan in 1967, and was made a Chevalier de l'Ordre national du Mérite, a Chevalier des Palmes académiques, and a Commandeur de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres.

He died at Autun on 9 July 2008, aged eighty-six, two months before Zarnecki. A square in the city bears his name. His position in the historiography is a distinctive one: not a university scholar, and not formally trained as an art historian, but a resident cleric whose knowledge of a single building was so complete that the international literature on Romanesque sculpture was obliged to build on it.

Grocock, Christopher

active late 20th-21st century

Christopher Grocock is a British classicist and historian whose work spans Roman military and educational culture and the historiography of early Anglo-Saxon monasticism. He is known both for studies of Roman elementary military training and the transmission of Vegetius, and for his contribution to the primary textual scholarship on Wearmouth-Jarrow.

With Ian N. Wood, Grocock edited and translated Abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow in the Oxford Medieval Texts series (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 2013), a critical edition of Bede's Historia abbatum and the anonymous Vita Ceolfridi that supersedes earlier editions and is now the standard basis for citation of these two texts. Since these are the two near-contemporary Northumbrian sources that describe the commissioning of the Codex Amiatinus and its sister pandects, and the departure of Ceolfrith for Rome in 716 carrying one of them as a gift for the tomb of St Peter, the Grocock–Wood edition underlies virtually all modern citation of the manuscript's documentary background. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database, which relies on this edition throughout for its account of the primary testimony.

Grondona, Marco

active late 20th century

Italian scholar associated with the historical studies of the Order of the Servites (Ordine dei Servi di Maria), working principally on the hagiography, iconography, and local cult of the order's founding saints in Umbria and Tuscany. With Davide M. Montagna, O.S.M., Grondona co-authored "Gli apporti dell'iconografia beniziana antica: l'affresco di Todi del 1346," published in Studi Storici dell'Ordine dei Servi di Maria (n. 49, anno XXXVI, 1986, pp. 35–47), a study combining a bibliographic survey of scholarship on the subject since 1980 with a close iconographic reading of the fresco itself.

The article addressed the large fresco of the Ascent of Souls from Purgatory into Paradise, discovered in 1975 in the former church of San Francesco at Todi, which had been attributed to Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio by Federico Zeri; Grondona and Montagna's contribution situated the image within the broader iconographic tradition surrounding the Servite saint Philip Benizi and the legend of Saint Patrick's Purgatory, with which the fresco's imagery is closely bound up. Grondona also co-authored, with C. Grondona, the local history Todi storica e artistica (Todi, 1981), reflecting a sustained scholarly engagement with the art and history of Todi and the Umbrian Servite tradition more broadly.

Grube, Ernst J.

Kufstein, 9 May 1932 - London, 12 June 2011

Ernst J. Grube was one of the foremost historians of Islamic art in the twentieth century and is often regarded as one of the last major representatives of rigorous German-trained art-historical scholarship. He is especially known as the first curator appointed to a dedicated Islamic art department, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Raised and educated in Berlin, he attended the Schiller-Gymnasium and received his doctorate from the Free University of Berlin in 1955. In the same year he entered the Art Library of the Berlin State Museums as an assistant and was later invited into the Islamic Department by Ernst Kuhnel, one of the founders of modern Islamic art history. In 1958 he received a research grant at the Metropolitan Museum, joining its Department of Near Eastern Art in 1959.

In 1962, Grube became Curator of the newly established Department of Islamic Art at the Met, and he taught Islamic art concurrently as an Adjunct Professor at Columbia University. His work at the Met helped shape one of the world's most important Islamic art collections, and his studies of Islamic pottery produced there remain standard references.

After leaving the Met in 1969 and teaching at Hunter College, he moved to Italy in 1972, where he built the next phase of his career. He taught at the University of Padua and then, from 1973, at the Oriental Institute in Naples, before being appointed in 1977 to the Chair of Islamic Art History at Ca' Foscari University of Venice, retiring in 1988. During these years he also founded the journal Islamic Art and served as co-editor with his wife, Eleanor Sims.

His scholarly output was substantial: twelve authored or co-authored books, 117 articles, and 32 reviews. Major works include Muslim Miniature Painting from the XIII to the XIX Century, The Classical Style in Islamic Painting, Cobalt and Lustre: The First Centuries of Islamic Pottery, and The World of Islam (translated into multiple languages). Portable arts, especially ceramics, miniature painting, and Fatimid rock crystal, remained central to his research throughout his career.

For medieval art and manuscript studies, Grube's work on Islamic miniature painting remains a key comparative framework. He highlighted how manuscript traditions developing from the thirteenth century onward, including the Baghdad school, formed sophisticated narrative and figural systems in dialogue with Byzantine and Italian visual cultures through trade, diplomacy, and the Sicilian context.

Guarnieri, Romana

The Hague, 1913 – Rome, 23 December 2004

Few twentieth-century scholars changed a medieval text's status as decisively as Romana Guarnieri did in a single newspaper article. She was, by her own description, a historian by vocation rather than by profession — she never held a university chair — yet her work on the Free Spirit and on female mysticism remains foundational.

She was born in The Hague in 1913 to an Italian father and a Dutch mother. Her father was Romano Guarnieri, a cultural mediator between Italy and the Low Countries connected with Papini, Prezzolini, Marinetti and Rebora, and among the founders of the Università per Stranieri in Perugia; her mother was Iete van Beuge, a painter from a Reformed background. Her parents separated when she was young, and she was for a time raised by agnostic, theosophically inclined grandparents; after her mother remarried an Italian architect she moved to Italy, settling in Rome. She arrived at the age of twelve, and after secondary school specialised in German language and literature at the Sapienza, completing her degree in 1939.

De Luca and the Edizioni di Storia e Letteratura

In 1938, introduced by Angela Zucconi, she met the Roman priest and érudit Giuseppe De Luca (1898–1962), who asked the young scholar to assist him in his editorial projects; the intellectual partnership that followed ended only with his death. Though baptised, Guarnieri had until then had no relationship with the faith; the encounter produced both her conversion and her research programme. Alongside De Luca she took part in founding the Edizioni di Storia e Letteratura and the Archivio italiano per la Storia della Pietà, which she directed from 1962.

De Luca's category of pietà — the lived presence of God in ordinary human history, pursued across individuals, groups and communities — gave her the frame within which she worked for the next sixty years.

On 16 June 1946, in an article in L'Osservatore Romano titled "Lo 'Specchio delle anime semplici' e Margherita Poirette", Guarnieri identified Marguerite Porete as the author of the Mirror of Simple Souls — reuniting an anonymous, widely diffused mystical treatise with the beguine burned at Paris in 1310. The attribution transformed the Mirouer into what is now recognised as the earliest known speculative work by a woman in Old French.

The scholarly apparatus followed over four decades:

  • 1961 — a provisional edition of the Chantilly manuscript (Musée Condé, F XIV 26), issued in 100 copies out of commerce by the Edizioni di Storia e Letteratura.
  • 1965 — "Il movimento del Libero Spirito. Testi e documenti", Archivio italiano per la storia della pietà 4, pp. 501–635, her magnum opus: a dossier of texts, inquisitorial records and manuscript witnesses. Its census of heresy cases (181 in total, with 29 references to the Speculum) remains a starting point for work on the Italian diffusion of the text.
  • 1986 — the critical edition prepared with Paul Verdeyen, Le mirouer des simples âmes / Speculum simplicium animarum, Corpus Christianorum Continuatio Mediaevalis 69 (Turnhout: Brepols), pairing the French text with the Latin version.

Her Dutch formation made her a pioneer of Italian nederlandistica: a study of Guido Gezelle (Morcelliana, 1941), a translation of Cyriel Verschaeve's Crocifisso (1942), and Hadewijch's Cinque poesie with Brabantine text (1947), followed much later by the Poesie Visioni Lettere of Hadewijch (Marietti, 2000).

On De Luca she wrote the first biographical profile, Don Giuseppe De Luca tra cronaca e storia (Il Mulino, 1974; new edition 1991), and the memoir Una singolare amicizia. Ricordando don Giuseppe De Luca (Marietti, 1998); their correspondence was later published as Tra le stelle e il profondo, edited by Vanessa Roghi (Morcelliana, 2010). From 1987 she directed the pietà section of the review "Bailamme". Her collected essays appeared as Donne e chiesa tra mistica e istituzioni, secoli XIII–XV (Storia e Letteratura 218, 2004).

She did not merely study beguinal life but practised it, consecrating herself by private vows to charity and study — an identification she explained as living in the world without being of it, belonging to everyone and to no one. Don Mario Sensi noted the difference: unlike the medieval beguines, hers was not a penitential choice but one of study understood as a means of sanctification. She died in a Roman hospital on 23 December 2004. Her library was donated by her nephews Adriano and Massimo to the Istituto Veritatis Splendor in Bologna, where it remains a working research collection.

Gudiol i Ricart, Josep

Vic, 1904 – Barcelona, 1985

Catalan art historian who specialised in Catalan Romanesque and Gothic painting and the broader field of Spanish medieval art, with a scholarly focus directly relevant to the twelfth through fourteenth centuries. Born Josep Maria Gudiol i Ricart in 1904 in Vic, Catalonia, he came from a family of art scholars: his uncle Josep Gudiol i Cunill was among the founders of Catalan art historiography. His work was distinguished by a systematic approach to cataloguing and stylistic analysis. During the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), he served as the Generalitat's commissioner for the preservation of artistic heritage, actively dedicating himself to the rescue of works of art — including the Romanesque frescoes of the Monastery of Santa Maria de Sixena in Aragon — documenting and removing wall panels to protect them from destruction. After the war he emigrated to the United States, where he taught as a professor, helping to disseminate knowledge of Catalan and Spanish art beyond European borders.

Gudiol Ricart directed the Institut Amatller d'Art Hispànic in Barcelona, a key centre for the study of Hispanic art, where he promoted restorations and research on medieval frescoes and sculptures. His most monumental contribution is the series Ars Hispaniae, a forty-volume encyclopaedia on the history of Spanish art, for which he edited the sections dedicated to the Middle Ages. Key publications within this programme include Las Pinturas Murales Románicas de Cataluña (1948, with José Pijoán), which analyses Catalan Romanesque frescoes with a focus on techniques, iconography, and attributions, and Arquitectura y Escultura Románicas (1948, with Juan Antonio Gaya Nuño), essential for understanding the evolution of sculpture in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. These works employ connoisseurship methods to distinguish local schools, offering a detailed picture of Romanesque painting traditions that preceded Catalan Gothic.

Gudiol died in 1985 in Barcelona, leaving a lasting legacy in the historiography of medieval Iberian art often compared to that of Chandler Rathfon Post for its coverage of Spanish painting. His daughter, Montserrat Gudiol i Corominas (1933–2015), was a painter trained in his studio for the restoration of medieval paintings, continuing the family's commitment to art; her research on Romanesque manuscripts and frescoes remains a reference for scholars of medieval iconography.

Gwynn, John

Larne, County Antrim, 28 August 1827 – Dublin, 3 April 1917

John Gwynn was born on 28 August 1827 in Larne, County Antrim, the eldest son of the Reverend Stephen Gwynne, rector of Larne and later of Portstewart, and grandson of the Reverend John Gwynne, rector of Kilroot. His mother drowned when he was ten years old. Educated at Enniskillen Royal School and, from 1845, at Trinity College Dublin, he proved a formidable linguist from the outset, mastering Latin, Greek, and Hebrew as an undergraduate; he took his BA in Mathematics in 1850, his MA in 1854, his Bachelor of Divinity in 1861, and his Doctorate of Divinity in 1880. Later in life, largely to occupy himself during the train journeys between his Ulster parishes and Dublin, he taught himself Syriac — a self-directed feat of philology that would eventually place him among the leading Syriac textual scholars of his generation.

Gwynn was elected a Fellow of Trinity College Dublin in 1853 and served as Warden of St Columba's College from 1856 to 1863, after which he spent two decades in parish and cathedral work in County Donegal and Londonderry, holding the deaneries of Raphoe and Derry. He returned to Trinity as a Divinity Lecturer in 1883 and was appointed Regius Professor of Divinity in 1888, a chair he held until 1907. Around 1862 he married Lucy Josephine, daughter of the nationalist leader William Smith O'Brien; the marriage produced ten children, several of whom became notable in their own right, including the writer and MP Stephen Lucius Gwynn, the future Provost of Trinity College Edward John Gwynn, and Robert Malcolm Gwynn, a Fellow of Trinity who would go on to assist his father's greatest editorial project.

Gwynn's Syriac scholarship culminated in his Two Memoirs on the Syriac Versions of the New Testament (1893) and The Apocalypse of St John in a Syriac Version Hitherto Unknown (1897); together with his editions of four short epistles missing from the received Peshitta text, this work was substantial enough to be incorporated into the standard Syriac Peshitta New Testament published by the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1905.

It is, however, as the editor of the Book of Armagh that Gwynn is principally remembered. The project had been begun many years earlier by the antiquary Bishop William Reeves, who assembled a great mass of preparatory material before his death in 1892; Gwynn carried the work forward over roughly two more decades of sustained labour, and in 1913 the Royal Irish Academy published his Liber Ardmachanus: The Book of Armagh, a full diplomatic transcription of the entire codex, with an extensive introduction and appendices, in a de luxe edition limited to four hundred copies. His son Robert M. Gwynn contributed a critical study of the Pauline text to the same volume. More than a century later, Gwynn's remains the only edition of the whole manuscript, and it is the foundation on which all subsequent study — including Ludwig Bieler's critical edition of the Patrician texts in 1979 — has been built. On the long-disputed question of how many scribes wrote the manuscript, Gwynn, who had lived with the codex for years in the course of his transcription, held the unitary view that it was substantially the work of Ferdomnach alone, a position later revisited, from different directions, by E. A. Lowe and by Richard Sharpe.

John Gwynn died in Dublin on 3 April 1917, having produced, in his eighties, the edition on which the whole of modern Book of Armagh scholarship still depends.

H

Hadermann-Misguich, Lydie

Belgium - 27 August 2018

Lydie Hadermann-Misguich was a Belgian art historian and one of the foremost specialists of twelfth-century Byzantine painting. Associated with the Universite Libre de Bruxelles, her career spanned more than half a century and produced scholarship of enduring authority on Komnenian frescoes, mosaics, and iconography across the Byzantine world and its Latin periphery.

She formed her scholarly identity within the Belgian tradition of Byzantine studies shaped by the journal Byzantion and the intellectual milieu around the Universite Libre de Bruxelles. From the early 1960s, she demonstrated striking range, publishing in 1964 on the Byzantine spirit in El Greco, on the mosaics of Byzantine Athens, and on the Modena Polyptych. Her involvement in the major 1964 exhibition Byzantine Art, An European Art in Athens placed her in direct contact with an international network of Byzantinists at a formative moment.

The cornerstone of her reputation is the monumental study Kurbinovo: Les fresques de Saint-Georges et la peinture byzantine du XIIe siecle (Editions de Byzantion, Brussels, 1975). In this 606-page work, she analyzed in exhaustive detail the fresco cycle of Saint George at Kurbinovo (dated 1191), situating it within the wider development of late Komnenian monumental painting and addressing workshop identity, stylistic sources, and the relationship between Constantinople and provincial centers. The book received the Prix Suzanne Tassier in 1977 and remains a foundational reference. In 1992, she returned to Kurbinovo in a bilingual French-Macedonian volume co-authored with Cvetan Grozdanov.

Throughout her career, Hadermann-Misguich explored the diffusion of Constantinopolitan models into peripheral zones, including Sicily, Cyprus, Latium, and Crusader territories, and studied how Byzantine workshops transmitted iconographic formulae through manuscript illumination, luxury textiles, and ivories. Her work on Sicilian mosaics, including Monreale, on churches of Kastoria, and on the fresco cycles of Ninfa in Lazio mapped the broad geographic reach of Komnenian style. Her volume Images de Ninfa: Peintures medievales dans une ville detruite du Latium (Fondazione Camillo Caetani, Rome, 1986) synthesized her research on the site and its Byzantine-Italian visual dialogue.

A recurrent thread in her scholarship was the Byzantine heritage in El Greco, especially the persistence of Orthodox pictorial conventions in his mature Spanish work. Beginning with a 1964 article in the Revue de l'Universite de Bruxelles, she returned to the subject repeatedly; these studies were reprinted in 1990 in a volume edited by Nikos Hadjinicolaou. In parallel, she devoted major studies to the sixteenth-century Cretan painter Georges Klontzas, including analysis of his illustrated manuscript of the Oracles of Leo the Wise in the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice, highlighting the interplay of Byzantine, Mannerist, and eschatological imagery.

Hadermann-Misguich also published important studies on Marian iconography, including the affective types of the Pelagonitissa and Kardiotissa, on the Epitaphios Threnos tradition, on the exterior decoration of Byzantine churches, and on spatial ambiguity in monumental painting. She was a long-standing member of the Groupe de Recherche en Histoire Medievale at the Universite Libre de Bruxelles. She died on 27 August 2018, returning from a journey that ended in Athens. The obituary published in Byzantion by Catherine Vanderheyde testifies to the high esteem in which she was held. Her later collected volume, Le Temps des Anges: Recueil d'etudes sur la peinture byzantine du XIIe siecle, ses antecedents, son rayonnement, gathered her most enduring essays and confirmed her place among the leading interpreters of Komnenian-era art.

Halpin, James

dates of birth and death not established in the accessible record; active in Ireland in the late 19th century

James Halpin was a contributor to the Irish Ecclesiastical Record, in which he published an account of the Book of Dimma in 1890. Writing within the antiquarian tradition exemplified by Eugene O'Curry, Halpin treated the manuscript as a genuine seventh-century production, copied by the scribe Dimma for Saint Crónán within the saint's own lifetime — the traditional dating and authorship that had stood essentially unchallenged for centuries and would not be overturned until Richard Irvine Best's demonstration, in 1926, that the manuscript's "Dimma" colophons had been altered over an erasure.

Halpin's article is of interest today chiefly as a representative specimen of pre-critical Book of Dimma scholarship: a marker of what was confidently believed about the manuscript's date, authorship and making before the palaeographic and codicological reassessments of the twentieth century set the record straight.

Hautecoeur, Louis-Eugene-Georges

Paris, 11 June 1884 - Paris, 17 November 1973

Louis-Eugene-Georges Hautecoeur was born on 11 June 1884 in Paris, the son of Alfred Albert Hautecoeur and Jeanne née Barrault, who were print merchants. He received a rigorous humanistic education at the prestigious Lycée Henri-IV before gaining admission to the École Normale Supérieure in 1905, one of the most selective academic institutions in France. He passed the agrégation examination in 1908, qualifying him for a high-level academic career, and subsequently spent two formative years (1908-1910) at the École française de Rome, where he was entrusted with the direction of archaeological excavations in Tunisia under the patronage of the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles Lettres. It was during this Roman sojourn that he developed his lifelong fascination with the classical tradition in European architecture, and in 1909 he married his first wife, Marcelle Charlotte Poullain.

Returning to France in 1910, Hautecoeur held teaching positions in Paris, Laon, and Amiens before the outbreak of the First World War. He was awarded his doctorate in 1912, the same year he published his first major scholarly work, L'architecture classique à Saint-Pétersbourg à la fin du XVIIIe siècle (H. Champion, 1912), a pioneering study arguing that Westernized Russian architecture was of cosmopolitan European - not exclusively French - origin. This nuanced, pan-European view distinguished him from contemporaries like Louis Réau, who emphasized French cultural primacy. Mobilized in 1914 as a Second-Lieutenant in the 152nd Infantry Division, he was eventually seconded to the Ministry of War in 1917 and posted as head of the Diplomatic Information Service in Lugano, Switzerland.

After the Armistice, Hautecoeur built a remarkable dual career as both scholar and museum administrator. He was appointed professor of art history at the Université de Caen (1919-1931) and simultaneously held the Chair of Architectural History at the École des Beaux-Arts and taught at the École du Louvre, both from 1920 to 1940. On the institutional side, he served in curatorial roles at the Louvre (1919-1927) and became the last conservator of the historic Musée du Luxembourg (1927-1937), the museum dedicated to the work of living artists. He then played a central role in organizing the Musée National d'Art Moderne at the Palais de Tokyo and served as its director until 1940, earning the rank of Knight in the Legion d'honneur in 1938 for this constellation of contributions.

The most contested period of Hautecoeur's career opened in July 1940 when he was appointed Directeur Général des Beaux-Arts under the Vichy regime, replacing Georges Huisman, who had been deemed too critical of the new government. From March 1941, he held the role of Secrétaire Général des Beaux-Arts and Conseiller d'Etat, and during this period he received the Ordre de la Francisque, Vichy's highest distinction. Scholars have debated his conduct: he appears to have used his position to maintain French cultural institutions and protect the artistic patrimony rather than to actively serve Nazi interests. Indeed, in early 1944 he was removed from office by direct order of Hermann Goring for "refusal to collaborate," and he subsequently became director of studies at the École Pratique des Hautes Études. Following the Liberation, he was reinstated as Secrétaire Général, a testament to the overall judgment that his wartime behavior was defensible, though his 1951 membership in the Association for the Défense of the Memory of Marshal Pétain remained a source of controversy.

Hautecoeur's enduring scholarly monument is the monumental Histoire de l'architecture classique en France, a project he began in the 1920s and published across seven volumes in eleven books between 1943 and 1957 (Éditions Picard). This encyclopedic work traces the development of classical architecture in France from the sixteenth century through the nineteenth, establishing a coherent interpretive framework for the relationship between French national identity and the classical tradition. The work became a foundational reference for subsequent generations of architectural historians and remains a standard scholarly source to this day. His student and interpreter Antonio Brucculeri later analyzed the intellectual genesis of this project in the monograph Du dessein historique à l'action publique. Louis Hautecoeur et l'architecture classique en France (Picard, 2007).

In 1952, Hautecoeur was elected to the Institut de France and took Seat No. 6 in the "Unattached" (Membres libres) section of the Académie des Beaux-Arts, succeeding Gabriel Cognacq. On 6 July 1955, he was elected Secrétaire perpétuel of the Académie des Beaux-Arts, the institution's highest permanent administrative office. He also served as President of the Comité Français d'Histoire de l'Art (CFHA) and vice-president of the Commission du Vieux Paris. A widower following the death of his first wife, he married the paleographer Marguerite Milliez (1918-2001) in 1956, a union that united two distinguished scholarly careers. He died in Paris on 17 November 1973, leaving behind an institutional and intellectual legacy that remains inseparable from the history of French art historiography.

Hawkins, Ernest Joseph Weaver

Dulwich, 1905 – Whiteley Village, 1993

Ernest Joseph Weaver Hawkins was born in 1905 in Dulwich, Southwark, London. He received no formal training in art history, instead apprenticing as a sculptor to the architectural carver Lawrence A. Turner from 1922 until 1927. As a sculptor he worked in a neo-Romanesque style, producing work for Westminster Cathedral — the staircase to the pulpit, added during the remodelling of 1934 — and the screen to St. Patrick's Chapel. He married Hilda Routen in 1930.

His path into Byzantine studies was accidental rather than vocational. In 1938 he joined the private Byzantine Institute of America, founded by the wealthy scholar Thomas Whittemore, as a technical assistant in Istanbul — motivated apparently by the need to make a living. That pragmatic beginning belied what would become a career of extraordinary scholarly consequence. Hawkins quickly became Whittemore's lieutenant in the field projects restoring the mosaics of Hagia Sophia, proposing the priorities for how the mosaics of the church should be revealed and leading the team that cleaned the gallery mosaics to uncover the Deësis, the imperial portraits, the apse mosaic and its archangel, and the saints of the north tympanum wall of the nave. When Whittemore died suddenly in 1950, Hawkins served under his successor Paul A. Underwood of the Dumbarton Oaks Center for Byzantine Studies, which gradually assumed control of the Institute's projects. This ensuing period resulted in the uncovering of the seventh-century pavement in the Church of the Pantocrator (Molla Zeyrek Camii), the restoration of mosaics in Fethiye Camii (Church of Theotokos Pammakaristos), and repair work at Fenari Isa (Lips Monastery).

In 1963 Hawkins became Assistant Field Director and Research Associate at the Dumbarton Oaks Center. He led the initiative to re-examine the apse mosaic of Hagia Sophia in 1964, conclusively proving that the Virgin and Child mosaics were completed in 867 AD — a milestone in Byzantine scholarship that resolved a long-standing art-historical dispute with evidence drawn directly from material examination of the mosaic surface itself. He also led campaigns to document and restore the buildings and decorations of the Kariye Camii, Fethiye Camii, Zeirek Camii, Bodrum Camii, Kalenderhane Camii, the Church of Constantine Lips, and St. Eirene, and participated in projects at Córdoba, San Marco in Venice, Jerusalem, and monuments in Cyprus. He campaigned — successfully in the case of the Chora church — against removing mosaics from the wall and resetting them, for fear that original surface nuances would be lost. Runciman later described Hawkins's restoration of the Kariye Camii as turning it into "the loveliest thing to see in all Istanbul."

Hawkins was invited to Cyprus in 1952 by Arthur Megaw, director of the Antiquities Department of the colonial administration of Cyprus. The church of Panayia Kanakaria, with its early sixth-century apse mosaic, was conserved in the years 1952–1970 by the Dumbarton Oaks Institute under his direction. The documentation Hawkins produced proved of critical historical value: the photographs he took in 1970 provide the most complete record of the monument prior to the Turkish invasion of 1974 and the subsequent looting that stripped or stole the mosaics entirely — as was the case both at Kanakaria and at the sixth-century apse of Livadhia.

What set Hawkins apart from academic art historians was his grounded, material understanding of medieval craft technique. He changed the widely held view of how medieval mosaics were created, demonstrating that the tesserae were set directly into the walls — not on panels in the studio and subsequently transferred — a fundamental correction that reshaped the understanding of Byzantine workshop practice. At the monastery of St. Catherine's at Sinai, he discovered that art historians had formed their conclusions about the Justinian-era mosaics without realising that the work was clouded by layers of nineteenth-century varnish, correcting generations of misattribution and misdating based on a distorted visual record. As a restorer, Hawkins was noted for his knowledge of medieval pigment and, just as importantly, where to buy it locally; he never remade or repainted pictures. His techniques were recorded in Helmut Schlunk's Die Mosaikkuppel von Centcelles (1988).

Hawkins received an OBE in 1971 and retired in 1975. His photographs and field notes reside at the Courtauld Institute of Art. He died in 1993 at Whiteley Village, Surrey; his obituary was written by Robin Cormack, his long-time collaborator, in The Independent of 10 June 1993. Hawkins was more than a craftsman and conservator: his co-operation with trained art historians helped set the standard and programme for Byzantine excavation and restoration for succeeding generations, and he carefully brought the mosaics to their present form without "restoration" — that is, without adding to them to make their appearance seem original. His career stands as one of the most consequential of any non-academic scholar in the history of Byzantine studies.

Henderson, George David Smith

born 1931, Aberdeen

George David Smith Henderson is a British art historian, Emeritus Professor of Medieval Art at the University of Cambridge, and the author of From Durrow to Kells, the standard interpretative study of the Insular gospel books.

He is the son of George David Henderson, professor of ecclesiastical history, and Janet Smith. He took his BA at the University of Aberdeen in 1953, moved to the University of London for an MA (1956), and was then admitted to Cambridge, where he took an MA and, in 1961, his PhD. In 1957 he married Isabel Bisset Murray, then a librarian at the National Library of Scotland — the Pictish scholar Isabel Henderson, with whom he would later collaborate.

He was appointed to Downing College, Cambridge, in 1961, remaining until 1964, and held a Research Fellowship at the Barber Institute of Fine Arts, University of Birmingham, in 1960–61. He was then Lecturer in the History of Art at the University of Manchester, 1963–66, and Lecturer in Art History at the University of Edinburgh, 1966–73. He remained at Edinburgh until 1973, when he was appointed at Cambridge as Lecturer in the History of Art and Fellow of Downing College, taking up the post in 1974. A specialist in Gothic and medieval art, he holds degrees from Aberdeen and London and a Cambridge doctorate. He rose to the chair of Medieval Art at Cambridge, from which he is now emeritus.

He was elected a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London in January 1975, is a member of the Association of Art Historians, and was awarded the Reginald Taylor Prize of the British Archaeological Association in 1962 for his paper "The Sources of the Genesis Cycle at St.-Savin-sur-Gartempe." He has been a visiting lecturer at the Courtauld Institute of Art, and has donated photographs to the Conway Library, currently being digitised. The Cambridge department places him in a line of descent from M. R. James and Robert Willis through S. C. Cockerell and C. R. Dodwell; his students included Michael Camille.

Henderson's early work lay in Romanesque and Gothic manuscript illumination and its late antique sources. His articles include "Late-Antique Influences in some English Mediaeval Illustrations of Genesis: the Caedmon, Aelfric and Egerton MSS," Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 25 (July 1962), pp. 172–198; "Apocalypse Manuscript in Paris: B.N. MS Lat. 10474," Art Bulletin 52 (March 1970), pp. 22–31; and "The Meaning of Leaf 5 of Fitzwilliam MS 330," Burlington Magazine 133 (October 1991), pp. 682–86. He also wrote the two short introductory volumes for Penguin's scholarly survey series — Gothic (1967) and Chartres (1968).

His major contribution to Insular studies is From Durrow to Kells: The Insular Gospel-Books, 650–800, published in 1987 (London: Thames & Hudson; 224 pp., 263 illustrations; ISBN 0-500-23474-4). The book treats Durrow, Lindisfarne, the Echternach and Durham gospel books, and Kells not as a sequence of stylistic stages but as a series of related intellectual projects, in which ornamental and iconographic invention answers to theological programme and to the demands of the gospel text itself. It remains the standard point of departure for situating Kells within the Insular tradition, and its account of the relationship between decoration and textual articulation underlies much subsequent work, including Farr's and Pulliam's.

His later publications include Vision and Image in Early Christian England (Cambridge University Press, 1999), and The Art of the Picts: Sculpture and Metalwork in Early Medieval Scotland, written with Isabel Henderson (Thames & Hudson, 2004) — a book of direct relevance to the current Portmahomack debate over the origins of Kells.

Henry, Françoise

Paris, 16 June 1902 – Auxerre, 10 February 1982

Françoise Henry was the dominant twentieth-century interpreter of early Irish art — a Frenchwoman who effectively founded the academic discipline of art history in Ireland, and whose 1974 study of the Book of Kells proposed the three-artist division that remained orthodoxy for a generation.

She was born in Paris, the only child of René Henry — deputy chef de cabinet to the president of the French Chamber of Deputies, professor at l'École des Sciences Politiques, and a writer on European affairs — and Jeanne Henry, née Clément, both of Paris. Her father left when she was young, so that her mother's family, of Swiss French Protestant stock, was the main influence on her upbringing and gave direction to her life's work. Her grandfather Charles Clément (1821–87) was a philosopher and writer on art; as a child she often stayed at her grandmother's house near Paris, surrounded by paintings and with discussions of art an everyday occurrence. She was brought up in the Limousin.

She studied under the medievalists Henri Focillon and Henri Hubert in Paris, who advanced her career by securing her a position at the Musée des Antiquités Nationales at Saint-Germain-en-Laye. She first came to Ireland in 1926, and her fascination with the stone high crosses at Ahenny and elsewhere in Tipperary and Kilkenny led her to write a doctoral thesis on Irish early Christian stonework, published in two volumes in Paris in 1933. The 1926 visit came at the invitation of Carrie Fitzgerald at Synone, Boherlahan, near Cashel; with Focillon's support Henry settled on Irish Celtic sculpture as her dissertation subject, and returned to Ireland for primary research, travelling the landscape by bicycle with Fitzgerald and Marie Duport. She secured an appointment in the French department at University College Dublin in 1932, the year her Doctorat d'État was awarded; the dissertation appeared in 1933 as La sculpture irlandaise pendant les douze premiers siècles de l'ère chrétienne, with a secondary thesis, Les tumulus du département de la Côte-d'Or, dedicated to Hubert.

Henry spent her working life in Ireland, moving from the French department into art history proper. At University College Dublin she founded the Department of History of European Painting in 1965 and headed it until her retirement in 1974. She is remembered there as the Department's founder and first Head; the Françoise Henry Reading Room, the School's dedicated art history library, was built around a nucleus of her own books. She is credited with founding the discipline of art history in Ireland.

She was also an excavator. Her fieldwork on the island of Inishkea, off the Mullet peninsula in Co. Mayo, became the subject of renewed interest when two versions of her excavation diary appeared — one in French edited by Barbara Wright, the other in English edited by Janet Marquardt — giving her elegantly written private impressions of digging on the island. She was a gifted photographer; her images, such as the Crucifixion pillar on Duvillaun Mór, remain in the Royal Irish Academy collections, some with details chalked in by her own hand to bring out the carving.

The three-volume survey published by Cornell University Press — Irish Art in the Early Christian Period, to 800 A.D. (1965), Irish Art During the Viking Invasions, 800–1020 A.D. (1967), and Irish Art in the Romanesque Period, 1020–1170 A.D. (1970) — established the chronology of the field; it grew out of her earlier volumes for Zodiaque (La Pierre-qui-Vire, 1963–64).

The Book of Kells: Reproductions from the Manuscript in Trinity College, Dublin appeared in 1974 (London: Thames & Hudson; New York: Knopf), with a substantial study of the manuscript and full-colour plates. In it Henry distinguished three scribes (conventionally A, B and C) and, more influentially, three artists, for whom she coined the designations still in use: the Goldsmith, responsible for the Chi-Rho and the eight-circle cross page, named for his fondness for yellow and for a metalwork-like fineness of finish; the Illustrator, who painted the Temptation and Arrest pages; and the Portrait Painter, responsible for the Virgin and Child and the Evangelist portraits. These are her own terms, not later shorthand — a point worth stating, since the labels circulate widely without attribution. Her tripartite division held the field until Bernard Meehan subdivided her Hand C to argue for a fourth scribe, and it remains the principal alternative reading of the manuscript's division of labour.

Her collected essays were assembled posthumously, in part with Geneviève Marsh-Micheli, as Studies in Early Christian and Medieval Irish Art (London: Pindar Press, 3 vols, 1983–85).

She was elected MRIA in 1949 — one of the first four women admitted to the Royal Irish Academy — and FSA in 1951, and received honorary doctorates from Dublin University (1963) and the National University of Ireland. Her papers are deposited in the Royal Irish Academy, the UCD Archives, and private hands. A self-portrait in conté drawn at nineteen and a pencil portrait of c. 1977 by Muriel Brandt are privately held; a head carved in Cashel sandstone by Domhnall Ó Murchadha (1982) is in the National College of Art. She was among the scholars celebrated in the Royal Irish Academy's Women on Walls exhibition. She died in 1982 at her house at Lindry in Burgundy, and is buried there; her death is recorded at Auxerre on 10 February 1982. Her photographic archive is being digitised by the Courtauld Institute of Art as part of the Courtauld Connects project.

Hermanin de Reichenfeld, Federico

Bari, 16 September 1868 – Rome, 29 June 1953

Federico Hermanin de Reichenfeld was born in Bari on September 16, 1868, to Federico Leopoldo, a general staff officer and honorary aide-de-camp to Umberto I, and Camilla Marstaller, both of Austro-German origin and Protestant faith. Although the family moved frequently due to his father's duties, their connection to the Germanic community in Italy remained strong, further strengthened by his marriage to Margherita Hausmann, daughter of the Danish consul in Bari. After settling in Rome, the city became the absolute center of his intellectual and professional life, decisively shaping his identity as a scholar.

In Rome, he earned his degree in 1895 with a thesis in Romance philology on the reception of the Tristan poem in Italy, under the guidance of E. Monaci, holder of the chair of Neo-Latin languages and literature. It was only beginning in 1896 that he turned toward art history, drawing closer to Adolfo Venturi, who that year had just secured the establishment of the first Italian chair of art history at the University of Rome, along with an affiliated advanced training school for future museum curators. His solid philological and positivist training proved decisive: Hermanin realized that the rigor of analyzing written sources was perfectly applicable to the critical study of works of art, a method that would characterize his entire scholarly output.

The most celebrated moment of Hermanin's scholarly career was the discovery, in October 1900, of the great thirteenth-century fresco of the Last Judgment in the Basilica of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, which he immediately attributed to the Roman painter Pietro Cavallini. This was a discovery of exceptional significance, destined to reignite critical attention on Roman medieval art and to fuel the historiographical debate for decades regarding the relationship between Cavallini and Giotto in the birth of modern Italian painting. Hermanin returned to the subject several times: in 1900 with a report on the discovery in the Archivio della Società romana di storia patria, in 1901 with a critical analysis in the journal L'Arte, and finally in 1902 with the seminal monograph Gli affreschi di Pietro Cavallini a Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, published in the Gallerie nazionali italiane.

In 1924, with the article Il maestro di Giotto, Hermanin explicitly stated his position: Cavallini preceded and influenced Giotto, being a key figure for understanding the Roman roots of the great pictorial turning point of the thirteenth century. This thesis, later discussed and reworked by successive generations of art historians, remains one of the most original and fruitful contributions to the entire field of Italian medieval historiography.

Having joined the Fine Arts administration in 1898, Hermanin worked for years at the National Print Cabinet in Palazzo Corsini, curating the catalog of engravings featuring Roman views and promoting a rich program of public exhibitions on graphic art. In 1908, he was appointed director of the National Gallery of Ancient Art at Palazzo Corsini, where he distinguished himself through an acquisition policy focused on the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, going against the grain of his mentor Venturi, who favored the Renaissance. It was he who secured the famous Narcissus by Caravaggio as a gift for the Gallery in 1914, organizing a small exhibition of Caravaggio-inspired paintings on that occasion.

On December 30, 1913, he was appointed Superintendent of the Galleries and Museums of Lazio and Abruzzo, a position he held until his retirement in 1938, although he continued to receive official assignments until 1945. In this capacity, he actively participated in the recovery of artworks damaged by the 1915 Marsica earthquake, saving a priceless heritage from dispersion and transferring many works to Rome.

The most ambitious museographic project of Hermanin's entire career was the creation of the Museum of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance at Palazzo Venezia, which became the focus of his professional life for over twenty years. As early as 1906, he had advocated for the establishment of a National Historical Museum at Castel Sant'Angelo, envisioning a space that would bring together paintings, sculptures, and the so-called "minor" arts — ceramics, ivories, textiles, small bronzes — to evoke the harmonious unity of the arts across every era, in contrast to the cold, positivist museum organized by schools and periods. Work began in 1916, and Hermanin gradually arranged over thirty rooms, completing the project in 1936, although the museum was never regularly opened to the public due to interference from the fascist regime, which designated Palazzo Venezia as the government's official residence.

In 1904, on a ministerial commission, Hermanin studied the paintings of the monasteries of Subiaco, producing a fundamental contribution in the collective volume The Monasteries of Subiaco (Rome, 1904), which remained for a long time the standard work for that geographical and artistic area. His magnum opus, Art in Rome from the 8th to the 14th Century, was conceived in the 1930s on commission from the National Institute of Roman Studies, but could only be published in 1945, symbolically crowning a lifetime of research. This work, still consulted today as a milestone in historiography, provides a systematic reconstruction of Roman artistic production from the early Middle Ages to the end of the fourteenth century, with a perspective that highlights Rome as the driving force behind Italian medieval painting.

Hermanin was also an active contributor to Venturi's journal L'Arte from 1898 to 1908, editing bibliographic reviews of foreign journals and publishing original research, including studies on Vatican miniatures. In 1923, he founded the journal Roma, later transferred to the National Institute of Roman Studies, and published a monograph on G. B. Piranesi. His popular works include La Farnesina (1927), Life in Old Italian Prints (1928), The Myth of Giorgione (1933), and The Borgia Apartment in the Vatican (1934), while his two-volume work on Italian artists in Germany was of greater scholarly rigor. He died in Rome on June 29, 1953, leaving a lasting mark on both the historiography of medieval Italian art and the history of Roman museum institutions.

Hort, Fenton John Anthony

Dublin, 23 April 1828 - Cambridge, 30 November 1892

Fenton John Anthony Hort was one of the foremost English biblical scholars of the nineteenth century, best known as the co-editor, with Brooke Foss Westcott, of the critical edition The New Testament in the Original Greek (1881), the text that did more than any other single work to establish the modern discipline of New Testament textual criticism on principles derived from the systematic evaluation of manuscript evidence rather than the received authority of the printed textus receptus.

Born in Dublin on 23 April 1828, Hort was educated at Rugby School and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took a double first in classics and mathematics and was elected a fellow in 1852. He was ordained in the Church of England and held college and parish appointments before returning to Cambridge as a fellow of Emmanuel College in 1872. In 1878 he was appointed Hulsean Professor of Divinity, and in 1887 he succeeded to the Lady Margaret's Professorship of Divinity, the senior theological chair in the university, which he held until his death.

Hort's collaboration with Westcott on the Greek New Testament occupied, by their own account, some twenty-eight years, from early private discussions in the 1850s to publication in 1881. The edition was accompanied by a substantial volume of Introduction and Appendix in which Hort set out, with great rigor, the genealogical method by which the two editors classified manuscripts into textual families and assessed the comparative reliability of readings — a method that, whatever refinements later scholarship has introduced, remains the ancestor of all subsequent work in the field. Hort was, alongside Westcott and J. B. Lightfoot, part of the informal "Cambridge triumvirate" whose combination of exacting philological method and theological seriousness reshaped English biblical scholarship in the later Victorian period.

Hort's part in the recovery of the true origin of the Codex Amiatinus, the vast Bible made at Wearmouth-Jarrow around the year 700 and long misattributed to sixth-century Italy, is a comparatively small episode within this larger career but one of exemplary method. Building on Giovanni Battista de Rossi's proposal of 1886–1888 that the manuscript's altered dedication concealed the name of the Northumbrian abbot Ceolfrith, and on the eighteenth-century observation of Angelo Maria Bandini that the dedicatory verses had been erased and rewritten, Hort located in the anonymous Vita Ceolfridi — a text that had long been in print but had escaped notice in this connection — a transcription of the original, unaltered dedication verses. Setting this recovered text against the manuscript's tampered page, Hort was able to demonstrate conclusively, in the late 1880s, that the codex had been made not in Italy but in Northumbria, at Ceolfrith's command, and carried toward Rome as a gift for the tomb of St Peter before Ceolfrith's death at Langres in 716. The demonstration converted a century of confident stylistic misattribution into a securely documented Anglo-Saxon origin and remains, in the historiography of the manuscript, the paradigmatic instance of textual recovery settling a question that connoisseurship alone had gotten wrong. For the full account, see the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database and the entry on de Rossi.

Hort died at Cambridge on 30 November 1892, before he could see the wider implications of the Amiatinus discovery fully absorbed into general scholarship, a process that in fact took another century. His reputation today rests chiefly on the Westcott-Hort text and its accompanying account of method, but his brief, decisive intervention in the case of the Amiatine Bible illustrates the same disposition that governed his life's principal work: an insistence that even the most venerable and confidently held readings of a text — biblical or codicological — must yield to what the manuscript evidence, properly examined, actually shows.

Hoskier, Herman Charles

Kent, 12 November 1864 – 1938

Herman Charles Hoskier was an independently wealthy, Eton-educated English textual critic who pursued New Testament and Old Latin scholarship entirely outside the university system, financing decades of manuscript collation from a career as a securities trader in Gilded Age Manhattan and, later, from private means. He interrupted this work to serve, and be twice wounded, with the French ambulance service during the First World War, an episode characteristic of a life that combined genuine scholarly obsession with an eccentric, almost anti-establishment relationship to the academic textual criticism of his day.

Hoskier's method was exhaustive collation rather than theory: he is credited with being the first scholar to collate, systematically and completely, every known Greek manuscript of the Apocalypse, a task occupying some thirty years and eventually published as the two-volume Concerning the Text of the Apocalypse (1929). His earlier Codex B and Its Allies, a Study and an Indictment (1914) used similarly minute collation to argue, against the prevailing Alexandrian-text consensus associated with Westcott and Hort, that Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus disagree with each other far more extensively than their reputation as the two best witnesses to the New Testament text would suggest — a position that put him generally, if not doctrinairely, on the Byzantine-priority side of early twentieth-century debate.

In 1919 Hoskier published The Text of Codex Usserianus 2., or2 ("Garland of Howth"), a "textual facsimile" transcription that reproduces, through special typefaces, the layout, abbreviation symbols, and letterforms of the Dublin manuscript. Sharply critical of T. K. Abbott's pioneering 1884 collation of the same book, which he called "deplorable," Hoskier's own transcription is generally very accurate, though it too has since been shown imperfect — he notably missed the opening words of Matthew 1:18 on the manuscript's first surviving page. His introduction confined itself to a selective list of readings marshalled in support of his own theory of a bilingual archetype behind the Latin version, rather than to any systematic account of the book's place in the Old Latin tradition, a gap not filled until Hugh A. G. Houghton's study nearly a century later. Hoskier died in 1938, by most accounts in much reduced circumstances, having spent a fortune and a working life on a body of collation that a largely indifferent academy left substantially unused until it was rediscovered by a later generation of textual scholars.

Houghton, Hugh A. G.

active 21st century

Hugh A. G. Houghton is a British scholar of New Testament textual criticism, Professor of New Testament Textual Scholarship at the University of Birmingham and Director of the Institute for Textual Scholarship and Electronic Editing (ITSEE). His research centers on the Latin biblical tradition, including the Vetus Latina and the Vulgate, and on the development of digital tools for the collation and editing of biblical manuscripts.

His book The Latin New Testament: A Guide to its Early History, Texts, and Manuscripts (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016) is now a standard reference work for the field, providing a systematic account of the surviving Old Latin and Vulgate New Testament witnesses and their relationships. The Codex Amiatinus, catalogued among the foremost of these witnesses under the siglum A (or am), is discussed there as the earliest surviving complete Latin Vulgate and a foundational text for every subsequent critical edition of Jerome's Bible, from Tischendorf's nineteenth-century work through to the modern Stuttgart Biblia Sacra. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller account of the manuscript's standing as a textual witness.

Hueck, Irene

born 1934

Irene Hueck is one of Germany's most distinguished art historians specializing in Italian painting of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Her career, spanning nearly four decades in both Germany and Italy, has made a fundamental contribution to the understanding of medieval painting in Tuscany, Umbria, and Rome.

Hueck trained at the University of Munich, where she earned her Ph.D. in 1961 with a dissertation titled Das Programm der Kuppelmosaiken im Florentiner Baptisterium (The Program of the Dome Mosaics in the Florentine Baptistery), published in Munich in 1962. This early work already announced her central interests: monumental decorative cycles, religious patronage, and the complexity of iconographic programs in Italian medieval art. After her doctorate, from 1961 to 1963, she worked as an assistant in the Department of Art History at the Technische Hochschule in Aachen.

In October 1963, Hueck moved to Florence as a fellow at the Kunsthistorisches Institut (KHI), one of the leading research institutes for European art history. After her fellowship period (until March 1965), she became head of the institute's Photo Library in April 1965. From December 1969 until her retirement in April 1999, she directed the Photo Library for nearly thirty years. This role gave her privileged access to a photographic archive of exceptional historical value and continuously nourished her research on dispersed and little-studied works.

Hueck's scholarship is distinguished by philological rigor and close attention to archival documentation. One of her most influential studies concerns Duccio di Buoninsegna's Madonna Rucellai: in 1990, she clarified the work's original location within Santa Maria Novella in Florence, in a study later described as well argued and exceptionally thorough in its use of documentation. In the same year, she published La tavola di Duccio e la Compagnia delle Laudi di Santa Maria Novella in the exhibition catalogue La Maestà di Duccio restaurata.

Equally significant is her contribution to studies on Cimabue and the decoration of the Upper Basilica of Assisi. Her 1981 article, Cimabue und das Bildprogramm der Oberkirche von San Francesco in Assisi, published in the Mitteilungen des Kunsthistorischen Institutes in Florenz, remains an indispensable reference for research on the Assisi cycles. Her rigorous positions on attributions, especially regarding Giotto and Assisi, generated substantial scholarly debate and confirmed the authority of her critical method.

Hueck's research was not limited to Tuscany. She published studies on the painter of the Apostles' scenes in the atrium of Old St. Peter's in Rome (Der Maler der Apostelszenen im Atrium von Alt-St. Peter), contributing substantially to scholarship on thirteenth-century Roman painting. She also examined the iconographic program of the Sala dei Notari in Perugia in Exempla: Das Bildprogramm der Sala dei Notari zu Perugia, published in volume 39 (2009-2010) of the Römisches Jahrbuch der Bibliotheca Hertziana. She further investigated Charles IV's visit to Padua and the paintings of Guariento, extending her work into fourteenth-century Venetian contexts.

Another major area of inquiry was illuminated manuscripts and historical drawings, where she demonstrated unusual skill in cross-referencing visual and documentary evidence. She identified lost works through the drawings of the German painter and traveler Johann Anton Ramboux (1790-1866), opening new perspectives on the dispersion of Umbrian medieval artistic heritage. Her studies on Tuscany, Assisi, and drawings connected to Piero della Francesca were later adopted by Italian scholars as points of departure for further research.

After retiring in 1999, Hueck continued independent research, first remaining in Florence and then moving in 2005 to Lüdenscheid in North Rhine-Westphalia. In this later phase she still produced original contributions, including the 2007 publication Fritz Selve, Luigi Calderini und der "Monumentalbrunnen" for the Geschichts- und Heimatverein Lüdenscheid, dedicated to the local history of her adopted city. She remains affiliated as a Research Associate at the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florence.

Hueck's body of work has helped redefine central questions in the history of Italian medieval art: the attribution of major pictorial cycles, the liturgical and devotional functions of altarpieces, and the role of religious patronage in shaping iconographic programs. Her influence is visible across subsequent generations of scholars, and her documentary analyses continue to be cited and debated in international art-historical literature.

Hughes, Kathleen

1926 – 1977

Kathleen Hughes was a British historian of the early Irish church, fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge, and one of the most influential Anglophone scholars of early medieval Ireland of the twentieth century. Her major works, The Church in Early Irish Society (1966) and the posthumously completed Early Christian Ireland: Introduction to the Sources (1972), established a framework for the study of Irish ecclesiastical organisation, hagiography and manuscript culture that remains a standard point of reference. She was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1975.

Hughes's classic distinction between the "rapid cursive" hands of the synoptic gospels and the "neat minuscule bookhand" of John in the Book of Dimma, drawn in her survey of the early Irish church, anticipated and helped set the terms for the more detailed multi-hand analysis later carried out by John Gillis and Bernard Meehan. Her scholarly authority was undiminished by the brevity of her career, cut short by her death in 1977.

I

Iakovleva, Maria I.

active early 21st century

Russian art historian specializing in Early Palaeologan Byzantine painting — the period of artistic efflorescence that followed the Byzantine recapture of Constantinople from the Latin occupiers in 1261 and unfolded across the first half of the fourteenth century, producing some of the supreme achievements of Byzantine pictorial culture. Her work has appeared in Actual Problems of Theory and History of Art, the peer-reviewed annual publication (indexed in Scopus and ERIH PLUS) of the international conference organized jointly by St. Petersburg State University and Lomonosov Moscow State University.

Her earlier contribution to that journal addressed "The Icon of Christ Emmanuel from the State Historical Museum — a Micromosaic of Early Palaeologan Period" (Икона «Спас Эммануил» из собрания ГИМ — микромозаика раннепалеологовской эпохи). The object — a Christ Emmanuel micromosaic from the GIM (Государственный Исторический Музей, Moscow) — places her within one of the most technically demanding and historically significant fields in Palaeologan art. Byzantine micromosaics, constructed from minute tesserae of glass, stone, and gold no more than a millimetre or two in dimension, represent the most exquisite and labour-intensive objects produced by the medieval world; the surviving corpus is small, concentrated in the fourteenth century, and associated with the highest levels of Byzantine imperial and aristocratic patronage. To publish a previously under-studied micromosaic from the GIM is a contribution of genuine scholarly weight both for the history of the individual object and for the reconstruction of the production and exchange networks within which such objects were made and transmitted.

Her contribution to Volume 7 (2017) of Actual Problems of Theory and History of Art — "Frescoes of the Church of Christ in Veroia (1314–1315) and the Issues of George Kalliergis' Oeuvre" (pp. 287–300) — addresses one of the most important and precisely documented monuments of Early Palaeologan painting. The Church of Christ in Veria (Βέροια), former katholikon of the Resurrection Monastery, retains a complete and accurately dated fresco ensemble: a dedicatory inscription above the western entrance records that the church was painted by the artist Kalliergis, called the best painter in all of Thessaly, and consecrated by the Constantinopolitan patriarch during the reign of Andronikos II Palaeologos in 1314–1315. Kalliergis's Veria church is accordingly one of the very few monuments of Byzantine painting in which the artist's identity, geographical origin, working date, and a measure of his contemporary reputation are simultaneously documented in the original inscription. Andreas Xyngopoulos, in 1955, proposed on the basis of the inscription and the stylistic evidence that Kalliergis was connected with Thessaloniki; this was subsequently confirmed by a document from the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos dated 1322.

Iakovleva's article addresses three interrelated aspects of the Kalliergis frescoes: the iconographic programme (including a marked preference for succinct iconographic variants attributed to the painter's desire for compositional clarity and expressive concentration); the stylistic character of the work and its place in the evolution of Early Palaeologan painting in Macedonia — in proximity to the Holy Apostles of Thessaloniki and the frescoes of the Protaton on Mount Athos; and the question of Kalliergis's wider oeuvre, using the securely documented Veria church as an anchor for broader attribution. The monument's date of 1314–1315 places it at the heart of the critical decade contemporary with both the Thessaloniki apostle-church and the opening phases of Theodoros Metochites's commission at the Chora Monastery in Constantinople — one of the central constellations of workshops, styles, and patronage networks in the ongoing scholarly debate about the Palaeologan Renaissance. The Veria church documented by Thanasis Papazotos in his 1994 monograph on Byzantine Veria provided the indispensable archaeological and historical groundwork on which Iakovleva's art-historical analysis builds.

J

Jackson, Eleanor

active 21st century

Eleanor Jackson is a manuscript scholar whose doctoral thesis, To Hold Infinity in the Palm of Your Hand: The Insular Pocket Gospel Books Re-evaluated (University of York, 2017), offered the first sustained critical re-examination of Patrick McGurk's "pocket gospel book" category since his foundational 1956 article defined it. Jackson argued that the term itself is a retrospective misnomer with no demonstrable connection to actual pockets, that several of the diagnostic features McGurk identified are inconsistently distributed within the group he defined, and that the common assumption that such books served as personal, portable copies has often been taken on faith rather than rigorously argued from the evidence.

Her reassessment has encouraged a more cautious, evidence-led treatment of the Book of Dimma and its relatives as a class, and she has subsequently continued to work in manuscript scholarship and curation.

Jalabert, Denise

active 1929–1966

Denise Jalabert was a French art historian and museum curator whose studies of the carved flora and fauna of medieval France created a descriptive vocabulary that the discipline still uses. She was curator at the Musée des Monuments français from 1930 to 1959 and subsequently honorary curator of the Musées nationaux.

Her subject was ornament, treated with a seriousness usually reserved for figure sculpture. In a long series of articles in the Bulletin Monumental she traced the descent of Romanesque motifs from ancient Near Eastern sources — successive studies were devoted to the sphinx (1935), the siren (1936) and the eagle (1938) — and mapped the development of carved foliage from the twelfth century to the fifteenth in "La flore gothique, ses origines, son évolution" (1932). Terms she coined or fixed in use, among them flore généralisée, flore naturaliste and flore réaliste, passed into standard archaeological description.

These investigations were gathered in La flore sculptée des monuments du Moyen Âge en France: recherches sur les origines de l'art français, prefaced by Paul Deschamps and illustrated throughout with her own drawings — a book whose combination of comparative range and first-hand draughtsmanship gives it a continuing usefulness. Her other work included studies of the sculpted flora of the Sainte-Chapelle (1947), the Romanesque flora of Burgundy (1960), and general accounts of French sculpture, Norman medieval art, and Notre-Dame de Paris.

Her place in the Autun literature belongs to the connoisseurial rather than the ornamental side of her work. It was Jalabert who observed the close kinship between the face of the Virgin on the Flight into Egypt capital and the face of Eve on the north portal lintel — an observation subsequently pressed into service both by those arguing for a single hand across the building's sculpture and by those interested in the theological pairing of Eve and the Virgin. Her precision as a describer of carved surface is what gives the comparison its weight.

Jaski, Bart

active late 20th – 21st century

Bart Jaski is a Dutch historian of early medieval Ireland and curator of manuscripts and rare books at Utrecht University Library. His research addresses early Irish kingship, law and genealogy, most substantially in his monograph Early Irish Kingship and Succession (2000), a standard reference for the mechanics of dynastic succession in early medieval Irish society.

In "Dianchride and the Book of Dimma," published in Peritia (volume 32) in 2021, Jaski engaged critically with the identification of the scribe Dianchride proposed by John Gillis and Bernard Meehan, challenging aspects of the resulting consensus view on who commissioned the manuscript's first three gospels, on the motive behind the substitution of the name Dimma, and on the date at which the gospel of John was joined to the rest of the book. His intervention keeps open, nearly a century after Best's discovery of the colophon forgery, questions about the manuscript's early history that might otherwise have seemed settled.

Johns, Jeremy

active late 20th-21st century

Jeremy Johns is Professor of the Art and Archaeology of the Islamic Mediterranean at the University of Oxford, based at the Khalili Research Centre for the Art and Material Culture of the Middle East (3 St John Street, Oxford). He is also a Fellow of Wolfson College. Since 2004 he has served as the first Director of the Khalili Research Centre, and in 2006 he was appointed to his full professorship.

Johns began doctoral research at Balliol College, Oxford, on the Muslims of Norman Sicily, with support from a Leverhulme Trust Study Abroad Scholarship. He completed his doctorate in 1983, after election to a Stipendiary Junior Research Fellowship at Wolfson College in 1981. In 1984 he was appointed New Blood Lecturer in Early Islamic Archaeology at the University of Newcastle upon Tyne, and in 1990 returned to Oxford as University Lecturer in Islamic Archaeology. This trajectory shaped his profile as a scholar bridging Islamic studies and medieval Latin history.

Johns's work is centrally concerned with relations between Muslim and Christian societies in the medieval Mediterranean as expressed through material and visual culture. His method emphasizes objects, buildings, documents, and images rather than purely theological or literary polemic, making coexistence and conflict historically legible through concrete evidence.

His research has two principal axes. The first addresses archaeological transformation from Late Antiquity to early Islam in the Levant. The second, for which he is especially renowned, concerns the archaeology, history, and art history of Sicily under Islamic and Norman rule, from the Muslim conquest of the ninth century to the destruction of Sicily's Islamic communities under Frederick II in the thirteenth.

Among his major ongoing initiatives is the project Documenting Multiculturalism, which studies the administrative and legal records of Norman and Hohenstaufen Sicily to reconstruct relations among Arabic-speaking Muslims and Jews, Greek-speaking Christians, and Latin Christians. This documentary work is fundamental for understanding how multilingual governance operated in the courts of Roger II and William II, where Arabic functioned institutionally alongside Greek and Latin.

His landmark monograph Arabic Administration in Norman Sicily: The Royal Diwan (Cambridge University Press, 2002) remains the foundational study of the Arabic bureaucratic structures maintained by the Norman kings after conquest. He has also published influential studies on the Cappella Palatina in Palermo, including work on its mosaics and courtly material culture, clarifying how visual programs and documentary practice articulate a single political ideology of rulership.

Johns occupies a distinctive position in medieval scholarship because he works across Arabic documentary sources, Byzantine and Islamic art history, Latin narrative texts, and archaeological evidence with equal authority. Against older historiographical separations, he reads Norman Sicily as an integrated Mediterranean formation: not merely a Latin kingdom with exotic ornament, nor an Islamic society under simple occupation, but a complex and genuinely hybrid political civilization that can only be understood through all of its linguistic and artistic traditions together.

K

Kaftal, George

1897 - 1987

George Kaftal was one of the most original and prolific iconographers of the twentieth century, the author of a monumental four-volume series on the iconography of saints in Italian painting that remains, more than seventy years after its first publication, an indispensable reference for the study of medieval and Renaissance art. His work transformed sacred iconography from an auxiliary field into an autonomous scholarly discipline by providing, for the first time, a systematic and comparative instrument of analysis.

Born in 1897, Kaftal conducted most of his studies and research career in England, where he lived for many years in Oxford. His formation unfolded in an intellectual milieu deeply shaped by the Viennese art-historical tradition (the Wiener Schule) and by the methodological innovations of Aby Warburg and the Warburg circle, whose iconological studies were reshaping approaches to medieval and Renaissance painting in the early twentieth century. Writing almost entirely in English, unusual in a field then dominated by German and Italian scholarship, he positioned his work within an international scholarly horizon.

Kaftal's scholarly debut was St. Francis in Italian Painting (London, 1950), where he mapped representations of the saint of Assisi across regional Italian schools with a new and rigorous method. He proceeded through iconographic cataloging based on each saint's visual attributes, classified variants of individual hagiographic episodes, and traced their geographical and chronological distribution.
