He is often credited as one of the first art historians to question systematically the traditional attributions to Donatello. His best-known specific proposal — that the bronze David in the Bargello might represent not David but Mercury (hence the occasional label "David-Mercury") — dates to around 1939. It is worth stressing, since it is easy to misstate, that Lányi never published this hypothesis himself; it entered scholarship posthumously, chiefly through John Pope-Hennessy, and remains contested (most quattrocento references to the statue call it David).

His death came in 1940. His father-in-law, Thomas Mann, by then in Princeton, secured passage for the couple to North America. Their ship, the SS City of Benares, was torpedoed by the German submarine U-48 in the North Atlantic on 17 September 1940 and sank — the same disaster, notorious for the child evacuees lost aboard, in which Monika Mann was injured but survived. Lányi drowned. (A caution on the record: because so many émigré scholars were lost in this period, his death is occasionally conflated with other wartime sinkings, but the City of Benares is the well-attested vessel.)

The afterlife of his work is the reason his name survives. The suitcases holding his Donatello notes were recovered and reached his widow, who carried them to the United States. His material was judged so important that H. W. Janson took it over, and it was published, incorporating Lányi's notes and photographs, as The Sculpture of Donatello (Princeton, 1957) — for decades the critical catalogue of the sculptor. Two of Lányi's own English articles appeared posthumously in the Art Bulletin and the Burlington Magazine, and his thinking is said to have influenced Pope-Hennessy. A recent doctoral project by Martina Medolago has begun the fuller reconstruction of his life and ideas that scholarship has long lacked.

Lanzi, Luigi

Treia (Macerata), 1732 – Florence, 1810

Luigi Lanzi was a Jesuit-trained antiquarian and art historian whose Storia pittorica della Italia (first edition 1792, definitive three-volume edition 1795–96) organised the entire history of Italian painting by regional school — Florentine, Sienese, Roman, Venetian, Bolognese, Neapolitan and others — a methodological innovation that shaped how the discipline subsequently periodised and classified its subject. After the suppression of the Jesuit order in 1773 Lanzi settled in Florence, where from 1775 he served as antiquarian and curator at the Uffizi Gallery, responsible among other things for the reorganisation of its collections of antiquities, a role that grounded his later writing on painting in a connoisseur's first-hand familiarity with a vast range of works.

Lanzi's history combined attention to documentary evidence with sustained stylistic characterisation of individual masters and schools, written in a lucid and judicious prose that made the Storia pittorica the standard synthetic account of Italian painting for the following century and a direct model for nineteenth-century connoisseurial historians, including Crowe and Cavalcaselle. He was also a noted authority on Etruscan antiquities and language, publishing the pioneering Saggio di lingua etrusca (1789); this second, epigraphic strand of his work reinforced the same philological rigour that distinguishes his treatment of painting. He died in Florence in 1810, having done as much as any single writer to establish the "school" as the basic organising unit of Italian art history.

Lasko, Peter

Berlin, 5 March 1924 - 18 May 2003

Peter Erik Lasko was a British art historian of German-Jewish birth who became one of the leading postwar authorities on the "luxury arts" of the early medieval West - metalwork, enamelling, gem-setting and ivory carving from the sixth to the twelfth century - while also building institutions: he was the first Professor of Visual Art at the University of East Anglia (UEA), where he founded the art history department and helped secure the Sainsbury collection that became the Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts, and he was Director of the Courtauld Institute of Art in London from 1974 to 1985, where he engineered the Institute's move to Somerset House.

Lasko was born in Berlin on 5 March 1924, the youngest child of the filmmaker Leo Lasko and his wife, who moved in the bohemian and "degenerate" circles that the Nazis, from 1933, condemned as entartete. An accident in Paris, where the family lived briefly from 1933, left him blind in one eye; a return to Berlin for treatment proved fruitless, and as a family of Jewish heritage associated with Modernist art circles their position in Germany grew untenable. Peter, then thirteen, arrived in England in 1937 with his mother and sister, following his father, who had left the previous year. His life during the Second World War is largely undocumented - he was between fifteen and twenty-one, and by one family account may have been interned as an enemy alien near Bristol - and he rarely spoke of this period afterward.

By 1946 he was back with his parents in London, studying at Hammersmith College of Art with the ambition of becoming a painter; within a year he judged, probably correctly, that he would never be a great one, though a picture of a clown he painted at the time reportedly hung in his various lodgings for years after. It was at art school that he met his future wife, Lyn Norman, whom he married in 1948. He had by then turned to the academic study of art, first under Nikolaus Pevsner at Birkbeck College before transferring to the Courtauld Institute of Art, where he graduated in 1949 under the mentorship of Christopher Hohler and the directorship of Tom Boase.

Within a year of graduating, Lasko was hired as a curator in the British Museum's Department of British and Medieval Antiquities, replacing Thomas Kendrick, who had become the Museum's director. In a small department where staff had to range widely, he took on the collection of clocks and watches, helping to secure the 2,000-object Courtenay Adrian Ilbert Collection for the Museum, and built a close circle of colleagues that included the future British Museum director David Wilson. His major acquisitions included a twelfth-century walrus-ivory reliquary tusk related in style to the Lewis chessmen and an English whalebone portable altar; the great prize that eluded him was the Cloisters Cross, lost to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York after Parliament declined to fund a purchase clouded by questions of wartime provenance. During these Museum years he also travelled widely to the church treasuries and museum collections of the Continent, often with the close friends and eventual rival Pelican-series authors George Zarnecki and C. R. (Reg) Dodwell - a research partnership that, around 1960, led Nikolaus Pevsner to commission from the trio three companion volumes, on painting, sculpture and the "luxury arts," for the Pelican History of Art; Lasko, in addition to writing his own volume, served as the group's driver and mechanic on their continental research trips.

In 1965 Lasko left the Museum to become founding Professor of Visual Art at the new University of East Anglia, appointed - on the recommendation, among others, of George Zarnecki - to build an art history department from nothing alongside his lieutenant Andrew Martindale. He completed his major book, Ars Sacra, 800-1200 (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1972; 2nd edn, New Haven and London: Yale University Press, 1994), delivered to Pevsner as series editor in 1968: a survey of Carolingian, Ottonian and Romanesque metalwork, enamelling and ivory carving that insisted, against the label "minor arts," on the aesthetic ambition and sculptural sophistication of these small-scale luxury objects, and that traced a shift across the book's three parts from art organised by royal and imperial patronage to a Romanesque section built around named makers such as Nicholas of Verdun and Godefroid de Claire. At UEA he also helped assemble the University's own Modernist art collection with Alastair Grieve, and was instrumental in persuading Robert and Lisa Sainsbury to donate their collection to the University, a gift realised in the Norman Foster-designed Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts.

Lasko succeeded Anthony Blunt as Director of the Courtauld Institute of Art in 1974, moving to London the following year. His directorship was contentious - he inherited a faculty with little loyalty to an outside appointee, and his efforts to invigorate the Institute's research culture met resistance - but his central achievement was strategic: unable to relocate the Courtauld to Bloomsbury, he negotiated instead a lease on part of Somerset House, uniting the Institute's galleries and collections with its students for the first time in a setting far grander than its previous home at 20 Portman Square. The financial strain of the move told on both his health and the Institute's finances, and in 1985 Lasko stepped down as director; the move to Somerset House was completed after his departure by his successor and friend, the fellow medievalist Michael Kauffmann. During and after his Courtauld years he served as President of the British Archaeological Association (from 1977), as a Trustee of the British Museum, and as general editor of the Pelican History of Art as the series transferred from Penguin to Yale University Press. He also chaired the founding committee of the Corpus of Romanesque Sculpture in Britain and Ireland (CRSBI), where as early as 1988 he insisted, prophetically, that the project be built as a digital resource rather than a printed corpus, well before the computing power to realise that vision was generally available.

Lasko's scholarly interests reached back to his student years in another direction as well: German Expressionism, a subject bound up with his own formation and, as his colleague and biographer Sandy Heslop has suggested, with a lifelong wish to see German contributions to modern art rehabilitated in English-speaking scholarship after the ruptures of two world wars. This research, renewed in the 1990s, produced a 1997 Art History article on the training of the four founders of Die Brücke and his last book, The Expressionist Roots of Modernism, published posthumously in 2003. Diagnosed with cancer in the mid-1990s, he refused chemotherapy after a single session; his energy and combativeness were undimmed to the end, including a quixotic 1999 run as Labour candidate in a solidly Conservative Norfolk council ward. Peter Lasko died on 18 May 2003. He had been elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1978.

Lavin, Marilyn Aronberg

St. Louis, Missouri, 1925-

American art historian of fourteenth- and fifteenth-century Italian painting, the leading Anglophone authority on Piero della Francesca, author of the first systematic study of narrative mural decoration in Italian churches across twelve centuries, and a pioneer - decades ahead of the field - of computing and digitized imagery in art-historical research. She built a major career largely outside the tenure system, and said so: because her research was driven by personal interest rather than employment, she could afford to publish books that were not written to persuade tenure committees.

She was born in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1925, the daughter of Charles Aronberg and Blanch Silverstone. Her family, like that of the man she would marry, was Jewish and of eastern European emigrant background.

She attended Washington University in St. Louis, studying under Horst Woldemar Janson - later famous, and later notorious, for the universally assigned survey textbook - and graduated in 1947. She took her M.A. in 1949, again under Janson, who was himself still working toward his doctorate at Harvard, and in the same year gained a certificate at the Free University of Brussels.

While serving as a graduate assistant in art history in 1949-1950, she met Irving Lavin (1927-2019), a student in her class taking his first art history course. They had in fact met as teenagers. They married in 1952; the marriage lasted sixty-six years, until his death.

Her career took an unconventional shape, and the shape is part of the story. From 1953 to 1955 she was curator of the Robbins Print Collection in Arlington, Massachusetts. From 1955 to 1957 she held a Fulbright fellowship in Rome. In 1957 she joined the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, as a staff writer, becoming a researcher in 1959. From 1965 she consulted for Time, Inc. and for the fine-press Heritage Press, for which she edited a two-volume Lives of the Most Eminent Painters by Vasari (1967).

When Irving Lavin was appointed at New York University in 1963, she worked at the Metropolitan while pursuing graduate study at NYU. Her Ph.D. came only in 1973, from New York University, with a dissertation on Piero della Francesca - by which point she had already published the Flagellation book. In 1975 she resigned from the Metropolitan to become visiting professor of art history at Princeton, followed by visiting posts at Yale (1977) and the University of Maryland (1979). She also taught at the Universita di Roma, La Sapienza.

When her husband was appointed in 1973 to the chair at the Institute for Advanced Study previously held by Erwin Panofsky and Millard Meiss, she found herself at Princeton with - initially - no title but "wife." That position, which required no teaching of him, also freed her: she could stop teaching and pursue her own research.

Her career was inescapably shaped by the dual-career marriage, and she has been candid about the costs. But her work stands entirely separate from her husband's in method and merit. She was never a derivative scholar.

Her work on Piero spans five decades and several registers.

Piero della Francesca: The Flagellation (London: Allen Lane / New York: Penguin, 1972), written for the Art in Context series, tackled what is probably the most contested small panel in Italian painting. It remains her best-known book.

Piero della Francesca's "Baptism of Christ" (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1981) is a monograph on the London panel.

Piero della Francesca: San Francesco, Arezzo (New York: George Braziller, 1994) treats the True Cross cycle, and she contributed texts to the Skira volume on the cycle edited by Maetzke and Bertelli (2001), published in the wake of the restoration.

She was the organizing scholar for the National Gallery of Art's 1995 exhibition and symposium volume Piero della Francesca and His Legacy (Studies in the History of Art 48), proceedings of "Monarca della pittura: Piero and his legacy," held in Washington on 4-5 December 1992 under CASVA, the Getty Museum, and the Getty Center.

Her synthetic Piero della Francesca (Phaidon, Art and Ideas series, 2002) analyses all the surviving works, benefiting from new photography of the freshly cleaned frescoes, and situates the paintings within early Renaissance religion and politics - a corrective to the long habit of reading Piero as a purely formal, geometrical intelligence. Piero's mathematics matter, she argues, but most of the paintings were commissioned to do religious work and were valued by contemporaries for their spiritual worth.

The Place of Narrative: Mural Decoration in Italian Churches, 431-1600 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1990) is her most ambitious book and the one of most direct use outside Renaissance studies. It asks not what Italian mural cycles depict but where they are put - how narrative sequences are disposed across the surfaces of a church, and what the disposition means. The chronological span, from the fifth century to the sixteenth, deliberately refuses the conventional break between medieval and Renaissance, treating the placement of pictorial narrative as a continuous problem with its own history.

For anyone working on programme, iconography, and the relation of image to liturgical space in Italian churches, this is a foundational reference - and its early medieval and Romanesque material is not incidental to it.

Seventeenth-Century Barberini Documents and Inventories of Art (1975) won the Charles Rufus Morey Award of the College Art Association. It was an early instance of primary-source documentation within the history of collecting, and it belongs to a strand of her work - archival, exhaustive, unglamorous - quite distinct from the interpretive monographs.

She is a genuine pioneer here, and the point deserves emphasis: she was building databases for art-historical analysis when the field regarded computers as clerical equipment. She directed the Piero Project, an electronic compendium of images and text (with a period of work at the Clark Art Institute), and in 1991 created and moderated a Listserv for art and architectural historians (caah@princeton.edu) that grew to some 800 scholars in 22 countries. She presented "New Technology Brings New Life to Art History: The Piero Project Story" at Museums and the Web in 2009.

She wrote a history of her adopted department - The Eye of the Tiger: The Founding and Development of the Department of Art and Archaeology, 1883-1923, Princeton University (1983) - and edited her husband's Festschrift, IL60: Essays Honoring Irving Lavin on His Sixtieth Birthday (New York: Italica Press, 1990). With Irving Lavin she published Images from the "Song of Songs" in the Art of Cimabue, Michelangelo, and Rembrandt (2002).

After his death in 2019 she edited into publishable form the article he left in drafts and notes on the Palestrina Pieta, filling gaps and resolving the question of when precisely Bernini became maestro. In 2022 she gave, in his honour, the black-and-white marble bust inscribed with the name of the jurist Prospero Farinacci - one of Irving Lavin's last Bernini discoveries - to the Republic of Italy via the non-profit LoveItaly; it is destined for the Castel Sant'Angelo, where a ceremony marked the gift on 20 March 2023.

In 2025 she published One Life for Two: The Autobiography of Irving and Marilyn Lavin (Deutscher Kunstverlag), a four-hundred-page account of two St. Louis children of Jewish emigrant families who became, together, central figures in the postwar discipline. She was interviewed about it at the age of one hundred. Writing from what she calls her "old age vantage point," she has continued to publish - a recent essay uses the view "from above, as it were," to trace relationships between Cavallini, Giotto, and Piero della Francesca in the planning of their major cycles.

She was living as of early 2026.

Leonardi, Claudio

Sacco di Rovereto, Trento, 17 April 1926 - Florence, 21 May 2010

Claudio Leonardi was an Italian historian, philologist and Latinist, the dominant figure in twentieth-century Italian mediolatinistica and the founder of the institutional apparatus - SISMEL, the Fondazione Ezio Franceschini, Medioevo latino - that still underpins medieval Latin studies internationally.

He was educated at the Liceo Antonio Rosmini in Rovereto, then studied at the Università Cattolica in Milan and at Fribourg in Switzerland, where he encountered Gianfranco Contini and Ezio Franceschini. He took his degree under Franceschini in 1950 with a thesis on the medieval fortuna of Martianus Capella's De nuptiis Philologiae et Mercurii - published as I codici di Marziano Capella in «Aevum» (1959-60), and still a foundational study.

The years immediately after his degree were difficult, but from 1953 Raffaello Morghen drew him into the work of the Istituto Storico Italiano per il Medio Evo, where he edited the first volume (Series collectionum) of the Repertorium fontium historiae Medii Aevi (1962). Only in 1960 did he become scriptor for Latin codices at the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, also working on the edition of the decrees of the medieval ecumenical councils (1962). In 1968 he took the chair of medieval Latin literature at the University of Lecce, remaining until 1971, then moved to Perugia (1971-74), Siena (Arezzo campus, 1974-76) and finally Florence (1976-2001).

His encounter with Gustavo Vinay and his relationship with Gianni Baget Bozzo, in the years of the student contestation and the Second Vatican Council, pushed him toward new historiographical instruments; he collaborated with «Renovatio», and in 1970 succeeded Vinay as director of «Studi medievali», which he held for over thirty years. From «Studi medievali» came, in 1978, the idea of «Medioevo latino (sec. VI-XV)», the great annual repertory of authors, texts and manuscripts, which began publication in 1980 and immediately became the reference tool of the discipline.

To sustain that enterprise, in 1984 Leonardi founded, with other Italian colleagues, the Società Internazionale per lo Studio del Medioevo Latino (SISMEL); the Fondazione Ezio Franceschini followed in 1987, presided over until 1992 by Oscar Luigi Scalfaro. In 1987 both institutions found a home in Florence at the Certosa del Galluzzo, and under Leonardi's direction became a decisive centre of research: a specialist library grown around Franceschini's own, prizes for young scholars, electronic infrastructure from 1992, publishing in its own right from 1996, and from 2001 a postgraduate course in medieval Latin philology and literature. By his death, SISMEL was issuing some forty series and eight journals, besides «Medioevo latino» and the digital archive of medieval culture, Mirabile. He left a bibliography of over a thousand titles.

Philology, understood as a historical science in the German tradition as rethought by Giorgio Pasquali and Contini, was the basis of everything he did. His editorial work includes the study of the tradition of Anastasius Bibliothecarius's Gesta octavae synodi quae Constantinopoli congregata est (1967) - the fullest documentation of the condemnation of Photius - the autograph Glossae on Martianus Capella by Ratherius of Verona (1984), the Latin recension of the Ascensio Isaiae (1995), Savonarola's De veritate prophetica (1997), and interventions on the text of the Opuscula of Francis of Assisi (2004). His major monographic studies appeared in «Studi medievali»: Anastasio Bibliotecario e l'ottavo concilio ecumenico (1967), Spiritualità di Ambrogio Autperto (1968), Alle origini della cristianità medievale: Giovanni Cassiano e Salviano di Marsiglia (1977).

He also curated large thematic anthologies: Scrittrici mistiche italiane (Genoa, 1988, the modern and contemporary section by Giovanni Pozzi); volumes 3-5 of Il Cristo for the Fondazione Valla (1989-1992); and La letteratura francescana in three volumes (Francesco e Chiara d'Assisi; Le vite antiche di San Francesco; Bonaventura: la perfezione cristiana), again for Valla-Mondadori. Two large retrospective collections gather his essays: Medioevo latino. La cultura dell'Europa cristiana (ed. F. Santi, Florence, 2004) and Agiografie medievali (ed. A. Degl'Innocenti and F. Santi, Florence, 2011), each of 47 studies.

Leonardi read the twentieth century as the crisis of modern culture, a crisis he saw fully articulated in Nietzsche, and held that the modern function of the intellectual had exhausted itself. Against both ideological historicism and a merely positivist retreat into erudition, he argued that philology restores the alterity of a past world through the language of its authors, and that the Middle Ages therefore matter as the space in which "reason is not everything" - where difference can be thought. He named the resulting programme a "storiografia del piacere" (Per una storiografia del piacere, «Micrologus», 1993), centred on what he called the gratuito: the non-predeterminable, generative element of history. This is also why medieval mysticism was central to him, refused as a primitive idealism and read instead as the testimony of a person who experiences freedom.

He was married to the philologist Anna Maria Chiavacci Leonardi. In 1981 the Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung in Bonn awarded him its Foreign Social Science Researcher Prize. The Zeno Karl Schindler Foundation's Claudio Leonardi Fellowship for Medieval Latin Studies, supporting young scholars, was established in his honour as founder and first President of SISMEL.

Essential secondary bibliography. E. Menestò, Claudio Leonardi (Sacco di Rovereto, 17 aprile 1926 - Firenze, 21 maggio 2010), «Studi medievali» 51 (2010), pp. 555-580, with an autobiographical note by Leonardi at pp. 574-580; L'esperienza intellettuale di Claudio Leonardi, Florence, 2011, with the complete bibliography; M. Lapidge, obituary in «Journal of Medieval Latin» 20 (2010); T. Gregory, Claudio Leonardi medievista, «Rinascimento» 50 (2010), pp. 1-18; A. Vauchez, Claudio Leonardi et l'hagiographie médiévale, «Studi medievali» 53 (2012), pp. 303-312.

Leone de Castris, Pierluigi

Bari, 26 January 1955

Pierluigi Leone de Castris was born in Bari on January 26, 1955. He completed his university studies in Naples in 1977, beginning an intellectual trajectory that would remain deeply anchored to the cultural and artistic world of Southern Italy. His formation took place in Naples at a moment of renewed scholarly interest in the art of the Mezzogiorno, and from early in his career he oriented his research toward the long arc of Neapolitan artistic production from the late thirteenth century to the early seventeenth century.

Leone de Castris built his academic career progressively, teaching first at the Universities of Lecce and Basilicata before joining the Universita degli Studi Suor Orsola Benincasa in Naples, where he became full professor (professore ordinario) of Medieval and Modern Art History. At Suor Orsola Benincasa he also teaches Museology and History of Collecting, and has directed both the Scuola di Specializzazione in Storia dell'arte and the Doctoral Programme in Art History and History of Ideas in Naples and Mediterranean Europe. He has served as President of the Consulta Universitaria Nazionale per la Storia dell'Arte, the national coordinating body for the discipline in Italian universities.

His teaching has reached well beyond Naples. He delivered seminars on patronage and the role of artists at the Angevin court at the Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa in 1990, lectured on Polidoro da Caravaggio at the National Gallery in London within the Renaissance Research Seminar in 2003, and again at the Musee du Louvre in Paris in 2007.

Before his full commitment to academic life, Leone de Castris worked as art historian inspector (ispettore) and then director (direttore storico dell'arte) at the Soprintendenza per i Beni Artistici e Storici della Campania e di Napoli. In this institutional role he oversaw the rehangings of the Museo di Capodimonte and the Museo Civico di Castel Nuovo, and organized numerous exhibitions in Naples, across Italy, in Europe, and in the United States. Among the most significant of these was the landmark exhibition L'Europe des Anjou. Aventure des Princes Angevins du XIIIe au XVe siecle, held at Fontevraud in 2001, and the more recent Ori, argenti, gemme e smalti della Napoli angioina, 1266-1381 (2014), whose catalogue he edited. He also serves as director of the prestigious journal Napoli Nobilissima and sits on the scientific committees of Rivista d'arte, Kronos, and Confronto.

Leone de Castris's scholarship is defined by a dual focus: on one hand, the art produced in Naples and the Mezzogiorno between the late thirteenth and the early seventeenth century, examined in its broader European and Mediterranean dimensions; on the other, the social role of the artist and the mechanisms of artistic patronage. His methodology is rooted in rigorous connoisseurship, extensive archival research, close comparison of literary sources, and a thorough command of the geographical distribution of artistic heritage across Southern Italy. He has also devoted significant attention to the goldsmith arts, manuscript painting, and wooden sculpture, fields often neglected by mainstream Italian art historiography.

A recurrent theme in his work is the relationship between Naples and the broader Mediterranean and transalpine worlds: how Angevin dynastic politics brought French, Flemish, and Tuscan artists to Naples; how the Aragonese succession opened the city to Catalan and Flemish influences; and how the Spanish Viceroyalty transformed the artistic landscape of the early modern city.

Leone de Castris is the author of a substantial body of monographs and catalogues that have become standard reference works in the field. His first major work, "Forastieri e regnicoli". La pittura moderna a Napoli nel primo Cinquecento (1985; second edition 1988), established his reputation. This was followed by Arte di corte nella Napoli angioina. Da Carlo I a Roberto il Saggio (Cantini, Florence, 1986), a foundational study of court art under the Angevins. He then produced the two-volume Pittura del Cinquecento a Napoli (1991 and 1996) and Quattrocento aragonese. La pittura a Napoli al tempo di Alfonso e Ferrante d'Aragona (1997).

His monographic studies of individual masters are particularly wide-ranging. He has devoted full volumes to Polidoro da Caravaggio (2001), Simone Martini (F. Motta, Milan, 2003), Giotto a Napoli (Electa, Florence, 2007), Gian Cristoforo Romano (2010), Pietro Cavallini, subtitled Napoli prima di Giotto (Arte'm, Naples, 2013), Andrea Sabatini da Salerno (2017), and the church of Donnaregina Vecchia a Napoli (2018). His most recent major contribution is La pittura del Quattrocento a Napoli 1400-1458. Da Ladislao D'Angio-Durazzo ad Alfonso d'Aragona (Naples, 2020). On his Academia.edu profile, he has made available over 45 scholarly papers covering topics from the social status of medieval artists, including a study on Petrarca, Giotto, Simone e lo status sociale dell'artista (2021), to manuscript painting and the rediscovery of the Neapolitan painter Colantonio.

Leone de Castris is recognized as one of the leading authorities on Neapolitan medieval and Renaissance art. His work has fundamentally reshaped scholarly understanding of Naples as a cosmopolitan artistic center in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, not a peripheral zone of Italian culture, but a dynamic crossroads where Angevin, Aragonese, Flemish, Tuscan, and Spanish artistic currents converged and transformed one another. His biographical and attributional studies of painters such as Pietro Cavallini and Simone Martini, both active in Naples, have been essential to understanding how the great artistic revolutions of the Duecento and Trecento radiated southward from Rome and Tuscany and found new creative expression in the Neapolitan kingdom.

Levison, Wilhelm

Düsseldorf, 27 May 1876 – Durham, 1947

Wilhelm Levison was born on 27 May 1876 in Düsseldorf, the elder son of Hermann Levison, a merchant, and his wife Josephine, née Goldschmidt. His family's roots lay in Siegburg on the Rhine, where his Jewish family had lived since the 17th century. Hermann Levison was an active member of the association for the propagation and advancement of skilled trades amongst Jews, and was remembered by his son particularly for his generous helpfulness that was by no means restricted to members of the Jewish community. After Hermann's early death in 1886, his widow eventually joined her son's household.

Directly after finishing high school, Wilhelm Levison went to Bonn to study classical philology and history, attaining his doctoral degree in 1898. He also studied at the University of Berlin before completing his degree. His doctoral dissertation, Die Beurkundung des Civilstandes im Altertum, already displayed his characteristic command of documentary evidence. The trajectory of his career, however, was decisively shaped by a chance encounter: with an article on the history of the Frankish king Clovis I, he gained the attention of Bruno Krusch, chief editor of the MGH series Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum. Although Levison originally intended to pursue a career as a librarian, Krusch was able to convince him to take up work for the Monumenta at the age of 23 in 1899. This was a decision that changed the direction of his life.

Levison's association with the Monumenta Germaniae Historica — the great German project for the critical edition of medieval sources — would define the first three decades of his scholarly output. He was well known as a contributor to the Monumenta, especially for the vitae from the Merovingian era. Working under Krusch, he co-edited volumes 5, 6, and 7 of the Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum (1910–1920), producing authoritative critical editions of numerous saints' lives from the Frankish period — texts of central importance for the history of early medieval religious culture, patronage, and liturgical practice.

A landmark in his hagiographic work was the edition of the Vitae sancti Bonifatii archiepiscopi Moguntini (MGH SS rer. Germ. 57, 1905), the collected lives of Boniface of Mainz. Levison spent his early career producing definitive editions of lives of Willibrord and Boniface — the two great Anglo-Saxon missionaries whose activity on the Continent would later become the central subject of his masterwork. His editorial standards set the benchmark for Merovingian hagiography for the entire twentieth century.

He carried this double workload — MGH editions and university teaching — until 1920, by which time he had become a leading specialist for early medieval Latin.

In 1903 Levison became a lecturer at the University of Bonn in the history of the medieval ages and auxiliary historical sciences, and became a full professor in 1912. He specialised in the early Merovingian and Carolingian periods, being the first scholar to treat Rhenish history as an integral part of German and European history.

In 1917, one year after the death of his mother, Levison married Dr Elsa Freundlich, a Jewish scholar and former student in his university classes. Their marriage remained childless. Bonn was the gravitational centre of his life and identity: in 1929 he turned down the offer of a professorship in Berlin in order to remain on the Rhine, where, as he wrote, "he felt himself rooted through his studies and at home with the people and the countryside."

Among the most remarkable products of his Bonn years was his massive 1927 study Das Werden der Ursula-Legende — a meticulous reconstruction of the development of the legend of St Ursula and the Eleven Thousand Virgins, published in the Bonner Jahrbücher and running to 164 pages. For historians of medieval art, this study is of direct relevance: the Ursula legend generated one of the richest iconographic traditions in Northern European art, from the Cologne reliquary shrines to Hans Memling's famous reliquary shrine in Bruges. Levison's philological and documentary analysis of how the legend evolved from a brief inscription to an elaborate narrative cycle remains a foundational point of reference.

In 1935, Levison was forced to retire from his professorship at Bonn University because of the Nuremberg Laws. He requested permission to emigrate but was initially refused. He was able to leave for Durham only in 1939. The circumstances of his departure were desperate: after the pogroms against Jews in November 1938, the Levisons decided to emigrate. They moved to Durham in north-east England, where Wilhelm Levison was given a stipend as an honorary fellow of Durham University.

The indignity did not end there. Like many Jewish refugees, he was interned as an "enemy alien" by the British government from 21 June 1940 until 2 September 1940. That a sixty-four-year-old Jewish scholar, who had fled the Nazi regime and whose career had been destroyed by German racial laws, should be classified as a threat to the British state speaks eloquently of the disorientation of wartime policy. He endured the internment without apparent bitterness.

Even in exile and under these conditions, Levison maintained contact with the MGH in Munich, continuing to work on editorial matters through clandestine correspondence. The MGH itself acknowledged this loyalty decades later, noting that no one was ever faced with greater challenges to his sanctus amor patriae — the old MGH motto, "holy love of the fatherland" — than he, a Rhenish Jew who never ceased working for the cause even as he was chased from the country.

From Durham, Levison produced the work for which he is most celebrated. He delivered the Ford Lectures at the University of Oxford in 1943, and they were published as England and the Continent in the Eighth Century (Oxford, 1946).

The book argued, through five richly documented lectures, that the eighth century represented England's period of deepest engagement with continental Europe — through the Roman church, the Frisian mission, the reforming activity of Boniface, and the scholarly networks linking figures such as Alcuin, Pippin, and Charlemagne. Levison argued that this period saw England's greatest influence on the continent until the industrial revolution. In his interpretation, Anglo-Saxon missionaries had saved a barbaric pre-Christian continent — a pattern he hoped to see repeated in his own life.

The work's significance for the historiography of medieval studies was considerable. Levison put the first crack in the insular exceptionalism which had plagued medieval English scholarship to that point; his work inspired many to take up his questions and aims in other places — Story, Rollason, Nelson, Reuter, and Leyser, among others, have all drawn on Levison's work. Conrad Leyser later described Levison as "one of the giants of twentieth-century historical scholarship, his England and the Continent in the Eighth Century one of its canonical texts."

Levison died of a heart attack in Durham in 1947. He died during the preparation of Aus Rheinischer und Fränkischer Frühzeit, a collected volume of essays published posthumously in 1948. His wife Elsa compiled a complete bibliography of his works, also published in 1948. His editions of Merovingian hagiographic texts for the MGH were completed and issued posthumously as well, including the critical edition of Gregory of Tours' Libri historiarum X (MGH SS rer. Merov. 1, 1951).

Five conferences have been held in commemoration of his work, and the lectures given at the 2007 meeting at Durham University were published in 2010. He also edited Wilhelm Wattenbach's Deutschlands Geschichtsquellen im Mittelalter, the standard guide to medieval German source materials, continued posthumously by Heinz Löwe. In Bonn, a street bears his name, the Wilhelm-Levison-Strasse — a belated civic recognition of one of the city's most distinguished scholars.

Levison's legacy operates on several levels simultaneously. As a textual scholar he produced critical editions of Merovingian saints' lives that remain indispensable tools for anyone working on early medieval hagiography, ecclesiastical organisation, or manuscript transmission. As a historian his England and the Continent demolished the artificial boundary between insular and continental medieval scholarship. And as a figure his biography embodies the tragic destruction wrought upon European intellectual culture by National Socialism — a destruction that stripped Germany of some of its greatest medievalists in the years when that discipline was reaching maturity.

For the historian of medieval art and manuscript culture in particular, Levison's work on the textual foundations of early medieval sanctity — the vitae, the missionary narratives, the hagiographic cycles — provides the documentary armature upon which iconographic programmes from the Carolingian period onward were systematically constructed.

Lindsay, Wallace Martin

Nairn, Scotland, 21 February 1858 – near St Andrews, 21 September 1937

Wallace Martin Lindsay was a Scottish classical scholar and palaeographer, Professor of Humanity at the University of St Andrews from 1899 until his death. One of the founders of modern Latin palaeography, he produced foundational studies of scribal abbreviation, notably Notae Latinae (1915), and of the history and classification of Insular and continental minuscule scripts, work that underpinned much subsequent codicological study of manuscripts such as the Book of Dimma.

Lindsay was among the first scholars to give the Cadmug Gospels (Fulda, Landesbibliothek, Codex Bonifatianus 3) sustained palaeographic description; in 1910 he characterised it as Saint Boniface's "pocket-copy" of the gospels, a phrase that entered the standard vocabulary later formalised by Patrick McGurk's category of the pocket gospel book. Lindsay drowned while swimming near St Andrews in 1937.

Lo Vullo, Gaetano

active first half of the twentieth century; documented into the 1950s

Gaetano Lo Vullo was one of the most important and influential painting restorers in twentieth-century Italy, and is closely associated with the golden age of postwar Florentine restoration. Born into a noble Sicilian family from Licata, he developed a rigorously practical vocation that distinguished him within a field often divided between scholarly theory and workshop practice. Trained in Florentine restoration ateliers, he absorbed the artisanal discipline that made Florence a major international center of painting conservation, and built a methodology grounded in philological respect for the original work combined with technically necessary intervention.

Lo Vullo worked within the circle directed by Superintendent Ugo Procacci, a pivotal figure in postwar Italian restoration culture. Alongside Augusto Vermehren and Vittorio Granchi, he formed part of the historic core of restorers active at the Uffizi, where he participated in major campaigns for the preservation of some of Italy's most significant pictorial heritage. In this environment, where technical operations were increasingly linked to historical research on artistic materials and processes, Lo Vullo became one of the most representative practitioners of a restoration model that united craft knowledge and emerging scientific standards.

Among the best-documented interventions of his career is the restoration in the 1950s of Beato Angelico's panel of the Last Judgment in the Museum of San Marco, Florence, prepared in the context of the 1955 commemorations for the fifth centenary of the artist's death. Lo Vullo cleaned the pictorial surface, removing yellowed varnishes and altered retouchings, but deliberately preserved the underlying patina because the available means at the time made deeper removal too risky. This decision has often been cited as exemplary of his methodological balance: intervention where necessary, restraint where material integrity required caution.

Contemporaries and later historians valued Lo Vullo for what was described as a pragmatic eclecticism between conservation and integration. Rather than applying a rigidly conservative or interventionist doctrine, he developed case-by-case solutions calibrated to each object's condition and historical complexity. This approach made him an important point of reference for subsequent generations, and later theoretical developments in Florence — including those associated with the International University of Art (founded 1969-70) and figures such as Umberto Baldini — have often been traced back to the practical culture of the Uffizi restoration team of which he was a leading member.

Lo Vullo was also fully integrated into the wider intellectual life of postwar Florence. A personal friend of Ugo Procacci and a supporter of Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti since the Liberation, he moved within anti-fascist and cultural networks that connected restoration, criticism, and exhibition culture. He served for many years as Secretary General of La Strozzina at Palazzo Strozzi and, in that role, was frequently delegated by the Superintendency to supervise the conservation of works lent to major exhibitions. In 2008, the publication of an English-language monograph by Rossella Beatrice Batassa confirmed the international scholarly recognition of his legacy as a central figure in twentieth-century Italian restoration practice.

Lollini, Fabrizio

Bologna, 3 February 1964

Fabrizio Lollini was born in Bologna on 3 February 1964, and his entire scholarly career has unfolded within the same city — a remarkable continuity that reflects both deep institutional loyalty and the extraordinary richness of Bologna as a centre of medieval artistic production. He completed his Laurea in Lettere classiche at the Università di Bologna, a foundation in classical philology and literature that informs the rigour and textual sensitivity of all his subsequent art-historical work. He then obtained a Diploma di Specializzazione in Storia dell'Arte medievale e moderna at the same institution, before going on to a doctorate. His training was thus doubly rooted: in the classical tradition and in the specialist art-historical methodology of the Bolognese school.

Lollini is currently Professore Associato in the sector ARTE-01/A (Storia dell'Arte Medievale) in the Dipartimento delle Arti of the Università di Bologna, one of Italy's oldest and most prestigious universities. He teaches three courses: Storia dell'arte medievale, Storia della miniatura, and Alimentazione e arti visive — the last of which reflects an original and growing area of his interests, namely the representation of food and nourishment in the visual culture of the Middle Ages. He has organised numerous international conferences and delivered lectures at foreign universities, and sits on the editorial boards of several scientific journals including La Rivista di Engramma. He has also been a member of the scientific committees of many exhibitions in Italy and abroad.

The Storia della miniatura course Lollini teaches reflects one of his deepest scholarly commitments: the study of illuminated manuscripts as primary historical documents. His investigation of the so-called Codice Parigi-Imola — a Dantesque manuscript produced at the Visconti court, split between Paris and Imola — has attracted considerable attention and was the subject of a dedicated public lecture that he delivered online in February 2021. In 2007 he contributed to the scholarly study of illuminated manuscripts preserved in Imola, including a 1506 manuscript biography of Cardinal Albornoz transcribed and illuminated by Girolamo Pagliarolo, demonstrating his command of the late medieval and humanist manuscript traditions of Emilia-Romagna. His work on Bolognese illumination connects directly to the long tradition of manuscript production for which Bologna was one of the great centres of medieval Europe, supplying the university and the mendicant orders with legal, theological, and liturgical codices from the twelfth century onward.

Beyond manuscripts, Lollini has written extensively on medieval sculpture in Bologna. His essay on Niccolò dell'Arca's Compianto in Santa Maria della Vita — one of the most celebrated and emotionally overwhelming groups of terracotta sculpture in Italian art — examines the devotional, institutional, and figurative sources that converged in that extraordinary work. He traces the complex visual culture of the sculptor, who came from Apulia but worked exclusively in Bologna, demonstrating how Niccolò drew on a European range of sources while remaining firmly embedded in the Bolognese artistic context. This interest in the intersection between imported stylistic currents and local tradition is a constant thread throughout Lollini's scholarship.

Lollini has been curator and scientific director of numerous exhibitions, making him one of the most publicly active medieval art historians of his generation in Italy. In July 2024 he gave a lecture entitled "Sentire" l'arte medievale: gli oggetti, il pubblico e i suoi sensi in Imola, a title that encapsulates an important dimension of his recent research: the sensory and affective dimensions of the medieval encounter with artistic objects. He has also lectured at the Museo della Città di Livorno and at the Fondazione Collegio San Carlo di Modena, bringing medieval art history to audiences well beyond the university. His collaboration with the publisher specialising in manuscript facsimiles further reflects his commitment to making medieval visual culture physically accessible to readers and institutions.

Lollini's declared research interests, as listed on his Academia.edu profile, include cinema and the visual arts, Late Byzantine history, and food studies alongside his core medieval art-historical work. This breadth is unusual among Italian medievalists and signals a scholar who thinks across disciplinary boundaries — connecting the medieval image to questions of sensory perception, material culture, and the long history of visual representation. His course on Alimentazione e arti visive is, to the best of current knowledge, one of the few such courses offered at an Italian university, reflecting his pioneering engagement with the anthropology of the image.

Longhi, Roberto

Alba, 28 December 1890 – Florence, 3 June 1970

Roberto Longhi is universally regarded as the greatest Italian art historian of the twentieth century: a figure who revolutionized critical methodology, discovered or reevaluated entire areas of Italian painting that had remained in the shadows, and trained generations of scholars—from Federico Zeri to Ferdinando Bologna—who reshaped the discipline.

Born in Alba, in the Langhe region, on December 28, 1890, to a middle-class family of Modenese origin, Longhi soon moved to Rome, where in 1913 he completed his advanced studies at the school of Adolfo Venturi, the great encyclopedist of Italian painting, of whom he became the most brilliant student and later the most formidable critic. Venturi opened the doors of the journal L'Arte to him, in which Longhi published his first essays, wittily dismantling established attributions and inaugurating his method of formal analysis—based on the examination of brushstroke, color, and compositional structure, rather than on documentary sources. The characteristics of his literary style emerged even in his very earliest works: a dense prose, rich in synesthetic metaphors and lexical inventions, which transformed the art-historical essay into an autonomous literary genre.

From 1913, he taught art history at the Tasso and Visconti high schools in Rome, where his students included Lucia Lopresti, a writer who would publish under the pseudonym Anna Banti and who would become his wife in 1924, as well as his intellectual collaborator for life. During his years in Rome, Longhi published essays destined to become milestones: Orione (1919), Piero della Francesca (1913, expanded in 1927), and the polemical Gentile da Fabriano e il Pisanello (1926), in which he attacked Croce's aesthetics and asserted the philosophical autonomy of figurative language. Between 1920 and 1922, he undertook a long journey through Europe with the collector Alessandro Contini Bonacossi, visiting museums and collections in France, Spain, Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary—experiences that extraordinarily broadened his visual and comparative horizons.

In 1934, he was appointed to the chair of Medieval and Modern Art History at the University of Bologna, where he began teaching in 1935, establishing his first academic school. That very year he published Officina Ferrarese, his study of painting in Ferrara during the fifteenth century—from Cosmè Tura to Ercole de' Roberti—which remains an unsurpassed model of reconstructing a regional pictorial tradition through stylistic analysis. In 1937, through Minister Giuseppe Bottai (a former student of his at the Visconti School), he obtained a position at the General Directorate of Fine Arts in Rome, where he worked for two years on organizing the Italian art exhibition at the EUR, which was ultimately not held due to Italy's entry into the war. In 1943 he founded the journal Proporzioni, and refused to serve under the Italian Social Republic, resulting in his suspension from teaching until the end of the war—one of the few explicit political gestures in a life deliberately focused on art criticism.

In 1950 he was appointed to a professorship at the University of Florence, where he remained until reaching the mandatory retirement age, forming his second school and teaching in the small villa at Villa Il Tasso, which had become his studio-museum. In 1950 he founded the journal Paragone, which he edited until his death and which became the leading organ of postwar Italian art criticism. Through Paragone, Longhi waged his cultural battles: he reevaluated forgotten artists, debunked erroneous attributions, championed contemporary painting (particularly Giorgio Morandi, of whom he was a close friend and the first systematic critic), and published the writings of his best students, including Federico Zeri, Mina Gregori, Luciano Bellosi, and Ferdinando Bologna himself. The magazine outlived its founder: Anna Banti continued it after Longhi's death until the 1980s, maintaining its polemical spirit and critical quality.

Longhi's two major contributions to the history of world art concern Caravaggio and Piero della Francesca. Regarding the latter, Longhi was the first 20th-century critic to fully grasp Piero's role in the Italian 15th-century art scene: his 1927 monograph, immediately translated into French and English, restored the artist from Sansepolcro to the ranks of the greatest painters, influencing all subsequent criticism and paving the way for a reevaluation by Bernard Berenson and Anglo-Saxon critics. As for Caravaggio, Longhi was the undisputed leading figure in the 20th-century rediscovery: following the Quesiti caravaggeschi (1928–1934) and the Ultimi studi caravaggeschi (1943), in 1951 he curated the monumental exhibition Caravaggio e i Caravaggeschi at the Palazzo Reale in Milan, which marked a turning point in the public and critical perception of the Lombard painter, definitively establishing him as the father of European naturalism. His 1968 monograph on Caravaggio remains his most mature contribution to the subject.

Longhi's method is based on the supremacy of the "visual fact": Longhi refused to rely on documents or literary sources for attribution when the analysis of pictorial form—of color, light, space, and "tone"—could offer more precise answers. This formalism, rooted in the traditions of Warburg and Berenson, was, however, always tempered in Longhi by a keen historical sensibility, which placed every artist within the network of relationships between workshops, patrons, and local traditions. Equally celebrated is his prose: rich in neologisms, daring constructions, and visual metaphors capable of translating the quality of light or the texture of a color into words, his writings have influenced generations of critics and writers, from Pier Paolo Pasolini to Andrea Zanzotto.

Roberto Longhi died in Florence on June 3, 1970, bequeathing his extraordinary art collection, library, photo library, and archive to the Roberto Longhi Foundation for Art History Studies, now based at Villa Il Tasso in Florence. Each year, the Foundation awards scholarships to young art history researchers, continuing the educational work of its founder. The photographic archive, now part of the Zeri Foundation's Photo Library, is an indispensable resource for research on Italian painting from the 13th to the 18th century.

Lowe, Elias Avery

Moscow, 15 October 1879 – Bad Nauheim, 8 August 1969

Elias Avery Lowe was born on 15 October 1879 in Moscow, then part of the Russian Empire, to a Jewish family headed by Charles Loew, a silk and embroidery merchant, and his wife, Sarah Ragoler. The family's roots lay in Lithuania, and he emigrated to New York City with his parents in 1892, becoming a citizen of the United States in 1900. He died on 8 August 1969 in Bad Nauheim, Germany; his ashes were interred at Corpus Christi College, Oxford.

After studying at the College of the City of New York from 1894 to 1897, Lowe obtained a BA at Cornell University in 1902. He then studied briefly at the University of Halle before moving to the University of Munich — a transition accidental in origin but consequential in effect. Georg Wissowa at Halle thought it would contribute to Lowe's development to spend a semester in Munich with Ludwig Traube. So taken was Lowe by Traube's personality and approach to Latin literature — with its emphasis on the manuscript traditions of the literature — that he never returned to Halle.

The intellectual debt to Ludwig Traube was absolute and lifelong. Traube — the founder of the modern science of Latin palaeography as an independent academic discipline — proposed as a dissertation subject the transmission of Latin classics through Monte Cassino. Lowe approached the problem on its most fundamental level, initiating an exhaustive study of the handwriting used in South Italy, on the basis of which extant manuscripts might be assigned to Monte Cassino as their place of origin and given their appropriate dates. Under Traube's supervision, Lowe completed his doctorate in 1908 with a dissertation on the oldest surviving calendars from Monte Cassino. Traube died prematurely in 1907, before the work was printed, and Lowe would carry his master's methods forward for the next six decades.

The first major publication to emerge from the Monte Cassino research was Studia Palaeographica: A Contribution to the History of Early Latin Minuscule and to the Dating of Visigothic Manuscripts (Munich, 1910). In this work Lowe established highly sophisticated criteria for dating Beneventan and Visigothic minuscule manuscripts, deploying for the first time systematically the principle that changes in letterform, ligature, abbreviation, and parchment treatment could serve as independent chronological indicators. This methodological rigour — the close comparison of formal features across a large number of dated exemplars as a basis for assigning undated manuscripts to a time and place — was Lowe's central contribution to the discipline, and it underpins everything that followed.

The Beneventan Script (Oxford, 1914) was the first full-scale study of a particular Latin script. It described, classified, and traced the history of the distinctive South Italian minuscule — the script associated with the great Benedictine scriptorium of Monte Cassino and its daughter houses — from its origins in the eighth century through its long florescence and eventual decline after the thirteenth. The script had previously been called Langobarda, Longobarda, or Gothica; it was Lowe who gave it the name Beneventan, now universally adopted. According to Lowe, the perfected form of the script was used in the eleventh century, while Desiderius was abbot of Monte Cassino, declining thereafter. The Beneventan Script remains, together with the facsimiles in Scriptura Beneventana, the model for treating the history of a script; a revised and expanded second edition, prepared by Virginia Brown, was published in Rome in 1980.

Lowe first lectured at the University of Oxford in 1913, and in 1914 gave the Sandars Lectures on bibliography at the University of Cambridge. He would be associated with Oxford — as lecturer, then reader, then honorary fellow — for over four decades, and nearly all of his palaeography teaching took place there. In parallel, from 1911 to 1953, he acted as research associate in palaeography for the Carnegie Institution of Washington, an affiliation that gave him both the financial independence and the institutional mandate to undertake sustained fieldwork across European libraries. During the 1910s he collaborated on the edition of the Bobbio Missal, a Gallican liturgical manuscript of the seventh–eighth century, producing the palaeographic analysis in a three-volume edition alongside André Wilmart and H. A. Wilson (London, 1917–1924).

The project that would consume the final forty years of Lowe's life arose from an encounter in 1921 with a sixth-century uncial fragment of the letters of Pliny the Younger, then at the Pierpont Morgan Library in New York. In order to establish a reliable date of origin for the Pliny fragment, Lowe began to assemble a list of all objectively dated uncial manuscripts that he could find, noting when various palaeographical or codicological features made their first appearance. The collecting and evaluating of data of this kind continued through the 1920s, well beyond the publication of the Pliny text, and eventually inspired Codices Latini Antiquiores. Work on this project began in 1929 and the final proofsheets of the last supplementary volume were in Lowe's hands when he died forty years later.

The Codices Latini Antiquiores (CLA) offers a palaeographical guide to all extant Latin literary manuscripts copied in scripts antedating the ninth century. Published 1934–1971, this monumental work covers over 1,800 manuscripts from repositories in twenty-one countries, providing detailed descriptions and one or more facsimiles for each manuscript. The eleven volumes are organised geographically — the Vatican City, Great Britain and Ireland, Italy, France, Switzerland, Germany, and a final volume covering Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Sweden, and the United States, among others — and were followed by a supplement in 1971 and two sets of addenda published in 1985 and 1992. To compile each volume, Lowe travelled in person to examine the originals, filling standardised forms with measurements, script identifications, and codicological observations. His assistant on many of these journeys was a young German palaeographer who would become his peer — Bernhard Bischoff, who later wrote a memoir of their travels together.

Lowe became one of the first professors at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study in 1936, where no teaching was required; he continued to lecture at Oxford during Trinity terms until 1948. He also acted as a consultant in palaeography for the Library of Congress. His collected short studies, spanning nearly sixty years of publication, were gathered posthumously in the two-volume Palaeographical Papers 1907–1965, edited by Ludwig Bieler and published by the Clarendon Press in 1972.

In 1911, Lowe married the translator Helen Tracy Lowe-Porter, who became celebrated as the English translator of Thomas Mann's novels — Buddenbrooks, The Magic Mountain, Doctor Faustus. They had three daughters. Among their descendants are the English artist Charlotte Johnson Wahl and her son, the politician Boris Johnson, the former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Although Lowe never abandoned his solidarity with the Jewish people, he declined to practise Judaism; towards the end of his life he told one of his daughters that, were he to adhere to a religion, he would opt for Roman Catholicism — a disposition not without irony in a scholar whose life's work was rooted in the manuscript culture of Benedictine monasticism.

Lowe received numerous recognitions from academies, institutes, and scholarly societies. He was awarded the Medieval Academy of America's Haskins Medal in 1957 and the gold medal of the Bibliographical Society in 1959, and received honorary doctoral degrees from the University of Oxford (1936), the University of North Carolina (1946), and the National University of Ireland (1964). From 1954 until his death he was an Honorary Fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He was also a corresponding fellow of the British Academy and a member of the Accademia dei Lincei in Rome and the Institut de France. A series of triennial lectures on palaeography, the E. A. Lowe Lectures, continues to be held at Corpus Christi College in his memory.

Lowe stands as the central figure in the twentieth-century transformation of Latin palaeography from an auxiliary discipline into an independent science. By insisting on the systematic analysis of letterforms against a controlled body of dated exemplars — and by applying this method with unmatched consistency across twelve volumes spanning the entire surviving corpus of pre-Carolingian Latin manuscripts — he gave to all subsequent medieval scholarship a reliable physical foundation for the study of manuscript transmission, textual history, and the geography of book production in the Latin West. For the historian of illuminated manuscripts in particular, the Codices Latini Antiquiores is not merely useful but foundational: it is the instrument through which the oldest stratum of Western manuscript art — the insular Gospel books, the great Italian uncial codices, the Merovingian liturgical books, the Visigothic and Beneventan traditions — can be assigned to their places and periods of origin with the precision that iconographic and art-historical analysis demands.

Ludovico da Pietralunga

16th century (fl. c. 1570-1580)

Ludovico da Pietralunga was a Franciscan Conventual friar, born at Pietralunga in the Alta Valle del Tevere (Umbria, in the territory of Città di Castello), who spent his mature years in the Sacro Convento at Assisi. He is consistently described in the literature as a frate-pittore — a friar who also practised painting, apparently at a modest artisanal level — though his own surviving output is negligible and this side of his career rests on slender evidence rather than on a documented corpus.

His claim on the attention of art historians rests entirely on one text: the Descrizione della Basilica di S. Francesco e di altri santuari di Assisi, compiled around 1570-1580 and preserved in manuscript 148 of the Biblioteca comunale di Assisi. It remained unpublished until the early twentieth century. The standard reference edition is Ludovico da Pietralunga, Descrizione della Basilica di S. Francesco e di altri santuari di Assisi. In appendice: Chiesa superiore, di Anonimo secentesco, ed. Pietro Scarpellini, Treviso, Canova, 1982 (series Fonti per la storia dell'arte) — cited in the scholarly literature as "Ludovico da Pietralunga, ed. 1982".

The Descrizione is the earliest systematic, room-by-room account of the decoration of the Basilica, and it is not a devotional inventory of relics but something closer to an artistic topography: Ludovico described the images, explained their iconography, recorded the names of illustrious donors — popes and cardinals — and dwelt at length on the names and merits of the painters. Because he wrote before the Baroque remodelling and the nineteenth-century interventions, he preserves evidence of things now lost.

Three examples of the kind of testimony he supplies:

  • He is the first to record the panel of St Francis against a gold ground, surrounded by four scenes of miracles, now in the Museo del Tesoro.
  • He recorded the tomb of Cardinal Gentile Partino da Montefiore in the pavement before the altar of the Cappella di S. Ludovico, of which no trace survives after the 1763 remodelling.
  • Read alongside Vasari, he documents heraldry in the Lower Church Passion cycle — the arms of Gualtieri di Brienne, recently identified in a badly worn portion of fresco by Michela Becchis exactly where Vasari and Ludovico had placed them, a find with consequences for the chronology of Pietro Lorenzetti at Assisi.

Lunghi, Elvio

Assisi, 1957

Elvio Lunghi was born in Assisi in 1957, a birthplace whose significance cannot be overstated: his entire scholarly life would orbit around the artistic heritage of that city and the Franciscan world it generated. He completed his Laurea in Lettere at the Università degli Studi di Perugia in 1981, and in 1987 defended his doctorate as an external candidate at the Università La Sapienza di Roma. His academic engagement began even before graduation: from 1983 to 1988 he served as professore incaricato at the Università per Stranieri di Perugia, a position that would prove the foundation of a career spent almost entirely at that institution. From 1988 to 1991 he taught as a tenured secondary school professor — an experience that cultivated his lifelong commitment to public communication of art history — before returning to the Università per Stranieri as professore comandato in 1991.

In 2004 Lunghi was appointed Professore Associato in Medieval Art History (sector L-ART/01) at the Università per Stranieri di Perugia, the post he has held ever since. His three declared research areas are: painting and sculpture in central Italy between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance; artistic patronage of the mendicant religious orders; and the popular promotion and dissemination of artistic heritage. These three axes are not parallel lines but deeply interwoven — the mendicant orders were the principal engine of visual culture in medieval Umbria, and understanding their patronage is inseparable from understanding the painters and sculptors Lunghi has spent his career studying.

No work has absorbed more of Lunghi's intellectual energy than the great artistic programme of the Basilica of San Francesco in Assisi. His monograph La Basilica di S. Francesco in Assisi (Scala Editrice, Florence, 1996) remains one of the most comprehensive single-volume accounts of the building's decoration. His 2012 volume Giotto e i pittori giotteschi ad Assisi (Editrice la Rocca, Marsciano, pp. 494) is the most systematic account yet written of the entire Giottesque workshop presence in the city. His article L'influenza di Pietro di Giovanni Olivi e di Ubertino da Casale nel programma iconografico della chiesa inferiore di S. Francesco ad Assisi, published in Collectanea Francescana in 1997, and the study La perduta decorazione trecentesca nell'abside della chiesa inferiore del S. Francesco, published in the same journal in 1996, together represent the most sustained scholarly engagement with the theological motivations behind the Lower Church's pictorial programme. His synthesis Immagini degli Spirituali. Il significato delle immagini nelle chiese francescane di Assisi (Il Formichiere, Foligno, 2019, pp. 313) crowns four decades of reflection on the relationship between Franciscan spirituality — particularly the Spiritual Franciscan movement — and the images produced for the order's churches.

Lunghi's contributions to the study of illuminated manuscripts in Umbria are among the most enduring in the field. In 2004 he wrote numerous entries for the Dizionario biografico dei miniatori italiani secoli IX–XVI (Edizioni Sylvestre Bonnard, Milan), covering artists including Bartolomeo Caporali, Giapeco Caporali, the Maestro dei Corali di Gubbio, the Maestro dei Corali di S. Lorenzo, the Maestro del Messale di Deruta, Marino da Perugia, Venturella di Pietro, and Vanni di Baldolo. Each of these entries represents original archival and stylistic research into artists who had received little or no dedicated scholarly attention. His essay Intorno ai codici liturgici del XIII e XIV secolo conservati nelle raccolte umbre, written with P.M. Della Porta and published in the catalogue Canto e colore: I corali di San Domenico di Perugia nella Biblioteca comunale Augusta (Perugia, 2006), accompanied catalogue entries for some twenty-three individual manuscripts preserved in the Augusta library. The 2018 exhibition Gubbio al tempo di Giotto, which Lunghi co-curated with Giordana Benazzi and Enrica Neri Lusanna, extended this manuscript work with entries on the Maestri dei corali di Gubbio, an anonymous Bolognese miniatore active in Gubbio, Venturella di Pietro, and Vanni di Baldolo.

Lunghi has also made a decisive mark on scholarship concerning wooden devotional sculpture in Umbria. His monograph La Passione degli Umbri. Crocifissi di legno in Valle Umbra tra Medioevo e Rinascimento (Orfini Numeister, Foligno, 2000, pp. 190) was the first systematic survey of the surviving corpus of wooden crucifixes in the Valle Umbra, tracing the artistic, liturgical, and devotional contexts that produced them. His essay La scultura lignea in Umbria nel XIII secolo, published in the CISAM volume L'Umbria nel XIII secolo in 2011, extended this analysis to the earliest documented phase of production in the region. Through the exhibition catalogues Da Giotto a Gentile (Fabriano, 2014) and Dal visibile all'indicibile (Foligno, 2012), he continued to catalogue individual crucifixes and place them in the broader context of mystical and penitential culture in central Italy.

As a connoisseur, Lunghi has proposed and refined a number of attributions that have entered standard art-historical usage. His early study Il Crocifisso di Giunta Pisano e l'icona del "Maestro di San Francesco" alla Porziuncola (1995) placed the two most important early devotional images at the Porziuncola in their full historical context, distinguishing the documented work of Giunta Pisano from the anonymous panel known as the Maestro di San Francesco. More controversially but very influentially, his essay Le arti del Duecento a Gubbio (2018) proposed an identification between the anonymous Maestro dei Crocifissi Francescani and the documented Bolognese painter Guido di Pietro da Gubbio, father of the miniatore Oderisi immortalised by Dante. In the catalogues of the exhibitions Da Giotto a Gentile (2014) and Gubbio al tempo di Giotto (2018), he systematically attributed multiple works to the Maestro dei Crocifissi Francescani across institutions in Assisi, Camerino, and Bologna. He also confirmed the presence of the Monteripido Crucifix within the corpus of the German sculptor Giovanni Teutonico, active in Umbria in the late fifteenth century.

While Lunghi's reputation rests primarily on medieval art, his scholarship extends naturally into the Quattrocento and early Cinquecento. He edited the major exhibition catalogue Nicolaus Pictor. Nicolò di Liberatore detto l'Alunno (Foligno, 2004, pp. 544) with Giordana Benazzi, the fullest account of the Foligno painter's life and workshop. He wrote Itinerari del Perugino in Umbria (Silvana Editoriale, 2004) and the monograph Il Martirio di san Sebastiano di Pietro Perugino a Panicale (2005), and in 2015 co-authored Cesare Sermei pittore devoto nell'Umbria del Seicento with P. Mercurelli Salari (Edizioni Orfini Numeister, pp. 330). A notable early contribution to Raphael studies was his 2003 monograph Raffaello a Cerqueto. Un affresco giovanile e l'esordio in Umbria and his article Una proposta per il giovane Raffaello (2002), which advanced a new attribution for the young Raphael's debut in Umbrian fresco painting.

Lunghi's scholarship has reached international audiences through publications in English and German. His essay Francis of Assisi in Prayer before the Crucifix in the Accounts of the First Biographers was published in the prestigious National Gallery of Art volume Italian Panel Painting of the Duecento and Trecento (Studies in the History of Art, XXXVIII, New Haven & London, 2002, pp. 341–353). He contributed a further study, Una proposta per il giovane Raffaello, to the Festschrift for Antje Middeldorf Kosegarten published in Dresden and Kassel in 2002. For the Enciclopedia dell'Arte Medievale of the Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana he wrote entries on Orvieto (1997), Spoleto (1999), and Giovanni di Bonino (1995). For many years he has maintained a regular column in the journal San Francesco Patrono d'Italia, writing each month on themes drawn from Franciscan art and spirituality, making scholarly research accessible to the widest possible audience. His most recent volume, Perugia. Cento storie, was presented in December 2025, confirming that at nearly seventy years of age his scholarly productivity shows no sign of abating.

M

Mabillon, Jean

Saint-Pierremont, 23 August 1632 - Paris, 27 December 1707

Jean Mabillon was born on 23 August 1632 in Saint-Pierremont, a small village in the Ardennes region of northeastern France, into a modest rural family. Little is recorded of his early childhood, but his evident intellectual gifts brought him to the attention of the local clergy, and he received his initial formation at the collège of Reims, where he demonstrated exceptional aptitude for Latin and the study of texts.

In 1653, at the age of twenty-one, Mabillon took his monastic vows at the Abbey of Saint-Rémi in Reims, entering the Congregation of Saint-Maur — the reformed Benedictine congregation founded in 1618, which would become the most distinguished centre of ecclesiastical scholarship in seventeenth-century Europe. The Maurists, as they were known, had made rigorous textual and historical scholarship central to their monastic vocation, producing critical editions of the Church Fathers, hagiographical collections, and historical documents on a scale unprecedented in the history of religious learning.

After his novitiate at Saint-Rémi, Mabillon was transferred to several abbeys for further formation — including Nogent-sous-Coucy and Corbie — before being definitively assigned in 1664 to the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, the intellectual heart of the Maurist congregation and home to one of the finest manuscript libraries in France. It was here that Mabillon would spend the greater part of his scholarly life, and where he would produce the works that secured his permanent place in the history of Western learning.

To understand Mabillon, it is essential to appreciate the extraordinary intellectual culture of the Maurists at Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Under the direction of scholars such as Luc d'Achery — who became Mabillon's mentor and guide — the congregation had undertaken the systematic editing of patristic and medieval texts, applying to sacred and historical documents the same rigorous philological methods that humanist scholars had brought to classical antiquity. D'Achery's own Spicilegium (1655–1677), a massive collection of previously unpublished medieval documents, set the standard for the enterprise in which Mabillon would surpass all his contemporaries.

Working under d'Achery's direction, Mabillon began his career with contributions to the edition of the works of St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1667), a task that required close familiarity with the transmission of twelfth-century manuscripts and the problems of attribution. This early experience sharpened his sensitivity to questions of textual authenticity and documentary evidence that would become central to all his subsequent work.

Mabillon's first major independent project was the nine-volume Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti, published between 1668 and 1701, which presented the lives and acts of Benedictine saints arranged chronologically from the sixth to the twelfth century. This monumental undertaking required Mabillon to survey and critically evaluate an enormous body of hagiographical material, distinguishing authentic documents from later forgeries and interpolations with a methodological rigour that was, at the time, genuinely revolutionary.

The Acta Sanctorum established Mabillon's reputation throughout learned Europe as a scholar of the first rank — meticulous, balanced in judgement, and possessed of an unparalleled command of the medieval manuscript tradition. It also brought him into correspondence with virtually every major historian and antiquary of the age, from Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz — with whom he maintained a prolonged and intellectually fertile exchange — to Antonio Magliabechi, the Florentine librarian and polymath. This network of correspondence, which Mabillon cultivated assiduously throughout his life, made Saint-Germain-des-Prés a nodal point in the pan-European République des Lettres of the late seventeenth century.

Mabillon's supreme achievement, and the work that assures his unique position in the history of scholarship, is the six-volume De Re Diplomatica libri VI, published in Paris in 1681.
