The immediate occasion for the work was a direct scholarly challenge: the Bollandist hagiographer Daniel van Papenbroeck had questioned the authenticity of a number of early medieval charters held by Benedictine monasteries, including documents foundational to the Maurists' own institutional history. Mabillon's response transformed what might have been a narrow polemical exchange into the founding document of an entirely new discipline.

De Re Diplomatica established, for the first time on a systematic basis, the criteria by which medieval documents — charters, diplomas, privileges — could be authenticated or identified as forgeries. Mabillon examined hundreds of original documents, developing rigorous criteria based on the analysis of script and handwriting, establishing a historical typology of Latin scripts from the Merovingian period through the high medieval era; the study of formulaic language (formulae) — the standardized phrases and clauses typical of different chanceries and periods; the material analysis of writing supports — parchment, vellum, papyrus — and of inks, seals, and authentication marks; and the examination of diplomatic protocol: the structure and sequence of clauses in official documents (invocation, intitulation, address, preamble, dispositio, sanctio, corroboration, dating, witness lists).

By synthesizing these multiple analytical approaches, Mabillon created what is essentially the discipline of Latin palaeography and the science of diplomatics as they are still practised today. Van Papenbroeck — with exemplary intellectual honesty — publicly acknowledged Mabillon's refutation of his arguments, and the two scholars parted in mutual respect. The work was immediately recognized as a masterpiece. Leibniz called it opus plane singulare, "a work altogether singular." It was translated, excerpted, and debated across Europe, and remains to this day the foundational text of the discipline.

In 1685–1686, Mabillon undertook an extended journey through Italy, commissioned by Jean-Baptiste Colbert's son the Marquis de Seignelay and by King Louis XIV himself, with the mission of identifying and acquiring manuscripts for the Royal Library. Accompanied by the Maurist Michel Germain, he traveled through Turin, Milan, Florence, Rome, Monte Cassino, Naples, and numerous other centres, visiting archives, monastic libraries, and collections both ecclesiastical and princely.

The journey was of incalculable scholarly significance. Mabillon gained direct access to document collections he had previously known only through correspondence or secondary description, and the experience deepened his understanding of Italian Benedictine manuscript traditions — particularly those of Monte Cassino, where he could examine the origins of the Beneventan script, a topic he would address in De Re Diplomatica. He also forged lasting relationships with Italian scholars, archivists, and librarians. The results of this journey were published as Museum Italicum (2 volumes, 1687–1689), a detailed account of the Italian libraries and manuscripts he had consulted, which remains an indispensable source for the history of Italian manuscript collections in the late seventeenth century.

In 1691, Mabillon entered a famous public controversy with Armand-Jean de Rancé, the austere reforming abbot of La Trappe and founder of the Trappist branch of the Cistercian order. Rancé had published a work arguing that monastic scholarship was fundamentally incompatible with the true spirit of the Benedictine vocation — that monks should devote themselves exclusively to prayer, manual labour, and penance, and that intellectual work was a form of spiritual vanity.

Mabillon's response, the Traité des Études Monastiques (1691), is a masterpiece of learned and dignified polemic. Without acrimony, he argued systematically that scholarly study had always formed an integral part of Benedictine life from the time of St. Benedict himself — that the copying, preserving, and interpreting of sacred and patristic texts was a form of lectio divina and an act of service to the Church no less spiritually valid than manual labour. The Traité drew on the full weight of Benedictine historical tradition to demonstrate that learning and contemplation were not enemies but natural complements, and that the great monastic culture of the Middle Ages had been inseparable from its scholarly activity.

The work was both an apologia for the Maurist enterprise and a profound meditation on the relationship between the intellectual and spiritual life. It remains one of the most thoughtful defences of the compatibility of scholarship and religious vocation ever written.

The last great project of Mabillon's life was the Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti, a comprehensive chronological history of the Benedictine order from its origins through the twelfth century. Mabillon published the first two volumes in 1703 and continued working on the project until his death, having completed four volumes; the remaining two were published posthumously between 1713 and 1739 from his notes and drafts.

The Annales represented the summation of a lifetime's engagement with medieval Benedictine sources — charters, chronicles, hagiographical texts, liturgical documents — and demonstrated once again Mabillon's extraordinary capacity to synthesize vast bodies of evidence into a coherent and critical historical narrative. Although inevitably superseded in many particulars by subsequent scholarship, the Annales remained an essential reference for historians of medieval monasticism well into the nineteenth century.

Mabillon was celebrated not only for the scale of his learning but for the exceptional quality of his personal character. Contemporaries consistently described him as humble, gentle, and entirely without intellectual vanity — qualities all the more remarkable in a scholar whose eminence was universally acknowledged. He bore controversy with equanimity, was generous in acknowledging the contributions of predecessors and colleagues, and maintained an extensive correspondence with scholars across confessional boundaries with unfailing courtesy.

He was elected a member of the Académie française and received recognition from learned societies across Europe. Louis XIV's minister Colbert sought his advice on the organization of the Royal Library, and Pope Clement XI received him in private audience during his Italian journey, honouring him as the foremost Latinist and medievalist of the age.

In his final years, increasingly affected by the physical decline of age, Mabillon continued to work at Saint-Germain-des-Prés with undiminished dedication. He died there on 27 December 1707, aged seventy-five, mourned across Catholic and Protestant Europe alike as one of the supreme intellectual figures of his generation.

The legacy of Jean Mabillon is at once disciplinary, institutional, and cultural. As the founder of Latin palaeography and diplomatics, he established the methodological foundations on which all subsequent study of medieval documents has been built. The analytical categories he developed in De Re Diplomatica — script typology, diplomatic protocol, formulaic analysis, material examination — remain the core instruments of the discipline to this day, and every palaeographer and archivist working with Latin medieval manuscripts works, however distantly, in his tradition.

His broader scholarly programme — the rigorous critical edition of medieval texts, the systematic cataloguing of manuscript collections, the application of philological method to hagiography and church history — defined the Maurist achievement and, through it, shaped the entire development of medieval studies as an academic discipline from the eighteenth century onward. The German historical school of the nineteenth century, Benedictine historical scholarship at Solesmes and Monte Cassino, and the modern institutions of palaeography and archival science all draw, in different ways, from the methodological capital accumulated by Mabillon and his Maurist colleagues.

For historians of medieval art and manuscript culture in particular, Mabillon's palaeographical typologies and his catalogues of Italian and French manuscript collections retain a documentary value that transcends their immediate historical context. His Italian journey and the Museum Italicum remain indispensable for the reconstruction of the state of monastic libraries at the end of the seventeenth century, before the catastrophic dispersals of the Revolutionary era.

Maginnis, Hayden B. J.

active 20th–21st century

Hayden B. J. Maginnis is an American art historian whose work on the painting of Trecento Siena has been especially concerned with reconstructing the material and documentary conditions of the medieval workshop, and with subjecting the connoisseurial tradition surrounding painters such as Duccio to sustained historiographical scrutiny.

His major books, Painting in the Age of Giotto: A Historical Reevaluation (1997) and The World of the Early Sienese Painter (2001), examine the documentary and institutional world in which Sienese Trecento altarpieces were commissioned, produced, and paid for, and have provided the archival basis for subsequent studies of individual painters' careers, including the documentation of major civic and ecclesiastical commissions such as the chapel of St Paul in Siena Cathedral.

Magister, Sara

active late 20th–21st century

Sara Magister is an Italian art historian trained in both classical archaeology and medieval and modern art history — she holds a research doctorate in classical antiquities alongside a diploma of specialization in medieval and modern art history — whose scholarship spans two seemingly distant fields: Trecento Sienese painting and the history of collecting, particularly of antiquities, in Renaissance and Baroque Rome.

For the Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana's Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, Magister contributed the standard modern biographical entry on the Sienese painter Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio (vol. 62, 2004), a synthesis that draws together Gaetano Milanesi's nineteenth-century documentary transcriptions, Roberto Longhi's and Pier Paolo Donati's reconstruction of the "Maestro degli Ordini," and Luciano Bellosi's 1972 identification of that anonymous personality with the documented painter, while carefully weighing later proposals — including Mojmír Frinta's punch-mark hypothesis linking Jacopo's father to the painter Mino Parcis, which Magister judged "di scarso fondamento" (of scant foundation).

Her principal monograph, Arte e politica: la collezione di antichità del cardinale Giuliano della Rovere nei palazzi ai Santi Apostoli (Atti della Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei, 2002), reconstructs the antiquities collection assembled by Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere — the future Pope Julius II — before his election, situating it within a broader survey of more than 160 Roman collecting families and establishing the documentary groundwork for the pontiff's later foundation of the Belvedere. She has since published widely on Renaissance and Baroque collecting, and in 2018 released Caravaggio, il vero Matteo. I capolavori per San Luigi dei Francesi a Roma, storia e significato (Campisano; 2nd ed. 2020), a study of Caravaggio's Contarelli Chapel paintings that won the national "Città Cristologica" prize the same year.

Alongside her published research, Magister has worked consistently to bring art history to a wider public, combining university teaching with print and television journalism, cultural tourism, and museum education — an orientation reflected in her continuing lecture courses for the online academy Schola Palatina.

Maguire, Henry P.

Bath, 1943

Henry P. Maguire is one of the most original and influential historians of Byzantine art of the second half of the twentieth century, Professor Emeritus at Johns Hopkins University and former Director of Byzantine Studies at Dumbarton Oaks. His contribution has often been described as transformative: with systematic rigor, he reintroduced literary rhetoric, poetry, and non-canonical objects as tools for analyzing medieval art, permanently expanding the traditional scope of Byzantine art history.

Born in 1943 in Bath, England, Maguire enrolled in 1962 at King's College, Cambridge, to study Archaeology and Anthropology, before moving to Art History after one year. His doctoral training took place at the Courtauld Institute of Art in London and at Harvard University, both attended through the Bliss Fellowship. At Harvard he studied under Ernst Kitzinger, whose Viennese-inflected method in early Christian and late antique art deeply shaped Maguire's stylistic and iconographic approach. His wife, Eunice Dauterman Maguire, herself a Byzantine art historian and later curator of the Johns Hopkins Archaeological Collection, followed the same advanced training and intellectual environment.

After a brief post at the University of Massachusetts in the early 1970s, Maguire held a joint appointment as assistant professor at Johns Hopkins and Dumbarton Oaks from 1973 to 1979. From 1979 to 2000 he taught at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he and Eunice Dauterman Maguire pursued pioneering work on domestic objects and the material culture of late antiquity. In 1991 he was appointed Director of Byzantine Studies at Dumbarton Oaks, a role he held until 1996. From 2000 to 2010 he held the Chair of Art History at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, where he is now Professor Emeritus.

Maguire's first major book, Art and Eloquence in Byzantium (Princeton University Press, 1981), established the methodological foundation of his later work. It demonstrated how classical rhetorical genres, especially ekphrasis and threnos, directly influenced Byzantine narrative pictorial conventions. The thesis was groundbreaking: instead of treating medieval art as a self-contained visual system, Maguire showed that painters and patrons worked within a shared semiotic field that included poetry, liturgy, homiletics, and rhetoric. A decisive early articulation of this line of inquiry is his 1977 Dumbarton Oaks Papers article, The Depiction of Sorrow in Middle Byzantine Art, where the Threnos at Nerezi is interpreted through the literary tradition of lament.

From the 1980s onward, Maguire expanded his research toward new and previously underexplored fields: nature in Byzantine art, magic and apotropaic imagery, and secular and domestic culture. Earth and Ocean: The Terrestrial World in Early Byzantine Art (1987) interpreted representations of earth, sea, and living beings in early Christian art as a coherent cosmological system. Rhetoric, Nature and Magic in Byzantine Art (1998) collected essays integrating aesthetics with magical-religious concerns, demonstrating how amulets, engraved gems, and textiles could be read within the same symbolic horizon as monumental works.

A mature synthesis of these themes appears in Nectar and Illusion: Nature in Byzantine Art and Literature (Princeton University Press, 2012), where Maguire analyzed how Byzantines represented and interpreted flowers, fruit, animals, and landscapes across monumental art, manuscripts, decorative arts, and texts. The volume is now indispensable for manuscript studies because it offers a strong theoretical framework for interpreting vegetal and zoomorphic ornament in margins, initials, and decorative programs.

Two parallel strands characterize the second half of his career. The first, focused on sanctity and the sacred image, culminated in Icons of Their Bodies: Saints and Their Images in Byzantium (Princeton University Press, 1996), a fundamental study of the relationship among saintly corporeality, relics, and representation. The second, devoted to secular culture, produced Other Icons: Art and Power in Byzantine Secular Culture (Princeton University Press, 2007), written with Eunice Dauterman Maguire, which shifted attention toward private and domestic objects, including textiles, jewelry, ceramics, and ivory. The book strongly influenced later scholarship on non-ecclesiastical medieval material culture.

His directorship at Dumbarton Oaks (1991-1996) was marked by intense editorial activity reflecting the full breadth of his interests. Under his supervision, major collective volumes appeared, including Byzantine Magic (1995), Byzantine Court Culture from 829 to 1204 (1997), and Byzantine Garden Culture (2002), all published by the Dumbarton Oaks Research Library and Collection. The volume San Marco, Byzantium, and Myths of Venice (2010), edited with Robert Nelson, further reflects his interest in interactions between Byzantine artistic traditions and their medieval Western reception.

In 2020, recognition of Maguire's scholarly legacy took the form of the Festschrift The Eloquence of Art: Essays in Honour of Henry Maguire, edited by Andrea Olsen Lam and Rossitza Schroeder for Routledge's Birmingham Byzantine and Ottoman Studies series. The twenty-three contributions, ranging from imperial iconography to Islamic-Byzantine visual culture and from Ravenna mosaics to Cypriot art, testify to the extraordinary thematic and geographical reach of his work and to an influence that spans generations and disciplines.

Mâle, Émile

Commentry, 2 June 1862 – Fontaine-Chaalis, 6 October 1954

Émile Mâle effectively created the study of medieval iconography as a discipline. His four-volume survey of French religious art, begun with the celebrated thesis of 1898, taught two generations to read a cathedral as an organised system of meaning rather than as an accumulation of ornament, and the method he established — reading images against the theological and liturgical texts of their period — dominated medieval art history for the better part of a century.

He was born at Commentry in the Allier in 1862 and entered the École normale supérieure, placing first in the agrégation in 1886. He was teaching rhetoric in provincial lycées when a journey to Italy that same year, and in particular a fresco by Andrea da Firenze showing Thomas Aquinas, turned him toward the history of Christian art. He defended his thesis, L'Art religieux du XIIIe siècle en France: étude sur l'iconographie du Moyen Âge et sur ses sources d'inspiration, in 1898; from 1906 he taught the history of Christian art at the Sorbonne, and in 1912 he received its chair of medieval archaeology, which he held until 1923.

The thirteenth-century volume was followed by companions on the twelfth century, the late Middle Ages, and the art of the Counter-Reformation, together forming the most influential body of iconographic scholarship ever produced in France. Its governing conviction — that "the Middle Ages had a passion for order", and that the imagery of a great church constitutes a mirror of knowledge, arranged and legible — gave the discipline both its method and its characteristic confidence.

He directed the École française de Rome from 1923 to 1937, was elected to the Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres in 1918 and to the Académie française in 1927, and died at Fontaine-Chaalis in 1954 at the age of ninety-two.

His authority has been qualified in two directions. Arthur Kingsley Porter challenged the national and regional priorities of his account of Romanesque sculpture — Mâle held for the primacy of Languedoc and treated Spanish work as downstream of French, a position sharpened by the nationalism of the period and weakened by the fact that he never travelled the pilgrimage roads himself. More recently, the textual model itself has been questioned: Linda Seidel, writing on Autun, argued against the Mâle tradition that a sculptural programme is not a fixed pictorial book to be read in sequence but a distributed field of associations activated by the movement of the viewer through the building. Both objections are a measure of how completely the field he founded was still his to be argued with.

Mango, Cyril

Istanbul, 14 April 1928 – 8 February 2021

Cyril Mango was born on 14 April 1928 in Istanbul, Turkey, the youngest of three sons of Alexander A. Mango, a descendant of a Genoese family who came to Istanbul via Chios, and Adelaide, known as Ada (née Damonov) Mango, a refugee from Baku. This cosmopolitan Levantine background — blending Italian, Greek, and Russian strands — proved formative for a scholar who would spend his life bridging cultures across centuries. His brother Anthony later became a multilingual interpreter at the UN, while brother Andrew became a prominent Turcologist and author of a seminal biography of Kemal Atatürk. Theirs was a very special, cosmopolitan universe, a remnant of the famous Pera, the bygone district of Constantinople.

After school, Mango began working for the British Council in Istanbul, where he crossed paths with Sir Steven Runciman, who was waiting out the war in the honorary position of Professor of Byzantine Art and History at Istanbul University. "His erudition, even when he was still in his teens, was extremely impressive," wrote Runciman of Mango in his memoirs many decades later.

Born in Constantinople in 1928, Mango was educated at the University of St Andrews, earning his MA in 1949, and then earned his doctorate in History from the University of Paris in 1953. His doctoral thesis, written under the supervision of Rodolphe Guilland, focused on the Imperial Palace of Constantinople — a subject that would anchor his scholarly interests for decades.

Mango's institutional career unfolded across the most prestigious centers of Byzantine studies in the world. At Dumbarton Oaks, he was a Junior Fellow (1951–1953), Fellow (1953–1954), and Research Associate (1954–1955) of Byzantine Studies, Instructor in Byzantine Archaeology (1955–1958), Lecturer in Byzantine Archaeology (1958–1962), Associate Professor of Byzantine Archaeology (1962–1963), and Executive Editor of Dumbarton Oaks Publications (1958–1963). His scholarly outlook was key for many research projects undertaken during this period.

He then held the Koraes Chair of Modern Greek and Byzantine History, Language, and Literature at King's College London (1963–1968), followed by the Bywater and Sotheby Professorship of Byzantine and Modern Greek at Oxford University (1973–1995). He was also a Visiting Associate Professor of Byzantine History at the University of California, Berkeley (1960–61). At Oxford he became an Emeritus Professorial Fellow of Exeter College, where, upon his death, the college flag was flown at half-mast in his honor.

Mango was also co-director of the Christian Monuments in Turkish Mesopotamia Project (1982–1990), and director of the Cathedral of Nisibis Project (1990–1991).

What distinguished Mango from most of his contemporaries was the extraordinary breadth of his scholarly command. A colleague at Oxford, Peter Frankopan, eulogised Mango as "prodigiously talented and astonishingly versatile, comfortable and adept not only in many languages, but also in disciplines ranging from art and architecture to archaeology, palaeography, epigraphy, numismatics and sigillography."

Mango's approach integrated archaeology and textual analysis, bridging gaps in Byzantine cultural history. He was particularly adept at using archival sources that others had overlooked. A celebrated example involved the 19th-century Swiss architect Gaspare Fossati, who had overseen restoration work on Hagia Sophia. In 1894, many mosaics and frescoes were destroyed by an earthquake. Mango had the genius to go to the cantonal archive of Ticino, the homeland of Fossati, and search for his drawings there — and he found them. Mango returned to humankind a lost piece of Hagia Sophia.

At Dumbarton Oaks, Mango directed significant restoration projects, like the mosaics of St. Sophia, enhancing scholarly understanding of Byzantine architecture. His collaboration with Ihor Ševčenko resulted in groundbreaking discoveries, including the lost church of St. Polyeuktos.

Mango's bibliography is both vast and foundational. His first major book, The Brazen House: A Study of the Vestibule of the Imperial Palace of Constantinople (1959), remains a classic of Byzantine topography. The Mosaics of St. Sophia at Istanbul (1962) details the history of the mosaics of the Hagia Sophia and is still considered an important work.

The Art of the Byzantine Empire 312–1453: Sources and Documents (1972) consists almost entirely of English translations of Byzantine primary sources about art, with commentary by Mango, organized from the age of Constantine through the Late Byzantine period — an indispensable anthology for any student of Byzantine visual culture. His Byzantine Architecture (1976) was a foundational textbook for more than one generation of Byzantinists.

His synthesis Byzantium: The Empire of New Rome remains one of his most celebrated works for broader audiences, and he also edited The Oxford History of Byzantium (2002), often recommended as the best introduction to the subject. As editor, Mango assembled many of the world's leading scholars of Byzantine studies to contribute essays for this ambitious volume — a narrative history covering over 1,100 years of civilization in under 400 pages.

Mango established Oxford as a premier center for Byzantine studies and mentorship. His legacy includes the Corpus of Dated Inscriptions project, enhancing the study of Byzantine inscriptions. By his death, into his tenth decade, Mango had become the sort of scholar for whom everyone seems to reserve the word "doyen." His younger colleagues relished his presence at Oxford's Byzantine seminars, and enthusiasts of Byzantine studies mourned Mango as a "titan" of their field.

At the time of his death, he was overseeing the final details of a major book on Constantinople ahead of its publication. He donated the rich holdings of his personal library to the Gennadius Library in Athens — a gift that will inspire students and scholars for decades to come.

He was a Fellow of the British Academy (FBA) and a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London (FSA). Cyril Mango died on 8 February 2021, at the age of 92.

Manuali, Giovanni

active late 20th-21st century

Giovanni Manuali is an Italian conservator-restorer and cultural-heritage curator, best known as conservatore dei Beni (keeper of the collections) of the Accademia di Belle Arti "Pietro Vannucci" in Perugia. His work centers on the custody, restoration, study, and exhibition of the academy's extensive historical patrimony.

In his role at the Accademia, Manuali is responsible for one of the richest academic collections in central Italy. By his own accounting, the holdings include roughly 12,000 drawings and 6,000 prints, along with original documents and autographs, including material connected to Canova, to the local eighteenth-century painter Carattoli, and to the Fondo Wicar (the drawings collection tied to Jean-Baptiste Wicar). The collection continues to grow through donations. He combines curatorial responsibility with active restoration practice, and local reporting identifies him specifically as conservatore dei beni e restauratore.

His name recurs in the Accademia's exhibition and conservation programs, often in coordinating or co-curating roles:

  • He coordinated the Accademia's section of Raffaello in Umbria e la sua eredita in Accademia (Palazzo Baldeschi, Perugia, 2020), the Raphael fifth-centenary exhibition. Its subsection L'Accademia di Perugia e Raffaello: da Minardi e Wicar al Novecento was curated by Alessandra Migliorati, Stefania Petrillo, and Saverio Ricci.
  • He co-curated, with critic Aldo Iori, a Giuliano Giuman exhibition at MUSA (the Accademia's museum) in 2021.
  • He promoted restoration and digitization of the Accademia's early drawings through a project supported by the Fondazione Cassa di Risparmio di Perugia and Art Bonus, carried out with the Soprintendenza archivistica e bibliografica dell'Umbria e delle Marche, to conserve and digitize a selected group of about fifty historic sheets.

Within the Accademia's institutional structure, Manuali serves among the governing bodies in the collections-keeper role, working in coordination with the academy's direction, including the years of Emidio De Albentiis as director and didactic coordinator.

Marabottini, Alessandro

Florence, 1926 - Florence, 12 June 2012

Alessandro Marabottini, known to friends and colleagues simply as "Sandro," was an Italian art historian, collector, and occasional novelist who held the chair of Storia dell'Arte Medioevale e Moderna at the universities of Messina and Perugia for over two decades. Although his scholarly output ranged across six centuries, from Trecento panel painting to the Macchiaioli, he is most closely associated today with his pioneering studies of Italian Baroque art and with the eclectic art collection he bequeathed to the city of Perugia.

Marabottini was born in Florence in 1926 into an old family of medieval Tuscan origin. He used his mother's surname, Marabottini, in preference to his father Piero's surname, Marabotti, a habit that distinguished him within the family. He grew up in a cultured, comfortable household in Florence, where he held particular affection for his great-grandfather Pitagora, who had served as Uruguay's consul in the city.

A formative episode is said to have occurred in his youth: travelling by train through Padua to join his parents on holiday in the Veneto mountains, he stopped to see Giotto's frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel, an encounter that left a lasting impression on him. He went on to take his degree in medieval art history under Mario Salmi, one of the most influential Italian medievalists of the twentieth century, whose other students included Enzo Carli and Umberto Baldini. Marabottini subsequently followed Salmi to Rome, working as his unpaid assistant in the early years of his career.

In Rome during the 1950s, Italian art history was largely divided between followers of Roberto Longhi and those aligned with Lionello Venturi. Marabottini deliberately avoided taking sides, preferring to remain on good terms with both camps. It was during this period, in 1951, that he met the British art historian Francis Haskell, who became a lifelong friend. Their exchanges are said to have shaped Marabottini's later book Mecenati e pittori. His Roman circle also included the art historians Giuliano Briganti and Luigi Salerno and the painter Arturo Cecchi, with whom he shared an early enthusiasm for artists such as Titian, Nicolas Poussin, and Pietro da Cortona, the latter studied at a time when Baroque art was still largely overlooked by Italian academia.

Marabottini won the chair of modern art history at the University of Messina in 1962, where he began his long engagement with Antonello da Messina, culminating in a major exhibition in 1979 marking the 500th anniversary of the painter's death, for which he also produced an illustrated booklet on the artist's life. From 1979 he taught at the University of Perugia, remaining there until his retirement in the mid-1980s.

Marabottini's bibliography spans the fourteenth through the twentieth centuries. His earliest major publication, the 1950 monograph on the Trecento painter Giovanni da Milano, remains his principal contribution to medieval art scholarship and was for some time a standard reference on the artist. His subsequent work moved chronologically forward and stylistically outward, including studies on Raphael's workshop and his early years, on Polidoro da Caravaggio, and full monographs on Pietro da Cortona, Jacopo da Empoli, and Pompeo Batoni. A 1981 monograph on Antonello da Messina consolidated his reputation as a leading authority on the painter. Later in his career he turned to nineteenth-century Italian painting, becoming one of the earliest scholars, beginning in the early 1980s, to take serious critical interest in Silvestro Lega and the Macchiaioli, to whom he dedicated a monograph and a 2000 exhibition at the Museo del Corso in Rome.

In 1981 he was elected a member of the Accademia Nazionale di San Luca in Rome.

An avid and discerning collector, Marabottini assembled an eclectic personal collection over decades, paintings, sculptures, drawings, prints, miniatures, glass, porcelain, and furniture, numbering well over 600 pieces and ranging from the sixteenth to the twentieth centuries, with objects also drawn from Central America, Africa, and Asia. He lived among the collection in his Florence apartment on Via Carducci from 1983. Having never married and leaving no direct heirs, he bequeathed the entire collection by will to the Fondazione Cassa di Risparmio di Perugia, with the stipulation that it serve as a hands-on teaching resource for art history students at the University of Perugia, where he had taught for twenty years. Since 2015 the collection has been on permanent public display across two floors of Palazzo Baldeschi in Perugia, with his former student Caterina Zappia overseeing its curation and reconstructing his study within the installation.

Beyond his academic output, Marabottini wrote fiction, publishing the mystery novel Le tentazioni di Sant'Antonio (2003) and leaving an unpublished campus mystery, Delitto accademico, set at the University of Perugia. A further novel, Collemammole, tracing his family's history from the mid-nineteenth century around the ancestral villa of the same name, was published posthumously by La nave di Teseo in 2022 to mark the tenth anniversary of his death.

Alessandro Marabottini died in Florence on 12 June 2012. A volume of essays in his honor, Scritti in onore di Alessandro Marabottini, had already been assembled by former students in Messina to mark his sixtieth birthday and final year of teaching. He is remembered as an unusually versatile and generous scholar whose interests moved fluidly between the medieval, the Baroque, and the modern, and whose collection continues to give Perugia's art history students direct, physical contact with works spanning four centuries.

Marcucci, Luisa

active mid-20th century

Luisa Marcucci was an Italian art historian and museum official who served within the Gallerie Nazionali di Firenze during the mid-twentieth century. Though biographical details about her personal life remain sparsely documented in available sources, her scholarly legacy is tangible and consequential: she produced two of the foundational systematic catalogues of the medieval Florentine collections, volumes that remain standard references in Trecento studies to this day.

Marcucci's work belongs to one of the most ambitious collective enterprises in twentieth-century Italian museum scholarship: the Cataloghi dei Musei e Gallerie d'Italia, published by the Istituto Poligrafico dello Stato under the auspices of the Ministero della Pubblica Istruzione — Direzione delle Antichità e Belle Arti. This series, launched in the postwar period, aimed to produce rigorous scientific catalogues of the state collections in a standardized format: each volume covering a defined school or period within a specific museum, with entries including physical description, provenance, critical history, bibliography, and photographic documentation. The series sat at the intersection of museum practice and academic scholarship, and its authors were typically the conservators and functionaries directly responsible for the works in question — custodians with daily, hands-on knowledge of the objects they catalogued.

Luisa Marcucci published Gallerie Nazionali di Firenze: I dipinti toscani del secolo XIII. Scuole bizantine e russe dal secolo XII al secolo XVIII with the Istituto Poligrafico dello Stato in 1958. This volume catalogued the thirteenth-century Tuscan panels in the Florentine national collections alongside Byzantine and Russian icons spanning the twelfth to eighteenth centuries — a pairing that reflects the collecting logic of the period, which grouped pre-Gothic and Byzantine material together as expressions of a shared pre-naturalistic tradition predating the Giottesque revolution.

The century covered — the Duecento — is among the most technically demanding in Italian art history: a period of transition from the Byzantine manner to the new pictorial language developing simultaneously in Florence, Siena, Lucca, and Pisa, when the distinction between individual artistic personalities and workshop traditions is often contested, and when documentary evidence is thin. Cataloguing this material with scientific rigour required both connoisseurial precision and a thorough command of the sparse archival record.

Her second volume, Gallerie Nazionali di Firenze: I dipinti toscani del secolo XIV, was published by the Istituto Poligrafico dello Stato in 1965, containing 210 pages and 170 black-and-white plates. This is the more widely cited of the two catalogues, covering the Trecento — the century of Giotto's legacy, the great Florentine workshops of the Gaddi family, Bernardo Daddi, Maso di Banco, Orcagna, and their circles, and the generation leading into the International Gothic. It is precisely the territory that Erling Skaug would later map through his punzoni research, and Bruce Cole addressed in his monograph on Giotto and Florentine painting.

The volume's entries are cited throughout the subsequent half-century of scholarship on Trecento Florence. A characteristic example of Marcucci's critical method appears in the museum database record for a Bernardo Daddi panel in the Galleria dell'Accademia: Marcucci considered this work particularly important because, being dated 1333, it confirmed that the stylistic change in the artist — due to his approach to Maso di Banco and Taddeo Gaddi — was occurring precisely at that date. This is a concise illustration of how she used individual dated works as chronological anchors for mapping the broader currents of stylistic evolution within the Florentine school.

Her engagement with the critical tradition was equally rigorous: where Richard Offner had assigned certain works to his anonymous grouping "Close Following of Daddi," Marcucci's attributions typically restored them to Daddi himself or to his documented workshop — a position subsequently confirmed by Angelo Tartuferi in later Accademia catalogues.

Marcucci's two catalogues occupy a specific and important position in the historiography of medieval Italian art. They were produced at a moment — the late 1950s and early 1960s — when the systematic, object-based approach to Trecento painting was gaining momentum, following the methodological groundwork laid by Richard Offner's Corpus of Florentine Painting (begun in 1930) and pursued in Italy by Roberto Longhi and his school. Her volumes provided the field with a reliable, systematic inventory of the Florentine state collections' medieval holdings at precisely the moment when scholars like Skaug, Cole, and Boskovits were building the modern critical literature on the period.

The consistent citation of her 1965 catalogue in subsequent scholarship — in attributional debates, in provenance research, in auction and exhibition literature, and in the MiBAC's national art database — confirms its enduring authority. Her name appears in the bibliographic apparatus of works on Giovanni del Biondo, Bernardo Daddi, and other major Trecento artists as a standard point of reference, functioning as the first systematic checkpoint between the older connoisseurial tradition and the more analytical scholarship that followed.

The relative biographical obscurity of Luisa Marcucci — a scholar whose contribution to the field is substantive and whose catalogues are cited by virtually every serious student of Trecento Florentine painting — reflects a broader pattern in twentieth-century Italian institutional art history, where the predominantly female workforce of the Soprintendenze and museum administrations produced scholarship of lasting value while remaining largely invisible in the biographical record that the discipline has maintained for its most prominent figures. Her case is analogous to that of several other women officials of the mid-century Florentine institutions whose cataloguing work underpins the field without their names having attracted the biographical attention they merit.

Mari, Fabio

Rome, 1993

Fabio Mari was born in Rome in 1993. He completed his undergraduate studies at the University of Rome Tor Vergata in the Faculty of Letters and Philosophy, earning a degree in Cultural Heritage. He is currently a Ph.D. candidate at the Department of Literary, Philosophical, and Art History Studies at the same university (36th cycle, Comparative Studies), where he is preparing a dissertation provisionally titled Caetani Patronage in Southern Lazio between the 13th and 14th Centuries under the supervision of Walter Angelelli and the co-supervision of Serena Romano.

The core of Mari's research concerns medieval painting in Lazio, with particular attention to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. His interests range from Gothic art to the history of collecting and patronage, from connoisseurship to medieval sculpture between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries. A recurring line in his work is the relationship between landscape, aristocratic power, and visual culture, examined through pictorial monuments in Benedictine areas and noble settlements in southern Lazio.

A significant part of his scholarship is devoted to Caetani patronage, the powerful medieval family that controlled broad territories in southern Lazio between the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Mari has studied the frescoes of the Caetani Palace in Fondi, especially the camera picta cycle dedicated to Virgil and commissioned by Roffredo III, presenting these results at the conference European and Mediterranean Middle Ages. Exchanges, Circulation, and Artistic Mobility. He has also explored the patronage context of the Lauri Chapel in the Cathedral of Anagni, publishing an essay in a 2021 anthology for the centennial of Giorgio Falco's I Comuni di Campagna e Marittima.

Among his most important contributions are two studies on Subiaco. The first, published in Convivium in 2022, analyzes the paintings in the lower church of the Sacro Speco through the theme of sacred landscape and visual culture. The second, published in 2023 in Horti Hesperidum under the title The Legitimizing Landscape: On the Paintings of the Cosmatesque Cloister of Santa Scolastica in Subiaco, interprets cloister paintings as a visual instrument for legitimizing abbatial power. Together, these studies argue that landscape in medieval monastic art is not merely decorative background but a politically and symbolically loaded visual language.

Mari has presented his research in many academic venues. In 2023 he participated in the international conference Aula micat medio clarificata suo. Rediscovering, Tracing, and Reconstructing Works and Monuments of Medieval Europe with a paper on reconstructing the Lauri Chapel in Anagni Cathedral. In 2025 he took part in the Giornate di storia del Lazio meridionale with a contribution on thirteenth-century painting in Priverno, and in a conference on noble chapels in the mendicant churches of Rome. He is also active in scholarly dissemination through work for ArtsLife and critical reviews for Horti Hesperidum, including pieces on Serena Romano's Apogeo e fine del Medioevo (Jaca Book, 2017) and Francesco Gandolfo's study of painting in Fondi between the eleventh and twelfth centuries.

Alongside traditional art-historical research, Mari contributes to the Tor Vergata initiative Digital Resources for the Study of Medieval Art and Art-Historical Sources, a Digital Humanities project aimed at improving access to medieval documentary heritage through digital tools. This methodological engagement reflects a new generation of scholars attentive both to archival sources and to digital research infrastructures.

Marković, Miodrag

Gacko, 1962

Miodrag Marković was born in Gacko in 1962. He is today one of the leading figures in the study of Byzantine and Serbian medieval art, and one of the most internationally connected Serbian scholars working in that field.

He pursued his academic career at the Faculty of Philosophy of the University of Belgrade, rising through the full sequence of academic ranks from Teaching Aide (1990–1999) to full Professor from 2015 onwards. He served as Director of the Institute of Art History of the Faculty of Philosophy, Belgrade from 2010 to 2018. He also held visiting positions as Guest Professor at Okayama University, Japan (May 2004) and at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (May 2009), and as Visiting Professor at the Faculty of Philosophy of the University of Eastern Sarajevo (2005–2011 and 2014–2016).

Marković became a Corresponding Member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts on 5 November 2015 and a Full Member on 4 November 2021; since 2023 he has served as SASA Vice-President. His accession speech to the Academy, delivered on 25 May 2016, was titled "Art in the Serbian Lands of the 11th Century" — a title that signals his particular interest in the formative, often understudied, early phase of Serbian medieval visual culture before the full consolidation of the Nemanjić dynasty.

Marković's scholarship centres on the art and architecture of medieval Serbia and its relationship with the broader Byzantine world, with special focus on monumental painting, iconography, and the cultural politics of patronage. Among his major monographs are The First Voyage of St. Sava to Palestine and Its Importance for Serbian Medieval Art (Belgrade, 2009) and Saint Niketas near Skopje: A Foundation of King Milutin (Belgrade, 2015), both published in Serbian with English summaries. The first reconstructs the formative pilgrimage of the Serbian archbishop St. Sava to the Holy Land and demonstrates how Palestinian iconographic models were absorbed into the nascent Serbian monumental tradition. The second offers a detailed monographic study of the monastery of St. Niketas near Skopje — one of the most important foundations of King Milutin (Stefan Uroš II, r. 1282–1321) and a key site for understanding the Palaiologan artistic renewal in the Serbian sphere. His research also extends to the social and institutional history of Byzantine art, as demonstrated by his study Painters in Byzantium and Beyond: Their Social Status and Reputation (Zbornik Radova Vizantološkog Instituta, 2023), which examines the position of painters within Byzantine society from the time of the Book of the Eparch in the tenth century.

Among Marković's most visible institutional achievements is his co-editorship, with Dragan Vojvodić, of a major publication dedicated to the artistic heritage of Kosovo and Metohija: the exhibition catalogue Artistic Heritage of the Serbian People in Kosovo and Metohija: Identity, Significance, Vulnerability (Belgrade, 2017) and the accompanying collection of scholarly papers Artistic Heritage of the Serbian People in Kosovo and Metohija: History, Identity, Vulnerability, Protection (Belgrade, 2017), which received the Special Award of the 63rd International Belgrade Fair. The contributions were written by renowned specialists including members of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, the Russian Academy of Arts, and the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters, alongside university professors and associates of scientific institutes, museums, and heritage protection institutions.

Marković served as Editor-in-Chief of Zograf — the principal Serbian journal of Byzantine and medieval art history — from 2008 to 2016. He has sat on the editorial boards of numerous journals and reference works, including the Serbian Encyclopaedia (Matica Srpska and SASA), the Dictionary of Visual Arts and Architecture (SASA), the Matica Srpska Journal of Fine Arts, the Collection of Papers of the Institute for Byzantine Studies, the proceedings of the Niš and Byzantium conference series, and the Italian journal Byzantina Lupiensia, founded by CISAM (Spoleto) and the University of Lecce. He served as Associate of the Board of Directors of the International Center of Medieval Art of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (2014–2018), was a member of the International Committee of the History of Byzantine Art under the auspices of the International Association of Byzantine Studies, and sat on the Organising Committee of the 23rd International Congress of Byzantine Studies, held in Belgrade in 2016.

Marković's career represents a sustained effort to situate Serbian medieval art within its proper Byzantine and trans-regional context, resisting any purely nationalistic framing while simultaneously insisting on the specificity and richness of the Serbian contribution to medieval visual culture. His work on iconographic programmes, on the social history of Byzantine painters, and on the monumental heritage of Kosovo and Metohija has secured his position as a central figure in twenty-first-century Byzantine studies, with a research profile that bridges Serbian, Greek, Italian, and broader international scholarly communities.

Markus, Robert Austin

Budapest, 8 October 1924 - 2010

Robert Austin Markus (1924–2010) was a Hungarian-born British historian widely credited, alongside Peter Brown, with helping to establish "Late Antiquity" as a distinct field of study. He was Professor of Medieval History at Nottingham between 1974 and 1982, and subsequently professor emeritus, and is best remembered for his work on Augustine of Hippo and Gregory the Great.

He was born Róbert Imre Márkus in Budapest, Hungary on 8 October 1924, into an assimilated Jewish family with, as the biographical record puts it, strong ties to Christianity. His father, Gyözö (Victor) Márkus, was the director of a heavy engineering firm founded by Robert's grandfather, and his mother, Lili Elek, was an internationally recognised ceramicist. Markus fled Hungary with his parents in 1939 amid rising antisemitism, settling in England, where he anglicised his name and pursued education at the University of Manchester, initially in chemistry before shifting to philosophy, earning an MA and PhD under Dorothy Emmet. At Manchester he studied medieval philosophy alongside figures such as Alasdair MacIntyre.

The intellectual trajectory that defined his life began with religious conversion. His philosophical turn was intimately connected with his conversion to Roman Catholicism in 1946, and after completing his doctorate he spent four years as a Dominican, reading deeply in the Church Fathers, especially Augustine. In 1954 he made the decision to leave the Dominicans. A year later he married a longstanding Catholic friend, Margaret Bullen, to whom he would later dedicate his first major book. He also became, and remained, an active supporter of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament — a detail worth noting, since his politics and his theology were not kept in separate compartments.

His teaching career ran first through Liverpool, where he taught medieval history from 1955 to 1974, and then Nottingham, where he held the chair in medieval history until his relatively early retirement in 1982. Retirement did not slow his output; his two most influential books both appeared afterward.

Markus's scholarly reputation rests on three works in particular. Saeculum: History and Society in the Theology of St Augustine (1970) advanced a then-radical reading of Augustine's concept of the "secular" — the saeculum as the shared temporal space of political communities, which Augustine, on Markus's account, effectively "liberated" from direct sacral control. It is worth flagging that this reading has been contested: critics have debated whether its true centre lies in Augustine's relation between sacred and secular history or in a broader "secularisation" of political institutions, and some have argued Markus read his own post-Vatican II sensibilities back into the fourth century. His The End of Ancient Christianity (1990) examined how Roman culture eroded from the time of Augustine to that of Pope Gregory the Great; Wolf Liebeschuetz regarded it as Markus's masterpiece, though it too generated debate about how sharply "ancient" Christianity can be said to have "ended." It was followed by Gregory the Great and His World (1997).

He was elected a Fellow of the British Academy and appointed OBE. He died of cancer in 2010, at the age of 86. His long intellectual friendship and productive disagreement with Peter Brown — who contributed the epilogue to Markus's Festschrift — is itself part of the story of how the study of Late Antiquity took shape in the anglophone academy. Obituaries appeared in The Guardian (by Dame Janet Nelson) and The Independent (by Wolf Liebeschuetz), and the ODNB carries a full entry.

Marrone, Raffaele

active 21st century

Raffaele Marrone is an Italian scholar specializing in medieval art history, with particular focus on late medieval visual culture, devotional practices, and the relationship between images and urban religious space in central Italy. His profile is especially relevant for research on Trecento Siena and the social uses of art in confraternal contexts.

Marrone is affiliated with the Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa, one of Italy's leading research institutions, and completed his doctoral work there under the supervision of Francesco Caglioti. In July 2025 he earned his PhD with a dissertation titled Images, Spaces, and Practices of Devotional Confraternities in Siena in the Late Middle Ages, a study that integrates visual analysis, documentary evidence, and urban topography.

His declared research interests include late medieval art and medieval iconography, with a concentration on fourteenth-century Sienese painting. Among his contributions is a study of the chapel in the cemetery of Santa Maria della Scala in Siena, decorated in 1341 by Ambrogio Lorenzetti, examined through archival sources and architectural evidence connected to the cult of Saint Cristina and to relics that arrived from Constantinople in 1359.

Marrone has also published on early fourteenth-century painting in Pistoia, including work on the pictorial cycle of the Stories of the Passion, expanding his research beyond Siena while maintaining a consistent focus on the interaction between narrative imagery, devotional practice, and local institutional history.

In November 2025 he presented the paper Images, Spaces, and Practices of Devotional Brotherhoods in the Late Middle Ages: The Case of Siena within the Medieval Networks series, further consolidating his position among emerging scholars working on confraternal visual culture and late medieval Italian art.

Marsden, Richard

active late 20th-21st century

Richard Marsden is a British scholar of Old English and Anglo-Saxon manuscript culture, Professor Emeritus at the University of Nottingham and general editor of The Cambridge Old English Reader. His scholarship on the transmission of the Bible in Anglo-Saxon England is foundational to the modern textual study of the Codex Amiatinus and its companion pandects.

His monograph The Text of the Old Testament in Anglo-Saxon England (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1995), and especially its long treatment of what are conventionally called the "Ceolfrith Bibles," remains the fundamental study of the editorial work behind the Northumbrian text and of its relationship to the Italian exemplars that reached Wearmouth-Jarrow through Benedict Biscop and possibly Hadrian of Canterbury. His article "Manus Bedae: Bede's Contribution to Ceolfrith's Bibles," published in Anglo-Saxon England in 1998, argued for Bede's active editorial participation in the pandect project — a hypothesis now widely, though not universally, accepted, since no primary source names Bede directly in connection with the Bibles.

Marsden's work is also frequently cited on the vexed question of the manuscript's scribal count, where the figure of seven hands associated with his research, and repeated by subsequent scholars including Peter Darby, remains the most frequently cited modern count, against earlier proposals of nine. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of both questions.

Masetti, Anna Rosa Calderoni

Italian art historian best known as a leading scholar of medieval art and of the artistic culture of Pisa and Liguria. Born in Pisa, she pursued a distinguished academic career and eventually became full professor of History of Medieval Art at the University of Genoa, where she taught for many years before retirement.

Her research has focused on the visual culture of the medieval Mediterranean, with particular attention to Pisa's civic and religious monuments, its role as a maritime republic, and its connections with the eastern Mediterranean, the Iberian world, and Byzantine artistic traditions. She has written extensively on Pisan Romanesque art, mosaics, sculpture, and the city's urban development, often bringing together art-historical analysis, urban history, and the study of maps and historical views of Pisa.

Calderoni Masetti has also studied smaller objects and systems of ornament, including enamelled belts and jewelry, addressing questions of technique, iconography, and courtly culture in the high and late Middle Ages. Her publications range from specialist scholarship to more accessible books, making her work a key reference for scholars and students interested in Pisan and Ligurian art as well as broader Mediterranean artistic exchanges. She continues to work as an independent researcher, publishing essays and participating in scholarly projects that deepen understanding of medieval visual culture in southern Europe.

Mather Jr., Frank Jewett

Deep River, Connecticut, 6 July 1868 - 11 November 1953

Frank Jewett Mather Jr. was one of the most influential American art critics, historians, and professors of the first half of the twentieth century. His career spanned militant journalistic criticism, innovative university teaching, and museum administration, making him a central figure in the dissemination of artistic culture in the United States.

Mather was born in Deep River, Connecticut, to Caroline Arms Graves and attorney Frank Jewett Mather Sr. (1835-1929). He was a direct descendant of Richard Mather, the seventeenth-century Puritan minister active in Boston, and thus deeply rooted in the intellectual traditions of New England. He graduated from Williams College in 1889 and earned his Ph.D. in 1892 at Johns Hopkins University in English philology and literature. He completed his formation through further study at the University of Berlin and at the École des Hautes Études in Paris.

Between 1893 and 1900, Mather returned to Williams College as an instructor and then assistant professor of English and Romance languages. During these years he established himself as an art critic: he wrote for the New York Evening Post, served as assistant editor of The Nation (1901-1906), and worked as art critic for the Post (1905-1906 and 1910-1911). From 1904 to 1906 he was American editor of the newly founded Burlington Magazine, later contributing regularly to journals such as Art and Progress and The Atlantic. In 1923 he became editor of the academic journal Art Studies.

In 1910, Mather was appointed professor of art history and archaeology at Princeton University, where he was the department's first scholar with a strong modern and post-classical orientation. His arrival marked a turning point by expanding Princeton's program beyond strictly classical studies to include systematic work on Italian medieval and Renaissance painting and on modern European and American art.

In 1922, he became director of Princeton's Museum of Historic Art (now the Princeton University Art Museum), a role he held until 1946. As director, he proved both intellectually ambitious and personally generous, donating numerous works from his own collection, including important Italian drawings. With colleague Charles A. Platt, he became a key figure in the growth of the museum's Italian drawings holdings, including works by Parmigianino and other Mannerist masters. Although he retired from teaching in 1933, he remained closely associated with Princeton until his death.

Mather was also a sharp and often polemical observer of the modern art world. During the 1913 Armory Show, the landmark exhibition that introduced European avant-garde currents to the United States, he took a critical stance toward the most radical Cubist and Futurist tendencies. His position, shared in part with figures such as Kenyon Cox and Royal Cortissoz, defended the values of formal quality and historical continuity without collapsing into simplistic conservatism.

His bibliography is remarkably broad, ranging from fiction to art history and from aesthetics to medieval studies. Among his major works are Estimates in Art (1916; Series II, 1923), The Portraits of Dante (1921), A History of Italian Painting (1923), Modern Painting: 1664-1914 (1927), The Isaac Master: A Reconstruction of the Work of Gaddo Gaddi (1932), Concerning Beauty (1935), and Western European Painting of the Renaissance (1939).

Mather was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1931 and to the American Philosophical Society in 1940. Throughout his life he donated works of art and acquisition funds to Princeton's museum. Since 1963, the College Art Association has awarded the annual Frank Jewett Mather Award for the best published contribution to art criticism in the previous year.

Over subsequent decades, the award has recognized critics including Clement Greenberg, Rosalind Krauss, Robert Hughes, Leo Steinberg, and Arthur C. Danto. It remains one of the highest institutional honors for published art criticism in the United States and confirms Mather's lasting centrality in American artistic culture.

Matthiae, Guglielmo

20th century

Guglielmo Matthiae was one of the most important Italian medievalists of the 20th century, trained in the school of Pietro Toesca and destined to become the leading scholar of medieval Roman mural painting, from late antiquity to the High Middle Ages.

Matthiae earned his degree in Medieval and Modern Art History at the University of Rome under the guidance of Pietro Toesca, whose assistant he later became. The influence of Toesca—the great systematizer of medieval Italian painting—was decisive: Matthiae absorbed his philological rigor and interest in the early Christian and early medieval traditions, directing his research from the outset toward the churches and pictorial decorations of Rome and Lazio.

Matthiae began his career in the Administration of Fine Arts, rising to the rank of Superintendent. He worked first in Abruzzo—where he acquired a deep knowledge of Romanesque painting in central Italy, studying in particular the frescoes of Bominaco and other monastic complexes—and then in Rome and Lazio, where his institutional role became inextricably intertwined with art-historical research and restoration work. He was appointed to teach Medieval Art History at the University of L'Aquila, where he passed on his methodology to subsequent generations.

The pinnacle of his scholarly output is represented by the two-volume work Pittura romana del Medioevo (Rome, Fratelli Palombi, 1965–1966): the first volume dedicated to the 4th–10th centuries, the second to the 11th–14th centuries. This work remains an indispensable reference today for anyone studying medieval pictorial decoration in Rome, from the catacombs and early Christian mosaic cycles to the great Romanesque and Proto-Gothic painting projects. The text was scientifically updated in a second edition (1987–1988) edited by Maria Andaloro and Francesco Gandolfo, attesting to its enduring historiographical relevance.

A parallel and equally important strand of his work concerns the early Roman churches: Matthiae edited the entry Churches of Rome from the 4th to the 10th Century in the series dedicated to Christian Rome, and published monographs on numerous Roman sacred buildings within the series Illustrated Churches of Rome. In 1961, he published in the Memorie della Pontificia Accademia Romana di Archeologia his research on the origins of the Basilica of San Pietro in Vincoli, conducted in parallel with the restoration of the building, which he himself had directed. In the final years of his life, he devoted himself with increasing intensity to the Abbey of Grottaferrata, studying its mosaics of the Greek-Byzantine tradition and overseeing their delicate removal.

A lesser-known but highly significant aspect of his work is his pioneering interest in the photographic documentation of works of art as a tool for research and conservation. His photographic collection, which was incorporated into the Photographic Library of the Federico Zeri Foundation in Bologna in the 1990s, constitutes a visual archive of extraordinary value for the study of the Middle Ages between East and West, documenting works and monuments that are today sometimes compromised or lost. Matthiae was a member of the Gruppo dei Romanisti, the association of the most distinguished scholars of Roman culture and history, further confirming his deep roots in the scholarly tradition of the city that was the center of his entire intellectual life.

Mazzalupi, Matteo

b. 1977

Matteo Mazzalupi was born in Rome in 1977. He graduated from the University of L'Aquila in 2004 with a dissertation on the fifteenth-century Camerino painter Girolamo di Giovanni, and took his PhD at the University of Udine in 2008; that thesis grew into the book-length study Pittori ad Ancona nel Quattrocento, co- edited with Andrea De Marchi (2008).

He subsequently held fellowships from the Fondazione Roberto Longhi in Florence (2008–09), the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York (2010–11), and the University of Florence (2011–14). He is currently a funzionario storico dell'arte in the Italian Ministero della Cultura.

His principal field is late medieval and Renaissance painting and sculpture in the Marches, though he has worked on artists of other regions and periods as well, always with a marked preference for archival research. That documentary orientation is the defining feature of his scholarship: much of his output consists of newly discovered notarial and testamentary material used to reset the biographies and chronologies of individual masters.

Representative finds include an archival document placing Piero della Francesca in Ancona in 1450, published for the first time in Nuovi studi, and the will and related Roman documents of the Umbrian painter Piermatteo d'Amelia, recovered from the Archivio di Stato di Roma.

He has contributed to a long series of exhibitions, among them Il Quattrocento a Camerino (2002), Fra Carnevale (2004–05), Gentile da Fabriano e l'altro Rinascimento, Officina pratese (2013), Luca di Paolo e il Rinascimento nelle Marche (2015) and Lorenzo de Carris e i pittori eccentrici nelle Marche del primo Cinquecento (2016); he also worked on the first two volumes of the corpus of the iconography of St Nicholas of Tolentino (2005, 2006) and on a catalogue of painted crosses in the Marches (2014).

With Andrea De Marchi he curated L'Autunno del Medioevo in Umbria. Cofani nuziali in gesso dorato e una bottega perugina dimenticata at the Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria (2019–20), and was involved in the Fabriano exhibition devoted to Allegretto Nuzi (c. 1315–1373).

He has written entries on Giovanni Angelo d'Antonio, Girolamo di Giovanni, Paolo da Visso, Piergentile da Matelica, Piermatteo d'Amelia and Pietro di Galeotto for the Allgemeines Künstler-Lexikon and the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani.

Two points relevant to the Trecento material in this site: his study on the Fabriano painters in Oro e colore nel cuore dell'Appennino. Allegretto Nuzi e il '300 a Fabriano (2021) and his attribution of the wooden St Anthony Abbot from Sant'Agostino at Civitanova Alta to the Master of the Fabriano Magi fall directly within the site's Trecento range — and his work on Paolo da Visso intersects with the Valnerina material.

Mazzoni, Cristina

active late 20th–21st century

Cristina Mazzoni is an Italian-American scholar of Italian studies and comparative literature whose work moves fluidly between medieval women's religious writing, modern literature and psychoanalysis, and the cultural history of food, ranging from a thirteenth-century Umbrian mystic to the oranges of Sicily. She holds a Ph.D. in Comparative Literature from Yale University and joined the faculty of the University of Vermont in 1993, where she was promoted to full professor in 2005. In November 2020 she was invested as the inaugural Wolfgang and Barbara Mieder Green and Gold Professorship in the Department of Romance Languages and Cultures, a chair recognizing her record of eight books and more than forty-five scholarly articles and book chapters; following the department's later reorganization, she now holds it as Professor of Italian in UVM's School of World Languages and Cultures.

Mazzoni's earliest book, Saint Hysteria: Neurosis, Mysticism, and Gender in European Culture (Cornell University Press, 1996), examined the overlapping discourses of clinical hysteria and female mystical experience in turn-of-the-century European culture, tracing how physicians and hagiographers alike struggled to interpret women's bodily and visionary excess. The theme of embodied female experience carried into Maternal Impressions: Pregnancy and Childbirth in Literature and Theory (Cornell University Press, 2002), a study of how pregnancy has been figured in literary and psychoanalytic writing.

For students of medieval sainthood, Mazzoni's most directly relevant contribution is her edition of Angela of Foligno's Memorial (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1999), translated into English by John Cirignano with an introduction by Mazzoni herself. Appearing in the same decade as Giovanni Pozzi's Italian critical edition of the text as Il libro dell'esperienza and Paul Lachance's earlier English translation of Angela's Complete Works, Mazzoni's volume helped consolidate the Memorial's place in Anglophone teaching and research on medieval women's visionary writing. She returned to the terrain of Italian sanctity with The Voices of Gemma Galgani: The Life and Afterlife of a Modern Saint (University of Chicago Press, 2003), co-authored with the historian Rudolph Bell, a study of the short and intensely documented life of the late nineteenth-century Lucchese stigmatic Gemma Galgani (1878-1903) and of the devotional cult that formed around her after death.

Mazzoni has also written extensively on the intersection of women's spirituality and domestic culture, most notably in The Women in God's Kitchen: Cooking, Eating, and Spiritual Writing (Continuum, 2005), which examines the recurring figure of food, fasting, and culinary metaphor in the writings of Italian women mystics. She edited the volume Capital City: Rome, 1870-2010 (Annali d'Italianistica, 2010) and published a cultural history of one of Rome's foundational symbols, She-Wolf: The Story of a Roman Icon (Cambridge University Press, 2010), tracing the Capitoline Wolf from antiquity to modern fascist and republican iconography.

Her more recent research has turned to material and popular culture: Golden Fruit: A Cultural History of Oranges in Italy (University of Toronto Press), which won the American Association for Italian Studies Book Prize in 2018, and an ongoing project on European fairy tales, reflected in her teaching on Italian food culture, travel writing, and children's literature at the University of Vermont. Across this varied output, Mazzoni's consistent method is to read canonical and marginal texts alike — mystical autobiography, medical case history, cookbook, and folk tale — as evidence of how culture inscribes itself on the female body and its appetites, a perspective that has made her editions and studies a recurring point of reference for scholars working on Angela of Foligno and on the broader tradition of Italian women's religious writing.

McGinn, Bernard

b. 19 August 1937

Bernard McGinn is an American Catholic theologian and historian of religion, and is widely regarded as the preeminent scholar of mysticism in the Western Christian tradition. He is the Naomi Shenstone Donnelley Professor Emeritus of Historical Theology and of the History of Christianity at the University of Chicago Divinity School, where he taught from 1969 until his retirement in 2003 and continues to publish prolifically.

He graduated cum laude from Saint Joseph's Seminary (Dunwoodie) in Yonkers, New York, earned a Licentiate of Sacred Theology from the Pontifical Gregorian University in Rome in 1963, and completed a Ph.D. in history at Brandeis University in 1970 with a dissertation on the twelfth-century Cistercian mystical author Isaac of Stella. After a year teaching at the Catholic University of America, he joined the University of Chicago Divinity School faculty in 1969, specializing in medieval intellectual history and the history of Christian spirituality.

McGinn's central achievement is the multivolume series The Presence of God: A History of Western Christian Mysticism, published by Crossroad beginning with The Foundations of Mysticism (1991) and continuing through The Growth of Mysticism (1994), The Flowering of Mysticism: Men and Women in the New Mysticism (1200-1350) (1998), The Harvest of Mysticism in Medieval Germany (1300-1500) (2005), The Varieties of Vernacular Mysticism (1350-1550) (2012), a three-part sixth volume on mysticism in the Reformation and Counter-Reformation (2016-2020), and The Crisis of Mysticism: Quietism in Seventeenth-Century Spain, Italy, and France (2021). Reviewers have consistently described the series as the most important contribution to the historical study of Christian spirituality in decades, prized for its exhaustive command of primary sources and its lucid synthetic analysis.

Alongside this project, McGinn is a leading authority on the fourteenth-century Dominican mystic and theologian Meister Eckhart, producing translations (with Edmund Colledge, for the Classics of Western Spirituality series) and interpretive studies including The Mystical Thought of Meister Eckhart (2001). He served as editor-in-chief of Paulist Press's Classics of Western Spirituality series from 1988 to 2015, co-edited the multivolume Encyclopedia of Apocalypticism, and has written extensively on apocalyptic thought in the Middle Ages, including Visions of the End: Apocalyptic Traditions in the Middle Ages (1979). He is a past president of the American Society of Church History and of the American Catholic Historical Association, and a Fellow of the Medieval Academy of America and of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

For the study of Angela of Foligno, McGinn's work is a central point of reference: he places her Liber at the summit of thirteenth-century Franciscan mysticism, treats her apophatic language of the abyss and annihilation alongside that of Mechthild of Hackeborn and Marguerite Porete in his study "Annihilation and Authorship: Three Women Mystics of the 1290s" (2016), and has judged her book to be "the premier text of all Franciscan women mystics."

McGurk, Patrick

dates of birth and death not established in the accessible record; formerly Reader in Medieval History, Birkbeck College, University of London; d. before 2024

Patrick McGurk was a British palaeographer and historian of the early medieval book whose long career centred on a single, enduring contribution: a systematic catalogue and analysis of the Latin Gospel book as a physical and textual object from Late Antiquity into the Anglo-Saxon period. For much of that career he was Reader in Medieval History at Birkbeck College, University of London.

McGurk's doctoral thesis, "The Architecture of Latin Gospel Books before A.D. 800" (1954), set out the method that would define his scholarship: rather than classifying Gospel manuscripts primarily by script or by decoration, McGurk analysed their "architecture" — the presence and arrangement of the prefatory apparatus that normally accompanies a Gospel text, including the Letter of Jerome to Damasus, the Eusebian canon tables, prologues, capitula and the interpretation of Hebrew names. This structural approach yielded a descriptive vocabulary that could be applied consistently across manuscripts of very different date, script and origin.

The thesis matured into Latin Gospel Books from A.D. 400 to A.D. 800 (Publications de Scriptorium V; Paris–Brussels, 1961), in which McGurk identified and catalogued 138 Gospel books surviving in European libraries, plus one in St Petersburg, assigning each a running catalogue number that remains in use as shorthand throughout the field. It is under this system, as no. 84, that the fragmentary Codex Usserianus Primus is entered — one of the three standard numbering systems, alongside those of J. J. G. Alexander and James F. Kenney, by which the manuscript is cited in the literature.

McGurk continued to work on the corpus of early Gospel books for the rest of his career. In 1986 he joined Jonathan Alexander, Simon Keynes, Bernard Barr and Nicolas Barker in producing the Roxburghe Club's commentary volume for the facsimile of the York Gospels. His article "The Anglo-Saxon Gospelbooks of Judith, Countess of Flanders: Their Text, Make-up and Function" (Anglo-Saxon England 24, 1995) and his chapter "Anglo-Saxon Gospel-Books, c. 900–1066" in The Cambridge History of the Book in Britain, volume I (1999), extended the architectural method he had developed for the earlier period into the study of the later Anglo-Saxon Gospel-book tradition. In 1998 his scattered articles on the subject were gathered as Gospel Books and Early Latin Manuscripts (Variorum Collected Studies), consolidating four decades of work into a single accessible volume.

Alongside the Gospel-book studies, McGurk devoted much of his later career to editing the twelfth-century Chronicle of John of Worcester for the Oxford Medieval Texts series: he co-edited volume II with R. R. Darlington and edited volume III alone. He was still at work on volume IV, the Chronicula, at the time of his death; it was completed by David A. Woodman and published by Oxford University Press in 2024, McGurk's name on the title page marked with the editorial dagger that records a contributor who did not live to see the volume in print.

McKitterick, Rosamond

Chesterfield, 31 May 1949

Rosamond Deborah McKitterick was born Rosamond Pierce on 31 May 1949 in Chesterfield, Derbyshire, England. From 1951 to 1956 she lived in Cambridge, where her father had a position at Magdalene College, before moving with her family to Western Australia, where she completed primary and secondary school and an honours degree at the University of Western Australia. In 1971 she returned to Cambridge to pursue her career, a return that proved permanent. She received the degrees of MA, PhD, and LittD from the University of Cambridge, and also studied for a year — 1974–75 — at the University of Munich under Bernhard Bischoff, the greatest Latin palaeographer of the twentieth century and the natural successor to the tradition of Traube and Lowe. This year of technical formation — absorbing the methods and rigour of the Munich school at their source — proved as decisive for McKitterick's intellectual identity as any element of her formal doctoral training.
