McKitterick's doctoral thesis, The Carolingian Renaissance: A Study in the Education of a Society, was submitted under her maiden name of Pierce and approved on 24 February 1976. Her supervisor was Walter Ullmann — an Austrian-Jewish scholar who had fled the Third Reich, settled in Britain, and become one of the foremost authorities on medieval political and ecclesiastical thought, whose doctoral students include Brian Tierney, Quentin Skinner, Janet Nelson, and McKitterick herself, a genealogy that stands among the most distinguished in twentieth-century medieval studies. The combination of Ullmann's jurisprudential and ecclesiastical focus with the palaeographic and codicological training absorbed at Munich under Bischoff created the methodological compound that is distinctively McKitterick's: the use of manuscript evidence not merely as the vehicle for text but as historical evidence in its own right, revealing the physical realities of literary production, circulation, and reception. She married David McKitterick, Librarian of Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1976.

She was a Fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge, and then became a professorial fellow of Sidney Sussex College. She was promoted to a Personal Chair in 1997 and from 1999 held the Chair in Medieval History in the University of Cambridge's Faculty of History, succeeding Barrie Dobson and holding it until her retirement in September 2016, when she was succeeded by John H. Arnold. Thomas F. X. Noble has described her as "one of the most original and productive historians of Europe's early Middle Ages," and she has been called a "doyenne in her field." She supervised 42 PhD theses to completion as of October 2015, with five more in progress at that date. Among her doctoral students are Sarah Foot — whose biography of the Anglo-Saxon king Æthelstan is a landmark of the field — and Matthew Innes, author of influential work on Carolingian local society and state formation.

McKitterick's first monograph, The Frankish Church and the Carolingian Reforms, 789–895 (Royal Historical Society, 1977), examined the ecclesiastical reform programme that the Carolingian rulers and their episcopal advisers pursued across the late eighth and ninth centuries — the capitularies, the attempts to regularise liturgy and canon law, the standardisation of the Rule of St Benedict, and the broader effort to create a uniformly Christian Frankish society through the written word. The Frankish Kingdoms under the Carolingians, 751–987 (1983) was a comprehensive political and institutional history of the Carolingian dynasty from Pippin's usurpation of the Merovingian throne to the Carolingians' effective extinction in the West, and served for a generation as the standard anglophone treatment of the subject.

The Carolingians and the Written Word (Cambridge University Press, 1989) is the book that definitively established McKitterick's scholarly identity and changed the terms of debate about early medieval culture. It studies the function and status of the written word in Carolingian society in France and Germany in the eighth and ninth centuries, demonstrating that literacy was by no means confined to a clerical élite but was dispersed in lay society and used for government, administration, and ordinary legal transactions. The book is structured to cover law and documentary practice, the evidence of charters, the production and economic organisation of books, the organisation of written knowledge in library catalogues, and the literacy of the laity — each chapter deploying a different category of manuscript evidence to build a cumulative argument that the Carolingian world was one in which the written word functioned as an active medium of social and political life across a considerably broader population than earlier scholarship had assumed. The research challenges the notion of separation between lay and clerical spheres and finds that Latin functioned more as a formal high register than a foreign language in the Carolingian realm, differing significantly from British and Irish contexts. Reviewers found it an essential reference book for questions of medieval European literacy and a contribution to current historical debate far in excess of its intended compass. It remains in print and in active use.

History and Memory in the Carolingian World (Cambridge University Press, 2004) developed the implications of her earlier work on literacy by examining how the Carolingians understood, constructed, and deployed their own historical past. Treating Carolingian historiography — the royal annals, the Liber historiae Francorum, the compilation and circulation of texts by Gregory of Tours, Paul the Deacon, and the Liber Pontificalis — as evidence not merely for events but for the construction of historical consciousness, McKitterick argued that the Carolingians were profoundly self-aware managers of historical memory, disseminating particular narratives of Frankish identity through the deliberate production and distribution of manuscripts. The book received a French translation (Histoire et mémoire dans le monde carolingien, Brepols, 2009). Perceptions of the Past in the Early Middle Ages (University of Notre Dame Press, 2006) extended these arguments in a series of interconnected lectures from a broader theoretical perspective.

Charlemagne: The Formation of a European Identity (Cambridge University Press, 2008) analyses the narrative representations of Charlemagne produced after his death before focusing on the evidence from his lifetime concerning the creation of the Carolingian dynasty, the growth of the kingdom, the court and royal household, communications and identities in the context of government, and Charlemagne's religious and cultural strategies. McKitterick identifies his reforms, particularly in administration and culture, as foundational to a unified European identity, synthesising Roman, Christian, and Frankish traditions during the Carolingian Renaissance. She challenges the notion of a primitive administration, revealing it as sophisticated, and demonstrates — contrary to earlier beliefs — that Charlemagne travelled minimally outside the Rhine-Moselle region.

McKitterick's most recent monograph, Rome and the Invention of the Papacy: The Liber Pontificalis (Cambridge University Press, 2020), is in many respects the culmination of a research trajectory that began with the Carolingian reform agenda and moved progressively towards Rome and the Franks' construction of Roman authority. The book offers a new analysis of this extraordinary combination of historical reconstruction, deliberate selection, and political use of fiction to illuminate the history of the early popes and their relationship with Rome, examining the content, context, and transmission of the text and the complex relationships between the reality, representation, and reception of authority that it reflects. Its sixth chapter, on the transmission, reception, and audiences of the early medieval manuscripts of the Liber Pontificalis, demonstrates most clearly the continuity with her lifelong method: the manuscript tradition is not incidental but constitutive evidence, revealing where the text was known, by whom, and how it was used to shape perceptions of papal authority across early medieval Europe.

Among McKitterick's most consequential editorial contributions is her editorship of The New Cambridge Medieval History, volume II: c.700–c.900 (Cambridge University Press, 1995), the standard collaborative reference work for the Carolingian period in the English-speaking world. She also edited The Uses of Literacy in Early Medieval Europe (1990), a collection that extended the arguments of The Carolingians and the Written Word to other regions and contexts; Carolingian Culture: Emulation and Innovation (1994); and the Times Atlas of the Medieval World (2003–2004), bringing her synthesis of early medieval history to a broad public audience.

In 2010 McKitterick was awarded the Dr A. H. Heineken International Prize in History by the Royal Dutch Academy, a biannual prize for outstanding scholarly achievement established in 1990, whose other awardees include Judith Herrin and Aleida Assmann. In 2015 she was elected to the Lectio Chair at the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven's Centre for the Transmission of Texts and Ideas in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance. In 2017 she was elected a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London. She is also a Fellow of the Royal Historical Society, the Royal Society of Arts, the Medieval Academy of America, the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, and the Austrian Academy of Sciences. She is Chair of the Faculty of Archaeology, History and Letters of the British School at Rome — a position reflecting her sustained engagement with Rome as a subject of research, especially following her Balsdon Fellowship there in 2002 — and was President of the Ecclesiastical History Society for 2018–19. In 2018 her former doctoral students published a Festschrift in her honour, Writing the Early Medieval West: Studies in Honour of Rosamond McKitterick, edited by Elina Screen and Charles West, with contributions from fifteen of her students.

McKitterick occupies a singular position in the historiography of the early medieval West because she works simultaneously at two registers that scholars more commonly keep apart: the technical analysis of manuscripts, scripts, and codicological features — the methods she absorbed from Bischoff in Munich — and the broad historical synthesis of political, cultural, and religious change across the Carolingian world and its Roman inheritance. The manuscript is not for her the passive vehicle of a text but an active historical object, carrying evidence of where it was made, who possessed it, how it was used, and how through its circulation it shaped the intellectual and political world of those who read it. For the historian of illuminated manuscripts and medieval book culture, her work is essential because she has established, across four decades of research, the social, economic, and institutional conditions under which early medieval manuscripts were produced, owned, catalogued, and read. Without understanding those conditions — the scriptoria, the library catalogues, the patterns of lay ownership, the Carolingian reform legislation that drove manuscript production to new intensity — the illuminated manuscripts themselves remain aesthetically admirable but historically opaque objects. McKitterick's scholarship provides precisely the contextual framework within which the physical evidence of the surviving books can be made fully intelligible.

McLynn, Neil B.

active late 20th-21st century

Neil B. McLynn is a British historian of Late Antiquity whose work centres on the religious politics of the fourth-century Roman world. He is University Lecturer in Later Roman History and a Fellow of Corpus Christi College at the University of Oxford, where he holds his post within the Faculty of Classics.

McLynn read classics and completed his doctorate (DPhil) at Oxford, before taking an unusual professional detour: in 1990 he moved to Japan, where until 2007 he taught in the Faculty of Law at Keio University, giving courses on subjects ranging from Shakespeare to International Relations. He returned to Oxford on 1 April 2007 to take up the University Lectureship in Later Roman History, a position he combines with a stipendiary lectureship at Corpus, teaching undergraduates in both classics and history. He has since become closely involved in the Oxford Centre for Late Antiquity, where he sits on the managing committee representing late-antique history, and much of his teaching is directed at graduate students, including the Late Antique and Byzantine Studies and Medieval History MSt programmes.

His scholarly reputation rests above all on his first book, Ambrose of Milan: Church and Court in a Christian Capital (University of California Press, 1994) — a study likely to interest you given its Milanese subject. Rather than treating Ambrose primarily as a theologian or saint, McLynn read the bishop's career as a sustained exercise in political manoeuvre, reconstructing how Ambrose negotiated his authority against the imperial court. The book is generally regarded as having reshaped scholarly understanding of episcopal power in the later empire, though it also drew criticism from those who felt its emphasis on political calculation risked flattening Ambrose's religious convictions — a debate worth weighing rather than taking McLynn's reading as settled.

Much of his subsequent output has orbited two figures. The first is Gregory of Nazianzus, on whom he has published extensively and around whom he has long described himself as writing a book examining the workings of secular, ecclesiastical, and cultural politics both in provincial Nazianzus and in Constantinople. The second is Augustine of Hippo, into whose more difficult biographical episodes he turned more recently. His shorter studies — collected in Christian Politics and Religious Culture in Late Antiquity (Variorum/Ashgate, 2009) — range across imperial churchgoing, Christian violence, the Donatist schism, and pagan-Christian relations in late-antique Rome. He also co-edited, with Anna Marmodoro, Exploring Gregory of Nyssa: Philosophical, Theological, and Historical Studies (Oxford University Press, 2018), and has supervised a substantial number of Oxford doctoral theses in late-antique history.

Meehan, Bernard

active late 20th – early 21st century

Bernard Meehan is an Irish manuscript scholar and curator, Head of Research Collections and Keeper of Manuscripts at Trinity College Dublin until his retirement at the end of 2016, and for a generation the custodian-scholar of the Book of Kells. His four-scribe division of the manuscript is the current working consensus.

Meehan spent his working life in the Manuscripts Department at Trinity College Library, rising to Keeper of Manuscripts and, latterly, Head of Research Collections; he holds an MA and a PhD. His curatorial responsibilities extended well beyond the medieval collections — he oversaw major modern Irish literary archives, including material relating to Samuel Beckett — and he served as chairman of the Irish Region of the Society of Archivists and as a member of the National Archives Advisory Council (1987–1997). He was Burns Visiting Scholar at Boston College in the spring of 1998.

His research divides into two substantial fields, which is worth knowing when searching his bibliography: Insular manuscripts, history and culture of the sixth to ninth centuries; and the history and manuscripts of Scotland and northern England from the Norman Conquest to about 1200 — with, as his own departmental profile puts it, excursions into modern literary and archival subjects.

His earliest published work belongs to the second of these. It includes "Outsiders, insiders and property in Durham around 1100," Studies in Church History 12 (1975), pp. 45–58; "The siege of Durham, the battle of Carham and the cession of Lothian," Scottish Historical Review 55 (1976), pp. 1–19; and "Geoffrey of Monmouth, Prophecies of Merlin: New Manuscript Evidence," Bulletin of the Board of Celtic Studies 28 (1978), pp. 37–46. He later contributed "Durham twelfth-century manuscripts in Cistercian houses" to Anglo-Norman Durham, ed. D. Rollason, M. Harvey and M. Prestwich (Boydell Press, 1994), pp. 439–449, and "Notes on the Preliminary Texts and Continuations to Symeon of Durham's Libellus de exordio" (1999).

From the Trinity collections came "A note on the Dublin Apocalypse (Trinity College Dublin MS 64)," Scriptorium 38 (1984), pp. 82–83; "The manuscript collection of James Ussher," in Treasures of the Library, ed. Peter Fox (Dublin, 1986), pp. 97–110; and, much later, "A fourteenth-century historical compilation from St Mary's Cistercian abbey, Dublin," Medieval Dublin XV (2016). He also edited Archives and Copyright, the proceedings of a 1982 conference of the Irish Region of the Society of Archivists (1983).

Meehan contributed to the commentary volume of the 1990 Faksimile Verlag Luzern facsimile, edited by Peter Fox. His The Book of Kells: An Illustrated Introduction to the Manuscript in Trinity College Dublin (London: Thames & Hudson, 1994; 95 pp.) became Thames & Hudson's best-selling title of all time and was subsequently reissued in a completely restructured, rewritten, redesigned and freshly illustrated edition (ISBN 9780500480243).

His large-format The Book of Kells (Thames & Hudson, 2012) was launched at Trinity with an introduction by Roger Stalley, Professor of the History of Art, and marked the tercentenary of the Old Library building. Presented in a cloth-bound slipcase, it features 84 full-size reproductions of complete pages together with enlarged details, and treats the manuscript through its historical background, the great decorated openings of the prefatory texts, comparison with earlier and related manuscripts, its symbols, themes and narratives, its scribes and artists, and the technical evidence supplied by recent scientific research. The Financial Times called it a triumph of scholarly investigation and interpretation.

His four-scribe scheme extends Françoise Henry's three-hand division (A, B, C) by identifying a fourth scribe, Hand D, distinguished by angular, elongated letterforms and a characteristic serif on the initial s, and reassigning to him much of what Henry had grouped under her Hand C. In the 2012 volume (p. 212) he suggested that a fifth hand, Scribe E, may yet await identification. He has also published on the manuscript's iconography — notably "'New' Narrative Scenes in the Book of Kells," in Making Histories: Proceedings of the Sixth International Conference on Insular Art, York 2011, ed. Jane Hawkes (Donington, 2013).

He was a co-author of the micro-Raman pigment study (Bioletti, Leahy, Fields, Meehan and Blau, Journal of Raman Spectroscopy 40, 2009, pp. 1043–49) and of the subsequent non-destructive analysis of the Codex Usserianus Primus, the Book of Durrow and the Book of Armagh (Burgio, Bioletti and Meehan, in Making Histories, 2013). Other work includes studies of the St Cuthbert Gospel and the Irish pocket gospels, "Book satchels in medieval Scotland and Ireland" (2005), and entries in Art and Architecture of Ireland, vol. 1, ed. Rachel Moss (2014).

His current projects, as listed by Trinity, include linked studies of Oxford, Bodleian Library, Rawlinson G. 167 and Auct. D. 2. 19 (the Macregol Gospels); St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek, 51; the Otho-Corpus Gospels; the Turin Gospels; and the Faddan More Psalter — together with a study of Françoise Henry and her predecessors, including J. O. Westwood, as interpreters of Insular manuscripts, which will be the natural companion piece to the historiographical section you are assembling.

Meier, Hans-Rudolf

Zurich, 9 November 1956

Hans-Rudolf Meier's path into art history was not a direct one: he trained first as a laboratory technician, worked in the chemical industry, and was active in trade-union and political life before turning to university study of art history, history, medieval archaeology and prehistory in Basel, Zurich and Freiburg im Breisgau. He completed his doctorate at the University of Basel in 1992 with a dissertation on high-medieval secular architecture in Sicily, and held a post as senior assistant at the Institute for Historic Preservation of ETH Zurich from 1992 to 2000, with further research stays in Basel, Rome and Zurich. He completed his habilitation in 2000.

His subsequent career has been spent almost entirely within Denkmalpflege, the German tradition of monument preservation understood as a historical and theoretical discipline rather than a purely technical one. He held an interim professorship in early art history at Basel in 2002/03, then a professorship in monument preservation and applied building research at the Technical University of Dresden from 2003 to 2007, before moving in 2008 to the Bauhaus-Universität Weimar as professor of monument preservation and building history, a chair he still holds. At Weimar he served as pro-rector for research from 2011 to 2012, directs the university's International Heritage Center, and is a spokesperson for the DFG-funded research training group "Identität und Erbe" ("Identity and Heritage"), run jointly with the Technical University of Berlin and the universities of Anhalt and Erfurt. His broader research concerns the theory and history of monument preservation, the reuse of architectural fabric across historical periods, and building archaeology.

Meier's engagement with Assisi dates to his 1990 article "Santa Chiara in Assisi. Architektur und Funktion im Schatten von San Francesco," published in Arte Medievale (2nd ser., IV/2, pp. 151–178), which read the basilica as a building shaped, formally and functionally, by its status as a memorial church subordinate to San Francesco — an interpretation that has become the organising thesis of the modern architectural literature on Santa Chiara. He expanded this analysis for the architecture section of the collaborative monograph La basilica di Santa Chiara in Assisi (Quattroemme, Perugia, 1994), co-authored with Marino Bigaroni and Elvio Lunghi, which remains the standard reference on the building.

Meiss, Millard

1904 – 1975

Millard Meiss was one of the most influential American art historians of the twentieth century, specializing in late medieval and early Renaissance painting, and later in manuscript illumination — areas of direct relevance to your own research interests. Born in 1904, Meiss first studied architecture at Princeton, graduating in 1926, before turning to art history. He taught at Columbia University from 1934 to 1953, then moved to Harvard as both professor and Curator of Painting at the Fogg Art Museum. In 1958, he left Harvard to assume the chair of Professor of Art at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton — a position vacated by his former teacher Erwin Panofsky, one of the giants of iconographic studies.

Meiss is celebrated for bridging traditional connoisseurship with a broader, socially informed art history. He sought to read paintings not merely as stylistic objects but as reflections of collective consciousness — a revolutionary stance at the time. His innovative interpretation held that artists of the mid-Trecento had absorbed the traumatic shocks of economic crises and the catastrophic Bubonic Plague of 1348, and that this suffering was visibly encoded in their work.

His landmark book Painting in Florence and Siena after the Black Death (1951) remains a cornerstone of Trecento studies, analyzing how the Black Death reshaped the spiritual and aesthetic character of Italian painting. He won the Haskins Medal in 1953 — awarded annually for a distinguished book in medieval studies — for this work. In 1962, he co-authored with Leonetto Tintori The Painting of the Life of St. Francis in Assisi, innovative in its use of technical analysis of mural painting to resolve major attribution debates.

Meiss's research broadened significantly in the 1960s to include manuscript illumination, an area now at the center of your own scholarly pursuits. His monumental multi-volume series French Painting in the Time of Jean de Berry (1967–74) is a definitive study of late Gothic manuscript illumination at the Valois court, covering French, Flemish, and Italian influences on the luxury manuscripts produced for Jean, Duc de Berry. This work remains an indispensable reference for anyone studying illuminated manuscripts of the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries.

Meiss was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the American Philosophical Society, and the British Academy, as well as several French and Italian scholarly societies. The College Art Association named its book illustration grant in his honor. A full-length reassessment of his scholarship, Millard Meiss, American Art History, and Conservation by Jennifer Cooke (University of Turin), was published in the Routledge Studies in Art Historiography series and provides a thorough modern evaluation of his methodology and lasting influence.

Mentré, Mireille

France - active late 20th-21st century

Mireille Mentré is a French art historian whose career was based at the Universite de Paris-Sorbonne (Paris IV), where she worked at the intersection of the history of art and the history of religion. This disciplinary positioning shaped her scholarship on Mozarabic illumination, privileging theological and spiritual interpretation alongside formal and historical analysis.

Her research environment at Paris IV linked her to the French tradition of religious art history associated with figures such as Emile Male, while her Iberian medieval specialization remained relatively rare in the French academy. She worked within a scholarly context closely connected to the cataloguing infrastructures of the Bibliotheque nationale and Sorbonne research institutes.

Mentré's doctoral thesis, La peinture mozarabe, submitted in 1981 in four dactylographed volumes at the Universite Paris-Sorbonne, was a pioneering and comprehensive treatment of Mozarabic painting in the Iberian Peninsula. It addressed origins, stylistic development, iconographic programs, and religious context, and represented the first systematic synthesis of the field in French scholarship.

A first published form appeared in 1984 from Presses Universitaires de Paris-Sorbonne as La Peinture "mozarabe". An expanded and retitled version, La Peinture mozarabe: Un art chretien hispanique autour de l'an mil, was published by Desclee de Brouwer in 1995, with extensive illustration and a broader synthetic framework.

In 1982, she co-authored with Francois Avril, Jean-Pierre Aniel, Alix Saulnier, and Yolanta Zaluska the reference volume Manuscrits enlumines de la peninsule iberique (Bibliotheque nationale), produced by the Centre de recherches sur les manuscrits enluminés. This catalogue of Iberian illuminated manuscripts in the BnF collections remains an indispensable tool for manuscript research in French collections.

Also in 1984 she published Creation et Apocalypse: Histoire d'un regard humain sur le divin in the series L'imaginaire medieval. More essayistic than her catalogues, the book clarified a key interpretive axis of her work: images as visual theologies that render the extremes of sacred history, Creation and Apocalypse, for communities living under historical pressure.

Her specialized studies include the 1985 communication "Le probleme de la couleur dans la peinture 'mozarabe'" (published in the Bulletin de la Societe nationale des Antiquaires de France, 1987), a technical analysis of Mozarabic chromatic practice; the 1986 article "Iconographie de la creation"; and the 1990 study "L'iconographie des bibles romanes catalanes" in Cahiers de Saint-Michel de Cuxa, where she connected Iberian manuscript traditions with wider regional Romanesque debates.

Her major international impact came with the English translation of the 1995 synthesis: The Illuminated Manuscripts of Medieval Spain (Thames & Hudson, 1996), translated by Jenifer Wakelyn with a foreword by Pierre Riche. The volume established Mentré, for English-language readers, as one of the two principal authorities on Mozarabic illumination alongside John Williams.

Mentré's method integrates three levels of analysis. At the formal level, she studies pictorial vocabulary such as striped color bands, flattened figural conventions, zoomorphic ornament, and architectural framing. At the historical level, she situates manuscripts in the political, liturgical, and cultural conditions of tenth- and eleventh-century Christian Iberia, in relation to al-Andalus and the eschatological horizon around the year 1000. At the theological level, she interprets images as expressions of religious experience, especially the tension between Beginning and End, Creation and Apocalypse.

Within the historiography of Mozarabic studies, her contribution is distinct from the classificatory work of Wilhelm Neuss, the socio-historical readings of Otto Karl Werckmeister, and the codicological and corpus-based syntheses of John Williams and Barbara Shailor. Mentré provided the major French art-historical synthesis of Mozarabic painting, grounded in sustained manuscript study and framed through religious history and spiritual phenomenology.

Metz, Peter

Mainz, 26 September 1901 - Berlin, 15 May 1985

Peter Metz was a German art historian and museum director whose long career spanned the interwar Rhineland museum world, wartime and postwar Berlin, a formative interlude at the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg, and, from 1955, the directorship of the Sculpture Department of the Berlin State Museums, which he rebuilt after the war and finally rehoused in a new museum building in Dahlem. He is best remembered in the field of medieval book illumination as the author of the standard monograph on the Codex Aureus of Echternach.

Born Ludwig Ferdinand Peter Paul Metz in Mainz on 26 September 1901, the elder of two children of the royal Bavarian court photographer Hanns Metz and Marie Metz, née Hilge, he was educated at the humanistic Altes Gymnasium in Mainz (later the Rabanus-Maurus-Gymnasium), taking his Abitur in 1920. He went on to study art history, archaeology and history at Frankfurt am Main, Munich, Göttingen, Cologne and Gießen, completing his doctorate at Gießen in 1924 under Christian Rauch with a dissertation on Mainz rococo sculpture, Mainzer Rokokoplastik.

His early career was rooted in his native Mainz: from 1925 to 1928 he was a scientific assistant at the University of Mainz, working on the cathedral and diocesan museum and organising the major sculpture exhibition Alte Kunst am Mittelrhein at the Hessisches Landesmuseum in Darmstadt (1927). In 1928 he moved to Berlin as a volunteer in the Kupferstichkabinett and the painting department of the Berlin State Museums, and assisted Ernst Friedrich Bange and Theodor Demmler on the reorganisation of the German department. A fellowship of the German Art Historical Institute took him to Florence in 1931-32. He married Ingeborg Sachse (1908-1994) in 1934.

The Nazi period disrupted his career sharply. He took a post as librarian at the state goldsmiths' school in Hanau but left it for political reasons; in 1935 he declined the directorship of the Frankfurt Historical Museum rather than accept the NSDAP membership the post required, and worked instead as an unpaid scientific assistant at the Berlin State Museums. He served in the military from September 1939 to 1945. After the war he was made a Custos, habilitated at the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität Berlin in 1946 with a study of Tuscan incrustation architecture (Toscanische Inkrustationskunst), and taught as Privatdozent at the Humboldt-Universität Berlin from 1948 to 1950. In 1950 he was appointed director of the Sculpture Department in what was now East Berlin, but fled soon afterward to West Germany.

Between 1950 and 1955 Metz worked at the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg as a conservator, while also lecturing at the University of Erlangen from 1951. He organised the exhibitions Deutsche Kultur von der Spätantike bis zum Rokoko at Schloss Cappenberg and Aufgang der Neuzeit, and led the museum's Augustinus-Seminar. It was in this Nuremberg period that he took on the task for which he is best known outside the world of sculpture studies: he directed the scholarly and organisational work behind the museum's acquisition of the Codex Aureus Epternacensis, the Golden Gospels of Echternach, and wrote the monograph that accompanied it, Das Goldene Evangelienbuch von Echternach im Germanischen Nationalmuseum zu Nürnberg (Munich: Prestel, 1956), published in English the following year as The Golden Gospels of Echternach: Codex Aureus Epternacensis (New York: Praeger, 1957). The book distilled the whole of his art-historical learning into a description of the manuscript's origins, history and iconographic and colour-symbolic programme, and it remained for decades the foundational full-length study of the Codex Aureus in any language; Metz was also the scholar who first proposed, and defended against later criticism, a dating of the manuscript to 1053-1056, after Abbot Humbert's death - a minority position followed by Peter Lasko but not generally accepted by subsequent scholarship.

In 1955 Metz returned to Berlin as the first postwar director of the Sculpture Department of the State Museums in West Berlin, a post he held until his retirement in 1966. He rebuilt the collection from wartime losses, acquiring 188 significant sculptures, and organised a series of major loan exhibitions, including Europäische Bildwerke von der Spätantike bis zum Rokoko at the Villa Hügel in Essen (1957) and, at Schloss Charlottenburg, Christliche Kunst Europas and Das Bild Christi (both 1958). His achievement was recognised in 1959 when Pope John XXIII made him a Knight of the Papal Order of Saint Gregory the Great. He was appointed adjunct professor at Erlangen in 1960, and the culmination of his Berlin directorship came on 16 April 1966 with the opening, in Berlin-Dahlem and with the architect Wils Ebert, of a new, purpose-built Sculpture Museum whose lighting and spatial design reflected his own theologically inflected views on how sculpture should be displayed. On his retirement later that year he declined the Bundesverdienstkreuz, First Class, after the Museums' refusal to extend his contract.

Metz's scholarship ranged from Rhenish cathedral sculpture and Ottonian book illumination to Late Antique ivories, and consistently sought to integrate art-historical description with Christian theology and symbolism; among his other books are Der Dom zu Mainz (1927), Zehn deutsche Dome (1939, with K. H. Clasen), Der Stifterchor des Naumburger Doms (1947), Idee und Erscheinungsform des Kunstwerkes (1953), Ottonische Buchmalerei (1959), and Elfenbein der Spätantike (1962). In retirement he pursued theological and scientific correspondence, was active in the Una Voce movement in support of the traditional Latin liturgy, and led study tours across Europe and Russia. Peter Metz died in Berlin on 15 May 1985 after a brief illness.

Meyer, Alfred Gotthold

Germany, 1864 – 1904

Alfred Gotthold Meyer was a German art historian born in 1864 whose scholarly work focused with exceptional precision on the medieval and early Renaissance sculpture and architecture of northern Italy, particularly Lombardy. Despite dying at just forty years of age, he produced two landmark works that remain indispensable references for the study of Lombard artistic heritage.

Principal Work on 14th-Century Lombardy

Meyer's most celebrated contribution is his monograph Lombardische Denkmaler des vierzehnten Jahrhunderts: Giovanni di Balduccio da Pisa und die Campionesen (1893), subtitled Ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der oberitalienischen Plastik - "A Contribution to the History of North Italian Sculpture". This ambitious study examines two of the most significant sculptural forces in 14th-century Lombard art: Giovanni di Balduccio da Pisa, the Tuscan sculptor who transplanted the refined Pisan Gothic tradition into Milan, and the Campionese masters, the dynasty of Lombard sculptors and architects from Campione d'Italia whose workshops dominated the decoration of the great northern Italian cathedrals and funerary monuments throughout the Trecento. The book remains a foundational text for any scholar researching the transmission of sculptural styles between Tuscany and Lombardy in this period.

Oberitalienische Fruhrenaissance

Meyer's second major work, Oberitalienische Fruhrenaissance: Bauten und Bildwerke der Lombardei ("North Italian Early Renaissance: Buildings and Sculptures of Lombardy"), appeared in two volumes, with the second part - Die Bluthezeit ("The Flowering") - published in Berlin by Wilhelm Ernst & Sohn in 1900. This expansive survey charts the transition from the Gothic to the Renaissance in Lombard artistic production, treating architecture and sculpture as interrelated phenomena shaped by the particular cultural context of the Po Valley. The work demonstrated Meyer's command of both formal analysis and historical documentation, synthesizing archival evidence with close stylistic observation in a manner characteristic of the rigorous German Kunstwissenschaft tradition of the late 19th century.

Significance and Scholarly Legacy

Meyer wrote at a time when the systematic study of medieval and proto-Renaissance Italian art was still being established as an academic discipline, and his focus on the often-overlooked Lombard school - long overshadowed by the Florentine and Sienese traditions - was itself a scholarly intervention of lasting importance. His analysis of the Campionese masters helped define how scholars understand the regional character of Lombard Gothic sculpture and its relationship to broader European currents. The digitized version of Oberitalienische Fruhrenaissance is preserved and accessible through the Universitatsbibliothek Heidelberg, and Lombardische Denkmaler is available through the Internet Archive, making both works accessible to researchers today. His premature death in 1904 cut short a scholarly career that, had it continued, would almost certainly have reshaped the historiography of Lombard medieval art more broadly.

Meyvaert, Paul

Belgium, 1921 - United States, 2011

Paul Meyvaert was a Belgian-born medievalist whose long career, conducted for the most part in the United States in close association with the Medieval Academy of America and its journal Speculum, made him one of the most consequential scholars of Bede, of the transmission of patristic texts, and, above all, of the Codex Amiatinus. Trained originally as a Benedictine monk before pursuing a full-time scholarly career, he brought to his work an intimate, practitioner's familiarity with the monastic textual and liturgical traditions he studied.

Meyvaert's article "Bede, Cassiodorus, and the Codex Amiatinus," published in Speculum in 1996, reoriented the entire modern discussion of the manuscript's models. He established that Bede possessed and used an Old Latin pandect associated with Cassiodorus at Jarrow, while arguing, more surprisingly, that Bede did not know Cassiodorus's Institutiones and was seemingly unaware that Cassiodorus had founded the monastery of Vivarium at all — meaning the Northumbrians had inherited a Cassiodoran book without Cassiodorus's own account of what he had made or why. In a second major article, "The Date of Bede's In Ezram and his Image of Ezra in the Codex Amiatinus" (Speculum, 2005), he dissented sharply from Rupert Bruce-Mitford's view that the manuscript's celebrated Ezra miniature was a relabelled portrait of Cassiodorus, arguing instead that the image was newly conceived at Wearmouth-Jarrow, very possibly with Bede's own close involvement in both its design and its accompanying couplet.

Meyvaert's two Amiatinus articles remain, more than any other single body of work, the fulcrum around which current debate on the manuscript's Cassiodoran background and its Ezra portrait turns; his qualification of Karen Corsano's 1987 argument for direct Cassiodoran dependence, and his dissent from Bruce-Mitford's identification of the Ezra figure, define the two principal axes of disagreement that later scholars, from Lawrence Nees to Celia Chazelle, have continued to negotiate. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller account of both debates.

Migne, Jacques Paul

Saint-Flour, 25 October 1800 - Paris, 24 October 1875

Jacques Paul Migne was born on 25 October 1800 in Saint-Flour, Cantal, in the Auvergne region of south-central France. After completing his university courses, Migne studied theology in Orléans, where he temporarily filled the position of professor at the college of Châteaudun. Ordained priest in 1824, the following year he was named curé at Puiseaux, in the Diocese of Orléans.

The parish of Puiseaux proved an uncongenial posting for a man of Migne's temperament. His uncompromisingly Catholic and royalist sympathies did not coincide with local patriotism and the new regime of the Citizen-King. He published a pamphlet, De la liberté, which brought him into conflict with his bishop, Brunault de Beauregard, in consequence of which he resigned his parish and went to Paris.

In 1833, after falling out with his bishop, he went to Paris, and on 3 November started a journal, L'Univers religieux, which he intended to keep free of political influence. It quickly gained 1,800 subscribers and he edited it for three years. The journal - which later became the ultramontane organ L'Univers under the co-editorship of Louis Veuillot - revealed the driving conviction that would shape his entire career: a belief in the power of the printed word, widely and cheaply distributed, as the primary instrument of Catholic revival in a France still convulsed by the cultural aftermath of the Revolution.

Migne believed in the power of the press and the value of information widely distributed. In 1836 he opened his great publishing house, the Ateliers catholiques, at Petit-Montrouge, in Paris's outlying fourteenth arrondissement. The establishment he built there over the following decades was unlike anything in the history of religious publishing.

The Ateliers catholiques were not a traditional publisher. They were an industrial complex - a factory of the sacred - in which steam-powered technology served theological ends. Migne's Ateliers catholiques employed five steam-powered presses, and by 1854 some 596 workers. The Ateliers were capable of turning out two thousand quarto volumes every 24 hours. They had approximately ten per cent of the printing capacity of a highly mechanised département.

According to the publisher Ambroise Firmin Didot, Migne undertook "the greatest publishing enterprise since the invention of printing." By Migne's own account, he intended to "render to the Church the greatest service that has ever been rendered," by publishing a complete edition of the Latin and Greek Fathers and thus reuniting a church divided by the Great Schism of 1054 and the Reformation.

The methods by which he achieved this output were characterised by their creator's ferocious pragmatism. Migne kept labour costs low; his workers were poorly paid - many of them were relatives, people networked from his hometown, and defrocked priests. He utilised the latest technologies, including the new steam-driven printing presses whose output was substantially higher than the previous technologies, so the per-unit cost was much less. He published numerous religious works in rapid succession meant for lesser clergy at prices that ensured wide circulation, and bypassed the bookselling establishment with direct subscriptions. These works were reproduced from the best available texts, generally without requesting permission.

Migne's workshop employed 596 workers in 1854, making him one of France's largest employers at the time. Rising literacy rates resulted in a growing reading public; advances in printing and paper manufacturing made books cheaper to produce; progress in transportation and communication made large-scale distribution and publicity possible. Bloch compares Migne's religious enterprise to the department store Le Bon Marché, showing how both used similar manufacturing, merchandising, and distribution techniques.

Migne trafficked illegally in masses and frequently reprinted editions that were not in the public domain. The police characterised him as one of the great schemers of the century. But the scheming was in the service of a genuine theological vision: the reconstruction of the library of Christian civilisation.

Before the great Patrologies, Migne had already demonstrated the ambition of his project through a series of encyclopaedic compilations. The best known of his publications are Scripturae sacrae cursus completus, which assembled a wide repertory of commentaries on each of the books of the Bible, and Theologiae cursus, each of them in 28 volumes, 1840-45; Collection des auteurs sacrés (100 vols., 1846-48); Encyclopédie théologique (171 vols., 1844-46).

In a desire to overturn the secularisation movement of the French Revolution, Migne attempted to produce a universal work that would match, and improve, other publications of a similar scope. In reading the volumes of the Patrologiae, many nineteenth-century readers might have recalled the greatest editorial enterprise of the previous century: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie. Migne was explicitly competing with the secular encyclopaedists on their own terrain, producing a Catholic counter-encyclopaedia of comparable scale, and using the same industrial logic of systematisation, coverage, and affordable pricing.

The first and in some respects the more immediately useful of the two Patrologies was the Patrologiae Cursus Completus, Series Latina - the Patrologia Latina (PL). The Patrologia Latina includes Latin works spanning a millennium, from Tertullian (d. 230) to Pope Innocent III (d. 1216), edited in roughly chronological order in 217 volumes: volumes 1 to 73, from Tertullian to Gregory of Tours, were published from 1841 to 1849, and volumes 74 to 217, from Pope Gregory I to Innocent III, from 1849 to 1855. Four volumes of indexes were published between 1862 and 1865, bringing the total to 221 volumes.

Relying on a clever system of subscriptions and on an aggressive publicity campaign through the publication of prospectuses and newspaper articles, Migne managed to publish this vast Latin corpus in two series spanning twenty years. The textual basis was not original scholarship: Migne reprinted the best available earlier editions, adding prefaces, indices, and supplementary material to enhance accessibility. Migne did not publish these texts as primary sources exclusively - alongside the patristic texts proper, the volumes include commentaries, vitae, sermons, liturgical texts, canon law compilations, chronicles, hagiographical dossiers, and documentary materials of every kind produced within the Latin Church across eleven centuries.

For the student of medieval art and iconography, the PL is a resource of first-order importance precisely because of this breadth. The exegetical tradition that governed the iconographic programme of every illuminated Bible, every apsidal mosaic programme, every tympanum and carved capital is documented here: in the biblical commentaries of Origen, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Bede, Hrabanus Maurus, Anselm, and Bernard of Clairvaux; in the liturgical texts and ordines that shaped the devotional context of manuscript production; in the hagiographical vitae that generated the cycles of saints' legends painted on church walls and woven into the imagery of psalters and breviaries; in the theological texts - from the Libri Carolini to Durandus of Mende's Rationale divinorum officiorum - that articulate the theological justifications and critiques of sacred imagery.

The Patrologia Graeca includes the printed works of Greek Christian writers down to the Council of Florence (1438-39). It was a still more ambitious project than the Latin series. The Patrologia Graeca consists of 161 volumes produced in 1857-1866 by J. P. Migne's Imprimerie Catholique, Paris. It includes both the Eastern Fathers and those Western authors who wrote before Latin became predominant in the Western Church in the third century.

The first series contained only Latin translations of the originals (81 vols., 1856-61). The second series contains the Greek text with a Latin translation (166 vols., 1857-66). The texts are interlaced, with one column of Greek and a corresponding column on the other side of the page that is the Latin translation. Where the Greek original has been lost, as in the case of Irenaeus, the extant Greek fragments are interspersed throughout the Latin text.

The PG includes the writings of the Apostolic Fathers, such as the Epistles of Clement and the Shepherd of Hermas, Eusebius, Origen, and the Cappadocian Fathers Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa, and it extends through the entire Byzantine theological and literary tradition - John of Damascus, the iconophile theologians of the second iconoclast controversy, the writers of the Macedonian and Comnenian periods, to the hesychast controversy of the fourteenth century. The PG is, for the student of Byzantine art and theology, what the PL is for the student of the medieval Latin West: the indispensable collected dossier of the theological tradition that generated and sanctioned the visual programmes under study.

On the night of 12-13 February 1868, a devastating fire, which began in the printing plant, destroyed Migne's establishment. "Five hundred thousand plates, stacked in piles, melted in an instant; they are now enormous blocks of the most bizarre forms," reported Le Monde illustré. Despite his insurance contracts, Migne was only able to retrieve a pittance.

In 1865 Migne had sold the literary rights to the Patrologia Latina to the Parisian publishing firm of Garnier. Only three years later the fire completely destroyed Migne's presses and stereotype plates, so that all subsequent Garnier editions were necessarily inferior because they had to rely on printed copies instead of the original plates.

The disasters compounded. Shortly afterwards, Georges Darboy, Archbishop of Paris, forbade the continuance of the business and even suspended Migne from his priestly functions. The Franco-Prussian War of 1870 inflicted further losses. Then from the curia of Pope Pius IX came a decree condemning the use of Mass stipends to purchase books, which specifically called out Migne and his publications.

The archbishop's hostility was long-standing: the Archbishop of Paris was averse to the commercial elements in the work, and had forbidden the continuance of the business. The Roman decree, in naming Migne and his publications specifically in the context of Mass stipend trafficking, dealt a severe blow to one of his primary mechanisms of revenue generation. He had long operated a system whereby priests in France and Belgium - regions with severe shortages of clergy - were subcontracted to celebrate masses at a fixed cost, receiving payment partly in kind through subscriptions to his publications. This brought controversy and resulted in the attempt by the Archbishop of Paris to unsuccessfully close his company.

Migne died in Paris on 24 October 1875 - one day before his seventy-fifth birthday. He died without ever regaining his former success, and his Imprimerie Catholique passed in 1876 into the hands of Garnier Frères.

It is important to distinguish clearly between Migne's scholarly deficiencies and his scholarly achievement. The deficiencies are real. The intention was to choose for the new issues the best editions of each author, with suitable introductions and critical additions, which plan, unfortunately, was not always realised. The printing, too, was frequently unsatisfactory, and in most of the Migne reprints we find a number of misprints and errata. Many of the editions Migne reprinted were already outdated when he reprinted them; the Greek texts in the PG frequently do not match their Latin translations, which were made in the Renaissance from inferior or corrupt manuscripts; and the whole enterprise was conducted at a pace that precluded any serious philological control.

Yet the achievement remains without parallel. Though scholars have always criticised them, these hastily edited, inexpensive, and widely distributed texts have only slowly been replaced during a century and a half with more critically edited modern editions. The cheap paper of the originals has made them fragile today, but the scope of the Patrologia still makes it unique and valuable when modern editions do not yet exist. It is a far more complete collection of Patristic and later literature than anything that has appeared subsequently.

The Patrologia Latina and the Patrologia Graeca, along with the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, are among the great nineteenth-century contributions to the scholarship of patristics and the Middle Ages. The comparison with the MGH is instructive: both are mid-century German and French responses to the same historical moment - the simultaneous recognition that the documentary basis of medieval civilisation was vast and largely inaccessible, and that only a systematic industrial mobilisation of editorial resources could make it available. The MGH applied the rigour of diplomatic and palaeographic criticism to the task; Migne applied the speed and economy of the new steam press. The results are complementary: the MGH gave scholars the best-edited texts of the most important documents; Migne gave them access to everything else.

The two Patrologia remain the standard edition for much of the religious Latin and Greek literature of the patristic and medieval periods. It usually gives the best texts which were available at the time of its publication, and it adds to them a store of notes, introductions, and dissertations by well-known Patristic scholars. The Latin series is furnished with four volumes of useful indices.

The output in summary is staggering in its dimensions. On average, it published a book every ten days for thirty years. In a career of forty years, Migne published, across all his series, well over a thousand volumes - a total of published text that dwarfs any comparable nineteenth-century editorial enterprise.

Migne's work has the peculiar status of a monument everyone uses and no one fully respects. Its column numbers - cited as "PL 120, col. 567" or "PG 44, col. 800" - appear in the footnotes of virtually every article and monograph in medieval studies, patristics, Byzantine history, liturgical history, and the history of Christian thought published in the last century and a half. No scholar of the medieval theological tradition, of the textual sources of iconographic programmes, of the history of ecclesiastical music, of canon law, of monastic culture, or of the Church Fathers themselves can work without reference to it.

What Migne provided was not critical scholarship in the sense that Quicherat, Levison, Lowe, or the scholars of the MGH would have recognised. He was not a philologist or a palaeographer; he was a systematiser and a publisher of visionary scale, who grasped that the primary need of the mid-nineteenth century was not better editions of individual texts but access to the totality of the tradition. The Patrologiae Cursus Completus fulfilled that need, and continues to fulfil it wherever modern critical editions do not yet exist - which, across the full span from Tertullian to the Council of Florence, is still true of a very great deal of the material.

For the historian of medieval art, the Patrologia is the theological library in which the visual culture of the Middle Ages was formed. The sermons, commentaries, hagiographies, liturgical texts, canonical decrees, and theological disputations that shaped the iconographic choices of every medieval illuminator, mosaicist, sculptor, and panel painter are assembled here. Without Migne, medieval art history would lack its textual infrastructure. With it - however imperfect - the full documentary universe of Christian visual culture from the second century to the fifteenth becomes, in principle, accessible to any researcher in any library that holds the collection.

Milanesi, Gaetano

Siena, 1813 – Florence, 1895

Gaetano Milanesi was an Italian philologist, archivist and art historian who, as director of the Archivio di Stato in Florence, placed the study of Tuscan art on a documentary footing that later generations of scholars have continued to build on. His early major undertaking, the three-volume Documenti per la storia dell'arte senese (1854–1856), assembled and published the archival record of Sienese painting, sculpture and building on a scale no previous scholar had attempted, establishing the model of source-based art history that Milanesi would apply on an even larger canvas to Florence.

That larger undertaking was his critical, annotated edition of Giorgio Vasari's Le vite de' più eccellenti pittori, scultori e architettori, published by Sansoni in nine volumes between 1878 and 1885. Milanesi did not merely reprint Vasari's text: he appended to each Life the archival documents — contracts, payments, guild registrations, wills — that could confirm, correct or contradict Vasari's often unreliable dates and attributions, converting the Vite from a literary monument into a working scholarly instrument. This annotated edition became, and for over a century remained, the standard reference text of Vasari used by art historians, and it is still routinely cited today wherever a Vasarian claim needs to be checked against the surviving documentary record. Milanesi also edited the correspondence of Michelangelo, applying the same rigorous, document-first method. He died in Florence in 1895, having done more than any other single scholar to give nineteenth- and twentieth-century Vasari studies their archival spine.

Miljković-Pepek, Petar

20th century

Petar Miljković-Pepek was the most prominent art historian and medieval archaeologist in twentieth-century Macedonia, the de facto founder of systematic research on Macedonian medieval monuments, and the mentor of generations of specialists who continued to shape the core of medieval studies at the University of Skopje. His work had international importance and brought him some of the most prestigious national and international academic distinctions, including the Herder Prize awarded through Vienna.

Miljković-Pepek worked within the Faculty of Philosophy at the "Sts. Cyril and Methodius" University of Skopje (Универзитет „Св. Кирил и Методиј”), which after the Second World War became Macedonia's principal center for historical-artistic and archaeological research. When the independent program in Art History and Archaeology was established there in 1973, the first academic offering of its kind in Macedonian history, he was among the seven founding professors charged with teaching in it, alongside Dimče Koco, Blaga Aleksova, Ivan Mikulčić, Boris Petkovski, and Cvetan Grozdanov. That founding group formed the intellectual nucleus that transformed Macedonian medieval studies from a peripheral specialty into a field recognized at the European level.

His influence within that school was extraordinary. Students such as Elizabeta Dimitrova, later a full professor and one of the leading figures of the department, explicitly dedicated scholarly works to him, acknowledging him as a formative mentor. Snezhana Filipova, another major scholar in the department, began her career in 1988 as his assistant. Miljković-Pepek's legacy therefore lies not only in his own publications but also in the scholarly lineage he created.

The central focus of his research was medieval Macedonia, spanning a chronology from the early Christian era of the fourth to sixth centuries to the late Palaiologan art of the fourteenth century. Among his most important contributions was his pioneering research on the ecclesiastical complex of Vodoča (Водоча) near Strumica, dedicated to Saint Leontius, a monumental episcopal center of the Samuelid period in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries. He identified the complex as a sacred structure of prime importance for understanding the art and architecture of Tsar Samuel's empire, and his investigations turned the fragmentary and heavily altered remains into a legible and scientifically documented architectural ensemble.

Equally significant was his work on the Church of the Virgin Eleousa at Veljusa, a small twelfth-century cave monastery near Strumica, founded in 1080 by Manuel, Bishop of Strumica. His monograph Veljusa, published in Skopje in 1981, remains the standard study of the monument's architecture and mural painting. The church exhibits close typological and stylistic ties to the monastery of Nerezi, sharing not only the same broader region but also related iconographic solutions, and the comparison between the two monuments, initiated by Miljković-Pepek, became a recurring theme in international scholarship.

Among his most frequently cited international publications is the monograph L'oeuvre des peintres Michel et Eutych, published in Skopje in 1967 with a French summary. That study was devoted to the identification and analysis of the work of the painters Michele and Eutichios, named in the inscription of the frescoes in the Church of Saints Anargyroi in Kastoria, dated around 1180. Because their inscription is one of the very few surviving signatures of Byzantine painters, the question of which other Macedonian and Greek monuments can be attributed to the same hands or workshop became one of the major debates in the history of medieval painting. Miljković-Pepek's method, based on comparative stylistic analysis across broad corpora of wall painting, established a model followed by subsequent scholarship.

Parallel to this work, he investigated foundation inscriptions and pictorial cycles of the tenth and eleventh centuries in Macedonia, paying special attention to artistic production after the Byzantine reconquest of 1018, when the Archdiocese of Ohrid became the ecclesiastical and cultural center of the region. In this way, his research linked the study of individual monuments to larger questions of political, religious, and artistic transformation in the medieval Balkans.

Among the honors he received, the most significant at the international level was the Herder Prize (Herderpreis) conferred in Vienna, one of the most distinguished European awards for scholars of Central, Eastern, and Balkan cultures. Nationally he received the "October 11" Award (11 Oktomvri), the highest cultural distinction of the Republic of Macedonia, as well as the "November 13" Award of the city of Skopje and numerous further medals of merit.

Miljković-Pepek's scholarly legacy is measured above all by the school he founded. The scholars trained under his guidance, including Elizabeta Dimitrova, Snezhana Filipova, Tatjana Filipovska, and others, expanded his lines of inquiry in international journals such as Niš and Byzantium, Zograf, Folia Archaeologica Balcanica, and the proceedings of the International Congresses of Byzantine Studies. The Department of Art History and Archaeology in Skopje, which he helped found in 1973, is now recognized as one of the most active centers of medieval studies in the Balkan region, a lasting institutional monument to his work.

Minello, Rosanna

active late 20th-21st century

Rosanna Minello is an Italian scholar and librarian associated with the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana in Florence, the institution that has held the Codex Amiatinus since the manuscript's transfer from the suppressed abbey of San Salvatore on Monte Amiata in the late eighteenth century.

She was a co-editor, with Luigi G. G. Ricci and Lucia Castaldi, of La Bibbia Amiatina: Riproduzione integrale su CD-ROM del manoscritto Firenze, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Amiatino 1 (Florence, 2000), the complete electronic facsimile of the manuscript prepared in connection with the removal of its nineteenth-century binding that same year. The facsimile has served as an essential research tool for subsequent scholarship, allowing scholars worldwide to examine the manuscript's disordered opening quire, its offsets, and the fine detail of its script and decoration without recourse to the fragile original. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the manuscript's modern conservation history.

Monck Mason, Henry

dates of birth and death not established with confidence in the accessible record; active in Dublin in the early 19th century

Henry Monck Mason was an Irish lawyer, librarian and antiquarian, librarian of the King's Inns in Dublin in the early decades of the nineteenth century. According to the provenance record kept by Trinity College Dublin, Monck Mason acquired the Book of Dimma sometime before 1816, unlawfully purchased without permission from a Dr Thomas Harrison of Nenagh, to whom the manuscript had merely been lent.

Monck Mason exhibited the book to the Society of Antiquaries of London and, on 24 May 1819, presented it to the Royal Irish Academy, accompanied by a paper describing "a rich and ancient Box, containing a Latin copy of the Gospels" — an early, if unsystematic, scholarly notice of both manuscript and shrine. He was also active in the affairs of the Hibernian Bible Society and wrote on the history of Bible translation into Irish. The manuscript subsequently passed from his hands to the antiquary William Betham.

Monneret de Villard, Hugo

Milan, 16 January 1881 - Rome, 4 November 1954

Hugo Monneret de Villard was one of the most extraordinary and multifaceted figures in twentieth-century Italian academia: trained as an engineer, he became Italy's leading scholar of Islamic, Coptic, and Eastern Christian art, as well as a pioneer in medieval archaeology. He stands as a rare bridge between the technical rigor of engineering and the encyclopedic breadth of Oriental studies.

Born in Milan on January 16, 1881, to Enrico Monneret and Anna Foli, Hugo belonged to a family of Burgundian origin that had moved to Piedmont during the French Revolution. He enrolled at the Polytechnic University of Milan, where he earned a degree in industrial chemical engineering in 1904. This technical training, however, did not lead him toward industry, but rather toward the history of medieval Lombard art and architecture, fields into which he ventured with an engineer's methodology and a humanist's passion.

Between 1913 and 1924, he taught History of Architecture at the Polytechnic University of Milan, becoming in 1913 the first Italian university professor of a subject called Medieval Archaeology. During this period, he engaged in depth with the medieval history of Lombardy and the Romanesque architecture of northern Italy, also contributing to the debate on the preservation of Milan's architectural heritage. These years marked the first phase of a career that would later take an increasingly Eastern and international direction.

In the second phase of his scholarly life, Monneret de Villard devoted himself to the art and archaeology of the Christian and Islamic East, working on behalf of the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Egypt, Nubia, Ethiopia, Iraq, Iran, India, and Central Asia. In Egypt and Sudan, he amassed an immense body of documentation on Nubian, Coptic, and Islamic art, compiling photographs, drawings, and architectural surveys that remain primary sources of great importance to this day. In 1937, following the Italian conquest of Ethiopia, he participated in excavation operations at Axum, contributing to the selection of the obelisk later transported to Rome, a controversial episode linked to fascist colonialism.

Monneret de Villard was the only Italian specialist in Islamic art of his time, and his bibliographic output effectively constitutes the entirety of Italian literature on the subject for that period. Among his most important works are studies on Roman and Christian Nubia, on Coptic and Muslim architecture in Egypt, and fundamental research on the art and architecture of medieval Iraq and Iran. He died before completing an ambitious catalog of Islamic art in Italy, which remained partially unpublished. His archive, comprising approximately 340 volumes and 750 pamphlets on Orientalist topics, was donated by his family to the Library of Archaeology and Art History in Rome at Palazzo Venezia in 1956 and 1966.

In 1944, after the fall of fascism in Rome, he taught archaeology at La Sapienza University for a year. In 1950, he was elected a member of the Accademia dei Lincei, the highest honor in Italian scientific culture. He died in Rome on November 4, 1954. His scientific legacy is particularly significant for anyone studying medieval art in its Mediterranean and Eastern dimensions: he demonstrated that one cannot fully understand European medieval art without taking into account the circulation of forms, techniques, and iconography among the Western Christian world, Byzantium, the Coptic world, and Islam, a perspective that anticipated the methodological debate in global art history by decades.

Mooney, Catherine M.

active late 20th–21st century

Catherine M. Mooney is an American historian of medieval religion and Associate Professor of Church History at Boston College's Clough School of Theology and Ministry, where she teaches courses on saints and sanctity, the papacy, spiritual autobiography, and Christian mysticism. She holds an A.B. in history from Saint Louis University, an M.T.S. from Harvard Divinity School, and an M.A., M.Phil., and Ph.D. in medieval history from Yale University. Before coming to Boston College she taught at Virginia Commonwealth University, the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg (where she also co-coordinated the graduate Gender Studies program), and Weston Jesuit School of Theology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Mooney's central scholarly concern is the mediated, often male-authored textual construction of female sanctity in the later Middle Ages — how the voices of holy women reach us only through the shaping hands of the confessors, scribes, and hagiographers who wrote (or wrote down) their lives. This is the organizing theme of the influential edited volume she produced, Gendered Voices: Medieval Saints and Their Interpreters (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1999), to which she contributed the chapters "Voice, Gender, and the Portrayal of Sanctity" and "Imitatio Christi or Imitatio Mariae? Clare of Assisi and Her Interpreters." The same concern underlies her major monograph, Clare of Assisi and the Thirteenth-Century Church: Religious Women, Rules, and Resistance (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2016), which won the Hagiography Society's Best Book Prize and reconstructs Clare's long, largely unsuccessful struggle to secure papal approval for a rule of absolute poverty against the resistance of a curia intent on regularizing female religious life.

She is a past and current leader of the field's professional institutions, serving as President of the Hagiography Society since 2019 and as an Advisory Council Member of the Bollandist Society, and has received research support from the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Women's Studies in Religion Program at Harvard Divinity School, and the Franciscan Institute at St. Bonaventure University, where she held the Joseph A. Doino Visiting Professorship of Franciscan Studies in 2009.

Mooney's contribution to the study of Angela of Foligno is foundational. Her essay "The Authorial Role of Brother A. in the Composition of Angela of Foligno's Revelations" (1994) was among the first sustained arguments that the scribe's mediating and shaping hand must be reckoned with before Angela's Liber can be read as an unmediated record of her voice — a position that helped set the terms for the "male scribe, female voice" debate later taken up by Dalarun, Coakley, and others. She returned to Angela in "The Changing Fortunes of Angela of Foligno, Daughter, Mother and Wife" (2007) and in "Interdisciplinarity in Teaching Medieval Mysticism: The Case of Angela of Foligno" (Horizons 34.1, 2007).

Morey, Charles Rufus

Hastings, Michigan, 20 November 1877 – Princeton, New Jersey, 28 August 1955

Morey was born in Hastings, Michigan, on 20 November 1877, and died in Princeton, New Jersey, on 28 August 1955. He graduated Phi Beta Kappa from the University of Michigan in 1899 and took his Master's degree there in Classics the following year, then held a three-year fellowship at the American School of Classical Studies in Rome. His first article, "The Christian Sarcophagus in S. Maria Antiqua," appeared in 1905. Those Roman years matter: he came to medieval art as a classicist, and the question that occupied him for fifty years — how antique form mutates into medieval form — was set by that training. Notably, he never took a doctorate.

He arrived at Princeton in 1903 as an instructor in Classics, and in 1906 Allan Marquand, founder and chairman of the Department of Art and Archaeology, invited him to transfer; this began a thirty-nine- year career in art history. He was made full professor in 1918, and on Marquand's death in 1924 succeeded him as chairman.

His institutional achievements outweigh, in the long run, his individual publications:

  • The Index of Christian Art, which grew out of an image collection of late antique, early Christian and medieval works he assembled in 1917; he handed its direction to his student Helen M. Woodruff in 1933. It survives as the Index of Medieval Art.
  • A deliberate programme of hiring his own medievalist students into the department — Albert M. Friend (1921), Ernest DeWald (1925), W. Frederick Stohlman (1929), Donald Drew Egbert (1935) — and, in 1935, the German refugee Kurt Weitzmann, welcomed warmly despite having published a book arguing against an early work of Morey's.
  • The Vatican Museo Sacro catalogue, begun in 1929; Morey wrote the ivories volume himself and distributed the others to Stohlman and Princeton colleagues. The first volume appeared in 1936, translated into Italian by Margaret Scolari Barr.
  • The "Laboratory-Library" pamphlet of 1932, a rethinking of the research library that combined faculty offices and student space; its ideas shaped both Firestone Library and the Marquand Library.
  • The Antioch excavations at Daphne, organised as a joint American–French campaign.
  • He was a founding member of the College Art Association and sat on its editorial board from 1922 to 1939, serving as its principal fundraiser.

In 1938 he was named to the Marquand Chair of Art and Archaeology.

His methodological breakthrough was "Sources of Mediaeval Style," Art Bulletin 7 (1924): 35–58 — a piece Panofsky said startled art historians as Kepler's work had startled astronomers. The two synthetic books of 1942, Early Christian Art and Medieval Art, restated the same thesis: that medieval style was formed by the interaction of three traditions — Hellenistic naturalism, Latin realism, and what he called "Celto-Germanic dynamism." It is a schema of continental temperaments rather than of workshops, and that is precisely where it has dated.

The Terence corpus belongs to this same period: The Miniatures of the Manuscripts of Terence Prior to the Thirteenth Century, with Leslie Webber Jones, Princeton University Press, 1930–31. The Adelricus/Corvey argument is a good specimen of Morey's method and its limits — a bold stylistic-genealogical reconstruction, later dismantled by Bischoff's palaeography.

He resigned the Princeton chair in 1945 to become the first Cultural Attaché at the American Embassy in Rome, assisted by Stohlman; Weitzmann succeeded him as department chairman. He worked on the repatriation of looted works of art, and — recognising that the great scholarly libraries in Rome were German-owned and therefore vulnerable — created a holding company, the International Union of the Archaeological and Historical Institutes of Rome, to preserve the collections of the Bibliotheca Hertziana and the Deutsches Archäologisches Institut. He was also Acting Director of the American Academy in Rome from 1945 to 1947. He was married to Sara Frances Tupper.

The Dictionary of Art Historians puts it bluntly: his writings, groundbreaking in their moment, proved less durable than those of contemporaries, and his datings of medieval objects have been superseded. What endured was the Index and the students — Walter W. S. Cook, George H. Forsyth Jr., Harald Ingholt, Glanville Downey, David Robbins Coffin, Joseph C. Sloane and others; Panofsky credited him personally with the fact that art history holds an undisputed place in American institutions.

Moskowitz, Anita Fiderer

b. 1937

Anita Fiderer Moskowitz is among the leading Anglophone authorities on Italian late-medieval and Renaissance sculpture, and Professor Emerita of Art at Stony Brook University (SUNY). Over four decades she has done as much as any scholar writing in English to establish Italian Gothic sculpture as a coherent field of study in its own right and, in a distinct second phase of her career, to open up the history of forgery, imitation, and the art market that grew up around Renaissance sculpture in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. For anyone working on the Pisano tradition, on Trecento tomb-shrines, or on the Lombard sculpture of Giovanni di Balduccio, her books are foundational reference points.

Life and training

She was born in Austria in 1937 and became an American scholar, taking her PhD at New York University's Institute of Fine Arts, one of the principal American centers for the study of Italian art. Her teaching career passed through adjunct appointments at Brooklyn College (CUNY), Union College, and Cooper Union before she settled at the State University of New York at Stony Brook, where she rose from assistant professor (from 1981) to associate professor and then full professor of art, and served for a time as director of graduate studies. She is now Professor Emerita there. Her birth in Austria and emigration place her within the notable cohort of Central-European-born scholars who shaped the study of Italian art in the American academy.

The sculpture scholarship

Moskowitz's core body of work is devoted to Italian sculpture of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, above all the tradition inaugurated by Nicola Pisano and carried forward by his successors.

Her early monograph, The Sculpture of Andrea and Nino Pisano (1986), treated two artists who had been comparatively neglected, arguing that their work stands at the meeting point of two great currents: the late diffusion of the Parisian court style and the emergence of a distinctively Italian sculptural language. She returned repeatedly to the Pisani across her career, including a study of the great pulpits of Nicola and Giovanni Pisano and a monograph on the facade reliefs of Orvieto Cathedral (Harvey Miller, 2005).

The book most directly relevant to the Lombard material is Nicola Pisano's Arca di San Domenico and Its Legacy (Pennsylvania State University Press, for the College Art Association, 1994). It analyzes the tomb-shrine of St Dominic, designed by Nicola Pisano in the 1260s for San Domenico in Bologna, not merely as a formal object but in relation to the specific concerns and controversies of the Dominican Order in the mid-thirteenth century, reading its unusual iconography against contemporary religious debate. Crucially, the book then traces the monument's legacy: the two most important descendants she identifies are Giovanni di Balduccio's Arca di San Pietro Martire in Sant'Eustorgio, Milan, and the Arca di Sant'Agostino in Pavia by a follower of Balduccio. Her sustained interest in Giovanni di Balduccio is also reflected in a dedicated article, "Giovanni di Balduccio's Arca di San Pietro Martire: Form and Function" (1991). This is the strand of her work that connects directly to the sculptural culture of Visconti Milan.
