Her most ambitious synthesis is the survey Italian Gothic Sculpture, c. 1250-c. 1400 (Cambridge University Press, 2001), which follows the tradition from Nicola Pisano's arrival in Tuscany around 1260 through the end of the fourteenth century, ranging across central Italy, Naples and Campania, Lombardy, and the Veneto. Its governing argument is a revisionist one, and it is the thesis for which she is best known: Italian Gothic sculpture is neither a provincial offshoot of Northern (French) Gothic nor a mere preparation for the Early Renaissance, but a body of work with its own distinctive visual language and syntax, deserving to be understood on its own terms. That framing, against both the "provincial" and the "proto-Renaissance" readings, has shaped how the period is taught and discussed.

The turn to forgery and the art market

In the later part of her career Moskowitz turned to a related but methodologically different subject: the fortunes of Renaissance sculpture in the modern imagination, and the questions of authenticity, imitation, and forgery that attend it. Beginning research at the National Gallery of Art in Washington in the early 2000s, she produced Forging Authenticity: Bastianini and the Neo-Renaissance in Nineteenth-Century Florence (Leo S. Olschki, 2013), a study of Giovanni Bastianini, arguably the most gifted nineteenth-century Florentine imitator of Renaissance sculpture, and the center of an authenticity controversy that has never entirely subsided. She situates Bastianini's pseudo-Renaissance production within the economic, political, and cultural context of the Risorgimento and the market of European and American collectors hungry for the aura of a lost golden age.

She followed this with Stefano Bardini, "principe degli antiquari": Prolegomenon to a Biography (Centro Di, 2015), the first English-language study of one of the most important and elusive Italian antiquarian dealers of the period between the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, tracing Bardini's dealings with collectors and museums across Europe and America. Together these books mark a shift from object-centered connoisseurship toward the history of taste, the sociology of the art market, and the problem of authenticity, a natural extension of a career spent looking very hard at how sculpture is made, copied, and attributed.

Honours and standing

Moskowitz has held a fellowship at Villa I Tatti (the Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies), three fellowships from the National Endowment for the Humanities (1988-89, 1993-94, and 2003-04), and a Visiting Senior Fellowship at the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts (CASVA) at the National Gallery of Art in 2003, where her research on Bastianini began.

Significance

Two things distinguish her contribution. The first is her insistence, most fully argued in the Cambridge survey, that Italian Gothic sculpture has an autonomous artistic identity, a corrective to older narratives that treated it as either derivative of France or merely a runway toward Donatello. The second is her characteristic method: reading monuments functionally and contextually, in relation to the religious orders, patrons, and controversies that produced them, rather than through style alone, an approach exemplified by the Arca di San Domenico book. Her late work on forgery and the market adds a third dimension, turning the tools of connoisseurship back on the very practices of attribution and authentication. For research on Trecento tomb sculpture and its Lombard diffusion, Giovanni di Balduccio and the world of Sant'Eustorgio and Visconti Milan, she remains an essential guide.

Selected bibliography

  • The Sculpture of Andrea and Nino Pisano (Cambridge University Press, 1986)
  • "Giovanni di Balduccio's Arca di San Pietro Martire: Form and Function" (article, 1991)
  • Nicola Pisano's Arca di San Domenico and Its Legacy (Pennsylvania State University Press / College Art Association, 1994)
  • Italian Gothic Sculpture, c. 1250-c. 1400 (Cambridge University Press, 2001)
  • The Facade Reliefs of Orvieto Cathedral (Harvey Miller, 2005)
  • Nicola and Giovanni Pisano: The Pulpits (study of the Pisano pulpits)
  • Forging Authenticity: Bastianini and the Neo-Renaissance in Nineteenth-Century Florence (Leo S. Olschki, 2013)
  • Stefano Bardini, "principe degli antiquari": Prolegomenon to a Biography (Centro Di, 2015)

Moss, Rachel

active 21st century

Rachel Moss is an Irish art historian and professor in the Department of History of Art and Architecture at Trinity College Dublin, where she became a fellow in 2022 and now serves as head of department. Her research centers on medieval Ireland, and especially on Insular art, medieval Irish Gospel books, and monastic history, examined through iconography, materials and methods, and the political and cultural settings in which such objects were made and used. She has been president of the Royal Society of Antiquaries of Ireland (elected 2013) and a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London since 2011.

Moss edited Art and Architecture of Ireland, Volume 1: Medieval c. 400–c. 1600 (Yale University Press, 2014), the standard modern synthesis of the field, and has since published An Insular Odyssey: Manuscript Culture in Early Christian Ireland and Beyond (Four Courts Press, 2017, co-edited), The Book of Durrow (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Modest and Civil People: Religion and Society in Medieval Galway (Four Courts Press, 2022), and, most recently, the co-edited Irish and Scottish Art, c. 900–1900: Survivals and Revivals (Edinburgh University Press, 2024), winner of the Historians of British Art Book Award for Exemplary Multi-authored Book.

With the Library's Keeper of Preservation and Conservation, Susie Bioletti, Moss directed the art-historical dimension of the Trinity College Dublin conservation and digitisation campaign — carried out between roughly 2014 and 2017 with support from the Bank of America Merrill Lynch Art Conservation Project — that comprehensively examined, conserved, and digitised four of the college's early Gospel books: the Codex Usserianus Primus, the Codex Usserianus Secundus (the Garland of Howth), the Book of Dimma, and the Book of Mulling. Bioletti and Moss co-authored an account of the project, Early Irish Gospel Books in the Library of Trinity College, Dublin (2016). The campaign was among the first to subject the Garland of Howth to sustained art-historical attention, a manuscript till then almost unknown to art historians, and Moss's contribution argued that its scribes and artists had drawn on exemplars of markedly different date and type, situating the book's modest, composite decoration within the wider circulation of models, materials, and technique across the Insular scriptoria.

Mouriki, Doula

Ampelokepi (Aigion), 1934 - Athens, 25 November 1991

Doula Mouriki was one of the most distinguished Greek Byzantinologists of the twentieth century, whose pioneering scholarship on Byzantine mosaics, frescoes, and icons transformed the field of medieval art history. Her career broke several academic barriers for women while producing enduring research on the visual culture of the Orthodox world.

Mouriki was born in 1934 in Ampelokepi, a village near the city of Aigion in the Peloponnese, the second of four children. Her father was a doctor and her mother a schoolteacher, a background that helped shape her intellectual vocation. In 1952 she moved to Athens to attend the University of Athens, where she came under the influence of a distinguished generation of Greek Byzantinists, including Professors Orlandos, Zakythinos, and Vlachos, and graduated with a degree in history and archaeology in 1956.

Her formation was decisively enriched by a scholarship year (1956-1957) at the Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes and the College de France in Paris, where she studied under two major figures of Byzantine scholarship: Andre Grabar and Paul Lemerle. On returning to Athens, she earned a second diploma in French literature from the University of Athens in 1958, reflecting an intellectual breadth that would mark all of her subsequent work.

In the early 1960s Mouriki joined the staff of the National Archaeological Museum of Athens and subsequently became a principal research assistant under Manolis Hatzidakis at the Byzantine and Christian Museum, a post she held from 1961 to 1965. In 1964, preparations were underway for the landmark Council of Europe exhibition Byzantine Art, An European Art, held at the Zappeion in Athens. Mouriki personally wrote 237 of the 740 catalogue entries, a remarkable contribution that attracted the attention of visiting international scholars such as Kurt Weitzmann, Hugo Buchthal, and Cyril Mango. The friendships forged during that exhibition led directly to her decision to pursue doctoral studies at Princeton University with Weitzmann.

Mouriki arrived at Princeton in 1965 and spent two years as a Junior Fellow at Dumbarton Oaks while writing her dissertation. She earned an MFA in 1968 and a PhD in 1970, completing a doctoral thesis entitled The Octateuch Miniatures of the Byzantine Manuscripts of Cosmas Indicopleustes, a meticulous study of miniature cycles in illustrated manuscripts of the Christian cosmographer Cosmas Indicopleustes. With this degree she became the first woman to earn a PhD from Princeton University's Department of Art and Archaeology.

After returning to Athens, Mouriki briefly worked at the Ethnikon Idruma Ereunon before taking a position in 1972 teaching art history at the National Technical University of Athens, where she remained for the rest of her career. She became the first woman to hold the rank of full professor in the university's School of Architecture, another landmark achievement in an era when women in academic leadership were rare.

Her research ranged across three principal areas: Middle Byzantine mosaics, Palaiologan monumental painting in Greece, and late medieval Cypriot icons. She was also deeply interested in the development of regional schools of medieval Orthodox painting, exploring how local workshops across the Byzantine world developed distinct stylistic identities while remaining connected to metropolitan Constantinople. She additionally produced important papers on Georgian fresco cycles, extending her comparative reach beyond the Greek-speaking world. Much of her work addressed Byzantine and Orthodox iconography, including representations of the Virgin Mary across different media and periods.

Mouriki's scholarly output was as broad in geography as it was in medium. Her 1975 monograph The Frescoes of the Church of St. Nicholas at Platsa in the Mani established her credentials as a leading interpreter of provincial Byzantine wall painting. Her 1981 article "Stylistic Trends in Monumental Painting of Greece during the Eleventh and Twelfth Centuries," published in Dumbarton Oaks Papers, remains a foundational text for the study of Middle Byzantine painting programs in Greek provincial churches. In 1978 she co-authored, with Hans Belting and Cyril Mango, The Mosaics and Frescoes of St. Mary Pammakaristos (Fethiye Camii) at Istanbul, a detailed analysis of one of the most important surviving Palaiologan decorative programs.

Her 1985 monograph The Mosaics of Nea Moni on Chios is widely regarded as her magnum opus. The Nea Moni, an eleventh-century imperial monastery endowed by Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, preserves one of the finest intact mosaic programs of the Middle Byzantine period, and Mouriki's exhaustive study of its iconographic program, stylistic sources, and workshop organization set the standard for all subsequent scholarship on the monument. The book was awarded the prestigious Gottfried von Herder Award in 1987. Her 1986 volume Thirteenth-Century Icon Painting in Cyprus addressed the rich and understudied tradition of Crusader-era icon production on the island, and in 1991 she co-edited with Slobodan Curcic The Twilight of Byzantium: Aspects of Cultural and Religious History in the Late Byzantine Empire.

Mouriki also served as a corresponding member of the Istituto di Studi Bizantini e Neogreci, as a member of the administrative council of the Greek Archaeological Society, and on an advisory committee to the Greek Ministry of Culture for the preservation of the historic monuments at Mistra. She died on 25 November 1991 in Athens, at the age of 57, cutting short a career that had lasted barely three decades but had transformed understanding of Byzantine visual culture. In her memory, a volume of essays was published in 1999 under the title Medieval Cyprus: Studies in Art, Architecture, and History in Memory of Doula Mouriki, edited by Nancy Patterson Sevcenko and Christopher Moss. Her posthumous collection Studies in Late Byzantine Painting brought together eight of her most influential essays, ensuring that her synthesis of stylistic analysis and iconographic interpretation would remain accessible to future generations of scholars.

Muller, Norman E.

active 20th–21st century

Norman E. Muller is an American paintings conservator and technical art historian long associated with the Princeton University Art Museum, where he built a career devoted to the close physical examination of early Italian panel paintings — their wooden supports, joinery, ground preparation, and painted stratigraphy — as a source of evidence independent of, and sometimes in tension with, purely stylistic analysis.

Muller's technical studies have repeatedly resolved questions of function and construction that connoisseurship alone could not settle. His 2025 article in the Zeitschrift für Kunstgeschichte on Luca di Tommè's Crucifixion at Montepulciano, the only known Sienese Trecento painting on cloth, examined the glued mounting of the linen support on its wooden strainer and argued, against the picture's long-standing interpretation as a processional banner, that its construction is consistent only with a fixed, single devotional image — a conclusion reached through material examination rather than stylistic comparison.

Mullins, Elizabeth

active late 20th – 21st century

Elizabeth Mullins is an Irish art historian specialising in the illumination and decorative apparatus of early medieval Irish gospel books. Her research on the Eusebian canon tables added to the Book of Mulling (Trinity College Dublin MS 60) — apparatus absent from the original core of that manuscript, as it is from the Book of Dimma, but supplied to it at a later stage — has clarified how members of the pocket gospel book group diverged from, and at points converged toward, the fuller display apparatus found in grander Insular gospel books such as the Book of Kells.

Her work situates the pocket gospels within the wider comparative study of Insular manuscript decoration inaugurated by Patrick McGurk's 1956 article and continued by later codicologists working on the group.

Murat, Zuleika

active 21st century

Zuleika Murat completed her MA in History of Art in 2007 and her PhD in the Study, Conservation and Enhancement of the Cultural Heritage in 2013, both at the University of Padova, an institution with which she has maintained a deep and continuous scholarly bond. Her doctoral research laid the groundwork for what would become a career defined by methodological innovation and a sustained engagement with the material, sensory, and devotional dimensions of medieval visual culture.

Following the completion of her doctorate, Murat received postdoctoral research fellowships from the University of Warwick (2013-2014) and the University of Padova (2014-2016), and was also appointed Teaching Assistant at Birkbeck, University of London, in 2015 and 2018. These formative years abroad enriched her scholarly profile with a comparative, pan-European perspective that later proved central to the design of her major funded projects.

Murat is Associate Professor of History of Medieval Art in the Department of Cultural Heritage at the University of Padova. She teaches MA-level modules on Visual and Material Culture in Medieval Europe and BA-level teaching on Making Art in Medieval Italy within Italian Medieval and Renaissance Studies.

Before winning European-level funding, Murat distinguished herself within the University of Padova's internal research landscape. In 2017 she won a STARS grant for ILAPA, leading a two-year multidisciplinary research project (2018-2020) as Principal Investigator. She has described that experience as decisive training for her later ERC success, both in proposal design and in presenting herself as an already established PI.

A crucial turning point in Murat's research emerged from an archival encounter while she was studying wood reliquary caskets produced in fourteenth-century Venice. In a 1489 pilgrim's chronicle, she found a report that a devotee's response had been triggered by the sweet smell emanating from one of the caskets. That detail prompted Murat to ask whether looking alone was the right way to grasp such artworks, and led her to rethink how medieval objects exerted agency and how their worshippers experienced them.

This question became the seed of SenSArt. Murat is Principal Investigator of the ERC Starting Grant project SenSArt - The Sensuous Appeal of the Holy. Sensory Agency of Sacred Art and Somatised Spiritual Experiences in Medieval Europe (12th-15th century) (2021-2026), funded under the European Union's Horizon 2020 programme with a total budget of EUR 1,499,328. The project investigates both quantitatively and qualitatively the perceptual schemes that oriented the reception of sacred art, studying how artworks solicited beholders through multiple sensory inputs and how, through sensorial stimulation or deprivation, they exercised social agency.

Murat's theoretical framework draws in part on Michael Baxandall's concept of the "period eye," extending it toward a reconstruction of a medieval "period sensorium" through the combined study of texts and objects. In this way, SenSArt seeks to recover how sacred art was experienced by medieval beholders and to expand the study of medieval visual culture beyond purely iconographic or stylistic analysis.

Alongside SenSArt, Murat serves as Principal Investigator of the FARE project SIDME - Sensory Impairment and Disability in Medieval Europe: Inclusive Approaches for Studying the Experience of Art (2022-2027). This five-year multidisciplinary project develops interpretive and inclusive analytical frameworks for studying how art was experienced by individuals with sensory and physical disabilities in medieval Europe, combining Disability Studies, Sensory Studies, and Material Culture Studies. Among its core lines of inquiry is the therapeutic agency of artworks in relation to healing objects and practices intended for people with impairments.

Murat's broader research has brought together sacred topography, church interiors as social constructions, gender, relics and devotion, visual and material culture in Western Christianity, domestic devotion, liturgy, the senses, and the history of disability and impairment. Across these areas, her work consistently approaches medieval art as something embodied, material, and experientially charged.

Her scholarly output includes monographs, edited volumes, and journal articles. Among the most notable are the co-edited volume English Alabaster Carvings and their Cultural Contexts (2019), with Luca Palozzi, Nigel Ramsay, and Andrew Kirkman; the article Contexts and Receptions of English Alabasters: Symbolic Meanings, Material Qualities, Aesthetic Values in Musica & Figura 9 (2022), pp. 9-34; the co-edited volume Pregare in casa. Oggetti e documenti della pratica religiosa tra Medioevo e Rinascimento (2018), with Giovanna Baldissin Molli and Cristina Guarnieri; the essay Il Paradiso dei Carraresi. Propaganda politica e magnificenza dinastica nelle pitture di Guariento a Sant'Agostino (2013); and the co-edited volume Il patriarcato di Aquileia. Identità, liturgia e arte (secoli V-XV), with Paolo Vedovetto. She also co-edits, with Teresa Martínez Martínez, the Brepols Gold Open Access series The Senses and Material Culture in a Global Perspective.

Murat is a member of the Governing Council of the Centro Interdipartimentale di Ricerca di Filosofia Medievale "Carlo Giacon" (CIRFIM), a member of the Accademia Galileiana di Scienze, Lettere ed Arti in Padova, a member of the Istituto Pio Paschini per la Storia Religiosa in Friuli, and a member of AcademiaNet following nomination by the Swiss National Science Foundation.

Murat stands among the most innovative medievalists currently working in Europe. By redirecting the study of medieval sacred art toward a sensory and experiential framework, and by pairing that work with a major project on disability and impairment, she has opened a new methodological horizon at the intersection of art history, liturgical studies, cognitive approaches, and disability studies. Her research is especially important for scholars concerned with the devotional, material, and embodied dimensions of medieval visual culture.

Mütherich, Florentine

1915–2015

Florentine Mütherich was an internationally recognised authority on early medieval book illumination and treasury art, whose expertise was drawn on by libraries, museums and the art trade alike. Her life's work was the edition of illuminated manuscripts of the Carolingian and Ottonian periods, which she made accessible both in commentary volumes to facsimile editions and in the eight-volume corpus of the Karolingische Miniaturen.

She was born on 26 January 1915 in Bestwig, a railwaymen's village on the upper Ruhr in Westphalia, and raised there. Her father Franz Mütherich, a railway worker from Enkhausen near Meschede, died in a field hospital on the Galician front in the year of her birth; her mother remarried in 1920. After the Abitur at the Oberlyzeum in Arnsberg in February 1935, and several weeks of compulsory labour service, she began studying art history, archaeology and history at Bonn in the same year. When Paul Clemen (1866–1947) retired she moved in 1936 to Königsberg, completing the so-called Ostsemester that qualified her for a place in Berlin, where from the winter semester of 1936/37 she studied art history with Wilhelm Pinder (1878–1947) and classical archaeology with Gerhart Rodenwaldt (1886–1945). Her dissertation on the ornament of Rhenish goldsmiths' work in the Hohenstaufen period — a subject suggested by the Cologne art historian Hermann Schnitzler (1905–1976) — earned her the doctorate under Pinder in 1940, though she kept her distance from his völkisch-nationalist positions.

From 1941 to 1945 she worked in monument conservation, on the inventory of architectural and artistic monuments in the Mark Brandenburg. In 1948 she went to the Gräflich Schönbornsche Bibliothek at Schloss Pommersfelden to catalogue medieval manuscripts.

In 1949 a research grant from the state of North Rhine-Westphalia took her to the newly founded Zentralinstitut für Kunstgeschichte in Munich, where in 1954 she was appointed a permanent research staff member. Her fellowship ran until 30 June 1954. She gave energetic support to the founding director Ludwig Heinrich Heydenreich (1903–1978) and helped make the Zentralinstitut a name in international scholarship. Until 1970 she also edited the Kunstchronik, which had appeared since 1948 and which she rapidly built into an internationally respected organ of reviews and reports for the discipline. She remained at the institute until her retirement in 1980. These years also brought her collaboration with the Göttingen historian Percy Ernst Schramm (1894–1970), which produced in 1962 the first volume of Denkmale der deutschen Könige und Kaiser — a much-noticed publication that became a standard work and appeared in an enlarged second edition in 1981.

The decisive turn came through Wilhelm Koehler. Koehler had resumed the corpus of the Karolingische Miniaturen in 1954 after war and exile; after his sudden death in 1959, Mütherich took over the continuation of the edition project, with its comprehensive palaeographical, codicological and text-critical investigations. Work on the Karolingische Miniaturen was to become her life's work, reaching a provisional conclusion in 2013 with a supplementary volume to the seven volumes devoted to the individual schools and groups. The volumes she saw through the press under the joint imprint with Koehler are: vol. 4, Die Hofschule Kaiser Lothars. Einzelhandschriften aus Lotharingien (1971); vol. 5, Die Hofschule Karls des Kahlen (1982); vol. 6, Die Schule von Reims, in two parts (1994–1999); vol. 7, Die frankosächsische Schule (2009); and vol. 8, Nachträge – Gesamtregister (2013). She also wrote the Neue Deutsche Biographie article on Koehler himself, published in 1980.

Meanwhile she contributed to the great Council of Europe exhibition Karl der Große at Aachen in 1965, writing the essay on book illumination at the Carolingian court for the accompanying publication. That essay — "Die Buchmalerei am Hofe Karls des Großen," in Wolfgang Braunfels and Hermann Schnitzler, eds., Karl der Große. Lebenswerk und Nachleben, vol. 3: Karolingische Kunst (1965), pp. 9–53 — remains a fundamental short account of the Court School.

The Aachen exhibition brought her a teaching appointment at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität in Munich in 1966; she became honorary professor there in 1969 and taught continuously until 1980. Research stays at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton followed in 1966 and 1971; in 1967 came the call to a visiting professorship at Columbia University in New York, to which she returned at intervals until 1982. Harvard and All Souls College, Oxford, each secured her for a semester, in 1975 and 1983 respectively. She was elected a corresponding member of the Medieval Academy of America in 1975, and received the Verdienstkreuz of the Federal Republic in 1991 and the Bavarian Order of Merit in 1993.

At the centre of her research stood the scholarly opening-up of illuminated manuscripts of the Carolingian, Ottonian and Romanesque periods, attested not least by her commentary volumes to major facsimile editions: the Stuttgart Psalter (1968), the Metz Sacramentary fragment (1972), the Gospels of Otto III (1978), the Leiden Aratea (1989), and the Bible of Charles the Bald from San Paolo fuori le Mura in Rome (1993). Methodologically, the broad interdisciplinary approach set by the Karolingische Miniaturen remained characteristic. The integration of text-critical and palaeographical analysis founded long and intensive collaborations with scholars such as Bonifatius Fischer OSB (1915–1997) and Bernhard Bischoff (1906–1991). That combination of art-historical connoisseurship with palaeography and biblical textual criticism is her most distinctive legacy, and it is what makes her volumes usable as research instruments rather than merely as descriptive catalogues.

She also made pioneering contributions to early medieval treasury art, above all the classification of the ivory decoration on the throne of Charles the Bald — the so-called Cathedra Petri in St Peter's — for whose extraction from Bernini's casing she was called in as a consultant in 1968.

Her students included Katharina Bierbrauer, Matthias Exner (1957–2020), Gude Suckale-Redlefsen, Ulrike Bauer-Eberhardt, Hans-Caspar Graf von Bothmer and Jolanda Drexler. She corresponded and maintained close friendships with Ernst Kitzinger, Francis Wormald, Kurt Weitzmann, Carl Nordenfalk, Hermann Fillitz and Joachim E. Gaehde, among many others; the extensive correspondence still awaits scholarly cataloguing.

She never married and had no children. She remained active with great discipline to the end — her publication list extends into her final years — and died on 12 June 2015 in Munich of a lung complaint, a few months after an academic celebration of her hundredth birthday. She is buried in the Velmede cemetery in her home community of Bestwig.

N

Nardinocchi, Elisabetta

active late 20th-21st century

Elisabetta Nardinocchi is an Italian art historian specializing in contemporary art, Christian art, iconography, and medieval sacred goldsmithing, as well as one of the leading experts on the work and legacy of the British collector and art historian Herbert Percy Horne. She is currently the Director of the Horne Museum in Florence, an institution of which she is also a member of the Foundation.

Nardinocchi teaches Christian Art, Symbolism, and Iconography of Sacred Goldsmithing, fields that reflect a background rooted in medieval religious visual culture and the history of liturgical objects. Her expertise thus spans both art history in the broadest sense and the history of sacred objects - an unusual profile that places her at the intersection of art history, Church history, and material culture. She has led tours and given lectures in collaboration with leading cultural institutions, including the Biblioteca dell'Accademia della Crusca and the British Institute of Florence.

The Horne Museum, located at Via de' Benci 6 in Florence, houses the extraordinary collection that Herbert Percy Horne (1864-1916) bequeathed to the Italian State upon his death, comprising 14th- and 15th-century panel paintings, sculptures, antiquities, and a substantial documentary archive.

Nardinocchi oversees the conservation and promotion of this heritage, while also supervising the Foundation's historical archive, which is accessible to scholars upon request with a letter of introduction. In recent years, she has overseen the restoration of the portrait of Herbert Percy Horne, an occasion on which she highlighted Florence's debt to the cultured and passionate foreigners who chose it as their second home, committing themselves to the protection of its art and urban fabric.

Among her major editorial contributions is the editing of the proceedings of the conference Herbert Percy Horne and Florence (Edizioni della Meridiana, 2005), the first comprehensive work dedicated to Horne in the Italian academic sphere.

She edited and authored the official guide to the Horne Museum (Polistampa, 2011), which remains the reference tool for visitors and scholars of the museum. In 2013, together with art historian Matilde Casati, she curated the exhibition and its accompanying catalog Horne & Friends: Florence, a Dream to Save (Horne Museum, May 27-December 7, 2013), an exhibition project that linked Horne to the network of foreign intellectuals and collectors who gravitated toward early 20th-century Florence. Together with Casati, she co-edited a publication featuring new photographic documentation and essays dedicated to the museum, highlighted in the newsletter of the Friends of Florence Foundation in 2023. She also wrote the entry Herbert Percy Horne for Treccani's Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, an authoritative recognition of her role as Italy's leading scholar of Horne.

Nardinocchi is an active participant in Florentine academic life. In 2022, she participated in the conference Herbert Horne: A New Perspective on the Unity of the Arts, held at Villa Bardini as part of the events organized by the Fondazione CR Firenze. Her collaboration with Francesco Caglioti, full professor of Medieval Art History at the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa, attests to the ties she cultivates with the high-level academic world. She recently shared with the public in-depth insights and previously unknown facts about Horne on the occasion of the restoration of his portrait, presented in 2026.

Nassar, Magdi A.M.

Peccioli, 8 April 1994

Magdi A.M. Nassar is a remarkably versatile intellectual, active in Tuscany and the Italian scholarly landscape as a researcher in history, numismatics, and medieval art history, while also maintaining a professional career in the business sector.

Born on 8 April 1994, Nassar grew up in Peccioli, in the province of Pisa. He graduated from the F. Niccolini Institute in Volterra, a city that later became central to his scholarly work. He then began university studies at the Faculty of Architecture of the University of Florence, where he enrolled in a master's degree program. His formation is therefore rooted in the humanities, with strong ties to Tuscany and its historical heritage.

Nassar is a member of the Italian Numismatic Society, a member of the Accademia dei Sepolti di Volterra, and National President of the Young Numismatists' Circle. His Academia.edu profile, linked to the University of Florence, presents him as a scholar of numismatics, history, and art history with a substantial publication record.

His best-known book is Le monete di Arezzo (2017), the first monographic study of the Arezzo mint from the Middle Ages to the modern era, where he proposes new attributions and datings by connecting coin production to the city's political and economic history. The volume received the 2017 NIA Literary Prize. This was followed by Le monete di Volterra. Il Medioevo e l'età moderna (Varesi Edizioni), dedicated to the coinage of the Volterra mint.

In 2025, he published a study in the Rivista Italiana di Numismatica e Scienze Affini titled La zecca medievale di Chiusi (XIII-XIV secolo). Aggiornamenti storico-numismatici e studio sui coni (pp. 175-219), reconstructing the historical-economic context of Chiusi in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries and analyzing surviving dies. He has also worked on the mint of Casole d'Elsa with the essay Sulla zecca di Casole e sul denaro del vescovo Ranuccio: monete, poteri comunali e faide familiari nella Toscana del Trecento.

For medieval art history, his essay on the Master of the Castelfiorentino Cross is especially relevant. That study addresses an anonymous thirteenth-century painter associated with the Volterra area and demonstrates Nassar's competence in attributional problems central to research on Duecento and Trecento Tuscan painting.

On the civic side, Nassar ran for mayor of Peccioli in 2019, receiving 46% of the vote, and served as minority council leader in the Municipality of Peccioli until 2024. In parallel, since 2013, he has worked as Sales Master for NIMS S.p.A., a Lavazza Group company in the coffee distribution sector.

Nassar thus represents a rare profile: a self-taught and highly committed scholar who, outside traditional academic structures, has produced recognized scientific contributions published in specialized national journals.

Nees, Lawrence

active late 20th-21st century

Lawrence Nees is an American art historian, Professor at the University of Delaware, and one of the most prolific and wide-ranging contemporary scholars of early medieval art, spanning the Insular, Carolingian, and broader Mediterranean traditions. His book Early Medieval Art (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2002), in the Oxford History of Art series, is a widely used synthetic account of the period, and his numerous articles have addressed questions of form, function, and meaning in early medieval illustrated manuscripts.

Nees has written specifically on the problem of form and function in early medieval illustrated Bibles from northwestern Europe, a body of work directly relevant to the Codex Amiatinus's prefatory quire. On the vexed question of the identity of the seated scribe in the manuscript's celebrated Ezra miniature, Nees has found Paul Meyvaert's positive reconstruction of a Wearmouth-Jarrow origin only partly persuasive, while agreeing that Rupert Bruce-Mitford's earlier hypothesis of a relabelled Cassiodorus self-portrait does not convince either — a position of careful, undogmatic skepticism that reflects the genuinely unsettled state of the question. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the Ezra portrait debate.

Neuss, Wilhelm

Montabaur, 24 July 1880 – Bonn, 31 December 1965

Wilhelm Neuss was born in Montabaur on 24 July 1880 and grew up in Aachen. His family background was solidly intellectual: his father, Johann Joseph Neuß (1847–1913), directed the Realgymnasium in Aachen from 1883 to 1913, and a great-uncle on his mother's side was the philosopher and poet Christoph Bernhard Schlüter (1801–1884). Young Wilhelm attended both the Realgymnasium and the Kaiser-Karls- Gymnasium in Aachen before graduating in March 1899.

After obtaining his Abitur, Neuss studied Catholic theology in Münster (1899–1900), Munich (1900–1901), and Bonn (1901–1902), where he was particularly influenced by the historian Heinrich Schroers. He also devoted himself to history and art history alongside his theological training. In the summer semester of 1902 he entered into contact with the Christian archaeologist Karl Künstler (1859–1932) in Freiburg im Breisgau, who drew his attention to the fresco cycle in the double church at Schwarzrheindorf.

During his Bonn years, Neuss was a member of the Catholic student fraternity W.K.St.V. Unitas Rhenania. On 24 August 1903 he was ordained as a priest and later became curate at St. Alban's Church in Cologne. In 1905 he was a religion teacher at the Cologne Ursuline School.

The intellectual trajectory Neuss had begun in Freiburg bore its first major fruit in 1911. Neuss wrote his dissertation on "The Book of Ezekiel in Theology and Art till the End of the 12th Century, with Special Consideration of the Painting in the Church of Schwarzrheindorf". The full publication followed in Münster in 1912.

In 1913 he submitted his post-doctoral habilitation thesis on "Catalan Bible Illustration at the Turn of the First Millennium", a study that signalled his pivotal interest in the Iberian Peninsula as a crucible of early medieval Christian iconography.

In 1917, Neuss was appointed associate professor of Church History at the University of Bonn, and a year later he became director of the Seminar for Christian Archaeology and Art Science in Bonn. From 1920 he held a full professorship in Church History at Bonn, and in 1927 he received the chair for Medieval and Modern Church History as well as the History of Christian Art. During these years he also formed an acquaintance with the constitutional lawyer Carl Schmitt.

The summit of Neuss's scholarly achievement came in 1931 with the publication of his two-volume work Die Apokalypse des hl. Johannes in der altspanischen und altchristlichen Bibel-Illustration: Das Problem der Beatus-Handschriften. It established the foundational classification of the Beatus manuscript tradition, dividing the surviving codices into the textual and pictorial branches (I, IIa, IIb) that scholars would continue to use, refine, and debate for the rest of the century.

Among the seminal studies on the Beatus manuscript group, Neuss's Die Apokalypse remains one of the three corner-stones of the field, alongside Peter Klein's 1976 corpus study and John Williams's five-volume The Illustrated Beatus (1994–2003).

The work was published as part of the Spanische Forschungen series of the Görres-Gesellschaft. Together with Heinrich Finke, Johannes Vincke, and J. Vives, Neuss co-directed this series, positioning German Catholic scholarship at the heart of Iberian medievalism.

Neuss's moral courage during the Third Reich is among the most significant chapters of his biography. In 1934–35, he co-edited the Studien zum Mythus des XX. Jahrhunderts ("Antimythus"), a critical examination of the racial ideology of Alfred Rosenberg. Cardinal Schulte originally prohibited this publication because he feared the possibility of termination of the Reich Concordat, but Münster Bishop Cardinal Clemens August von Galen declared himself willing to include the "Studies" as a contribution to the Church Office Magazine (Amtsblatt). In all, around 200,000 copies of the Studies were published.

After 1933, Neuss also managed to bring numerous artworks to safety, saving them from confiscation by the National Socialists.

From 1938 to 1947, Neuss served as director of the Diocesan Museum in Cologne — the institution that would later become the Kolumba Museum — navigating its collections through the devastation of Allied bombing.

From 1923 to 1965 Neuss was chairman of the "Society for Christian Art in the Archbishopric of Cologne and the Bishopric of Aachen" and thus also chairman of the museum board. From 1935 to 1954 he was chairman of the Society for the Publication of the Corpus Catholicorum. In 1936 he became non-resident curate of Cologne Cathedral.

In 1947, Neuss became a corresponding member of the Institut d'Estudis Catalans. That same year he published Kampf gegen den Mythus des 20. Jahrhunderts. Ein Gedenkblatt an Clemens August Kardinal Graf von Galen.

Neuss was granted emeritus status in 1949. Pope Pius XII appointed him Papal House Prelate on 4 January 1953. In his final years he co-authored (with Friedrich Wilhelm Oediger) the first volume of the history of the Archbishopric of Cologne, covering the period from the foundation of the diocese to the end of the 12th century, published in 1964 by the Kölner Bachem Verlag.

Wilhelm Neuss died in Bonn on 31 December 1965 and was buried in the Bonner Südfriedhof. A street in Bonn was subsequently named in his honour.

For researchers working on medieval illuminated manuscripts, Neuss occupies a place of enduring methodological importance. His approach was rigorously comparative and iconographic: he sought to trace the transmission of biblical imagery across scriptoria, centuries, and regions, reading the visual evidence in conjunction with theological and liturgical texts. His work on the Beatus manuscripts demonstrated that the illustrated Apocalypse commentary tradition of northern Iberia constituted a coherent and classifiable corpus, shaped by distinct textual recensions and connected pictorial archetypes. His habilitation on Catalan Bible illustration and his doctoral study of the Ezekiel iconography at Schwarzrheindorf together show a career built on the intersection of biblical exegesis, monumental painting, and book illumination.

Neri Lusanna, Enrica

active late 20th-21st century

Enrica Neri Lusanna is an Italian art historian, one of the most authoritative living specialists on Italian medieval sculpture, painting, and manuscript illumination, and the scholar most closely identified with the modern reassessment of Arnolfo di Cambio.

Training and early career. She graduated in 1972 under Roberto Salvini at Florence. Between 1974 and 1980 she held fellowships from the Fondazione Roberto Longhi, the Courtauld Institute Summer School in London, and the CNR. From 1981 to 1985 she served as a functionary of the Ministero per i Beni Culturali e Ambientali, attached to the Soprintendenze of Florence and Pistoia. The Longhi/Salvini formation plus soprintendenza fieldwork accounts for the connoisseurial-philological cast of everything she has written since.

Academic career. After teaching at the University of Florence, she became professor ordinario of Storia dell'arte medievale at the University of Perugia. She was elected Accademico Corrispondente of the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in 2009 and Accademico Ordinario in 2014, and presided over its Class of Art History from December 2015 until October 2023. She sits on the scientific committee of Studi di Storia dell'Arte.

Research. Her declared method is philological and interdisciplinary, applied across sculpture, painting, and illumination.

  • Arnolfo di Cambio. Alle origini del Rinascimento fiorentino (Museo dell'Opera del Duomo, Florence, 2005): she conceived and curated the exhibition and edited the catalogue, and has presented Arnolfian material at international conferences before and since, including the study day on the restored Guillaume de Braye monument.
  • Maso di Banco. La cappella di San Silvestro (Electa, 1998): monograph on the Bardi di Vernio chapel in Santa Croce.
  • Pistoia. Un'officina di libri in Toscana (Florence, 2011): study of a Tuscan book-producing workshop.
  • Percorrendo giardini di virtu. Affreschi del Trecento a Firenze nel Canto dei Pecori al Boldrone (2005), with Mirella Branca and Francesca Carrara, and Dante, non-Dante (Paragone, 2014): part of a sustained turn toward civic and secular Trecento fresco cycles.
  • She directed the PRIN 2008 project Testi e contesti. Arti e tecniche a confronto tra Umbria e Marche (XI-XIII secolo) and edited the proceedings, Umbria e Marche in età romanica (Todi, 2013).
  • Co-curator of Bagliori dorati (Uffizi, 2012); contributor to catalogues of Florentine museum exhibitions in 2000, 2008, 2014, and 2015; co-curator with Giordana Benazzi and Elvio Lunghi of the 2018 Gubbio exhibition on art from 1200 to the later Trecento, which reinterpreted Guido di Oderisi, the Maestro Espressionista di Santa Chiara, Palmerino di Guido, and Guiduccio Palmerucci. She also edited Le chiese di Montefollonico: Arte e storia (Olschki, 2019), reviewed in Speculum.

Nessi, Silvestro

active 20th century

Silvestro Nessi was an Italian scholar active in the study of Umbrian medieval painting, especially the Trecento artistic culture of the Trevi-Spoleto area. He is cited in modern historiography as a key contributor to the reconstruction of local artistic personalities otherwise known only through connoisseurship and surviving works.

His best-known intervention is the article I dipinti trecenteschi di Trevi, published in Spoletium 21 (1976), pp. 29-40. In that study he brought critical attention to the monumental painted cross from San Francesco at Trevi and aggregated it to the corpus of the painter now generally known as the Maestro della Croce di Trevi.

This attributional move had long-term historiographical consequences: from Nessi onward, the label "Maestro della Croce di Trevi" became the most stable and widely used name for that anonymous master, replacing or reordering earlier designations tied to other works. Later scholarship has repeatedly returned to Nessi's 1976 proposal when discussing the master's catalogue, chronology, and geographic setting in southern Umbria.

Although his profile in international literature is often linked above all to this specific contribution, Nessi remains an indispensable point of reference for studies of Trevi's medieval painted heritage and for the methodological history of Umbrian connoisseurship in the second half of the twentieth century.

Nicco Fasola, Giusta

Turin, 23 February 1901 - Fiesole, 8 November 1960

Giusta Nicco Fasola was an Italian art historian, philosopher of art, teacher and anti-fascist partisan, author of the monograph on Nicola Pisano that reoriented Italian scholarship on the origins of Tuscan Gothic sculpture.

She was born in Turin on 23 February 1901, the daughter of Carlo Nicco and Marianna Rosa Cumino, and was registered at birth as Giustina Maria Rosa. Her entire education took place in the city: private schooling, then the Regio Ginnasio Massimo D'Azeglio, then the Regia Università degli Studi di Torino, where she took not one degree but two — philosophy on 8 July 1922, and letters on 29 June 1924, the second obtained by enrolling directly in the fourth year immediately after the first. Her final assessment was awarded 110 cum laude.

At Turin she was a pupil of both Adolfo Venturi and Lionello Venturi. The dual training — philosophical and art-historical — is the single most useful fact for reading her later work: she came to medieval sculpture with the habits of an aesthetician, interested less in connoisseurial attribution for its own sake than in the formal and conceptual principles by which a style is constituted. Her degree thesis, on Ravenna and the compositional principles of Byzantine art, was published in L'Arte in 1925.

From 1924 she taught art history, philosophy and pedagogy in a succession of Turin schools — among them the Liceo Classico Cavour, where one of her pupils was the young Giulio Carlo Argan — while serving from 1923 to 1933 as a voluntary assistant to the chair of art history at the university. She passed two state competitions and entered the regular teaching corps in 1927.

In 1934 she married Cesare Fasola (1886-1963), librarian of the Uffizi and later one of the Italian officials who worked with the Allied Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives programme to recover Florentine works displaced during the war. She adopted the name under which she published, Giusta Nicco Fasola, and the couple settled at Fiesole, where both would spend the rest of their careers.

Her first monograph, on Jacopo della Quercia, appeared with Bemporad in 1934. In 1938 the Reale Accademia d'Italia awarded her a Borsa Volta of two thousand lire; at the solemn session of 21 April 1941 the same body gave her its award for the historical sciences, on the strength of her work on Nicola Pisano.

The documentary record here requires care, and is worth stating precisely rather than smoothing over. Nicco Fasola was enrolled in the Partito Nazionale Fascista from 1933 to 1943 — a fact she herself declared on her 1 September 1944 application to the Florence section of the Partito d'Azione, the same document recording that she had been "denounced and kept under surveillance," had conducted clandestine political activity after 8 September 1943, and had belonged to the Partito d'Azione since 1941. PNF membership was in practice a condition of continued state employment in those years; the two facts stand side by side in her own hand.

She was secretary of the Comitato di Liberazione Nazionale of Fiesole and held several posts for the Tuscan committee between 1943 and 1945; after February 1944 she sat on the emergency committee in Florence. She served on the committee that found lodgings for refugees, for those being hunted, and for Jews. She was recognised as a partigiano combattente, having belonged to the Giustizia e Libertà division of Florence, and was awarded the war merit cross. From 1945 to 1947 she sat on the building commission of the Comune di Firenze; in 1948 she and her husband left the Partito d'Azione for the Partito Socialista Italiano.

In the academic year 1944-45 she was given the teaching of Italian literature in the Faculty of Architecture at Florence, a post she herself converted into a chair of estetica e trattatistica dell'architettura — aesthetics and architectural treatise literature — which was judged highly effective in forming the critical conscience of future architects. On 28 February 1949 she was appointed professor of medieval and modern art history at the University of Padua, thereby entering the regular university ranks; in practice she held that chair, first as straordinaria and then as ordinaria, in the Faculty of Letters at Genoa, where she taught until her death and where she is regarded as the founder of art-historical teaching and of the Institute of Art History. She was one of the first women in Italy to hold a university chair in the discipline.

Her published work moves freely between the medieval and the early modern, and between history and theory:

  • Jacopo della Quercia (Florence: Bemporad, 1934)
  • Nicola Pisano. Orientamenti sulla formazione del gusto italiano (Rome: Palombi, 1941)
  • Piero della Francesca, De prospectiva pingendi, critical edition (Florence: Sansoni, 1942)
  • Pontormo o del Cinquecento (Florence: Arnaud, 1947)
  • Ragionamenti sulla architettura (1949)
  • La fontana di Perugia, with Francesco Santi's report on the restoration of 1948-49 (Rome: Libreria dello Stato, 1951)
  • Storiografia del manierismo (Rome: De Luca, 1956)
  • "Giulio Romano e il manierismo," Commentari 11 (1960)

For the study of thirteenth-century sculpture two of these matter most. The Nicola Pisano of 1941 is not a catalogue but an argument: the subtitle, orientamenti sulla formazione del gusto italiano, announces a thesis about how an Italian visual sensibility was constituted, with Nicola as its hinge. Its appendix of documents remains in use — the Sienese charter of 13 March 1284 that records Nicola as already dead is still cited from her edition. La fontana di Perugia (1951) is the fundamental modern study of the Fontana Maggiore, published in the immediate wake of the 1948-49 restoration and still the reference point for any discussion of the division of hands between Nicola and Giovanni across the two basins. Reviewing it, Harald Keller credited her with dislodging working hypotheses that had been favoured for generations; Rudolf Wittkower, writing in The Burlington Magazine in 1953, praised the independence of her readings of father and son from the surviving documentation.

She died at her house in Fiesole on 8 November 1960, after an illness of two years during which she continued to receive students and colleagues at home when the journey to Genoa became too much for her. She was working to the last, with her husband's help, on the entry Jacopo della Quercia for the Enciclopedia universale dell'arte — the subject of her first book closing the circle of her final one. She is buried in the family tomb at Bra.

Her personal library was given by Cesare Fasola to the Institute of Art History at Genoa; her photographic collection of glass slides, assembled for teaching between 1948 and 1960 and heavily weighted towards Nicola and Giovanni Pisano, Arnolfo di Cambio and the Perugia fountain, survives there in part, having been damaged by a fire at the Institute in the 1970s. Her papers are conserved with her husband's in the Cesare and Giusta Nicco Fasola archive, catalogued by the Soprintendenza archivistica e bibliografica dell'Umbria; they include correspondence with Lionello Venturi, Benedetto Croce and Pietro Nenni. A memorial volume, Studi in onore di Giusta Nicco Fasola, appeared as a special number of Arte Lombarda in 1964-65, with a bibliography of her writings compiled by Carla Musso Casalone.

Nicolaïdès, Andréas

active late 20th–21st century

Andréas Nicolaïdès is a French scholar of Byzantine art and archaeology whose career has been built around the painted churches of Cyprus — above all the church of Panagia tou Araka at Lagoudera, whose 1192 fresco cycle he subjected to the definitive iconographic study that remains the standard scholarly reference nearly thirty years after its publication. He completed his doctoral thesis, "L'église de la Panagia Arakiotissa à Lagoudera et la peinture byzantine du 12ème à l'aube du 13ème siècle à Chypre," at Aix-Marseille I in Art and Archaeology in 1993. His institutional career has been spent almost entirely at Aix-Marseille University, where he holds the position of Maître de conférences in Byzantine art history and archaeology, affiliated with LA3M (Laboratoire d'Archéologie Médiévale et Moderne en Méditerranée), CNRS UMR 7298.

Three years after completing his doctorate, Nicolaïdès published the iconographic study of the Lagoudera frescoes that has become the indispensable reference for the monument: "L'église de la Panagia Arakiotissa à Lagoudéra, Chypre: Étude iconographique des fresques de 1192," Dumbarton Oaks Papers 50 (1996), pp. 1–137. At 137 pages, an exceptionally substantial monograph-length study even by the standards of the journal, the article undertook a comprehensive iconographic analysis of the entire fresco programme commissioned by Leon Authentes in December 1192, situating it within the chronology of late Komnenian painting on the eve of the Frankish conquest's full consolidation. Its analysis of the Panagia Arakiotissa — the Virgin of the Passion image on the church's southeastern wall — remains the foundational scholarly account of one of the earliest known depictions of that iconographic type, a depiction that, in Nicolaïdès's reading, combines the tenderness of the mother-child relationship with a deeper theological meaning concerning Christ's future Passion. Subsequent scholarship on Lagoudera, including the 2018 Leventis Foundation volume edited by Papageorgiou, Bakirtzis, and Hadjichristodoulou, and the Winfields' study of the paintings' painterly significance, builds upon rather than supersedes this 1996 iconographic framework.

Before his career became centred on Cyprus, Nicolaïdès's early publications addressed the Roman and medieval archaeology of Aix-en-Provence, including excavation reports on the Maison d'arrêt on the Rue Peyresc published in Archéologie médiévale (1993) and a co-authored study of ancient houses on the Rue des Magnans published in Gallia (1994). His Cypriot research extended beyond individual monuments into landscape archaeology: he was among the contributors to "Potamia-Agios Sozomenos (Chypre): La constitution des paysages dans l'Orient médiéval," Bulletin de correspondance hellénique 125/2 (2001), pp. 655–678, a multi-disciplinary project integrating pottery, geomorphology, ceramics, and Byzantine art history. His co-authorship on that project with Demetrios Michaelides — who was also Ioanna Kakoulli's co-author on the 2010 study of painted rock-cut tombs in Cyprus — links the landscape-archaeology and materials-science strands of Cypriot research examined across this series.

Nicolaïdès's most direct institutional link to Kakoulli's work lies in his co-editorship, with Annemarie Weyl Carr, of the major Dumbarton Oaks volume Asinou Across Time: Studies in the Architecture and Murals of the Panagia Phorbiotissa, Cyprus (Washington DC, 2012). Kakoulli, together with M. Schilling and J. Mazurek, contributed "The Murals of Panagia Phorbiotissa: A Technical Examination" to this volume — making Nicolaïdès the co-editor of the publication in which Kakoulli's laboratory delivered its scientific findings on the third great Troodos painted church, alongside Lagoudera and the Enkleistra. His continuing engagement with Asinou is reflected in his paper "Le cycle sanctoral de la Panagia Phorbiotissa à Asinou en 1105–1106," presented at the conference "Melusine of Cyprus" at CAARI in Nicosia in May 2017 — the same institution of which Kakoulli was, from 2011, a member of the Board of Trustees.

Beyond his monument-specific studies, Nicolaïdès has produced broader syntheses for major exhibition catalogues. His "La peinture monumentale byzantine en Chypre du Xe au XIIIe siècle" appeared in Chypre: entre Byzance et Occident, IVe–XVIe siècle, edited by Jannic Durand and Dorota Giovannoni (Louvre/Somogy, 2012), pp. 112–123. He has also worked on the iconography of female sanctity in Cypriot wall painting, co-authoring "Sainte souveraine et saintes princesses dans la peinture monumentale des églises byzantines de Chypre" with Ourania Perdiki, in a volume he himself co-edited: Impératrices, princesses, aristocrates et saintes souveraines de l'Orient chrétien et musulman (Presses Universitaires de Provence, 2014), pp. 25–36.

Nicolaïdès occupies, for Lagoudera, the position that Mango and Hawkins occupy for the Enkleistra: the author of the foundational scholarly study upon which all subsequent work depends. His 1996 Dumbarton Oaks Papers article transformed the church of Panagia tou Araka from a remote and beautiful Troodos monument into a fully documented art-historical object — one whose patron, painter, iconographic programme, and place within the chronology of Komnenian painting on the eve of the Lusignan conquest are now established with a precision that, before 1996, did not exist. His later career — moving outward from Lagoudera to Asinou, to landscape archaeology, to broader syntheses for the Louvre, and to co-editorship of the Dumbarton Oaks Asinou volume alongside contributions from Kakoulli's laboratory — traces, in microcosm, the entire arc of this biographical series: from a single fresco cycle, outward to the network of monuments, scholars, patrons, and scientific collaborators that together constitute the study of medieval Cypriot Byzantine art.

Nordenfalk, Carl

Stockholm, 13 December 1907 – Stockholm, 13 June 1992

Carl Nordenfalk was born in Stockholm on 13 December 1907 and died there on 13 June 1992. He belongs to a generation of Northern European art historians who rebuilt the discipline of medieval manuscript studies on rigorously comparative, iconographic, and stylistic foundations.

Nordenfalk studied at the University of Uppsala between 1926 and 1928 and at Göteborg University from 1928 to 1929. His formation, however, extended well beyond Scandinavia. During research travels in Germany he studied with Georg Swarzenski in Frankfurt and with Adolph Goldschmidt and Albert Boeckler in Berlin. In Berlin he also worked with Wilhelm Koehler, the founder of the Deutscher Verein für Kunstwissenschaft and the driving force behind the comprehensive corpus publication of Carolingian illuminated books. These encounters grounded Nordenfalk in the most rigorous philological tradition of German Kunstwissenschaft while simultaneously exposing him to the ambitions of large-scale, systematic corpus scholarship.

During his research travels Nordenfalk also became acquainted with an international group of art historians who shared similar interests: Francis Wormald and Hugo Buchthal in London, Otto Pächt in Vienna, and Meyer Schapiro and André Grabar in Paris. Several of these were to become lifelong friends.

In 1938 Nordenfalk published his doctoral thesis on the Eusebian canon tables. This study marked the start of his long and successful academic career and also signalled his life-long interest in illuminated and decorated manuscripts. The work, Die spätantiken Kanontafeln: kunstgeschichtliche Studien über die eusebianische Evangelien-Konkordanz in den vier ersten Jahrhunderten ihrer Geschichte (Göteborg, 1938), is a two-volume study in art history and theology. The Eusebian canon tables are the columnar concordance systems devised by Eusebius of Caesarea that allow the reader to cross-reference parallel passages across the four Gospels; when reproduced in illustrated codices, these tables were enclosed within elaborate arcaded architectural frameworks that became one of the most sophisticated and varied decorative programmes in all of medieval art.

Nordenfalk's monograph on the canon tables remains the only full monograph on the subject from an art-historical standpoint, and its importance has only grown with renewed scholarly interest in the relationship between Gospel book structure and the visual imagination of Late Antiquity and the early medieval period. This pioneering work contributed immensely to scholarship on the history of the medieval book and is still recognised for its long-lasting scholarly value. His dissertation became the standard work on canonical typologies of Gospel illumination.

Nordenfalk was appointed assistant curator at the museum in Göteborg in 1935. Articles on Insular illumination had already begun appearing from his pen in the early and mid-1930s, and his combination of museum work and independent research would characterise his entire professional life. In 1944 he moved to the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm, where he was put in charge of loans, exhibitions and education. In 1949 he was promoted to the department of painting and sculpture.

A pivotal interlude followed when, at the nomination of Erwin Panofsky, Nordenfalk spent a year at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, 1949–1950. The intellectual environment of the Institute — where Panofsky, Kurt Weitzmann, and other European émigré scholars had reconstituted a world-class centre for art-historical research — left a decisive mark. For his Princeton project he returned to his favourite research area, examining the origins and oldest types of medieval ornamental letters, work that would eventually lead to his 1970 book on illuminated initials. The materials were selected from the Codices latini antiquiores of Elias Avery Lowe, whom Nordenfalk was able to consult in Princeton, and to whom he was to dedicate the resulting book.

Nordenfalk rose to director of the Nationalmuseum in 1958. As director he presided over one of Sweden's most internationally respected cultural institutions, overseeing both acquisitions and exhibition programmes. As director he organised several important shows, including the Queen Christina of Sweden exhibition of 1966. He retired in 1968, spending a second term at the Institute for Advanced Study from 1968 to 1970.

Alongside his technical scholarly production, Nordenfalk played a decisive role in bringing medieval painting to an educated general readership through the celebrated Skira series. In 1957 and 1958, in collaboration with the Byzantine art historian André Grabar, he authored two magisterial volumes: Early Medieval Painting from the Fourth to the Eleventh Century (1957) and Romanesque Painting from the Eleventh to the Thirteenth Century (1958). Produced in Geneva and distributed internationally in multiple translations, these volumes set a benchmark for accessible yet scholarly synthesis of medieval pictorial culture that remained authoritative for decades.

Nordenfalk's research emphasized Celtic influences in Insular illumination over Northumbrian influence, the latter felt to be the predominant origin at the time. He also studied the contribution of Insular style to continental illumination, tracing pathways of transmission that German and English scholarship had tended to examine in isolation.

In the United States he taught as guest professor at the University of California, Berkeley, 1971–1972, and at the University of Pittsburgh, 1971–1976, interrupted by the 1972–1973 year as both Slade Professor at Cambridge and Kress Professor in Residence at the National Gallery of Art, Washington DC. The Slade Professorship — the oldest visiting chair in art history at Cambridge, endowed since 1869 — placed him alongside some of the most distinguished art historians of the twentieth century to have held it.

His Celtic and Anglo-Saxon Painting (1976) brought another underpublished subject to English readers with intelligence and economy. The volume offered commentary on forty-eight folios from the major Insular codices — the Book of Kells, the Lindisfarne Gospels, the Book of Durrow among them — combining analytical precision with genuine descriptive elegance.

He further taught at the University of California, Los Angeles, 1977–1978, and was a fellow at the National Humanities Center, North Carolina, 1980–1982, before returning to Sweden.

Nordenfalk was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1970 and to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1974. In 1987, on the occasion of his eightieth birthday, his colleagues Per Bjurström, Nils-Göran Hökby, and Florentine Mütherich edited the Florilegium in honorem Carl Nordenfalk octogenarii contextum (Stockholm: Nationalmuseum, 1987), a Festschrift that assembled contributions from the leading manuscript scholars of three continents.

His wife, Cecilia, died in 1991. In the last year of his life Nordenfalk prepared his final book for press: Studies in the History of Book Illumination (London: Pindar Press, 1992). This volume compiles twenty-three significant papers spanning four decades, from late antiquity to Ottonian illumination, all extensively revised by the author just prior to his death in 1992.

The publisher's assessment, which served as the volume's blurb, may stand as the most succinct appraisal of his career: Nordenfalk's work over the last forty years has represented perhaps the most important effort made in these decades to clarify the development of book illumination in the late antique and early medieval periods. His papers on late antique and Insular manuscript painting in particular are recognised as standard works on the subject.

Nordenfalk possessed an excellent narrative style, taking somewhat dry topics and turning them into engaging discussions by, among other things, describing the search for evidence. His English- language treatments of manuscript painting were the finest and most accessible in the language for many years.

Unlike many art historians whose range is defined by a single period or medium, Nordenfalk moved fluently between disciplines. Most unusual were his numerous forays into the Baroque — he wrote a major study of Rembrandt's only monumental painting, The Batavians' Oath of Allegiance (Stockholm: Nationalmuseum, 1983) — and into the modern era with his study of van Gogh, published in Swedish in 1946 and translated into English as The Life and Work of van Gogh (New York: Philosophical Library, 1953).

For anyone working on medieval illuminated manuscripts, Nordenfalk is an unavoidable reference point across three distinct domains. His dissertation on the Eusebian canon tables remains the foundational art-historical study of one of the most ubiquitous and visually complex decorative programmes in Gospel book production, from Late Antiquity through the full flowering of Carolingian, Insular, and Ottonian illumination. His work on Insular manuscripts reframed the debate about Celtic versus Northumbrian origins with a rigour and comparative breadth that shaped research for the rest of the century. And his Skira volumes with Grabar provided generations of students — and museum professionals — with the most visually generous and intellectually reliable introduction to the field that the mid-twentieth century produced.

Nordhagen, Per Jonas

active late 20th century

Per Jonas Nordhagen was a Norwegian art historian, Professor at the University of Bergen, and a leading specialist in early medieval Roman wall painting and its Byzantine connections, particularly the extensively studied fresco cycles of Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum. His work situated early medieval Rome within a Mediterranean-wide artistic culture in close contact with Byzantium, rather than treating it as a purely local or purely Western tradition.

In his Jarrow Lecture of 1977, The Codex Amiatinus and the Byzantine Element in the Northumbrian Renaissance, Nordhagen argued that the manuscript's late-antique Mediterranean pictorial idiom — its modelling, foreshortening, and treatment of drapery, which have no genuine Insular parallel — was most plausibly explained by the direct presence of an Italo-Byzantine painter working in Northumbria, brought there as part of the same continental recruitment that furnished Benedict Biscop's monastery with glaziers and masons. The position has an obvious attraction, but it has been challenged by subsequent pigment analysis identifying orpiment, a material characteristic of Insular rather than Italian workshops, in the Amiatinus's painting — evidence now generally taken to favour a Northumbrian artist copying imported models rather than a visiting Mediterranean painter. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of this debate.

Novello, Roberto Paolo

b. 1958

Roberto Paolo Novello is an Italian art historian and educator whose scholarship centres on Italian Gothic sculpture and the medieval "minor" or decorative arts. He took his laurea with honours in Lettere Moderne (art-historical track) at the University of Pisa, followed at the same institution by the Diploma di Perfezionamento in the history of ancient and medieval-modern art (1986) and a Dottorato di Ricerca in Storia dell'Arte (1991). His doctoral work was a monographic study of the Pisan sculptor Giovanni di Balduccio da Pisa. He has long taught art history at the Istituto Statale d'Arte "Stagio Stagi" in Pietrasanta (Lucca), the historic art school in the heart of the Apuan marble district.

His research has developed largely independently within two closely linked fields: the sculpture of the Pisan and Campionese schools (Giovanni Pisano, Giovanni di Balduccio, Tino di Camaino, Matteo da Campione) and the arti minori, especially wood intarsia (tarsie) and marble work. Among his signature contributions is the 2006 monograph Giovanni Pisano. Il Pergamo di Pisa in Franco Cosimo Panini's Figure series, alongside essays and catalogue entries on the Trecento sculpture, mosaics, and inlays of the Pisa Duomo, and studies of the Pisan pergami of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

Novello sat on the scientific committees of two landmark marble exhibitions - Niveo de Marmore. L'uso artistico del marmo di Carrara dall'XI al XV secolo (Sarzana, 1992) and I Marmi di Lasinio (Pisa, 1993) - and contributed to the great Panini Mirabilia Italiae corpora directed by Salvatore Settis, including the Duomo di Pisa, Duomo di Modena, the Basilica di San Francesco ad Assisi, and the Scrovegni Chapel volumes. He collaborated repeatedly with the Opera della Primaziale Pisana and the Pisa Soprintendenza on cataloguing thirteenth- to fifteenth-century sculpture and painting, and took part in the virtual reconstruction of the tomb of Emperor Henry VII (Arrigo VII) for the multimedia installation displaying Tino di Camaino's facade angels.

His institutional ties to the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa are significant: he ran a continuous seminar in collaboration with Enrico Castelnuovo's art-history course, and from its foundation he has belonged to the research group behind the Corpus delle opere firmate del Medioevo italiano - later Opere firmate nell'arte italiana / Medioevo. Rinascimento - directed by Maria Monica Donato. That project on the medieval artist's signature produced several of his sharpest philological studies, including work on indirect textual transmission such as the Orlandi-Roncioni codex. He is also a contributor of numerous artist entries to the Saur Allgemeines Künstler-Lexikon. His authority record is VIAF 33155637.

One caveat is worth marking for the present context: despite the "signed works" strand touching on scribal and epigraphic questions, Novello's corpus is essentially sculptural and lapidary rather than codicological. He is therefore a strong reference point on the Pisan sculptural milieu, on Giovanni di Balduccio and related masters, and on the broader problem of the medieval artist's signature, but not a specialist in illuminated manuscripts as such.

O

O'Curry, Eugene

Dunaha, County Clare, 20 November 1794 – Dublin, 30 July 1862

Eugene O'Curry was an Irish scholar of language, literature and manuscripts, one of the towering figures of nineteenth-century Irish antiquarian scholarship despite having received no formal university education. Largely self-taught in Irish palaeography and the Irish language, he worked from 1835 for the Ordnance Survey of Ireland under George Petrie, and subsequently as a cataloguer of Irish manuscripts for the Royal Irish Academy, Trinity College Dublin and the British Museum, work that gave him an unrivalled first-hand knowledge of the surviving corpus of medieval Irish manuscripts.

In 1854 O'Curry was appointed the first Professor of Irish History and Archaeology at the newly founded Catholic University of Ireland, where his lectures were published as Lectures on the Manuscript Materials of Ancient Irish History (1861) and, posthumously, On the Manners and Customs of the Ancient Irish (1873). O'Curry described the Old Irish verse following the John colophon of the Book of Dimma as among the oldest specimens of pure Irish writing then known.

Writing before the palaeographic redating of the manuscript in the twentieth century, O'Curry's broader account of the Book of Dimma exemplifies the romantic, largely uncritical antiquarian tradition that Richard Irvine Best's 1926 study of the colophons would later overturn.

Oertel, Robert

Leipzig, 1907 – Freiburg im Breisgau, 1981

Robert Oertel (Leipzig, October 30, 1907 – Freiburg im Breisgau, December 1, 1981) was one of the most important German art historians of the twentieth century, specializing in medieval and Renaissance Italian painting, with particular emphasis on the period between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries.

He studied art history, history, classical archaeology, and philosophy at Leipzig, Vienna, Munich, Hamburg, and Freiburg im Breisgau. In February 1932 he completed his doctorate in Frankfurt am Main under Hans Jantzen, one of the major theorists of medieval German art, and in 1948 he obtained his habilitation in art history, consolidating his return to academic and museum life after the war.

Between 1935 and 1939, Oertel served as director of the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florence, where he deepened his firsthand knowledge of Tuscan medieval and Renaissance painting. After 1939 he moved to the Gemaldegalerie Alte Meister in Dresden, working under Hans Posse and later Hermann Voss on inventories and acquisitions. During the war he was chiefly responsible for the relocation and safeguarding of the gallery's holdings. Drafted in 1944, he fought on the Eastern Front as an artilleryman, was captured by Soviet forces in May 1945, and was released in August of the same year.

After a brief return to work with the Dresden collections, Oertel was dismissed because of his past NSDAP membership. He rebuilt his career in West Germany, becoming chief curator at the Alte Pinakothek in Munich, where he was appointed Oberkonservator in 1960 and Landeskonservator in 1962. The peak of his institutional career came in November 1964, when he was appointed director of the Gemaldegalerie of the Prussian State Museums in Berlin-Dahlem, a role he held until 1973. There he oversaw the reinstallation of the Italian Renaissance painting section and planned the new Gemaldegalerie building at the Tiergarten.

For medieval studies, his most enduring contribution is Early Italian Painting to 1400, a major critical synthesis of Italian painting from its origins through the end of the fourteenth century. He also published a monographic study on Fra Filippo Lippi in 1942, combining broad historical framing with close analysis of a single master. His photographic archive, preserved at the Zentralinstitut fur Kunstgeschichte in Munich, documents Italian painting from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century and remains a valuable research resource.

Oettinger, Karl

Vienna, 4 March 1906 - Peschiera del Garda, 8 May 1979

Karl Norbert Julius Oettinger was an Austrian art historian and medievalist whose career spanned the Vienna museum and university world of the interwar and wartime periods and, from the 1950s, a long professorship at the University of Erlangen, where he became an influential figure in the study of medieval sculpture and archaeology in Franconia. In the historiography of the Codex Aureus of Echternach he is remembered for a striking and much-discussed intervention on the date of the treasure cover's central ivory plaque.

Born in Vienna on 4 March 1906, Oettinger studied classical archaeology, German studies and art history from 1924, in Berlin under Adolph Goldschmidt and in Vienna under Julius von Schlosser and Karl Maria Swoboda, taking his doctorate at the University of Vienna in 1928 with a dissertation on early Bohemian painting (altböhmische Malerei) and spending 1928/29 at the Institute for Austrian Historical Research. In 1930 he joined the Austrian Museum for Applied Art (the Österreichisches Museum für angewandte Kunst) as a scientific officer, and from 1934 he contributed artist biographies to the Thieme-Becker Allgemeines Lexikon der bildenden Künstler. He habilitated in art history at the University of Vienna in 1936 and, from 1942 to 1945, served as associate professor there, during part of this period acting as substitute for the chair-holder, Hans Sedlmayr.
