Oettinger did not obtain a permanent Vienna chair in the immediate postwar years; his major publications of the later 1940s and early 1950s — Das Wienerische in der bildenden Kunst (1948) and, above all, Das Werden Wiens (1951), a study proposing a continuous development of the city from antiquity into the Middle Ages that broke with earlier scholarly consensus and helped establish medieval archaeology as an independent discipline in Austria — were accompanied by fieldwork at St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna, where his excavations clarified the configuration of the medieval high altar. He took a full professorship at the University of Erlangen in 1953/54, remaining there until his retirement as professor emeritus in 1971, and held guest lectureships at Ankara University in 1962 and 1965. His scholarly method moved over his career from a stylistic-critical approach toward the historical analysis of stylistic change, and his earlier work included Altdeutsche Bildschnitzer der Ostmark (1939), a study of late Gothic wood sculptors in the Austrian lands.

Oettinger's contribution to the study of the Codex Aureus of Echternach is a single, pointed article: "Der Elfenbeinschnitzer des Echternacher Codex Aureus und die Skulptur unter Heinrich III. (1039-56)," Jahrbuch der Berliner Museen, n.F. 2 (1960), 34-54. Against the standard view that the cover's central ivory Crucifixion plaque was carved in Trier in the late tenth century as an original component of Archbishop Egbert's treasure binding, Oettinger connected the ivory carver's hand to sculpture produced under Henry III in the mid-eleventh century, implying a significantly later date for the ivory and effectively decoupling it from the rest of the late-tenth-century metalwork. The proposal has not displaced the majority view, but it remains a live element of the unresolved debate over the ivory's date and origin, cited alongside Peter Metz, John Beckwith and Peter Lasko in every subsequent survey of the question.

Karl Oettinger died in Peschiera del Garda, on Lake Garda, on 8 May 1979.

Offner, Richard

Vienna, 1889 - Florence, 1965

Richard Offner was one of the most rigorous and influential art historians of the twentieth century, specializing in medieval and early Renaissance Florentine painting. His career marked a turning point in the systematic and critically grounded study of Duecento, Trecento, and early Quattrocento masters.

Born in Vienna on June 30, 1889, Offner moved with his family to New York in 1891. He studied at Harvard between 1909 and 1912, then trained as a Fellow at the American Academy in Rome, where he developed his visual method on early Italian painting. In 1914, he completed his doctorate at the University of Vienna under Max Dvorak, a foundational figure of the Viennese school. This formation gave Offner the strict formal and methodological discipline that would define his connoisseurship.

He began teaching at the University of Chicago in 1915, moved to Harvard in 1920 as a Sachs Fellow, and joined New York University in 1923. Promoted to full professor in 1927, he served as head of the fine arts department from 1930 to 1933 and remained at NYU until retiring in 1961. He died in Florence on August 26, 1965, after a lifetime devoted to Florentine painting.

Offner's scholarly identity was rooted in connoisseurship understood as a disciplined reading of artistic personality through style. Influenced by Bernard Berenson but also by the analytical rigor of the Viennese school, he treated line, form, and structure as historically legible evidence. He was skeptical of color photography as a primary analytical instrument, preferring black-and-white documentation to minimize interpretive distortion and isolate compositional relations.

His central achievement was A Critical and Historical Corpus of Florentine Painting, an extraordinarily ambitious, multi-volume cataloguing project conceived in the 1920s to provide exhaustive critical coverage of Florentine painting from its medieval foundations through the Renaissance. Planned across six sections and thirty volumes, the Corpus was organized by artists and structured through detailed historical and attributional analysis. Offner published twelve volumes, working closely with Klara Steinweg, but the enterprise remained unfinished at his death.

After 1965, the Corpus was continued by Miklos Boskovits (1984-2011) and remains active under the direction of Sonia Chiodo, with Andrea De Marchi in a leading institutional role and support from the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz. Offner's early books, including Studies in Florentine Painting: The Fourteenth Century (1923) and Italian Primitives at Yale University (1927), remain foundational references.

His documentary legacy is equally significant: the Offner photographic archive, now preserved at the National Gallery of Art in Washington through the Institute of Fine Arts, contains roughly 50,000 photographs, negatives, notes, clippings, and teaching materials. Preserved with his original attributional structures intact, it remains one of the most important research tools for scholars of Florentine medieval painting.

Ó Floinn, Raghnall

active late 20th – 21st century

Raghnall Ó Floinn is an Irish archaeologist and museum curator, Director of the National Museum of Ireland from 2013 to 2018 and, before that, Keeper of Irish Antiquities. A specialist in medieval Irish metalwork, reliquaries and book shrines, he is the author of the standard account of the Book of Dimma's cumdach, "The Shrine of the Book of Dimma," published in Éile: Journal of the Roscrea Heritage Society (volume i, 1983).

Ó Floinn's reading of the shrine's inscription corrected the older antiquarian identification of its patrons, dating the surviving gilding and inscription to a refurbishment of about 1380–1407 under Tadhg Ailbhe Ó Cearbhaill, king of Éile, rather than to the shrine's original twelfth-century manufacture — a distinction fundamental to any accurate account of the shrine's composite history. His broader work has done much to place Irish ecclesiastical metalwork, including the cumdachs of Dimma, Mulling and the Cathach, within its proper archaeological and historical context.

Okunev, Nikolai Lvovich

1885 - Prague, 1949

Nikolai Lvovich Okunev was one of the most important historians of medieval art in the first half of the 20th century, a leading authority on Byzantine mural painting as well as ancient Russian, Armenian, Georgian, and medieval Serbian art. His career, marked by political exile after the Russian Revolution of 1917, took him from the University of St. Petersburg to Prague, where he became professor at Charles University and founded academic institutions that endured long after his lifetime.

From 1905 to 1911, Okunev studied at the Faculty of History and Philology of the University of St. Petersburg under Dmitry Ainalov, one of the founding figures of Russian Byzantine studies and author of the seminal essay Ellenisticeskie osnovy vizantijskogo iskusstva. This training decisively shaped Okunev's method, grounded in rigorous analysis of material evidence - architecture, mural painting, and manuscript illumination - and in the broad historical framing of Eastern Mediterranean artistic cultures.

After graduating in 1911, he participated in the excavations at Ani, the ancient capital of the Armenian Bagratid Kingdom in eastern Anatolia, led by Academician Nikolai Marr. That expedition opened a field of inquiry he would pursue throughout his life: the relationship between Eastern Christian traditions (Armenian, Georgian, Syriac) and Byzantine artistic heritage. On Marr's recommendation, he was admitted to the Imperial Russian Archaeological Society.

Between 1913 and 1914, Okunev served as secretary of the Russian Archaeological Institute in Constantinople, one of the leading European centers for Byzantine art and archaeology. There he worked in direct contact with the monuments of the imperial capital and with the international scholarly network surrounding the institute, including Fyodor Uspensky, its director and a central figure in Russian Byzantine studies.

In June 1917, shortly after the February Revolution, Okunev was appointed assistant professor at the University of Petrograd. Soon after, Marr invited him to lead an expedition to the Caucasian province of Kars to document and preserve Christian monuments in Ottoman Armenia, then temporarily occupied by Tsarist troops during World War I. During the summer of 1917, Okunev and photographer Bulbenko traveled through Tao-Klardjeti - Otkhta Eklesia, Parkhali, Ishkhani, Oshki, Khakhuli - producing over 400 photographs of early Christian and medieval wall painting in southern Georgia. Preserved today in the Photographic Archive of the Institute for the History of Material Culture in St. Petersburg, these images remained unpublished for decades and are still irreplaceable primary documentation, since many recorded frescoes were later destroyed or whitewashed.

The October Revolution radically altered his trajectory. For political reasons he left Russia and, between 1920 and 1923, lived in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, where he entered a favorable intellectual milieu and began focusing on Serbian and Macedonian medieval monuments. During this phase he carried out field surveys and documentation work that became central to his later publications.

In 1923, Okunev settled permanently in Prague, where he remained until his death in 1949. At Charles University (Karlova Universita), he held the chair of medieval art history for over two decades, training a new generation of scholars who continued research across the Balkans and Eastern Europe. He was active in the Institute of Slavic Studies in Prague, where he founded both the Archive and the Gallery of Slavic Art for systematic documentation of medieval Slavic artistic heritage. He was also among the founding editors of Byzantinoslavica, which soon became the leading international journal for the art and culture of the Byzantine-Slavic world.

Okunev's most enduring contribution lies in medieval mural painting in Serbia and Macedonia. His investigations of Serbian monasteries, especially in the Raska region, were pioneering surveys of monuments then scarcely known in Western scholarship. Of exceptional importance was his work on the Church of St. Panteleimon in Nerezi (Macedonia), whose 1164 painted cycle commissioned by Alexios Angelos Komnenos was first published and systematically analyzed by Okunev in 1927. That publication triggered a debate, still active today, over the identification of the votive portraits and established Nerezi as a landmark in the history of medieval painting in the Balkans. Okunev also carried out conservation work at Nerezi and at the Basilica of Saint Sophia in Ohrid, one of the most complex monuments of medieval and Palaiologan mural painting in present-day North Macedonia.

His scholarship is distinguished by extraordinary geographical and chronological range: from pre-Mongol Russian art to Armenian medieval architecture, from tenth-century Georgian painting to fourteenth-century Serbian manuscript illumination. His field expeditions, often in difficult conditions and politically unstable zones, produced photographic and documentary archives of exceptional value, in many cases the only surviving record of monuments now lost or severely deteriorated.

Jirina Jancarkova's 2012 monographic study published in Frankfurt, Istorik iskusstva Nikolai L'vovich Okunev, 1885-1949. Zhiznennyj put' i naucnoe nasledie, offered the first comprehensive reconstruction of Okunev's intellectual biography and scholarly legacy within the major currents of twentieth-century medieval studies. Okunev emerges as a bridge between the Russian fieldwork-based school of art history and the Central European academic world in which he continued to produce research of the highest level despite the constraints of exile.

O'Loughlin, Thomas

active late 20th-21st century

Thomas O'Loughlin is an Irish theologian, Professor of Historical Theology at the University of Nottingham, and one of the most prolific contemporary scholars of early medieval biblical exegesis and Hiberno-Latin intellectual culture. His work ranges from critical editions and studies of Adomnán's De Locis Sanctis to broader accounts of how early medieval Christians organized and understood the structure of Scripture itself.

His article "The Structure of the Collections that make up the Scriptures: the Influence of Augustine on Cassiodorus," published in the Revue Bénédictine in 2014, demonstrated that the nine-volume arrangement displayed in the bookcase of the Codex Amiatinus's Ezra miniature follows the canon list set out by Augustine in De doctrina christiana II.8.13, a scheme that Cassiodorus had himself adopted at Vivarium. The finding adds a further layer to the manuscript's opening quire, showing it to transmit an Augustinian scheme at one remove, mediated through Cassiodorus and realized in a Northumbrian book. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the Ezra miniature and its bookcase.

Oltrogge, Doris

b. 1959

Doris Oltrogge is a German art historian and art technologist, and one of the leading specialists in the technical and material study of medieval book illumination. Since 1996 she has taught and researched at the Cologne Institute of Conservation Sciences (CICS), part of the Technische Hochschule Köln (formerly the Fachhochschule Köln), where her long-standing partnership with the chemist Robert Fuchs has produced one of the most substantial bodies of art-technological research on European manuscript painting of the past three decades.

She began her studies in 1977, reading art history, history, classical and Christian archaeology, and prehistory at the Georg-August-Universität Göttingen; in 1980 she moved to the Rheinische Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität Bonn, where she completed her doctorate in 1987 with a dissertation on the illustration cycles of the Histoire ancienne jusqu'à César, 1250-1400 - an early instance of the interest in the transmission of pictorial cycles across manuscript traditions that would recur throughout her later career.

After the doctorate she returned to Göttingen as a research assistant on the DFG-funded Forschungsstelle für Technik mittelalterlicher Buchmalerei (Research Unit for the Technique of Medieval Book Painting), and carried out a period of art-technological examination work at the J. Paul Getty Museum. Between 1992 and 1993 she held a postdoctoral fellowship of the Fritz Thyssen Foundation for a study of the underdrawings of the Master of the Registrum Gregorii, the Trier Ottonian illuminator whose style stands behind much of the following century's Ottonian and Salian book painting, including the Echternach golden Gospels. From 1993 to 1995 she worked with the Byzantinist Peter Schreiner at the Fachhochschule Köln on the project Byzantinische Tintenrezepte: Rekonstruktion und technischer Kommentar (Byzantine ink recipes: reconstruction and technical commentary), reconstructing historical ink formulae from textual recipe sources - a method of working from written recipe to reconstructed material practice that became a hallmark of her subsequent research.

Since 1996 Oltrogge has been based at the CICS, teaching art-historical sources and documentation, codicology, the technology of illumination, bindings and prints, and building - together with Fuchs, a chemist by training - an interdisciplinary programme that unites documentary and archival method with non-invasive scientific analysis (reflectography, spectroscopy, pigment and dye identification) of the physical object. The partnership has produced technical studies of, among others, the Registrum Gregorii tradition, the manuscripts of Ottonian Hildesheim associated with Bishop Bernward, and the World Chronicle of Rudolf of Ems and its miniatures. The study for which she is most cited in the literature on the Codex Aureus of Echternach is Die Maltechnik des Codex Aureus aus Echternach: ein Meisterwerk im Wandel (Nuremberg: Verlag des Germanischen Nationalmuseums, 2009), the systematic technical examination, co-authored with Fuchs, of every painted and ornamental page of the Nuremberg manuscript, which established that roughly a third of its leaves had been reworked - in most cases already in the course of the book's original production, for aesthetic reasons and using nearly the full range of pigments available in the eleventh century.

Oltrogge's broader research concerns the painting technique and materiality of medieval book illumination, art-technological written sources and the practical contexts that produced them, and the history, manufacture and non-destructive analysis of historical painting materials. She directs the Kunsttechnologische Rezeptsammlung at TH Köln, a growing database transcribing and translating German-language art-technological recipes preserved in manuscripts from the medieval period to the sixteenth century - covering pigment and colour preparation, painting media, binders and adhesives, and the working of textiles, leather, parchment, paper, metal and glass - built on the corpus of pre-1500 recipe manuscripts identified by the art historian Mark Clarke. More recently she has been involved in WELTBUNT, a BMBF-funded collaborative project examining the early German chemical dye industry for textile production up to 1940, again pairing spectroscopic analysis of surviving dyes and textiles with archival research. She is a member of ICOM-CC and of the Arbeitskreis Archäometrie und Denkmalpflege (Working Group for Archaeometry and Monument Conservation).

Together, Oltrogge and Fuchs represent one of the most productive art-historian/chemist partnerships in the technical study of European medieval manuscripts, and their 2009 Codex Aureus volume remains, alongside the Germanisches Nationalmuseum's own catalogues, the primary source for understanding the material genesis of the Nuremberg manuscript.

O'Reilly, Jennifer

1938 - 2016

Jennifer O'Reilly was an Irish art historian, long associated with University College Cork, and one of the most influential scholars of her generation in the study of Insular art as a vehicle of patristic and Bedan exegesis. Her work on the Book of Kells, the Lindisfarne Gospels, and related manuscripts consistently argued that their decoration could be fully understood only in relation to the theological and exegetical traditions their makers inhabited, and above all in relation to the writings of Bede.

Her article "'All that Peter stands for': The Romanitas of the Codex Amiatinus Reconsidered," published in the Proceedings of the British Academy in 2009, is among the most important single studies of the manuscript's meaning. O'Reilly argued that the Amiatinus's alignment with Rome — visible in its script, its layout, its late-antique pictorial idiom, its Hieronymian text, and above all in its destination at the tomb of St Peter — was a theological claim rather than a merely stylistic preference: an assertion that Northumbria belonged to the universal Roman communion not as a distant periphery but as a full participant, capable of producing for the apostle's tomb a book finer than anything then available in Rome itself. Her reading remains the fullest and most persuasive account of what the manuscript's Romanitas actually meant. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion.

Ovcharova, Olga V.

active late 20th-21st century

Olga V. Ovcharova is a Russian historian of medieval and Byzantine art, currently a senior researcher at the State Institute for Art Studies (Gosudarstvennyi institut iskusstvoznaniia; Государственный институт искусствознания) in Moscow, located at 5 Kozitsky Pereulok. She holds a Ph.D. and works within the department dedicated to Byzantine art at this important Russian research center.

Her interests focus primarily on middle- and late-period Byzantine art, with particular attention to painting, both mural and panel, and to the miniatures of illuminated manuscripts. A recurring theme in her studies is the relationship between metropolitan centers, especially Constantinople, and provincial schools, specifically the ways in which Constantinopolitan artistic models were adopted, reinterpreted, and transformed in the empire's peripheral regions. In this context, she has devoted studies to the style of twelfth-century Byzantine painting as an indicator of artistic trends and individuality, a central theme in historiographical debate on anonymity and creative personality in Eastern medieval art.

Among the iconographic subjects she has addressed is the archangel Michael on horseback, the iconographic type known as "Archangel Michael Voivode," analyzed in terms of its transformations across Byzantine, post-Byzantine, and Russian iconography. She also presented research on the miniatures of the Acts of the Apostles in Byzantine manuscripts at the 23rd International Congress of Byzantine Studies (Venice, 2022).

Ovcharova has played a prominent role in organizing Russian academic life in the field of Byzantine studies. She served as secretary of the organizing committee for the international conference "Art of the Byzantine World: Individuality of Artistic Creativity," held in Moscow jointly by the State Institute for Art Studies and Lomonosov Moscow State University. She is also co-editor, together with Irina Oretskaia, of a collection of papers from that conference, published by the State Institute for Art Studies. She participated as a member of the organizing committee at the 22nd International Congress of Byzantine Studies (Sofia, 2011), where she also presented a paper on the genesis of certain Byzantine iconographic traditions.

Ovcharova publishes regularly in the journal Iskusstvoznanie (Art Studies Journal), the periodical of the State Institute for Art Studies, and contributes to the collective volume Actual Problems of Theory and History of Art, a primary forum for methodological discussion among art historians in the post-Soviet region. Her ORCID (0000-0001-5074-8082) and Scopus ID (57205690917) confirm her active presence in internationally indexed scholarly output.

P

Pace, Valentino

Lanciano (Abruzzo), 2 October 1944

Valentino Pace is one of Italy's leading scholars of medieval and Byzantine art. His academic career has spanned universities across Europe and North America and has brought him recognition from major international scholarly institutions.

Pace earned his degree in Humanities with a specialization in Medieval Art History at the University of Rome (academic year 1968-69). Between 1982 and 1994 he worked in Rome as a researcher at the Institute of Art History at La Sapienza, consolidating a methodological approach centered on early Christian and early medieval art and on the relations between Rome, the Latin world, and the Byzantine East.

From the 1980s onward he established an international profile through teaching appointments in Heidelberg, Bonn, Basel, Johns Hopkins University, and Princeton. He also held a chair in Early Christian and Medieval Art at Trinity College (Hartford, Connecticut), on the Rome campus. These experiences fostered sustained dialogue with Germanic, Anglo-Saxon, and Scandinavian historiographical traditions.

In 1998 he was appointed associate professor of Medieval and Byzantine Art History at the University of Udine, becoming full professor in 2004 and serving until retirement in 2014. Between 2000 and 2005 he also taught Byzantine Art History at Roma Tre. International recognition followed: foreign member of the Academy of Sciences and Letters at the University of Oslo (from 2003), recipient in 2010 of the University of Belgrade award for outstanding medieval and Byzantine art-historical research, Richard-Krautheimer-Professor at the Bibliotheca Hertziana / Max-Planck-Institut fur Kunstgeschichte in Rome (2010-2012), and Rudolf-Arnheim-Gastprofessur at Humboldt University in Berlin (2015-2016).

His primary field is the medieval art of Southern Italy and the Mediterranean, with particular attention to the penetration of Byzantine figurative language into the Latin West. His major contributions include studies on Romanesque frescoes in Campania, Venetian mosaics (especially the Baptistery of San Marco and the role of Paolo Veneziano), medieval bronze doors, and painted crosses of central and southern Italy. He was also among the first to study systematically the Greek-Byzantine pictorial traditions of Salento, including the frescoes of Santa Maria di Cerrate, interpreted as evidence of the interaction of Greek monasticism, manuscript culture, and Italo-Byzantine visual language.

Among his most significant publications are Apulien - Basilicata - Kalabrien (Darmstadt, 1994), Campania Romanica (Milan, 1997, with Mario D'Onofrio), and Medieval Art in Southern Italy, Vol. 1: Campania (Naples, Liguori, 2007), collecting essays written between 1975 and 2003. In his honor, the anthology Un Medioevo in lungo e in largo. Da Bisanzio all'Occidente (VI-XVI secolo) was published, confirming his importance in international medieval studies. On Academia.edu he has made 232 essays freely available and has built a substantial scholarly following.

Padoa Rizzo, Anna

active late 20th–21st century

Anna Padoa Rizzo is an Italian art historian whose career has been devoted to the study of Florentine painting from the Trecento through the Quattrocento. Associated with the Istituto di Storia dell'Arte dell'Università di Firenze — a scholarly lineage rooted in the tradition founded by Mario Salmi and continued under Roberto Salvini — her scholarship is fundamentally archival and attributive in character: the close reading of documents, registers, and visual evidence in combination, brought to bear on problems of attribution, workshop identity, and the reconstruction of artistic personalities that had been either misidentified or left without a name.

The central axis of her published work is Benozzo Gozzoli (c. 1421–1497), the prolific Florentine painter who worked across the whole of central Italy during the second half of the Quattrocento. Her first monograph, Benozzo Gozzoli pittore fiorentino (Editrice Edam, Florence, 1972), established the documentary and critical foundations she would continue to build upon. Twenty years later came Benozzo Gozzoli: catalogo completo (Cantini, Florence, 1992), the complete catalogue of the painter's works in the series I Gigli dell'Arte, providing the standard reference for Gozzoli's entire painted production. In 1997, on the occasion of the fifth centenary of Gozzoli's death, she curated the exhibition Benozzo a Firenze, San Gimignano, Val d'Elsa e Val d'Era, Pisa, Pistoia (OCTAVO, Florence), working alongside Annamaria Bernacchioni, Nicoletta Pons, and Lisa Venturini; the same year saw the publication of Benozzo Gozzoli in Umbria (Octavo, Florence), tracing the painter's Umbrian activity. The arc concluded with the large illustrated volume Benozzo Gozzoli: un pittore insigne, pratico di grandissima invenzione (Silvana Editoriale, Cinisello Balsamo, 2003), a monograph of 272 pages with 230 colour illustrations tracing chronologically the entirety of the painter's life and work.

A defining feature of Padoa Rizzo's method is the patient disentanglement of anonymous hands from within workshop production. Her most consequential attribution in this domain concerns Alesso di Benozzo (1473–1528), Gozzoli's son: she proposed that the more refined and elegant figures in works produced by the Gozzoli sons jointly are by Alesso, while the coarser passages are by Francesco, apparently of lesser renown. More strikingly, Padoa Rizzo identified Alesso as the anonymous artist previously known by two names — the "Maestro Esiguo," invented by Roberto Longhi in reference to the painter's exiguous figures, and the "Alunno di Benozzo" invented by Bernard Berenson — simultaneously resolving two critical pseudonyms into a single documented personality, a model of connoisseurship at its most consequential. Her 1989 article on the altar of the Compagnia dei Tessitori in San Marco, Florence, attributed to the same painter the spectacular Volto Santo with Saints, originally on the choir screen of San Marco, described by Vasari and erroneously attributed to Cosimo Rosselli. On Giovanni di Francesco del Cervelliera she corrected Vasari's claim that Giovanni and his cousin were pupils of Andrea del Castagno, noting on documentary grounds that Castagno was ten years younger than Giovanni. In the field of late Trecento and early Quattrocento painting, Padoa Rizzo and Cecilia Frosinini extended research into Stefano di Antonio di Vanni, proposing to identify his hand in secondary parts of altarpieces and frescoes executed within Bicci di Lorenzo's bottega.

Padoa Rizzo's scholarship is not confined to monographic studies of individual painters. Her Arte e committenza in Valdelsa e Valdera: con Benozzo, catalogo di un itinerario pittorico (Florence, 1997) traced the pictorial heritage of the Elsa and Era valleys in relation to Gozzoli's presence. She contributed essays to major collaborative catalogues including Bagliori dorati: Il Gotico Internazionale a Firenze 1375–1440, the landmark exhibition on International Gothic painting in Florence, and to the exhibition catalogue dedicated to painters in the territory of Castelfiorentino and the Valdelsa in the second half of the Quattrocento, alongside Antonio Natali, Nicoletta Pons, and Annamaria Bernacchioni.

Within the landscape of Italian art-historical scholarship, Anna Padoa Rizzo belongs to a tradition — centred on Florence and rooted in archival documentary research — that produced the great critical catalogues of Florentine painters of the Quattrocento. Her generation inherited the methods of Richard Offner, Federico Zeri, and Miklós Boskovits, and applied them with systematic care to the reconstruction of individual artistic personalities within the dense web of the Florentine bottega system. Her work on Gozzoli in particular has made that painter, long underestimated in comparison with his more celebrated contemporaries, substantially more legible as an artistic personality: a figure of extraordinary productivity, geographical mobility, and technical versatility who merits serious reassessment alongside the canonical masters of the Quattrocento.

Palanque, Jean-Rémy

Marseille, 7 March 1898 - Aix-en-Provence, 2 June 1988

Jean-Rémy Palanque was a French historian of late antiquity and early Christianity whose work helped renew the historical study of the later Roman Empire in the French academy. He is remembered especially for his major study of Saint Ambrose, produced at almost exactly the same moment as Frederick Homes Dudden's work on the same figure, but in complete independence and with a distinctly historical rather than Anglican-ecclesiastical emphasis.

Born in Marseille on 7 March 1898, the son of a merchant, Palanque studied at the Lycée Thiers, took his baccalauréat in 1914, and entered the École normale supérieure on the rue d'Ulm in 1917. He was licencié ès lettres in 1918 and placed first in the agrégation in history and geography in 1921. Appointed that same year to the lycée at Montpellier, he began lecturing in ancient history at the Faculty of Letters there from 1925, laying the foundations for a career that moved steadily from school teaching to university research and major scholarly synthesis.

His first publications already announced the subject that would make his name. In 1924 he published two studies on Ambrose: a critical examination of Paulinus of Milan's Vita Ambrosii in the Revue des sciences religieuses, and an analysis of the testimony of Socrates Scholasticus on Ambrose in the Revue des études anciennes. These studies fed directly into the doctoral thesis he defended in 1933, Saint Ambroise et l'Empire romain: contribution à l'histoire des rapports de l'Église et de l'État à la fin du IVe siècle, printed at Bordeaux in 1933 and issued in Paris by de Boccard in 1935, hence the double dating by which the book is often cited. His complementary thesis was the Essai sur la préfecture du prétoire du Bas-Empire (1933), showing the extent to which his Ambrose study emerged from a wider command of the late Roman administrative world.

The Ambrose book is structured in two large movements: first the history of the bishop of Milan's personal and political dealings with the emperors Gratian, Valentinian II, and Theodosius; then, drawn from that narrative, a reconstruction of Ambrose's political ideas. Palanque rightly insisted that Ambrose never set out a formal doctrine of Church and State in systematic fashion; his position emerges instead from letters, occasional writings, and texts produced in the pressure of events. The chronological framework Palanque established, especially for the letters and the sequence of confrontations with imperial authority, remains a standard point of departure for later work on Ambrose and on the late fourth-century relationship between episcopal authority and imperial government.

Palanque's academic career advanced rapidly thereafter. He became maître de conférences at Montpellier in 1937, professeur sans chaire in 1938, and in 1940 transferred to the chair of ancient history at Aix-en-Provence. His public life extended beyond the seminar room: he was decorated with the Medal of the Resistance in 1945, and in the elections to the constituent assembly that same year he stood in second place on a list associated with the Resistance. In 1950 he was behind the creation of the Fédération historique de Provence, strengthening the scholarly infrastructure of regional history in southern France. He also taught for a period in Tananarive, Madagascar, in 1961.

Scholarly recognition followed at the highest level. Palanque was elected to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres on 15 November 1968 and later presided over the Société d'histoire religieuse de la France. His wider work ranged well beyond Ambrose. In collaboration with Henri-Irénée Marrou, he helped renew the historical reading of the later Roman Empire and of early Christianity, and he translated and completed in French the late antique studies of the Austrian historian Ernst Stein. He contributed the volume De la paix constantinienne à la mort de Théodose to the Fliche–Martin Histoire de l'Église, wrote Les impérialismes antiques (PUF, "Que sais-je?", 1948) and Le Bas-Empire (1971), collaborated with Latreille and Delaruelle on the three-volume Histoire du catholicisme en France (Spes, 1957–62), and edited the diocesan histories of Marseille (1967) and Aix-en-Provence (1975) for the Histoire des diocèses de France.

Particularly important for late antique and early medieval prosopical work was his role, together with Marrou, in the long-term project of the Prosopographie chrétienne du Bas-Empire, launched in publication from 1982. The second volume, Italie (313–604) by Charles and Luce Pietri, remains one of the essential research tools for anyone working on Milanese or north-Italian ecclesiastical names in the age of Ambrose, Gregory, and the post-imperial church. Palanque died in Aix-en-Provence on 2 June 1988, leaving behind a body of work that remains central to the historical study of Ambrose, Church-State relations in the late Roman Empire, and the Christian prosopography of late antiquity.

Paoli, Emore

active late 20th–21st century

Emore Paoli is an Italian philologist and one of the leading living scholars of medieval Latin hagiography, with a research profile centred on Umbria and on the textual transmission of saints' lives from late antiquity through the Counter-Reformation. He is professore ordinario of Medieval and Humanistic Latin Literature (Letteratura latina medievale e umanistica) at the Università per Stranieri di Perugia, having previously taught the same discipline for many years at the Università degli Studi di Roma "Tor Vergata," where he served as director of the Dipartimento di Studi letterari, filosofici e di storia dell'arte from November 2015 to October 2021. From February 2021 to April 2024 he was President of the Consulta per il Medioevo e l'Umanesimo Latini (CoMUL), the principal Italian coordinating body for university teaching in medieval and humanistic Latin.

Paoli's career began within the network of scholars associated with Claudio Leonardi, one of the founders of modern Italian medieval Latin philology. From 1989 to 1999 he collaborated on Medioevo Latino. Bollettino bibliografico della cultura europea dal secolo VI al XIII, directed by Leonardi, and in the early 1990s on the Bibliografia Umbra, directed by Leonardi together with Enrico Menestò — the same Menestò whose editorial projects on Umbrian sources and mystics recur throughout Paoli's later bibliography. Between 1993 and 1997 he was scientific coordinator, with Andrea Tabarroni, of a research group at the Centro italiano di studi sull'alto medioevo in Spoleto working on the CNR strategic project "Medioevo Europa," building a database of medieval historical sources and authors writing in Latin and in the other languages of the period.

The core of Paoli's scholarship lies in the critical study of hagiographic texts as evidence for the politics, liturgy, and social uses of sanctity. His edition of the Dominican Bartolomeo da Trento's Liber epilogorum in gesta sanctorum (Florence, SISMEL–Edizioni del Galluzzo, 2001) is his major critical edition, and he has continued to work on the same author's Liber miraculorum beatae Mariae Virginis. He also edited the anastatic reprint of Petrus de Natalibus's fourteenth-century Catalogus sanctorum et gestorum eorum (Spoleto, 2012), contributed the chapter on the thirteenth century to Claudio Leonardi's handbook Letteratura latina medievale (secoli VI-XV) (Florence, 2002), and took part in the multi-volume cataloguing project on the medieval manuscripts of the Biblioteca Comunale of Todi directed by Enrico Menestò, describing dozens of codices for the Todi collections.

For the study of medieval women's mysticism, Paoli's most directly relevant contributions concern Angela of Foligno. His essay "Le due redazioni del 'Liber' [di Angela da Foligno]: il perché di una riscrittura," in Angèle de Foligno. Le dossier, edited by G. Barone and J. Dalarun (Rome, 1999), addresses the textual problem of the two surviving redactions of Angela's Liber, a question closely bound up with the editorial choices later made by Giovanni Pozzi in his own critical edition of the text. Paoli returned to Angela in "Le visioni di Angela da Foligno" (2009) and, more broadly, in "Parole di donna, scritture di uomini: Angela da Foligno, Margherita da Cortona, Chiara da Montefalco" (2011), a study that places Angela alongside Margaret of Cortona and Clare of Montefalco to examine how the spoken or dictated words of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century women mystics were shaped, in each case, by the male scribes and confessors who committed them to Latin — the same dynamic explored from a different angle in this database's entries on John W. Coakley and Catherine M. Mooney.

Much of Paoli's other work is anchored in Umbrian local hagiography: studies of the cults of San Fortunato of Montefalco (with Silvestro Nessi, 1995), San Terenziano of Todi, San Valentino, and San Gemino; the "vite antiche" of the poet-friar Iacopone da Todi (2003); the legend of the Orvietan penitent Vanna da Orvieto, edited with Lucia Gualdo Rosa Ricci (1996); and the hagiography and cult of saints in Todi, Perugia, and the Piceno across the early and later Middle Ages. A recurring theme across this body of work is the reception and rewriting of medieval saints' lives in the post-Tridentine period, examined for instance in his study of the early modern afterlife of the medieval lives of St Ubaldo of Gubbio.

Paoli sits on the scientific council of the Società Internazionale per lo Studio del Medioevo Latino (SISMEL) and of the Fondazione Ezio Franceschini in Florence, where he is responsible for the foundation's Mariology section; on the governing board of the Centro italiano di studi sul basso medioevo–Accademia Tudertina in Todi; and on the scientific council of the Edizione Nazionale dei Testi Mediolatini d'Italia. Since 1994 he has been a member of the editorial committee, and one of the secretaries, of Hagiographica. Rivista di agiografia e biografia della Società internazionale per lo studio del Medio Evo Latino, the principal international journal in the field. Author of more than a hundred scientific publications, he remains one of the central figures connecting the philological tradition of Claudio Leonardi and Enrico Menestò to the ongoing study of Umbrian sanctity and of the great thirteenth- and fourteenth-century women mystics.

Paolini, Gilberto

L'Aquila, 22 December 1928; later active in the United States

Gilberto Paolini was born in L'Aquila on 22 December 1928 and later emigrated to the United States. He developed his academic career at Tulane University in New Orleans, where he taught in the Department of Spanish and Portuguese and eventually became Professor Emeritus. His institutional profile was therefore primarily situated in Hispano-medieval studies rather than in Italian medieval studies, while still reflecting his Italian origins and literary training.

Paolini's scholarship engaged with medieval Iberian literature and culture, especially the world of Alfonso X of Castile (Alfonso el Sabio, 1221-1284), whose court produced the Cantigas de Santa Maria. A JSTOR study, Iconography and Literature: Alfonso Himself in Cantiga 209, identifies Paolini as a member of the Relations Committee overseeing scholarship in this field, confirming his active role within Alfonsine and medieval Iberian studies.

Earlier in his career, Paolini also published in Forum Italicum: A Journal of Italian Studies, including the 1968 article La moralita zeniana, indicating that his interests extended to modern Italian literary culture alongside medieval Iberian research.

The scope and impact of his scholarly contribution were recognized by the publication of Studies in Honor of Gilberto Paolini in the Juan de la Cuesta Hispanic Monographs series. Contributions to that volume include work explicitly addressing medieval tradition and Islamic cultural currents, suggesting an intellectual horizon centered on the cross-cultural dimensions of the medieval Mediterranean and Iberian worlds at the intersection of Christian, Islamic, and Jewish learning.

Papazotos, Thanasis

Agios Athanasios, Drama, 1951 – Athens, 20 November 1996

Greek Byzantinologist and archaeologist whose brief but concentrated career — cut short by illness at the age of forty-four — produced the most comprehensive scholarly study of the Byzantine monuments of Veria and its icons, a contribution that won the Prize of the Academy of Athens and remains the standard reference for the late Byzantine heritage of one of the most significant cities in medieval Macedonia. He graduated in History and Archaeology from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in 1975 and completed his doctoral dissertation at the Faculty of Philosophy of the University of Crete — a trajectory placing him within the methodological traditions of two of the most important centres of Byzantine studies in Greece.

The institutional home of Papazotos's career was the 11th Ephorate of Byzantine Antiquities at Veria, where he served as curator-archaeologist and eventually as head of the Ephorate; he had previously served at the 9th Ephorate in Thessaloniki. In 1989–90 he held the position of visiting researcher at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he also gave courses and lectures at American universities and research centres. Veria (ancient Beroea, Byzantine Βέρροια) — an episcopal centre preserving more than seventy Byzantine and post-Byzantine churches spanning the eleventh through the eighteenth centuries, many with their original painted decoration — was an extraordinarily rich field of study for a Byzantine archaeologist with scholarly ambitions.

The culminating achievement of his career was Η Βέροια και οι ναοί της, 11ος–18ος αι. Ιστορική και αρχαιολογική σπουδή των μνημείων της πόλης (Veria and Its Churches, 11th–18th Centuries: A Historical and Archaeological Study of the City's Monuments; Athens, 1994), awarded the Prize of the Academy of Athens in 1995. Spanning seven centuries of architectural typology — domed basilicas, cross-in-square churches, and single-nave chapels, each with its painted programme and specific context of episcopal, monastic, or civic patronage — the work provides the definitive inventory of the Macedonian provincial painting tradition from the Comnenian period through the Palaeologan Renaissance. Βυζαντινές Εικόνες της Βέροιας (Byzantine Icons of Veria; Athens: Akritas, 1995; translated into English by John C. Davis as Byzantine Icons of Verroia in the same year) documents the portable icon painting tradition of the city and its region — complementing the earlier architectural volume and constituting together the most comprehensive visual and historical record of a single Byzantine Macedonian city's artistic heritage. Papazotos completed the icons volume during the final years of his illness, writing against pain and debility in full knowledge of his prognosis. A third volume, Μακεδονικά Αποσημειώματα, Βυζαντινά-Μεταβυζαντινά (Macedonian Notes, Byzantine and Post-Byzantine), was published posthumously by the Institute for Historical Research of the National Research Foundation, gathering unpublished articles on archaeological, historical, prosopographical, and iconographic problems related to Byzantine and post-Byzantine Macedonia.

Alongside his scholarly career, Papazotos was a practicing visual artist — a dimension consistently noted by his colleagues — whose trained eye informed the quality of his visual analysis and descriptive prose when addressing individual works of art. His personal library of approximately 1,700 items, with Byzantine archaeology and history as its central focus, is preserved at the Aikaterini Laskaridis Foundation. A memorial event organized by the Ephorate of Antiquities of Thessaloniki on 5 June 2026 marked the thirtieth anniversary of his passing. His two volumes on Byzantine Veria complement the work of Pelekanidis on the churches of Kastoria and of Theocharidis on the documentary history of Byzantine Macedonia, providing the detailed object-based analysis that neither the iconographic survey nor the historical synthesis alone can furnish; for anyone researching Byzantine panel painting or Macedonian ecclesiastical architecture, they remain an indispensable starting point.

Palladino, Pia

active 20th–21st century

Pia Palladino is an American art historian and curator specialising in Italian painting of the late medieval and early Renaissance periods. She built her early career in the department of European Paintings at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, where she worked closely with Laurence Kanter on the reconstruction and study of Sienese Trecento and Quattrocento altarpieces.

With Kanter she organised the exhibition Painting a Tuscan Town: Sassetta in 15th-Century Siena (2003–04) and, earlier, curated Art and Devotion in Siena after 1350: Luca di Tommè and Niccolò di Buonaccorso at the Timken Museum of Art, San Diego (1997–98), one of the first exhibitions to present Luca di Tommè to a general public as an artist in his own right. Palladino subsequently worked as a specialist in Old Master paintings at Sotheby's, and returned to museum scholarship as co-author, with Kanter, of the first volume of the catalogue of Italian paintings at the Yale University Art Gallery (2025).

Parenti, Daniela

active late 20th-21st century

Daniela Parenti is an art historian and long-serving curator at the Galleria dell'Accademia di Firenze.

Parenti is the curator responsible for the medieval and early-Renaissance painting collections at the Galleria dell'Accademia, the major holding of Florentine gold-ground panels from the Duecento to the early Quattrocento, including Pacino di Bonaguida's Tree of Life and the Lorenzo Monaco group. Her work belongs to the connoisseurship tradition associated with Miklos Boskovits and Angelo Tartuferi: attributive, catalogue-based, and focused on the Florentine Trecento and International Gothic.

Her name is attached to many of the defining Accademia exhibitions of the last two decades, often co-curated with Tartuferi:

  • Da Puccio di Simone a Giottino. Restauri e conferme (Galleria dell'Accademia, 2005), co-curated with Tartuferi.
  • Intorno a Lorenzo Monaco. Nuovi studi sulla pittura tardogotica (conference proceedings, Fabriano-Foligno-Firenze 2006, published Livorno 2007), co-edited with Tartuferi, a foundational volume on late Gothic in central Italy linking Florence to the Marche and Umbria.
  • L'eredita di Giotto. Arte a Firenze 1340-1375 (2008) and related scholarship on the generation after Giotto.
  • Work on Giovanni dal Ponte and on the parallel currents of late Gothic and early Renaissance painting in the first three decades of the Quattrocento in Florence, mirroring the Accademia's collection displays.

She has also contributed to the museum's collection catalogues and to the philological reorganization of its Duecento and Trecento rooms, including the 2019 arrangement that brought Pacino and Jacopo del Casentino panels from the Uffizi to sit in continuity with the Accademia holdings.

Park, Katharine

active late 20th-21st century

Katharine Park (known as "Katy" Park) is an American historian of science and medicine, Samuel Zemurray, Jr. and Doris Zemurray Stone Radcliffe Professor of the History of Science emerita at Harvard University. She specializes in the history of gender, sexuality and the female body in medieval and Renaissance Europe, and in categories and practices of experience and observation in the Middle Ages.

Park took her A.B. in History and Literature (Renaissance and Reformation) at Radcliffe College, an M.Phil. in Combined Historical Studies of the Renaissance at the Warburg Institute, University of London, and her Ph.D. in the History of Science at Harvard. She was awarded a Marshall Scholarship in 1974, and received the Harvard doctorate in 1981.

Her research and teaching centre on the history of science and medicine in medieval and early modern Europe, with particular attention to gender, sexuality and the history of the body. Her work insists on the interconnection of knowledge and practice, and on relating both to the social, institutional and cultural contexts that produced them. At Harvard she also chaired the programme in Women's Studies from 1998 to 2003.

Her first book, Doctors and Medicine in Early Renaissance Florence (Princeton University Press, 1985), argued for studying artisanal and empirical practitioners, male and female, alongside university-trained physicians. It examines the guild, the university, hospitals and confraternities, Church and state as the institutional frame of Florentine medicine, the social position and intellectual life of the doctors themselves, and argues that the arrival of plague marked a crisis that transformed the composition of the profession and the conditions of practice. The Dan David Prize citation described her method there as surveying "the entire world of medical practice" in the wake of the 1348 epidemic.

With Lorraine Daston she wrote Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150-1750 (Zone Books, 1998), a study of the place of the marvellous in European natural philosophy across six centuries. Her monograph Secrets of Women: Gender, Generation, and the Origins of Human Dissection (Zone Books, 2006) reconstructed the emergence of human dissection in late medieval Italy, showing - against the received account of anatomy as a Renaissance rupture - that the earliest dissected bodies were largely women's, and that the practice grew out of concerns with generation, holiness and the interior of the female body. She also co-edited, with Daston, The Cambridge History of Science, vol. 3: Early Modern Science (2006).

She has been at work on A New History of Medieval Science, co-authored with Ahmed Ragab, premised on the argument that Greek, Arabic and Latin science were contemporary and in continuous communication throughout the medieval period, rather than three successive phases of a linear development culminating in the "birth of modern science" in early modern Europe. The book, spanning the eighth to the seventeenth centuries, is organised chronologically as a series of chapters, each set in a different city and built around a particular object of scientific knowledge.

Wonders and the Order of Nature, which has appeared in Italian and German translation, received in 2001 the Pfizer Award of the History of Science Society and the Roland H. Bainton Prize of the Sixteenth Century Studies Conference. Secrets of Women won the Margaret W. Rossiter History of Women and Science Prize of the HSS in 2007 and the William H. Welch Medal of the American Association of the History of Medicine in 2009, appearing in French the same year. Park was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and awarded the Sarton Medal in 2016. In 2021 she was named a Dan David Prize laureate in the "Past" category (History of Health and Medicine), alongside Alison Bashford and Keith Wailoo.

Parkes, Malcolm Beckwith

1930 - 2013

Malcolm B. Parkes was one of the foremost palaeographers of the twentieth century, Professor of Palaeography at the University of Oxford and a Fellow of Keble College. His books English Cursive Book Hands, 1250–1500 (1969) and, above all, Pause and Effect: An Introduction to the History of Punctuation in the West (1992) reshaped the study of medieval script and layout by treating punctuation, word separation, and page design as historically meaningful systems of visual communication rather than incidental scribal habit.

Parkes brought this same attention to the material discipline of the page in his 1982 Jarrow Lecture, The Scriptorium of Wearmouth-Jarrow, in which he argued that the community responsible for the Codex Amiatinus had developed its own graded system of uncial script, including a working variety he termed "Capitular Uncial," reserved for subsidiary elements of the page. The observation is significant because it points to institutional method rather than individual virtuosity: a scriptorium capable of distinguishing and teaching different grades of script for different textual functions was operating at a level of organizational sophistication matched by very few contemporary houses. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the manuscript's script and the scriptorium that produced it.

Parlato, Enrico

b. 1955

Distinguished Italian art historian specializing primarily in Renaissance and Baroque art, with significant contributions to medieval studies, including illuminated manuscripts and the masters of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries. Born in 1955, he earned a Ph.D. from Columbia University (GSAS) in 1985, and has developed a scholarly career since the 1980s across subjects ranging from the Middle Ages to the nineteenth century, with a core focus on fifteenth-century painting and sculpture in Rome and Florence.

Parlato has been Full Professor of Italian Art History from the Renaissance to the Baroque at the University of Tuscia in Viterbo since 1987. He is a member of the advisory committee of the National Institute of Archaeology and Art History (INASA), Scientific Secretary at the same institute, and a corresponding member of the National Institute of Roman Studies. His international teaching profile includes service as adjunct professor in Cornell University's Rome program and visiting lectures at multiple European and U.S. universities.

His research addresses the rediscovery of antiquity in the Renaissance, artistic exchanges between Rome and Venice in the sixteenth century, and the reworking of early Christian and medieval Rome in early modern visual culture. He has also published on medieval patronage in the Mediterranean, including work connected to Jill Caskey's studies on Amalfi, and has contributed to projects such as the Enciclopedia Farnesiana (since 2020) with collaborators including Paolo Marini.

Alongside academic publications, Parlato has been active in curatorial work, including the Filippo Lippi exhibition at Palazzo Barberini (2017–18) and the curatorial committee for the Pietro Aretino project at the Uffizi. He has also worked within RIASA (Journal of the National Institute of Archaeology and Art History), where he has served as secretary, in a framework spanning archaeology and art from antiquity to the Middle Ages.

His bibliography includes books, articles, edited volumes, and conference activity on topics such as Rome-Venice-Cyprus connections and artistic epistolary culture. On Academia.edu, he maintains an active profile with broad scholarly engagement (including 151 research papers), and his work is frequently cited in discussions that bridge medieval and Renaissance attributional and iconographic problems.

Parronchi, Alessandro

Florence, 26 December 1914 - Florence, 7 January 2007

Alessandro Parronchi was one of the most versatile Italian intellectuals of the twentieth century: poet, art historian, critic, essayist, translator, and amateur painter. He spent almost his entire life in Florence, which he rarely left except for brief stays related to travel and university teaching.

The only child of Augusto Parronchi, a notary, and Annunziata Paoletti, he was deeply marked in adolescence by the loss of his father, who died by suicide under circumstances never fully clarified. This biographical fracture has often been associated with the elegiac and melancholic tone of his poetry.

After classical studies, he enrolled in 1933 in the Faculty of Letters at the University of Florence, where classmates included Franco Fortini and Giorgio Spini. He graduated in November 1938 with highest honors with a thesis in art history under the medievalist Mario Salmi.

Together with Mario Luzi and Piero Bigongiari, later joined by Alfonso Gatto, Parronchi formed what Carlo Bo called the "triad" of Florentine Hermeticism, the literary movement often considered the most important in Italian culture after Futurism. For Parronchi and his generation, Hermeticism was also a gateway to European culture in the 1930s and 1940s, including Mallarme, Rimbaud, and Rilke, all authors with whom he maintained a lasting intellectual dialogue.

His poetic debut came in 1938 in Frontespizio with the poem Eclisse, introduced by Carlo Betocchi. He took active part in Florence's avant-garde journals, including Frontespizio, Campo di Marte, Letteratura, and Corriere Fiorentino. His first major collection, I giorni sensibili (1941), established him as one of the most authentic voices of Hermetic poetry. Later books, including Per strade di bosco e citta (1954), Coraggio di vivere (1961), and Quel che resta del giorno (2001), show a path from strict Hermeticism toward more narrative and existential tones while preserving a constant elegiac quality. In 2000, Polistampa gathered his poetic work in Le poesie, and in 2001 he received the Premio Dino Campana for his complete oeuvre.

In parallel with poetry, Parronchi developed a distinguished body of scholarship on medieval and Renaissance art. Already active as an art critic before completing his degree, he published in newspapers and journals such as Il Bargello. In 1959 he began university teaching, with appointments at the Florence Institute of Art, the Academy of Fine Arts in Bologna, and the University of Urbino, before becoming full professor of Medieval and Modern Art History at the University of Florence (1973-1989).

His major art-historical work is Studi su la dolce prospettiva (Aldo Martello Editore, Milan, 1964), a monumental 675-page collection of essays on fourteenth- and fifteenth-century art. The volume reconstructs the optical, perspectival, and mathematical frameworks within which figures such as Brunelleschi, Donatello, Paolo Uccello, and Filippo Lippi worked, and remains an important reference for studies of Renaissance perspective and the scientific foundations of vision.

He also published significant studies on Michelangelo and Donatello. Particularly well known is his attribution of the Fanciullo Arciere, now at the Cultural Institute of the French Embassy in New York, to the young Michelangelo. Proposed in 1968 after examining a photograph of the work, this attribution was later supported by specialists in the late 1990s.

Parronchi was also an important translator, rendering into Italian works by Stephane Mallarme, Arthur Rimbaud, and Gerard de Nerval, thereby contributing to the diffusion of French Symbolism in Italy. He also served as President of the Venice Biennale, confirming his role in major national cultural institutions.

In 1936 he wrote the libretto for the opera Giuoco del Barone in 9 e piu colpi di dadi for the composer Valentino Bucchi. The work was performed in 1939 and later won the Premio Italia in 1953, attesting to his broad engagement with literary and musical culture.

Throughout his life he maintained close relationships with many of the leading intellectuals of the century. During World War II, his Florentine home hosted figures including Eugenio Montale and Carlo Emilio Gadda. His large correspondence, much of it still insufficiently explored, is preserved at the Humanities Library of the University of Siena.

Parronchi died in Florence on 7 January 2007, a few days after turning ninety-two, leaving his wife Nara Somigli, whom he had married in 1954, and his daughters Rosa and Agnese. His scholarly and literary production has been systematically cataloged in the bibliography of works and criticism (1937-2014) edited by Bassi and Manigrasso and published by the University of Siena. Often described as "the last of the Hermetics," he is recognized both as one of the major Italian poets of the second half of the twentieth century and as a pioneering scholar of Renaissance perspective and medieval optics.

Pasqualetti, Cristiana

active late 20th-21st century

Cristiana Pasqualetti is an Italian art historian specializing in medieval painting and sculpture in Umbria and the central Apennine area, with particular attention to the fourteenth century and to the mobility of artists, workshops, and devotional objects between Spoleto and L'Aquila.

Her research is especially associated with the historiography of the anonymous masters of the Trecento in the old Duchy of Spoleto, including the Maestro della Croce di Trevi and the closely related painter-sculptor workshop problem around the Maestro della Croce di Visso. In this field, she is frequently cited for methodological precision in distinguishing secure attributions from proposals and in preferring workshop-based explanations when documentary proof is lacking.

A major contribution is her 2020 study that reexamined the evidence for the master's trans-Apennine geography, with focused analysis of the lunette in San Silvestro at L'Aquila and related Abruzzese material. That intervention helped reactivate the debate on whether the so-called "Spoletan" masters should be interpreted within a broader Umbrian-Abruzzese cultural continuum rather than through modern regional boundaries.

Pasqualetti's work is marked by close visual reading of physiognomic types, ornamental motifs, and painting technique, combined with careful control of provenance and restoration history. Her studies are regularly used in current scholarship on central-Italian Trecento art for questions of attribution, chronology, workshop structure, and the circulation of forms across the Apennines.

Pasqui, Ubaldo

Arezzo, 20 March 1859 – Arezzo, 29 November 1939

Ubaldo Pasqui was born in Arezzo on 20 March 1859 to Pietro Pasqui, an appreciated woodcarver, and Angelo (Angiolo) Pasqui, the archaeologist who became famous as the discoverer of the Ara Pacis Augustae. He left the local technical schools quite early and undertook a largely self-directed course of study in the libraries and archives of his native city, a choice that shaped his entire intellectual identity. Before the age of twenty he had already conceived the ambitious plan of writing an organic, document-based history of Arezzo, inspired in part by the massive Memorie manoscritte della città di Arezzo left by the marchese Antonio Albergotti. This early project explains the precocious breadth of his archival explorations and his life-long attachment to municipal history in a decidedly Romantic and Risorgimento-influenced key.

His first publication, written together with his brother Angelo, was La cattedrale aretina e i suoi monumenti (1880), a broad and systematic study of the cathedral of Arezzo and its artworks, illustrated with drawings by his own hand. Two years later, in 1882, on the occasion of the great Guidonian celebrations, he published the Guida di Arezzo, explicitly presented as "nuova" and "compilata sui documenti", already signalling his programmatic insistence on archival foundations for any description of the city. In order to collect documentary material on Arezzo — whose medieval communal archive had been destroyed in the fire of 1384 — Pasqui frequented the archives of Florence, Rome, Siena and Perugia, an activity that broadened both his documentary base and his scholarly network.

Pasqui's professional life was deeply rooted in archival work. From the 1880s he collaborated with the distinguished scholar Gian Francesco Gamurrini and came into contact with the great diplomatist Cesare Paoli, who between 1889 and 1891 published three of Pasqui's monographs in the prestigious Archivio Storico Italiano. In 1890–1892 he reorganized the pre-unification historical archive of the Comune di Arezzo, serving for decades as its conservator and compiling an inventory that, reworking earlier tools by Gustavo Mancini and Pasquale Leoni, remained the principal instrument for accessing the material for more than a century.

His archival career coincided with his broader role within the emerging Italian state archival administration; later surveys of the Archivio di Stato di Arezzo recall that some of the earliest concentrations of historical fonds in the city were the result of Pasqui's efforts from 1885 onwards. His training and practice as a diplomatist and paleographer shaped his methodological stance: he was deeply convinced that only rigorous archival investigation and critical analysis of documents could yield reliable, scientifically grounded historical knowledge. This conviction underpinned not only his documentary editions but also his work in local historiography and art history, making him a key figure in the renewal of humanistic studies in Arezzo at the turn of the century.

Although archivist and diplomatist by profession, Pasqui cultivated a remarkably wide range of scholarly interests, being described by the Società Storica Aretina as a man of "multiforme ingegno". He worked as historian, art historian, archaeologist, glottologist, bibliographer and sigillography specialist, publishing around forty studies on Arezzo and its territory. Among his main works are studies on the Casa del Petrarca (1900, 1904, 1933), on the family of Giorgio Vasari (1911), on Aretine painters of the late Middle Ages and Renaissance (notably the 1917 essay on painters active from the mid-twelfth century to 1527), on pottery (vasi fittili, 1921), on Bartolomeo della Gatta (1926) and on the Aretine dialect (1928).

His best-known and most substantial achievement is the monumental Documenti per la storia della città di Arezzo nel medio evo, published in four volumes between 1889 and 1937 and amounting to over two thousand pages. This collection, conceived as preparatory to a complete Storia di Arezzo that he never managed to write, gathers nearly 900 documents dated between 650 and 1385, along with some ten chronicles, including the third-rhyme chronicle of ser Bartolomeo di ser Gorello, whose authorship Pasqui correctly identified. The enterprise, with its strong "Muratorian" spirit, became a fundamental quarry for all subsequent studies on medieval Arezzo and remains a standard reference in diplomatic and historical research.

In parallel, Pasqui's Guida illustrata storica, artistica e commerciale di Arezzo e dintorni, published in 1925 together with Ugo Viviani and enriched with an extraordinary photographic apparatus, represented a synthesis of his activity as historian, art historian and archaeologist. For Pasqui, the description of monuments and the review of the city's illustrious men formed an organic part of local history, an approach that prefigures later notions of integrated cultural heritage. This guide, which combines historical narrative, topographical description and artistic documentation, is still considered an indispensable working tool for art historians dealing with Arezzo.

Beyond his archival post, Ubaldo Pasqui held several public and cultural positions in the city and province. From 1890 to 1913 he served as regio ispettore of monuments and excavations for the province of Arezzo, then as conservator of the municipal picture gallery (pinacoteca), and in 1914 he was made a knight of the Kingdom of Italy. He was a member of various Tuscan learned societies, including the Accademia Etrusca of Cortona, the Florentine society "La Colombaria", and the Deputazione di storia patria per la Toscana, and later also entered the Accademia Petrarca in Arezzo. The city itself commemorates him with plaques and a small monument near his birthplace, where he is paired with his older contemporary and sometime mentor Gamurrini.

Contemporary testimonies and later assessments present Pasqui as a figure of difficult and somewhat angular character, inclined to non-conformist positions and often isolated within the Aretine cultural milieu. His vision of the city's past was strongly marked by a narrow, municipal patriotism of Romantic and Risorgimento derivation, a mindset widespread in many Italian smaller cities between the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In at least one case this led to a significant historical misunderstanding: it was Pasqui's interpretation that prompted the podestà Guidotti Mori, in 1929, to formalize an anomalous version of Arezzo's civic coat of arms. Yet the very body of archival evidence assembled and published by Pasqui has since allowed later scholars to move beyond some of his interpretative limits, demonstrating how his empirical groundwork outlived his ideological framework.

Ubaldo Pasqui died in Arezzo on 29 November 1939, having spent his entire life working for and on his native city. The archival fonds he concentrated and inventoried formed the initial nucleus of what later became the local section of the Archivio di Stato, established in the city by ministerial decree in 1941, ensuring institutional continuity for his work as archivist and diplomatist. Generations of Aretine scholars — historians, philologists, art historians and archaeologists — have depended on his documentary editions and guides, which remain essential points of reference for the medieval and early modern history of the city.

Modern evaluations underline the dual nature of his legacy: on the one hand, an at times restrictive municipal perspective; on the other, an extraordinary depth of archival research and methodological rigour that renewed historical and humanistic studies in Arezzo. Because of this, current historiography on Arezzo routinely treats Pasqui as both an object and an instrument of research: his writings are critically scrutinized, yet his Documenti and guides are still used daily as basic tools. In short, Ubaldo Pasqui can be seen as an exemplary figure of late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Italian local erudition at its best: deeply rooted in place, passionately attached to municipal history, but also capable of producing documentary work of lasting national scholarly value.

Pasut, Francesca Rosa

active late 20th–21st century

Francesca Rosa Pasut is one of Italy's leading specialists in medieval illuminated manuscripts, with a scholarly career spanning nearly three decades and focused primarily on Florentine and Bolognese manuscript painting from the thirteenth to the fifteenth centuries. Her work sits at the intersection of art history, codicology, and Dante studies, making her a central figure in contemporary research on Italian medieval book culture.

Pasut received her graduate training at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan, and then pursued a three-year specialization (Scuola di Specializzazione triennale in Storia dell'Arte) at the Università degli Studi di Milano. A decisive formative experience came through her fellowship at the prestigious Fondazione di Studi di Storia dell'Arte Roberto Longhi in Florence, where she held a scholarship for the academic years 1997–98 and 1998–99. This institution, founded by the great art historian Roberto Longhi, has long been a crucible for connoisseurship-based approaches to Italian painting, and its influence is clearly visible in Pasut's method of close stylistic and attributional analysis.

Her institutional career has centered on two major universities. She has been affiliated with the Università degli Studi di Firenze, within the Department of History, Archaeology, Geography, Art and Performing Arts (SAGAS), where she held a post-doctoral position. More recently, she has been associated with the Università degli Studi di Napoli "Federico II," within its Department of Humanistic Studies. These affiliations reflect the broad national reach of her scholarly network, connecting the great Florentine tradition of art historical research with the important medieval manuscript holdings of Southern Italy.

One of Pasut's most significant early scholarly contributions is her volume Ornamental Painting in Italy, 1250–1310: An Illustrated Index (Florence: Giunti, 2003), published as part of the foundational Corpus of Florentine Painting series edited by Miklós Boskovits. This work systematically catalogued decorative painting in Italian manuscripts of the late Duecento and early Trecento, providing the field with an essential reference tool for understanding the stylistic relationships between workshops operating during a period of remarkable artistic transformation. The volume addresses a category of medieval visual production — border and ornamental work in manuscripts — that had often been treated as peripheral, but which Pasut demonstrated to be a rich source of evidence for questions of dating, attribution, and inter-workshop exchange.

Pasut has dedicated a substantial portion of her career to the study of Pacino di Bonaguida, the early fourteenth-century Florentine painter and illuminator who was among the first artists to create illustrated copies of Dante's Divine Comedy. She contributed the authoritative entry on Pacino to the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (vol. 80, Treccani, 2014), the national biographical encyclopedia of Italy. Her essay "Codici miniati della Commedia a Firenze attorno al 1330: questioni attributive e di cronologia" (Rivista di Studi Danteschi, 2007) is considered a landmark study on the attribution and dating of the earliest Florentine illustrated Dante manuscripts, having accumulated over 2,400 views on Academia.edu. She also published research on Pacino's illumination of the Trivulzian Bible (Codice Trivulziano 2139), co-authored with M. Pontone in Libri & Documenti (2014), demonstrating the collaborative, workshop-based nature of this major commission.

A particularly original thread in Pasut's research concerns the Danti del Cento, a compact cluster of Florentine Commedia manuscripts identifiable through shared philological, graphic, and codicological features — replicated from one exemplar to the next in codified form. At the 2021 Bargello Museum exhibition marking the seventh centenary of Dante's death, she argued that the key impulse for producing illustrated Commedia manuscripts emerged around 1337, the year Giotto's image of Dante appeared among the blessed in Paradise in the Bargello's Cappella del Podestà. This thesis connects the production of illustrated Dante manuscripts directly to a specific historical and devotional moment in Florentine civic life, and was central to the exhibition's scholarly apparatus.

Alongside her Florentine research, Pasut has made lasting contributions to the study of Bolognese manuscript painting, particularly the work of Nicolò di Giacomo, the most prominent illuminator of late Trecento Bologna. Her early article "Qualche considerazione sul percorso di Nicolò di Giacomo miniatore bolognese" (Arte Cristiana, 1998) established key aspects of his chronology and stylistic development. She later published an essay on his illustrations for the Ambrosian manuscript of Seneca's Tragedies (co-authored with C.M. Monti, in Miscellanea Graecolatina, 2013), a study that showed how classical literary texts circulated in richly illustrated form within the learned milieu of Trecento Northern Italy. She also wrote a profile of the master for the popular illumination journal Alumina. Pagine Miniate (2009), bringing her specialist research to a wider audience.

Pasut's interests extend naturally to the other two crowns of the Trecento literary canon. Her essay "Il Dante illustrato di Petrarca: problemi di miniatura tra Firenze e Pisa alla metà del Trecento" (Studi Petrarcheschi, 2007) traced the illuminated copy of the Commedia owned by Petrarch, addressing complex questions about artistic interchange between Florence and Pisa around 1350. Her contribution to the 2013 exhibition catalogue Boccaccio autore e copista (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana) treated Boccaccio as a visual artist, analyzing his drawings in relation to the broader manuscript culture of his time.

Pasut's chronological range extends into the Quattrocento through her research on manuscript production connected with the early Vatican Library. Her major essay "Libri, miniatori e artisti alle origini della Vaticana tra Niccolò V e Sisto IV" appeared in the volume Le origini della Biblioteca Vaticana tra Umanesimo e Rinascimento (Vatican City, 2010), exploring the illuminators and artists who contributed to the Library's founding collections under popes Nicholas V and Sixtus IV. This work positions her as a scholar equally at home in the Trecento world of Gothic illumination and in the transitional moment of the early Renaissance.

Beyond her individual research, Pasut has played an important role in organizing the field. She co-edited the conference proceedings Da Giotto a Botticelli: Pittura fiorentina tra Gotico e Rinascimento (Florence, 2008), the acts of an international symposium held at the University of Florence and the Museo di San Marco in 2005. This volume brought together international specialists on Florentine painting and illumination across a critical century of artistic transformation. She has also contributed to the Illuminated Dante Project (IDP), an international digital humanities initiative cataloguing the approximately 280 illuminated manuscripts of the Divine Comedy from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

Pelekanidis, Stylianos

Constantinople (Phanar), 1909 – Thessaloniki, 1980
