Greek archaeologist and professor of Byzantine archaeology whose career united three complementary identities — field conservator, academic scholar, and documentary editor — in a sustained engagement with the material heritage of early Christian and Byzantine Greece. Born in the Phanar district of Constantinople, he entered the Theological School of Halki (Heybeliada) in 1923, graduating in 1931 with a diploma in Orthodox theology. This liturgically grounded formation in Byzantine sacred culture preceded his academic studies at the University of Berlin from 1935, where he encountered the rigorous methodological traditions of German art-historical and archaeological scholarship. The transit between Halki's Orthodox theological culture and Berlin's secular academic apparatus was the characteristic movement of the most productive Greek Byzantinologists of the twentieth century.

Pelekanidis served as Ephor of Byzantine Antiquities in Thessaloniki from 1943 to 1962 — a tenure that began under the Axis occupation of Greece and continued through the civil war and its aftermath. In this capacity he held administrative and scholarly responsibility for the care, conservation, and study of Byzantine monuments in the city and its region. He oversaw the completion of the restoration of the Basilica of Saint Demetrios in 1948, following the catastrophic fire of 1917, and coordinated the systematic conservation of the mosaics of the Rotunda on the occasion of the Ninth International Congress of Byzantine Studies in Thessaloniki in 1953. These conservation campaigns required sustained, technically demanding contact with the most important monuments of early Christian pictorial art in Greece and forged the connoisseurial expertise that informed all his subsequent scholarship. After his years as Ephor, he joined the faculty of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki as Professor of Byzantine Archaeology, affiliated with the Centre for Byzantine Studies (Κέντρο Βυζαντινών Ερευνών).

The Byzantine painted churches of Kastoria — a lakeside town in western Macedonia with an exceptionally dense concentration of medieval frescoes spanning the eleventh to the fifteenth centuries — were the subject of his first and most sustained monographic engagement. His Καστορία, τόμος I: Βυζαντιναί τοιχογραφίαι (Kastoria, Volume I: Byzantine Wall Paintings; Thessaloniki, Society of Macedonian Studies, 1953) was the first systematic scholarly treatment of the Byzantine painted decoration of the town's churches, documenting the foundational Comnenian cycles of Hagios Stephanos, Hagioi Anargyroi, and Hagios Nikolaos Kasnitzi. The authority of this documentation was confirmed three decades later in the volume Kastoria (Melissa Publications, 1985), produced in collaboration with Manolis Chatzidakis in the prestigious Byzantine Art in Greece series — a posthumous confirmation of the enduring value of his fieldwork. His collected essays, Μελέτες Παλαιοχριστιανικής και Βυζαντινής Αρχαιολογίας (Studies in Early Christian and Byzantine Archaeology; Institute of Balkan Studies, Thessaloniki, 1977; 502 pp., also known in German as Studien zur frühchristlichen und byzantinischen Archäologie), represent the mature summation of his scholarly contributions to the field.

For the study of illuminated manuscripts, the most directly relevant dimension of his career is his editorial supervision of the multi-volume photographic catalogue Θησαυροί του Αγίου Όρους: Εικονογραφημένα χειρόγραφα (Treasures of Mount Athos: Illustrated Manuscripts), produced under the auspices of the Aristotle University's Centre for Byzantine Studies — the most systematic documentation of the illuminated manuscripts preserved in the monasteries of the Athonite peninsula. Pelekanidis supervised and edited volumes covering the manuscripts of the Great Lavra, Pantocrator, Dochiariou, Karakalou, Philotheou, Saint Paul, Iviron, Saint Panteleimon, Esphigmenou, and Chilandari. The series spans the full range of Byzantine book production — Gospels, Psalters, Lectionaries, theological and hagiographic texts — from the earliest surviving examples of the ninth and tenth centuries through the Palaeologan Renaissance and into the post-Byzantine tradition, and constitutes an indispensable reference for the study of Byzantine manuscript illumination across its full chronological and typological range.

In 1974 Pelekanidis was awarded the Herder Prize, conferred by the Alfred Toepfer Foundation through the University of Vienna, recognizing his contributions to the cultural life of Central and Eastern European nations through the documentation of the Byzantine heritage of northern Greece and Macedonia. A philological memorial volume was published in his honour in 1982, gathering the tributes of colleagues and students from the Thessaloniki academic community.

Perkins, Frederick Mason

Boston, 1874 – Assisi, 1955

Frederick Mason Perkins, who published under the name F. Mason Perkins, was an American-born connoisseur and art historian who spent almost the whole of his adult life in Italy and became one of the most prolific and internationally consulted authorities on Sienese and Umbrian painting of the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries. Settling first in Assisi and later dividing his time between Assisi and Florence, he built an extensive private collection of early Italian panels alongside his scholarly work.

Between 1908 and the 1920s Perkins published a long series of articles, principally in the Rassegna d'arte senese, that drew together and reattributed scattered panels then circulating under mistaken or generic names, work that formed an essential precondition for the twentieth-century reconstruction of numerous Sienese painters' corpora, Luca di Tommè among them. Perkins's residence in Fascist Italy through the Second World War, and his sympathies with the regime, later complicated his reputation; his collection of early Italian paintings passed after his death to the Pinacoteca Comunale of Assisi.

Perrin, Michel Jean-Louis

born 1944

Michel Perrin was born in 1944 and is a specialist in Latin Christian literature. He was the author of an undergraduate thesis in Classical Letters at the University of Nancy 2 in 1969 on the illustration of the rhetorical precepts of the fourth book of Augustine's De doctrina christiana through examples drawn from his sermons, an early engagement with the relationship between textual argument and formal expression that would prove prophetic of his life's work.

His doctoral thesis, directed by Jacques Fontaine at the Universite de Paris IV (Sorbonne), was defended in 1977 under the title Homo christianus: christianisme et tradition antique dans l'anthropologie de Lactance, a major study of how Lactantius (c. 250-325) absorbed, transformed, and re-articulated classical anthropological concepts within Christian prose. Perrin became Professor of Latin Language and Literature at the University of Picardie in 1976 and has long worked in Amiens, where he directed the research laboratory trAMe (EA 4284: "Textes, Representations, Autorites, Archeologie, Memoire") at the Universite de Picardie Jules-Verne.

His scholarship is structured across three principal domains: Late Antiquity (especially the fourth century), the Middle Ages (especially the ninth century), and the history of biological and medical sciences. The Lactantius studies that emerged from his doctoral work, including articles in the Cahiers de Fontenay between 1984 and 1991, established him as an authority on Christian Latin intellectual culture in the Constantinian age.

The decisive turn in his career came through manuscript proximity at the Bibliotheque municipale d'Amiens, which preserves one of the key ninth-century witnesses to Hrabanus Maurus's In honorem sanctae crucis (BAM 223 F). In 1988 Perrin published the first French translation of De laudibus sanctae crucis, with reproductions, drawings, and a substantial introduction. This publication made one of the most complex Carolingian verbal-visual works accessible to a wider francophone scholarly public.

The object of Perrin's central research, Hrabanus's cycle of 28 carmina figurata, is a uniquely difficult corpus in which letter-grids, poetic composition, and image formation are inseparable. Read continuously, each grid yields hexametric text; read selectively through highlighted versus intexti, it generates theological images and inscriptions. Around eighty manuscripts survive, confirming the broad diffusion of the work in Carolingian and post-Carolingian intellectual networks.

In 1989 Perrin published two foundational studies. The first, "Le De laudibus sanctae crucis de Raban Maur et sa tradition manuscrite au IXe siecle" (Revue d'histoire des textes, 19, 1989, pp. 191-252), offered the first systematic reconstruction of the ninth-century manuscript tradition. The second, "Le De laudibus sanctae crucis de Raban Maur: de la codicologie a la theologie en passant par la poetique" (Revue des Etudes Latines, 67, 1989, pp. 213-235), articulated the methodological triad that defines his work: codicology, theology, and poetics.

This research proved decisive for understanding the Vienna codex tradition centered on Codex Vindobonensis 652 (Osterreichische Nationalbibliothek). Perrin did not treat Vienna as an isolated masterpiece; he located it within a dynamic transmission network including Vatican Reginensis 124, Amiens BAM 223 F, and other Fulda, Tours, and related witnesses. His analysis clarified recension differences and showed that Vienna preserves the earlier textual state of the cycle.

Perrin's critical edition in Corpus Christianorum, Continuatio Mediaevalis (CCCM 100-100A, Brepols, 1997) transformed the field. It was the first truly critical edition since Jakob Wimpfeling's 1503 editio princeps; intervening print traditions, including PL 107, had largely recycled non-critical text. The CCCM edition includes an extensive introduction, full manuscript-based apparatus, translation, explanatory notes, and indexed tools for navigating the corpus.

Perrin subsequently extended this philological foundation into systematic iconographic documentation with L'iconographie de la "Gloire a la sainte croix" de Raban Maur (Brepols, 2009-2010), the first volume of the RILMA series, which he directed. This initiative sought to provide medieval literary illustration with the same documentary rigor that critical editions provide for texts, enabling comparative analysis of visual programs across the full manuscript tradition.

Beyond Hrabanus, Perrin co-organized and co-edited Bede le Venerable entre tradition et posterite (2005, with Stephane Lebecq and Olivier Szerwiniack), directed work on court Latin poetry and political culture (La lyre et la pourpre, with Nathalie Catellani-Dufrene), and published studies on the relationship between Alcuin and Hrabanus in the genesis of In honorem sanctae crucis.

Michel Perrin's contribution is foundational for historians of Carolingian art, manuscript studies, and medieval visual theology. His integrated method, codicology, theology, and poetics, his mapping of the manuscript tradition, his critical edition, and his iconographic repertory together established the modern scholarly framework for studying Hrabanus Maurus and the transmission of Carolingian word-image culture, including the Vienna Codex Vindobonensis 652.

Picchiarelli, Veruska

b. Umbria, 1978

Veruska Picchiarelli is an Italian art historian specialising in medieval and early modern painting, and one of the leading scholars of Umbrian art of the Duecento and Trecento.

Training. She took her degree in Conservazione dei Beni Culturali at the University of Siena, followed by a specialisation diploma and a doctorate in Storia delle Arti Visive at the University of Pisa. She also holds a diploma from the school of archival science, palaeography and diplomatics at the Archivio di Stato in Perugia, a philological grounding that shows in her work on documentary sources and on manuscript-adjacent material.

Career. Since 2017 she has been a staff art historian (funzionaria storica dell'arte) at the Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria in Perugia, where she curates the medieval and early modern collections, organises exhibitions, and has coordinated the museum's educational services. Her earliest museum work there goes back much further: she collaborated on landmark Perugia exhibitions including Perugino il Divin Pittore (2004), Arnolfo di Cambio. Una rinascita nell'Umbria medievale (2005-06), and Pintoricchio (2008).

Since December 2020 she has been scientific director of Castello Bufalini at San Giustino (PG), where she has overseen a restoration and access programme, funded under the Ministry's Piano Strategico Grandi Progetti Beni Culturali, to open currently unvisitable rooms, with completion targeted for 2026. She is also cultore della materia for the teaching of Economia e gestione dei Beni Culturali e del Turismo at the University of Perugia, and is active in ICOM Italia.

On 24 June 2026 the Ministry of Culture appointed her interim head of the Musei nazionali di Perugia - Direzione regionale Musei nazionali Umbria, following Costantino D'Orazio's move to the Direzione generale Creativita contemporanea; she will serve until a new director is appointed through the international competitive procedure introduced by the 2014 Franceschini reform.

Scholarship and exhibitions. Her research centres on late medieval painting in Umbria, the Foligno diocese, minor masters of the Trecento, and the artistic geography of the Valnerina, and on the Perugino orbit. Notable curatorial work includes:

  • Taddeo di Bartolo (GNU, 2019), for which she wrote on Benedetto di Bindo in Umbria
  • L'Autunno del Medioevo in Umbria. Cofani nuziali in gesso dorato (GNU, 2019-20), on Perugian gilded-gesso marriage caskets
  • L'eta dell'oro (GNU, 2024-25), co-curated with Alessandra Mammi and Carla Scagliosi, spanning nine centuries from the Middle Ages to the contemporary
  • Il Maestro di San Francesco e lo stil novo del Duecento umbro, with Andrea De Marchi and Emanuele Zappasoldi (Silvana Editoriale, 2024), the first major attempt to reconstruct the anonymous Duecento master's oeuvre

She has also published previously unknown preparatory drawings connected to Perugino's Adoration of the Child fresco from San Francesco al Monte, now in the GNU.

Piccirilli, Pietro

Sulmona, 18 July 1849 – Sulmona, 8 March 1921

Pietro Piccirilli was the first scholar from Abruzzo to approach the history of medieval art and architecture in his region in a systematic and critically grounded manner, documenting the artistic heritage of inland Abruzzo through rigorous methodology and tireless fieldwork, which established him as an irreplaceable figure in southern medieval studies.

Born in Sulmona on July 18, 1849, Piccirilli was entirely self-taught, graduating with top honors in August 1875 from the Institute of Fine Arts in Naples, then directed by Edoardo Dalbono. By 1872 he was already working as a teacher in Sulmona's secondary schools, a career he never abandoned until his death, alongside his historical-artistic research: he was responsible for founding the School of Arts and Crafts in Sulmona, an institution that had a tangible impact on the technical and artistic education of local generations. An acquaintance and friend of Benedetto Croce, he was the second scholar from Abruzzo—after Antonio De Nino—to engage systematically and not merely sporadically with the region's historical and artistic heritage, distinguishing himself from his predecessors precisely through his ability to compare sources and subject attributions to a precise stylistic examination, without succumbing to the parochial biases that had marred many local studies.

Piccirilli's most enduring contribution concerns two distinct yet complementary fields: medieval architecture in Abruzzo and the luxury arts—goldsmithing, silversmithing, and woodcarving. In 1888, he published in Lanciano Monumenti architettonici e artistici di Sulmona (Architectural and Artistic Monuments of Sulmona), the first critical survey of medieval architecture in the Peligna region, followed between 1893 and 1898 by the volumes La Basilica di San Clemente a Casauria (The Basilica of San Clemente in Casauria) and Monumenti sulmonesi architettonici descritti ed illustrati (Described and Illustrated Architectural Monuments of Sulmona) (ten issues with thirty-six plates). At the same time, Piccirilli was the first scholar to reconstruct, with historiographical rigor, the great medieval goldsmithing tradition of Sulmona and to systematically analyze the work of the leading 15th-century goldsmith of Abruzzo, Nicola da Guardiagrele, grouping the relics scattered throughout the region's churches into coherent stylistic families through an attributive method that anticipated the formalistic approach later codified by Longhi's criticism. His essays on medieval goldsmithing were published in Adolfo Venturi's journal L'Arte, which attests to the recognition of his expertise by the national scholarly community.

Piccirilli was the first scholar to provide a detailed and systematic description of the frescoes in Santa Maria ad Cryptas a Fossa and the oratory of San Pellegrino a Bominaco, the two most important medieval pictorial cycles in inland Abruzzo. These descriptions, published in local journals between the late 19th century and the first decade of the 20th century, remained for decades the sole scientific reference for anyone wishing to study those monuments, and were explicitly cited by all the great medievalists who studied Abruzzese painting during the 20th century—from Guglielmo Matthiae to Ferdinando Bologna.

In 1897, together with Giovanni Pansa, Piccirilli founded the Rassegna Abruzzese di Storia e Arte (RASA), the first scholarly journal entirely dedicated to the region's historical and artistic heritage. He was also among the founders of the Società Regia di Storia Patria degli Abruzzi (later the Deputazione Abruzzese di Storia Patria), based in L'Aquila, an institution that brought together scholars and historians from the region in a joint project of archival and monumental research. Among his foreign scholarly counterparts were Émile Bertaux—author of the seminal L'art dans l'Italie méridionale (1903)—and G. Rohault de Fleury, with whom he collaborated on studies of medieval goldsmithing, fostering dialogue between Abruzzo research and French medieval studies.

The most emblematic moment in Piccirilli's life was his response to the Marsica earthquake of January 13, 1915, which completely destroyed Avezzano and devastated dozens of towns in western Abruzzo, burying sculptures, frescoes, liturgical furnishings, and archives of immense value under the rubble. Piccirilli, by then sixty-five years old, rushed to the affected areas and remained there for weeks, working in conditions of extreme cold and hardship, leading the recovery of salvageable works with an energy and determination that Superintendent Carlo Ignazio Gavini, in his seminal History of Architecture in Abruzzo (1927), recalled as one of the most shining examples of dedication to artistic heritage. His son Guido Piccirilli (1885–1968) continued his father's research, becoming himself a scholar of Abruzzo art history. Pietro Piccirilli passed away on March 8, 1921, leaving behind a bibliographic output of over fifty-five contributions published between 1882 and 1919 in journals such as Venturi's L'Arte, Napoli Nobilissima, the Rassegna Abruzzese, and the Rassegna d'Arte.

Pope-Hennessy, John

London, 13 December 1913 - Florence, 31 October 1994

Sir John Wyndham Pope-Hennessy was one of the most influential art historians and museum directors of the twentieth century, especially in the study of Italian sculpture from the medieval period through the Renaissance and Baroque. Trained in the British connoisseurship tradition but intellectually cosmopolitan, he combined close visual analysis with archival awareness and an unusually elegant literary style, producing books that shaped generations of scholars, curators, and students.

Born in London into a prominent Anglo-Irish family, Pope-Hennessy was educated at Downside School and later at Balliol College, Oxford. Early in his career he turned decisively toward Italian art, with a particular focus on sculpture as a central rather than secondary field of historical inquiry. At a time when painting still dominated most narratives of Italian art, he argued that sculpture offered an equally rigorous route to reconstructing patronage, workshop practice, devotional culture, and civic ideology.

His scholarly reputation was established by a sequence of landmark studies that remain foundational: Italian Gothic Sculpture, Italian Renaissance Sculpture, and Italian High Renaissance and Baroque Sculpture. Together, these books provided a coherent long-duration history of Italian sculpture, notable for clear periodization, strong attributional judgement, and sensitive stylistic reading. He also authored major monographs on individual masters, including Donatello and Cellini, and influential museum catalogues, among them the work on Italian sculpture in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

Pope-Hennessy also played a major public role in museum leadership. He served as Director of the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, then as Director of the British Museum, and later became Director of The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Across these institutions he promoted rigorous object-based scholarship, strengthened curatorial standards, and expanded the international profile of museum research. His directorships helped bridge the worlds of academic art history, conservation, and public museum culture at a global level.

Methodologically, his work is associated with disciplined connoisseurship: careful formal comparison, attention to material and carving technique, and strong interest in historical context without reducing visual problems to documentary summaries. His writings on Trecento and Quattrocento sculpture were especially important for integrating provincial and regional centers into broader narratives, rather than treating Florence as the sole axis of development. In this respect, he contributed decisively to a more plural map of Italian artistic production.

Beyond specialist monographs, Pope-Hennessy wrote and lectured with a rare clarity that made demanding art-historical arguments accessible to non-specialist audiences without sacrificing scholarly precision. His prose style, precise but never dry, became a model for museum catalogues and synthetic histories alike. He was widely honored in Britain and internationally, and his authority extended across both European and American scholarly communities.

For researchers of medieval and early Renaissance visual culture, Pope-Hennessy remains indispensable not only for specific attributions but for historiographic method: his insistence that sculpture be read as a primary historical source transformed how Italian art is taught and interpreted. His legacy survives in the continued use of his books, in the curatorial standards he championed, and in the enduring centrality of sculpture within narratives of Italian medieval and Renaissance art.

Porter, Arthur Kingsley

Stamford, Connecticut, 6 February 1883 – Inishbofin, County Donegal, 8 July 1933 (disappeared)

Arthur Kingsley Porter was the first American scholar of Romanesque art to achieve international standing, the author of the ten-volume Romanesque Sculpture of the Pilgrimage Roads, and the central figure in the most consequential controversy in the field's early history. He disappeared from a Donegal island in 1933 in circumstances that have never been explained.

He was born at Stamford, Connecticut, in 1883, the son of a banker; his mother died when he was eight and his father during his first year at Yale, leaving him independently wealthy. He was educated at the Browning School in New York, graduated from Yale in 1904, and studied at the Columbia School of Architecture — a training in building rather than in connoisseurship that marked all his later work. In 1912 he married Lucy Bryant Wallace, who managed his affairs and his vast photographic campaigns. He took a Harvard B.F.A. in 1917, joined the Fine Arts department there in 1920, taught at the Sorbonne in 1923, and from 1925 held the William Dorr Boardman chair.

Medieval Architecture (1909) and the four volumes of Lombard Architecture (1915–17) established him, but Romanesque Sculpture of the Pilgrimage Roads (1923) made him famous and contentious in equal measure. Its thesis was that twelfth-century sculptural style was not the property of nations or regions but travelled, fluid as the pilgrims themselves, along the roads to Santiago de Compostela — and that Spanish monuments could hold chronological priority over French ones. This ran directly against Émile Mâle and the received primacy of Languedoc, and the ensuing quarrel, sharpened by the nationalist temper of French scholarship after 1918, was among the defining episodes of twentieth-century medieval art history. Porter, unlike Mâle, had actually travelled the Camino. Spanish Romanesque Sculpture followed in 1928.

His documentary ambition was as important as his arguments. He and Lucy Porter assembled a photographic archive of Romanesque architecture and sculpture on a scale no individual scholar had attempted, and the plate volumes of his books put the monuments themselves before readers who would never see them. The method — comparison at scale, from photographs, across national boundaries — became standard practice.

From about 1929 Ireland absorbed him. He bought Glenveagh Castle in County Donegal, built a cottage on the island of Inishbofin off the Donegal coast, and turned to Irish material in The Crosses and Culture of Ireland (1931). On 8 July 1933, having spent the night at the Inishbofin cottage, he vanished without trace; the inquest was the first held in Ireland without a body. He was presumed drowned, though the absence of any remains has sustained a long afterlife of speculation, including the suggestion that he arranged his own disappearance. He was fifty.

His name survives in the Gislebertus literature in a minor but characteristic register: it was Porter who compared the Eve of Autun to El Greco and Gauguin, one of the earliest of those modernist analogies — André Malraux's "Romanesque Cézanne" is the other — by which twentieth-century critics claimed Romanesque sculpture for the history of expressive form.

Post, Chandler Rathfon

Detroit, 1881 – Foxborough, 1959

American art historian renowned for his expertise in Spanish and Italian Renaissance art, particularly iconography and painting traditions. Born on December 14, 1881, in Detroit, Michigan, Post pursued his education at Harvard University, earning a BA in Spanish literature in 1904. He later studied Greek literature at the American School of Classical Studies in Athens and returned to Harvard for a PhD in 1909, with a thesis on fifteenth-century Castilian allegory influenced by Dante. Post joined Harvard's faculty in 1914 as assistant professor of Greek art and fine arts, advancing to the William Dorr Boardman Professor of Fine Arts by 1934 and teaching until 1950, when he became professor emeritus. He served as an interpreter for the American Red Cross Commission to Italy during the First World War, blending his linguistic skills with art historical pursuits.

Post's scholarship focused on comprehensive art surveys, beginning with the two-volume History of European and American Sculpture (1921), one of the earliest such works produced in America. His magnum opus, the fourteen-volume A History of Spanish Painting (1930–1953), meticulously documented Spanish art from the medieval to the Renaissance period, with the final volumes completed posthumously by Harold Edwin Wethey. This series remains a foundational reference for understanding regional styles, attributions, and iconographic developments in Iberian painting, and provides valuable context for transitional periods relevant to twelfth- to fourteenth-century iconography.

A member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the American Philosophical Society, Post's rigorous methodologies advanced connoisseurship and stylistic analysis in Renaissance studies. Among his notable students were the writer John Dos Passos and the art historian Walter William Spencer Cook, reflecting his influence on future scholars. He died on November 2, 1959, in Foxborough, Massachusetts.

Potestà, Gian Luca

Genoa, 15 November 1952

Gian Luca Potestà is an Italian historian of Christianity, and one of the leading international authorities on medieval prophetism and apocalypticism — above all on Joachim of Fiore.

Formation and academic career

He studied at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan, where he graduated in philosophy. He remained at the same university as a fellow and then as a researcher in the Dipartimento di Scienze Religiose. In 1998 he became associate professor of medieval history at the University of Palermo, where in 2001 he obtained the chair of History of Christianity and of the Churches (as straordinario, 2001–2004). From 2004 to 2023 he held the chair of History of Christianity at the Università Cattolica, where he is now professor emeritus in the Facoltà di Lettere e Filosofia.

His international career includes a fellowship of the Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung at the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in Munich (1990–1992), a Senior Fellowship at the Historisches Kolleg in Munich (2008–2009), visiting professorships in medieval history at the University of Konstanz (1996 and 2000), and a directeur d'études invité appointment at the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales in Paris (2007). He has directed the scientific committee of the Centro Internazionale di Studi Gioachimiti at San Giovanni in Fiore since 2021, and in the same year became a Corresponding Fellow of the Medieval Academy of America. He is a member of the International Commission for the critical edition of the Opera omnia of Joachim of Fiore.

His work began with the biographical and doctrinal trajectories of the Franciscan Spirituals and the fraticelli of the early fourteenth century. To this belong Storia ed escatologia in Ubertino da Casale (Vita e Pensiero, 1980), which won the "Paola e Antonio Malipiero" prize for Franciscan studies in 1982, Angelo Clareno: dai poveri eremiti ai fraticelli (Istituto Storico Italiano per il Medio Evo, Rome, 1990), his critical edition of Ubertino da Casale's Tractatus de altissima paupertate Christi et apostolorum eius ("Oliviana", 4, 2012), and most recently Frati contro. Dissidenti, cospiratori, fuggiaschi (Edizioni Biblioteca Francescana, 2025).

From the early 1990s he turned intensively to Joachim of Fiore and to the prophetic and apocalyptic figures and movements attached to his doctrinal legacy. Within the Opera omnia he produced the critical edition of Joachim's Dialogi de prescientia Dei (Rome, 1995; Italian translation with facing Latin text, Rome, 2001). His best-known book is Il tempo dell'Apocalisse. Vita di Gioacchino da Fiore (Laterza, 2004), translated into Spanish as El tiempo del Apocalipsis (Trotta, Madrid, 2010).

Other principal works include L'Anticristo, in three volumes with Marco Rizzi for Mondadori–Fondazione Valla (2005–2019); L'ultimo messia. Profezia e sovranità nel medioevo (il Mulino, 2014; Czech translation Argo, 2017; French translation Les Belles Lettres, 2018); Dante in conclave. La lettera ai cardinali (Vita e Pensiero, 2021; revised and expanded French translation, Macula, 2025); and Segni dei tempi. Figure profetiche e cifre apocalittiche (Vita e Pensiero, 2023). With Giovanni Vian he co-authored the widely used textbook Storia del cristianesimo (il Mulino), of which chapters 1–16 are his.

He directs the series Dies Nova. Fonti e studi per la storia del profetismo (Vita e Pensiero); he sits on the editorial board of «Aevum. Rassegna di scienze storiche linguistiche e filologiche», which he directed from 2014 to 2022, and of the «Rivista di Storia del Cristianesimo», which he helped to found. He is also on the editorial committee of «Oliviana. Mouvements et dissidences spirituels XIIIe–XIVe siècles» and the scientific committee of the «Annali di Scienze religiose», which he directed from 2008 to 2013.

Powell, Roger

Kimbolton, Herefordshire, 1896 – Hampshire, 1990

Roger Powell was a British bookbinder and manuscript conservator, among the most celebrated craftsmen in twentieth-century book conservation. Trained originally in the Arts and Crafts binding tradition, Powell went on to rebind or conserve an extraordinary run of the most important surviving medieval manuscripts of the British Isles, including the Book of Kells, which he rebound into four volumes, one per gospel, in 1953.

In 1957 Powell rebound the Book of Dimma with wooden boards and modern vellum, work that stood until the manuscript was disbound, conserved and rebound again by John Gillis in 2016. His other major commissions included conservation work associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls fragments and historic bindings held at the Bodleian Library and elsewhere. Powell's combination of traditional craft skill with a scholarly, historically informed respect for the physical integrity of the object set a professional standard for manuscript conservation that later conservators, including Gillis himself, would continue to develop.

Pozzi, Giovanni

Locarno, 20 June 1923 - Lugano, 20 July 2002

Giovanni Pozzi was a Swiss-Italian Capuchin friar and philologist of international renown, one of the most versatile literary critics working in Italian studies during the second half of the twentieth century. Baptized Paolo, he entered the Capuchin convent of Faido, in the Canton Ticino, at the age of eleven, took his novitiate at Cesena under the religious name Giovanni da Locarno, and was ordained priest in 1947. In his scholarly publications, however, he always signed simply as Giovanni Pozzi.

He began his literary studies in 1948 at the University of Fribourg in Switzerland, where he formed himself in the exacting school of Gianfranco Contini and Giuseppe Billanovich. He went on to hold the chair of Italian literature at the same university from 1960 to 1988, nearly three decades during which Fribourg became, under his guidance, an unlikely but productive outpost of Italian philology north of the Alps.

His earliest scholarly interests lay in medieval and humanist philology. Contini, then at work on his anthology Poeti del Duecento, enlisted him to edit Brunetto Latini's Tesoretto and Favolello. Spurred on by Billanovich, Pozzi then turned to the literature of Italian Humanism, producing with Lucia A. Ciapponi the monumental modern critical edition, richly annotated, of Francesco Colonna's Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (Padua, Antenore, 1964), the allegorical dream-romance printed by Aldo Manuzio in 1499, which remains the standard reference edition of that famously difficult text. He devoted the following decade to a four-volume critical edition of Ermolao Barbaro's Castigationes Plinianae et in Pomponium Melam (1973-1979), a project on which he trained a first generation of Fribourg doctoral students, assigning them dissertations on figures such as Biondo Flavio, Leon Battista Alberti, Sebastiano Serlio, and Felice Feliciano. With Maria Teresa Casella he also edited the spiritual letters of the Florentine Dominican Giovanni Dominici.

Pozzi investigated Seicento literature with equal rigour, beginning with his university thesis on the sacred oratory of the Capuchin preacher Emmanuele Orchi and continuing with his edition of Giovan Battista Marino's Dicerie sacre and La strage degli innocenti (Einaudi, 1960). This line of research culminated in his critical edition, with extensive commentary, of Marino's masterpiece Adone (Mondadori, 1976; revised 1988), a work that did much to rehabilitate a poet then still widely dismissed as an emblem of Baroque bad taste, and which Pozzi instead situated within a century that, in his own phrase, "gave the heavens a new order."

Alongside his editorial work, Pozzi developed an influential theoretical strand of research into the relationship between text and image. Building on Ernst Robert Curtius's study of literary commonplaces, he analysed the descriptive conventions, or topoi, through which the female body is evoked in Italian poetry and prose. In parallel, he catalogued the figurative and iconic potential of written language itself, from Alexandrian and medieval technopaegnia to the calligrammes of Guillaume Apollinaire, gathering this research in La parola dipinta (Adelphi, 1981), a study of poetry made to be seen as much as heard.

In the last two decades of his life, Pozzi turned with particular intensity to the study of Italian women's mystical writing, a body of texts he treated as a singular and largely unexplored register of literary and religious expression. He edited Maria Maddalena de' Pazzi's ecstatic utterances as Le parole dell'estasi (1984), and, most consequentially for students of medieval sainthood, produced the modern critical edition of the Memoriale of Angela of Foligno, published as Il libro dell'esperienza (Adelphi, 1992; revised 2001) — the edition that underlies most subsequent scholarship on the text, including the study of Angela's Franciscan "frater scriptor" discussed in this database's entry on Mario Sensi and the reading of the Angela-scribe relationship offered by John W. Coakley. Pozzi also prepared an edition of writings attributed to Clare of Assisi. With Claudio Leonardi he co-edited the wide-ranging anthology Scrittrici mistiche italiane (1988), spanning women's religious writing from the twelfth to the twentieth century and opened by his own foundational essay "L'alfabeto delle sante" — a collaboration that places Pozzi within the same Italian scholarly milieu of critical hagiographical editing, centred on Leonardi and the Florentine SISMEL circle, from which the editions of Adele Simonetti on Umiltà da Faenza would later emerge. His final book, Tacet (2002), a meditation on silence in mystical experience, appeared in the year of his death.

Pozzi received the Premio Galileo Galilei of the Italian Rotary clubs for the history of Italian literature (1992), the Premio Viareggio-Répaci for Alternatim (1996), the career prize of the Premio Chiara (1998), and the Centenary Prize of the Banca della Svizzera Italiana (2000). As a Capuchin friar he also contributed to the renewal of Franciscan conventual libraries, collaborating at times with the Ticinese architect Mario Botta on the restoration of the library of the Capuchin friary at Lugano, where his own extensive personal library is now preserved. He died suddenly on 20 July 2002 and was buried in the cemetery of the convent of Bigorio, near Lugano.

Previtali, Giovanni

Florence, 4 March 1934 - Rome, 3 February 1988

Italian art historian, the most restless and methodologically ambitious of Roberto Longhi's pupils. In a career cut short at fifty-three he produced a founding study of the modern reception of medieval art (La fortuna dei primitivi, 1964), a reframing of the Giotto problem (Giotto e la sua bottega, 1967), a body of essays that effectively created the map of Gothic sculpture in central and southern Italy, and as founder of Prospettiva and coordinator of Einaudi's Storia dell'arte italiana, some of the most consequential editorial projects of postwar Italian art history.

Previtali was born in Florence on 4 March 1934, into a family of prominent musicians: his father was the conductor Fernando Previtali (1907-1985), and his mother the daughter of the conductor Vittorio Gui (1885-1975). He initially inclined toward law, but in the summer of 1952 decided on letters instead; his letters to his mother from those years, published by Galansino, record both that choice and his impatience with the disorder of the University of Rome.

He began in Rome under Lionello Venturi, but found the teaching unsatisfying and moved to Florence in 1954 to follow Roberto Longhi, then at the height of his authority. It was a deliberate act of self-apprenticeship, and the bond held until Longhi's death in 1970. On 15 March 1957 Previtali discussed his thesis with Longhi, with Francesco Arcangeli as correlatore, on the critical fortune of the Italian primitives in the eighteenth century. In 1966 he took the libera docenza in the history of art criticism.

The thesis became the book that made his name. Published by Einaudi in 1964 as La fortuna dei primitivi. Dal Vasari ai neoclassici, it traced how the art of the Italian Middle Ages was seen, misprized, rediscovered, and finally canonized across three centuries of criticism and collecting. It was a pioneering study of reception, and it did not look like other art-historical books of its moment: its plates were as innovative as its argument. A revised and expanded edition appeared posthumously in 1989, with an introductory note by Enrico Castelnuovo.

For anyone working on medieval art today, this remains the indispensable prehistory of the field: it explains why the "primitives" became visible at all, and on whose terms.

In 1964 Previtali also published a Giotto (Fabbri), followed by volumes on the Assisi and Padua frescoes (1965) and, in 1967, the monograph Giotto e la sua bottega (Fabbri), dedicated to Longhi. The book placed Giotto within his workshop and his following rather than in isolation.

On the vexed question of the St Francis cycle at Assisi, Previtali sided with Longhi, Toesca, and their Italian colleagues in holding the cycle to be Giotto's conception but not his execution. His distinctive move, as Castelnuovo observed, was to reframe the problem: rather than the binary "Giotto or non-Giotto" of Richard Offner's connoisseurship, he asked what specifically Giotto's achievement consisted in. The Assisi attribution remains one of the genuinely unresolved questions of Trecento studies, and Previtali's position should be cited as a considered stance within a live controversy, not as a settled outcome.

Alongside his work on painting and historiography, Previtali opened up a field that had been left at the margins: the Gothic sculpture of central and southern Italy. His investigations of Umbrian sculpture between the Duecento and Trecento, and of the Marche and Abruzzo, produced new results in an area then poorly mapped, and culminated in the Siena exhibition Scultura dipinta. Maestri di legname e pittori a Siena 1250-1450 (1987).

The essays were gathered posthumously as Studi sulla scultura gotica in Italia. Storia e geografia (Turin: Einaudi, 1991, "Biblioteca di storia dell'arte," n.s. 15), with a prefatory memoir by Luciano Bellosi, "Previtali e la scultura." The volume assembles the Umbrian studies with a Florentine corollary on Tino di Camaino and a Lucchese one on the Crocifisso di Camaiore; the great essay on Marco Romano; two studies on the sculptures of the Loggia degli Osii in Milan and on the tomb of Giovanni d'Aragona at Tarragona; and three pieces on Quattrocento subjects (the late Donatello, Vecchietta, Domenico di Niccolò dei Cori).

Bellosi judged the Marco Romano essay Previtali's masterpiece, for its method and for its capacity, in the total absence of documents, to bind together major works on stylistic evidence alone. The subtitle, storia e geografia, is the point: Previtali integrated stylistic, technical, and formal observation into larger structures, yielding unusual geographical cross-sections and unexpected definitions of artistic milieu. The Milanese essays in particular, on the Loggia degli Osii, sit directly adjacent to the Lombard sculptural questions of the mid-Trecento.

Previtali entered the editorial board of Longhi's journal Paragone in spring 1961 and served as its secretary from 1962, collaborating with it for about a decade. By the early 1970s disagreements arose among the Longhi pupils on the board, notably over whether classical art belonged in its pages. In 1975, with the archaeologist Mauro Cristofani (1941-1997), he founded Prospettiva, a quarterly open to ancient and modern art alike and conceived as an organ of scientific and political debate within the discipline.

He edited the Arte 2 volume of the Feltrinelli-Fischer encyclopedia (1971) and coordinated the first four volumes of Einaudi's Storia dell'arte italiana, writing its weighty introductory essay, "La periodizzazione della storia dell'arte italiana" (1979). The project was fought over: within Einaudi, Paolo Fossati backed him only partway while Giulio Bollati favored an alternative scheme presented by Federico Zeri, and the compromise produced a work split into two hard-to-reconcile halves. Previtali also wrote introductions to the Italian translation of George Kubler's The Shape of Time (1976) and to the Einaudi edition of Bellori's Vite (1976, edited by Evelina Borea).

His Marxism and his engagement with the PCI were not incidental to the scholarship. Giovanni Romano's assessment, that Previtali was a philologist with impeccable credentials who nonetheless kept reopening his own professional statute against other masters and other disciplines, and an inexhaustible animator of books, exhibitions, and conferences, has become the standard verdict. Arturo Galansino's monographic study is aptly titled storico dell'arte militante.

He taught at the universities of Messina, Siena (professor of medieval art history from 1973), and Naples, where he was called to the chair of medieval and modern art history in 1983. His research on southern Italy produced La pittura del Cinquecento a Napoli e nel Vicereame (Einaudi, 1978) and continued with the Andrea Sabatini exhibition at the Certosa di Padula and its catalogue, Andrea da Salerno nel Rinascimento meridionale (1986). In 1986 he was visiting senior fellow at CASVA, the National Gallery of Art's Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts in Washington, where he sketched the plan for a corpus project.

Early in 1987 he learned he had cancer. He died in Rome on 3 February 1988, not yet fifty-four.

His archive was donated by Evelina Borea to the University of Siena, which also received his library and photographic collection; the Fondo Giovanni Previtali entered the Biblioteca Umanistica in May 2014. Prospettiva devoted two double issues to his memory (Scritti in ricordo di Giovanni Previtali, nn. 53-56 and 57-60, 1988-1990), the second containing his complete bibliography. Gert Kreytenberg donated a pencil drawing by Previtali to the Siena library in 2018.

La fortuna dei primitivi and Studi sulla scultura gotica in Italia remain in active use, the latter routinely set alongside Gnudi's L'arte gotica in Francia e in Italia on university reading lists for Italian Gothic sculpture.

Procacci, Ugo

Florence, 31 March 1905 – Florence, 19 February 1991

Ugo Procacci was born in Florence on 31 March 1905 into a lower-middle-class family; his father Virgilio worked as a railway inspector and his mother Amelia Faini was a housewife. He studied at the University of Florence, where he graduated in 1927 with a thesis in art history, coming into contact with the environment of the Rivista d'Arte and with the Florentine school of historians of medieval and Renaissance art. After a short period as an assistant at the university, he entered the Soprintendenza alle Gallerie of Florence at the end of the 1920s, beginning a career as a state official that would last more than four decades. In 1932 he became director of the newly founded Gabinetto dei Restauri of the Florentine Soprintendenza, a laboratory that he built up into a crucial centre for the study and restoration of panel painting.

During the 1930s Procacci combined his work as a civil servant with an intense scholarly activity, publishing in the Rivista d'Arte and other journals studies on Tuscan painting between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries. He participated in the organization of major exhibitions such as the 1933 Tesoro di Firenze sacra and the 1937 Mostra giottesca, for which he carried out systematic surveys of churches, pievi and minor collections in the Florentine countryside, including the Mugello. These campaigns led to the identification and "rediscovery" of many neglected medieval and early Renaissance works, which Procacci studied and often re-attributed on the basis of stylistic and documentary analysis.

From an early stage, Procacci was recognized as a specialist in medieval and early Renaissance painting, particularly in the Tuscan and Florentine context. His research addressed both major figures — Giotto, Masaccio, Vasari — and lesser-known masters, insisting on the importance of documentary evidence and on the study of the "life" of works of art, including their later alterations and restorations. At the same time, he developed an innovative conception of restoration, which he helped to ground on scientific, technical and historical bases through the work of the Florentine restoration laboratory.

Under his direction, the Gabinetto dei Restauri became a pioneering institution in which art historians, chemists, photographers and restorers collaborated closely. Among the best-known episodes of his technical and connoisseurship acumen is the discovery, during investigations on Masaccio's Trinità in Santa Maria Novella, of the painted skeleton underlying the lower part of the fresco, a memento mori long hidden by later interventions. In other cases, like the cleaning of the Madonna with Child from San Giovanni Battista a Remole, the laboratory under Procacci experimented with mechanical cleaning techniques using a scalpel, inaugurating practices that would become widely discussed in the theory of restoration.

His approach to restoration sought to "return to the work its authentic image" through the removal of repaintings and accretions, but also insisted on respect for the material history of the object and on prudence in reconstruction, often opting for neutral reintegration and reversible solutions. Because of these contributions, later accounts describe him as one of the founders of modern scientific restoration in Italy and as a fundamental reference point for debates on conservation ethics.

Procacci's career as a civil servant and historian intersected dramatically with the events of the Second World War and the flood of 1966. During the war he was among the Italian officials who organized the transfer and protection of artworks from Florence and Tuscany, actions that later earned him recognition as a kind of civilian "monuments man". After the devastating flood of the Arno in November 1966, by then Soprintendente of Florence, he was among the first to rush to Santa Croce, where Cimabue's great Crocifisso and many other works had been gravely damaged.

In his report to the Ministry of Education of 30 November 1966, Procacci described the destruction as worse than any "più infausta previsione" and recounted how, in the absence of fire brigade support, the staff of the Soprintendenza and the restorers had to work alone in the mud to dismantle and secure the crucifix. He took the crucial decision, later considered decisive, to carry out all restoration work in Florence, despite difficulties and international offers of help from laboratories abroad. This choice ensured homogeneity of methods, central coordination of operations and the creation, in Florence, of an extraordinary experimental hub that accelerated the development of restoration techniques and research.

In the decades after the flood, Procacci continued to oversee restoration campaigns and to publish on the results, helping to shape both the practical and theoretical framework within which Italian conservation was reinvented. His role as Soprintendente and as a public intellectual made him a central figure in discussions on the relationship between modernization, urban planning and the protection of historic centres, especially in Florence.

Alongside his activity as official and restorer, Ugo Procacci was also a prolific scholar and editor. He published numerous studies on Florentine and Tuscan art from the Trecento to the Seicento, many of them in the Rivista d'Arte, a journal with which his career was closely intertwined and which he eventually directed. His writings combined connoisseurship, archival research and technical observation, often reattributing works, clarifying workshop practices and reconstructing the historical contexts of commissions.

Even after his retirement from the Soprintendenza in 1970, Procacci continued to work as a professor at the University of Florence, where he transmitted his integrated vision of art history — concerned with the material, social and institutional life of artworks — to new generations of scholars. Colleagues and pupils later described him as a master of a history of art attentive to "la vita degli artisti e delle opere in tutti i loro aspetti", from creation to conservation and reception. His essays were later collected and re-read in volumes such as Tra Giotto e Vasari, which emphasize his contribution to understanding the long continuity of Florentine artistic traditions.

Recognition of his importance continued after his death: in 2006 the library of the Opificio delle Pietre Dure in Florence was named "Biblioteca Ugo Procacci" in honour of his role in founding the first modern restoration laboratory in Italy. A prize for young scholars in the field of art history and conservation, the "Premio Ugo Procacci", further testifies to his lasting prestige and to the desire to link his name to innovation in research.

Ugo Procacci died in Florence on 19 February 1991. By then he was widely regarded as one of the foremost Italian art historians of the twentieth century, particularly in the field of medieval and early Renaissance painting, and as a founding father of scientific conservation in Italy. His connoisseurial discoveries contributed to the re-evaluation and "rediscovery" of many medieval works and contexts, both in the great museums and in minor ecclesiastical settings.

Perhaps even more important is the model he offered of an art historian who is simultaneously scholar, civil servant and custodian of a city's heritage, actively engaged in protecting and rescuing works in times of crisis. Thanks to his decisions during the flood and to his long work at the Gabinetto dei Restauri, Florence became an international centre of excellence for restoration, attracting expertise and resources from around the world. For these reasons, recent commemorations in Florence and in the scholarly world continue to present him as a "custode di Firenze" and as a reference figure for those working at the intersection of medieval art history and conservation.

Q

Quicherat, Jules

Paris, 13 October 1814 – Paris, 8 April 1882

Jules Étienne Joseph Quicherat was born on 13 October 1814 in Paris, the son of a working cabinet-maker who had come from Paray-le-Monial to the capital to support his large family. Despite these modest, even straitened circumstances, he was admitted to the Collège de Sainte-Barbe, where he received a thorough classical education. His debt to that institution was lifelong: he showed his gratitude by writing its history in three volumes, published between 1860 and 1864. He was also the younger brother of Louis Quicherat, a celebrated Latin scholar and lexicographer, who survived him.

The decisive intellectual turning point of his youth came through an encounter with the historian Jules Michelet. At the end of his studies he hesitated for some time before deciding what career to follow, until Michelet ended his indecision by inspiring him with a taste for history. In 1835, Quicherat entered the École des Chartes, and left two years later at the head of the college.

The first monumental achievement of Quicherat's career was in the field of documentary history. Inspired once more by the example of Michelet, who had just written an admirable work on Joan of Arc, he published the text of the two trials of Joan, adding much contemporary evidence on her heroism in his Procès de condamnation et de réhabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc (5 vols., 1841–1849), as well as a supplementary volume of Aperçus nouveaux sur l'histoire de Jeanne d'Arc, in which it seems that the last word has been said on important points. This edition, a landmark in the critical editing of primary sources, transformed Joan of Arc studies and demonstrated his rigorous command of palaeographic method.

Quicherat extended his archival energies deeply into late medieval French history. In 1844, he published memoirs of the adventures of the brigand Rodrigue de Villandrando, which gradually grew into a volume full of fresh matter. He produced full biographies of two chroniclers of Louis XI: the obscure Jean Castel, and Thomas Basin, Bishop of Lisieux, who was, on the contrary, a remarkable politician, prelate, and chronicler. Between 1855 and 1859, Quicherat published the latter's works, most of which were brought out for the first time. He also edited Fragments inédits de Georges Chastellain and Lettres, mémoires et autres documents relatifs à la guerre du bien public en 1465.

Quicherat's most enduring institutional contribution was the creation of archaeology as a formal academic discipline in France. In 1847, he inaugurated a course of archaeological lectures at the École des Chartes, and in 1849, was appointed professor of diplomatics at the same college. His students circulated his principles throughout France, recognizing him as the "founder of national archaeology."

His pedagogical influence was profound even beyond the lecture hall: although he was not eloquent and had a nasal voice, his hearers were loath to miss any of his thoughtful teachings, which were unbiased and well-expressed. He began transcribing his lectures towards the end of his life, but only the introductory chapters, covering material up to the 11th century, were found among his papers at his death. These were subsequently reconstructed and published posthumously by his students Robert de Lasteyrie and Arthur Giry.

For scholars of medieval art, Quicherat's contributions are of particular significance. In 1849, he wrote his Notice sur l'Album de Villard de Honnecourt architecte du XIIIe siècle, the first serious scholarly study of the famous portfolio of the thirteenth-century architect and draughtsman — a foundational text for the interpretation of Gothic architectural practice and workshop culture. This essay was published posthumously in the collected Mélanges d'archéologie et d'histoire (1885–1886).

On the question of Gothic origins, he published in 1850 a memoir De l'ogive et de l'architecture ogivale, where he advanced his theory on the structural role of the pointed arch in the history of religious architecture. In an 1874 article on L'âge de la cathédrale de Laon, he proposed an exact date for the birth of Gothic architecture. These contributions placed him at the centre of the heated nineteenth-century debate over the national and structural origins of the Gothic style.

Quicherat was also the first French historian to develop a systematic theory of the history of dress, analysing material artefacts alongside pictorial, textual, and philological sources. His Histoire du costume en France, depuis les temps les plus reculés jusqu'à la fin du XVIIIe siècle (1875) was a key text that established a method, theory, and framework for understanding dress history — a discipline that is today indispensable for the iconographic study of medieval imagery and manuscript illumination.

Not all of Quicherat's positions proved correct. With warmth and pertinacity worthy of a better cause, he maintained the identification of Caesar's Alesia with Alaise in the Doubs, and he died without becoming a convert to the opinion, now almost universally accepted, that Alise-Sainte-Reine is the place where Vercingetorix capitulated. Yet even this error had a productive side: some well-directed excavations at Alaise brought many Roman remains to light, which were subsequently sent to enrich the museum at Besançon.

From 1871 to 1882, Quicherat served as director of the École des Chartes, the institution he had attended as a student nearly four decades earlier. He filled this post with the same energy he had shown in the many scientific commissions he had taken part in. In 1878 he relinquished his duties as professor of archaeology, which then fell to the most prominent of his pupils, Robert de Lasteyrie.

He died suddenly in Paris on 8 April 1882, a short time after correcting the proofs of Supplément aux témoignages contemporains de Jeanne d'Arc, published in the Revue Historique. His brother Louis outlived him.

Quicherat published over three hundred and sixty-three works during his lifetime, a bibliography reconstructed in full by his student Arthur Giry. Among his posthumous papers were important fragments of his archaeological lectures, though his Histoire de la laine, with which he had been occupied for many years, was never found.

Quicherat stands as one of the pivotal figures of nineteenth-century European medievalism: a rigorous palaeographer, a founding theorist of French archaeology, a pioneer of Gothic architectural history, and one of the first scholars to treat medieval artefacts — whether buildings, costumes, or manuscripts — as structured evidence for historical interpretation. His study of Villard de Honnecourt's album alone would secure him a permanent place in the historiography of medieval art.

Quintavalle, Arturo Carlo

Parma, 12 May 1936 - living

Arturo Carlo Ottaviano Quintavalle is an Italian art historian whose career has decisively shaped the modern study of Emilian Romanesque sculpture while ranging, with unusual breadth, from the twelfth century to contemporary photography and design. Professor of art history at the University of Parma and founder of its Centro Studi e Archivio della Comunicazione (CSAC), he is best known to medievalists for his sustained, philologically exacting work on Wiligelmo, on Benedetto Antelami, and on the sculptural programme of the Parma Baptistery. In May 2026 the city of Parma marked his ninetieth birthday with a public celebration at the Teatro Regio, an occasion that gathered civic and academic authorities together with several of the scholars and artists formed in his orbit.

Quintavalle was born into a household already at the centre of Italian connoisseurship. His father, Armando Ottaviano Quintavalle (Naples 1894 - Modena 1967), served as superintendent (soprintendente) for the provinces of Parma and Piacenza from 1933 to 1959; a scholar first of Campanian Romanesque and then of Emilian Renaissance painting, he is remembered above all for having sheltered roughly nine thousand works from the Galleria Nazionale di Parma in the Castello di Torrechiara during the Second World War. His mother, Augusta Ghidiglia Quintavalle (1904-1988), was herself a leading twentieth-century authority on Correggio and Parmigianino. The younger Quintavalle thus inherited both a scholarly vocation and a lifelong preoccupation with the conservation of the artistic patrimony.

He studied at Pisa, at the University and at the Scuola Normale Superiore, where his principal masters were the art historian and cultural critic Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti and the medieval historian Arsenio Frugoni. Ragghianti's eclectic, anti-Crocean model, which admitted cinema and design alongside the traditional canon, left a lasting imprint on Quintavalle's later refusal of disciplinary boundaries. In 1963-64 he taught briefly in the United States at the University of Chicago; returning to Italy in June 1964, he entered the Soprintendenza at Bologna under Cesare Gnudi, with responsibility for the Romagna. He has said that the decision to return was deliberate: the study of urbanism, territory and monuments, in his view, cannot be conducted by correspondence but demands presence in Europe.

Quintavalle's academic career was thereafter bound to the University of Parma, where he became professor of medieval and modern art history and eventually professor emeritus. In 1968 he founded the Centro Studi e Archivio della Comunicazione (CSAC), which he directed for roughly two decades, latterly in partnership with Gloria Bianchino. Conceived as an archive of contemporary visual culture in the broadest sense, CSAC grew into one of the most important collections of its kind in Italy, today housing several million items spanning painting, sculpture, photography, drawing, design and graphic projects, and installed in the former Cistercian Abbey of Valserena (the "Certosa di Paradigna") outside Parma. Within Italian medieval studies his institutional legacy is equally significant: he founded and, for some fourteen years, presided over the Associazione Italiana Storici dell'Arte Medievale (AISAME), and coordinated a long series of international congresses in the field.

Quintavalle's contribution to medieval art history is concentrated on the Romanesque and early Gothic sculpture of the Po valley, and it is characterised throughout by a materially grounded, workshop-centred method. His early monograph on Modena Cathedral (La Cattedrale di Modena, 1964-65) established a framework he would refine for decades: the reconstruction of the officina, the workshop as a working organism with its masters, apprentices, borrowings and internal chronology, rather than the isolated attribution of masterpieces to named individuals. Wiligelmo, the sculptor of the Modena facade reliefs, remained a recurrent subject, as did the vexed relationship between the Modenese enterprise and the later Campionese masters.

His most conspicuous single achievement was the great Parma exhibition of 1990, Benedetto Antelami, held at the Salone delle Scuderie in the Pilotta from 31 March to 30 September and accompanied by a monumental catalogue published by Electa for the Centro Studi Medievali of the University of Parma, with the catalogue of works itself edited by Arturo Calzona and Giuseppa Z. Zanichelli. There Quintavalle marshalled some hundred pieces, several long hidden or little known, to argue for Antelami as an architect-sculptor who assimilated the Ile-de-France and Provencal currents and, alongside Nicola Pisano, mediated the Gothic into Italy in a distinctively classicising key. He returned to the same master at the end of his career with a study of the Antelamic workshop at the cathedral of Fidenza (Borgo San Donnino) in 2020, and he authored the Benedetto Antelami entry for the Treccani Enciclopedia dell'Arte Medievale (1991).

The Parma Baptistery lies at the centre of this body of work. Quintavalle reads its sculptural and architectural programme as, first of all, an evolving architectural project shaped by the city's political position between papacy and Empire, and he has advanced the interpretive thesis that its iconography was conceived in part to rebut Cathar heresy, the denial of the sacraments, of the works of mercy, and of the Cross as instrument of Christ's Passion. This reading is a strong interpretive claim rather than a settled fact, and it should be weighed against the work of other specialists on the same monument, notably Chiara Frugoni, whose studies of the Antelamic Months and of the Baptistery (I mesi antelamici del battistero di Parma, 1992; Benedetto Antelami e il Battistero di Parma, 1995) approach the cycle from a different interpretive tradition. That Quintavalle and Frugoni, the latter a daughter of his own teacher Arsenio Frugoni, could reach divergent conclusions on the same reliefs is a useful reminder of how open these questions remain.

Beyond his own publications, Quintavalle formed a genuine school of Emilian medievalists. Scholars such as Arturo Calzona, Giuseppa Z. Zanichelli, Francesca Stroppa and Michele Luigi Vescovi, among others, emerged from or worked closely with the Parma circle, and their continued activity is part of his lasting influence on the field.

What distinguishes Quintavalle from most medievalists of his generation is the deliberate extension of the same critical apparatus to the modern and contemporary. From the 1970s he became one of the principal Italian advocates of authorial photography, introducing American work, the Farm Security Administration photographers, Lee Friedlander and others, through his contact with John Szarkowski of the Museum of Modern Art, and serving as an intellectual point of reference for Luigi Ghirri and the generation of the 1984 Viaggio in Italia. His Il territorio della fotografia (1979) and his editorship of the six-volume Enciclopedia pratica per fotografare (also 1979) treated photography as a structured visual language demanding the same historical rigour as any older art. Through CSAC he pressed this argument still further, gathering design, graphics, advertising, fashion and even comics into a single field of visual communication. He also wrote extensively on the Renaissance, including on Correggio, the subject of his parents' scholarship, and on twentieth-century Italian art.

Quintavalle sustained an unusually prominent public role. From the early 1970s he wrote the art column for the weekly Panorama for about twenty-five years, and for some three decades he contributed to the Corriere della Sera, where he remained a widely quoted commentator on questions of heritage, his comparison, after the 2019 fire, of Notre-Dame de Paris to the loss of the Sistine Chapel being a characteristic intervention. This combination of specialist scholarship and public advocacy for conservation is central to how he is understood in Italy.

He is a member (socio nazionale) of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei, earlier sources describe him as a corresponding member, reflecting his advancement within the academy over time, and he has been affiliated with a British society of architectural historians in London. Among his distinctions are a gold medal conferred by the President of the Republic for services to culture, a silver medal for the protection of cultural heritage, the Ariosto d'Oro of the Liceo Romagnosi alumni association (2011), and the Gold Medal of the Premio Sant'Ilario awarded by the city of Parma in 2017, the citation praising his rigour and his commitment to the conservation of the contemporary artistic patrimony.

R

Ragghianti, Carlo Ludovico

Lucca, 1910 – Florence, 1987

Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti (Lucca, March 18, 1910 - Florence, August 3, 1987) was one of the leading Italian art historians, critics, and theorists of the twentieth century. His career united rigorous methodological reflection with an exceptional level of civic and political engagement, making him a central figure in modern Italian intellectual life.

He received his early formation in Lucca and developed a precocious anti-fascist stance by the mid-1930s. He then moved to Pisa, studying art history at the Scuola Normale Superiore and the University of Pisa in an environment of high critical discipline. Giovanni Gentile, despite deep ideological differences, recognized Ragghianti's intellectual gifts and supported him at the start of his career. In 1935, together with Ranuccio Bianchi Bandinelli and with Gentile's backing, he founded Critica d'Arte, a journal that also involved Roberto Longhi and became one of the key instruments for methodological renewal in postwar Italian art history.

Ragghianti's most original contribution was his formulation of a rigorous aesthetic historicism, grounded in both formal analysis and historical interpretation. He rejected both pure formalism and reductive social-documentary readings of art, seeking instead to reconstruct the internal development of visual language over time. In contrast to approaches centered on stylistic rupture, he emphasized continuity and progression, a perspective that shaped his reevaluation of neglected periods, including nineteenth-century Italian art, and also informed his long-range inquiry into prehistoric visual culture, culminating in L'uomo cosciente, arte e conoscenza nella paleostoria (1981).

His biography was inseparable from political action. During the Resistance he became one of the main leaders in Tuscany, heading the Actionist Military Committee, founding and commanding the Rosselli Brigades until June 1944, and then presiding over the Tuscan National Liberation Committee. In this role he directed the provisional government that led the uprising against Nazi-Fascist forces in Florence, liberated on August 11, 1944. In 1945 he served as Undersecretary of Education in the Parri government, with responsibility for Fine Arts and Performing Arts, promoting urgent measures for postwar cultural reconstruction.

His institutional work remained marked by a reformist vision. In 1957 he founded the Cabinet of Drawings and Prints at the University of Pisa, developing it into both a major twentieth-century graphic collection and a center for research and exhibitions. In 1964 he founded and directed the Italian Society of Archaeology and Art History to strengthen collaboration between university and heritage administration. In 1967 he curated the landmark exhibition Arte moderna in Italia 1915-1935 at Palazzo Strozzi, a major application of his historical-critical method to twentieth-century art.

Ragghianti's legacy is preserved through the Fondazione Centro Studi sull'Arte Licia e Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti in Lucca, established according to his and his wife Licia's wishes as a permanent institution for research, exhibitions, and cultural dissemination. His archival papers, conserved in the Tuscan State Archives, remain a primary source for the history of twentieth-century Italian art criticism. He continues to be an essential reference point for scholars studying the relationship between artistic interpretation, public responsibility, and intellectual vocation in modern Europe.

Ramsey, J. Boniface

b. 6 October 1945

J. Boniface Ramsey (born 6 October 1945) is an American Catholic priest, patristics scholar, and translator, known in two quite distinct capacities: as a prolific editor and translator of early Christian texts, and as the priest who tried, over nearly two decades, to alert Church authorities to the misconduct of Theodore McCarrick.

He was ordained in 1973 as a member of the Dominican Order, and earned a doctorate in theology in 1983 following studies at the Institut Catholique in Paris. He taught patrology at institutions including The Catholic University of America and, from 1986 to 1996, at Immaculate Conception Seminary at Seton Hall University in New Jersey (the seminary serving the Archdiocese of Newark). In 2004 he left the Dominicans to join the Archdiocese of New York, his hometown, where he has served as pastor and administrator in several Manhattan parishes — over the years associated with St. Vincent Ferrer, St. Joseph-Yorkville, and, most recently, St. Rita's in Long Island City.

Ramsey's scholarly reputation rests principally on his work with the Church Fathers. His introductory survey Beginning to Read the Fathers (Paulist Press, 1985), a thematic guide to the principal Greek and Latin patristic writings, remains widely used as a teaching text. He is the general editor of The Works of Saint Augustine: A Translation for the 21st Century (New City Press), the ambitious project begun in 1990 in conjunction with the Augustinian Heritage Institute to render Augustine's entire corpus — some 132 works — into modern English for the first time. Within that series he served as editor of volumes including The City of God, and himself translated Augustine's Revisions (Retractationes). Beyond Augustine, he produced the standard modern English translations of John Cassian's monastic works — The Conferences (1997) and The Institutes (2000) in the Ancient Christian Writers series — and translated the sermons of Maximus of Turin. He also edited the volume on Ambrose in Routledge's Early Church Fathers series (1997), which may be of particular interest given your work on Milan.

The second strand of his public life concerns McCarrick. While on the Immaculate Conception faculty in the early 1990s — when McCarrick was Archbishop of Newark — Ramsey heard persistent reports that the archbishop invited seminarians to his beach house and shared his bed with them. In November 2000, after McCarrick was appointed Archbishop of Washington, Ramsey wrote to the Apostolic Nuncio, Archbishop Gabriel Montalvo, setting out these allegations; by his own later account, he did so on his own initiative, having phoned the nunciature beforehand. As a Dominican rather than a diocesan priest, he was not under McCarrick's supervision, which gave him a measure of independence in speaking out. He received no formal reply, but a 2006 letter from the Vatican's Leonardo Sandri confirmed the 2000 complaint had been received in Rome. Ramsey later renewed his warnings, including a 2015 letter to Cardinal Seán O'Malley. When the McCarrick scandal broke publicly in 2018, and Archbishop Carlo Maria Viganò cited Ramsey's letter in his own dossier, Ramsey emerged as the central whistleblower in the affair — though he has been careful to distinguish his documented factual claims from Viganò's broader and more contested accusations, and has resisted framing the matter as a campaign against gay priests.

Ranucci, Cristina

active 20th-21st century

Cristina Ranucci is an Italian art historian specializing in medieval painting, particularly the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, with research interests that also extend to late antique archaeology. Her work is especially relevant for studies of Italian Duecento and Trecento visual culture and regional workshop traditions.

Ranucci is active as an independent art historian and lecturer, with a research profile centered on thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italian painting. Her Academia.edu profile lists 17 published articles and identifies her principal interests as 13th- and 14th-century painting and late antique archaeology, situating her among independent scholars engaged in sustained scholarly production outside a permanent university chair.

Among her most significant contributions is the entry on Gentile da Rocca in Treccani's Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (vol. 53, 2000), where she examines a painter active in Abruzzo in the second half of the thirteenth century. The study includes a detailed discussion of a 1283 Virgin Enthroned Nursing the Child, combining technical and iconographic analysis with attention to stylistic attributes, Gothic inscriptions, and regional context.

Her research also includes studies on thirteenth-century painting in Terni and the contribution La maesta di Otricoli, presented in the proceedings of the Third Week of Studies in Medieval Art History at the University of Rome. In collaboration with Monica Zorzan, she has worked on fragments of painted plaster from the presbytery of the ancient Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls, a topic of particular importance for the study of early medieval painted decoration. She also published The Hermitage of San Cataldo in Cottanello: From Research to Conservation (Miligraf, 2011), a volume that links historical-artistic investigation with conservation issues.

Ravalli, Gaia

active 21st century
