Gaia Ravalli is an Italian art historian whose research is centred on panel and mural painting in Florence in the second half of the fourteenth century, with particular attention to the workshop associated with the brothers Andrea, Nardo and Jacopo di Cione. Her work continues, and in places revises, the connoisseurial tradition established by Richard Offner and carried forward by Gert Kreytenberg, applying close comparative analysis of technique, documentary record and archival dating to a body of material whose attributions have shifted repeatedly across the twentieth century.

Her most consequential contribution to the study of Andrea di Cione, called Orcagna, is a monographic study of the Chiostrino dei Morti at Santa Maria Novella, published in 2015. The essay reopens the question of the two fresco fragments in the Tornaquinci-Trinciavelli burial chapel — a Nativity and a Crucifixion long associated with Andrea and his immediate circle — setting them against the securely dated campaign of the vault quatrefoils in the basilica's cappella maggiore and testing the conventional dating of 1340-47 against the surviving documentary record. Her conclusions bear directly on the vexed question of hand: whether the Chiostrino frescoes are autograph work of Andrea or the product of one of the subordinate painters distinguishable elsewhere in the choir vault, a distinction on which the chapel's status as an early, formative work in Andrea's career depends.

More broadly, Ravalli's work is representative of a strand of recent Trecento scholarship that treats the Cione workshop not as a single hand extended by anonymous assistants but as a genuinely collaborative enterprise whose internal division of labour can, with sufficient care, be partially reconstructed — an approach that has steadily narrowed the secure corpus attributed to Andrea himself while sharpening understanding of how a large fourteenth-century Florentine shop actually produced its work.

Recanati, Maria Grazia

Bergamo, 1962

Maria Grazia Recanati was born in Bergamo in 1962. She studied at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan, where she graduated in lettere moderne with a specialization in art history and medieval history, writing her thesis on late medieval Lombard art history under the supervision of the distinguished Hungarian-Italian art historian Miklos Boskovits. After her degree she further refined her methodological training at the Fondazione "Roberto Longhi" in Florence, one of Italy's most prestigious institutes for the advanced study of art history.

Following her postgraduate formation at the Longhi Foundation, Recanati collaborated with the chair of medieval and modern art history at the Università Cattolica and simultaneously worked with the Pinacoteca Carrara in Bergamo. These early institutional ties established her dual profile as both a researcher engaged with the scholarly community and a museum professional committed to the public communication of art history. Her research output in this period included, notably, a 1992 study of the late-14th-century secular allegorical fresco cycle at the Castello di Bianzano in the Val Cavallina, a rare example of profane pictorial decoration in the Bergamo area that she was among the first scholars to analyze systematically.

Recanati's contribution to the 1998 volume Il Protiro settentrionale di Santa Maria Maggiore in Bergamo, edited by Enzo Mangili and published by the Banca Popolare di Bergamo, positioned her as a key voice in the scholarly reassessment of Giovanni da Campione's masterwork. The northern protiro, built between 1351 and 1353, is one of the finest examples of Campionese Gothic sculpture in Lombardy, featuring red Veronese marble lion-bearers and a rich sculptural program that connects Lombard Romanesque typology with the refined Trecento workshop tradition of the Campionesi. The volume, produced in conjunction with a major restoration campaign of the monument carried out between 1997 and 1998, brought together several specialists; among the contributors also noted in related scholarship is Saverio Lomartire, who addressed the theme of Giovanni di Ugo da Campione and the civic myth of the Campionesi.

The central axis of Recanati's scholarly activity has consistently been medieval Lombard painting and miniature. In 1989 she co-authored Codici e incunaboli miniati della Biblioteca civica di Bergamo, a foundational catalogue of the illuminated manuscripts held by Bergamo's civic library. She also contributed to the monumental multi-volume series La pittura in Lombardia, the Cariplo-sponsored survey coordinated by Mina Gregori and published between 1987 and 1999, where she co-authored with Carla Travi the section on Lombardy, Piedmont, and Liguria in the volume dedicated to mural painting from the late 13th to the early 15th century. In 2018 she delivered a public lecture at the Biblioteca Angelo Mai in Bergamo on the little-known illuminated Messale MA 298, using it as a lens to reconstruct the largely uncharted context of Lombard manuscript painting in the second half of the 13th century.

From 2000 to 2010, Recanati served as Director of the Accademia Carrara di Belle Arti di Bergamo, one of the major art academies in northern Italy. This decade-long directorship reinforced her standing as a central figure in Bergamo's cultural institutions. She has also served as a member of the Commission for Mobile Cultural Heritage of the Diocese of Bergamo, and as president of the cultural commission of the Biblioteca Angelo Mai, Bergamo's principal civic research library.

One of Recanati's most important recent scholarly contributions is the first volume of the scientific catalogue of the Accademia Carrara, dedicated to the panel paintings of the 14th and 15th centuries, published in September 2018. The catalogue was the result of years of archival and connoisseurial research and established significant new attributions within the collection, making it an essential reference tool for the study of Lombard and northern Italian painting of the Trecento and Quattrocento. She continues to teach art history at the Accademia di Belle Arti "G. Carrara" - now known as the Politecnico delle Arti di Bergamo - where her courses address medieval and modern art.

Ricci, Luigi G. G.

active late 20th-21st century

Luigi G. G. Ricci is an Italian philologist and palaeographer whose work is closely tied to the manuscript holdings of the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana in Florence, and in particular to the study and conservation of the Codex Amiatinus, the great Northumbrian Bible that has been housed there since the late eighteenth century.

Ricci was the lead editor, with Lucia Castaldi and Rosanna Minello, of La Bibbia Amiatina: Riproduzione integrale su CD-ROM del manoscritto Firenze, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Amiatino 1 (Florence, 2000), the complete electronic facsimile prepared alongside the manuscript's removal from its nineteenth-century binding — a conservation milestone that also permitted new non-destructive scientific analysis of the codex between 1999 and 2001. The facsimile remains a standard research tool, giving scholars direct access to the manuscript's full page sequence, including the disputed and disordered opening quire, without recourse to the fragile original. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the manuscript's modern conservation and study.

Richa, Giuseppe

Florence, 1689 – Florence, 1764

Giuseppe Richa was a Florentine Jesuit priest and ecclesiastical historian whose ten-volume Notizie istoriche delle chiese fiorentine divise ne' suoi quartieri (1754–1762) is the most exhaustive early-modern survey of Florence's churches, compiled parish by parish and quarter by quarter over the course of nearly a decade of research and writing. For each church Richa set out its foundation and building history, its patronage and burial rights, and a detailed inventory of its altars, tombs, and decoration, citing archival and inscriptional evidence throughout.

Because so many Florentine church interiors were subsequently reordered, stripped, or damaged — by eighteenth- and nineteenth-century remodelling, by Napoleonic suppressions, and by the losses of the twentieth century, including the flood of 1966 — Richa's Notizie istoriche frequently constitutes the only surviving record of an altarpiece's original location, a chapel's patron, or a fresco cycle's subject before its destruction or removal. Alongside Bocchi–Cinelli and Del Migliore, Richa completes the trio of great topographical guides on which modern reconstructions of Trecento and later Florentine decorative campaigns still depend, and his parish-by-parish method makes him particularly valuable for tracing a single family's chapels and commissions across the city.

Richter, George Martin

San Francisco, 27 March 1875 - June 1942

George Martin Richter was born on 27 March 1875 in San Francisco, California, the son of Dr. Clemens Max Richter (1848-1936), a noted surgeon, and his wife Emma. He pursued his art-historical training in Germany, writing his doctoral dissertation on the sixteenth-century German painter Melchior Feselen under a professor described as a leading chair in art history and noted scholar of Bavarian art history from the Middle Ages to the early modern era. His doctorate was conferred in 1907, and it was during these formative German years that Richter absorbed the rigorous, object-centred methodology of the German academic tradition.

Richter's intellectual formation was decisively shaped by his encounter with Giovanni Morelli, the Italian senator and connoisseur who had revolutionized art historical attribution by insisting on the close examination of small, unconsciously rendered details - ears, hands, fingernails - as fingerprints of individual artistic personality. Richter famously introduced Morelli to Bernard Berenson, a meeting that proved consequential for the entire field of Italian Renaissance connoisseurship, as Berenson adapted and extended the Morellian method throughout his long career. This placed Richter at the very nerve centre of the connoisseurial world at the turn of the twentieth century.

From approximately 1910 to 1912, Richter worked at the Galerie Helbing, a prominent gallery and auction house, where his scholarly expertise and his growing photo archive were both developed and refined. In 1918 he returned to Munich and established his own art dealership, and in July 1919 he co-founded the luxury publishing company Phantasus-Verlag with H. H. Schlieper. Over the following years his scholarly attention shifted increasingly toward Italian Renaissance art, with a particular concentration on the Venetian master Giorgione and on Florentine painters of the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. On 24 March 1925, the Richters were invited to tea with Bernard and Mary Berenson at the Villa I Tatti in Settignano, cementing a connection between the two most prominent connoisseur-scholars of Italian art of the day.

While most art historians of his era collected photographs as part of their research practice, Richter accumulated them on an exceptional scale, ultimately assembling an archive of some sixty thousand photographs along with an unspecified quantity of press clippings, all arranged in hundreds of green slip-case boxes according to his own classification system: first by school, then by artist attribution, and finally by chronology. He recorded the system in a small leather-bound notebook that survives in the National Gallery of Art. This archive was conceived as a tool for connoisseurship and authentication - a visual memory bank against which new attributions could be tested - and it anticipated the kind of photographic reference libraries that would later become standard in major art research institutions.

With the rise of fascism in Italy, Richter relocated his family and his archive from Florence to England in 1929, continuing to write, lecture, and advise clients on Italian art from his new base. Eventually he emigrated to the United States, where Hilla von Rebay - the pioneering director of what would become the Guggenheim Museum - helped introduce him to the New York art world and encouraged him to resume his research. He took up again his work on the Florentine painter Andrea dal Castagno (a book eventually published posthumously) and began a new project linking Giorgione to the modernist painting movements of the early twentieth century.

Finding it difficult to establish himself as a dealer in New York and discovering that income from writing and lecturing was insufficient, Richter recognized that his library and archive were his most valuable assets. From February 1940 he began negotiating with David Finley, director of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, offering the entire archive of sixty thousand photographs for fifty thousand dollars. In February 1942, already in failing health, Richter presented his last paper at Johns Hopkins University, accompanying an exhibition on Giorgione. He died in June 1942. It was only after his death that Solomon Guggenheim, at the urging of Hilla von Rebay, stepped in and provided the funds for the National Gallery to purchase the archive from Mrs. Richter, while his books were sold at auction. In 1943 the National Gallery announced with great fanfare the donation of what it called the George M. Richter Archive of Illustrations on Art, emphasizing its vital role in authenticating works of art and establishing provenance in the turbulent aftermath of the Second World War.

Within this broader career, Richter's article Megliore di Jacopo and the Magdalen Master (Burlington Magazine, Vol. 57, No. 332, November 1930) represents his engagement with the problems of Duecento Florentine painting that naturally arose from his long residence in Florence during the 1920s. The article is entirely consistent with his method: placing anonymous and semi-anonymous painters within networks of stylistic affiliation, drawing on his vast photographic archive for comparison, and contributing to the same connoisseurial project that Offner and Berenson were simultaneously pursuing. For a scholar of your specialization, Alberto, the Richter Archive at the National Gallery of Art in Washington would itself be a remarkable resource - its sixty thousand photographs of Italian paintings, organized by school and artist, constitute an extraordinary document of how early-twentieth-century scholarship constructed the corpus of Italian medieval and Renaissance art.

Romagnoli, Ettore

Siena, 22 October 1772 - Siena, 13 January 1838

Ettore Romagnoli was one of the most versatile figures in early nineteenth-century Sienese culture: art historian, musicologist, composer, and interpreter of the city's heritage for Italian and foreign visitors. For scholars of medieval Sienese art, he remains an indispensable historical source, especially for the reconstruction of local artistic biographies and archival traditions.

Born in Siena, he remained closely tied to the city throughout his life and also performed a quasi-diplomatic cultural role, accompanying foreign dignitaries on behalf of local noble circles. He was a member of the Societa Colombaria Fiorentina, one of the major learned societies of Grand Ducal Italy, and collaborated with the music theorist Carlo Gervasoni on the drafting of the Nuova teoria di musica.

His magnum opus is the autograph manuscript Biografia cronologica de' Bellartisti senesi dal secolo XII a tutto il XVIII, organized in twelve volumes plus a thirteenth volume of indexes, for a total of roughly 11,000 pages. Donated by the author to the Municipal Library of Siena in 1835, it gathers biographies of painters, sculptors, architects, and artisans, with documentary transcriptions, archival references, and critical observations. The first volume, dedicated to artists active between 1100 and 1300, is directly relevant to research on Duecento and Trecento Siena.

The manuscript was used by contemporaries such as Rumohr, Gaye, and Milanesi, later noted by Julius von Schlosser in Letteratura artistica (1924), and consulted by John Pope-Hennessy in his 1937 study of Giovanni di Paolo. After long periods of relative neglect, it has returned to the center of scholarship thanks to the complete digital transcription project promoted by Fondazione Memofonte. A facsimile reprint in thirteen volumes was published by S.P.E.S. (Studio per Edizioni Scelte) in 1976.

Among his printed works, Romagnoli published the Guide to the City of Siena for Lovers of the Fine Arts (Siena, Marco Ferri e Figlio, 1832), one of the earliest systematic guides to the city's artistic heritage. Posthumously appeared the Historical and Artistic Notes on Siena and Its Suburbs (Siena, Onorato Porri, 1840), republished in a third edition in 1852 with a biographical essay on the author and his writings. Together with the manuscript corpus, these works confirm his role as a foundational mediator between local erudition and modern art-historical method.

Romanini, Angiola Maria

Legnano, 26 February 1926 - Rome, 18 January 2002

Angiola Maria Romanini was one of the most influential Italian art historians of the second half of the twentieth century, especially in the study of medieval architecture and sculpture. Her work combined close formal analysis with broad historical interpretation, and helped shape modern scholarship on Lombard, Romanesque, and Gothic art in Italy.

Romanini taught medieval art history at the University of Pavia and later at Sapienza University of Rome, where she trained generations of students and researchers. Her university activity was matched by a major institutional profile: she became a member of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei and also held roles in high-level heritage bodies concerned with conservation policy and monument protection.

Her research focused in particular on Lombard art, the development of Romanesque and Gothic architectural language, and the artistic culture of monastic orders. Among her most cited works are studies on fourteenth-century Lombard architecture and on Arnolfo di Cambio, including the landmark volume Arnolfo di Cambio e lo "stil novo" del gotico italiano (1969), which became a reference point for discussions of the transition from Duecento classicism to early Trecento innovation.

Romanini also played a foundational role in scholarly publishing. She founded and directed the journal Arte Medievale and worked on major encyclopedia projects dedicated to medieval art, helping to create durable research infrastructure for the field. Her output is notable not only for specialized monographs, but also for synthetic contributions that connected stylistic analysis, workshop practice, and cultural history.

For the study of Assisi and early Trecento painting, Romanini's essay Gli occhi di Isacco. Classicismo e curiosita scientifica tra Arnolfo di Cambio e Giotto (1987) remains an important reference. The article is frequently cited in debates on the Isaac Master, the emergence of spatial naturalism around 1300, and the intellectual context in which Giotto's pictorial language developed.

Romano, Serena

Italian-Swiss scholar, active 20th–21st century

Serena Romano is an Italian-Swiss scholar and art historian best known for her work on medieval art, Roman visual culture, and Lombard art under the Visconti and Sforza. She combines institutional experience in the Italian Ministry of Culture with a long academic career in Switzerland, where she held a professorship in Medieval Art and is now emerita.

Romano studied art history at the University of Rome "La Sapienza," earning a degree focused on medieval art. She began her professional life as an art historian in the Italian Ministry of Culture, working in Venice and Rome, and later shifted into academia, becoming professor of medieval art at the University of Lausanne (Universite de Lausanne), where she served until her retirement and is now professor emerita. She has also taught in the "Art History in Rome" program at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, offering graduate-level courses on medieval visual culture.

Her research centers on painting and visual culture in Rome from Late Antiquity through the Middle Ages, as reflected in major synthetic books such as Arte e iconografia a Roma. Da Costantino a Cola di Rienzo and related volumes on Roman art from Late Antiquity to the end of the Middle Ages. She has written extensively on the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore and on the frescoes of the Lower Church at Assisi, where she was involved in early research projects on the Assisi fresco cycles. Another strong line of work concerns Lombard art under the Visconti and Sforza, including studies on arte lombarda and the role of court patronage in the later Middle Ages and early Renaissance.

Romano has published monographs and edited volumes with major Italian publishers such as Jaca Book and Vita e Pensiero, and her titles appear in both scholarly and museum-oriented catalogues. She has also curated or co-curated exhibitions, for example the 2015 show Arte lombarda dai Visconti agli Sforza, which brought together paintings, manuscripts, and decorative arts to trace the development of Lombard visual culture under those dynasties. Her bibliography ranges from technical studies of individual fresco cycles to broader synthetic accounts of Roman and Italian medieval art, making her a key reference for students and researchers working on Italian medieval painting and iconography.

Rothe, Andrea

active 20th–21st century

Andrea Rothe is a paintings conservator whose career bridges the Italian restoration tradition and the American museum world. He trained and worked in Florence, where he was active in the restoration laboratories that undertook the emergency conservation of works damaged in the flood of 1966, gaining an unusually broad practical grounding in the technical construction and condition of early Italian panel and canvas paintings before their treatment became a matter of laboratory science.

Rothe later moved to the United States and served for many years as a senior paintings conservator at the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, where he treated numerous Italian Renaissance panels entering the Getty's collection. His 1979 restoration of Luca di Tommè's Crucifixion at Montepulciano, carried out at the Palazzo Pitti, forms part of the documented conservation history of that painting and of the broader modern effort to stabilise and re-examine early Sienese panel and canvas works.

Rotili, Mario

Benevento, 12 August 1920 - Benevento, 26 February 1981

Mario Rotili was one of the most multifaceted figures in twentieth-century Southern Italian culture: a historian of medieval and modern art, museologist, librarian, archivist, and politician, he combined a distinguished academic career with direct civic commitment to the reconstruction of his city. His figure uniquely combines scientific research with administrative responsibility, in an intellectual profile reminiscent of certain civic humanists of the fifteenth century.

He was born in Benevento on August 12, 1920, and spent most of his life there. After attending a classical high school in his hometown, he enrolled in the Faculty of Letters at the University of Naples, where he earned his degree and took his first steps in art-historical research. He also began teaching art history at the classical high school in Benevento and contributed to local newspapers with articles on literary, theatrical, and film criticism, revealing from a young age a cultural openness that would characterize his entire body of work.

A member of the Christian Democrats, Rotili entered city politics at a delicate moment: between 1952 and 1956 he led the opposition to right-wing administrations, and in 1956 he was elected mayor of Benevento, a position he held for seven years, until June 1963. His term was marked by a measured and careful policy of reconstruction of the areas destroyed by Anglo-American bombing in 1943, with a General Urban Plan entrusted to the renowned urban planner Luigi Piccinato. He took stock of that period in the book Seven Years in the Service of My City (Benevento, Abete, 1963), and for his civic commitment he was awarded the title of Grand Officer of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic. Nearly ninety percent of the City Council's resolutions were approved unanimously during his tenure, a sign of his exceptional ability to mediate.

In 1959, while still serving as mayor, Rotili assumed the directorship of the city's cultural institutions: the Museo del Sannio, the Provincial Library, and the Provincial Historical Archives of Benevento. During his eleven years as director, until 1970, he completely reorganized the museum, established an art gallery within it, divided it into four specialized sections, and promoted exhibitions, conferences, concerts, and meetings with leading figures in Italian and international culture, envisioning the museum as a public hub of cultural life and not merely a repository of objects. He oversaw the restoration of the rich collection of parchment materials preserved in the museum's holdings, and for this work he was awarded the Gold Medal of Merit for Education, Culture, and the Arts by presidential decree in 1965.

After obtaining the title of Lecturer in Medieval and Modern Art History, Rotili initially taught at the Academy of Fine Arts in Naples, then at the University of Naples as an adjunct professor, and finally as a full professor, holding the chair of History of Miniature and Minor Arts and subsequently of Medieval and Modern Art History. He also taught at the Suor Orsola Benincasa University Institute of Education in Naples and was a lecturer in the Advanced Culture Courses at the Italian University for Foreigners in Perugia. A full member of the Pontaniana Academy and the National Society of Sciences, Letters, and Arts of Naples, he was also an Honorary Academician of the Pontifical Insigne Academy of the Virtuosi al Pantheon.

The core of Rotili's work is the history of medieval art in southern Italy, with Benevento and the Lombard duchy at the center of his focus. His first major volume, L'Arte nel Sannio (Benevento, 1952), won the Premio Napoli for Art History in 1956. This was followed by a series of studies on early medieval architecture and sculpture in the Benevento area, culminating in the monumental edition of L'Arco di Traiano a Benevento (Rome, Istituto Poligrafico dello Stato, 1972), which examined one of the most important monuments of classical art in Southern Italy. The volume Byzantine Art in Calabria and Basilicata (Cava dei Tirreni, Di Mauro, 1980) broadened the scope to encompass the landscape of late antique and medieval art in southern Italy. Rotili also contributed to the Corpus della scultura altomedioevale edited by the Italian Center for Studies on the Early Middle Ages in Spoleto, for which he authored the volume dedicated to the Diocese of Benevento (1966).

A second, equally original line of research concerns the history of miniature painting: Rotili was among the first Italian scholars to devote systematic research to book illustration in medieval Southern Italy. His major works in this field include La miniatura gotica in Italia (Naples, Libreria Scientifica, 1968-1969), Introduzione alla storia della miniatura e delle arti minori in Italia (1970, with Antonella Putaturo Murano), The Illuminated Dante Manuscripts of Naples (1972) and, above all, the two-volume work Miniature Painting in the Abbey of Cava (Cava dei Tirreni, Di Mauro, 1976-1978), dedicated to the Benedictine scriptorium of the Abbey of the Trinity in Cava. In 1963, he published Origins of Italian Painting (Bergamo, Italian Institute of Graphic Arts), a richly illustrated volume offering an overview of Italian painting from its Christian origins through the High Middle Ages, in which he included, among others, G. Salvi's thesis on the true identity of the painter Conxolus of the Sacro Speco in Subiaco.

His interest in architecture is also evident in his studies on Filippo Raguzzini, the Neapolitan architect of the Roman Rococo, to whom Rotili dedicated a volume in 1951 and a posthumous concluding essay in 1982; and in the series of studies on Luigi Vanvitelli, beginning in 1954, which culminated in the critical edition of the Vita di Luigi Vanvitelli written by his son (Naples, Banca di Roma-S.E.N., 1975). He contributed numerous entries to the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani and the Enciclopedia Dantesca, and contributed to the major collective work L'art dans l'Italie meridionale, the updated edition of Emile Bertaux's monumental work edited by Adriano Prandi (Rome, École française, 1978).

Mario Rotili died in his hometown of Benevento on February 26, 1981, at the age of sixty. One year after his passing, the City Administration, the Provincial Administration, and the Rotary Club organized an official commemoration, the proceedings of which were published in 1987. In 1984, friends and students published Studi di Storia dell'Arte in memoria di Mario Rotili (Naples, Banca Sannitica, 2 vols., 954 pp.), a miscellaneous collection featuring his complete bibliography, edited by Alessandra Perriccioli Saggese, and a tribute by the great historian Giuseppe Galasso. The City of Benevento later named a street in his honor.

Ruskin, John

London, 8 February 1819 – Coniston, 20 January 1900

John Ruskin was the most influential English art and architecture critic of the Victorian age, a passionate advocate of the moral and social value of Gothic art, and, for the study of Giovanni Pisano in particular, the first major critical voice writing in English to recognize the sculptor's individual genius and expressive force, an appraisal that ran well ahead of the more cautious Italian scholarship of his own century.

The only child of a prosperous sherry merchant, Ruskin was educated largely at home before matriculating at Christ Church, Oxford. His parents took him on extended tours of Britain and the European continent from early childhood, journeys that fostered the close, almost obsessive observation of landscape, geology, and architectural detail that would characterize his mature writing; repeated visits to Italy, and to Tuscany in particular, gave him direct and prolonged experience of the cathedrals, pulpits, and sculpture of Pisa and Siena.

Ruskin first won public attention with Modern Painters, published in five volumes between 1843 and 1860, begun as a defense of J. M. W. Turner against critics who found his late work unintelligible and expanded into a sweeping theory of art founded on truth to nature. The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849) and, above all, The Stones of Venice (1851-1853) established him as the leading English theorist of Gothic architecture; the central chapter of the latter work, "The Nature of Gothic," argued that the roughness and irregularity of medieval craftsmanship expressed the dignity of free labor, an argument that would exert enormous influence on William Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement.

It was within this framework that Ruskin arrived at his celebrated judgment of Giovanni Pisano, whom he called the "Canova of the thirteenth century," crediting him with combining the grace of Ghiberti, the tenderness of Raphael, and the majesty of Michelangelo. Coming decades before the documentary and stylistic work of later Italian and German scholarship had disentangled Giovanni's individual contribution from his father Nicola's workshop, Ruskin's enthusiasm belonged to the same wave of foreign rediscovery of the Pisano pulpits, alongside artists such as Ingres and Delaroche, that restored Giovanni Pisano to art-historical visibility after centuries of neglect.

Ruskin held the Slade Professorship of Fine Art at Oxford from 1869, lecturing on subjects ranging from Florentine sculpture to political economy, and his later career turned increasingly toward social criticism, most notably in Unto This Last (1860) and through the utopian Guild of St George, which he founded in 1871. Recurrent mental illness shadowed his final decades, and he died at his home at Brantwood in the Lake District in 1900, having shaped, through his voluminous writing, the taste, the conservation movement, and the social conscience of an entire generation.

Rutenburg, Nina

Boston, 1956 – New York, 20 May 2013

Nina Rutenburg — later, professionally, Nina Gray, after her marriage — is credited on the single most cited modern study of Andrea Orcagna's tabernacle at Orsanmichele, an article she wrote as an undergraduate with her Connecticut College professor Nancy Rash Fabbri. It was not the direction her career subsequently took.

Rutenburg attended Phillips Academy, Andover, before taking a bachelor's degree at Connecticut College, where she won the college's Lyman Allyn Museum Prize in art history — the training ground, and the collaborator, that produced "The Tabernacle of Orsanmichele in Context," The Art Bulletin 63, no. 3 (1981), 385–405. She went on to a master's degree at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University, and from there into a curatorial career that left Trecento Florence behind for American decorative arts of a much later period.

As Nina Gray she was a staff curator at the New-York Historical Society from 1985 to 1990, and thereafter worked as an independent curator, consulting for institutions including the Brooklyn Museum, the Munson-Williams-Proctor Arts Institute, and several National Park Service properties. Her later scholarship centred on the glass and metalwork produced by Louis Comfort Tiffany's studios and, specifically, on the women who worked there: she was co-curator of the 2007 New-York Historical Society exhibition A New Light on Tiffany: Clara Driscoll and the Tiffany Girls, which established Driscoll's authorship of major Tiffany lamp designs long credited to the studio's men, and a contributor to the related scholarship on "the women of Tiffany Studios" written with Margaret K. Hofer and Martin Eidelberg.

The distance between the two projects associated with her name — a co-authored article on a fourteenth-century Florentine confraternity shrine, and a body of curatorial work recovering the women artisans erased from the Tiffany Studios attribution record — is worth pausing on. Both are, in their different registers, exercises in the same kind of historical attention: asking who actually did the work behind a monument or an object, and why the standard account obscures it. She died in Manhattan in 2013.

S

Sacchetti, Franco

Florence, c. 1332/1334 – San Miniato, 1400

Franco Sacchetti was a Florentine merchant, statesman and writer whose Trecentonovelle, a collection of vernacular short stories composed in the last years of the fourteenth century, is among the most vivid documentary windows onto the everyday life, speech and artistic culture of Trecento Florence. Born into a Guelph merchant family of ancient standing, he spent part of his youth engaged in trade in the eastern Adriatic, at Ragusa (Dubrovnik) and along the Slavonian coast, before returning to Florence to take up the civic and mercantile life of his class.

From the 1360s Sacchetti held a long succession of public offices in the service of the Florentine Republic, serving on councils and magistracies in the city and repeatedly as podestà and capitano in subject and allied towns, including San Miniato, Bibbiena, Faenza and elsewhere. This administrative career, pursued across four decades, gave him direct and repeated exposure to provincial as well as Florentine society, an experience that feeds directly into the social breadth of his narrative writing. He belonged to the same literary and civic milieu as Giovanni Boccaccio, with whom he corresponded, and his work is everywhere marked by the example of the Decameron, even as it pulls decisively away from Boccaccio's aristocratic and idealising registers toward a rougher, more anecdotal realism rooted in contemporary Florentine fact.

His principal work, the Trecentonovelle, was planned as three hundred novelle but survives in some two hundred and twenty-odd tales, composed mostly in the 1390s and left unfinished at his death. Populated by merchants, friars, magistrates, wits and artisans rather than by princes and nobles, the collection is prized by historians as much for its incidental testimony as for its literary merit: it preserves anecdotes, nicknames and turns of phrase current in late Trecento Florence that survive nowhere else. Painters and sculptors of the earlier fourteenth century recur as protagonists of his tales, Giotto above all, whose proverbial wit Sacchetti records in several of the collection's best-known novelle; it is in this same casual, undocumented register that Sacchetti uses the nickname "Orcagna" for the painter and sculptor Andrea di Cione without troubling to explain it, evidence that the sobriquet was already common currency within a generation of the artist's death. Sacchetti's other writings include a substantial body of lyric verse — sonnets, ballate and cacce collected as the Libro delle Rime — together with moral and political letters and a commentary on Dante, the Sposizioni di libri. He died in 1400, probably of plague, while serving as podestà of San Miniato, leaving the Trecentonovelle incomplete.

Salmi, Mario

San Giovanni Valdarno, 14 June 1889 – Rome, 16 November 1980

Mario Salmi was one of the most influential Italian art historians of the twentieth century, specializing in Romanesque architecture, Tuscan sculpture, and the early Italian Renaissance. Born in San Giovanni Valdarno on 14 June 1889, he died in Rome on 16 November 1980, leaving behind a scholarly legacy of extraordinary breadth and depth.

In 1910, Salmi earned his law degree from the University of Pisa with a pioneering thesis titled La tutela del patrimonio artistico nazionale, demonstrating from the very beginning an exceptional sensitivity toward the protection of cultural heritage. From 1911 to 1914, he pursued advanced studies in Art History at the University of Rome under the guidance of Adolfo Venturi, one of the founding fathers of the discipline in Italy. This rigorous training laid the foundation for a philological method that would characterize his entire career: always starting from a direct and meticulous observation of the work — "stone by stone," as he liked to say — and then arriving at critical assessments within a broader historical perspective.

In 1917 he taught Art History at the Academy of Fine Arts in Parma, and beginning in 1918 he served as inspector of monuments in various Italian regions, from Puglia to Molise, from Umbria to Lombardy. In 1923 he became a professor at the University of Pisa, where he founded the Institute of Art History, which opened in 1929. He then moved to the University of Florence, where he taught from 1929 to 1949 and where he established the National Institute of Renaissance Studies in 1937. From 1950 to 1964, he held the chair of Medieval Art History at the University of Rome, where he was named professor emeritus upon his retirement.

His institutional influence extended far beyond the university lecture halls. In 1952, he was among the founding members of the Italian Center for Studies on the Early Middle Ages, an institution that helped bring a historical period previously considered marginal back into the center of scholarly attention. In 1949 he founded the art history and criticism journal Commentari, and was also co-editor of the journal Rinascimento. He served as editor-in-chief of the monumental fifteen-volume Enciclopedia Universale dell'Arte, published between 1958 and 1967, promptly translated into English as Encyclopedia of World Art by McGraw-Hill in New York.

Salmi's most distinctive trait was his tireless visual empiricism: at a time when the aesthetic perspective marked by Croce's idealism dominated in Italy, he instead favored a rigorous historical-philological approach, always accompanied by a direct examination of the works. To reach monuments scattered across the most remote countryside, when few roads were yet passable, Salmi would walk dozens of kilometers, sometimes spending the night in farmhouses. During visits to restoration sites, those working there recalled the arrival of this tall, solemn figure who "immediately and rapidly observed, read, and analyzed everything, comparing it with distant monuments, aided by a prodigious memory." His writings, even the most specialized ones, are characterized by a linear and essential prose, accessible even to non-specialists — which reflected his conviction that formal clarity was an expression of an orderly and harmonious vision of reality.

The chronological scope of Salmi's scholarly work ranges from early Christian and Coptic art to the Baroque, spanning architecture, sculpture, painting, and the so-called minor arts. His primary fields of expertise, however, were the Romanesque and the Renaissance: the two-volume set Romanesque Architecture in Tuscany and Romanesque Sculpture in Tuscany (1926–1927) remains a fundamental reference in the field to this day. Salmi was one of the first scholars to devote academic attention to the minor arts, a field then still neglected in academic circles, even establishing a chair for it at the University of Florence.

A field to which Salmi devoted particular attention was that of Italian medieval miniature painting. Notable among his works on the subject are La miniatura fiorentina gotica (1954), Italian Miniatures (1954, translated into English and published by H. N. Abrams), La miniatura italiana (1956, Electa), and the study of the Grimani Breviary (1974). These works earned him international recognition as the foremost authority on the tradition of Italian miniature painting.

His deepest passion remained Piero della Francesca. In 1979, at the age of ninety, he published his last and most laborious work, The Painting of Piero della Francesca, confessing that he had "exhausted what remained of his extraordinary vitality" in it. His student Umberto Baldini recalled that his love for Piero had been "one of the focal points of his life as a scholar and teacher," almost a symbol of the order and divine harmony of the Renaissance.

His career was not without controversy. When he was chosen over Roberto Longhi for the chair of Art History at the University of Rome, Bernard Berenson uttered the famous — and ruthless — phrase: "A genius has been neglected in favor of an insect." Salmi was also involved in the controversial affair surrounding the breakup of the Contini-Bonacossi Collection, which led to the export of numerous masterpieces (including works by Zurbarán, Piero della Francesca, and Giovanni Bellini), resulting in parliamentary inquiries and a complaint for "fraud against the state." No less combative was his stance regarding the doors of Orvieto Cathedral, for which he resigned as vice president of the Higher Council of Antiquities and Fine Arts when there were plans to include a work by Emilio Greco.

Salmi was a member of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei — to which he bequeathed his vast library, including numerous manuscripts, upon his death — and a foreign member of the Académie de France. He served as president of the Accademia Petrarca di Lettere, Arti e Scienze in Arezzo from 1945 to 1979, transforming it into an institution of international significance. He received the Gold Medal of Merit for Education, Culture, and the Arts, and an honorary doctorate from the University of Algiers. He donated a significant portion of his private art collection to the Museum of Medieval and Modern Art in Arezzo.

Among his most illustrious students were Enzo Carli, Paola Barocchi, Umberto Baldini, Vittoria Kienerk, and Giovanni Carandente, a school that profoundly shaped Italian art history in the second half of the twentieth century. At the age of eighty-five, he still regretted no longer being able to work fourteen to fifteen hours a day as he had done for decades — eloquent testimony to a total dedication to art history that has few parallels in the Italian academic landscape.

Salvini, Roberto

Modena, 1912 – Florence, 1985

Roberto Salvini was one of the most important Italian art historians of the twentieth century, making fundamental contributions to the study of medieval art, Romanesque sculpture, and Flemish painting. A student of the medievalist Mario Salmi, Salvini received his education in Florence, Munich, and Berlin, acquiring a European methodological perspective that would characterize his entire body of work. In 1937, he joined the Fine Arts administration, serving as superintendent of galleries in various locations — Trento, Palermo, and Modena — during the years of World War II. His institutional career culminated in his directorship of the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, where he promoted significant museographic innovations.

In 1956, Salvini began his university career as a professor at the University of Trieste, before moving to the University of Florence, where he taught for many years. He was actively engaged in the methodology of teaching art history, a topic he had already addressed in his theoretical essay La pura visibilità (1947), which reflected the influence of the German formalist tradition on his education. In 1983, he was elected a National Member of the Accademia dei Lincei, the highest academic honour in Italy. He also served as President of the Art History Section of the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence and held the position of Secretary General.

His studies ranged from Italian medieval art to the Renaissance, from Flemish art to European Romanesque sculpture. Among his most significant works in medieval studies are Medieval Mosaics in Sicily (1949), Wiligelmo and the Origins of Romanesque Sculpture in Europe (1956) — a pioneering study on the origins of Romanesque sculpture — and The Cloister of Monreale (1962). He also made significant contributions to Byzantine studies, writing seminal volumes such as The Cathedral of Modena (1966) and the volume Medieval Sculpture for the international series History of Western Sculpture.

A recurring theme throughout his work was his interest in the relationship between Italian patrons and Flemish painting, explored both in Flemish Painting (1958) and in his last published work, Florentine Bankers and Flemish Painters (1985), released in the year of his death. Salvini left a profound mark on half a century of national and international art history, and in 2018 and 2022 his legacy was celebrated with conferences and publications dedicated to his scholarly contributions.

Sánchez Ameijeiras, Rocío (María del Rocío)

active late 20th-21st century

Rocío Sánchez Ameijeiras, full name María del Rocío Sánchez Ameijeiras, is a professor of History of Art at the University of Santiago de Compostela and one of the most intellectually distinguished medievalists working in Spain today. Her scholarship occupies a distinctive position in the landscape of Hispanic medieval art history: deeply grounded in the Galician and Castilian material record, yet theoretically ambitious in ways that situate her work firmly within international currents of image theory, visual studies, and the relationship between verbal and pictorial rhetoric.

Sánchez Ameijeiras earned her doctorate in History of Art from the University of Santiago de Compostela, with a thesis on the iconography of thirteenth-century funerary sculpture in Castile and León. She subsequently completed her formation at the Istituto di Storia dell'Arte of the Università di Roma I (La Sapienza) and at the Warburg Institute in London.

Her doctoral thesis was directed by Serafín Moralejo, the great Galician art historian of the generation of Yarza Luaces and Bango Torviso, whose encyclopaedic mastery of Romanesque art, pilgrim culture, and the visual world of Santiago de Compostela made him the presiding genius of his field. To be Moralejo's doctoral student was to inherit the most demanding of intellectual traditions: one grounded simultaneously in formal analysis, classical iconographic method, and extraordinary sensitivity to the entanglement of text and image in the medieval world. Sánchez Ameijeiras received that inheritance and has done more than any other scholar of her generation to transform it.

Her postdoctoral years at the Warburg Institute proved equally formative, exposing her to the tradition of cultural iconology, the study of symbolic images in their widest cultural and literary context, that Aby Warburg founded and E. H. Gombrich, Michael Baxandall, and their successors developed. This immersion in the Warburgian method is palpable in her later theoretical writing, with its attention to the migration of motifs, the classical substrate of medieval visual language, and the rhetorical structures that govern both pictorial and literary production.

Funerary Sculpture in Gothic Castile and León

The subject of her doctoral thesis, iconographic investigations into thirteenth-century funerary sculpture in Castile and León, has remained one of the defining axes of her career. Her research into Gothic royal and aristocratic tombs is exceptional for the range of questions it brings to bear on apparently circumscribed objects: questions of dynastic identity, liturgical function, gender representation, political propaganda, and the theology of death and intercession all converge in her analyses.

Among the most celebrated of her early articles is "Lament for a Lost Queen: the Sarcophagus of Doña Blanca in Nájera" (The Art Bulletin, vol. 78, no. 2, 1996), which placed a major Castilian funerary monument in a richly documented historical and visual context and was subsequently reprinted in the influential anthology Memory and the Medieval Tomb. Her study of the tomb ensemble at Villalcázar de Sirga (Palencia), the sepulchres of Infante Felipe and a noblewoman, reconstructed both the identity of the commissioning patron and the theological significance of the distinctive heart-offering gesture shown in the effigies, revealing the complex layering of political vindication, Marian devotion, and funerary liturgy encoded in a single monument.

Her research on Romanesque sculpture in Galicia has encompassed both individual monuments and the broader problem of model circulation, addressing her contribution to the Enciclopedia del Románico en Galicia on the provinces of A Coruña and Ourense, as well as studies of the Codex Calixtinus and the Tumbo A. Her long essay "Dreams of Kings and Buildings: Visual and Literary Culture in Galicia (1157-1230)," published in the Brill volume Culture and Society in Medieval Galicia (2015), offered a panoramic account of visual production under Fernando II and Alfonso IX, addressing the intersection of royal patronage, Arthurian literary culture, and architectural ambition in Galician Romanesque.

Her engagement with the Tumbo A of Santiago Cathedral, published in 2008 alongside Manuel Cecilio Díaz y Díaz and Fernando López Alsina, provided a searching analysis of the functions and modalities of images in one of the most politically charged illustrated cartularies of medieval Iberia, showing how illuminated charters served as instruments of institutional memory, territorial claim, and sacred authority simultaneously.

Her research on the illuminated manuscripts of Alfonso X the Learned, above all the codices of the Cantigas de Santa María, represents one of her most sustained and original contributions. Her study "Del Salterio al Marial: sobre las 'fuentes' de las imágenes de los Códices de las Historias de las Cantigas de Santa María" (Alcanate, 2012-2013) traced the iconographic sources of the miniature cycles, demonstrating the transformation of psalter imagery into a Marian narrative mode through a nuanced reading of both visual and theological tradition. Her essay "Ymagines sanctae: fray Juan Gil de Zamora y la teoría de la imagen sagrada en las Cantigas de Santa María" situated the visual programme of the manuscripts within a specific Franciscan theory of sacred imagery, connecting the production of court manuscript culture to the wider intellectual world of mendicant theology. She also directed a major inter-university and international research project on visual culture in post-Alfonsine Castile.

Sánchez Ameijeiras's major theoretical work, Los rostros de las palabras: Imágenes y teoría literaria en el Occidente medieval (Akal, 2014), is a study of the relationship between images and literary theory in the medieval West, pursuing two interrelated questions: the relationship between the predicatory arts and the figurative programmes of Gothic cathedrals, and the comparison between formulas codified in Latin and vernacular grammars and poetics with the visual translation of verse discourse, with the aim of defining a specific visual genre, that of images in verse.

The book adopts a circular structure in which the Cathedral of León and the illustrated codices of the Cantigas de Santa María serve as both starting and ending points of a journey that visits French Gothic cathedrals, illuminated manuscripts from the Utrecht Psalter to the Psalter of Blanche of Castile, and ivory objects from Carolingian book covers to Parisian fourteenth-century mirror-cases. The work is at once a contribution to the theory of medieval images and a practical hermeneutic tool: its argument is that rhetorical figures, tropes, schemes, figures of thought, are not merely verbal phenomena but structural principles that organise both the production and the interpretation of visual art. Reviewing the book in Cahiers de civilisation médiévale, Herbert L. Kessler, the most eminent American scholar of medieval imagery, engaged it as a work of the first importance.

Her more recent work has pushed further into questions of time, movement, and cosmology in Gothic art. Her article "From the End to the Beginning: Time, Movement and Cosmology at the Dawn of Gothic" (Codex Aquilarensis 37, 2021) explored the temporal and spatial logic of early Gothic programmes, and "Rebellious Architecture: Movement, Subversion and Transubstantiation in the Visionary Mode" (Codex Aquilarensis 35, 2019) investigated the ways in which Gothic architecture can be understood as enacting theological concepts, particularly transubstantiation, through formal means. Her essay "If the Sea Were Made of Ink: A Word on Medieval Visual Poetry," contributed to Tributes to Paul Binski (Harvey Miller, 2021), extended her long-standing inquiry into visual poetics, addressing the intersection of liquid materiality, ink, writing, and image in medieval devotional culture.

Sánchez Ameijeiras is a member of the editorial and scientific committees of numerous prestigious journals, including Codex Aquilarensis, and has contributed to major international collaborative volumes. She co-edited with Francisco J. Hernández and Emma Falque the volume Medieval Studies in Honour of Peter Linehan (SISMEL-Edizioni del Galluzzo, Florence, 2018), a tribute to the distinguished Cambridge medievalist and historian of the medieval Iberian Church. She has also co-edited with José Luís Senra the important collective volume El tímpano medieval: imágenes, estructuras y audiencias (Santiago de Compostela, 2003), which remains a foundational reference for the study of Romanesque portal sculpture.

As a doctoral supervisor she has directed theses on subjects ranging from the illuminated Books of Hours and the Penitential Psalms to the Gothic cloister of León Cathedral, to the visual culture of the Castilian monarchy in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Her supervision of the 2012 thesis Thesaurum. La Crónica Troyana de Alfonso XI (Escorial, h.I.6) y los libros iluminados de la monarquía castellana (1284-1369) gave the field one of the most substantial recent monographs on royal Castilian illuminated manuscripts.

Within the tradition established by Yarza Luaces and Bango Torviso, Rocío Sánchez Ameijeiras represents both continuity and transformation. She inherits their commitment to rigorous archival and iconographic scholarship while opening the discipline toward the theoretical ambitions of image studies, visual poetics, and the anthropology of art. Her work on Gothic funerary sculpture, the Alfonsine manuscripts, and the rhetoric of medieval images has earned her a place in the first rank of European medievalists, a scholar for whom the Galician Romanesque and the Parisian Gothic, the Marian miracle and the liturgical rite, the sermon and the stone effigy all illuminate one another within a single, extraordinarily capacious intellectual vision.

Sandberg-Vavalà, Evelyn

Compton, Berkshire, 1888 – Florence, 8 September 1961

Evelyn Sandberg-Vavalà was born Evelyn May Graham Sandberg in Compton, Berkshire, in 1888. She was the only child of the Reverend George Alfred Sandberg (1848-1910), vicar of the church of Saints Mary and Nicholas, and Annie Sandberg (1858-1894), who died when Evelyn was still a child. She studied geography and went on to teach in a girls' grammar school and at a university college — an education and career path typical of the small number of professionally active women of her generation in Britain. She was also known by her married name, Evelyn Kendrew, though it was her pseudonym, Sandberg-Vavalà, that she used exclusively in her scholarly life.

In 1921 Sandberg-Vavalà made the decisive choice of her intellectual life: she moved to Florence, where she would remain for thirty-five years — interrupted only by the years of the Second World War. In Florence she placed herself under the guidance of Bernard Berenson, the great Lithuanian-American connoisseur and art historian who had established his villa I Tatti as the pre-eminent centre for the study of Italian Renaissance painting. Under Berenson's influence she developed into a rigorous scholar of iconography and early Italian painting, and she established close intellectual relationships with the most important art historians of the age: John Pope-Hennessy, Roberto Longhi, and Giuseppe Fiocco. She became well known in Florence not only as a researcher but also as a tutor and guide for students of art at the Galleria degli Uffizi, accompanying them on visits throughout Italy.

Her first and most enduring major work was published in 1929: La Croce Dipinta Italiana e l'Iconografia della Passione (Italian Painted Crucifixes and the Iconography of the Passion). This book remains a foundational reference in the study of the medieval painted cross — the croce dipinta — a distinctly Italian devotional form that was central to the visual culture of the Duecento and Trecento. For the first time, Sandberg-Vavalà subjected the entire corpus of surviving Italian painted crucifixes to systematic iconographic and stylistic analysis, tracing the development of the form from the Christus Triumphans of the Romanesque period to the suffering Christus Patiens of the Gothic age. Her work in this field was so foundational that a full century later, the Römisches Jahrbuch of the Bibliotheca Hertziana published a special section entitled Aspekte der Tafelkreuzforschung im Jahrhundert nach Evelyn Sandberg-Vavalà — "Aspects of panel cross research in the century after Evelyn Sandberg-Vavalà", a tribute to the lasting relevance of her pioneering study.

In 1934 she published her study on the iconography of the Virgin and Child in thirteenth-century Italian painting: L'iconografia della Madonna col bambino nella pittura italiana del Dugento, a work that brought the same systematic iconographic method she had applied to the crucifix tradition to bear on the Madonna type. She also made important contributions to the study of Venetian Trecento painting: she is cited by scholars of Venetian art — alongside Roberto Longhi — for her analyses of the workshop of Paolo Veneziano and his followers. Her 1926 monograph La pittura veronese del Trecento established her as one of the first scholars to treat Veronese medieval painting with the rigour it deserved.

In the postwar years Sandberg-Vavalà produced two major synthetic works that confirmed her reputation as the leading English-language authority on central Italian medieval and early Renaissance painting. Uffizi Studies: The Development of the Florentine School of Painting appeared in 1948, followed by Sienese Studies: The Development of the School of Painting of Siena in 1953. Both works combined iconographic analysis with careful attention to stylistic development and workshop tradition, and both remain useful reference tools. Her final monograph, Studies in Florentine Churches (Olschki, Florence, 1959), extended the investigation to the specific devotional and institutional contexts in which Florentine painting was produced and displayed.

One of the most remarkable legacies of Sandberg-Vavalà's scholarly life was her photographic archive of over 25,000 photographs of Italian paintings from the thirteenth to the sixteenth centuries. This archive, which she assembled and organised over four decades, constitutes an extraordinary documentary resource covering medieval mosaics and frescoes, Romanesque sculpture, and applied arts including cassoni, ivories, and jewellery. From 1957, aware of her declining health, Federico Zeri worked to ensure that the archive would be preserved intact. He persuaded Count Vittorio Cini to purchase it, and the archive passed after her death to the Fondazione Giorgio Cini in Venice, where it is preserved today as the Fondo Sandberg-Vavalà. A further portion of her photographic materials is held at the Fondazione Federico Zeri at the Università di Bologna.

Sandberg-Vavalà died in Florence on 8 September 1961, cared for in her final illness by the nuns of a religious community. She was buried in the small cemetery of Moggiona, a hamlet of Poppi in the Casentino, the forested valley southeast of Florence that she evidently loved. She was seventy-three years old. Her scholarly achievement was remarkable not only for its range and depth but for the era in which it was accomplished: as a self-taught British woman working in Florence in the interwar years, without a university chair or institutional support, she produced a body of work that shaped the study of medieval Italian painting for generations. The centenary of her great work on the painted crucifix has been marked by new international scholarship, the best possible tribute to an historian whose questions have not yet been fully answered.

Sanders, Henry A.

Livermore (Maine), 22 October 1868 - Ann Arbor (Michigan), 16 November 1956

American classicist, papyrologist, and textual scholar, professor of Latin at the University of Michigan, and editor of the standard early twentieth-century edition of the Latin text of Beatus's Commentary on the Apocalypse. Sanders took his A.B. at Michigan in 1890 and his A.M. in 1894, studied in Berlin in 1895–96, and received his doctorate at Munich in 1897. After two years at Minnesota he returned to Michigan in 1899, where he taught Latin until his retirement in 1939, rising from instructor to professor and chairing the department of speech and general linguistics from 1932 to 1939.

An interest in the Oxyrhynchus epitome of Livy drew Sanders from Roman history into papyrology, and he became the principal architect of the University of Michigan's celebrated papyrus collection, editing the bulk of its documentary Latin papyri and demonstrating the extent of Latin's use in the legal documents of Roman Egypt. He is equally known for his editions of the biblical manuscripts of the Freer Collection — the Washington codices of the Gospels, the Pauline Epistles, the Psalms, and the Minor Prophets — published in facsimile and transcription in a series of volumes that remain fundamental to New Testament textual criticism. He served as president of the American Philological Association in 1936–37 and twice directed the School of Classical Studies at the American Academy in Rome, in 1915–16 and from 1928 to 1931.

It was under the auspices of the American Academy in Rome, during his second term as director of its School of Classical Studies, that Sanders published in 1930 Beati in Apocalipsin libri duodecim, the critical edition of the Latin text of the Commentary of Beatus of Liébana. The edition established a textual classification of the manuscripts which, arrived at independently, corresponded closely to the family groupings that Wilhelm Neuss reached from the illustrations in the following year — a convergence of textual and pictorial evidence that gave the resulting stemma much of its authority. Sanders's text remained the standard edition of the Commentary until the appearance of modern critical editions in the later twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

Santanicchia, Mirko

active late 20th-21st century

Mirko Santanicchia is an Italian art historian and professore associato of Storia dell'arte medievale at the University of Perugia (Dipartimento di Lettere - Lingue, Letterature e Civilta antiche e moderne). He specializes in painting and the applied arts of central Italy between the late Middle Ages and the early Renaissance.

What distinguishes him within the Umbrian school is his sustained focus on arti applicate, not only panel painting. His core research territory includes goldsmithing (oreficeria), manuscript illumination (miniatura), and wooden furnishings and inlay (arredo ligneo and intarsia), treated with the same rigor usually reserved for painting. This integrated method reads miniatures and metalwork as a single visual culture.

Representative work includes:

  • In Istrumento: la sede puo fare la differenza? La rappresentazione del paesaggio urbano e naturale in alcuni documenti miniati e oreficerie del Trecento (in Paesaggio e arti figurative in Umbria tra Gotico e Rinascimento, 2014/2017), on Trecento illuminators and goldsmiths and their treatment of urban and natural landscape, keyed to Perugian illumination.
  • Un campanile ravennate per l'antica cattedrale di Perugia (Studi di Storia dell'Arte, 25, 2014), based on a 1343 miniature by the Perugian illuminator Vanni di Baldolo in the Biblioteca Augusta (ms. 975), used as visual evidence for the lost cathedral bell tower.
  • San Bevignate di Perugia. Storia e iconografia (Studi di Storia dell'Arte, 27, 2016), on the Templar church and the Statuto degli Ortolani in the Vatican Library.
  • L'Antependium di Citta di Castello e l'oreficeria sacra in Umbria in eta romanica (in Enrica Neri Lusanna's Umbria e Marche in eta romanica, Todi, 2013), on Romanesque liturgical metalwork.
  • La croce in cristallo di rocca del Duomo di Foligno e la circolazione di opere veneziane in Umbria nel Trecento (Arte Medievale, 2010-2011), on Venetian rock-crystal work circulating in Umbria.

Santanicchia has combined research with editorial and curatorial activity. He co-edited Paesaggio e arti figurative in Umbria tra Gotico e Rinascimento (2017) with Enrica Neri Lusanna, and Gli ordini di Terrasanta. Questioni aperte, nuove acquisizioni (XII-XVI secolo) (2021). He worked on the Pintoricchio centenary exhibition and its arti minori strand (Spello/Perugia, 2008), co-authored Storie di pittori tra Perugia e il suo lago (2008) and Il mobile in Umbria. Aspetti storici, artistici, tecnici e produttivi dal Medioevo al primo Novecento (2012), and contributed to Lo studiolo di Federico da Montefeltro e il suo doppio (Gubbio, 2023). He also lectures at the Festival del Medioevo and teaches the history of artistic techniques at Perugia.

Santi, Francesco

Perugia, 1914 – 1993

Italian art historian and long-serving custodian of the artistic patrimony of Umbria, born in Perugia in 1914. He took a degree in law at the University of Perugia in 1938, was called up for military service, and after the armistice of 8 September 1943 took part in anti-fascist Resistance activity and served on the local Liberation Committee; in its aftermath he turned to the study of art history in Rome.

In 1945 Santi entered the Soprintendenza of Perugia as an auxiliary official, beginning a career devoted almost entirely to the protection, study, and display of Umbrian art. He became director of the Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria in 1966, when he expanded its exhibition space to include the top floor of the Palazzo dei Priori; he was named Soprintendente in 1973 and director of the Soprintendenza in 1975, overseeing the restoration of historic buildings across the region. He retired from public office in 1979 but continued to research and publish, contributing regularly to the Bollettino d'Arte and to the museum's own catalogues; he compiled two of the fundamental catalogues of the Galleria Nazionale dell'Umbria, in 1969 and 1985, works that remain standard references for the collection — including its Perugia triptych attributed to Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio, which Santi had published in 1969 with an attribution to Bartolo di Fredi. He died in 1993; his private library was later donated to the Galleria, becoming its single most substantial acquisition.

Sauerlander, Willibald

Bad Waldsee, 29 February 1924 - Munich, 18 April 2018

Willibald Sauerlander was one of the most influential art historians of the twentieth century, renowned for fundamentally rewriting the history of medieval French sculpture and shaping postwar German art historical scholarship. Born on February 29, 1924, in Bad Waldsee, Wurttemberg, Germany, he passed away on April 18, 2018, in Munich, leaving behind a legacy that transformed how scholars understand Gothic art and its broader cultural contexts.

Sauerlander grew up in an artistic household as the son of a late-Impressionist painter who, ironically, disliked art historians. Surrounded by works of old and modern art, he nevertheless chose to pursue art history, beginning his studies in 1946 at the University of Munich when the city was still in ruins from World War II. The intellectual atmosphere was severely truncated by the war's aftermath, and the academic focus centered on medieval art studied through what he later characterized as a "curious kind of secular, aesthetic mystical spiritualism," an approach he found unappealing. He received his doctorate in art history from Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat Munchen in 1953 under the supervision of Hans Jantzen, with a dissertation on French Gothic portal sculpture.

After completing his doctorate, Sauerlander spent the years between 1954 and 1959 in Paris, working as a German lecturer and tour guide, an experience that profoundly shaped his scholarly focus on French medieval art. He then served as an assistant at the University of Marburg from 1959 to 1961, where he completed his Habilitation. His international connections deepened when he became a Visiting Member at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1961-1962, marking the beginning of regular scholarly exchanges with American institutions. He held a professorship at the University of Freiburg from 1962 to 1970, also serving as a visiting professor at New York University in 1964-1965 and 1970.

In 1970, Sauerlander assumed the directorship of the prestigious Zentralinstitut fur Kunstgeschichte in Munich, a position he held until 1989. During these nearly two decades, he served simultaneously as an honorary professor at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat Munchen and continued his international engagement through visiting professorships at Harvard University (1984-1985), Berkeley (1989), and New York (1992). In 1991, he delivered the prestigious Mellon Lectures in Washington, a recognition of his scholarly eminence. After retiring from the Zentralinstitut, he became a freelance contributor to the Suddeutsche Zeitung from 1993 onward, bringing art historical expertise to a broader public audience.

Sauerlander's most celebrated achievement was his fundamental reconceptualization of early French Gothic sculpture, moving beyond the formalist approaches that had dominated prewar German art history. His landmark work "Gothic Sculpture in France, 1140-1270," published in 1970 and translated into English in 1972, established him as the leading authority on the subject. Rather than focusing solely on stylistic analysis, he pioneered a contextual approach that examined sculpture within its political, intellectual, and religious frameworks. His methodology represented a deliberate break from the contaminated nationalist concepts of his predecessors, particularly Hans Sedlmayr's reactionary fundamentalist views, which he actively opposed.

His scholarly approach was characterized by an explicitly transnational perspective, emphasizing the continuous artistic exchange between French and German art rather than treating them as isolated national traditions. When examining German monuments such as the Naumburg Stifterfiguren or Bamberg Cathedral, he deliberately sought parallels beyond Germany's borders. This internationalist stance, nurtured by his extensive time in Paris and frequent travels to the United States, constituted a form of methodological anti-nationalism that distanced postwar German scholarship from its problematic heritage.

Beyond Gothic sculpture, Sauerlander's scholarly interests encompassed Romanesque art, about which he published two volumes of collected papers, as well as Nicolas Poussin and French eighteenth-century art. His later work extended to Baroque and modern art, including studies on Rubens's religious altarpieces in "Der katholische Rubens" (2011) and on Manet's depictions of Monet in "Manet malt Monet" (2012). He published extensively on the history and methodology of art history itself, with his most important studies on Romanesque and Gothic art collected in "Cathedrals and Sculpture" (1999-2000) and "Romanesque Art" (2004). His critical essays were gathered in "Die Luft auf der Spitze des Pinsels" (2002) and "Geschichte der Kunst - Gegenwart der Kritik" (1999).

Sauerlander received numerous honors throughout his career, including honorary doctorates from the University of Strasbourg (1987) and Scuola Normale Pisa (1999). He was awarded the Bavarian Maximilian Order for Science and Art in 1995, became a Correspondant etranger de l'Academie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in 1994, and received the Grand Prix de la Societe francaise d'archeologie in 2007. France honored him with the Commandeur de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres in 1990 and the Chevalier de la Legion d'Honneur in 1999. He was elected to the Academy of Europe in 1988 and held membership in numerous German and international academies. In 2011, international colleagues organized a conference in his honor at Princeton University, resulting in the volume "Gothic Art and Thought in the Later Medieval Period," which highlighted the breadth of his methodological innovations. After his death, the Zentralinstitut fur Kunstgeschichte established the Willibald-Sauerlander-Preis to honor early career research in the history of art history, preserving his memory and commitment to rigorous scholarship.

Scarpellini, Pietro

Rome, 4 April 1928 – Perugia, 29 September 2010

Scarpellini was one of the central figures in the twentieth-century study of Umbrian art, and for more than half a century the effective interpreter of Perugia's artistic patrimony.

Born in Rome to Luigi Scarpellini and Virginia Pancrazi, he was the nephew of the literary scholar Pietro Pancrazi, who is credited with transmitting to him an early love of art. He took a diploma at the Accademia di Belle Arti in Rome in 1951 and a degree in letters at the University of Rome in 1952, training under Lionello Venturi — a formation that left a lasting mark on his attention to style and to the critical tradition.

He taught at the Istituto d'Arte in Perugia from 1955, then at the Universita per Stranieri di Perugia from 1957 to 1981, becoming full professor in 1981 and moving to the Facolta di Lettere e Filosofia of the Universita degli Studi di Perugia in 1987, where he held the chair of medieval art history.

His scholarship spanned the medieval and Renaissance centuries in central Italy. He is remembered above all for his monographs on Luca Signorelli, Perugino and Bernardino di Betto (Pintoricchio), and for his critical edition of Fra Ludovico da Pietralunga's guide to Assisi, in which he drew together the vast bibliography on the Franciscan basilica and its fresco cycles — the Descrizione della basilica di S. Francesco e di altri santuari di Assisi (c. 1570), published at Treviso by Canova in 1982 and still routinely cited as a primary source in the literature on the Maestro di San Francesco and the Assisi cycles. His Perugino. L'opera completa appeared with Electa, Milan, in 1984. Equally valued are his studies on the interplay between medieval Umbrian poetry, the sacre rappresentazioni and the figurative arts, and his work on Giotto and the giotteschi.

Alongside his academic career he was a committed conservationist. He was among the founders, in 1959, of the Perugia section of Italia Nostra, which he presided over for twenty-three years (1978–2001), leading campaigns against the building speculation of the 1960s and 1970s. He was described after his death as a free thinker and the critical conscience of the city, a defender of Article 9 of the Italian Constitution. In 2015 the Perugia city council moved to install a commemorative plaque in his honour. His collected papers have since been published as Pietro Scarpellini. Scritti d'arte.

Schapiro, Meyer

Šiauliai, 1904 – New York, 1996

Pioneering American art historian, critic, and teacher whose interdisciplinary approach revolutionised the study of medieval, Romanesque, and modern art. Born on September 23, 1904, in Šiauliai, Lithuania, he immigrated to the United States with his family in 1907, settling in New York City, where he was profoundly shaped by the city's vibrant intellectual and artistic milieu.

Schapiro attended Columbia University, earning his bachelor's degree in 1924, his master's in 1926, and his Ph.D. in 1929 with a groundbreaking dissertation on twelfth-century Romanesque sculpture in Burgundy, which challenged prevailing stylistic chronologies and emphasised socio-political contexts. His early work — including articles on Mozarabic art and cloister frescoes at Santo Domingo de Silos — established him as a meticulous scholar who integrated formal analysis with historical, theological, and economic factors, methods that contrasted sharply with the era's more rigid iconographic or formalist schools. Joining Columbia's faculty in 1928, he taught there for over fifty years, mentoring figures including Arthur Danto and Robert Rosenblum, and fostering dialogues between art history, Marxism, psychoanalysis, and phenomenology.

His seminal publications include Romanesque Art (1977) and essays collected in Words and Pictures (1973), which dissected the emotional expressivity in medieval sculpture — arguing, for instance, that the "chaotic" sculptural heads at Moissac reflected deliberate spiritual intensity rather than primitivism — as well as later monographs on Van Gogh (1950) and Cézanne (1952), which humanised modern masters by linking their innovations to personal psychology and cultural upheaval.
