His insistence on viewing art as a dynamic interplay of form, content, and human agency — epitomised in his critique of Erwin Panofsky's iconology — bridged medieval monastic traditions with twentieth-century abstraction, influencing fields from semiotics to New York School painting; he was personally acquainted with artists including Willem de Kooning. He died on March 26, 1996, leaving an enduring corpus that taught generations to see art not as isolated objects but as vital expressions of historical consciousness.

Schmarsow, August

Schildfeld (Mecklenburg-Schwerin), 26 May 1853 - Baden-Baden, 19 January 1936

August Schmarsow was a German art historian whose career united two distinct and lasting legacies: the foundational theory of architectural space that bears his name, and the institutional act that created what is now the most important research library for Italian art history in the world. He occupied the chair of art history at Leipzig for twenty-six years and trained a generation of scholars that would reshape the discipline for the following century.

Schmarsow was educated in Zurich, Strasbourg, and Bonn. He came under the decisive influence of Carl Nicolaus Heinrich Justi, one of the great scholar-connoisseurs of nineteenth-century German art history, whose philological rigor and biographical method left a permanent mark on his student's approach to the Italian masters. He became docent of the history of art at Gottingen in 1881, professor there in 1882, at Breslau in 1885, moved to Florence in 1892, and then to Leipzig in 1893.

The Breslau years were the crucible of his most consequential institutional initiative. It was as professor at Breslau that Schmarsow organized the winter seminar in Florence that would lay the groundwork for what became the Kunsthistorisches Institut.

The winter semester of 1888-89 produced one of the most remarkable gatherings in the history of the discipline. August Schmarsow, professor of art history at Breslau, taught courses at various locations in Florence. He lectured on Italian sculpture in the Circolo Filologico in the Palazzo Ferroni, on Masaccio and Masolino, and held tutorials on the history of Italian sculpture and painting in his private apartments. The nine students attending this seminar were Aby Warburg, Ernst Burmeister, Hermann Ulmann, Max J. Friedlander, Albert Kollmann, Johannes Seger, Max Semrau, August Winkler, and Ernst Zimmermann.

The roll-call is extraordinary: Aby Warburg, who would go on to found the Warburg Institute and transform cultural history, and Max J. Friedlander, who became the supreme connoisseur of Early Netherlandish painting, were both young students in Schmarsow's Florence seminar. Schmarsow's idea was to found the German Institution of Art History, the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz, with the aim of promoting research in the field of Italian art. In this occasion, Warburg had the task of writing an essay regarding Masolino and Masaccio's frescoes from the Brancacci Chapel, highlighting the differences between the two.

August Schmarsow proclaimed with this pioneering feat in 1888 the establishment of the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz. The formal history of the institution, however, is somewhat more complex: at the second Kunsthistorischer Kongress in Nuremberg, it was decided to establish a research institute in Florence, the most distinguished centre of art-historical studies. An executive committee was formed, headed by Adolph Bayersdorfer, August Schmarsow, and Max Georg Zimmermann. Considerable funds were donated via Wilhelm von Bode, the influential Berlin museum director. Schmarsow proposed Heinrich Brockhaus from Leipzig for the post of director. On 16 November the Kunsthistorisches Institut provisionally opened in the largest room in Brockhaus's private apartments.

The model that animated the project was explicit: he became devoted to the idea of founding an institute for art in Florence akin to the Deutsche Archaologische Institut in Rome. The DAI had given German classical scholarship a permanent base at the source of its materials; Schmarsow wanted to do the same for the study of Italian art. The institution he initiated, now the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz, part of the Max Planck Society since 2002, possessing a library of over 360,000 volumes and one of the most comprehensive photographic archives on Italian art in the world, is the enduring monument to that ambition. It is precisely the institution where, seventy-eight years later, both Bruce Cole and Erling Skaug were working as fellows when the Arno flooded Florence in November 1966.

In 1893 Schmarsow succeeded Anton Springer as chair of art history at the University of Leipzig, beating out Heinrich Wolfflin. The competition between the two figures was not merely institutional but intellectual: they represented divergent approaches to the foundational question of what art history was and how it should proceed. Wolfflin would develop his theory of Kunstgeschichtliche Grundbegriffe, the formal categories of Renaissance and Baroque, into the most widely taught method in the discipline; Schmarsow contested him from the outset with an alternative rooted in bodily experience and spatial psychology rather than the optical analysis of form.

At Leipzig, Schmarsow incorporated ideas similar to Wolfflin's as well as concepts from the anthropology of his Leipzig colleague, the psychologist Wilhelm Wundt (1832-1920). Wundt, the founder of experimental psychology and the author of the monumental Volkerpsychologie, was Schmarsow's closest intellectual neighbour at Leipzig, and the cross-fertilization between Wundt's empirical investigations of perception and Schmarsow's theory of architectural experience was direct and consequential.

Schmarsow's inaugural lecture at Leipzig in 1893, Das Wesen der architektonischen Schopfung (The Essence of Architectural Creation), is the founding text of his theoretical legacy. In his inaugural lecture at Leipzig, Schmarsow focused on defining architecture exclusively as the spatial art, in contrast to Wolfflin's formalism.

Schmarsow was the first to formulate a comprehensive theory of architecture as a spatial creation at the frontiers of the paradigm of perceptual empiricism. He differed most from other theorists in his insistence that bodily movement through space rather than the stationary perception of form was the essence of architecture.

The implications of this position were radical. Schmarsow fundamentally altered the balance between space and mass in favour of the former: prior to his work, space was considered to be a void inside the solid building, while modern architecture treats structures as means to define the extensions of space. Schmarsow declared that architectural form should be understood through the movement of visitors through space and not as an object of stationary observation.

This reorientation from mass to space, from optical form to embodied experience, placed the human body, its bilateral symmetry, its sense of forward movement, and its proprioceptive awareness of enclosure and extension, at the centre of architectural analysis. The book also outlined Schmarsow's three principles of human organization: symmetry, proportionality, and rhythm.

The theoretical elaboration continued in Grundbegriffe der Kunstwissenschaft am Ubergang vom Altertum zum Mittelalter (1905): following the ideas of Alois Riegl in his recently published Spatromische Kunstindustrie, Schmarsow argued that the significance of space is part of the psychological expression of a particular period of history. This move, making spatial conception a historically determined phenomenon rather than a universal one, connected his theory to the broader Kunstwollen debate and gave it a historiographical as well as perceptual dimension.

Alongside his theoretical and institutional work, Schmarsow maintained a sustained engagement with specific artists and periods of Italian art, producing monographs that reflect the full scope of his interests from the medieval through the Baroque.

His early publications ranged from the Umbrian Quattrocento, Raphael und Pinturicchio in Siena (1880), Melozzo da Forli (1886), Giovanni Santi, der Vater Raphaels (1887), to medieval Tuscan sculpture: St. Martin von Lucca und die Anfange der toskanischen Sculptur im Mittelalter (1889). This last work, devoted to the origins of Tuscan sculpture in the Romanesque period, exemplifies the chronological range that distinguished him from contemporaries more narrowly focused on the High Renaissance.

The Masaccio-Studien (1895-1899), published in five parts with an atlas of photographs, a format designed to put visual evidence directly before the reader alongside the argument, was among the most systematic treatments of that pivotal painter produced before Roberto Longhi's generation. Masaccio was the hinge figure between the Trecento world of the Compagnia di San Luca and the new naturalism of the Quattrocento, and Schmarsow's sustained engagement with his work placed him at the centre of the debate about how that transition should be understood.

Gherardo Starnina (1912) addressed an important but elusive late Trecento and early Quattrocento painter active in Florence and Spain, a figure at the threshold between the International Gothic and the early Renaissance, whose work intersects with the tradition of Florentine workshop painting that runs through Orcagna, Agnolo Gaddi, and the circle studied by Skaug and Cole.

Barock und Rokoko (1897) represented his first major intervention in the rehabilitation of Baroque art at a moment when its reputation was only beginning to recover from Burckhardt's disparagement, a pioneering move that Schmarsow shared with his contemporary Cornelius Gurlitt. Federigo Barocci (1909-10) extended the argument into the Mannerist generation.

The 1888 Florence seminar had placed Schmarsow at the origin point of two of the most consequential careers in twentieth-century art history. Aby Warburg's lifelong obsession with the survival of antiquity in the Renaissance, his concept of the Pathosformel, his theory of cultural memory, and the library that became the Warburg Institute, traces its beginning to the encounter with Masaccio and Masolino that Schmarsow assigned him in Florence. Max J. Friedlander became the foremost connoisseur of Early Netherlandish painting, producing the fourteen-volume Early Netherlandish Painting that remains the standard reference.

His students included scholars who went on to occupy major positions in the German and international art-historical establishment. The institutional legacy through the Kunsthistorisches Institut is equally direct: generations of scholars from every country have used its library, worked in its seminar rooms, and published in its series, all of them inheritors of the ambition that Schmarsow articulated in his private apartments in Florence in the winter of 1888.

Schmarsow stands at the intersection of three distinct but related contributions: monographic scholarship on Italian Renaissance and medieval art, the institutional initiative that gave the international community of Italian art historians its most important research base, and the theoretical argument about space, movement, and embodied perception that made him one of the founding figures of architectural phenomenology.

His contest with Wolfflin, the two greatest art historians of their generation competing for the same chair, defined the methodological poles around which the discipline organized itself for decades. Where Wolfflin proposed an art history of pure visibility, grounded in the analysis of formal categories independent of historical content, Schmarsow proposed an art history grounded in bodily experience, psychological response, and the historically specific spatial imagination of a culture. The subsequent century has vindicated elements of both positions: the phenomenological tradition in architectural theory, from Merleau-Ponty through Christian Norberg-Schulz to Juhani Pallasmaa, descends in large part from the argument that Schmarsow first articulated in his Leipzig inaugural lecture of 1893.

Schmidt, Victor Michael

active late 20th-21st century; retired May 2024

Victor Michael Schmidt is a Dutch art historian specializing in Italian medieval and Renaissance painting, with a particular focus on panel painting, the typology and function of art objects, iconography, and the origins of art theory. For decades, he served as Associate Professor of Art History at Utrecht University, where he remained until his retirement in May 2024.

Schmidt's research focuses on Italian painting of the 13th and 14th centuries, employing an approach that integrates typological analysis, liturgical function, and the private devotion associated with pictorial objects. He is one of the foremost living specialists in late medieval Italian panel painting, with a specific focus on the Marche, Tuscany, and the Umbrian region.

His perspective is distinctly interdisciplinary: in addition to stylistic attribution, he investigates the artist's social status, patronage, and the reception of the works within the religious and civil context of the Middle Ages.

Schmidt's most influential publication is his editorship of the volume Italian Panel Painting of the Duecento and Trecento (Studies in the History of Art, 61), published by the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 2002, which brings together twenty-three essays by international specialists and grew out of a symposium held in Florence in 1998.

This volume has become an indispensable reference tool for anyone studying the origins of Italian panel painting. Equally significant is Painted Piety: Panel Paintings for Personal Devotion in Tuscany, 1250-1400 (Centro Di, Florence, 2005), a monographic study on private devotion and the relationship between patron and sacred image in 13th- and 14th-century Tuscany. In 2010, he co-edited with Justin Kroesen The Altar and Its Environment, 1150-1400 (Brepols, Turnhout), a collective volume on the altar as a physical, liturgical, and visual space in the Middle Ages. More recently, he published Processional Banners and Gonfalons from the Marche. Late Middle Ages and Renaissance (Edizioni Centro Studi "G. Mazzini," Fermignano, 2020), exploring processional painting in the Marche region.

Schmidt is a member of the editorial boards of some of the most authoritative Italian journals of medieval and Renaissance art history, including Prospettiva, La Diana (journal of the School of Specialization in Historical and Artistic Heritage at the University of Siena), Arte marchigiana, and Studi montefeltrani.

He is also a member of the board of directors of the Stichting voor Nederlandse Kunsthistorische Publicaties, the Dutch organization that publishes the journal Simiolus, one of the most respected art history publications in the Netherlands. He has maintained academic ties with the Dutch University Institute of Art History in Florence, an institution that has traditionally fostered the relationship between Dutch art historiography and Italian art.

Until his retirement, Schmidt trained entire generations of art historians in Utrecht, supervising theses and research on topics related to medieval Italian painting. As evidenced by his students still active in 2025-2026, his influence extended far beyond his direct teaching: a recent example is the presentation of a bachelor's thesis on Francesco da Bologna at Utrecht University in May 2026, supervised by Schmidt himself. The National Gallery of Art in Washington has also included his bibliography in online catalogs dedicated to 13th- and 14th-century Italian painting, a recognition of the institutional significance of his work.

Schubert, Ernst

Bemerode near Hannover, 23 May 1941 - Hannover, 18 March 2006

Ernst Schubert was a German historian best known for his work in medieval and regional history. He spent most of his academic life at the University of Gottingen, where from 1985 until his death he held the chair in Niedersachsische Landesgeschichte, the regional history of Lower Saxony.

Schubert studied history and the auxiliary historical disciplines, with a strong focus on the Middle Ages, and completed both his doctorate and habilitation in this field. After several academic appointments, he became Professor fur Niedersachsische Landesgeschichte at Gottingen in 1985, where he helped shape regional history as a major area of research and supervised numerous doctoral students.

His main research interests lay in the social and constitutional history of the Middle Ages and the early modern period, especially in Lower Saxony and northwestern Germany. He also worked on environmental and agrarian history, examining how land use, settlement patterns, and legal institutions influenced medieval society.

Schubert's studies regularly combined close archival research with a sustained focus on institutions such as lordships, towns, and ecclesiastical jurisdictions. This methodological combination made his work particularly valuable for understanding regional structures of power and long-term historical change.

He remained active in research and teaching until shortly before his death in 2006 at the age of sixty-four. His books and edited volumes continue to be cited in scholarship on medieval and early modern German regional history, especially for studies concerning Lower Saxony and neighboring territories.

Scudieri, Magnolia

active late 20th-21st century

Magnolia Scudieri is an Italian art historian specialising in Renaissance and medieval art, particularly known for her scholarship on Beato Angelico and fourteenth- and fifteenth-century miniature painting. She devoted the greater part of her career to the Museo di San Marco in Florence, where she held key positions in conservation, restoration, and curation.

Scudieri earned her degree in Medieval and Modern History from the University of Florence, where she studied under Giorgio Bonsanti, whose assistant she served from 1982 to 1992. She began her professional career at the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, working in the Restoration Office of the Superintendency for Artistic and Historical Heritage of Florence and Pistoia, with specific assignments in the Fiesole area and at the Museo di San Marco. This initial phase allowed her to combine scientific rigour with curatorial practice, and her work on restorations revealed previously unknown aspects of Renaissance interiors, including the original green colour of the walls of Michelozzo's library, which emerged in 2000 from beneath a nineteenth-century patina.

From 1992 until her retirement after approximately thirty years of service, Scudieri directed the Museo di San Marco, transforming it into a centre of excellence for conservation and public engagement. Under her leadership, the museum oversaw restorations of the Sala Greca — including the polychrome wooden ceiling — and of key works by Beato Angelico: the San Marco Altarpiece, the Crucifixion in the Chapter House, and the Annalena Altarpiece. She reorganised sections of the collection, including the tombstones from San Pancrazio and the paintings by Fra' Bartolomeo, improving security, accessibility, and conservation standards while preserving the site's monastic character.

A specialist in fourteenth- and fifteenth-century manuscript illumination, she contributed to exhibition catalogues in Italy and abroad, curating exhibitions on subjects including the illuminated choir books of San Marco and the relationship between Beato Angelico and miniature painting. Her publications include Gli affreschi dell'Angelico a San Marco (2004), Fra Giovanni Angelico. Pittore miniatore o miniatore pittore? (2007), the biographical entry on Guido di Pietro (Beato Angelico) in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (2004), and the official museum guide Museo di San Marco. La guida ufficiale (1999). Her research on Sister Plautilla Nelli's Lamentation over the Dead Christ contributed to the rediscovery of Nelli as the first Florentine female painter, a contribution recognised by the Nelli Prize awarded in 2004 by Advancing Women Artists.

Antonio Paolucci, former superintendent of the Florentine museums, praised Scudieri's ability to combine scientific rigour with humanity. Her "diachronic" approach to the museum — emphasising San Marco's spiritual and historical continuity from the Renaissance to the twentieth century — has been widely acknowledged as a defining contribution to the site's identity. She led distinguished tours, including that for Emperor Akihito of Japan in 1993.

Seidel, Linda

b. 1939

Linda Seidel is an American historian of medieval art, Hanna Holborn Gray Professor Emerita of Art History at the University of Chicago, and the author of the study that dismantled the modern legend of Gislebertus. Her work is characterised by a persistent scepticism toward the received identities of famous monuments — she has repeatedly shown that what the discipline takes to be medieval fact is often a nineteenth- or twentieth-century construction — combined with an early and influential turn toward reception theory.

Born in 1939, she took a B.A. in French literature at Barnard College, an M.A. at Radcliffe, and her Ph.D. in art history at Harvard in 1965 under Frederick B. Deknatel. She taught at Harvard, in the Fine Arts department and at the Fogg Art Museum, before joining the faculty of the University of Chicago in 1977; she was named the first Hanna Holborn Gray Professor in Art History, received the Burlington Northern Distinguished Graduate Teaching Award in 1990, and retired in 2004.

Her method announced itself early. "A Romantic Forgery: The Romanesque 'Portal' of Saint-Étienne in Toulouse" (1968) demonstrated that one of the standard monuments of the French Romanesque canon was in fact a nineteenth-century composite, an argument that overturned a good deal of accepted French scholarship and set the pattern for her later work. Songs of Glory: The Romanesque Façades of Aquitaine (1981) read western French church fronts as public rhetoric rather than as illustrated theology, and Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait: Stories of an Icon (1993) applied the same suspicion to the most over-interpreted panel in Netherlandish painting, treating the accumulated readings as themselves the object of study.

Legends in Limestone: Lazarus, Gislebertus, and the Cathedral of Autun (Chicago, 1999) is her most contested book and the one most directly relevant here. It takes as its subject two cults — that of the saint and that of the sculptor — and shows how "Gislebertus, sculptor" was discovered, elaborated and effectively canonised over the course of the twentieth century, above all by the 1960 monograph of Denis Grivot and George Zarnecki. Against that reading she argued that the inscription GISLEBERTVS HOC FECIT commemorates a lay benefactor rather than a carver, proposing a late Carolingian count as its referent, and that its placement beneath the feet of Christ suits a patron's memorial better than a craftsman's boast.

The reception was respectful of the historiographical achievement and sceptical of the patron thesis in particular: William Diebold, reviewing the book in The Medieval Review (2000), allowed that a patron is entirely plausible on medieval conventions while noting that the displacement of artist by patron was hardly news to medievalists, and Christine Verzár in Speculum (2001) joined others in complaining that the book sets up and demolishes straw men drawn from an older iconographic art history. The fair verdict is that Seidel destabilised the confident biography of "Gislebertus the sculptor" without securing "Gislebertus the patron" in its place — which is itself a substantial result.

She also edited Meyer Schapiro's Charles Eliot Norton Lectures as Romanesque Architectural Sculpture (Chicago, 2006), an act of scholarly stewardship toward the tradition she had spent her career interrogating. Her wider argument against the older iconographic method associated with Émile Mâle — that a church's imagery is a fixed pictorial book to be read in sequence — has proved more durable than any single attribution: at Autun she describes a distributed programme whose meanings are made and remade by the moving body of the pilgrim.

Seidel, Max

Basel, 9 February 1940

Max Seidel is a Swiss art historian and, for a generation, one of the pre-eminent authorities on the art of medieval and early-Renaissance Tuscany, above all the sculptors Nicola and Giovanni Pisano. Director of the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz (KHI) from 1993 to 2005, he presided over that institute's transformation into a Max Planck research center, and he remains its Director Emeritus. His career has run along the same terrain covered by this set of notes, the Pisano workshop, Sienese Trecento painting, and the political imagery of Lucca, which makes him a natural counterpart to Anita Moskowitz on the sculpture side and a scholar whose Lucca work touches directly on the world of Castruccio Castracani.

Life and career

He was born on 9 February 1940 in Basel and studied art history at the universities of Basel and Florence. He took his doctorate at Basel in 1967 with a dissertation on the relationship between central-Italian and northern-French art in the thirteenth century, a theme (the Italian encounter with French Gothic) that would recur throughout his work. He completed his Habilitation at Zurich in 1973.

His academic path then moved steadily southward and upward: university lecturer (Universitatsdozent) at Zurich (1973-1979); professor at Gottingen (1979-1982); full professor (Ordinarius) and director of the Kunsthistorisches Institut of the University of Heidelberg (1982-1993); and finally director of the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz (1993-2005). During his tenure the KHI passed to the Max Planck Society in 2002; Seidel became a Scientific Member of the Max Planck Society that year and has been the institute's Director Emeritus since 2005. Under his directorship the institute's research capacities were substantially expanded, and it advanced into a leading international center for art-historical scholarship.

Seidel's standing in Italy is reflected in an unusual density of honours: he was made an honorary citizen of Florence in 2005, and he holds the rank of Grande Ufficiale of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic and Commendatore of the papal Order of St Sylvester, along with the Italian state medal Benemerito della cultura e dell'arte (1997) and civic honours from Lucca (2008) and the cathedral works (Opera del Duomo) of Pisa (2014). The concentration of Lucchese, Pisan, and papal recognition mirrors exactly the geography of his research.

Research and the Pisano problem

Seidel's scholarship centers on Tuscan art of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, with excursions into the nineteenth. He has written extensively on Nicola and Giovanni Pisano, on the Sienese painters Simone Martini and Ambrogio Lorenzetti, and on Luca Signorelli, and he pursued the political iconography of the Tuscan communes. With Peter A. Riedl he co-directed the vast corpus project Die Kirchen von Siena (The Churches of Siena), one of the great topographical-inventory undertakings of Italian art history.

His engagement with the Pisani culminated in the two-volume monograph Father and Son: Nicola and Giovanni Pisano (Munich: Hirmer Verlag, 2012; 2 vols, c. 989 pp., c. 928 illustrations; ISBN 978-3-7774-5101-5), issued in the series of the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florenz. It is the summation of a lifetime's work, and it is built around a single, deliberately narrow problem: the artistic relationship between father and son. Against the long-dominant view, encapsulated in Adolfo Venturi's image of an "abyss" separating Giovanni from Nicola, Seidel argues for the essential continuity of their art and outlook, tracing the emergence of Giovanni's manner directly out of his apprenticeship under his father and their joint labour on the Siena Cathedral pulpit.

The book's method is characteristic and worth noting for anyone using it: it eschews the conventional monographic apparatus (there is no chronological life-and-works survey), and it leans heavily on close reading of the surviving documents. From the Siena pulpit payment records, for instance, Seidel shows that Giovanni was the most highly paid sculptor on the project after Nicola himself, earning substantially more than any other assistant, Arnolfo di Cambio included, and he uses fiscal and property records to demonstrate the comparatively high social standing the two artists enjoyed (Giovanni's Siena house was appraised above those of Duccio or Segna di Bonaventura). He gives particular weight to the Pisani's confrontation with the Gothic art of France and with Roman antiquity. Reviewers in The Burlington Magazine, Speculum, and the Sculpture Journal received it as a landmark that sets a new standard for the study of Italian late-medieval sculpture, while noting that its problem-driven structure can be demanding for the non-specialist.

Among his other books is Dolce liberta: iconografia politica a Lucca (Venice: Marsilio, 2004; also issued in English), a study of the political iconography of Lucca, the very city whose Ghibelline fortunes Castruccio Castracani embodied, which reads the commune's visual self-representation as an instrument of civic ideology.

Significance and connections

Seidel's importance is twofold. As an institution-builder, he shaped the modern KHI and helped anchor German-language art history at the center of Italian medieval studies. As a scholar, he brought a rigorously documentary and iconographic method to bear on artists long treated through style alone, and his continuity thesis in Father and Son reframed the central narrative of Italian Gothic sculpture.

For the thread running through these biographies, the connections are direct. His lifelong subject, the Pisani, is the same tradition whose tomb-shrine legacy Anita Moskowitz traced from Nicola Pisano's Arca di San Domenico down to Giovanni di Balduccio in Milan; where Moskowitz argued for the autonomy of Italian Gothic sculpture against the French model, Seidel's doctoral and later work foregrounds precisely the Italian engagement with French Gothic, a productive counterpoint rather than a contradiction. And his Lucca iconography places him, unexpectedly, in the same civic and political world as the first figure in this series.

Selected bibliography

  • Doctoral dissertation (Basel, 1967) on central-Italian and north-French artistic relations in the thirteenth century
  • Die Kirchen von Siena (corpus project, co-directed with Peter A. Riedl)
  • Dolce liberta: iconografia politica a Lucca (Marsilio, Venice, 2004; English edition also published)
  • Father and Son: Nicola and Giovanni Pisano, 2 vols (Hirmer Verlag, Munich, 2012; ISBN 978-3-7774-5101-5)
  • Numerous studies on Simone Martini, Ambrogio Lorenzetti, Giovanni Pisano, and Luca Signorelli

Sensi, Mario

Assisi, 15 August 1939 - 25 May 2015

Don Mario Sensi was an Italian priest-historian and one of the most prolific scholars of medieval and early modern religious life in Umbria and the Marche, with a bibliography reaching some 387 titles by 2008. A doctor in both Theology and Philosophy, he was ordained for the Diocese of Foligno and served as parish priest of Colfiorito from 1963 for many years before becoming episcopal chancellor; at his death he was prior of the Chapter of Canons of Foligno Cathedral, a chaplain and Prelate of Honour of His Holiness, and professor emeritus at the Pontifical Lateran University in Rome. He also served as a consultor to the Congregation for the Causes of Saints and as a member of the Pontifical Committee of Historical Sciences.

Sensi's scholarship traced what the medievalist Attilio Bartoli Langeli described as a "climb" from Foligno up to Colfiorito and the Altopiano di Plestia, over the Apennine watershed into the Alta Valle del Chienti, and from there outward across the interior Marche to Camerino, San Ginesio, Macerata, and the Piceno — a geography he treated not as a border but as a corridor of shared religious and social culture. Within this Umbro-Marchigian frame, he became a leading authority on penitential and quasi-religious movements — the *bizzoche* (lay female penitents) and Franciscan tertiaries — publishing extensively on their transition into Observant Poor Clare communities, on hospital confraternities and *xenodochia*, and on the typology of Marchigian sanctuaries and rural devotions. His edited volume with Ettore Orsomando, Studi sull'ambiente naturale degli altipiani di Colfiorito (2002), reflects the same integration of local topography with religious history that runs through his life's work. A festschrift, Amicitiae Sensibus: Studi in onore di don Mario Sensi, filled an entire volume (XXXI-XXXIV, 2007-2011) of the Bollettino Storico della Città di Foligno.

For Angela of Foligno, Sensi's most consequential intervention concerns the identity of her scribe. In "Fra Berardo Arnolti, il 'frater scriptor' del Memoriale di Angela?" (1992), he proposed identifying the anonymous "Brother A." with the archivally-attested Franciscan Berardo Arnolti — a hypothesis he himself flagged as uncertain with the question mark in his own title. He was also, alongside Jacques Dalarun, among the historians who judged the evidence for dating Angela's conversion to 1285 too weak to be treated as securely established, contributing to the broader critical reassessment of the traditional Ferré chronology of her life. His identification of the "frater scriptor" engages directly with the text established, in the same year, in Giovanni Pozzi's critical edition of the Memoriale, Il libro dell'esperienza (1992), which remains the standard modern edition of Angela's book.

Shailor, Barbara A.

New Haven - active late 20th-21st century

Barbara Shailor was born in New Haven and studied at Hamden High School, Wilson College, and the University of Cincinnati, where she received her PhD in 1975. Her doctorate in Classical Philology gave her work a distinct profile among medievalists: she approached manuscripts primarily through palaeography and codicology, with close attention to script, physical construction, and textual transmission. In Visigothic manuscripts, where script, decoration, and pictorial cycles are inseparable, this training proved especially influential.

Shailor is a specialist in Latin manuscript studies, the transmission of classical texts in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, and women in classical antiquity and the Middle Ages.

She was a faculty member and administrator at Bucknell University from 1975 to 1996. During these years, alongside full-time teaching and leadership responsibilities, she carried out one of the most sustained scholarly projects in North American manuscript studies: the systematic cataloguing of Yale Beinecke Library's medieval and Renaissance manuscript holdings.

From 1970 to 1995, through summer research and sabbatical leaves in New Haven, she completed the three-volume Catalogue of Medieval and Renaissance Manuscripts in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. Published in 1984, 1987, and 1993 (Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies), the catalogue remains the standard starting point for work on these collections. Each entry combines physical description, provenance, textual identification, palaeographical analysis, and bibliography.

In 1988 she curated a Beinecke exhibition that generated The Medieval Book, first issued as an exhibition catalogue and then published by the University of Toronto Press in association with the Medieval Academy of America in 1991. The book's first part explains the physical making of medieval books from the shift away from papyrus scroll; the second part examines manuscript genres and their cultural settings.

Reprinted repeatedly and widely adopted in university teaching, including in Rare Book School contexts, The Medieval Book became one of the most used English-language introductions to the physical and cultural history of the medieval codex.

In parallel, Shailor developed major expertise in Latin palaeography and codicology of Visigothic manuscripts from tenth- and eleventh-century northern Spain, publishing extensively on Visigothic script and monastic book production.

This specialization connected directly with the Beatus tradition. In A Spanish Apocalypse: The Morgan Beatus Manuscript (1991), her codicological analysis complemented John Williams's iconographic study, demonstrating the productive intersection of technical manuscript scholarship and interpretive art history in the study of MS M.644.

In 1989 she co-directed with Robert G. Babcock an NEH Summer Seminar on palaeography and codicology, reinforcing her commitment to training researchers through direct work with primary materials.

Shailor served as Dean of Douglass College and Professor of Classics at Rutgers University from 1996 to 2001, then joined Yale in 2001 as Director of the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. In 2003 she became Yale's Deputy Provost for the Arts, a role she held until 2012, overseeing museums, performing-arts centers, and broader cultural programming.

After retiring from administration in 2012, she continued as Senior Research Scholar and Senior Lecturer in Classics, and as Co-PI of the Mellon-funded initiative on digitally enabled scholarship for Yale's medieval manuscripts. This work placed her at the intersection of long-standing object-based manuscript expertise and the digital humanities.

She retired from teaching in Spring 2020. Her honors and institutional roles include support from NEH, ACLS, the American Philosophical Society, and the National Science Foundation; election to the Comité International de Palaeographie Latine (2000); Fellowship of the Medieval Academy of America (2006); trusteeship at the Samuel H. Kress Foundation (from 2003); and election to the Grolier Club of New York.

The volume Medieval Manuscripts and their Provenance: Essays in Honour of Barbara A. Shailor (2024) reflects the central thread of her scholarly legacy: the reconstruction of manuscript histories through ownership marks, annotations, bindings, textual traditions, fragments, and archival evidence.

Shailor's contribution stands on three interconnected registers. As a palaeographer and codicologist, she produced one of the most rigorous institutional manuscript catalogues in North America. As a teacher and communicator, she authored a foundational introduction to the medieval codex. As an institution-builder, she shaped the Beinecke and Yale's arts infrastructure while helping open manuscript collections to global digital research communities.

Sharpe, Richard

17 February 1954 – 22 March 2020

Richard Sharpe was educated at St Peter's School, York, and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took a first-class degree in 1977. He began in Classics before moving toward the study of Anglo-Saxon, Norse, and Celtic, working under Simon Keynes and Michael Lapidge — a training that gave him, unusually among British medievalists of his generation, a genuinely comparative command of the historical cultures of early medieval England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales alike. His doctoral research was on Latin hagiography from Ireland, a subject that would remain at the centre of his work for the rest of his career.

Sharpe spent his working life at Oxford, eventually as Professor of Diplomatic and a Fellow of Wadham College. From 1981 to 1990 he assisted in the editing of the Dictionary of Medieval Latin from British Sources, and for three decades he was general editor of the Corpus of British Medieval Library Catalogues, the British Academy project that gathers, prints, and interprets the scattered documentary evidence for the ownership and organisation of books in the medieval British Isles. He delivered the Lyell Lectures on medieval libraries and book economies in 2018–19 and served as President of the Surtees Society from 2002 until his death.

His 1991 book Medieval Irish Saints' Lives: An Introduction to Vitae Sanctorum Hiberniae grew directly out of his doctoral work and remains the standard guide to that body of hagiography. A Handlist of the Latin Writers of Great Britain and Ireland before 1540 (1997) supplied the field with an indispensable reference tool of a kind previously lacking, and his edition and translation of Adomnan's Life of Columba (1995) reshaped scholarly understanding of the Latin culture of Iona. Throughout, his method combined first-hand palaeographical and codicological examination of manuscripts with a historian's scepticism toward inherited scholarly consensus.

That scepticism was applied directly to the Book of Armagh in "Palaeographical considerations in the study of the Patrician documents in the Book of Armagh," published in Scriptorium 36 (1982), together with companion studies of the same period on Patrick and the see of Armagh and on Armagh's relations with Rome. Reopening a question that had seemed settled since E. A. Lowe's attribution, in Codices Latini Antiquiores, of three contemporary hands to the manuscript, Sharpe argued for essential scribal unity: that the observable variation in the script was more plausibly the work of a single accomplished scribe writing in different registers than evidence of several distinct hands. The argument returned the debate to something closer to John Gwynn's original position, and it stands, alongside Lowe's and Bieler's, as one of the three positions any serious account of the manuscript's production must weigh.

Sharpe was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 2003, an Honorary Member of the Royal Irish Academy in 2018, and a Corresponding Fellow of the Medieval Academy of America in the year of his death. He died on 22 March 2020, aged sixty-six, remembered as one of the most exacting codicologists and textual historians of his generation, whose insistence on returning to primary evidence rather than received judgement — nowhere more consequentially than in the case of the Book of Armagh — set a standard the field has continued to measure itself against.

Simi Varanelli, Emma

Italian scholar, active late 20th-21st century

Emma Simi Varanelli is an Italian historian of medieval art whose work is especially associated with the study of late Duecento and early Trecento painting in central Italy. She is frequently cited in scholarship on Assisi, the Isaac cycle, and the formation of Giotto's early pictorial language.

Publicly available biographical data about Simi Varanelli's personal life and institutional trajectory are limited in comparison with the documentation available for many other twentieth-century art historians. For this reason, her profile is best reconstructed through her published scholarship and its reception in later historiography.

Her most widely cited contribution is the essay Dal Maestro d'Isacco a Giotto. Contributo alla storia della perspectiva communis medievale (1989), a study that links stylistic analysis to the intellectual history of medieval optics and perspective theory. The article has become a recurrent reference in debates on the so-called Isaac Master, on the relationship between Roman and Florentine currents at Assisi, and on the technical-intellectual foundations of early Trecento naturalism.

Methodologically, Simi Varanelli's work is valued for combining close visual reading with attention to the conceptual vocabulary of medieval image-making. Rather than isolating style from ideas, her approach treats pictorial innovation as part of a broader cultural field in which workshop practice, scholastic thought, and scientific curiosity interact.

In studies of Umbrian and central Italian painting around 1300, her scholarship is regularly cited alongside major contributions by Angiola Maria Romanini and Bruno Zanardi. Within that constellation, Simi Varanelli remains an important voice for understanding how questions of space, vision, and representation shaped the transition from Duecento modes to early Giottesque pictorial language.

Simonetti, Adele

active late 20th-early 21st century

Adele Simonetti is known to scholarship almost entirely through her work rather than through any public account of her life. The standard biographical data one would expect for such a profile, such as date and place of birth, education, academic appointments, and institutional affiliation, are not documented in reliable publicly accessible sources. This entry therefore presents her scholarly contribution and intellectual milieu rather than a conventional life-biography. Personal particulars have been deliberately left blank rather than filled with conjecture. If such details are needed, they should be sought in Italian academic directories, in the front matter of her own volumes, or through the institutions with which she has published.

A preliminary caution is necessary. The surname is common in Italian medieval and patristic studies, and Adele Simonetti should not be confused with Manlio Simonetti (1926-2017), the eminent historian of patristics and early Christian literature, nor with other scholars of the same name. Catalogue indices of Florentine medievalist publishers accordingly distinguish "Simonetti, A." from "Simonetti, M." and "Simonetti, R."

Simonetti is a philologist of medieval Latin, a practitioner of filologia mediolatina, the discipline devoted to the critical edition and study of Latin texts of the Middle Ages. Her published work situates her within the principal Italian institutional network for the field: the Florentine and central-Italian scholarly constellation around medieval Latin studies that developed in the later twentieth century. Her editions appeared under the imprint of Edizioni del Galluzzo at the Certosa del Galluzzo near Florence, the publishing house associated with the Societa Internazionale per lo Studio del Medioevo Latino (SISMEL) and the Fondazione Ezio Franceschini, and also in series of the Centro Italiano di Studi sull'Alto Medioevo (CISAM) at Spoleto.

This is the milieu shaped above all by Claudio Leonardi and his collaborators, whose ambition was to provide medieval Latin literature, and Italian hagiography in particular, with rigorous critical editions furnished with introduction, apparatus, and where appropriate facing Italian translation. Simonetti's work belongs squarely to that enterprise, and her name is attached to major series dedicated to editing medieval Latin texts. It was with Leonardi that the Capuchin philologist Giovanni Pozzi co-edited the anthology Scrittrici mistiche italiane (1988), a collaboration that situates Simonetti's editorial labour on Umilta da Faenza within the same broader project of recovering the Latin and vernacular textual record of medieval Italian women's religious writing.

Her particular specialism is hagiography and religious literature, and more specifically the textual dossier of Umilta da Faenza. Simonetti's scholarly identity is deeply bound to this medieval saint, whose Latin and vernacular remains she edited more completely than any predecessor. By editing both the hagiographic Lives written about Umilta and the sermons attributed to Umilta herself, she effectively became the modern custodian of the saint's literary record. Through the Umilta corpus, her contribution is chiefly measured. Her work exemplifies the strengths of her tradition: patient manuscript-based establishment of the text, careful reconstruction of textual transmission, and sober historical framing that does not smooth away evidentiary difficulty.

The foundation of Simonetti's reputation rests on three closely related publications, each concerning the writings of or about Umilta da Faenza and together constituting the critical basis on which serious modern study of the saint depends.

The first is I sermoni di Umilta da Faenza. Studio e edizione, published at Spoleto by CISAM in the series Biblioteca di "Medioevo Latino" (no. 14) in 1995 (xciv + 194 pages). The volume presents the Latin Sermones attributed to Umilta, preceded by a substantial study organized around the saint's identity (from Rosanese Negusanti to Umilta da Faenza), the character of the sermons and their Johannine spirituality, and manuscript transmission. A point of major importance is that the edition prints fifteen sermons, numbered Sermo I through Sermo XV, correcting the older and frequently repeated figure of nine sermons found in earlier reference literature and popular accounts.

The second is her edition of the hagiographic Lives, Le Vite di Umilta da Faenza. Agiografia trecentesca dal latino al volgare, published in the Per Verba series of the Fondazione Ezio Franceschini by Edizioni del Galluzzo in the later 1990s (dated 1997 in some catalogues and 1998 in others; citation should be checked against the book itself), LIV + 70 pages. Simonetti provides the first critical edition of the Latin redaction of the Vita, established from six manuscripts, together with a transcription of an independent vernacular redaction. Her framing is historically acute: she treats the two fourteenth-century redactions as independent witnesses, both attributed to Vallombrosan hagiographers, and places them within an early-fourteenth-century Vallombrosan project to model female sanctity in monastic and penitential terms, a minority current beside dominant mendicant hagiography.

The third, and most extensive, is the bilingual critical edition Sermones, issued under Umilta da Faenza (Humilitas) in the Edizione Nazionale dei Testi Mediolatini (Serie II, 6) by SISMEL - Edizioni del Galluzzo in 2005 (VIII + 553 pages). The volume was edited by Lea Montuschi, with the Latin critical edition by Adele Simonetti and Italian translation by Lea Montuschi and Luigi G. G. Ricci. The Latin text appears in a new critical edition with facing Italian translation and a set of critical essays on the corpus. Inclusion in the Edizione Nazionale marks the definitive scholarly status accorded to Umilta's sermons.

Simonetti's importance lies in transforming the study of Umilta da Faenza from devotional tradition and inadequate older printings into a properly critical enterprise. Before her editions, texts by and about Umilta were chiefly accessible through seventeenth- and eighteenth-century compilations and reference summaries. After her work, scholars gained critically established texts with reconstructed manuscript transmission and historically grounded framing. This kind of intervention is foundational, because it clarifies what the texts are and thereby enables further inquiry into spirituality, Latinity, women's preaching, and the relation between written remains and visual cult.

Her work is also significant for the broader history of medieval women's religious writing. By providing rigorous editions of a corpus of Latin sermons attributed to a thirteenth- and fourteenth-century woman, Simonetti supplied primary materials for one of the very few surviving female Latin preaching corpora of the period. Her distinction between independent Latin and vernacular redactions of the Vita, and her identification of their Vallombrosan authorship and purpose, also illuminated strategies by which a monastic order fashioned and promoted the sanctity of a foundress against prevailing mendicant models.

For researchers on manuscript culture, Trecento visual programs, and the relation of text and image, Simonetti's editions have direct practical utility. Her critical Latin Vita, established from six manuscripts, provides the dependable textual basis needed to test correlations with painted narrative cycles, including those associated with Beata Umilta. Where visual programs illustrate episodes of a saint's life, interpretive security depends on identifying the operative textual redaction. Simonetti's separation of independent Latin and vernacular versions is therefore a central analytical tool, not a merely philological detail.

Beyond Umilta specifically, her scholarship stands as a model of source-critical method for medieval studies more generally. The discipline of establishing a text from surviving witnesses, weighing relationships among them, and refusing assertions beyond documentary support is directly analogous to responsible work on script, decoration, localization, and iconography in manuscript and art history. For scholarship on the meeting of hagiographic text and image in the devotional culture of the Italian Middle Ages, Simonetti's editions are both a practical resource and an exemplary method.

Singer, Charles Joseph

London, 2 November 1876 - 10 June 1960

Charles Joseph Singer was a British physician, historian of science, and one of the founding figures of the academic discipline of the history of medicine. Over the course of a long career that bridged active medical practice and painstaking archival scholarship, he became the most internationally prominent English-speaking historian of science and technology of the first half of the twentieth century - a man whose work touched directly on medieval illuminated manuscripts, early anatomical texts, and the transmission of ancient knowledge.

Singer was born on 2 November 1876 in London, the son of the Reverend Simeon Singer, a Hebrew scholar of considerable distinction, and Charlotte Pyke. He was educated at the City of London School and then entered University College London in 1896 before winning a scholarship to Magdalen College, Oxford, where he read zoology and took his BA in 1900. Medicine was always his true aim, however, and he completed his clinical training at St. Mary's Hospital, qualifying in 1903. Almost immediately upon qualifying, he departed as medical officer on an expedition under Sir John Harrington to delimit the Abyssinian frontier with Sudan, spending nearly a year collecting biological specimens and studying medical cases in the field.

Singer's transformation from practicing physician to professional historian of medicine was set in motion in 1910, when browsing a second-hand bookshop he encountered a copy of Benjamin Marten's early eighteenth-century text on contagion and was captivated by the problem of how scientific ideas are transmitted across centuries. He began writing papers on medical history alongside his hospital work at the Dreadnought Hospital for Seamen and the Cancer Hospital, Brompton. In the spring of 1914, at the age of thirty-eight, he made the decisive and financially costly choice to give up consulting medicine entirely, accepting an invitation from Sir William Osler, then Regius Professor of Medicine at Oxford, to devote himself full-time to historical research. Singer and his wife Dorothy, largely at their own expense, established a history of science research room in the Radcliffe Camera at Oxford, installing a safe to hold manuscripts and opening it as a working space for researchers.

After serving in the Royal Army Medical Corps during the First World War, Singer returned to Oxford as Lecturer in the History of the Biological Sciences. When Osler died in 1919, the hopes of securing Singer an Oxford professorial chair died with him, and in 1920 he moved to University College London, where he was appointed Lecturer on the History of Medicine, a post which the University of London upgraded to an honorary professorship in 1930. He retired as Professor Emeritus in 1942. His international standing was extraordinary: he presided over the Third International Congress of the History of Medicine in 1922 and the Second International Congress of the History of Science and Technology in 1931. He lectured at Johns Hopkins and the University of Pennsylvania, and was visiting professor at the University of California in 1931-1932. He held Oxford doctorates in all three faculties - medicine, letters, and science - a distinction without parallel among British scholars of his generation.

Singer's bibliography spans an extraordinary range. His early collaboration with Dorothy on The Development of the Doctrine of Contagium Vivum, 1500-1750 (1913) established his method: close reading of primary sources, careful attention to manuscript transmission, and resistance to teleological narratives of progress. His two-volume edited collection Studies in the History and Method of Science (1917-1921) gathered the most important international scholarship of the era. A Short History of Anatomy from the Greeks to Harvey (1925, revised 1957) remains a foundational text. His edition and translation of A Prelude to Modern Science (1946), presenting the complete text of Vesalius's Tabulae anatomicae sex of 1538 with detailed analysis, was one of his crowning achievements.

Perhaps his most enduring monument is the monumental A History of Technology (five volumes, 1954-1958), which Singer co-edited and to which he contributed substantially, covering the full sweep of human technological history from prehistoric times through the Industrial Revolution. His From Magic to Science (1928), especially relevant to students of medieval intellectual history, examined the scientific content of illuminated manuscripts from the medieval period, particularly medical and natural-philosophic manuscripts, bringing textual scholarship into productive dialogue with art-historical analysis.

No account of Charles Singer's work can omit his wife, Dorothy Waley Singer (1882-1964), a scholar of Jewish history, Giordano Bruno, and manuscript cataloguing who was an equal intellectual partner throughout their shared life. She participated in virtually every major research project, sustained the correspondence networks that kept the Radcliffe Camera research room functioning during the war years, and produced her own substantial independent scholarship on Renaissance science and Hermeticism.

During the 1930s and 1940s, Singer's commitments extended well beyond the archive. He helped found the Society for the Protection of Science and Learning, the principal British organisation dedicated to rescuing Jewish and anti-fascist scholars fleeing Nazi persecution, and he and Dorothy personally sheltered and assisted many academic refugees. In 1956 he received the Osler Medal of Oxford University and shortly afterward the George Sarton Medal of the American Society for the History of Science - the two highest honours in his field. A Festschrift of ninety essays in his honour, Science, Medicine and History (1953), gathered contributions from leading historians of science on both sides of the Atlantic. Singer died on 10 June 1960, leaving behind a discipline he had done more than almost anyone else to establish as a rigorous and internationally recognized academic field.

Sinkević, Ida

active late 20th-21st century

Ida Sinkević is one of the world's leading specialists in late antique, Byzantine, and medieval art and architecture. A professor at Lafayette College in Pennsylvania, she is especially known for her monographic study of the Church of Saint Panteleimon at Nerezi, the monument founded by Alexios Angelos Komnenos in 1164.

Sinkević earned her Ph.D. in Art and Archaeology from Princeton University in 1994. Her dissertation was devoted entirely to the church at Nerezi and offered a systematic analysis of the monument's architecture, painting, and sculpture. Princeton, with its historic ties to classical and late antique studies and its proximity to the Index of Christian Art (now the Index of Medieval Art), provided an ideal environment for research that combined architectural history, pictorial iconography, and Byzantine aristocratic patronage. The choice of Nerezi as a dissertation topic was an ambitious one: although the monument had been discussed in the specialized literature, especially by Okunev in the 1920s and by André Grabar, it had never before received an exhaustive monographic treatment in English.

After completing her doctorate, Sinkević pursued her academic career at Lafayette College in Easton, Pennsylvania, where she holds the Arthur J. '55 and Barbara S. Rothkopf Professorship of Art History, a privately endowed chair recognizing the significance of her work. Within the liberal arts environment of Lafayette, she has developed a teaching program spanning an unusually broad chronological and geographical range: from Greek and Roman art to post-revolutionary Russian art, from early Christian architecture to medieval Serbian miniature painting.

From the outset, her research has been marked by an approach that integrates formal and stylistic analysis of monuments, the study of literary and liturgical sources, and close attention to patronage and strategies of self-representation. This method, indebted in part to Panofsky's iconological tradition while also drawing on the social history of art, is evident both in her monograph on Nerezi and in her subsequent articles.

Sinkević's seminal book is The Church of St. Panteleimon at Nerezi: Architecture, Programme, Patronage, published in 2000 by Ludwig Reichert in Wiesbaden. The 209-page volume, accompanied by 88 figures and 27 plates, systematically develops the themes of her doctoral dissertation: the analysis of the church's architecture in its typological context, the description and interpretation of the pictorial iconographic program, and, in a particularly original way, the reconstruction of the personality and motivations of the patron, Alexios Angelos Komnenos. In this book, and in the precursor article published in Gesta in 1996, Alexios Angelos Komnenos, a Patron without History?, Sinkević advanced the thesis that Alexios consciously adopted the surname Komnenos as a strategy of social legitimation, and that the church's iconographic program was aligned with theological positions independent of the imperial court of Manuel I.

Among her later contributions, the essay Western Chapels in Middle Byzantine Churches: Meaning and Significance, published in Starinar in 2002, stands out for its examination of the liturgical and compositional function of western chapels in Middle Byzantine churches, including the northwestern chapel at Nerezi. She has also published studies on Serbian royal mausoleums as sites of cultural identity construction for the Nemanjić dynasty, and on five-domed churches in Middle and Late Byzantine architecture.

In recent years, Sinkević has broadened her interests to include innovative technological applications in medieval art history. She collaborates with ZeuxisVR, a virtual reality project dedicated to the reconstruction and interpretation of historical monuments, where she serves as a senior researcher with expertise in Byzantine and medieval art. This work reflects a sustained commitment to widening access to medieval artistic heritage, especially monuments preserved in geographically remote locations such as Nerezi itself in North Macedonia.

Sinkević is also active as an editor of major collective volumes. Her most recent and significant editorial project is Type and Archetype in Late Antique and Byzantine Art and Architecture, published by Brill in 2023 and edited together with Jelena Bogdanović, Marina Mihaljević, and Čedomila Marinković. Bringing together papers first presented at the 23rd International Congress of Byzantine Studies in Belgrade in 2016, the volume addresses the problem of typology in late antique and Byzantine art, namely the relationship between model and archetype, across case studies ranging from early Christian architecture to late Palaiologan painting. The project confirms Sinkević's place among the leading contemporary scholars of Byzantine art and architecture working across the Anglo-American and Central European scholarly worlds.

Sirén, Osvald

Helsinki, April 6, 1879 – Stockholm, June 26, 1966

Osvald Sirén was one of the most important and versatile art historians of the twentieth century, a figure bridging the European tradition of connoisseurship and the new horizons of scientific Orientalism, and the author of a monumental body of work that uniquely encompasses both medieval and Renaissance Italian painting and Chinese art.

Born in Helsinki on April 6, 1879, into Finland's Swedish-speaking minority, Sirén grew up in a culturally vibrant environment open to the most advanced European intellectual currents. He completed his university studies in art history, training in the tradition of the connoisseurship method of Morelli and Berenson, which in those years dominated the discipline throughout Europe. From the outset, his scholarly work was deeply influenced by the formalist methods of Bernard Berenson, with whom he shared an interest in medieval Tuscan painters and Leonardo da Vinci, aiming to situate works within their historical context without making a priori aesthetic judgments.

In 1908, Sirén was appointed to the J.A. Berg Chair of Art History and Theory at the University of Stockholm, thus becoming the first professor of art history in Sweden, a distinction that attests both to his exceptionally early academic success and to the youth of the discipline as an independent university subject in the Nordic world. He held that chair until 1923, devoting himself with great systematic rigor to the study of medieval and Renaissance Italian painting. During this period, he produced fundamental contributions: in 1905, he proposed attributing a painting preserved at the Bandini Museum in Fiesole to the Florentine painter and illuminator Lorenzo Monaco, a proposal that ushered in a new era of studies on late Gothic Florentine art. He published studies on Giotto, on the early Tuscan and Pisan painters, and was among the first to attempt a systematic organization of the corpus of the Maestro di Tedice, the anonymous thirteenth-century Pisan painter whose stylistic identification Sirén proposed by grouping under that conventional name a coherent body of thirteenth-century works.

Sirén belongs to that extraordinary generation of art historians born between 1870 and 1890 who transformed the discipline: he corresponded with Lionello Venturi and shared with him an interest in medieval Tuscan painters and Leonardo. Like Venturi, Sirén was influenced by the aesthetic thought of Benedetto Croce, by Alois Riegl's Kunstwollen, the concept of "artistic will" as a key to interpreting style, and by Berenson's Kennerschaft. His intellectual circle also included Tancred Borenius and Onni Okkonen, other Finnish art historians working internationally with similar methodologies. He was also a member of the theosophical movement, of which he was among the first adherents in the Scandinavian region, and this spiritual sensitivity toward Eastern traditions likely paved the way for his subsequent turn to Chinese art.

After World War I, Sirén made the most surprising intellectual shift of his career: he gradually abandoned the history of Italian art to devote himself increasingly exclusively to Chinese art, a field that was virtually unexplored by Western historiography at the time. This change of course was not sudden: the scholarly method he had applied to Italian primitives, meticulous formal analysis, classification by hand, and the construction of attributive corpora, proved extraordinarily well suited to the study of a figurative tradition that was itself extremely rich and still largely unknown in the West. From 1928 to 1945, he served as Curator of Paintings and Sculptures at the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm, thus combining his research activities with a leading role in museum operations.

The fruits of Sirén's Orientalist period were of extraordinary magnitude. In 1924, he published The Walls and Gates of Peking, a documentary work on imperial Beijing. In 1926, Chinese Sculpture: Fifth to Fourteenth Centuries was published in five volumes, accompanied by an impressive collection of photographs. In 1929, he published A History of Early Chinese Painting, published by the Medici Society in London. In 1935, he published La scultura e la pittura cinesi in Italian for ISMEO in Rome. His magnum opus was Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles (1950-1958), a seven-volume work that compiled, updated, and systematized decades of research, becoming the indispensable reference text for anyone studying Chinese painting in the English-speaking world. He also taught courses on Chinese art at Harvard University, bringing his research to the heart of American academia.

In 1956, Sirén was awarded the Charles Lang Freer Medal, the most prestigious American honor in the field of Asian art studies, presented by the Smithsonian Institution, an award that cemented his status as the world's foremost authority in the field. He died in Stockholm on June 26, 1966, at the age of eighty-seven, leaving a bibliographic legacy of rare breadth and quality.

Osvald Sirén stands out for his dual excellence: very few art historians have achieved leading positions in two fields as diverse as medieval Italian painting and Chinese art. For scholars of Italian medieval art, his contributions to fourteenth-century studies, on Pisan painted crosses, the Maestro di Tedice, Lorenzo Monaco, and fourteenth-century Florentine frescoes, remain historiographical reference points that are still discussed and cited. For the world of East Asian studies, his monumental work on Chinese painting still retains irreplaceable documentary value today, the result of decades of travel, access to private and public collections, and a systematic application of Western connoisseurship to a visual tradition of extraordinary complexity.

Skaug, Erling Sigvard

15 December 1938 – 7 March 2022

Erling Sigvard Skaug was a Norwegian art conservator and art historian whose career bridged the practical work of conservation and the exacting discipline of connoisseurship in Italian medieval panel painting. He is principally remembered for his monumental and methodologically innovative research on punch marks in Tuscan art.

Skaug began his career at the National Gallery of Norway, and also worked as a conservator at the Norsk Folkemuseum and the Oldsakssamlingen. A decisive turning point came in November 1966 when, as an intern at the Istituto Centrale per il Restauro in Rome, he participated in restoration work following the catastrophic Florence flood, assisting efforts to treat paintings damaged by floodwaters from the Arno. His own account of the experience is characteristically modest: "I was a nobody, but I watched and I did everything I was asked to do. They had to get me a pair of boots because I had brought trainers or something like that… I never conceptualised myself as one of the great people who came to save things." The personal and professional impact of those weeks in Florence would leave a permanent mark on the entire arc of his subsequent scholarship.

From the 1960s onward, Skaug dedicated himself to the systematic study of punzoni — the small metal tools used by Florentine and Tuscan panel painters to impress decorative patterns into gold leaf grounds. Working in parallel with the art historian Mojmir Frinta, he began investigating the potential of studying these patterns quantitatively to draw connections between art pieces. The probability that a punch pattern is unique is very high, given that the limited technology of the period made exact reproduction virtually impossible; Skaug manually catalogued a very large number of punches, their exact measurements, the art pieces they are connected to, and the potential author or authors involved in their production. This work took him more than thirty years and remains not exhaustive of all panel paintings making use of punched decoration in the region. The fruit of these decades of field research was his landmark two-volume publication: Punch Marks from Giotto to Fra Angelico: Attribution, Chronology, and Workshop Relationships in Tuscan Panel Painting c.1330–1430 (Oslo: IIC-Nordic Group, 1993–1994), covering artists including Giotto, Bernardo Daddi, Taddeo Gaddi, Pietro Lorenzetti, Simone Martini, Orcagna, and Fra Angelico, among many others. The publication set an example for future work in its comprehensive presentation of the evidence regarding how the motif punch serves in art-historical analysis and how it is positioned within the wider range of decorative practices used at the time. This publication also formed the basis of his doctoral work: in 1995 he took the dr.philos. degree.

In 1997 Skaug was hired as professor of conservation at the University of Oslo, retiring in 2004. He was a guest scholar at the Harvard Center for Italian Renaissance Studies (Villa I Tatti, Florence) in 2008–09, and was a Fellow of the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters. In 2006 he was awarded the title Cavaliere dell'Ordine della Stella d'Italia by the Italian government for his work to save Italian cultural heritage after the 1966 flood — a distinction that closed the circle between that early formative experience and a lifetime of service to Italian art.

Beyond his punch-mark corpus, Skaug also explored the historical figure of Giotto in broader cultural context, publishing Giotto and the Flood of Florence in 1333, a study proposing that Giotto's appointment in 1334 as architect of the Cathedral of Florence may be understood in relation to the disastrous flood of 4 November 1333 — the worst catastrophe of its kind until 1966 — and that this angle of approach enables a new interpretation of several connected elements of Florentine art history of that moment. In his final years he also turned his attention to Norwegian cultural politics, publishing the polemical book Spillet om Nasjonalgalleriet. En politisk skandale (2018), in which he criticised the process of discontinuing the National Gallery of Norway and moving its collections to the National Museum of Norway.

Skaug's punch-mark research has continued to generate scholarly and scientific interest well after his death. His catalogues now underpin computational approaches to attribution, with machine-learning researchers using his corpus as training and reference data for automated punch recognition in digitised works. He remains one of the most original methodologists in the history of medieval art studies — a Norwegian scholar who, across six decades, made the gold grounds of Tuscan altarpieces yield their secrets with rigour, patience, and a craftsman's eye.

Skerl Del Conte, Serena

active late 20th century

Italian art historian based in Trieste, specializing in Tuscan Trecento painting and, in particular, the diffusion of the styles of Taddeo Gaddi, Antonio Veneziano, and Spinello Aretino beyond Florence in the second half of the fourteenth century. Her monograph Antonio Veneziano e Taddeo Gaddi nella Toscana della seconda metà del Trecento (Campanotto) traces the reach of the Gaddi workshop's manner through the careers of painters who absorbed and transmitted it, and her essay on the shared bottega of Agnolo Gaddi and Spinello Aretino, published in the journal Arte in Friuli, arte a Trieste, extends the same method — the tracing of workshop filiation across regional boundaries — to the following generation.

In a 1996 article in Critica d'Arte, Skerl Del Conte proposed to extend this line of enquiry to Siena, arguing that certain strongly Gaddesque passages in the decoration of the vault and western wall of the Cappellone degli Spagnoli in Santa Maria Novella, Florence — the chapter house frescoed in its final campaign by Andrea di Bonaiuto between about 1365 and 1368 — belonged to an earlier phase of work, datable to around 1355–1365, and were the work of the Sienese painter Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio. The proposal, reported neutrally by the Treccani Dizionario Biografico as a recent addition to Jacopo's catalogue rather than an accepted attribution, is characteristic of Skerl Del Conte's broader project of tracking the Gaddesque idiom as it moved between workshops and cities in the decades after the Black Death.

Smith, Allyson

active early 21st century

Allyson Smith is a conservator and conservation scientist associated with Trinity College Dublin's early Irish manuscripts project of the 2010s. With Susie Bioletti, she carried out non-destructive pigment analysis of the Book of Dimma and related pocket gospel books, published as "Shining a Light on the Pigments of Early Irish Manuscripts" in An Insular Odyssey: Manuscript Culture in Early Christian Ireland and Beyond (2017).

Their analysis overturned the long-held assumption that the intense blue found in these manuscripts derived from imported lapis lazuli, showing instead that the illuminators achieved a comparable visual effect using an indigo blue mixed with gypsum, and more generally relied on local materials used with expertise rather than costly imports — a finding that substantially revised the understanding of materials, trade and technical skill in early Irish scriptoria.

Solberg, Gail E.

active late 20th–21st century

American art historian resident in Florence, and one of the leading modern authorities on Sienese painting of the early Quattrocento. Solberg holds degrees in history and art history from Stanford University and completed her doctorate at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University, in 1991 with a dissertation, written under John Pope-Hennessy, titled Taddeo di Bartolo: His Life and Work. She has spent much of her subsequent career expanding and refining that research, publishing extensively on Taddeo di Bartolo's documented commissions, workshop practice, and place within the network of painters who carried the Sienese Trecento tradition into the fifteenth century; this work culminated in the monograph Taddeo di Bartolo: Siena's Painter in the Early Quattrocento (Harvey Miller, 2025), praised for its meticulous documentation, detailed chronology, and comprehensive bibliography.

Solberg has also contributed to the conservation and cataloguing of Sienese Trecento panels outside the Taddeo di Bartolo corpus, including the scheda for the Madonna 'Belverde' in the Restituzioni conservation campaign of 2018, in which technical examination and archival research together established that the panel — long attributed on documentary grounds to Jacopo di Mino del Pellicciaio — is in fact a work of Taddeo di Bartolo of around 1405, made after Jacopo's death had left an earlier commission unfulfilled. Her explicit characterization of Jacopo as Taddeo's master, advanced in that scheda, gives documentary and technical weight to a relationship the field had previously inferred chiefly from style.

Sophocleous, Sophocles

Nicosia, active late 20th–21st century

Sophocles Sophocleous was born and educated in Lefkosia (Nicosia). He studied at the University of Human Sciences of Strasbourg and at Paris-X-Nanterre, and at ICCROM in Rome — the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property, which provided him with rigorous grounding in the theory and practice of conservation. He obtained his Doctorat, Sciences de l'Antiquité at the University of Human Sciences of Strasbourg in 1990, with a thesis on the heritage of icons in the Diocese of Limassol, Cyprus, from the 12th to the 16th century, written in French under the title Le Patrimoine des icônes dans le diocèse de Limassol, Chypre, 12–16e siècle.
