His research areas span Classical, Byzantine, and post-Byzantine art and archaeology, European and Middle Eastern art history, cultural heritage, religious and mythological imagery, iconographic analysis, the history of aesthetics, the theory and practice of conservation and restoration, and museology.

The foundation of Sophocleous's fieldwork lies in a sustained, systematic survey of Cyprus's ecclesiastical heritage. He worked at the Bishopric of Limassol for five years, recording the Byzantine and post-Byzantine heritage of more than 100 communities and municipalities of the district of Limassol and in various monasteries of the area, before appointment as District Archaeological Officer at Paphos within the Department of Antiquities of Cyprus. This dual experience — diocesan survey and state archaeological service — gave Sophocleous an unusually comprehensive grasp of Cyprus's dispersed and fragile sacred heritage, spanning churches, monasteries, and rural chapels often overlooked by institutional scholarship.

In 1991 he created, and has since directed, the Centre of Cultural Heritage in Nicosia, which has become the primary instrument through which he has pursued a threefold mission of research, conservation, and public education. The conservation atelier focuses on icons, murals, and archaeological finds; the educational department organises special programmes for children involving visits to churches and monasteries; and the museum of the Byzantine Heritage of Palaichori, inaugurated on 11 January 1998, showcases ecclesiastical art from Frankish rule to the present, reflecting social and economic life in a rural Cypriot community. He was Invited Professor (Directeur d'Études Invité) at the École Pratique des Hautes Études, Sorbonne, Paris (1996–1998), and Professor of Art History, Archaeology and Cultural Heritage at the University of Nicosia (2005–2011).

Sophocleous's most significant book-length contribution is his Icons of Cyprus: 7th–20th Century (Nicosia, 1994), a pioneering work intended for both the expert and the layman that investigates the history of Byzantine painting in one of the most fascinating provinces of the Byzantine Empire. Byzantine province, Crusader kingdom, and Venetian stronghold in the Eastern Mediterranean, Cyprus continued its Byzantine artistic traditions under Ottoman and British rule and renewed them in the modern Byzantine painting of the twentieth century. The volume presents for the first time a panorama of 116 icons from the seventh to the twentieth century and three iconostases of the sixteenth century, as well as three mural mosaics and six mural paintings from the sixth to the eleventh century. A complementary volume, Icons of Cyprus: Diocese of Limassol, 12th–16th Century (Nicosia, 2006), developed from his doctoral research into a comprehensive catalogue of a regionally specific corpus.

His published exhibition catalogue contributions include "L'évolution de la peinture chypriote durant la période franque et vénitienne" in La France aux portes de l'Orient: Chypre XIIe–XVe siècle (Paris, 1991) and "L'art des icônes byzantines et post-byzantines à Chypre" in À l'image de Dieu: Icônes byzantines de Chypre du 12e siècle à nos jours (Mulhouse/Strasbourg, 1994). At the 25th Spring Symposium of Byzantine Studies (Birmingham, 1991), he presented recently discovered medieval Cypriot icons from his diocesan surveys — 235 icons from the twelfth to the sixteenth century — exploring the implications of Western influences in Cypriot iconography and the interconnections between Byzantine and Crusader art. His paper "Cypriot icons before the 12th century: A critical reconsideration" (Nicosia, 2011) argued for the necessity of more rigorous scientific analyses to overcome the sparse data and aesthetic subjectivity on which pre-iconoclastic dating had previously relied.

In 2011 the French Republic honoured him with the distinction of Chevalier de l'Ordre des Arts et Lettres, and in 2012 he was honoured by the Cyprus Green Party with the Prize of Architectural Heritage in memory of Neoptolemos Michaïlidis.

Sordini, Giuseppe

Spoleto, 6 September 1853 - Spoleto, 8 June 1914

Italian archaeologist, art critic, and heritage official - self-taught, uncompromising, and the man who effectively excavated the Spoleto we see today. A lawyer by degree, he became Ispettore ai monumenti e agli scavi by public competition, served briefly and unhappily as mayor of his own city, and spent nearly two decades recovering, defending, and documenting its Roman and medieval fabric. For medievalists his importance lies in the restoration of Sant'Eufemia, his documentary study of the Duomo of Spoleto, and his archival work on Umbrian painters, above all the Sparapane of Norcia.

Sordini was born at Spoleto on 6 September 1853, the son of Oreste Sordini. He attended the city's classical liceo Pontano-Sansi and took a degree in law, studying at the universities of Perugia and Rome. He then worked as a tutor (precettore) for the Marignoli family in Rome.

Archaeology, however, was the real vocation, and he pursued it as an autodidact, extending his study to the history of art and architecture. His self-education was thorough enough to win him a public competition at the Ministry of Public Instruction, Divisione Antichità e Belle Arti. This is the essential fact about him: he had no formal training in the discipline he came to command, and he acquired his authority entirely by work.

The Ministry sent him to Palermo in 1888 as Ispettore ai monumenti e agli scavi. In 1890 he obtained a transfer to Florence. Only in 1896 did he return definitively to Spoleto, where he carried out the great bulk of his research, protection, and interpretation of the city's archaeological and artistic heritage, exercising what his biographers describe as a tenacious guardianship over every monument in it.

His archive - some seventy buste now in the Sezione di Archivio di Stato di Spoleto - contains his inspectorate papers, personal documents, a collection of early charters and parchments, epigraphic casts, prints, drawings, and correspondence. The names in that correspondence indicate his standing: Theodor Mommsen, Wilhelm Henzen, Eugen Bormann, Wolfgang Helbig, Paul Fridolin Kehr, Thomas Ashby, Luigi Pigorini, Corrado Ricci, Cesare Bazzani, Ugo Ojetti, Lionello Venturi. A provincial inspector with no university chair was corresponding with the leading epigraphers and archaeologists of Europe.

Elected town councillor on his return in 1896, and a member of the Commissione per l'ornato pubblico, he resigned from both - and from the various bodies and associations to which he belonged - over disagreements about the lighting of the Teatro Nuovo and, more revealingly, over the demolition of a medieval arch in via Cecili. He would not compromise with his own civic conscience, and the pattern repeated: appointed mayor of Spoleto in September 1902, he lasted seven months before the whole giunta resigned over political disputes. As mayor he planned the Piazza della Signoria, its gardens, and the panoramic terrace - a scheme realized only in the late 1920s, after the expropriations went through.

He succeeded Achille Sansi as director of the Accademia Spoletina. His contribution to the founding of the city's Pinacoteca and Museo Civico was decisive: housed in the so-called Palazzo della Signoria, the museum was inaugurated in 1910 but assembled by him slowly from 1903 until his death.

Working from old books and documents and then digging, Sordini recovered a series of major sites. He identified the Roman theatre - locating it from a drawing by Baldassarre Peruzzi - and published on its remains in Notizie degli Scavi (1891). He discovered the Casa Romana near the Palazzo Comunale in 1885 and worked on it until his death; the Ponte Sanguinario; the building in via della Sinagoga; and the Lex Spoletina. He reported a polygonal wall found at Spoleto in the Mitteilungen of the German Archaeological Institute in 1886.

He founded and directed periodicals of archaeological and art-historical character - among them La Nuova Umbria - and published in Notizie degli Scavi (the organ of the Accademia dei Lincei), the Bollettino d'Arte, and the Bollettino dell'Istituto Archeologico Germanico. His output ran to more than fifty essays.

Three strands matter most for the study of medieval art.

Sant'Eufemia. The Romanesque church within the courtyard of the Archbishop's Palace had been disfigured from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries onward: divided horizontally into two storeys, the ground floor left for worship while the upper level - at the height of the galleries - was absorbed into the episcopal palace, the facade plastered over, the bell-cote demolished. In 1907, on Sordini's initiative, the complete restoration of the building was undertaken; it was carried through, in a campaign concluded only in 1954 by the Soprintendenza umbra, with the adjoining parts of the Palazzo Vescovile demolished. The result restored to view the only church in Umbria with high matronei - a building of Lombard-inflected Romanesque whose closest comparison is San Lorenzo in Verona, and whose recovery is the foundation of all subsequent discussion of Spoletan Romanesque. Mario Salmi's Sant'Eufemia di Spoleto (Spoletium, 1954) belongs to the conclusion of that story.

A caution worth recording: the church's original high altar was accidentally destroyed during the early twentieth-century restoration, and the marble frontal now in place came from the high altar of the Duomo. The restoration recovered a great monument and lost something in the process - a point to state plainly rather than smooth over.

The Duomo. Il duomo di Spoleto: delle origini, secondo i documenti (Spoleto: Panetto & Petrelli, 1908) is a short but exacting piece of documentary archaeology. Working from the cathedral's capitular archive - the Lezionari, the Vita of St John of Spoleto commissioned by the abbess Berta from John of Montecassino, the diploma of Henry II - Sordini established where the primitive episcopio actually stood and demolished the tradition, repeated by Bernardino di Campello and other late writers, that the tribune of S. Primiano had formed part of a ducal chapel or basilica. His verdict on that tradition was characteristically blunt: an unsupported amplification, of a kind produced in ages that thought monuments, families, and cities were honoured by resounding but gratuitous claims. He also published Di alcuni lavori nel Duomo di Spoleto eseguiti dal 6 gennaio 1904 a tutto l'agosto 1905, and a paper on the trifora in the facade of S. Gregorio in Spoleto (Bollettino d'Arte, 1908).

Painting and documents. Gli Sparapane da Norcia. Nuovi dipinti e nuovi documenti (Bollettino d'Arte, 1910) added both works and archival evidence to the corpus of that Nursine workshop. He also brought to light the Madonna col Bambino by Giovanni di Pietro, lo Spagna, in the church of Sant'Ansano at Spoleto, and published on a diploma and a fresco in the archiepiscopal palace (1890), on the tomb of Gabriello Garofoli (1895), on an underground Christian cemetery in Umbria (read at the international congress of Christian archaeology, Rome 1900), and on the oldest church and crypt of San Benedetto at Norcia (1913).

An untreated stomach ulcer turned bad; an operation attempted in extremis failed to save him. He died at Spoleto on 8 June 1914, aged sixty. He is buried in the city's Cimitero Monumentale, and a plaque placed by the Accademia Spoletina - of which he had been president - marks the house he inherited from an uncle he had cared for. A piazza in Spoleto bears his name, as does an annual schools competition on the city's heritage, now in its third decade.

His archive was the subject of a round table at the Archivio di Stato in 1993 and an accompanying exhibition, Giuseppe Sordini: luoghi e documenti di un archeologo spoletino.

Sotirakoglou, Christina

active 2024

Christina Sotirakoglou works as a court consultant based in Thessaloniki, specialising in the identification and authentication of handwriting in criminal cases. Her primary professional domain is forensic document examination — the discipline used in criminal investigations to match anonymous writings to known authors, verify signatures, and authenticate disputed texts. It is precisely this forensic expertise, applied with rigorous methodology to a medieval manuscript, that brought her into the field of Byzantine art history in 2024.

The investigation built upon prior research by Father Cosmas Simonopetritis, a Greek monk, linguist, and former senior administrator at Mount Athos. The trail started with earlier research linking the painter conventionally known as Manuel Panselinos — a name meaning "full moon" in Greek, long celebrated as one of the supreme masters of the Macedonian School of Byzantine painting and a contemporary of Giotto — with the artist and scholar who wrote and illustrated the Marcian Codex GR 516, an early fourteenth-century Greek handwritten text treating subjects from astronomy to music theory, among whose painted illustrations was a depiction of a full moon. Father Cosmas identified this image as a signature clue to the painter's identity and concluded that the name "Panselinos" was a nickname — "full moon" — eventually applied to the painter Ioannis Astrapas of Thessaloniki. With a name found for the hand that produced the manuscript, the next step was to check its script against the painted inscriptions on the Protaton frescoes, traditionally linked with "Panselinos." Father Cosmas turned to Sotirakoglou to undertake that comparison.

Since women have been banned from entering Mount Athos for more than a thousand years, Sotirakoglou was compelled to conduct her analysis from high-resolution photographic documentation of the inscriptions on the frescoes — a significant methodological constraint that she nonetheless managed to turn into a productive approach. The investigation cross-referenced the handwriting of the Marcian Codex GR 516 with inscriptions on the Protaton frescoes. Sotirakoglou identified distinctive similarities in the letterforms, particularly the Greek Phi (Φ), T, and K. "When the unique Phi was identified, it unlocked the code of the writing, making further matches much easier," she stated. This approach — applying forensic graphology to the painted inscriptions within a Byzantine church interior — represents a genuinely novel methodological crossover between criminal document examination and medieval art history, extending the evidentiary standard of forensic science into a domain where attribution had previously relied on stylistic analysis alone.

Father Cosmas Simonopetritis stated that the research "clearly proves" Panselinos's real identity: "Panselinos was a real person, and the name was just the nickname by which Ioannis Astrapas became known." The response from the wider scholarly community has been cautiously positive but not unconditional. Constantinos Vafiadis, a professor of Byzantine art in Athens not involved in the studies, found merit in the nickname theory and the Astrapas link, while noting that more than one painter appears to have undertaken the Protaton project: "I agree with attributing part of the paintings to Ioannis Astrapas." The qualification is significant — the Protaton church at Karyes is a large and complex decorative programme, and the possibility of workshop participation by multiple hands complicates any single attribution.

Sotirakoglou's contribution exemplifies a growing trend in medieval art history: the application of forensic and scientific methods — spectroscopic analysis, radiocarbon dating, digital imaging, and now graphological comparison — to problems that traditional connoisseurship and document study alone have been unable to resolve. Her work on the Panselinos question is particularly consequential given the painter's canonical status: the frescoes of the Protaton church have been described as among the most important achievements of late Byzantine art and were included in the UNESCO World Heritage inscription of the Mount Athos monastic community in 1988. The research was brought to wide international attention in December 2024 through an Associated Press report, prompting renewed interest in the question of artistic identity in the Byzantine world — a field where, because of the deeply collective and anonymous character of medieval workshop practice, individual painters remain extraordinarily difficult to identify.

Sotiropoulou, Sophia

active late 20th–21st century

Sophia Sotiropoulou is a physicist, graduating from the University of Athens in 1991, with postgraduate studies in Physical Methods in Archaeology and Museography at the University of Bordeaux in 1993, and a PhD in Chemical Engineering at the National Technical University of Athens in 2000, with a thesis addressing the optimisation of colour measurements in paintings using non-destructive techniques — a subject that defined the methodological axis of her entire subsequent career. The trajectory from physics through archaeometry to chemical engineering reflects the genuinely interdisciplinary formation required for the field she would help build: one in which the physics of light interaction, the chemistry of pigments and binders, and the historical understanding of artistic traditions must all be held in simultaneous focus.

From 1993 to 1996 she was Research Associate at the National Centre for Scientific Research "Demokritos," Institute of Materials Science, Laboratory of Archaeometry. From 1996 to 2017 she served as Senior Researcher at the "Ormylia" Foundation — Art Diagnosis Centre, the institution she helped to found and define alongside Sister Daniilia. Since 2018 she has been Senior Research Associate at the Foundation for Research and Technology–Hellas, Institute of Electronic Structure and Laser (FORTH-IESL), Heraklion, Crete, where she works within the Photonics for Heritage Science (PhoHS) team, developing laser-based methods — including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), laser-induced fluorescence, and coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy — for the analysis, diagnosis, preservation, and restoration of archaeological and historical objects. From 2010 she has also served as Assistant Module Coordinator at the Hellenic Open University, School of Applied Arts, for the Master's course in Lighting Design.

Sotiropoulou and Sister Daniilia formed the core intellectual partnership of the Ormylia Art Diagnosis Centre from its inception. Their collaboration produced the foundational publications that established the scientific study of Byzantine iconography as a coherent, internationally recognised research field. In the landmark 2000 paper on the Protaton frescoes, published in the Journal of Cultural Heritage, they co-authored the first systematic technical examination of the Panselinos wall paintings at the Protaton Church on Mount Athos — establishing the mixed al fresco/al secco technique of the Palaiologan workshop and determining egg and animal glue as the binding media, a paper that remained for many years the primary scientific reference for the most important Byzantine fresco cycle accessible to scholarly investigation. In the 2010 review published in Accounts of Chemical Research — the first such review to appear in one of the flagship journals of the American Chemical Society — Sotiropoulou is the corresponding author and Sister Daniilia the co-author, surveying the state of the field across more than a decade of collaborative work.

Sotiropoulou's distinctive contribution lies in the development and optimisation of methodological frameworks that can be deployed across radically different object types and historical periods while maintaining the non-invasive or minimally invasive constraint essential when studying objects of active religious use. Her arsenal includes micro-Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared imaging (FTIR and μFTIR), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (FORS), SEM-EDS, and high-performance liquid chromatography with diode array detection (HPLC-DAD). A recurring theme is the integration of in-situ non-invasive methods with laboratory micro-analysis, allowing first-pass characterisation in the field to guide the selection of the very small number of samples that may, where strictly necessary, be removed for more detailed laboratory investigation.

Her 2008 paper "Microanalytical investigation of degradation issues in Byzantine wall paintings," published in Applied Physics A with Sister Daniilia, Miliani, Rosi, Cartechini, and Papanikola-Bakirtzis, studied the St. Euthymios wall paintings in the Cathedral of Thessaloniki (dated 1303 AD, stylistically attributed to the School of Panselinos) within the Eu-ARTECH MOLAB project, combining in-situ XRF, mid-FTIR, and UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy with μFTIR, SEM-EDS, and μRaman on micro-samples. The identification of degradation products — in particular the alteration of minium (lead tetroxide) to plattnerite (lead dioxide), which produces a characteristic darkening — carries direct implications for conservation treatment decisions. Among the highest-profile applications of the Ormylia Centre's programme is the scientific study of El Greco's Baptism of Christ, co-authored by Sister Daniilia, Andrikopoulos, Sotiropoulou, and Karapanagiotis: "Analytical Study into El Greco's Baptism of Christ: Clues to the Genius of His Palette," Applied Physics A 90(3) (2008). The study identified the distinctive combination of Byzantine egg tempera with Venetian-inspired oil glazing in a single panel, providing the first scientific mapping of the transition between El Greco's Cretan Byzantine formation and his Venetian period, visible in the very stratigraphy of a single painting.

A significant strand of Sotiropoulou's research extends far beyond the Byzantine period into the Prehistoric Aegean. Her paper "Review and New Evidence on the Molluscan Purple Pigment Used in the Early Late Bronze Age Aegean Wall Paintings," published in Heritage (2021), investigated an assemblage of approximately 500 colouring materials and related objects from different contexts at Akrotiri, Thera, dating to the Early, Middle, and Late Cycladic Bronze Age (c. 3000–1600 BC). The identification of Tyrian purple — the prestigious dye extracted from Hexaplex trunculus and related molluscs — in the wall paintings of the Bronze Age Aegean, achieved through a comprehensive methodology combining micro-Raman, FTIR spectroscopies, and HPLC-DAD, connects the biochemistry of ancient pigment production with the archaeology of Cycladic civilisation. Her 2018 paper "Advanced analytical investigation on degradation markers in wall paintings," published in Microchemical Journal, co-authored with researchers from the University of Bologna, the Getty Conservation Institute, the University of Pisa, and CNR in Perugia, represents the large-scale international consortium research that characterises the mature phase of her career: moving from the case-study-driven investigation of individual monuments to the systematic characterisation of the chemical mechanisms by which wall painting materials age and decay across different traditions, climatic zones, and historical periods.

Sophia Sotiropoulou occupies a central position in the generation of Greek heritage scientists who transformed the study of Byzantine art from a discipline dependent entirely on stylistic connoisseurship and historical documentation into one in which chemistry, physics, and optics contribute structurally to understanding, attribution, and conservation. Her two-decade partnership with Sister Daniilia at the Ormylia Art Diagnosis Centre produced the foundational literature of the field. Her subsequent work at FORTH-IESL has extended the reach of those methods across a much wider chronological and geographical range, from the Bronze Age Aegean to the Ottoman-period monasteries of northern Greece. She is, in the fullest sense, a co-founder of the scientific study of Byzantine iconography as an internationally recognised discipline.

Spilner, Paula

active late 20th–21st century

Paula Spilner is an American art and architectural historian whose scholarship has been centred on the built environment of late medieval Florence. Her work sits at the intersection of urban history, architectural analysis, and archival research — an approach that draws on legal and administrative documents to reconstruct the physical transformation of a city during one of the most consequential centuries of its existence.

Spilner completed her doctoral dissertation at Columbia University in 1987 under the title 'Ut Civitas Amplietur': Studies in Florentine Urban Development, 1282–1400 — a work whose Latin title, taken from a communal provision of the period, translates as "so that the city may be enlarged." The phrase encapsulates her central concern: the deliberate, politically directed expansion of Florence as a physical and institutional project, pursued by the republican commune from the foundation of the Priorate of the Guilds to the close of the Trecento.

The dissertation provides a descriptive and analytical account of major aspects of urban development and planning in Florence from the foundation of the republic under the Priorate of the Guilds in 1282 to the end of the fourteenth century, utilizing a wide range of archival sources, many hitherto unstudied, to illuminate both civic and private contributions to urban form. Its scope is systematically conceived, covering: the legal and administrative aspects of planning; the construction of new fortifications; the evolution of the street network; the development of new residential districts by ecclesiastical institutions; and the evolution of the Piazza della Signoria.

Chapter I summarizes what is known about the topography of the city in about 1280. Chapter II focuses on legal and administrative aspects of planning and public works under the republic: the legislative process and powers of expropriation; the extensive planning responsibilities vested in the Six in Charge of Rights in the late thirteenth century and the evolution of this office in the fourteenth century; the duties of the city surveyors' office and the role technical experts played in planning. This is, in essence, a document-based anatomy of how a medieval commune organized, legislated, and administered its own growth — a subject that touches on the legal history of property, the politics of public space, and the administrative machinery through which architectural ambition was translated into stone.

Spilner's most widely cited published contribution is her 1993 article in the Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians: "Giovanni di Lapo Ghini and a Magnificent New Addition to the Palazzo Vecchio, Florence." In a previously unnoticed provision of 1371, the Signoria and Councils of Florence approved a plan to construct an addition to the Palace of the Priors, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio. The article analyzes the main features of the provision, including financing for the project, selection of a building committee, and appointment of the architect Giovanni di Lapo Ghini as superintendent of the work.

The conceptual centre of the article reaches beyond the building itself. The implications of the term "magnificence" used in the provision to justify the project are examined in the context of the contemporary understanding of Aristotle's theory of magnificence. The word magnificenza, deployed in a practical communal document, connects the civic building programme to the Aristotelian tradition of the Nicomachean Ethics, in which magnificent expenditure on public works is identified as a political virtue befitting those who govern a great city. Spilner's reading thus situates a piece of Florentine administrative prose within the broader intellectual culture of Trecento civic humanism. Her conclusion, following a review of an earlier addition proposed by the Duke of Athens in 1343, is that very little of that duke's project had been realized, and that the provision of 1371 effectively revived and recast the earlier idea.

A further dimension of her scholarship concerns the evolution of the Piazza della Signoria as a civic space — treated in the doctoral dissertation and cited repeatedly by later scholars as a foundational reference. Her archival reconstruction of the Trecento development of the Piazza — tracing the sequence of expropriations, demolitions, paving decisions, and competing architectural ambitions that shaped the space — has become a standard point of departure in subsequent studies of Florentine urban form and civic imagery. The detail she identified — that the delay between the granting of planning permission and its actual execution coincided with a reassertion of the Signoria's political authority — is characteristic of her method: a small archival finding that carries a large interpretative charge, illuminating the relationship between political contingency and the built fabric of the city.

Spilner contributed to the entry on Florence in Grove Art Online, the standard scholarly reference work for the history of art published by Oxford University Press, consolidating her standing as a recognized specialist on the medieval and early Renaissance city.

Spilner's work belongs to a strand of scholarship on late medieval Florence — alongside that of Marvin Trachtenberg, Diane Finiello Zervas, Richard Trexler, and Nicolai Rubinstein — that treats the built environment not as a backdrop to cultural history but as its central object. Her particular contribution is the sustained archival investigation of the administrative and legal machinery of urban planning: how the commune decided to build, how it acquired land, how it hired architects, and how it formulated and justified its ambitions in the language of civic virtue. The doctoral dissertation, though unpublished as a book, has circulated widely in the scholarly literature on Trecento Florence and remains the most comprehensive archival study of Florentine urban development in the period it covers. Its influence is traceable in a generation of subsequent work on medieval Italian urbanism, the Piazza della Signoria, and the civic architecture of the Palazzo Vecchio.

Steinhoff, Judith B.

active 20th–21st century

Judith B. Steinhoff is an American art historian, a professor of art history at the University of Houston, whose research has reframed the interpretation of Sienese painting in the decades following the plague of 1348. Her work challenges the older thesis that the Black Death produced a uniform retreat into a more hieratic and abstract mode of religious image-making, arguing instead that Sienese painting after 1348 exhibited a deliberate stylistic pluralism, in which patrons chose among coexisting registers according to the demands of function and commission rather than painters collectively regressing into archaism.

Steinhoff's article "Artistic Working Relationships after the Black Death: A Sienese Compagnia, c. 1350–1363(?)" (Renaissance Studies, 2000) and her monograph Sienese Painting after the Black Death: Artistic Pluralism, Politics, and the New Art Market (Cambridge University Press, 2006) proposed that a group of Sienese painters, including Bartolomeo Bulgarini, Niccolò di Ser Sozzo, and Luca di Tommè, operated after the plague as a loosely structured cooperative pooling resources, equipment, and commissions — a thesis that has substantially reshaped the interpretation of joint signatures, joint payments, and shared punch tools among Sienese Trecento painters.

Steinweg, Klara

Westphalia, 18 May 1903 - Meerbusch, 10 June 1972

Klara Steinweg was a German art historian specializing in Italian medieval and early Renaissance painting, best known for her decades-long collaboration with Richard Offner on the Critical and Historical Corpus of Florentine Painting - one of the most ambitious scholarly enterprises in the history of art historical studies. Although she worked largely in the shadow of her more celebrated partner, her contribution to the understanding of fourteenth-century Florentine painting was indispensable and lasting.

Steinweg was born on 18 May 1903 in Westphalia, Germany. The details of her early academic training are not fully documented in available sources, but her subsequent career demonstrates a thorough grounding in connoisseurship, archival methodology, and iconographic analysis. Like many German-trained art historians of her generation, she was shaped by the philological rigour that characterized the German Kunstwissenschaft tradition - a systematic, evidence-based approach to attributing and dating works of art.

The defining relationship of Steinweg's scholarly life was her partnership with Richard Offner (1889-1965), the American art historian whose A Critical and Historical Corpus of Florentine Painting aimed to catalogue and analyze, with exhaustive documentary precision, the entire body of Florentine painting from the twelfth century onwards. Steinweg became his primary collaborator from 1930 to 1965, contributing research, attribution analysis, and critical apparatus to multiple volumes. The project was published through the Institute of Fine Arts at New York University, and the volumes produced under their joint authorship covered pivotal figures of Trecento painting.

When Offner died in 1965, Steinweg assumed sole direction of the Corpus, continuing to produce volumes under the joint imprint of "Offner and Steinweg". Her contributions included landmark volumes on Jacopo di Cione (1965), Giovanni del Biondo (1967), and Niccolo di Pietro Gerini (1969). On attribution questions - such as the contested dating and authorship of major altarpieces by Orcagna and Jacopo di Cione - her positions were frequently cited and debated by subsequent scholars including Miklos Boskovits, Mirella Levi d'Ancona, and Carl Huter. Her final volume, on Andrea Bonaiuti, was published posthumously in 1979, seven years after her death.

Steinweg lived and worked in Florence for most of her adult life, immersing herself in the city whose artistic heritage she spent her career documenting. Her Florentine residence made her a central figure in the community of international art historians active in Italy during the mid-twentieth century. One of her research assistants in her final years was the young Patricia Rubin, who would go on to become a distinguished professor at the Institute of Fine Arts, NYU - a direct testimony to Steinweg's role as an informal teacher and mentor. She also had a significant influence on the formation of Miklos Boskovits, who made contact with her during his early career and who would later take over the direction of the Corpus after her death.

Steinweg's work was inseparable from the practice of photographic documentation that underpinned the Corpus. Her handwritten annotations on the backs of archival photographs - still preserved in the project's archives - record her first-hand observations of specific works, including notations made during direct inspection of paintings. This material evidence underlines how deeply her methodology depended on sustained, in-person confrontation with the objects of study, a practice central to the connoisseurship tradition she inherited from Offner.

Steinweg died on 10 June 1972, aged 69, in Meerbusch, in the Rhein-Kreis Neuss district of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany - apparently having returned to her homeland at the very end of her life after decades in Florence. After her death, the Corpus was continued under the direction of Miklos Boskovits and Mina Gregori, a continuation that acknowledged the structural foundations she had laid. The Corpus of Florentine Painting remains, to this day, the essential reference for the study of Trecento Florentine painting, and Steinweg's name - paired with Offner's on volume after volume - ensures her permanent place in the historiography of Italian medieval art.

Stokes, Whitley

Dublin, 28 February 1830 – London, 13 April 1909

Whitley Stokes was born in Dublin on 28 February 1830, the eldest son of the physician William Stokes and grandson of the physician Whitley Stokes the elder; both father and grandfather had held the chair of Regius Professor of Physic at Trinity College Dublin. His sister, Margaret Stokes, became a noted writer and archaeologist of early Christian Irish art, so that the study of Ireland's medieval heritage ran in both directions through the same household. Stokes was educated at St Columba's College, Dublin, where he began the study of Irish, and entered Trinity College Dublin in 1846, taking his BA in 1851; there he studied Sanskrit and comparative philology with Rudolf Thomas Siegfried, the teacher who set him on the course of Celtic scholarship he would pursue, in the margins of an entirely separate career, for the rest of his life.

Called to the bar at the Inner Temple in 1855, Stokes practised in London as an equity draughtsman and conveyancer, devoting his spare hours to philology. In 1862 he went to India as Secretary to the Legal Department, and he remained in Indian government service for twenty years, becoming Law Member of the Council of the Governor-General in 1877 and president of the commission on Indian law in 1879. He was responsible, in this capacity, for a substantial part of the codification of Anglo-Indian law. He retired and returned permanently to London in the early 1880s. He married Mary Bazely in 1865, with whom he had four sons and two daughters before her death in India; he married Elizabeth Temple in 1884.

It is a measure of Stokes's capacity that a career spent almost entirely in law produced a scholarly output — reckoned at somewhere in the region of fifteen thousand printed pages — that made him, in the judgement of his contemporaries, the greatest of living Celtic philologists. He worked mainly on Irish but also on Cornish and Breton, editing sagas, saints' lives, and glossarial material with a combination of textual rigour and sheer productivity that no successor has matched. With Kuno Meyer he founded the Archiv fur celtische Lexicographie, one of the discipline's principal journals.

His single most consequential achievement for the study of the Book of Armagh was undertaken jointly with the Manchester Celticist John Strachan: the two-volume Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus (1901–03), which gathered and analysed the entire corpus of Old Irish glosses surviving in manuscripts across Europe. Its second volume, published in 1903, prints and phonologically analyses all the Irish-language material in the Book of Armagh — the charter-like notes of the Additamenta and the compressed jottings of the Notulae — and remains, more than a century later, the indispensable starting point for anyone working on that material, which includes some of the oldest continuous Irish prose to survive.

Stokes was elected a founder Fellow of the British Academy, a foreign associate of the Institut de France, and an honorary Fellow of Jesus College, Oxford; he held honorary doctorates of laws from Trinity College Dublin and the University of Edinburgh and a doctorate of civil law from Oxford, and was appointed CSI in 1887 and CIE in 1889. He died in London on 13 April 1909, at the end of a scholarly life that had been conducted, almost without exception, in the hours left over from an unrelated profession.

Strachan, John

Keith, Banffshire, 31 January 1862 – Prestwich, Lancashire, 25 September 1907

John Strachan was born in Keith, in the Scottish county of Banffshire, on 31 January 1862. He was educated at Keith Grammar School and the University of Aberdeen before proceeding to Pembroke College, Cambridge, and, briefly, the University of Jena, acquiring along the way a command of Sanskrit and Greek as well as of the Celtic languages that would become his principal field. In 1886 he married Mina Grant.

Strachan spent his entire academic career at Owens College, Manchester, and its successor institution, the Victoria University of Manchester (from 1903 the University of Manchester), where he held the Hulme Chair of Greek from 1885 until his death in 1907 and was, simultaneously, Professor of Sanskrit and Comparative Religion from 1890. This combination of chairs — Greek, Sanskrit, and comparative philology held by one man — reflects a scholarly formation now vanished from the modern university, in which Celtic studies grew directly out of, and remained answerable to, the methods of Indo-European comparative linguistics.

It was as a grammarian, rather than as a literary interpreter, that Strachan made his lasting contribution. Working alongside Whitley Stokes, seventeen years his senior and already the most productive Celtic scholar of the age, Strachan brought a comparative philologist's precision to material Stokes supplied in extraordinary quantity; the partnership produced the two-volume Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus (1901–03), the great collection of Old Irish glosses from the continental manuscripts at Wurzburg, Milan, St Gall, and Turin, alongside the vernacular material preserved in Irish manuscripts including the Book of Armagh. His Old-Irish Paradigms and Selections from the Old-Irish Glosses (1904–05) distilled this documentary mass into a working grammar that became, and long remained, the standard teaching text for the language; revised after his death by Osborn Bergin, it was still in use generations later. He also edited Stories from the Tain as a teaching selection from the great epic, and his comparative reach extended to Brittonic in the posthumously published An Introduction to Early Welsh (1909).

Strachan died in Prestwich, Lancashire, on 25 September 1907, at forty-five, his career cut short at the height of its productivity. The Thesaurus he built with Stokes nevertheless endures as the necessary point of departure for any editor of Old Irish glossarial or documentary material, the Book of Armagh's Additamenta and Notulae included, and his grammar shaped how the language itself was taught for the better part of a century after his death.

Strehlke, Carl Brandon

active late 20th-21st century

Carl Brandon Strehlke is an American art historian and museum curator whose career has been centred on the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where he served as Adjunct Curator of the John G. Johnson Collection and subsequently as Curator Emeritus. A renowned expert on Fra Angelico and other Florentine Renaissance painters, he has produced across four decades a body of scholarship combining the close visual analysis of individual panels with technical examination of their material constitution - a dual practice that places him in the tradition of scholarship inaugurated by scholars like Erling Skaug, who brought the physical evidence of punched goldwork into the service of attributional argument, and continued in the collaboration between art historians and conservators that has defined the most productive institutional research of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

The institutional foundation of Strehlke's career is one of the most important and least widely discussed early Italian collections in North America: the paintings assembled by the Philadelphia lawyer John G. Johnson and bequeathed, on his death in 1917, to the city of Philadelphia. When the Philadelphia lawyer John G. Johnson began to collect art in the late nineteenth century, he defied contemporary taste by acquiring Italian paintings from the early Renaissance. He eventually donated his distinguished collection to the City of Philadelphia, and it is now housed at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

The Johnson Collection is a remarkable and idiosyncratic accumulation: Johnson was a self-taught collector of exceptional visual intelligence who acquired early Italian panels - Duccesque Sienese altarpieces, Trecento Florentine polyptychs, early Quattrocento panels - at a moment when such objects were generally undervalued by the market and dismissed by prevailing taste. The collection he assembled spans the full range of the period from the mid-thirteenth century through the mid-fifteenth, with particular strengths in Sienese Dugento-Trecento painting and early Florentine Quattrocento.

Although there have been several catalogues of these paintings, including one by Bernhard Berenson in 1913, Carl Brandon Strehlke, Adjunct Curator of the Johnson Collection, prepared the first complete scholarly examination. His discussion of such art historical questions as dating and attribution combines extensive archival research with information he gained through his technical study of the paintings with Mark S. Tucker, the Museum's Vice Chairman of Conservation and Senior Conservator of Paintings.

The collaboration with Tucker is methodologically significant. Over more than twenty years - for over twenty years, Carl Strehlke, adjunct curator of the collection; Mark S. Tucker, the Philadelphia Museum's vice chairman of conservation and senior conservator of paintings; and Tucker's extensive team have focused scrutiny on ninety-seven early Italian pictures in the Johnson Collection and another twenty among the museum's holdings. Their work has long constituted a vibrant force in the prolific, ever-dynamic scholarship of that field.

The examination of 117 panels over more than two decades - subjecting each to infrared reflectography, X-radiography, cross-section paint sampling, dendrochronological analysis of wooden supports, and the full range of technical methods available to a major conservation laboratory - placed the Johnson Collection catalogue in a category substantially different from its predecessors. Berenson's 1913 catalogue was a product of pure connoisseurship: the attribution of works to artists or schools on the basis of visual comparison, conducted without technical evidence and without archival consultation of the kind that subsequent generations would pursue. Strehlke's catalogue of 2004 is the product of a fundamentally different methodology - one in which the evidence of the paint itself, its material composition and its underdrawing, is integrated with the evidence of documents and with the comparative visual analysis of a connoisseurial tradition transformed by technical knowledge.

The catalogue, published jointly by the Philadelphia Museum of Art and Pennsylvania State University Press in 2004, runs to 600 pages with 130 colour illustrations and 700 black-and-white plates - a physical scale commensurate with the scholarly ambition of its content. Strehlke's introduction sheds new light on Johnson's collecting and traces the history of the acquisition, conservation, and installation of the Philadelphia paintings.

The individual entries - covering works attributed to or associated with Cimabue, Duccio, Simone Martini, Pietro and Ambrogio Lorenzetti, Bernardo Daddi, Maso di Banco, Orcagna, Fra Angelico, Lorenzo Monaco, Masolino, Masaccio, and many other named and anonymous Tuscan painters of the period - represent the most comprehensive systematic treatment of the collection since Berenson's catalogue ninety years earlier. The choice of the date range 1250-1450 mirrors Van Os's Sienese Altarpieces (which ends in 1460) and Erling Skaug's punch-mark corpus (which runs from Giotto to Fra Angelico, c. 1330-1430): it is the terrain of the Trecento and the early Quattrocento, the period bounded by the Giottesque revolution at one end and the early Renaissance at the other, that defines the core of Strehlke's scholarly engagement.

The attribution work in the catalogue advances several debates of lasting importance. His outright attribution of a Virgin of Humility to Lorenzo Monaco (c. 1420) and of a predella panel to Fra Angelico (c. 1425, where the influence of Masaccio's lost Sagra is argued) exemplifies the combination of visual analysis and contextual argument that characterizes the best attributional scholarship. The discussion of the Masaccio-Masolino panels in the collection - works that occupy one of the most contested zones in the historiography of the early Florentine Renaissance - drew on the technical examination to clarify questions of priority, collaboration, and relative chronology that purely visual analysis had left unresolved.

Reviewers recognized it as a model of the genre. "This handsome, lavishly illustrated, and meticulously researched volume is the first comprehensive and scholarly treatment of the collection and the collector."

Strehlke's most widely cited collaborative contribution to the study of Sienese painting was the catalogue produced for the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition of 1988-89: Painting in Renaissance Siena: 1420-1500, co-authored with Keith Christiansen and Laurence B. Kanter (New York: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1988). The first comprehensive study in English devoted to Sienese painting published in four decades, it covered the generation from Sassetta through Giovanni di Paolo, Francesco di Giorgio Martini, Matteo di Giovanni, and the painters of the late Quattrocento - the period immediately following the chronological scope of Van Os's Sienese Altarpieces and completing the coverage of Sienese painting from the Dugento through the end of the fifteenth century. The combination of Christiansen's work on the early Sienese Quattrocento, Kanter's expertise in later Sienese painting, and Strehlke's specific knowledge of the Florentine-Sienese boundary zone produced a catalogue of extraordinary range and authority.

Fra Angelico (Guido di Pietro, c. 1395/1400-1455) is the artist to whom Strehlke has devoted the most sustained and consecutive scholarly attention. The Florentine Dominican friar-painter occupies a peculiar position in the historiography of Italian art: revered in the nineteenth century as a painter of uniquely spiritual vision, subsequently reassessed as a transitional figure between Gothic elegance and Renaissance spatial rationality, and most recently re-examined through the technical study of his materials and methods.

Strehlke's Angelico (Jaca Books, 1998; original Italian edition, translated into English by Anna Maria Agosti) was the first full monograph on the painter in the English-speaking world for a generation. His article "Fra Angelico and Early Florentine Renaissance Painting in the John G. Johnson Collection at the Philadelphia Museum of Art" (Philadelphia Museum of Art Bulletin, Spring 1993) addressed the specific Fra Angelico panels in the Johnson Collection, establishing the arguments that would later be developed in the 2004 catalogue.

With Laurence B. Kanter and Clay Dean, he produced Rediscovering Fra Angelico: A Fragmentary History (Yale University Art Gallery, 2001), examining four fifteenth-century panels recently confirmed as belonging to a single dispersed triptych by Fra Angelico - a problem in the reconstruction of dismembered polyptychs analogous to the challenges that occupied Van Os in his work on the Antwerp-Baltimore Altarpiece.

The capstone of his Fra Angelico scholarship was the Prado exhibition of 2019. Curated by Carl Brandon Strehlke, Curator Emeritus at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and a renowned expert on Fra Angelico and other Florentine Renaissance painters, the exhibition is on display in Rooms C and D of the Jerónimos Building. The exhibition, presented with almost eighty works, focused on the crucial decade 1420-30 - the moment at which Fra Angelico simultaneously absorbed the innovations of Brunelleschi's perspective architecture, Masaccio's chiaroscuro naturalism, and Donatello's sculptural expressivity while remaining committed to the refined colour and decorative richness of the late Gothic tradition he had absorbed as Lorenzo Monaco's pupil. This generously illustrated catalogue by Carl Brandon Strehlke, author of numerous studies on 15th-century Renaissance masters, includes two essays: one on Florence of the period seen through the eyes of the artists and one on Fra Angelico's formation and working methods. The accompanying Thames and Hudson volume made the exhibition's arguments available to a wide international readership.

Among Strehlke's most methodologically significant publications was the volume The Panel Paintings of Masolino and Masaccio: The Role of Technique (Milan: 5 Continents, 2002), co-edited with Cecilia Frosinini - the same Cecilia Frosinini who had collaborated with Anna Padoa Rizzo on research into Stefano di Antonio di Vanni. The volume brought together technical studies of the panels produced by the two painters - working separately and in documented collaboration - whose careers defined the transition from late Gothic Florentine painting to the revolutionary naturalism of the early Renaissance. The technical evidence - the analysis of panel preparation, underdrawing, pigment application, and the sequence of laying in figures and backgrounds - provided new grounds for addressing questions about the relative chronology of Masaccio and Masolino's collaboration on the Brancacci Chapel frescoes and the panels associated with the two painters, questions that had been debated for generations on purely formal and visual grounds.

A dimension of Strehlke's scholarship less immediately connected to his core work on early Italian painting is his engagement with the history of collecting and with the figure of Bernard Berenson - the most influential connoisseur of Italian art in the Anglo-American world of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Berenson had produced the first scholarly catalogue of the Johnson Collection in 1913, and the relationship between his attributional judgements and those of subsequent scholarship is a recurring subtext of Strehlke's 2004 catalogue.

His essay "Bernard Berenson and Asian Art" in the Villa I Tatti conference volume Bernard Berenson: Formation and Heritage (eds. Joseph Connors and Louis A. Waldman, Florence, 2014) placed him within the community of scholars engaged with Berenson's reception and legacy at the Harvard Center for Italian Renaissance Studies - the same institution where Van Os had held a visiting position and where Skaug had spent his fellowship year. The essay addressed a dimension of Berenson's intellectual life - his engagement with non-Western art - that the conventional image of him as the arbiter of Italian connoisseurship had largely obscured.

Carl Brandon Strehlke belongs to a generation of American museum-based scholars - alongside Keith Christiansen and Laurence Kanter at the Metropolitan Museum, Burton Fredericksen at the Getty, and Miklós Boskovits at the Florentine Art Historical Society - who brought the rigour of European art historical training to the systematic documentation of early Italian paintings in American institutional collections. His particular contribution is the sustained, technically grounded analysis of the Johnson Collection over more than two decades, producing in the 2004 catalogue a work of permanent reference value for the study of the period from Dugento Tuscany through the early Quattrocento.

The chronological span of his research - 1250 to 1450, Italian painting from its medieval origins to the threshold of the High Renaissance - encompasses the entire territory that recurs throughout this research thread: the Trecento world of Giotto, the Lorenzetti, Simone Martini, Bernardo Daddi, and their documented patrons, as well as the transitional generation of Masolino, Masaccio, Fra Angelico, and Lorenzo Monaco that closes the medieval epoch. His combination of archival documentary research, technical examination, and connoisseurial comparative analysis represents the fullest integration of the methodological traditions available to the student of this material.

Strzygowski, Josef Rudolph Thomas

Biala (Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria), 7 March 1862 - Vienna, 2 January 1941

Josef Rudolph Thomas Strzygowski was a Polish-Austrian art historian and one of the most controversial and provocative scholars of his era, celebrated for radically expanding the geographical horizons of art history while simultaneously drawing condemnation for his ideologically compromised later work. He is remembered as a central figure of the Vienna School of Art History and, arguably, Europe's first professor of non-Western art history.

Strzygowski was born on March 7, 1862, in Biala, in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria (present-day Poland, then part of the Austrian Empire). His mother, Edle Trass von Friedelfeldt, came from minor nobility, while his father was a cloth manufacturer. Following family tradition, the young Strzygowski began an apprenticeship at a weaving plant in 1880, but abandoned this path in 1882 to enroll at the University of Vienna. He soon transferred to the University of Munich, where he immersed himself in art history and completed a dissertation on the iconography of the Baptism of Christ, published in 1885 under the title Ikonographie der Taufe Christi.

After completing his studies, Strzygowski spent three years in Rome, where he produced Cimabue und Rom (1887), an early and significant work that emphasized the Byzantine sources underlying the painting of Cimabue, a subject of direct relevance to the study of medieval Italian art. This work already signaled his lifelong conviction that the roots of Western European art lay not in Rome alone but in the broader Eastern Mediterranean world. He subsequently traveled to Thessaloniki, Mount Athos, Saint Petersburg, and Moscow, deepening his knowledge of Byzantine and Russian art.

In 1892, Strzygowski was appointed to the faculty of the University of Graz. Between 1894 and 1895, he lived in Cairo, where he studied early Byzantine and Islamic art in Egypt and compiled a landmark catalogue of Coptic art held in the Cairo Museum. This fieldwork positioned him as a pioneer in areas that were then largely unexplored by Western scholars, and his expertise soon attracted the attention of major institutions: Wilhelm von Bode, director of the Berlin Museums, enlisted Strzygowski to help build the Byzantine collection before the opening of the Kaiser-Friedrich Museum in 1904, expanding the holdings from fewer than 100 to approximately 2,000 objects.

The most intellectually explosive moment of Strzygowski's career came in 1901, with the publication of Orient oder Rom: Beitrage zur Geschichte der spatantiken und fruhchristlichen Kunst ("The Orient or Rome: Contributions to the History of Late Antique and Early Christian Art"). In this polemical work, he directly challenged the dominant paradigm that Rome was the fountainhead of early Christian and medieval art, arguing instead that the Near East, particularly Syria, Mesopotamia, Armenia, and Egypt, played the decisive formative role. This thesis shook the foundations of the discipline and ignited a scholarly debate that resonated for decades.

Upon the death of Franz Wickhoff, Strzygowski was appointed in 1909 to his successor's chair at the University of Vienna, a position secured in part through the breadth of his research and, reportedly, the advocacy of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. From this prestigious platform, he continued to publish prolifically on Byzantium, Islam, Armenia, Norse art, and Slavic visual culture, developing a sweeping, non-Eurocentric theoretical framework for art history that was radical for its time.

His two-volume Die Baukunst der Armenier und Europa (1918), "The Architecture of the Armenians and Europe," advanced the daring claim that the origins of Gothic architecture could be traced to Armenian building traditions, a thesis that was largely rejected by subsequent scholarship. He also entered a notable controversy with the archaeologist Ernst Herzfeld over the origins of the Mshatta facade; in this dispute, Herzfeld's position was ultimately vindicated.

Strzygowski retired from the University of Vienna in 1933 and founded the Gesellschaft fur vergleichende Kunstforschung ("Society for Comparative Art History") in 1934 to propagate his theoretical views. Tragically, in his final years he embraced the nationalist and racist ideology of National Socialism, a drift that scholars have interpreted not merely as political opportunism but as the disturbing logical conclusion of the ethnic and racial categories that had gradually infiltrated his art historical thinking.

He died on January 2, 1941, in Vienna. His private library was bequeathed to the Art History Department of the University of Vienna, where it remains.

Despite his methodological inconsistencies and the deep ideological stain on his later work, Strzygowski's intellectual legacy is complex and cannot be dismissed outright. His insistence on looking beyond the Greco-Roman world helped legitimize Islamic art, Coptic art, and non-Western visual traditions as serious fields of academic inquiry. Several of his most gifted students, most notably Otto Demus and Fritz Novotny, successfully pursued these broadened horizons without adopting their teacher's ideology. Today, in an era of global art history and decolonized museum practice, Strzygowski's restless geographical curiosity finds a kind of posthumous vindication, even as his racial theorizing remains a cautionary chapter in the history of the discipline.

Stubblebine, James H.

1920 – 1987

James H. Stubblebine was an American art historian who specialized in early Italian painting, especially the Sienese school of the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. He is regarded as one of the leading scholars of Italian Duecento and Trecento painting and made a major contribution to the institutional development of art history as a discipline in the United States.

Educated at Harvard University, where he graduated in 1942, Stubblebine became professor of art history at Rutgers University and was later named Distinguished Professor II. He helped build Rutgers' graduate program in art history and also taught at New York University's Institute of Fine Arts in the late 1970s and 1980s. His long-standing association with major American research institutions and museums, including the National Gallery of Art, anchored his work in both scholarly and curatorial practice.

Stubblebine's primary research focused on thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italian panel painting, with particular emphasis on Duccio di Buoninsegna and his circle in Siena. His monumental two-volume study Duccio di Buoninsegna and His School combines iconographic, stylistic, and document-based analysis with an extensive photographic archive, reproducing essentially all of Duccio's surviving works and many by his contemporaries. He also published extensively on related figures such as Coppo di Marcovaldo and Guido da Siena, and his essays on Byzantine influence and the development of throne imagery in Duecento Tuscan painting remain frequently cited in debates on Italo-Byzantine transition.

For scholars working on twelfth- to fourteenth-century Italian painting and illuminated manuscripts, Stubblebine's work remains essential for understanding chronology, workshop practice, and stylistic evolution in late Duecento and early Trecento Siena. His method, combining meticulous formal analysis with documentary and archival research supported by systematic photographic evidence, continues to serve as a model for attributional and school-based studies in medieval Italian art.

T

Tambini Strocchi, Anna

c. 1942 - 2025

Anna Tambini Strocchi was one of the most authoritative Italian scholars of medieval and Renaissance art in the Romagna region, particularly celebrated for her pioneering studies on the Giottesque School of Rimini and on manuscript illumination between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries. She died at the age of 82, mourned by the cultural community of Faenza and beyond.

Tambini studied Art History at the Università di Bologna under the guidance of Carlo Volpe, obtaining her Diploma di perfezionamento in Storia dell'Arte in 1979. Her graduation thesis became the foundation for her first major book, Pittura dall'Alto Medioevo al Tardogotico nel territorio di Faenza e Forli (Faenza, 1982), which established her as a rigorous and original voice in the study of Romagnole art history.

Her primary field was the art of the Middle Ages and Renaissance in Romagna, though she also devoted significant attention to eighteenth-century painting. Among her most appreciated contributions are studies on the Giottesque Riminese School, on Forli's medieval painting tradition, on Late Gothic art in Romagna, and on manuscript illumination in Romagna from the Duecento to the Quattrocento.

Over the course of her career, Tambini produced more than one hundred publications in specialized journals, including international venues. She contributed to the catalogues of the Pinacoteca di Ferrara and the Pinacoteca di Bologna, and she curated the medieval and Renaissance painting section in the catalogue of the Pinacoteca Comunale di Ravenna (2001). She also wrote entries for the Enciclopedia Treccani and the German Kunstler Lexikon.

Her most ambitious publishing project was a three-volume series on the history of figurative arts in Faenza: Le origini (2006), Il Gotico (2007), and Il Rinascimento (2009), followed by a contribution on Faentine painters of the first half of the sixteenth century in a fourth volume. These works, together with her cataloguing activity at the Biblioteca di Faenza and her contributions to the five-volume series on Faenza's historic neighborhoods edited by Lorenzo Savelli, form a major scholarly corpus on local art history.

In 2001 she also co-authored with Morelli and Tabanelli Quella chiesa nata dalle acque. L'oratorio di Croce Coperta a Lugo, a focused study on a lesser-known but artistically significant oratory in the Ravenna province.

Tambini lectured at the universities of Trieste and Urbino and supervised theses in both institutions. She presented papers at symposia in Mercatello, Tolentino, Vignola, Camerino, and Urbino, reflecting the breadth of her recognized authority across central Italy. In 2021 she received the honorary distinction Faentina Lontana, conferred by the city of Faenza.

Her legacy is that of a meticulous and passionate researcher who dedicated her scholarly life to recovering and illuminating an artistic heritage that might otherwise have remained largely forgotten.

Tartuferi, Angelo

Florence, 16 August 1957

Angelo Tartuferi is one of Italy's most authoritative art historians in the field of medieval and early Renaissance Tuscan painting, with a particular focus on the period from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century. His scholarship combines connoisseurship, archival discipline, and museum practice, and has made him a major reference point in studies of Florentine painting between the Duecento and the Quattrocento.

He graduated with honors in Art History at the University of Florence in 1982 under Mina Gregori, the same teacher as Giordana Benazzi. He later earned his Specialization Diploma at La Sapienza University of Rome (1986), followed by a PhD in 1989 with a dissertation titled La pittura a Firenze nel Duecento. Decisive to his formation was also his collaboration with Miklós Boskovits, a leading scholar of medieval Florentine painting at the Germanic Institute of Art History in Florence, an experience he has described as a true scholarly bottega in the most concrete and demanding sense.

On 25 July 1990 he entered the Italian Ministry for Cultural Heritage as an art-historical official. He served as Deputy Director of the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence, then moved in 2006 to the Uffizi as Director of the Department of Duecento-to-Quattrocento painting. Between 2009 and 2013 he also held the position of Deputy Director of the Uffizi. In 2013, after the retirement of Franca Falletti, he became Director of the Galleria dell'Accademia, a role he held until the 2015 ministerial reform. From 2016 to 2020 he directed the department dedicated to Michelangelesque sculpture and Duecento-to-Quattrocento painting at the same museum. From 2020 to 2024 he served as Director of the Museo di San Marco in Florence, where he oversaw, among other projects, the new installation of the room dedicated to Fra Angelico.

Tartuferi has authored numerous monographs, essays, and articles in leading journals, including Paragone Arte, Arte Cristiana, Antichità Viva, Commentari d'arte, Revue de l'Art, and Studi di Storia dell'Arte. His research spans Duecento Florentine painting, late Gothic culture, and the early Renaissance, with special attention to attributional questions and to the reconstruction of minor or anonymous artistic personalities. He obtained the Italian National Scientific Qualification in 2012 for associate-professor rank and in 2020 for full-professor rank (sector 10/B1, Art History), and he has taught university courses at the University of Perugia and other institutions.

His scholarly stature has been recognized by a collective Festschrift, Scritti di Storia dell'Arte in his honor, published by Campisano Editore and featuring contributions from numerous international scholars on medieval and early Renaissance topics. After retiring in August 2024, he has continued to work as an independent researcher and exhibition curator.

Theocharidis, Georgios Ioannis

active mid–late 20th century

Greek Byzantine historian associated with the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and the Society of Macedonian Studies, whose scholarly life was devoted to the institutional, documentary, and prosopographical history of Byzantine Macedonia from late antiquity through the final decades before the Ottoman conquest. His work represents the specifically historical complement to the archaeological investigations of Stylianos Pelekanidis: where Pelekanidis read the material fabric of Byzantine Macedonia — its churches, mosaics, and manuscripts — Theocharidis read its documentary fabric, the charters, wills, legal proceedings, and council decisions that illuminate the social and institutional world within which those monuments were built and those manuscripts produced.

Theocharidis worked within the dense network of Thessalonian scholarly institutions whose primary publication vehicles were the journal Μακεδονικά and the monographic series of the Institute for Balkan Studies (Ίδρυμα Μελετών Χερσονήσου του Αίμου). His foundational source base was the extraordinary documentary archive of the Athonite monasteries — Vatopedi above all, but also the Great Lavra, Chilandari, and smaller foundations — which preserve chrysobulls, praktika, wills, and records of legal proceedings providing direct access to the economic, social, and institutional history of Byzantine Macedonia in the eleventh through fourteenth centuries.

Among his contributions to Μακεδονικά was a foundational prosopographical study of the Tzamphakonoi (Οι Τζαμπλάκωνες. Συμβολή εις την βυζαντινήν μακεδονικήν προσωπογραφίαν του ΙΔ΄ αιώνος — The Tzamphakonoi: A Contribution to Byzantine Macedonian Prosopography of the 14th Century). The Tzamphakonoi were one of the most powerful Byzantine aristocratic families in Macedonia during the fourteenth century — the period of Palaeologan civil war that nonetheless produced the mosaics of the Holy Apostles in Thessaloniki and the frescoes of the Chora monastery in Constantinople. Prosopographical research of this kind is indispensable for the history of art patronage: knowing who the Tzamphakonoi were, what properties they held, what religious foundations they were connected to, and what documents they left in the Athonite archives is a precondition for understanding the material culture of the world they inhabited.

His most substantial independent publication was his edition and analysis of Μια διαθήκη και μια δίκη βυζαντινή. Ανέκδοτα Βατοπεδινά έγγραφα του ΙΔ΄ αιώνος περί της μονής Προδρόμου Βεροίας (A Testament and a Byzantine Trial: Unpublished Documents from Vatopedi of the 14th Century concerning the Monastery of Prodromos at Veria; Supplement 2 of Μακεδονικά). The work exemplifies his characteristic method: the identification, transcription, and critical analysis of unpublished archival documents brought to bear on a specific historical problem. Such documentary editions serve art history directly: testamentary documents and property records of monasteries frequently mention icons, liturgical vessels, embroideries, and books that constitute their moveable heritage, establishing the existence of works no longer surviving and occasionally providing precise dates or attributions for objects still preserved.

The synthetic summation of his scholarly life was Ιστορία της Μακεδονίας κατά τους μέσους χρόνους, 285–1354 (History of Macedonia in the Middle Ages, 285–1354; Society of Macedonian Studies, Institute for Balkan Studies series, vol. 55, Thessaloniki, 1980). The dates of its scope are precisely chosen: 285 AD marks the administrative reorganization under Diocletian when Macedonia first emerged as a distinct late antique province; 1354 marks the definitive Serbian occupation under Stefan Dušan, after which the specific political identity of Byzantine Macedonia effectively dissolved. The work covers the entire arc of Byzantine Macedonia — from its late antique formation through the Macedonian dynasty, the Komnenian prosperity of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, the Latin occupation after 1204, the Nicaean reconquest of 1246, and the turbulent Palaeologan decades of civil war and artistic efflorescence — providing the essential historical framework within which the individual Athonite documents acquire their intelligibility.

Thode, Heinrich

Dresden, 13 January 1857 - Copenhagen, 19 November 1920

Heinrich Thode was a German art historian, renowned for his studies on the Italian Renaissance and especially on Saint Francis of Assisi, and for his role in shaping the discipline of art history in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Germany. He combined rigorous archival research with a strongly personal, often romantic vision of Italy and of the development of modern individuality out of medieval spirituality.

Thode was born in Dresden in 1857 into a respected North German bourgeois family. His father, Robert Thode (1825-1898), was a banker who had founded the "Dresdener Bank Robert Thode & Co." in Dresden, later incorporated into the Dresdner Bank in 1891, which placed the family in a comfortable financial and social position. His mother, Adolfine Dzondi (1822-1900), was the daughter of a Saxon Lutheran pastor, and Thode grew up as the third of four children in a protected, cultivated milieu where Protestant religiosity and bourgeois culture intersected.

From an early age he received a solid humanistic education: after the Gymnasium at Gorlitz he moved in the typical fashion of the German Bildungsburger between schools and university cities, building the classical and philological foundation that would later support his art-historical work. This combination of banking-bourgeois pragmatism and clerical-intellectual background helps explain both his practical engagement in institutional life and his persistent preoccupation with religious questions in art.

Thode initially enrolled in law at the University of Leipzig, following a conventional path for a young man of his class. However, he soon turned away from jurisprudence and, after being sent to Vienna, discovered art history, then still a relatively young academic discipline, which he continued to study in Berlin and Munich. In Vienna he wrote his doctoral dissertation under the guidance of Moritz Thausing, completing it in 1880 and thus entering the circle of the great positivist-philological school of Central European art history.

In 1886 he obtained his Habilitation at the University of Bonn as Privatdozent in art history, which gave him the formal right to teach at the university. These years of formation placed him at the crossroads of several methodological traditions: the documentary, source-critical Viennese school; the museum-based connoisseurship associated with figures like Wilhelm von Bode; and, increasingly, an idealist interest in the spiritual and cultural "sense" of historical periods. This plural background would mark his later work, which moves continually between archival precision and broader cultural interpretation.

In 1886 Thode married Daniela von Bulow (1860-1940), whom he had met in Venice during a study trip to Italy. Daniela was the daughter of Cosima Liszt (later Cosima Wagner) and of her first husband, the conductor Hans von Bulow, and thus part of the circle surrounding Richard Wagner and the Bayreuth enterprise. Through this marriage Thode entered the complex world of late nineteenth-century German musical and cultural elites, tied to the cult of Wagner and to a network of artists, intellectuals and patrons.

This connection to Bayreuth and to Cosima's family reinforced Thode's interest in the ideological and spiritual dimensions of art, since the Wagnerian milieu cultivated an almost religious conception of the artist and of the artwork as vehicles of a new Germanic spirituality. Socially, the marriage placed him in the border zone between academic art history and broader cultural debates, a position that would later shape his strong, sometimes polemical interventions on contemporary German art and on the threat he perceived in French Impressionism.

In 1889, thanks to the recommendation of Wilhelm von Bode, Thode was appointed director of the Stadelsches Kunstinstitut in Frankfurt am Main. This prestigious museum-directorship placed him at the heart of German museum practice at a time when museums were becoming key instruments for the formation of national taste. During his Frankfurt years he met the painter Hans Thoma, with whom he established a long friendship, indicative of his closeness to certain strands of German naturalism and of his appreciation for contemporary artists who, in his view, remained faithful to a specifically German sensibility.

However, disagreements with the museum administration led Thode to resign in October 1891, only two years after his appointment. The conflict reflected both institutional tensions and Thode's strong personality: he was not simply a curator but an intellectual with pronounced ideas about what a museum should collect and how it should present art to the public. His departure from Frankfurt marked a shift from primarily curatorial work back toward the university and gave him greater freedom to develop his own interpretive projects.

In 1893 Thode was appointed extraordinarius (associate professor) of art history at the University of Heidelberg, and in 1896 he became ordinarius, the first full professor of art history at that university. This position placed him among the central figures of German academic art history, a generation that included scholars who were institutionalizing the field within the university system. At Heidelberg he built a thriving art-historical seminar, training students in both archival research and close formal analysis, while integrating literary and theological materials into his lectures.

His teaching at Heidelberg reflected his dual interest in Italian Renaissance art and in the contemporary German artistic scene. On the one hand he offered historic courses on Michelangelo, the Renaissance, and the spiritual origins of modern art; on the other he took clear positions in the debates about what constituted "true" German art at the end of the nineteenth century.
