In this way he helped shape both the historical canon and the taste of a generation of educated German viewers.

Beyond the university, Thode nourished an intense personal and intellectual relationship with Italy. He settled for long periods on Lake Garda, where he acquired and developed a villa that became an "officina della maturita," a workshop of his mature years, filled with books, artworks, and memories of ancient and Renaissance art. This villa, later to become Gabriele D'Annunzio's Vittoriale degli Italiani, preserved many traces of Thode's presence and of the art-historical and literary work he carried out there.

In this Italian retreat he constructed something like a hortus conclusus, a closed garden of study and contemplation, embodying both his love of Renaissance culture and his romantic, almost Goethean idea of a fusion between scholarly research and the aesthetic experience of place. The Italian critic Silvia Urbini has highlighted how Thode's essays and Kunstnovellen (art novellas), written in this context, belong to a tradition of "romantic science" where documentary and philological research intertwine with narrative forms. For Thode, Italy was not merely an object of study but a lived environment that shaped his historiographical imagination.

Thode's most famous work is his study on Saint Francis and the origins of Renaissance art: Franz von Assisi und die Anfange der Kunst der Renaissance in Italien, first published in 1885. In this book he argued that the Renaissance should be understood as a process of emancipation from medieval values in which the modern individual emerges, yet in his view this emancipation remains deeply marked by the spirituality of Saint Francis of Assisi. The work was widely read, translated (for example into French and later into Italian), and helped consolidate the idea of Franciscan spirituality as a crucial factor in the birth of Renaissance art.

Alongside this seminal study, Thode devoted important monographs and essays to Michelangelo and to various aspects of Italian Renaissance art, confirming his reputation as a specialist in this period. At the same time, he wrote extensively on German art of the late nineteenth century, championing what he regarded as "great German art," characterized by technical skill, realism and a distinct national spirit, and sharply opposing the dominance of French Impressionism and other foreign currents. He insisted that art should be intelligible to the broader public, not only to academics and the bourgeois elite, which aligned his scholarship with broader debates on culture and nation.

In his writings on modern art, Thode expressed strong criticism of Impressionism and of what he perceived as a cosmopolitan trend undermining specifically German artistic traditions. He accused modern French art of attempting to destroy both "true" German art and the "true" German spirit, formulating an opposition between rooted national realism and foreign, decadent experimentation. These positions, while part of broader contemporary debates, were later regarded as important antecedents for the cultural policies of the Third Reich, particularly the condemnation of so-called "degenerate art."

This retrospective association has complicated Thode's reputation, as his work is now seen both as a significant contribution to the historical understanding of the Renaissance and as a source of ideas that could be instrumentalized for nationalist and exclusionary cultural politics. Modern scholarship, such as the monographic study Henry Thode (1857-1920): Leben und Werk, has sought to reassess his oeuvre in its historical context, emphasizing his role as the first full professor of art history at Heidelberg and as a key figure in the institutional consolidation of the discipline, while also critically examining the ideological dimensions of his thought.

Thode's personal life became increasingly unsettled in the years surrounding the First World War. His strong German nationalism and his Italian ties, combined with the political upheavals of the period, contributed to a sense of displacement; he and his wife moved around Germany until 1919, eventually leaving the country. In 1919 they settled in Copenhagen, where Thode sought a degree of peace after the traumas of war and professional conflict.

He died in Copenhagen in November 1920, reportedly depressed following complications from a gastric operation. His death in relative exile, away from both his native Dresden and his beloved Lake Garda, gives his biography a somewhat tragic cadence, contrasting with the secure, bourgeois beginnings of his life. Yet his writings continued to circulate, especially his work on Saint Francis and the Renaissance, which remained a reference point for discussions on the spiritual origins of modern art well into the twentieth century.

Thode stands as a representative of a generation of art historians who experienced and theorized a "time of upheaval" in art and culture, bridging the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. As the first ordinarius for art history at Heidelberg, he played a central role in institutionalizing the subject within German universities and in forming a generation of students who would continue to develop the discipline. His work on Saint Francis, the Renaissance, and Michelangelo contributed to the canonization of certain narratives about the birth of modern individuality and the relationship between medieval spirituality and Renaissance art, narratives that continue to interest scholars today.

At the same time, his conservative cultural politics, his hostility to Impressionism, and his insistence on an essentialized "German spirit" mark him as a figure in whom scholarly insight and ideological rigidity coexist in tension. Contemporary historians of art and culture read Thode not only for his factual contributions but also as a case study in how art history can participate in wider national and ideological projects. This dual legacy-scholarly and ideological-makes him a particularly instructive figure for understanding the history of art history as a discipline.

Tischendorf, Constantin von

Lengenfeld, 18 January 1815 - Leipzig, 7 December 1874

Constantin von Tischendorf was a German biblical scholar and textual critic, Professor at the University of Leipzig, and one of the most celebrated manuscript hunters of the nineteenth century. He is best remembered for his discovery, at St Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, of the Codex Sinaiticus, one of the two oldest surviving complete manuscripts of the Greek Bible, and for the numerous critical editions of the Greek New Testament he produced over a long and prodigiously productive career.

Tischendorf's connection to the Codex Amiatinus lies in his having published its New Testament text, in 1850 and again in an improved edition in 1854 — the publication that first made the manuscript widely known and consulted among biblical scholars internationally, more than three decades before its true origin was established. Tischendorf accepted, as did every other scholar of his generation, the manuscript's apparent identity as a sixth-century Italian production, an attribution seemingly confirmed by its own dedication page. He also noted the comparative textual inferiority of the Amiatinus's rendering of Maccabees, an observation that remains part of the standard account of the manuscript's uneven textual quality. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller account of the manuscript's textual history and its historic misattribution.

Todd, James Henthorn

Dublin, 23 April 1805 – Dublin, 27 June 1869

James Henthorn Todd was an Irish clergyman and scholar, fellow and later librarian of Trinity College Dublin, Regius Professor of Hebrew from 1849, and President of the Royal Irish Academy from 1856 to 1861. A central figure in the mid-nineteenth-century revival of Irish historical and manuscript scholarship, Todd was a founding member of the Irish Archaeological Society (1840) and edited a series of medieval Irish historical texts, including Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh: The War of the Gaedhil with the Gaill (1867) for the Rolls Series.

As Trinity's librarian, Todd oversaw the college's growing collection of early Irish manuscripts during the very period in which the Book of Dimma itself entered the library's holdings, purchased from William Betham in 1836. His editorial standards helped establish the more rigorous, source-critical approach to Irish manuscript scholarship that would culminate, a generation later, in the work of Whitley Stokes, John Strachan and Richard Irvine Best.

Todini, Filippo

Rome, 1957–

Italian art historian best known for his studies on Umbrian painting and the painting schools of Central Italy between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries. Todini specializes in Italian art history with a particular focus on Umbria and on the artistic dynamics between Bologna, Perugia, and Florence from the late Middle Ages to the modern era. His work is frequently cited in studies on minor painters, anonymous masters, and attributional problems, and he is regarded as an authority on the cataloging and reconstruction of Perugian and Umbrian workshops.

Among his best-known works is the two-volume set La pittura umbra dal Duecento al primo Cinquecento (1989), which functions as a large-scale critical survey and catalogue-style reference for Umbrian painting. He has also edited volumes such as Studi di storia dell'arte (conference proceedings and research collections) and has published studies on seventeenth-century Umbrian painting, continuing his analysis of local history, patronage structures, and workshop formation.

Todini has repeatedly intervened in attribution debates, proposing or confirming identities of "anonymous masters" and reattributing works to lesser-known painters or collaborative workshop contexts. His criteria are often cited in articles and exhibition catalogues for their close attention to stylistic details, internal workshop chronology, and the circulation of forms between Umbria and Tuscany.

Toesca, Pietro

Pietra Ligure, 12 July 1877 – Rome, 9 March 1962

Giovanni Pietro Toesca was one of the greatest Italian medieval art historians of the twentieth century, whose work laid the methodological foundations of the discipline for generations of scholars. Born in Pietra Ligure, Liguria, to a noble family originally from Saorgio, he was orphaned at the age of twelve. He died in Rome on 9 March 1962 after dedicating over six decades to research, philological cataloging, and the critical evaluation of a vast body of artworks.

Toesca was trained in Rome under the guidance of Adolfo Venturi, the patriarch of Italian art history, of whom he became the most worthy successor in the teaching of medieval and modern art history. In 1905, he began his career as a lecturer at the Scientific-Literary Academy of Milan, and in 1907 he was appointed to the newly established chair of Art History at the University of Turin. These Turin years were extraordinarily productive: in 1908 he published a seminal essay in L'Arte on fourteenth- and fifteenth-century Italian gold-leaf stained glass with graffiti, and in 1909 he identified the illuminator Francesco Marmitta as the creator of Domenico Della Rovere's Missal.

In 1912, La pittura e la miniatura nella Lombardia fino alla metà del Quattrocento was published, a work that represented the first systematic attempt to reconstruct the landscape of Lombard figurative art from the Middle Ages onward and established its significance on a European scale. From May 1912 to December 1913, he also served on the Board of Directors of the Civic Museum of Turin, strengthening his ties with the city's cultural institutions.

In 1913, the first issue of the monumental Storia dell'arte italiana was published. Its first volume, Il Medioevo, would be completed in 1927 after years of uninterrupted research. The work became a central reference for the study of Italian medieval art and remained one of the most influential syntheses in twentieth-century historiography.

In 1914, Toesca moved to Florence, where he formed a deep intellectual friendship with Bernard Berenson, sharing the method of direct stylistic analysis of works. This Florentine phase strengthened his confidence in saper vedere, the ability to observe the distinctive stylistic characteristics of a work directly, as an indispensable foundation of art history. In 1926, he moved permanently to Rome, where he succeeded Venturi as professor of Medieval and Modern Art History at La Sapienza, concluding his teaching career in 1948.

Toesca's method was based on rigorous philological analysis of styles, combined with close visual observation. He theorized this approach in two articles published in the Annali della istruzione media: Una lezione su Giotto (1929) and Saper vedere (1932). In these texts, rare examples of explicit methodological reflection, he argued that understanding the distinctive stylistic qualities of a work constitutes the true foundation of the discipline.

He also made continuous and thoughtful use of photography as a tool for analyzing and documenting artworks, anticipating practices that would later become standard in art-historical research. This integration of direct viewing, philology, and visual documentation was one of the strongest features of his method.

In addition to university teaching, Toesca held institutional roles of the highest order. From 1929 to 1937, he served as director of the History of Medieval and Modern Art section of the Treccani Enciclopedia Italiana, leaving a lasting methodological imprint on the treatment of medieval artists. In 1939, he joined the Technical Council of the Central Institute for Restoration, helping to define scientific criteria for restoration in Italy.

From 1944 to 1952, he served as president of the National Institute of Archaeology and Art History (INASA) in Rome, guiding the institution through the difficult postwar years and returning it to its headquarters at Palazzo Venezia in 1945. His chair in Rome was also an extraordinary breeding ground for talent.

Among his most illustrious students were Roberto Longhi, Federico Zeri, Giulio Carlo Argan, Ernst Kitzinger, Carlo Bertelli, Sergio Bettini, Ferdinando Bologna, and Giovanni Carandente. Roberto Longhi, destined to become the most influential art critic of postwar Italy, took his first steps under Toesca's guidance, though he later developed a more dynamic and literary critical approach than his mentor's philological sobriety.

Toesca's definitive masterpiece remains the two-volume Storia dell'arte italiana. The first volume, Il Medioevo (1913-1927), covers Italian art from its Christian origins through the thirteenth century, while the second, Il Trecento (1951), resumes the discussion from the age of Giotto and Duccio. Also central are Monumenti e studi per la storia della miniatura italiana (1929) and La pittura fiorentina del Trecento (1929), testifying to his specific and lasting influence on the study of manuscript illumination and Trecento painting.

Toesca married Elena Berti (1900-1967), also an art historian and author of numerous essays; they had one daughter, Ilaria Toesca, who followed in her parents' footsteps. From 1946, he was a national member of the Accademia dei Lincei, the highest academic honor in Italy. Critics have described him as an example of exemplary moral consistency as both a teacher and a historian, qualities that made him not only a rigorous scholar but also a master in the fullest sense of the word.

Tomei, Alessandro

active late 20th - 21st century

Alessandro Tomei studied art history in Rome and Paris, taking his degree in Letters at the University of Rome with a thesis on the medieval painter and mosaicist Jacopo Torriti. He was a confirmed researcher at the Institute of Art History of the Faculty of Letters at Rome's Sapienza from 1981 to 1993, then associate professor of medieval art history at the Università "G. d'Annunzio" of Chieti from 1993 to 2000, when he was promoted to full professor of medieval art history, a post he held until his retirement in November 2022. He directed the university's Department of Medieval and Modern Studies from 2006 to 2012 and later coordinated its doctoral programme in cultural heritage and languages (2015-2018), and also taught medieval art history and the history of manuscript illumination at Rome Tre and at L'Aquila.

Tomei's research centres on central Italian painting and manuscript illumination of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and on Roman Duecento painting and mosaic in particular. His monograph Iacobus Torriti pictor. Una vicenda figurativa del tardo Duecento romano (Argos, Rome, 1990) remains the standard study of the mosaicist of the apses of San Giovanni in Laterano and Santa Maria Maggiore, and his Pietro Cavallini (Silvana Editoriale, Milan, 2000) was the first monograph on that painter in over two decades, incorporating the results of intervening restorations. From 1981 to 1999 he was a contributing author and editor for the Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'arte medievale, writing, among other entries, the entry on Pietro Cavallini. He curated the exhibitions Fragmenta picta (Rome, 1989), Le Biccherne di Siena (2002-2003), and Giotto e il Trecento (Rome, 2009) — the last drawing more than 200,000 visitors — and has served on the editorial or scientific committees of Arte medievale, Rivista d'arte, Art e Dossier, and the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence.

For Assisi, Tomei edited the volume Santa Chiara in Assisi. Architettura e decorazione (2002), commissioned in the wake of the 1997 Umbria earthquake to accompany the restoration of the basilica's frescoes and panels; despite its title, the volume is overwhelmingly concerned with the painted decoration rather than the architecture already treated by Hans-Rudolf Meier. In it Tomei argued for a substantially Giottesque paternity for much of the right-transept decoration and proposed the pontificate of Nicholas IV (1288-1292) as a terminus post quem for the Old Testament cycle in the transept, establishing the volume as the standard modern account of the basilica's post-earthquake decorative programme.

Torriti, Piero

Montisi, 1924 – Siena, 2015

Italian art historian, critic, and museum professional who played a central role in the study and stewardship of Sienese art throughout the second half of the twentieth century. Born in the hill town of Montisi in the Sienese countryside, he developed an enduring sensitivity to local artistic traditions and devotional imagery. He studied art history at the University of Florence under Mario Salmi, receiving a formation grounded in connoisseurship, contextual analysis, and the critical use of archival sources. Entering the state art-heritage administration after graduation, he eventually became Superintendent of the Soprintendenza per i Beni Artistici e Storici for the provinces of Siena and Grosseto, a role that placed him at the intersection of conservation policy, museum management, and scholarly research. As a scholar, Torriti focused especially on Sienese painting and sculpture from the Duecento to the early modern period, studying artists such as Duccio, Jacopo della Quercia, and the Lorenzetti circle, while also addressing the devotional culture, architecture, and urban image of Siena and its territory, including Pienza and the impact of the Renaissance papacy on local commissions. He curated important exhibitions and restorations, edited catalogues that combined archival documentation, technical analysis, and iconographic discussion, and wrote widely used books and guides such as Siena, storia e capolavori and Arte a Siena, making Sienese art accessible to a broad public without sacrificing scholarly precision. Through his work as superintendent, scholar, and popularizer, he helped define the modern understanding of Sienese art and left a lasting legacy in both academic and museum circles.

Toscano, Bruno

Spoleto, 9 April 1930-

Bruno Toscano is one of the leading Italian art historians of the second half of the twentieth century, as well as a painter, and he has played a fundamental role in the study and preservation of historical and artistic heritage, particularly in Umbria and Italy.

Born in Spoleto in 1930, Toscano initially trained as a painter and, beginning in the 1950s, participated in exhibitions in various Italian cities, joining the so-called "Spoleto Group" within the Informal art movement. He was among the promoters of the "Spoleto Prize" (1953-1963), which helped make the city one of the most vibrant centers of postwar contemporary art, fostering a close dialogue between artistic practice and historical-critical reflection. Parallel to his early work as a painter, he enrolled in the Faculty of Letters at La Sapienza University in Rome and in 1952 published his first study on fourteenth-century Umbrian painting, an early sign of a structural interest in medieval art.

After his formative years, Toscano embarked on a long academic career, becoming a full professor of the History of Art Criticism at the Faculty of Education at La Sapienza and later of the History of Modern Art at the same university. From 1992 to 2002, he taught Modern Art History at Roma Tre University, where he directed the Department of Historical-Artistic, Archaeological, and Conservation Studies, helping to define a strongly interdisciplinary approach to heritage studies. Institutional recognition of his work is reflected in the President of the Republic's Gold Medal for Cultural Merit (2003) and in his appointment, in 2016, as a member of the Scientific Committee of the National Gallery of Umbria.

Toscano's extensive and multifaceted scholarly output spans medieval, modern, and contemporary art history, with studies published in Italian and international books and journals. One of the cornerstones of his work is the definition of criteria for a systematic understanding of Italy's historical and artistic heritage, including not only preserved works but also those lost or stolen, and emphasizing the relationship between artists, patrons, and local contexts. His research on the relationship between museums and their local contexts and on artistic geography aims to reconcile the formal autonomy of the artwork with the multiple cultural, social, and material contexts in which it is created and transmitted, making art history an explicitly critical and problematic discipline.

Alongside art-historical research in the strict sense, Toscano has dedicated numerous contributions to restoration, museology, and heritage policy. In programmatic texts and in works such as the Vademecum for an Art History That Does Not Exist, he proposes tools for interpreting the Italian reality based on awareness of the gaps, dispersions, and stratifications of heritage, calling for the systematic integration of documentation, works in situ, and museum collections. In this context, the museum is never conceived as an isolated entity, but as a node in a network of relationships with the territory, urban and rural memory, and cultural landscapes, particularly in a "laboratory region" such as Umbria.

The relationship with Umbria, his homeland, is a constant in both his artistic practice and his historical-critical reflection, from the pioneering Spoleto in pietre (1963) to his most recent interventions on the city and landscape. Toscano is often presented as a leading figure in the awareness of Umbrian heritage, capable of combining cultural activism, scientific research, and educational activities, and of engaging with local authorities, heritage agencies, and museum institutions. His participation, as a member of the scientific committee, at the National Gallery of Umbria reaffirms this role as a mediator between local communities and the national historical-artistic tradition.

Although he became best known as an art historian, Toscano did not abandon painting, as evidenced by his watercolor exhibitions from 2013 to 2018, accompanied by catalogues that intertwine personal memory, landscape observation, and a critical awareness of the figurative tradition. In these works, that dual identity of artist and scholar emerges, in which the problems of seeing, of constructing space, and of the relationship with historical time are put to the test directly in practice. The same attention to the distinction and dialogue between the preserved and the lost, central to his studies, becomes in painting a meditation on the fragment, on urban or natural detail, and on light, in continuity with his long-standing reflection on Umbrian landscapes.

Tronzo, William

active late 20th-21st century

William Tronzo received his Ph.D. in the History of Art and Architecture from Harvard University (1973-1982) and his undergraduate degree in History from Haverford College (1969-1973). After completing his doctorate he taught at Johns Hopkins University, Duke University, and Tulane University before settling at the University of California, San Diego (UCSD), where he currently holds the position of Senior Teaching Professor in the History of Art, Architecture and Landscape, and serves as Director of European Studies.

Tronzo has held research fellowships and appointments at many of the most prestigious institutions in art-historical scholarship, including the American Academy in Rome, Dumbarton Oaks in Washington, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts (CASVA) at the National Gallery of Art, the Bibliotheca Hertziana in Rome, the École des hautes études en sciences sociales in Paris, the Huntington Library, the Clark Art Institute, and the Stanford Humanities Center. This range of affiliations reflects the interdisciplinary breadth of his work across Byzantine studies, medieval Latin history, Islamic art history, and Renaissance studies.

He is also a member of the Collegio dei Docenti del Dottorato di Ricerca in the Department of Humanistic Studies at Università degli Studi Roma Tre, consolidating his ongoing connection to Italian academic life.

Tronzo's most celebrated and controversial contribution to medieval art history is his monograph The Cultures of His Kingdom: Roger II and the Cappella Palatina in Palermo (Princeton University Press, 1997). The study advanced a major reinterpretation of the Cappella Palatina, arguing that the building in its present form reflects two distinct planning projects with divergent aims in the twelfth century, rather than a single unified program of multicultural display. This thesis generated sustained debate because it challenged the long-dominant narrative of Norman Sicilian harmony and instead emphasized political tension and competing ideological agendas in the chapel's formation. The book remains a standard reference for scholarship on the monument.

His interpretation emphasizes not only decoration, but also patronage process: who commissioned what, in what sequence, and for what political purpose. This focus reflects his broader interest in the relationship between visual culture and power in the medieval world.

Beyond the Cappella Palatina, Tronzo has pursued sustained research on what he calls the hybrid culture of the Italian South, the multicultural civilization of Sicily and southern Italy from the Norman period through the court of Frederick II and into the early Renaissance. He has co-directed major projects on buildings, cities, and landscapes of the later medieval Italian South funded by the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH), as well as a three-year program of research, seminars, and conferences on the medieval Mediterranean at the American Academy in Rome, funded by the Getty Foundation.

His monograph Petrarch's Two Gardens: Landscape and the Image of Movement (Italica Press, 2014) extends this inquiry into the early Renaissance, with a significant opening chapter on La Zisa and La Cuba in Palermo, surviving Fatimid-Norman garden pavilions of the twelfth century. Through these sites, Tronzo explores landscape as a social network and as a mediator of images. The study illustrates his characteristic method: beginning with a specific object or place to open broader questions of cultural exchange, representation, and the movement of ideas across time and space.

He has also published extensively on historiography and method in art history, examining how the discipline constructs narrative and what assumptions underlie scholarly judgment. For research on the art of the twelfth-century Mediterranean, including Monreale and the Cappella Palatina, Fatimid elements in Norman art, and the interplay of Byzantine, Arab, and Latin visual traditions, Tronzo is essential reading. If Jeremy Johns approaches Norman Sicily primarily through documentary and archaeological evidence grounded in Islamic studies, Tronzo approaches it through formal analysis and the interpretation of buildings and images; together, their work offers complementary lenses on Roger II's kingdom and its artistic legacy.

Tsigaridas, Euthymios

active late 20th–21st century

Euthymios Tsigaridas is Professor of Christian Art and Architecture at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. Over a career spanning more than four decades, he has established himself as the foremost living authority on the art of Mount Athos — its mosaics, wall paintings, and portable icons — and one of the most productive scholars of Byzantine and post-Byzantine painting in the Greek-speaking world. His position at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the principal academic institution of northern Greece and the natural intellectual capital of Byzantine Macedonia, has given him both privileged access to the monuments of the Holy Mountain and the institutional standing to produce the monumental publications that the field requires. Throughout his career he has collaborated closely with Dr. Katia Loverdou-Tsigarida, whose expertise in Byzantine metalwork, revetments, and minor arts complements his own focus on monumental painting and portable icons.

Tsigaridas's scholarly career opens with a study of one of the most significant and enigmatic monuments of early Christian and Byzantine Thessaloniki. His monograph Latomou Monastery (The Church of Hosios David), published by the Institute for Balkan Studies in Thessaloniki in 1988 and translated into English by D. Whitehouse, remains the primary scholarly reference for this UNESCO World Heritage monument. The church of Hosios David — the former katholikon of the Latomos Monastery — preserves in its apse one of the most extraordinary mosaics of the early Christian period: a fifth-century Theophania depicting a youthful Christ in a radiant mandorla surrounded by the symbols of the four evangelists and flanked by the prophets Ezekiel and Habakkuk. The mosaic was concealed during the Ottoman occupation of Thessaloniki, rediscovered in 1921, and has since attracted intense scholarly attention for its iconographic programme, its unusual youthful typology of Christ, and its relationship to the broader tradition of apsidal decoration in the early Christian East. Tsigaridas's monograph was the first comprehensive study to integrate the architectural analysis, the mosaic's iconography, and its later medieval fresco decoration into a single scholarly treatment, and it established the interpretive framework within which all subsequent work on the monument has operated. The same year saw the publication of his essay "Monumental Painting in Greek Macedonia during the 15th Century" in the catalogue of the landmark exhibition Holy Image, Holy Space: Icons and Frescoes from Greece (Athens, 1988), addressing a period relatively neglected by Byzantine scholarship in favour of the more celebrated fourteenth-century Palaiologan Renaissance and seeking to characterise the distinct qualities of Macedonian monumental painting in the century of Ottoman conquest and consolidation.

The centrepiece of Tsigaridas's scholarly output on Mount Athos is his sustained engagement with Vatopedi — the second largest and one of the oldest and most richly endowed of the twenty ruling monasteries of the Holy Mountain. On the Holy Mountain, mural mosaics have survived only in the katholikon of the Vatopaidi Monastery; these mosaics, limited in extent but of high artistic quality, were not well known because of their poor state of preservation, and no special study was devoted to them until Tsigaridas filled the gap in 1994. The surviving mosaics comprise four separate subjects — two with the Annunciation, one with the Deisis, and one with a bust of St. Nicholas — belonging to three different periods. His analysis of their date, iconographic programme, and stylistic relationships with Constantinopolitan and Thessalonian workshops addressed a lacuna that Xyngopoulos had identified decades earlier but never fully resolved. "The Mosaics and the Byzantine Wall Paintings," published in the first volume of The Holy and the Great Monastery of Vatopaidi: Tradition, History, Art (Mount Athos, 1998), extended this analysis to the complete ensemble of wall paintings in the monastic complex, including the early fourteenth-century frescoes of the exonarthex of the katholikon. "Portable Icons," published in volume II of Moni Vatopediou in 1996, runs to nearly four hundred pages and constitutes a comprehensive art-historical catalogue of all the portable icons in the Vatopedi collection, proposing attributions to Constantinople, Thessaloniki, or Athos workshops as appropriate.

The magnum opus of this sustained engagement with Vatopedi came in 2007 with Holy Great Monastery of Vatopaidi: Byzantine Icons and Revetments (Monastery of Vatopaidi, 447 pp.), co-authored with Dr. Katia Loverdou-Tsigarida. The first part, written by Tsigaridas, covers the portable icons — describing each work, characterising its style and iconography, and concluding in each case on its date and the probable location where the artist worked, generally choosing between Athos, Constantinople, or Thessaloniki. Robin Cormack, reviewing the volume, described it as a highly important discussion of understudied materials, noting that it offers new information on the history of the Byzantine icon from the thirteenth century onwards — and in particular the fourteenth century — comparable in value to what the progressive publication of the Sinai icons has achieved for that collection. Among the most consequential findings is Tsigaridas's analysis of two royal doors from the monastery's library tower, which he concludes were made by an early fifteenth-century workshop in Constantinople and whose influence on the Russian artist Andrei Rublev he demonstrates — a significant contribution to the question of how late Byzantine artistic models were transmitted across Orthodox Christendom in the final decades before the fall of Constantinople.

Tsigaridas is the principal art-historical authority on the frescoes of the Protaton Church at Karyes — the oldest and most venerated church on Mount Athos and the site of the supreme achievement of the Macedonian School of Byzantine painting. His characterisation of the Panselinos style — the monumentality of the compositions, the autonomy and self-sufficiency of the figures, the delicacy of the colours, and the revival of themes from classical antiquity — established the evaluative vocabulary that all subsequent scholarship has engaged with. He wrote the museological study of the exhibition "Manuel Panselinos: From the Holy Church of the Protaton," organised by the Mount Athos Center in Thessaloniki in April–June 2003 as part of the Cultural Olympics, which presented for the first time an accurate reconstruction of the painted decoration of the Protaton and a second section showing the work attributed to Panselinos including the frescoes of the Chapel of St. Euthymios in the Church of St. Demetrios in Thessaloniki. His analytical passage characterising the style of the Protaton paintings — the olive green shadows, the warm ochre of the flesh, the linear white highlights above the eyebrows, the red parallel lines on the bridge of the nose, the schematisation of the sternum at the base of the neck, the fleshy half-open lips, and the reflective gaze — has served as a reference point in all subsequent attribution debates around Astrapas, Panselinos, and the Macedonian School. He also served as one of the principal contributors to the 700-page catalogue of the 1997 Treasures of Mount Athos exhibition in Thessaloniki, providing the scholarly apparatus for the icon sections and the presentation of key artefacts drawn from the collections of multiple monasteries — the first time that many of these objects had been publicly exhibited outside the Holy Mountain.

Euthymios Tsigaridas occupies a position in Byzantine art history that is, in the most precise sense, irreplaceable: no other scholar has devoted equivalent sustained attention to the art of Mount Athos across its full chronological range, from the early Christian period through the Palaiologan Renaissance to the post-Byzantine era, and across its full material spectrum, from mural mosaics and monumental frescoes to portable icons and metalwork revetments. His monograph on Hosios David, his comprehensive studies of the Vatopedi collections, and his authoritative texts on the Panselinos frescoes of the Protaton together constitute a scholarly corpus without which the understanding of Byzantine art in Macedonia would be fundamentally impoverished. He represents, in the tradition of Xyngopoulos and Chatzidakis before him, the continuation of a distinctly Greek scholarly commitment to the systematic documentation and interpretation of the sacred art of the Orthodox world.

Tuchman, Barbara W.

New York City, 30 January 1912 - Greenwich, 6 February 1989

Barbara W. Tuchman (1912-1989)

Barbara Wertheim Tuchman was an American historian and journalist, twice winner of the Pulitzer Prize, and perhaps the most widely read narrative historian of the second half of the twentieth century. She held no doctorate and never taught in a university, yet she shaped the popular historical imagination of her era more powerfully than most tenured medievalists, a fact of consequence for anyone writing about the fourteenth century today, since her A Distant Mirror (1978) remains, for a very large general readership, the book through which the Trecento is understood.

Born in New York City on 30 January 1912, she was the second of three daughters of the banker Maurice Wertheim and Alma Morgenthau. The family was wealthy, cultivated, and deeply engaged in public life. Her father founded the investment bank Wertheim & Co., owned The Nation, was a founder of the Theatre Guild, and was a serious art collector; his collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings went to the Fogg Museum at Harvard. Her mother founded the Walden School, New York's first progressive school, which Barbara attended, and was a patron of contemporary American music.

Her maternal grandfather was Henry Morgenthau Sr., Woodrow Wilson's ambassador to the Ottoman Empire; her uncle Henry Morgenthau Jr. was Secretary of the Treasury under Franklin Roosevelt. She was, by her own description, a voracious reader from the age of six, formed early by G. A. Henty, Lucy Fitch Perkins, and the historical novels of Alexandre Dumas.

One biographical curiosity she planted quietly in her own work: as a two-year-old travelling with her grandfather's family, she was aboard a steamer that reached Constantinople in August 1914 having witnessed the British pursuit of the German warships Goeben and Breslau. In The Guns of August she describes the arrival of "the daughter, son-in-law and three grandchildren of the American ambassador" without disclosing that one of the grandchildren was herself, a detail she confirmed only later in Practicing History.

She took her B.A. at Radcliffe College in 1933, in history and literature, and never pursued a graduate degree. She was unembarrassed about this and came to argue that the absence of doctoral training had freed her: the discipline of writing for readers rather than for examiners was, in her account, a methodological advantage rather than a deficiency.

After graduating she accompanied her grandfather to the World Economic Conference in London, then worked as a researcher at the American Council of the Institute of Pacific Relations. In 1934-35 she spent a year in Tokyo, a month in Peking, and returned via the Trans-Siberian Railway, Moscow, and Paris. She wrote for Foreign Affairs at twenty-four. As a correspondent for The Nation, the magazine her father owned, she reported from Valencia and Madrid on the Spanish Civil War, sympathetic to the Republican cause. Her first book, The Lost British Policy: Britain and Spain since 1700 (1938), grew out of that work.

In 1940 she married Lester R. Tuchman (1904-1997), an internist and professor of clinical medicine at Mount Sinai. They had three daughters, Lucy, Jessica, and Alma; Jessica Mathews later became president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. During the war she worked on the Far East desk of the Office of War Information. She then spent roughly a decade raising her children while researching what became Bible and Sword: England and Palestine from the Bronze Age to Balfour (1956), after which she produced a book about every four years for the rest of her life.

Major works

  • Bible and Sword (1956)
  • The Zimmermann Telegram (1958)
  • The Guns of August (1962), the prelude to and first month of the First World War. Pulitzer Prize, 1963. Famously read by John F. Kennedy, and often credited with informing his caution during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
  • The Proud Tower: A Portrait of the World Before the War, 1890-1914 (1966)
  • Stilwell and the American Experience in China, 1911-45 (1970/71). Pulitzer Prize, 1972.
  • Notes from China (1972)
  • A Distant Mirror: The Calamitous 14th Century (1978)
  • Practicing History: Selected Essays (1981)
  • The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (1984)
  • The First Salute (1988)

Tuchman practised history as a literary art. She favoured explanatory narrative over archival discovery, and she was explicit that she did not consider it her task to unearth new documents; her gift lay in the shaping of known material into story. She insisted that "the material must precede the thesis," disclaimed any philosophy of history, and set as the historian's first duty staying within the evidence and refusing to judge past cultures by hindsight. One assessment often quoted against her, that she was a layperson's historian rather than a historian's historian, she would probably not have entirely disputed.

In the introduction to A Distant Mirror she formulated the principle that has outlived most of the book's specific claims: the fact of being reported multiplies the apparent extent of any deplorable development several-fold. Disaster looks continuous and ubiquitous in the record because the record is made of disasters; the persistence of ordinary life is systematically underrepresented. This is a genuinely useful corrective, and it applies as much to reading chronicles as to reading newspapers.

Tuchman spent roughly seven years on A Distant Mirror. Her organising device was the life of Enguerrand VII de Coucy (1340-1397), a French nobleman whose lifespan neatly bracketed the century, whose marriage to Isabella, eldest daughter of Edward III, gave him a foot in both kingdoms, and who was present at or near most of the era's decisive events, dying in Ottoman captivity after the catastrophe at Nicopolis. Around him she assembled the Hundred Years' War, the Black Death, the Papal Schism, the free companies, the Jacquerie and other risings, persecution of Jews, and, unusually for a popular history of the period, the Little Ice Age and the material conditions of every social class.

The title declares the thesis: the fourteenth century as a mirror of the twentieth, a violent and disordered age legible to a readership living through Vietnam.

Popular reception was enthusiastic; scholarly reception was not. The main lines of criticism are worth knowing precisely, because they bear on how the book can responsibly be cited:

  • Charles T. Wood, reviewing in Speculum, allowed her narrative power but judged the book dated and old-fashioned in conception, and argued that it was shaped by American political preoccupations of the late 1960s and early 1970s, that is, the mirror distorted in the direction its maker was facing.
  • Bernard S. Bachrach (1979) objected to her dependence on secondary literature and on old translations of the medieval narrative sources rather than archival work, and to the thinness of the critical apparatus and gaps in the bibliography.
  • David Donald, in Commentary, made the structural objection: too little is known about Coucy to carry the weight placed on him. No authentic likeness survives; almost nothing of his words or opinions remains; the sole preserved detail of his appearance is that he went bald. Tuchman is therefore repeatedly driven to constructions of the he doubtless saw / he may have known variety. Worse, because Coucy's actual role in events was consistently secondary, sustaining him as protagonist forced her to narrate the whole Hundred Years' War at a scale disproportionate to her subject.

Underlying all three is her heavy reliance on Froissart, a chronicler whose flattery, chronological looseness, and aristocratic sympathies are precisely what modern scholarship has learned to discount, an irony, given that Tuchman's own Law describes the problem exactly.

A Distant Mirror is not a source. It is a reception-history document: the single most important vector by which the "calamitous fourteenth century" (plague, schism, chivalric collapse) entered the general imagination in the English-speaking world. When a museum label, a documentary, or a lay reader treats the Trecento as an age of catastrophe whose art is best read as a response to trauma, Tuchman is very often the unacknowledged ancestor of that framing.

For work on Italian art this matters in a specific way. The "calamitous" model is French- and northern-centred, built on the Hundred Years' War, and it fits Italy badly: Balduccio was carving in Milan for the Visconti in the 1330s and 1340s, in a peninsula whose crisis chronology, patronage structures, and civic institutions ran on different rhythms. Millard Meiss's Painting in Florence and Siena after the Black Death (1951) had already proposed a trauma-driven reading of Italian art, and that thesis has been substantially contested since. Tuchman is useful to cite as evidence of how the century has been imagined; she is not useful as evidence of what happened in it.

Her Law, though, is worth keeping. Applied to Trecento sources, chronicles, obituaries, records of catastrophe, it is a sound warning that the archive over-reports rupture and under-reports the workshop that simply kept working.

She won the Pulitzer Prize for General Non-Fiction twice (1963, 1972) and the St. Louis Literary Award (1971), was elected a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1978), and served as the first woman president of the American Academy of Arts and Letters. Her books were translated into some thirteen languages. A tower of Currier House at Harvard is named for her; a graduate paper prize in historical international relations carries her name.

She died in Greenwich, Connecticut, on 6 February 1989, of complications following a stroke. Her papers are at Yale University Library (Barbara Wertheim Tuchman papers, MS 574).

U

Unterkircher, Franz

St. Jakob in Defereggen, 29 September 1904 – Vienna, 28 January 1989

Franz Unterkircher was born on 29 September 1904 in St. Jakob in Defereggen, a remote village in the Defereggen valley of East Tyrol, then part of the Austrian Empire. He attended the Gymnasium in Brixen from 1914 to 1922 — schooling in that ancient episcopal city which had been Austrian territory when he began his studies but became Italian under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919, a transition that unfolded around him during his secondary education. He then studied scholastic philosophy and theology at the University of Innsbruck, completing the doctorate in theology in 1932. He died on 28 January 1989 in Vienna, at the age of eighty-four; an obituary and assessment was published the following year by Eva Irblich in Codices manuscripti 15 (1990), and his estate is held in the inventory of scholarly and cultural papers at the ÖNB.

The theological formation at Innsbruck — an institution with deep Jesuit roots — placed Unterkircher within the tradition of scholastic method, a rigorous training in textual analysis and deep familiarity with the liturgical and devotional literature of the medieval Church. These foundations would prove directly serviceable to his later work on liturgical manuscripts, Books of Hours, and Carolingian sacramentaries.

In 1939 he was forcibly retired from his post for political reasons. Austria had been annexed by the Third Reich in March 1938, and the Nazi regime's systematic dismantling of Catholic educational institutions and the suppression of clerical academic life followed swiftly. Rather than retreating from scholarly life, Unterkircher pivoted with striking intellectual energy: he studied art history at the University of Vienna, completing a second doctorate in 1942 with the dissertation Der Sinn der deutschen Doppelchöre (The Meaning of German Double Choirs), a study of the structural and symbolic function of the double-choir arrangement in medieval German ecclesiastical architecture that bridges his theological training and his emerging art-historical identity, treating architectural form as liturgical expression. From 1943 he worked at the Bundesdenkmalamt — the Federal Monuments Office responsible for the documentation and protection of Austria's cultural heritage — before taking a position at the library of the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.

In 1947 Unterkircher moved to the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, whose manuscript collection he directed from 1950 to 1969. The Handschriftensammlung of the ÖNB is one of the most important repositories of medieval manuscripts in the world, holding thousands of codices ranging from late antique papyri and early medieval Gospel books to the great Flemish illuminated masterpieces of the Burgundian court. Unterkircher's nineteen years as its head produced two parallel bodies of work: a systematic programme of scholarly cataloguing, and a sustained effort to make the collection's greatest treasures accessible through facsimile editions.

The most structurally significant of Unterkircher's contributions to the scholarly infrastructure of manuscript studies was his leadership of the Katalog der abendländischen Handschriften der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek — Series nova, produced jointly with Otto Mazal between 1963 and 1997, which constitutes the authoritative finding guide for researchers working with the collection. Parallel to this, Unterkircher directed and largely authored the Austrian contribution to the international series of catalogues of dated Latin-script manuscripts. The volumes Die datierten Handschriften der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek appeared in four parts between 1969 and 1976, covering manuscripts up to 1400, 1401–1450, 1451–1500, and 1501–1600 respectively, each with a text volume and a plates volume. He then extended the series to the Viennese collections outside the ÖNB: Die datierten Handschriften in Wien außerhalb der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek bis zum Jahre 1600, with catalogue descriptions by Heidelinde Horninger and Franz Lackner, appeared in 1981 in two parts.

Catalogues of dated manuscripts occupy a peculiar but essential position in the discipline. By identifying every manuscript that carries an explicit date — whether in a colophon, a dedication, a calendar entry, or an internal reference — they provide the fixed points against which undated manuscripts can be calibrated. In the method pioneered by E. A. Lowe and carried forward by Bernhard Bischoff, dated exemplars are the anchors of palaeographic chronology. Unterkircher's contribution to this framework for the Austrian collections gave subsequent researchers the chronological armature needed for localising and dating the thousands of manuscripts in the ÖNB and the collections surrounding it.

Alongside the technical cataloguing work, Unterkircher developed an equally significant role as interpreter and editor of the ÖNB's greatest treasures, working closely with the Akademische Druck- und Verlagsanstalt (ADEVA) in Graz — the publisher that, under his intellectual guidance and that of his colleagues, established itself as the world's leading producer of scholarly facsimile editions of illuminated manuscripts. His introductory survey Abendländische Buchmalerei: Miniaturen aus Handschriften der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek (Vienna, 1966), published in English translation by Thames & Hudson in 1967 as European Illuminated Manuscripts in the Austrian National Library, presented sixty full-colour plates with discussion of illumination from the eighth century to the late sixteenth, and served as the standard introduction to the collection for decades.

Among his most celebrated editorial achievements was his contribution to the facsimile edition of the Hours of Mary of Burgundy (Codex Vindobonensis 1857), produced by ADEVA in 1969 with a commentary volume by Unterkircher and Antoine de Schryver. Completed in Flanders around 1477, probably for Mary, ruler of the Burgundian Netherlands, the manuscript contains 187 folios with 24 calendar roundels, 20 full-page miniatures, and 16 quarter-page illustrations, its foremost illuminator being the artist known as the Master of Mary of Burgundy. It has been described as among the most important works of art made in the late Middle Ages. Unterkircher's editorial work placed this pinnacle of Flemish manuscript illumination before the scholarly community in a form that could be studied independently of the fragile original.

He devoted comparable attention to the Livre du cœur d'amour épris (Codex Vindobonensis 2597) by King René of Anjou, whose sixteen extraordinary miniatures are among the most poetically conceived and technically accomplished paintings in any surviving manuscript. His presentation of the miniatures, published as Vom liebentbrannten Herzen (ADEVA, Graz, 1975) and simultaneously in a French edition with Daniel Poirion and Marie-Thérèse Gousset, introduced the allegorical imagery of this late medieval masterpiece — with its nocturnal tonalities, fantastic landscapes, and personifications of the inner life — to a wide international readership. His study of the Drogo Sacramentary (Paris, Bibliothèque nationale, MS lat. 9428), published in 1977 as Zur Ikonographie und Liturgie des Drogo-Sakramentars, brought his theological formation directly to bear on a monument of Carolingian book illumination — written and painted around 850 AD for the personal use of Drogo, Bishop of Metz, a son of Charlemagne — uniting iconographic analysis with liturgical exegesis in a way that few scholars, lacking his combination of theological and art-historical training, could have achieved. In 1983 he published Maximilian I: Ein kaiserlicher Auftraggeber illustrierter Handschriften, a study of Emperor Maximilian I as a commissioner of illustrated manuscripts. His final book, Tiere, Glaube, Aberglaube: Die schönsten Miniaturen aus dem Bestiarium (Graz, 1986), drew on the bestiary tradition in medieval manuscript illumination, tracing the intersection of natural history, theology, and visual imagination in one of the most characteristic genres of medieval manuscript art.

Unterkircher's career traces a remarkable arc across the disruptions of the twentieth century — from a Tyrolean theological education to forced removal under National Socialism, from a wartime pivot to art history to the postwar reconstruction of Austrian cultural institutions, and ultimately to the directorship of one of Europe's greatest manuscript repositories. What makes his trajectory unusual is not only its resilience but its coherence: the liturgical sensibility formed in Innsbruck, the architectural vision of his second doctorate, and the intense engagement with devotional manuscripts — Books of Hours, sacramentaries, bestiaries — all draw on the same formation. For the historian of illuminated manuscripts, his legacy operates on two complementary levels. The Katalog der datierten Handschriften provides the dateable chronological anchors on which manuscript scholarship depends, extending the international network of such catalogues to the Austrian collections. The facsimile editions — produced at a time when high-quality colour reproduction of complete manuscripts was technically ambitious and financially formidable — made the greatest treasures of the ÖNB, above all the Hours of Mary of Burgundy and the Cœur d'amour épris, permanently accessible to researchers who could not travel to Vienna. In both respects his work remains active and indispensable.

Ussher, James

Dublin, 4 January 1581 – Reigate, Surrey, 21 March 1656

James Ussher was Church of Ireland Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland, and one of the most formidable scholars and book collectors of seventeenth-century Britain and Ireland. He is remembered today chiefly for his biblical chronology, but his contemporaries valued him at least as highly as a patristic textual critic and historian of the early British and Irish churches, and his personal library became, after his death, the founding acquisition of what is now the Library of Trinity College Dublin.

Ussher was born in Dublin on 4 January 1581, the son of Arland Ussher, a clerk in chancery, and Margaret Stanihurst, whose father James Stanihurst had been speaker of the Irish House of Commons; his brother Ambrose Ussher became a noted scholar of Arabic and Hebrew. James entered the newly founded Trinity College Dublin on 9 January 1594, at the age of thirteen, among the first cohort of students at an institution barely two years old. He took his B.A. by 1598 and his M.A. by 1600 or 1601, was elected a fellow, and was ordained deacon in 1602. In 1613 he married Phoebe Challoner, daughter of a former vice-provost of the college; their only child, Elizabeth, was born in 1619.

His ecclesiastical and academic career advanced together. He became Chancellor of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, in 1605, and in 1607 was appointed Professor of Theological Controversies at Trinity, the university's senior chair in divinity. He was consecrated Bishop of Meath in 1621 and translated to the archbishopric of Armagh — the primatial see of the whole Irish church — in 1625, an office he held until his death thirty-one years later.

Ussher's scholarship pursued several distinct programmes at once. His Discourse of the Religion Anciently Professed by the Irish and British (1622, expanded 1631) argued that the early insular Church had held doctrines closer to the reformed than to the Roman position, a polemical thesis that gave the Church of Ireland an ancient pedigree independent of the papacy, and his Britannicarum Ecclesiarum Antiquitates (1639) was the most substantial history of the British churches produced to that date. In patristics his most durable achievement was his 1644 edition of the epistles of Ignatius of Antioch, in which he identified the shorter Middle Recension as the authentic corpus against the interpolated Long Recension that had circulated for centuries — a piece of textual criticism later vindicated in its essentials by nineteenth-century scholarship and still cited as a landmark in the history of the discipline.

It is on his chronological work that Ussher's wider fame rests. In Annales Veteris Testamenti (1650) and its continuation Annalium Pars Posterior (1654), he synthesised biblical genealogies with ancient Near Eastern and astronomical chronography to construct a continuous dated history of the world from Creation — placed at nightfall on the eve of 23 October 4004 BC — down to the fall of Jerusalem. The dates were later printed in the margins of many editions of the King James Bible, and "4004 BC" became, for generations of readers, effectively synonymous with the idea of biblical chronology itself, a popular afterlife that has obscured how the Annales was received in its own day: as a work of rigorous, up-to-date scholarship, drawing on the best available classical and Near Eastern sources, by a scholar whose command of the ancient chronographic literature was unmatched among his contemporaries.

The Irish Rebellion of October 1641 cost Ussher his revenues and much of his property in Ireland, and he never returned. Parliament voted him a pension of £400, and Charles I assigned him the income of the vacant see of Carlisle; from January 1642 he lived at royalist Oxford, then successively at Bristol, Cardiff and St Donat's Castle as the Civil War shifted around him, before settling in London in 1646 under the protection of Elizabeth, Dowager Countess of Peterborough. Parliament's abolition of episcopacy stripped him of the Carlisle income in October 1646, and he spent his final years as a preacher at Lincoln's Inn, a royalist bishop surviving on the goodwill of parliamentarian friends. He was present at the execution of Charles I in January 1649, watching from the Countess's house, and is said to have fainted before the axe fell.

Ussher died at the Countess of Peterborough's house at Reigate, Surrey, on 21 March 1656. Despite his lifelong royalism, Oliver Cromwell insisted on a state funeral, and Ussher was buried in the Chapel of St Erasmus in Westminster Abbey on 17 April 1656 — a mark of the respect in which his scholarship was held even by his political opponents. His library of some ten thousand books and manuscripts, one of the great private collections of the age and reportedly sought by both the King of Denmark and Cardinal Mazarin, could not simply be given to Trinity College as he had hoped: his straitened finances required that it be left as the sole provision for his widowed daughter. Cromwell forbade its export from the country, and the officers and soldiers of the army in Ireland subscribed a sum — usually given as £2,200, though a figure of £2,500 also appears in the record — to purchase the collection for a library in Dublin. The books were held at Dublin Castle from about 1658, exposed to some loss, until the Restoration, when they were formally granted to Trinity College Dublin in 1661, nominally as the gift of Charles II.

That bequest transformed Trinity's library into one of the great manuscript repositories of the British Isles, and Ussher's name still attaches to a number of its most celebrated holdings, including the two Gospel books catalogued as the Codex Usserianus Primus and the Codex Usserianus Secundus (the Garland of Howth). As the codicological literature on the Primus is careful to stress, however, no direct evidence places either manuscript in Ussher's own hands: the name records the collection through which each book reached Trinity, not a documented act of personal ownership. Ussher survives in the library's holdings, in other words, chiefly as a mark of institutional inheritance — a distinction his own exacting historical method would very likely have insisted upon.

V

Valagussa, Giovanni Francesco Maria

Milan, 1963 –

Giovanni Francesco Maria Valagussa (born 1963, Milan) is one of Italy's most distinguished art historians specializing in medieval and Renaissance painting, best known for his long tenure as curator of the Accademia Carrara in Bergamo and his fundamental contributions to the study of Italian Trecento and Quattrocento art.

Valagussa graduated in Lettere with a specialization in Art History from the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan, where the eminent Hungarian-Italian medievalist Miklos Boskovits served as co-supervisor of his thesis. This formative relationship with Boskovits, one of the great connoisseurs of Italian medieval painting, would leave a lasting imprint on his scholarly approach. He then deepened his training at the prestigious Fondazione Roberto Longhi in Florence, studying under Mina Gregori, and subsequently completed his PhD at the Università degli Studi di Torino under the guidance of Giovanni Romano. His educational path from 1982 to 1994 thus united three of Italy's most rigorous schools of art historical connoisseurship.

After a brief period teaching in secondary schools in Milan following his graduation, Valagussa entered the museum world by winning a competitive examination for the post of conservatore at the Museo Civico Ala Ponzone in Cremona (1998-1999), an experience he did not find entirely fulfilling. He subsequently held the role of conservator at the Accademia Tadini in Lovere (2000-2001), a small but significant institution on Lake Iseo, where he worked with great satisfaction. Simultaneously, beginning in 1998, he began teaching regularly at the Università Cattolica, both in Milan and in Brescia, offering courses in art history and museology that he has continued to this day.

In 2001, Valagussa won the competitive selection for the position of conservator at the Accademia Carrara in Bergamo, a contest promoted by the then-director Francesco Rossi. He would remain in that role for over twenty years, until April 2022, becoming the institution's most enduring scholarly figure of the modern era. During the museum's lengthy closure for renovation (2008-2015), he was the principal curator of the Accademia Carrara's travelling exhibitions, bringing the collection to Lausanne, Rome, Brussels, Canberra, and Moscow, among other international venues. He also co-curated with Simone Facchinetti important publications on the collection, including catalogues covering Italian Renaissance and eighteenth-century painting.

Valagussa's most significant single publication is the Catalogo completo dei dipinti italiani del Trecento e Quattrocento dell'Accademia Carrara (Officina Libraria, 2018), the first volume of the museum's scientific catalogues. The work is notable for introducing a number of relevant new attributions and providing a complete bibliographic apparatus for the collection, making it an essential reference for anyone working on Italian medieval and early Renaissance painting. His attribution of a Virgin and Child (Forli, Pinacoteca Civica) to the Master of the Borgo Crucifix is among the scholarly contributions that have drawn international attention, cited even in the National Gallery's catalogues. Beyond the catalogue, he has published numerous essays and articles focusing primarily on medieval and Renaissance art.

Throughout his career, Valagussa has curated a wide range of major monographic exhibitions, including those dedicated to Fra Galgario, Giovanni Battista Moroni (Piccio), Carlo Ceresa, and Andrea Mantegna. In 2017, he co-curated the exhibition Serenissime Trame at the Ca' d'Oro in Venice. In 2021, he organized an exhibition of masterpieces from the Accademia Carrara in Shanghai, demonstrating the international reach of his curatorial work. He has also presented individual works for broader public audiences, including a presentation of Lorenzo Lotto's Madonna col Bambino e i santi Giovanni Battista e Caterina d'Alessandria for RAI Radio 3's Museo Nazionale.

Since January 2022, following the conclusion of his curatorial post, Valagussa has continued as a studioso associated with the Comune di Bergamo and remains a docente a contratto in the Department of History, Archaeology, and Art History at the Università Cattolica. He is described by those who know him as a reserved and modest person (una persona schiva, modesta), dedicated entirely to scholarship rather than public visibility. Married with two children, he has spent much of his professional life in the Bergamo area, contributing enormously to the visibility and scholarly reputation of one of northern Italy's most important picture galleries. His expertise in the attributional study of medieval Italian painting, shaped by the Boskovits and Longhi traditions, makes him a key reference figure for researchers working on Trecento and Quattrocento art today.

Valentiner, Wilhelm

Karlsruhe, 2 May 1880 - Raleigh, 6 September 1958

Wilhelm Reinhold Valentiner, known in the United States as William R. Valentiner, was a German-American art historian, connoisseur, critic, and museum director trained in the tradition of Wilhelm von Bode. He transplanted German museum scholarship into American museology in the decades before the wartime diaspora of German scholars and is remembered chiefly as a Rembrandt authority and as the architect of the modern Detroit Institute of Arts.

Valentiner was born on 2 May 1880 in Karlsruhe, the youngest of four children. His father, Karl Wilhelm Valentiner, was an astronomer and professor at Heidelberg, and his mother, Anna Lepsius Valentiner, belonged to the distinguished Lepsius family of scholars. He attended schools in Karlsruhe and Heidelberg before studying at the universities of Leipzig and Heidelberg, where Henry Thode supervised his doctorate on Rembrandt and his environment.

He then trained in the Netherlands, working alongside Cornelis Hofstede de Groot and Abraham Bredius and serving as Bredius's assistant at the Mauritshuis in The Hague. On the strength of this early work he was called to Berlin by Wilhelm von Bode, under whom he worked at the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum and the Kunstgewerbemuseum. In that environment he absorbed Bode's encyclopedic conception of the museum and the connoisseur's method of attribution by eye, which remained central to his later career.

Around 1907-08 Valentiner moved to New York to become the first curator of the newly created department of decorative arts at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He returned to Germany during the First World War and served in the German army until 1918, then worked again at the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum and chaired the Arbeitsrat fur Kunst, placing him at the centre of Berlin's avant-garde. In 1919 he married Marie Cecilia Odefey; their daughter Brigitta later married the sculptor Harry Bertoia.

Valentiner returned to the United States in 1921, first cataloguing the Widener collection and advising on acquisitions, then organising one of the first American exhibitions of German Expressionism in New York. In 1924 he was appointed director of the Detroit Institute of Arts, a post he held until his retirement in 1944-45. His Detroit years were his most consequential institutional achievement: he built a curatorial staff, pursued an encyclopedic collection, acquired German Expressionism, Pre-Columbian art, and African art, and commissioned Diego Rivera's monumental Detroit Industry murals under Edsel Ford's patronage. He also founded Art Quarterly and helped shape the 1939 Chicago World's Fair art exhibition.

After leaving Detroit he continued to advise museums in Los Angeles and California, and in 1955 became the first director of the North Carolina Museum of Art in Raleigh, holding the post until his death. Alongside his Rembrandt studies he produced an influential body of work on Dutch and Flemish painting, including the survey The Art of the Low Countries, catalogues of Rembrandt and Frans Hals, and late in life Rembrandt and Spinoza (1957). His attributions should now be read historically, since many were later revised by the Rembrandt Research Project.

Valentiner's significance for medievalists lies in a set of early studies on Italian Gothic sculpture, especially Tino di Camaino. His 1923 article on Tino in Art in America, his 1925 study of Gothic sculpture from Siena and Pisa, and his 1935 monograph Tino di Camaino: A Sienese Sculptor of the Fourteenth Century helped establish the first modern anglophone framework for the sculptor's work. That framework mattered directly for the study of Giovanni di Balduccio, since Tino's sepulchral forms became the model that Balduccio carried northward in works such as the Arca di San Pietro Martire at Sant'Eustorgio.

Valentiner worked in the grand connoisseurial manner of the Bode school, relying on attribution by eye, expansive corpora, and close involvement with the art market. The method produced real discoveries but also many attributions that later scholarship has narrowed or rejected, both in the Rembrandt corpus and in Italian sculpture. He is best treated as a foundational but dated source: indispensable for the history of the discipline and provisional on specific attributions.

He received the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1957 and died on 6 September 1958, while serving as director of the North Carolina Museum of Art. His papers survive in the Smithsonian's Archives of American Art and the North Carolina Museum of Art, and his influence remains visible in the transatlantic museum culture he helped shape.

Van Marle, Raimond

The Hague, 1887 – Perugia, 18 November 1936

Valentin Raimond Silvain van Marle was a Dutch art historian of remarkable versatility and ambition, best remembered today as the author of the monumental The Development of the Italian Schools of Painting - a work that remains one of the most comprehensive surveys of Italian painting ever attempted. Though largely self-funded and working outside the formal academy, he produced a body of scholarship that still serves as a fundamental reference for anyone studying medieval and Renaissance Italian art.

Van Marle was born in The Hague in 1887 to a family of mixed European origins: his mother was Hungarian and his father was of distant Picard descent, which explains the French-sounding surname. In 1906, at the age of nineteen, he moved to Paris to pursue higher studies, enrolling at two of France's most prestigious scholarly institutions - the Ecole des Chartes, renowned for its training in the analysis of historical documents and manuscripts, and the Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes. In 1910 he was awarded a doctorate from the Sorbonne, a considerable intellectual achievement that shaped his rigorous, source-based approach to historical inquiry.

His first published works were not about Italian art but about medieval Northern European history and philosophy. In 1908 - while still a student - he published Le Comte de Hollande sous Philippe le Bon, a study of the County of Holland under Philip the Good of Burgundy. In 1916 he produced a Dutch-language monograph on the German mystic Meister Eckhart, titled De mystieke leer van Meister Eckhart, demonstrating his command of both religious thought and vernacular scholarship. These early works revealed a scholar equally at ease with political history, mystical theology, and archival research.

The decisive turning point in van Marle's life came in 1918, when, following his marriage, he relocated to a villa in the San Marco district of Perugia, in the heart of Umbria. Blessed with a private income that freed him from institutional obligations, he committed himself entirely to the study of Italian painting. Perugia was an ideal base: surrounded by Umbrian altarpieces, frescoes, and the artistic heritage of central Italy, he could conduct direct visual research while corresponding with scholars across Europe. He began contributing regularly to the Bollettino d'Arte and other international specialist journals, establishing himself as a serious voice in the growing field of Italian art history.

Van Marle's supreme achievement was the encyclopaedic The Development of the Italian Schools of Painting, a project of almost inconceivable scope covering Italian painting from the Romanesque era to the end of the fifteenth century. Published between 1923 and 1938 in Dutch, French, English, and Italian, the work was originally planned in 21 volumes, though van Marle lived to complete only 17 of them. After his death in 1936, the art historian Frederick Mason Perkins and his widow Charlotte van Marle continued the work, completing the 19th volume and the general index. The first two volumes were subsequently translated into Italian by Alba Buitoni in 1938. The series remains a touchstone for scholars of medieval and early Renaissance Italian painting, offering detailed artist-by-artist and school-by-school analysis that has not been fully superseded.

Beyond Italian painting, van Marle turned his attention to the broader visual culture of the medieval period. His two-volume Iconographie de l'art profane au Moyen-Age et a la Renaissance, et la decoration des demeures (1931-1932) explored secular iconography - the imagery of everyday life, allegory, and decoration that adorned private dwellings alongside the more thoroughly studied religious art of the period. This work demonstrated his sensitivity to sociological dimensions of art history, treating images not merely as aesthetic objects but as documents of medieval and Renaissance culture and society.

Van Marle was also a collector of photographic documentation, and his personal photo library became part of a distinguished archival tradition. His collection is preserved today at the Fondazione Giorgio Cini in Venice, alongside the photographic archives of scholars such as Evelyn Sandberg Vavala - a testament to the importance of visual documentation in early twentieth-century art historical method.

Van Marle was part of an international network of art historians active in Italy during the interwar period. His name appears in the correspondence archives related to Belle da Costa Greene, the celebrated director of the Morgan Library, connecting him to the transatlantic circuits of medieval manuscript scholarship and connoisseurship. His collaboration with Frederick Mason Perkins - himself a specialist in Sienese and Umbrian painting - further anchored him within the community of foreign scholars who made central Italy their intellectual home.

Van Marle died in Perugia on 18 November 1936, with two further manuscripts still in preparation. The political climate of Fascist Italy cast a shadow even over his burial: the regime's hostility toward foreign scholars meant that he could not be interred in the city where he had lived and worked for nearly two decades. Instead, he was buried in the remote village of Pozzale, a district of Pieve di Cadore in the Dolomites - a poignant geographical displacement that reflects the precarious position of cosmopolitan scholarship under nationalist politics. His work was nonetheless reissued in the postwar period, with Hacker Art Books producing a reprint edition as late as 1970, confirming the enduring utility of his surveys for generations of art historians.

van Os, Hendrik Willem

Harderwijk, 28 February 1938 - 14 June 2025

Hendrik Willem van Os (28 February 1938 - 14 June 2025) was a Dutch art historian. He served as professor of Art and Cultural History, director of the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, and presenter of television programs on art. In the specific field of Italian medieval and early Renaissance painting, he was the author of the most comprehensive treatment of Sienese altarpiece production from the thirteenth through the fifteenth century produced in the twentieth century - a two-volume work that established the functional study of the altarpiece as a scholarly programme and whose influence has been permanent and wide.
