That the same scholar directed the Rijksmuseum and presented popular television programmes on art to a mass Dutch audience in the same years he was producing his most rigorous scholarly work makes him, among the historians encountered in this research thread, one of the most unusual in the range of his public and institutional commitments.

Hendrik Willem van Os (Harderwijk, 28 February 1938) studied History and Art History at the University of Groningen from 1957-1964, where he also obtained his doctorate cum laude with a thesis entitled "Iconological problems in Sienese painting from 1300-1450." While working on his PhD, he resided in Florence and Siena for several years.

Henk van Os studied art history at the University of Groningen, where his father, Frederik van Os, served as rector magnificus during two terms. The institutional connection between the van Os family and Groningen was thus biographical as well as intellectual: his formation in the university where his father held its highest office embedded him in a specific institutional culture that shaped his later commitment to the public responsibilities of the senior academic. He also spent time studying in Rome - the essential Italian complement to his Sienese specialization - before completing his doctorate in 1969.

The doctoral dissertation, published in German as Marias Demut und Verherrlichung in der sienesischen Malerei 1300-1450 (Mary's Humility and Glorification in Sienese Painting 1300-1450, The Hague, 1969), established the programmatic concerns that would govern his scholarly work for the next fifty years: the iconological analysis of religious imagery, the specific tradition of Sienese Marian devotion, and the function of images as instruments of prayer and theological statement rather than purely as aesthetic objects. The German-language publication - unusual for a Dutch scholar's doctoral work - signalled an immediate orientation toward the international German-language art historical community that had dominated the field of Italian medieval painting since Schmarsow and his successors.

In parallel with the doctoral dissertation, Van Os produced the first of his contributions to the study of Italian paintings in Dutch collections: Sienese Paintings in Holland (Groningen, 1969) and, in collaboration with Marian Bisanz-Prakken, The Florentine Paintings in Holland 1300-1500 (Amsterdam: De Arbeiderspers/Netherlands Institute for Art History, 1974). These catalogues of Italian medieval and Renaissance panels in Dutch public and private collections performed a service analogous to Luisa Marcucci's catalogue of the Florentine national collections - systematic documentation of a defined corpus, providing the scholarly community with reliable physical descriptions, attributions, and bibliographic apparatus for objects that had not previously been comprehensively treated.

His 1974 monograph Vecchietta and the Sacristy of the Siena Hospital Church: A Study in Renaissance Religious Symbolism (New York: A. Schram, 1974) turned the lens onto a single Sienese painter-sculptor of the mid-fifteenth century and a single institutional commission - the painted programme of the sacristy of the Spedale di Santa Maria della Scala - in a study that combined attributional analysis with the kind of contextual interpretation, rooted in the specific liturgical and civic function of the decorated space, that would become his signature method.

Van Os was appointed professor of Art and Cultural History at the University of Groningen in 1974, and subsequently became dean of the Faculty of Arts in 1984. The fifteen years between his professorial appointment and his move to the Rijksmuseum were the period of his most sustained scholarly production. He continued to publish on Italian painting in Dutch collections - the Early Venetian Paintings in Holland (Maarssen: G. Schwartz, 1978) extended his systematic catalogue work to the Venetian school - while simultaneously conducting the research that would produce his major scholarly monument.

The two-volume Sienese Altarpieces, 1215-1460: Form, Content, Function (Groningen: Bouma's Boekhuis, 1984 and 1990) is Van Os's principal scholarly legacy. Volume I covers the period 1215-1344 - from the earliest surviving examples of the Sienese altarpiece tradition through the death of Simone Martini; Volume II extends to 1460, covering the post-plague generation and the Quattrocento. His many publications include Mariological Themes in Sienese Painting: The Art of Devotion in the Late Middle Ages in Europe and Sienese Altarpieces, 1215-1460: Form, Content, Function.

The title's three terms - Form, Content, Function - are the programmatic declaration of Van Os's method. Where earlier scholarship on Italian altarpieces had concentrated primarily on formal and attributional questions (who painted it, when, in what style), Van Os insisted on the necessity of understanding the altarpiece as a functional object: an artefact designed for a specific liturgical setting, addressing a specific congregation, in service of specific patterns of devotion shaped by the particular theology, hagiography, and institutional culture of its commissioners. The Tarlati Polyptych, commissioned by Guido Tarlati for the high altar of Santa Maria della Pieve; the Orsini Polyptych, designed for Cardinal Napoleone Orsini's private prayer: both are illuminated by this methodology, which asks not only what an altarpiece represents but what it was for.

The Sienese Altarpieces is cited in every subsequent serious study of the Sienese Trecento - in the literature on Duccio, Simone Martini, the Lorenzetti brothers, Sassetta, and Giovanni di Paolo - as the standard systematic treatment of the context within which each of these painters' works functioned. The range of material covered, from the earliest surviving Sienese frontal paintings of the early Duecento to the late Quattrocento works that close the medieval tradition, encompasses the entire arc of Sienese devotional painting, making it the Sienese equivalent of what Erling Skaug attempted for Florentine punch marks or what Lambros attempted for the Athonite manuscript catalogue: a comprehensive scholarly survey that provides the foundational reference for all subsequent work.

From 1989 to 1996, Van Os was general director of the Rijksmuseum. The directorship of the Rijksmuseum - the principal museum of the Netherlands and one of the great encyclopaedic collections in the world, housing Rembrandt's Night Watch, Vermeer's The Milkmaid, and the most comprehensive collection of Dutch Golden Age painting in existence - was the institutional pinnacle available to a Dutch art historian. Van Os brought to it the same combination of scholarly rigour and public commitment that had characterized his Groningen years.

He organised numerous exhibitions, such as "Prayer Embedded in Beauty" (Gebed in Schoonheid). This exhibition, presented in 1994-95, brought together forty-four objects of private medieval devotion from Dutch and other collections - ivory diptychs, small panel paintings, Books of Hours, sculpted altarpieces, limewood Christ children - and presented them not as art objects but as instruments of prayer, each addressed to a specific kind of devotee: nun, duke, pilgrim, merchant wife. The exhibition and its accompanying publication, The Art of Devotion in the Late Middle Ages in Europe, 1300-1500 (Princeton University Press, 1994), translated the functional methodology of the Sienese Altarpieces into a format accessible to the general museum-going public while maintaining its scholarly integrity. For Alberto's research on illuminated manuscripts and private devotional objects, The Art of Devotion remains a foundational reference: the analysis of the Book of Hours as a specifically tailored instrument of lay piety - its calendar personalized, its devotional emphases calibrated to the owner's particular needs, its images selected to support the prayers that frame each of the canonical hours - draws directly on Van Os's insistence that medieval religious objects must be understood through the devotional practices they were designed to serve.

During his Rijksmuseum directorship, Van Os also developed the television work for which he became most widely known to the Dutch public. Van Os became widely known to the public through his presentation of TV programs such as Beeldenstorm (AVRO) and Museumschatten (VARA), which aimed to popularize art, especially painting. The programme Museumschatten (Museum Treasures) invited Van Os to present individual works from the national collection in terms accessible to a general audience, drawing on his gifts as a teacher and communicator to make the specific visual and historical arguments of art history legible to viewers with no prior preparation. The programme reached audiences of millions and established Van Os as the most publicly recognized art historian in the Netherlands - a position analogous to that which Kenneth Clark had occupied in Britain through the Civilisation series a generation earlier.

In 1996, he stepped down as director of the Rijksmuseum and was appointed University Professor holding the chair in Art and Society at the University of Amsterdam (UvA). The chair title - Art and Society rather than Art History - reflected the programmatic commitment of his Amsterdam years to the study of art as a social practice embedded in specific communities, institutions, and patterns of use, rather than as an autonomous aesthetic phenomenon to be evaluated by formal criteria alone.

He has held teaching positions at Princeton University, Harvard University, Heidelberg University, the Harvard Center for Renaissance Studies, and Smith College. The Harvard Center for Renaissance Studies - Villa I Tatti in Florence, the same institution where Erling Skaug had spent his postdoctoral years - was among the institutions at which Van Os held visiting appointments, placing him within the international scholarly community of Italian Renaissance specialists gathered around that extraordinary Florentine research library.

His later publications extended the range of his public engagement beyond his core Italian medieval specialization: The Discovery of the Netherlands: Four Centuries of Landscape Painting by Dutch Masters (Rotterdam: Nai Publishers, 2008) addressed the canonical Dutch landscape tradition in the accessible register of his television work; Young in Groningen: Art from the Period 1945-1975 (Groninger Museum, 2009) returned to the city of his formation to document its postwar artistic culture. A series of popular books in Dutch - including reflections on the pleasures of art history (De vreugden van de kunst(geschiedenis)), on looking (Zien is genoeg - Seeing is Enough), and on individual meditations on works he loved - established his Dutch-language voice as one of the most readable and intellectually serious in the genre of accessible art writing.

The collected essays published as Studies in Early Tuscan Painting (London: Pindar Press, 1992) gathered contributions to specific attributional and iconographic problems in Trecento Florentine and Sienese painting that complement and extend the systematic treatment of the Sienese Altarpieces. The essay "From Rome to Siena: the Altarpiece of San Stefano alle Lizza" (Mededelingen van het Nederlands Instituut te Rome, 43, 1981) traces the specific artistic and institutional history of a single Sienese altarpiece with the documentary precision of a scholar who has absorbed both the Italian archival tradition and the iconological method of the Warburg school.

His "Reassembling a Giovanni di Paolo triptych" (The Burlington Magazine, 119, 1977) exemplifies the connoisseurial contribution - the identification and physical reconstruction of a dispersed polyptych's original ensemble - that Van Os pursued alongside his broader cultural and functional analyses. The dual commitment to connoisseurship and function is characteristic of his generation of Italian Trecento specialists, trained in the tradition that runs from Richard Offner through Federico Zeri and Miklos Boskovits, who understood that the close visual analysis of individual objects and the contextual interpretation of their social function were complementary rather than competing activities.

Van Os died on 14 June 2025 at the age of eighty-seven, having spent the better part of six decades bringing the art of late medieval Siena to scholarly and public audiences. His career represents one of the most successful integrations of specialist scholarship and public communication in the history of art history: the man who wrote the standard treatment of the Sienese altarpiece was the same man who explained Rembrandt's Night Watch to millions of Dutch television viewers, and who made private medieval devotional objects accessible to visitors without prior art historical preparation. The Sienese Altarpieces and The Art of Devotion remain the starting points for any serious engagement with the function of painting and the sculpted or painted altarpiece in the religious life of the late medieval period - precisely the territory that Alberto's research on illuminated manuscripts, Trecento patronage, and Byzantine devotional imagery inhabits.

Vapheiades, Konstantinos

active late 20th–21st century

Konstantinos Vapheiades is affiliated with the Higher Ecclesiastical Academy of Athens, where his research interests span medieval art and Byzantine art. He is one of the most productive and methodologically wide-ranging Greek scholars currently working in the field of Byzantine and post-Byzantine painting, with a profile that extends from the twelfth century through the Ottoman period, and from the monumental ensembles of Constantinople and Mount Athos to the portable icons and workshop culture of Venetian Crete. His work is situated at a productive intersection of connoisseurship, epigraphy, iconographic analysis, and cultural history. He was cited by the Associated Press in 2024 as a scholarly commentator on the research linking the painter Panselinos to the identity of Ioannis Astrapas.

The cornerstone of Vapheiades's scholarly output is his major monograph Ύστερη βυζαντινή ζωγραφική: Χώρος και μορφή στην τέχνη της Κωνσταντινούπολης, 1150–1450 — Late Byzantine Painting: Space and Form in the Art of Constantinople, 1150–1450 — published by Barbounakis Editions in Thessaloniki in 2020 (397 pp.). The monograph has become an essential reference in the field and is cited across a broad range of international publications dealing with Byzantine monumental painting, attribution problems, and the artistic culture of the Palaiologan period. Its chronological scope — deliberately extending from the mid-twelfth century to 1450 — places the late Byzantine artistic flowering within a long arc of development rooted in Komnenian Constantinople, offering a coherent narrative of stylistic transformation across three centuries.

Perhaps Vapheiades's most consequential single contribution to Byzantine art history is his reattribution of the wall paintings of the Protaton Church on Mount Athos — the most important monumental ensemble of early Palaiologan painting on the Holy Mountain. During conservation work on the frescoes, a number of letters were found that can form the name "Eutychios" or "Eutychiou" — the name of one of the two painters who decorated the Peribleptos Church in Ohrid. This discovery overturned the findings of previous research, and Vapheiades addressed its implications in "The Wall-Paintings of the Protaton Church Revisited," published in Zograf in 2019. He there attributes the wall paintings to two painters — Michael Astrapas and the painter of the Chapel of St. Euthymios in Thessaloniki — and dates them to between 1309 and 1311/1312. An earlier essay, "Protaton: A Fundamental Monument of Late Byzantine Painting," published in Athonika Tetradion in 2015, had already staked out the church's pivotal position in the development of the Palaiologan aesthetic. This attribution carries major ramifications for the identity question long surrounding the enigmatic "Manuel Panselinos": according to the well-documented opinion of Miodrag Marković, if the name in the inscription between St. Merkourios' thighs is restored in the genitive form, it constitutes a patronym, given that Michael Astrapas liked to sign his works as Μιχαήλ Ευτυχίου (Michael son of Eutychios). Vapheiades engages directly with this hypothesis and with the broader problem of Macedonian School workshop dynamics, offering a revised reconstruction of Astrapas's artistic development. In a subsequent article in Zograf in 2021, "A Reassessment of Middle Byzantine Monumental Painting on Mount Athos: Patronage, Dating and Style," he extended his focus further back, offering an overall assessment of the extant fragments based on epigraphic, iconographic, and stylistic evidence and raising new questions as to their style, dating, and patrons.

Vapheiades contributed a substantial study, "The Byzantine Painting after 1341: Stylistic Tendencies and Devices," to Byzantina (vol. 35, Thessaloniki, 2017), addressing one of the most debated problems in Palaiologan studies: the nature and coherence of Byzantine painting after the theological rupture of the Hesychast controversy, when the victory of Palamite theology in 1351 coincided with profound political disintegration and the beginnings of Ottoman encroachment.

One of the most distinctive and theoretically ambitious dimensions of Vapheiades's research is his sustained attention to the relationship between ecclesiastical and imperial authority as expressed through monumental painting. His paper "Sacerdotium and Imperium in Late Byzantine Art," published in Niš i Vizantija XVIII (2020), explores the intricate relationship between sacramental and imperial power in late Byzantine art. A companion essay, "Sacerdotium and Regnum in Late Byzantium: Some Notes on the 'Imperial Deesis'," published in the American Journal of Arts and Design, examines how the iconographic motif of Christ as High Priest and King functioned as a visual instrument of ecclesiological argument in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. He also authored a monograph published in Athens in 2017, Η τέχνη της δουλείας και η δούλη τέχνη, 15ος–17ος αι. Η «κρητική» ζωγραφική ως τεκμήριο της μεταβυζαντινής πολιτικής θεωρίας και Ηθικής — The Art of Servitude and the Servile Art, 15th–17th Centuries: Cretan Painting as Evidence of Post-Byzantine Political Theory and Ethics — which reads the flourishing of Cretan workshop production under Venetian and Ottoman domination as a document of Byzantine political thought in exile, tracing how the visual culture of post-Byzantine Christianity encoded theological and moral responses to the loss of the empire.

In an article published in I Quaderni del MAES (2018), "Byzantine Painting Treatises: The Case of Codex Panteleimoniensis 259," Vapheiades examines a manuscript copy of a late Byzantine constitutio textus regarding the descriptions of saints' physiognomy alongside quotations from their dicta and verses related to biblical events. He argues that Byzantine painting manuals were not merely collections of technical and iconographic advice, as post-Byzantine ones tend to be, but primarily a corpus of theoretical knowledge necessary for the intellectual formation of artists — a distinction with important implications for understanding the status and self-understanding of Byzantine painters.

Beyond the capital and Mount Athos, Vapheiades has invested considerable research in the monastic artistic culture of Thessaly, centred on the extraordinary rock monasteries of Meteora. In a study on the artistic activity of Theophanes the Cretan in western Thessaly, published in the Analecta Stagorum et Meteororum, he expands knowledge of Theophanes Strelitzas's prolific activity under monastic patronage in the region by presenting unpublished icons pertaining to his artistic idiom from ecclesiastical collections of the wider area, and critically questions the prevailing art-historical narrative on the Cretan style's dissemination in Thessaly and continental Greece.

Vapheiades stands as a distinctive voice in contemporary Byzantine studies for the breadth of his chronological and geographical range — covering Middle Byzantine Athos, late Byzantine Constantinople, the Macedonian School's Palaiologan masterpieces, post-Byzantine Cretan workshop culture, and the monastic art of Ottoman Thessaly — and for his integration of formal analysis with broader cultural and theological interpretation. His reattribution of the Protaton frescoes, his monograph on space and form in Byzantine painting, and his politically inflected readings of post-Byzantine art place him among the most intellectually ambitious scholars currently working in the field.

Vassilaki, Maria

active late 20th–21st century

Maria Vassilaki is Professor of Byzantine Art at the University of Thessaly, Greece, and Scientific Advisor at the Benaki Museum in Athens. This dual affiliation — a full academic chair combined with a senior consultative role at one of Greece's most important cultural institutions — defines the character of her career: rigorously scholarly and at the same time deeply engaged with museum practice, curatorial work, and the public presentation of Byzantine and post-Byzantine heritage. Her research spans Byzantine art and archaeology, icon painting, Cretan painting of the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, workshop practices, and the material and technical study of icons — a range that places her at the intersection of traditional art-historical analysis and the newer interdisciplinary approaches that have transformed the field since the 1990s.

The central and most sustained thread of Vassilaki's scholarship concerns the painting culture of Venetian Crete in the period following the fall of Constantinople in 1453, when the island — then under Venetian rule — became the principal centre of Orthodox icon production in the Mediterranean world. Large painters' workshops were established in Crete's urban centres, in particular Candia, and they undertook commissions for icons in substantial quantities. Vassilaki's research has approached this phenomenon from multiple angles: the social history of painters and their contracts, the iconographic structures governing the reproduction of devotional images, and — with particular originality — the material tools of the workshop itself. An examination of the methods by which Cretan painters of the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth centuries reproduced and transferred their iconographic material shows that this was done with the aid of working drawings (anthivola), which allowed iconographic themes to be copied identically, down to the last detail. This investigation into the technology of icon production — treating the physical tools of the Cretan workshop as primary historical evidence — represents one of Vassilaki's most distinctive methodological contributions.

One of the most celebrated results of Vassilaki's archival and connoisseurial work is her reconstruction of the career and œuvre of Angelos Akotantos, one of the most significant Cretan icon painters of the early fifteenth century. His will, drawn up in 1436, has survived, and he signed his works with the simple formula Cheir Angelou — "The Hand of Angelos" — a phrase taken as the title of the major exhibition and catalogue she edited. Her study The painter Angelos Akotantos: his work and his will (1436) is among her most cited works and established the foundation for all subsequent scholarship on the Cretan school at its formative stage. His art draws on Constantinopolitan painting and contains certain echoes of the decoration of the Chora Monastery, while also being influenced by the Italian Renaissance and recalling, for example, Paolo Veneziano — a cultural synthesis that Vassilaki's work has brought into sharp focus as characteristic of Cretan painters decades before the more celebrated case of El Greco. The fruits of this research were gathered in the exhibition The Hand of Angelos: An Icon Painter in Venetian Crete, hosted at the Benaki Museum in Athens from November 2010 to January 2011, with contributions by Angeliki Laiou, Cryssa Maltezou, David Jacoby, Robin Cormack, Maria Kazanaki, and Nano Chatzidakis.

A particularly important discovery in Vassilaki's career came through her collaborative work with Robin Cormack on Domenikos Theotokopoulos's Baptism of Christ in the Benaki Museum's Conservation Department. The cleaning and conservation of the panel revealed the date MDLXVII (= 1567) on its lower left side — a finding published in the Benaki Museum Journal in 2005 that provided a firm documentary anchor for the early Cretan phase of El Greco's career and confirmed what art historians had long suspected on stylistic grounds. The examination further demonstrated that in this work El Greco succeeded in combining traditional techniques of Byzantine icon painting with the innovative practices of Venetian Renaissance art.

Vassilaki's monograph Working Drawings of Icon Painters after the Fall of Constantinople: The Andreas Xyngopoulos Portfolio at the Benaki Museum (A. G. Leventis Foundation, Leventis Gallery & Benaki Museum, Athens, 2015) brought together years of research into the material culture of post-Byzantine icon workshops. The book focuses on the Xyngopoulos Portfolio — the largest known collection of such workshop materials — exploring its composition, history, and the importance of working drawings in the post-Byzantine icon-painting tradition. The catalogue is organised thematically across fourteen sections covering the full range of Orthodox iconography, from Christological cycles and scenes from the life of the Virgin to individual saints and hagiographic cycles, giving a comprehensive view of how Cretan painters organised and transmitted their iconographic repertoire across generations.

Beyond her monographic research, Vassilaki has been a driving force in the production of landmark exhibition catalogues that have shaped international access to Byzantine and post-Byzantine art. She organised the Mother of God exhibition at the Benaki Museum (October 2000 – January 2001), a landmark event in Byzantine studies that assembled representations of the Theotokos across more than a millennium of sacred art; the accompanying scholarly volume Images of the Mother of God brings together leading international authorities across the disciplines of art history, archaeology, theology, philology, and social anthropology to survey how the Theotokos was perceived in the Byzantine world. In 2008 she co-edited with Robin Cormack the monumental catalogue Byzantium: 330–1453, published by the Royal Academy of Arts in London to accompany one of the most ambitious exhibitions of Byzantine art ever mounted in the West. Highlighting over three hundred works from the holy monasteries of Sinai and Mount Athos, the Treasury of Saint Mark's in Venice, and institutions across the globe, the publication explores the artistic identity of Byzantium and its influence on European and Islamic traditions, illustrated with 465 full-colour images.

Maria Vassilaki occupies a prominent position in contemporary Byzantine studies as a scholar who has consistently combined archival precision, iconographic analysis, and material science to deepen understanding of icon painting as both a theological practice and an economic and social phenomenon. Her work on Cretan workshop practices — particularly the role of working drawings (anthivola) in transmitting iconographic models — has opened a methodological avenue that is now a recognised sub-field of post-Byzantine art history. Her curatorial achievements, above all the Mother of God and Byzantium: 330–1453 exhibitions, have played a central role in bringing Byzantine art to wider international audiences while maintaining the highest standards of scholarly rigour.

Vedova, Massimo

active late 20th–21st century

Massimo Vedova is an Italian Franciscan friar of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual and a scholar of medieval and early-modern spirituality, best known for his sustained philological and theological work on the writings of Angela of Foligno. He teaches the history of medieval spirituality at the Pontificia Università Antonianum in Rome, where he holds a position on the Faculty of Theology, and also at the Pontificia Facoltà Teologica Teresianum. Before entering theological studies, he trained as a physicist, earning a degree in Fisica from the Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II in 1993, a scientific formation that preceded his later vocation to the friary and to the study of mystical texts.

Vedova's research centres on the history of monasticism and the papacy, hagiography, and above all the mystical and prophetic literature produced between the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The core of his published work addresses the textual and theological problems posed by the corpus attributed to Angela of Foligno (c. 1248-1309), the Umbrian mystic whose Memoriale and Instructiones occupy a central place in the history of medieval women's religious writing. In essays such as "Leggere" il Memoriale di Angela Da Foligno (published in Antonianum, 2010), Esperientia Dei: memoriale di Angela da Foligno, tracce di una teologia "alternativa"?, and L'immagine di Maria nel Liber di Angela da Foligno, he has pursued close readings of the text's theological vocabulary and its representation of Mary, poverty, and mystical experience, while Tematiche spirituali fondamentali nelle Instructiones di Angela da Foligno (Frate Francesco, 2019) examines the relationship between the Instructiones and the Memoriale within the wider Angelan corpus.

A recurring concern in his scholarship is the history of the reception and translation of Angela's writings across languages and centuries, treated in La (dis)avventura del tradurre (2019), an essay on the difficulty and the interpretive richness of translating the Memoriale. This interest culminated in his co-editorship, with Alessandra Bartolomei Romagnoli, of the collective volume Il Libro di Angela da Foligno e le sue traduzioni (Spoleto, Fondazione CISAM, 2019), which gathers studies on the hermeneutic problem of translation and on the reception of the Liber in various linguistic traditions, including its Polish fortunes. The two scholars subsequently co-edited Santa Angela da Foligno: la canonizzazione di una mistica medievale, again for CISAM, addressing the process and cultural context of Angela's formal canonization.

Alongside his work on Angela of Foligno, Vedova has published on other figures of Franciscan and broader Catholic mysticism, including studies of the Franciscan Beato Egidio of Assisi ( L'esperienza contemplativa del Beato Egidio and Il beato Egidio, la preghiera e il demonio), of the seventeenth-century ecstatic friar Giuseppe da Copertino ( La mistica di san Giuseppe da Copertino: piste di studio, 2017, and Metamorfosi di un'estasi: San Giuseppe da Copertino e la cupola della Santa Casa di Loreto, in Collectanea Franciscana, 2018), and of the theme of poverty in the spirituality of Angela of Foligno and of St Maximilian Kolbe. His broader theoretical interests include the symbolism of mystical union with God in medieval religious literature, addressed in L'amplexus simbolo dell'unione dell'anima con Dio nel contesto della letteratura mistica medievale (Miscellanea Francescana, 2012).

Combining a scientific formation with theological and philological training, Vedova belongs to a tradition of Franciscan scholarship, centred on institutions such as the Antonianum, that treats the medieval mystical corpus as a subject demanding rigorous textual criticism alongside spiritual and theological interpretation. His essays are regularly cited in the scholarly literature on Angela of Foligno alongside the work of Giovanni Pozzi, Paul Lachance, and Cristina Mazzoni, and his collaborative volumes with Alessandra Bartolomei Romagnoli have become standard points of reference for the study of the transmission and translation of her writings.

Venturi, Adolfo

3 September 1856 - 10 June 1941

Overview

Adolfo Venturi was the founding figure of modern art history as an academic and institutional discipline in Italy. Born in Modena the year before the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed, he devoted his life to constructing the first systematic, archivally grounded history of Italian art on an Italian scholarly foundation - independent of the German, English, and French traditions that had previously dominated the field. His monumental Storia dell'arte italiana, published across nearly four decades in twenty-five volumes, remains a foundational reference from Early Christian art through the sixteenth century. He also created Italy's first university chair in art history, built the professional infrastructure for the protection and cataloguing of the national heritage, and formed the generation - Longhi, Brandi, Argan, Ragghianti - that shaped Italian art historical thought throughout the twentieth century.

Venturi was born on 3 September 1856 in Modena, son of Gaetano Venturi and Maria Barbieri, a family of modest means in a city that was still, at the moment of his birth, a duchy under the Este house. His son Lionello Venturi (1885-1961) became a distinguished art historian in his own right, continuing the family tradition at the University of Turin and, after his exile under Fascism, in North America.

Venturi's education was in many ways a self-construction. He attended the academy and technical school in Modena, but - lacking the means for formal study - largely taught himself classical history and art history by means of the private library of G. B. Toesca, to which he obtained access. To fund further study he worked as a private tutor, saving enough to attend the Istituto di Studi Superiori in Florence. He then undertook an intensive personal survey of the Italian artistic heritage, travelling systematically through Bologna, Venice, and Milan, studying monuments, collections, and archives directly.

In 1878, at the age of twenty-two, Venturi was appointed curator (ispettore) of the Galleria Estense in Modena - the Este ducal collection, one of the oldest and richest in Emilia. In a professional environment where the role of museum curator had no established guidelines in newly unified Italy, Venturi effectively shaped the profession from scratch. His governing principle was that understanding each work of art required reconstructing its individual history through archival research. He spent his years at the Estense systematically mining the Emilian state archives, linking documents to objects, establishing provenance, and grounding attribution in evidence rather than tradition or received opinion.

This empirical approach brought him into direct contact with the Morellian tradition. Venturi knew Giovanni Morelli personally. A celebrated anecdote - recorded by art historian Claudio Strinati at the 1992 Venturi conference - captures the relationship well: Morelli, in his Milan apartment, showed Venturi a painting and asked him to name the artist. Faced with Venturi's uncertainty, Morelli teased him for not recognizing a fellow Modenese, identifying it as Francesco Bianchi Ferrari. Venturi subsequently studied the work in detail and published an article reversing the attribution to a lesser painter, Michele Coltellini - a calculated riposte that demonstrated how archival and formal scrutiny could check even the authority of the master connoisseur. The combination of Morelli's close formal analysis with systematic documentary investigation became Venturi's methodological signature.

In 1882 he published La R. Galleria Estense in Modena, his first substantial contribution to the literature.

In 1888 Venturi was called to Rome as general inspector of the Belle Arti at the Ministry of Public Instruction, a position of national scope. There he was instrumental in two significant reforms: he instituted Italy's first formal training programme for the treatment of works of art - a rudimentary but foundational step towards professional conservation - and he developed the framework for a systematic national catalogue of the artistic heritage. From 1891 to 1898 he served as deputy director of the Kingdom's museums, and subsequently directed the National Gallery of Ancient Art at Palazzo Corsini in Rome. These institutional roles gave him an unparalleled overview of the national patrimony and deepened his conviction that Italian art history required a comprehensive, rigorous, and specifically Italian treatment.

That same year, 1888, Venturi co-founded with Count Domenico Gnoli (1838-1915) the journal Archivio storico d'arte - renamed L'Arte in 1901. He edited it continuously until 1940, making it for half a century the principal Italian venue for archivally grounded art historical scholarship across all periods. Crucially, L'Arte also published the early work of the next generation: in 1914 Venturi assigned the journal's book review section to the young Roberto Longhi, who published monographic studies on Orazio Borgianni, Battistello Caracciolo, and the Gentileschi family in its pages between 1914 and 1916.

In 1896 Venturi left the ministerial bureaucracy to take up an academic appointment at the Universita degli Studi di Roma "La Sapienza" as its first Professor of Medieval and Modern Art History - a chair created specifically for him, and the first university chair in art history in Italy. He held it until his retirement in 1931. He also established at La Sapienza a Scuola di Perfezionamento in Storia dell'Arte Medievale e Moderna, a postgraduate specialisation school whose alumni shaped the discipline for decades. The school was notably open to women students at a time when the Italian academic world was largely closed to them, and Venturi's seminars attracted a disproportionate number of female scholars, a circumstance that contemporaries remarked upon.

Intellectually, Venturi's work at this period was shaped by Benedetto Croce's aesthetics - specifically Croce's emphasis on the creative individual and on the artwork as expression of a singular historical consciousness - alongside the continuing influence of the Morellian connoisseurship tradition and, through his son Lionello, of Heinrich Wolfflin's formal analysis. His students at La Sapienza included Giuseppe Fiocco (who became the leading authority on Venetian Renaissance painting), Margaret Scolari Barr (who later worked closely with Alfred H. Barr at MoMA), and, more broadly, Cesare Brandi, Giulio Carlo Argan, and Carlo Ludovico Ragghianti - four of the most influential Italian art historians and critics of the twentieth century.

In 1901 Venturi was elected to the Institut de France in Paris, succeeding Giuseppe Verdi (1813-1901).

Venturi's magnum opus, the Storia dell'arte italiana, was published by Ulrico Hoepli in Milan in twenty-five volumes between 1901 and 1940, spanning early Christian art through the architecture of the sixteenth century. It was conceived from the outset as a monument: a comprehensive, illustrated, archivally anchored account of the totality of Italian artistic production across fifteen centuries - an enterprise without precedent in the Italian literature, and one that effectively demonstrated that Italians could construct their own art history rather than receive it from Rumohr, Waagen, or Ruskin. The project consumed Venturi's working life; in his final years, suffering from cataracts that left him practically blind, he relied on his students to help draft the later volumes.

The structure of the work is of particular relevance to researchers in medieval and Trecento art. The volumes dedicated to the pre-modern period are:

  • Vol. I (1901): Dai primordi dell'arte cristiana al tempo di Giustiniano - Early Christian to Justinianic art
  • Vol. II (1902): Dall'arte barbarica alla romanica - the transition from late antique and barbaric art to Romanesque
  • Vol. III (1904): L'arte romanica - Romanesque painting, sculpture, and architecture
  • Vol. IV (1906): La scultura del Trecento e le sue origini - Trecento sculpture and its origins
  • Vol. V (1907): La pittura del Trecento e le sue origini - Trecento painting and its origins

Volumes IV and V constitute the most comprehensive treatment of Dugento and Trecento Italian art produced up to that date, and despite their age remain indispensable for the breadth of their documentary apparatus, their coverage of regional schools, and the sheer range of works catalogued and illustrated. They are also primary sources for early attributions in the field, since Venturi was often writing from direct examination and from archival sources that had not previously been published.

The work was abridged and translated into English as A Short History of Italian Art (Macmillan, New York, 1926), translated by Edward Hutton, and was the subject of an unpublished fuller translation produced by the Illinois Works Project Administration in 1939.

As Italy's pre-eminent authority on Italian art, Venturi was called repeatedly to adjudicate questions of attribution in legal and public contexts. In 1929 he testified in the celebrated American case of Hahn vs. Duveen, in which a Kansas City couple sued the dealer Sir Joseph Duveen for publicly dismissing their painting - claimed to be a Leonardo La Belle Ferroniere - as a copy. Venturi sided with Duveen, declaring the Hahn picture a low copy. He also expressed scepticism regarding the Isleworth Mona Lisa (1923), attributing its execution primarily to Ambrogio de Predis on Leonardo's design, and expressed doubts (1928) about a painting claimed to be Leonardo's Leda and the Swan, finding it too finished and elegant to be entirely by Leonardo's hand.

Adolfo Venturi died on 10 June 1941 at Santa Margherita Ligure, on the Ligurian coast, at the age of 84. His obituary appeared in the New York Times the following day. A commemorative conference held at Modena in 1989 - a century after his appointment to the ministry - resulted in a facsimile reprint of his Galleria Estense catalogue and a series of essays assessing his role in the institutionalization of Italian art history.

His legacy is threefold: as the architect of Italy's first modern art historical institution (the La Sapienza chair and postgraduate school); as the founder and decades-long editor of L'Arte, the central journal of the discipline; and as the author of the Storia dell'arte italiana, the most comprehensive account of Italian art ever undertaken by a single scholar. In the Dictionary of Art Historians he is characterised as a "pioneer of the modern school of art history in Italy" - a judgment that substantially understates the scope of his achievement: he did not merely pioneer, he founded.

For researchers working on Italian medieval painting, Venturi's Volumes IV and V of the Storia dell'arte italiana are primary reference tools - both as evidence of what was known and attributed at the turn of the twentieth century, and as catalogues that preserve documentary references and early photographic records of works that have since been dispersed, damaged, or insufficiently studied. Volume V (La pittura del Trecento e le sue origini, 1907) treats Giotto, the Sienese school, and the major regional schools of the Dugento and Trecento in systematic detail.

Venturi's attention to miniature painting and manuscript illumination as part of the continuous history of Italian art, rather than as a separate technical speciality, also makes his work relevant to Alberto's current focus: illuminated manuscripts are treated within the broader pictorial tradition in the Storia, and L'Arte published significant articles on Italian manuscript illumination throughout its run from 1901 to 1940.

Venturi, Lionello

Modena, 25 April 1885 – Rome, 14 August 1961

Lionello Venturi was one of the greatest Italian art historians and critics of the twentieth century, distinguished both by the breadth and originality of his scholarship and by the civic courage with which he opposed fascism, refusing allegiance to the regime even at the cost of exile. His work spans medieval, Renaissance, and modern art, and remains foundational for the international historiography of art criticism.

Born in Modena to Adolfo Venturi and Giovanna Zanni, he grew up in an intellectually formative environment and moved early to Rome with his family. He graduated in Literature and Philosophy at La Sapienza in 1907 and in 1911 obtained his qualification to teach medieval and modern art history at the University of Padua. After graduation, he held a rapid sequence of museum and administrative posts: inspector of the Venice Galleries (1909-1910), inspector of the Galleria Borghese in Rome (1911-1912), and, at only twenty-eight, Director and Superintendent of the National Gallery of Urbino (1913-1914).

Between 1914 and 1915 he entered university teaching at Turin, where he was soon appointed associate professor. With Italy's entry into World War I he volunteered for military service; wounded in combat in 1917, he was discharged with a decoration for military valor. From 1915 to 1931 he held the chair of Art History at the University of Turin, where he trained a major generation of students including Giulio Carlo Argan and Mario Soldati. His teaching combined methodological rigor with sustained attention to both the aesthetic quality of the work and its historical context.

In October 1931, Venturi was among the very small group of Italian university professors who refused the oath of allegiance imposed by the fascist regime. The decision led to his immediate exclusion from university teaching in Italy. In 1932 he left for Paris, where he remained until 1939, developing contacts with the anti-fascist movement Giustizia e Libertà and teaching and lecturing in Paris, Lyon, London, and Cambridge. After the introduction of racial laws, he promoted the Italian section of the International League Against Racism and Anti-Semitism. With the outbreak of World War II he moved to New York (1939), taught at American universities, took leadership roles in the Mazzini Society, and chaired the Italian Emergency Rescue Committee.

His years in exile were also among his most productive intellectually. Major works include Histoire de la critique d'art (1936; expanded Italian edition, 1948), still a central text in the history of art criticism; the two-volume Cezanne (1936), which established him as a leading interpreter of modern painting; Archives de l'Impressionisme (2 vols., 1939), a key documentary corpus for Impressionist studies; and Come si guarda un quadro, one of the most widely read twentieth-century Italian books on aesthetic education. For medieval and Renaissance studies, Il gusto dei primitivi (1926) remains especially significant for the reassessment of early Italian painting.

After the Liberation, Venturi returned to Italy in 1945 and resumed teaching at La Sapienza, remaining there until 1955 and contributing decisively to the reconstruction of postwar Italian art-historical culture. He was elected to the Accademia dei Lincei, the Accademia di San Luca, and the Accademia delle Scienze di Torino, and became a corresponding member of the Institut de France. He died in Rome on 14 August 1961.

Vervat, Muriel

active in Florence since 1984

Muriel Vervat is a paintings conservator based in Florence, active in the field since 1984. Working principally for the Soprintendenza Speciale per il Polo Museale Fiorentino, she has undertaken conservation campaigns for the city's major state collections, among them the Galleria degli Uffizi, the Galleria Palatina, the Galleria d'Arte Moderna at Palazzo Pitti, and the Galleria dell'Accademia, as well as for churches including Florence's Duomo, Santo Spirito, and Santa Trinita. Her practice has also extended beyond Florence, to commissions for the Soprintendenze of Siena and Parma.

At the Galleria dell'Accademia, Vervat carried out the restoration of Andrea di Cione (Orcagna)'s Pentecost triptych, the high altarpiece of Santi Apostoli painted in the 1360s. Her intervention proceeded in two cleaning phases — first removing degraded adhesive responsible for micro-lifting of the paint surface, then thinning the discoloured varnish left by a restoration of 1953 — followed by the filling of losses and the selective reapplication of gold leaf to worn metallic passages. In the course of the work she drew attention to the sophistication of the panel's original gilding technique: layered gold and silver leaf applied over red bole, individually patterned haloes, and passages of "fantastical animals" rendered in silver over gold to suggest a bronzed finish, executed, in her account, in single strokes that allowed no correction. She presented these findings in 2023 in a video made for the Galleria dell'Accademia's public-facing "Scopri la Galleria" series.

Verzár, Christine

active late 20th–21st century

Christine Verzár — who published her earlier work as Christine Verzár Bornstein — is a historian of medieval art and Professor Emerita at the Ohio State University, and one of the principal Anglophone authorities on twelfth-century Italian sculpture. She took her doctorate at the University of Basel, and something of that school's tradition remains visible in her work; she has written on the Basel department itself and on the legacy of Jacob Burckhardt and Heinrich Wölfflin as its founders.

Her first monograph, Die romanischen Skulpturen der Abtei Sagra di San Michele (1968), studied the sculpture of the great Piedmontese abbey. Her central book is Portals and Politics in the Early Italian City-State: The Sculpture of Nicholaus in Context (Parma, 1988), which set the work of the sculptor Nicholaus within the civic and political circumstances of the emerging communes — an approach that treats a carved doorway as a public instrument rather than as an isolated aesthetic object, and which has been widely followed since. She has also worked extensively on Matilda of Canossa and on the representation of authority, on the relation of text to image in Romanesque sculpture, and on late medieval German sculpture.

A sustained interest in artistic exchange across the Mediterranean during the Crusades produced the co-authored exhibition volume The Meeting of Two Worlds: The Crusades and the Mediterranean Context (1981). She has served on the boards of the International Center of Medieval Art, of Assaph at Tel Aviv University, and of Fifteenth Century Studies, and has acted as an assessor of medieval works for the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Metropolitan Museum of Art and museums in San Francisco. Her photographic collection of more than six hundred and fifty images, weighted toward Italian Romanesque architectural sculpture, is held by the Index of Medieval Art at Princeton.

In the Gislebertus literature she appears as a reviewer. Her notice of Linda Seidel's Legends in Limestone in Speculum (2001) is among the substantial critical responses to that book, and voices the objection heard across its reception: that its case is built in part against straw men drawn from an older iconographic art history, and that dismantling the sculptor does not by itself install the patron.

Villani, Matteo

Florence, c. 1283 – Florence, 1363

Matteo Villani was a Florentine merchant, communal officeholder and chronicler whose continuation of his brother Giovanni Villani's Nuova Cronica is the principal eyewitness narrative source for Florentine history in the fifteen years following the Black Death of 1348. Like his brother, Matteo was active in the family's mercantile and banking affairs and held a succession of civic offices in the Florentine Republic, including terms as prior; this direct involvement in communal government gave his chronicle an insider's grasp of politics, taxation and guild affairs that complements its narrative of war and calamity.

When Giovanni Villani died of plague in 1348 partway through his universal chronicle of Florence, Matteo took up the task of continuation, explicitly framing his own book as a record of the plague's aftermath and of the profoundly altered world it had left behind. His chronicle, composed in eleven books covering the years from 1348 to 1363, opens with an extended and often-cited account of the epidemic's mortality and its social and moral consequences — the collapse of labour discipline, the inflation of wages, the ostentation and moral laxity Matteo perceived among the survivors — before proceeding to the wars against Milan under the Visconti, the conflicts with Pisa and other Tuscan powers, the depredations of mercenary companies of ventura moving through Italy, and the continuous business of Florentine guild and communal politics.

Matteo's chronicle is markedly more interpretative and moralising than his brother's more annalistic manner, reading contemporary events as evidence of a providential and penitential history; it is for this reason that modern historians of art and society researching the psychological and religious climate of post-plague Tuscany — including the interpretative literature on Florentine and Sienese painting after 1348 — have drawn on Matteo's testimony as documentary counterpart to the visual evidence. He died in 1363, almost certainly a further victim of plague, leaving his own chronicle unfinished; it was continued in turn by his son Filippo Villani, who carried the family's chronicle project into a fourth generation of Florentine historical writing.

Vittorini, Marta

L'Aquila, c. 1975-1976; active 21st century

Marta Vittorini is an Italian scholar, archivist, and medievalist from L'Aquila, currently serving as Director of the Archivio di Stato dell'Aquila. Her profile bridges academic research in medieval philosophy and manuscript studies with institutional leadership in the preservation and enhancement of Italy's archival and bibliographic heritage.

Vittorini studied Philosophy at the Università degli Studi dell'Aquila (Univaq), graduating with 110/110 con lode. Her thesis, Il problema dell'onnipotenza divina tra il XIII e il XIV secolo: Tommaso, Scoto e Ockham in dibattito, addressed a core issue of late medieval theology and anticipated her sustained engagement with scholastic thought.

She later completed a doctorate in Medieval Philosophy with the dissertation Predicabili e categorie nell'ultimo commento di Walter Burley all'Isagoge di Porfirio, including a critical edition based on three principal manuscripts. This work placed her within high-level textual scholarship on late medieval Aristotelianism, with research interests centered on theology, metaphysics, and philosophy of nature in the late Middle Ages.

Alongside philosophical training, Vittorini pursued advanced specialization in the material study of manuscripts. She obtained the Diploma di Archivista Paleografo at the Scuola Vaticana di Paleografia, Diplomatica e Archivistica, where her thesis examined the manuscript tradition of Walter Burley in codices of the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana. She also earned a Diploma di Conservatore di Manoscritti at Università La Sapienza di Roma, strengthening her expertise in manuscript conservation.

Her disciplinary range includes Latin and Greek paleography, codicology, history of manuscript illumination (storia della miniatura), history of manuscript transmission, library science, and cultural heritage legislation. She additionally attended Arabic language training and a seminar on Arabic paleography and codicology taught by Adam Gacek (McGill University), extending her methodological competence toward Arabic manuscript traditions.

The central focus of Vittorini's scholarly research is Walter Burley (c. 1274-c. 1344), the English scholastic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle. Her work analyzes Burley's logic and metaphysics through both philosophical argument and manuscript evidence, integrating history of ideas with codicological investigation.

She presented this research in international venues, including the XII International Congress of Medieval Philosophy (SIEPM, Palermo, 2007) with the paper Some Notes about the Metaphysical Composition of Individuals in Walter Burley. She also delivered Walter Burley on the Role of Difference at the Scuola Normale Superiore and presented at the Pisa workshop Conoscenza e contingenza nella tradizione aristotelica medievale (Convento di Santa Croce in Fossabanda, 2006).

In July 2007 she took part in the Workshop in Editing Medieval Texts at Georgetown University (Washington, D.C.) and later completed a two-month research stage at the Biblioteca dei Gesuiti in Salamanca, further consolidating her editorial and manuscript-based methods.

From February 2018 to December 2021, Vittorini served as Funzionario Archivista di Stato (Area III, F1) at the Soprintendenza in Rome, where she handled declarations of historical interest, authorizations for restoration and archival arrangement, and supervision of archives belonging to major institutions, including Confindustria, Confartigianato, INAIL, and sectors of the antiquarian market.

On 1 January 2022, by decree of the Director General of Archives (rep. 898/2021), she was appointed Director of the Archivio di Stato dell'Aquila, succeeding Sebastiana Ferrari. In this role she oversees the three archive sites in L'Aquila, Avezzano, and Sulmona, with responsibility for staff, conservation of archival and bibliographic patrimony, maintenance, and public services. She has also promoted the institute's collections through exhibitions, web communication, and social media, and collaborates with the Carabinieri TPC unit on expert evaluations of archival and bibliographic materials under investigation.

Vittorini has maintained an active publication record in medieval philosophy, manuscript studies, archival law, and the protection of non-state archives, including a 2023 contribution on the duties of Soprintendenze archivistiche e bibliografiche. She has also authored a book-interview with Professor Colapietra, reflecting her engagement with the wider cultural life of Abruzzo. Her profile exemplifies the intersection of medieval scholarship, technical manuscript expertise, and institutional leadership in the safeguarding of documentary heritage.

Vnouček, Jiří

active late 20th-21st century

Jiří Vnouček is a Czech-born parchment specialist and conservator, long associated with the Royal Danish Library (Det Kongelige Bibliotek) in Copenhagen, whose research combines close visual and microscopic examination of historical parchment with practical, hands-on experimental reconstruction of medieval skin-preparation techniques. His work has been influential in establishing species identification and manufacturing method as central, rather than incidental, evidence in the study of medieval manuscripts.

His study "The Parchment of the Codex Amiatinus in the Context of Manuscript Production in Northumbria Around the End of the Seventh Century," published in the Journal of Paper Conservation in 2020, challenged the long-standing assumption that all three of Ceolfrith's pandects were written on calfskin. On the basis of visual and microscopic examination combined with experimental reconstruction, Vnouček argued that the text-block of the Codex Amiatinus itself is composed of goat and sheep skins, while the surviving leaves of the two lost sister Bibles are calf — a finding that, if sustained, complicates the assumption that the three volumes were produced from a single uniform supply and unsettles the broader association of high-grade Insular bookmaking with calfskin specifically. The conclusion awaits confirmation by non-destructive peptide mass fingerprinting (ZooMS) and is not yet universally accepted, but it stands as a striking recent instance of long-held assumptions about the manuscript being overturned by direct examination of the physical object. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion.

Volpe, Carlo

Bologna, 11 giugno 1926 - Bologna, 2 febbraio 1984

Carlo Volpe è stato uno dei più influenti storici dell'arte italiani del secondo Novecento, formatosi alla scuola di Roberto Longhi e protagonista degli studi sul Duecento e Trecento, in particolare sul Trecento riminese e bolognese.

Volpe nasce a Bologna nel 1926 e cresce in un ambiente che lo porta presto a confrontarsi con la grande tradizione degli studi storico-artistici italiani. La sua formazione decisiva avviene all'Università di Bologna, dove è allievo di Roberto Longhi, del quale assimila il metodo filologico basato sul confronto diretto con le opere, l'attenzione alla qualità visiva e l'uso serrato della fotografia come strumento di indagine. Nel novembre del 1949 discute con Longhi una tesi dedicata a Pietro Lorenzetti ad Assisi, che già rivela il suo interesse per la pittura trecentesca e per i rapporti fra scuole regionali. In questi anni si forma anche nel clima longhiano delle riviste e della critica militante, che mette in dialogo antico e contemporaneo.

Poco dopo la laurea, Volpe comincia a collaborare al Nuovo Corriere con interventi e recensioni che spaziano dall'arte antica alle ricerche contemporanee, mostrando una curiosità ampia e non settoriale. Parallelamente, entra nel gruppo di giovani redattori legati all'esperienza di Paragone, la rivista fondata da Longhi, dove debutta nel 1951 con un saggio su Ambrogio Lorenzetti e i rapporti fra Firenze e Siena nel quarto decennio del Trecento. Questa precoce attività critica lo pone subito in dialogo con figure come Francesco Arcangeli, Giuliano Briganti e Mina Gregori, con cui condivide una riflessione comune sul metodo e sui confini della storia dell'arte.

Dopo un lungo periodo di insegnamenti "secondari" presso l'Istituto di Storia dell'arte dell'Università di Bologna, Volpe ottiene nel 1974 la cattedra di Storia dell'arte medievale e moderna. Il suo insegnamento si colloca in continuità con la lezione longhiana ma introduce una particolare attenzione alla sistematicità degli studi sul Trecento e sulla tradizione emiliana, contribuendo a formare una generazione di storici dell'arte sensibili al dato visivo e, insieme, alle strutture critiche di lungo periodo. Nel 1982 diventa il primo direttore del neonato Dipartimento delle Arti Visive dell'Ateneo bolognese, trasformando l'eredità dell'Istituto di Storia dell'arte in una struttura dipartimentale più ampia, che integra storia dell'arte, studi visivi e nuove metodologie.

La sua morte prematura nel 1984 interrompe una carriera critica e accademica ancora in pieno corso, proprio nel momento in cui stava consolidando il suo ruolo istituzionale e la sintesi teorica dei suoi interessi. A distanza di decenni, l'Università di Bologna e vari centri di ricerca continuano a ricordarlo come una figura cardine nella storia del loro Dipartimento, anche attraverso convegni dedicati alla sua eredità scientifica accanto a quella di Francesco Arcangeli, altro grande allievo di Longhi.

Accanto all'insegnamento, Volpe sviluppa una intensa attività di critico militante, che attraversa quotidiani e riviste specialistiche. Oltre al Nuovo Corriere, lavora stabilmente nella redazione di Paragone, dove interviene regolarmente su temi di arte italiana, dall'età medievale al Seicento, consolidando il proprio profilo di conoscitore capace di misurarsi con problemi attributivi e con questioni di metodo. Dal 1958 affianca Stefano Bottari nella redazione di Arte antica e moderna, altra sede in cui la sua scrittura si esercita nel dialogo con i dibattiti più vivi della storiografia artistica.

Pur celebre per gli studi trecenteschi, Volpe mantiene un'attenzione costante all'arte contemporanea, seguendo artisti come Morlotti, Morandi, Cavaglieri, Ruggeri e Licini. Questa duplice inclinazione, verso il Medioevo e verso il Novecento, alimenta una concezione dell'arte come storia lunga, in cui le categorie formali e la questione della "moralità" dell'arte vengono ripensate alla luce del presente. Un saggio tardo, Il lungo percorso del "dipingere dolcissimo e tanto unito", mette bene in luce il suo sforzo di tenere insieme analisi stilistica, storia sociale e riflessione critica sui valori etici dell'opera.

La ricerca di Volpe si distingue per un'impressionante vastità di interessi, che vanno dal Duecento al Seicento, ma è soprattutto nel campo del Trecento italiano che il suo nome resta centrale. Il libro La pittura riminese del Trecento, pubblicato nel 1965, rappresenta una pietra miliare: in esso Volpe coglie per la prima volta con piena consapevolezza la precocità e la portata della ricezione della lezione assisiate di Giotto in area riminese, ridefinendo un intero capitolo della pittura italiana del tempo. Più tardi, nel 1979, dedica un'ampia sintesi alla pittura bolognese trecentesca all'interno del saggio La pittura emiliana del Trecento, contribuendo a chiarire il ruolo dell'Emilia come cerniera fra tradizioni diverse.

Un'altra linea importante dei suoi studi riguarda l'arte emiliana fra Cinque e Seicento, testimoniata, tra l'altro, dal volume Il fregio dei Carracci e i dipinti di Palazzo Magnani in Bologna, uscito per il Credito Romagnolo nella seconda metà degli anni Settanta. In questi lavori Volpe esercita con rigore il mestiere di conoscitore, affinando attribuzioni, ricostruendo cicli decorativi e riflettendo sulle dinamiche del collezionismo e del mecenatismo cittadino. Il suo contributo più ambizioso e teoricamente denso è considerato Il lungo percorso del "dipingere dolcissimo e tanto unito", apparso nel quinto volume della Storia dell'arte italiana, dove riconosce un ruolo centrale alla Lombardia nella rielaborazione di formule giottesche che a Firenze, al contrario, risultano "perdenti" in una certa fase del percorso del maestro.

Per l'ambito che interessa particolarmente gli studi sul Duecento e Trecento, Volpe si impone come figura chiave nella rilettura del cosiddetto "cantiere assisiate" e delle sue propagazioni regionali, dal riminese all'Emilia e oltre. La sua attenzione a maestri come Pietro e Ambrogio Lorenzetti, ai rapporti Firenze-Siena e al ruolo delle scuole periferiche lo colloca fra gli interpreti più raffinati delle vicende pittoriche del Medioevo italiano, influenzando anche la successiva valorizzazione di contesti allora considerati marginali.

Volpe è unanimemente riconosciuto come uno dei più rigorosi esponenti del metodo filologico longhiano, applicato con particolare finezza al lavoro di conoscitore. La sua pratica quotidiana di studio si fonda su un uso sistematico della fotografia: nel corso della vita costruisce una vasta fototeca personale di opere dal Duecento al Cinquecento, oggi organizzata e valorizzata come Fototeca Carlo Volpe, che rappresenta una risorsa di primo piano per la connoisseurship della pittura italiana. Questa raccolta, conservata e resa consultabile in ambito accademico, documenta non solo il suo interesse per singoli autori, ma anche la volontà di mappare interi territori figurativi con sguardo capillare.

Nel giudizio degli storici dell'arte, Volpe si afferma presto, accanto a Federico Zeri, come uno dei maggiori conoscitori a livello internazionale, capace di proporre attribuzioni e letture destinate a modificare il quadro critico di riferimento. Le iniziative recenti, convegni, studi sulla sua "moralità dell'arte" e ricerche dedicate alla sua fototeca, mostrano come la sua figura continui a essere un punto di riferimento per chi si occupa di Trecento italiano e di metodologia della storia dell'arte nel solco longhiano.

von Campenhausen, Hans Freiherr

Rosenbeck (Livonia), 16 December 1903 - Heidelberg, 6 January 1989

Hans Erich Freiherr von Campenhausen was one of the most important Protestant church historians of the twentieth century, known above all for his work on the early Church, the formation of canon, and the political and theological history of late antiquity. He also occupies a particular place in Ambrose studies, because his first major work on the bishop of Milan appeared almost simultaneously with the great books of Jean-Rémy Palanque and Frederick Homes Dudden, yet was conceived entirely independently and with a sharply argumentative, historically focused method of its own.

Campenhausen was born on 16 December 1903 at Rosenbeck in Livonia, then part of the Russian Empire, into a Baltic-German baronial family of large landowners whose ancestors had come from Germany into the still-pagan Baltic in the High Middle Ages. The Russian Revolution destroyed that world. His father was killed in the upheavals of 1919 as a representative of the "feudal class," and the young Campenhausen himself was imprisoned before the family eventually escaped to Germany. He had begun his schooling at Dorpat and Riga and completed his Abitur at Heidelberg in 1922, bringing to German academia the experience of violent political rupture that marked so many scholars of his generation from the Baltic provinces.

He studied theology and history at Heidelberg and Marburg, with periods in Berlin and Rome. His formation was shaped above all by Rudolf Bultmann and Hans Freiherr von Soden, while the methodological influence of Martin Dibelius was especially decisive. In 1926 he took his doctorate at Heidelberg under Hans von Schubert with a study of Ambrosius von Mailand als Kirchenpolitiker, published by de Gruyter in 1929. He habilitated at Marburg in 1928 with a work suggested by von Soden on the Passion sarcophagi, Die Passionssarkophage: Zur Geschichte eines altchristlichen Bildkreises, a study of direct importance for Christian archaeology and iconography because it traces the formation of an early Christian image-cycle in sculpted stone rather than treating late antique Christianity only through texts.

His Ambrose dissertation asked the sharpest single question in the field: what kind of church politician Ambrose was. This was not merely a biography but an inquiry into episcopal action, political tactics, and relations with imperial power under Gratian, Valentinian II, and Theodosius. In later historiography, Palanque's great thesis supplied the chronological and epistolary scaffolding for Ambrose's career, while Dudden's two volumes offered the full English narrative; but Campenhausen's book remained the shortest, most pointed, and most argumentative of the three, and it set enduring terms for the debate over Ambrose's political posture and practical dealings with the late Roman court.

Campenhausen's early academic career unfolded under the increasingly difficult conditions of the Third Reich. In 1930 he became Privatdozent for church history and Christian archaeology at Göttingen, and from 1931 to 1935 held the modest office of Inspector at the Theological Stift there. A compromised fact of his record is that on 11 November 1933 his name appeared among the signatories of the professors' declaration supporting Hitler and the National Socialist state. Yet he kept his distance from the regime, joined the Confessing Church, and paid for that distance professionally. From 1935 onward he survived on a sequence of stand-in lectureships at Giessen, Greifswald, Göttingen, Kiel, Heidelberg, and Vienna. Two academic chairs were blocked for political reasons: first the succession to Heinrich Bornkamm at Giessen in 1935, and then, in 1937, the Heidelberg chair of church history vacated by Walther Köhler, where he had already received favourable support from the dean, the faculty, and even student representatives before the office of the Deputy of the Führer vetoed him because of his Confessing Church ties.

Only after the collapse of the regime was he finally called, in 1945, to Heidelberg as successor to his own teacher Hans von Schubert. He was elected Rector of the university in 1946 and taught there until 1968, making Heidelberg the center of his mature scholarly life. The major books of these decades include Die Idee des Martyriums in der alten Kirche (1936), Kirchliches Amt und geistliche Vollmacht in den ersten drei Jahrhunderten (Mohr, 1953), Griechische Kirchenväter (1955), Lateinische Kirchenväter (1960), Die Jungfrauengeburt in der Theologie der alten Kirche (1962), Aus der Frühzeit des Christentums (1963), and above all Die Entstehung der christlichen Bibel (Mohr, 1968), which remains one of the classic accounts of the formation of the Christian canon. The two small books on the Greek and Latin Fathers became especially influential in teaching and were long available in English translation as The Fathers of the Greek Church and The Fathers of the Latin Church.

His later years brought extensive honors. He received honorary doctorates from Göttingen, Oslo, St Andrews, and Uppsala; belonged for more than forty years to the Heidelberg Academy; was a member of the German Archaeological Institute; and served as corresponding fellow of the British Academy and the Göttingen Academy, as well as honorary member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences from 1972. Severe visual impairment gradually made research more difficult and eventually impossible. His scholarly legacy remained institutional as well as bibliographical: fifteen of his students became university teachers, a school often said to be the largest left by any Protestant church historian since Harnack. His son Axel von Campenhausen later became a professor of canon law. Hans Freiherr von Campenhausen died in Heidelberg on 6 January 1989 and was buried in the Bassermann–Campenhausen family plot in the Bergfriedhof, leaving a body of work central to early Christian studies, late antique church politics, and the historical interpretation of figures such as Ambrose.

W

Walram of Naumburg

died April 12, 1111

Walram of Naumburg was one of the more intellectually active German bishops of the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries, positioned at the intersection of the great political and theological controversies of his age — the Investiture Controversy between the papacy and the Empire — and remembered also for his role in the documentation of the cult of Saint Leonard of Noblac.

Walram was appointed to the Diocese of Naumburg-Zeitz, in Saxony, around 1089, succeeding Bishop Günther I von Wettin, and was formally consecrated bishop around 1091 by Hartwig of Spanheim. He held the see until his death in 1111, when he was succeeded by Dietrich I von Naumburg. His episcopate was dominated by the bitter conflict known as the Investiture Controversy, the struggle between Pope Gregory VII (and his successors) and Emperor Henry IV over the right to appoint — or "invest" — bishops and abbots with the symbols of their office. Walram was a committed imperialist, firmly siding with Henry IV against the reforming papacy, and this political alignment shaped his entire career and literary output.

Walram's most significant intellectual contribution is the treatise Liber de unitate ecclesiae conservanda ("Book on the Preservation of the Unity of the Church"), attributed to him and published in a critical edition in 1883 by the Monumenta Germaniae Historica (Impensis bibliopolii Hahniani). This polemical work defended the imperial position in the Investiture Controversy, arguing that the unity of the Church required cooperation between the sacerdotium and the imperium — pope and emperor — rather than papal supremacy over temporal appointments. It is a document of considerable importance for understanding the ideological arguments marshalled in defence of Henry IV and stands as one of the more sophisticated pro-imperial theological texts of the period.

A preserved letter from Walram to Anselm of Canterbury — held in the Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF, ark:/12148/btv1b10544536g) — reveals that he was engaged in theological correspondence with one of the greatest minds of the age. Anselm of Canterbury, though himself a reformist sympathetic to Gregorian ideals, maintained contacts across the theological spectrum, and Walram's letter to him testifies to the intellectual climate in which German bishops of the period operated, exchanging arguments and seeking legitimacy from renowned ecclesiastical figures even across political divides.

In 1103, Walram was present at the Abbey of Noblac in the Limousin (modern Saint-Léonard-de-Noblat, France) during the celebrated pilgrimage of Bohemond I of Antioch, the Norman crusader prince who had been captured by the Danishmend Turks and attributed his release to the intercession of Saint Leonard. This event was a moment of extraordinary publicity for Leonard's cult, drawing European-wide attention to the abbey. Walram seized the occasion to compose or commission a new hagiographic vita of Leonard, incorporating the miraculous liberation of Bohemond and other contemporary miracle accounts. The resulting text — whose authorship was later critically examined by the Bollandist Albert Poncelet, who questioned whether it was genuinely Walram's own composition or attributed to him posthumously — marked the moment when Leonard's veneration expanded from a regional Limousin devotion into a major European pilgrimage cult.

Walram died on April 12, 1111. His legacy is twofold: as a political theologian, he left the Liber de unitate ecclesiae conservanda as a testament to imperialist ecclesiology in the age of the Investiture Controversy; as a hagiographer, his presence at Noblac in 1103 and the vita associated with his name played a decisive role in amplifying the cult of Saint Leonard across Latin Christendom, making him an unexpectedly important figure in the history of medieval devotion to one of the most widely venerated saints of the central Middle Ages.

Wander, Steven

active late 20th-21st century

Steven Wander is an American art historian specializing in Late Antique and early Byzantine art, whose work includes studies of early Byzantine silver, notably the sixth- and seventh-century David plates depicting scenes from the life of the biblical king, and broader questions of iconographic transmission between text and image in the late antique Mediterranean world.

Wander's research on the Codex Amiatinus demonstrated that the manuscript's Tabernacle diagram and its Ezra miniature correspond more closely, in points of specific detail, to Cassiodorus's Latin version of Josephus's Jewish Antiquities than to the biblical text of Exodus itself. The finding both strengthens the case for a Vivarium connection behind the manuscript's prefatory images and complicates any simple derivation of those images directly from a Bible, showing instead a more intricate chain of transmission running through Cassiodorus's broader library and its Josephan material. See the essay on the Codex Amiatinus in this database for the fuller discussion of the Tabernacle diagram and its models.

Ward, Benedicta (Florence Margaret Ward)

Durham, 4 February 1933 - 23 May 2022

Sister Benedicta Ward was one of the most significant medievalists of her generation: an Anglican contemplative nun who combined a life of strict monastic enclosure with a prodigiously productive career as a scholar of early Christian spirituality, hagiography, and medieval theology.

Benedicta Ward's intellectual formation began with undergraduate studies in history at Manchester University in the early 1950s. This period proved decisive in two respects: she discovered her vocation as a historian, and she converted from the Methodism of her northern English upbringing to Anglicanism and to the contemplative religious life.
